roles.title: Slaughterers and Meat Packers
roles.description: Perform nonroutine or precision functions involving the preparation of large portions of meat. Work may include specialized slaughtering tasks, cutting standard or premium cuts of meat for marketing, making sausage, or wrapping meats. Work typically occurs in slaughtering, meat packing, or wholesale establishments.

tasks.label: Remove bones, and cut meat into standard cuts in preparation for marketing.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Large beef packing plant fabrication floor: worker at a chain station receives quarters/primals (chuck, round, loin, brisket) and hand-bones them with knife and hook into boneless subprimals to spec, at line speed, in a cold, wet room.

Large beef plant rib/loin station: cutting the rib primal along the scribe line and sawing/removing the striploin from the chine — a bone-and-cut operation performed with a powered saw at a fixed station on the fabrication line.

High-volume pork plant cut floor: hams and shoulders are boned out and middles are worked into deboned loin/back and belly (rib pulling, chine removal, trimming) to standard cut specs, hundreds of pieces per hour.
Broiler further-processing plant: front halves/breast caps and whole legs/thighs are deboned into fillets, tenders and boneless thigh meat for retail packs, at several thousand birds per hour.

Small or very small USDA/state-inspected slaughter-and-cut plant or custom-exempt locker: one worker breaks whole carcasses or sides (beef one day, hogs or lambs the next, occasional game) into standard retail/wholesale cuts on a table or rail, with widely varying carcass size and condition.
Lamb/sheep boning room: carcasses broken into forequarter, middle and hindquarter and worked into racks, loins, backstraps and boneless legs/shoulders.

tasks.label: Sever jugular veins to drain blood and facilitate slaughtering.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-speed red-meat plant (beef or hog) kill floor: the sticker stands at the bleed rail and, seconds after captive-bolt or electrical/CO2 stunning, plunges a sticking knife into the throat/thoracic inlet of a shackled, hoisted, still-convulsing animal to sever the carotid arteries and jugular veins, often using a hollow knife when blood is collected for food. Animals swing and vary in size; line speeds run several hundred head per hour; hot, wet, blood-covered conditions.

High-speed broiler kill line: birds hung in shackles on the overhead conveyor pass, after stunning, through the in-line killing station where the neck vessels are cut so the bird bleeds out before the scalder; routine, correctly presented birds at line speeds of thousands per hour.

Poultry kill room backup killing: the attendant watches the shackle line and manually knife-cuts the necks of birds the automatic killer missed or presented badly (undersized, oversized, twisted or partly unshackled birds) before they reach the scald tank.

Small or very-small USDA-inspected plant slaughtering a handful to a few dozen head a day of mixed species (cattle, hogs, sheep, goats, sometimes bison or deer): the slaughterer stuns, shackles and hoists with a chain hoist and sticks the animal by hand, adjusting to widely varying animal size and to a cramped, non-standard kill room layout.

Religious slaughter at a kosher or halal certified plant: a trained shochet or Muslim slaughterman makes the single uninterrupted throat cut severing the jugular veins and carotid arteries of a restrained (often upright or rotating-box) animal, with certification requirements on who performs the cut and how.

Mobile/on-farm custom slaughter: the operator shoots or stuns the animal in a farm pen or paddock, then sticks it on the ground or after hoisting on the mobile unit's boom; uneven terrain, mud, weather, and a layout that differs at every farm.

tasks.label: Tend assembly lines, performing a few of the many cuts needed to process a carcass.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Hog dressing/slaughter line in a large pork plant: worker stands at one station on a machine-paced rail line (700–1,300 head/hour) making one or two assigned cuts on each carcass as it passes — dropping the bung, opening the belly/breast, cutting the aitchbone or neck, splitting the carcass with a saw. Hot, wet, noisy; carcasses vary in weight and conformation.

Beef slaughter floor saw/primal-separation station: worker splits the hanging cattle carcass down the spine with a powered saw, opens the brisket, or quarters/rib-scribes the side as it hangs on the rail at 150–400 head/hour under USDA inspection.

Beef knife stations — hide opening and legging on the kill floor, and boning/trimming a chilled beef chuck, round or loin to a customer spec on the fabrication line. Freehand knife work that follows seams and bone contours on highly variable carcasses, judged on yield, trim spec and bone-chip freedom.

Pork or lamb boning/cut floor station: deboning hams, shoulders or loins, or breaking chilled lamb carcasses into bone-in primals, at a table or conveyor position in the plant's cut room at line pace.

Poultry slaughter and cut-up line station: very high-speed work (5,000–10,000+ birds/hour) at one position on the shackle or cone line — removing wings, drums and thighs, cutting breast caps, deboning thighs or breasts, in a chilled, institution-run plant.

Small, very small, custom-exempt or specialty (halal/kosher, mixed-species) abattoir: worker performs several of the cuts by hand as beef, hogs, sheep, goats or game come off a short rail; low volume, varied species and product mix, layout and sequence differ day to day.

tasks.label: Shackle hind legs of animals to raise them for slaughtering or skinning.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-speed hog plant, kill floor: pigs come out of the CO2 stunner and are tipped from the gondola onto a belt conveyor lying on their sides, still twitching/kicking. The worker grabs one hind leg, snaps a shackle chain around the hock, hooks the shackle onto the elevator hook, which lifts the pig to the sticking/bleed rail. Roughly 1,000-1,400 pigs/hour, wet floor, blood, other workers alongside.

Large beef plant, knock box exit: the stunned steer/heifer drops from the box onto the shackling table or conveyor with legs still flailing. The worker throws a shackle chain around a hind leg above the hock, hooks it to the bleed rail trolley/roller, and the hoist raises the 1,200+ lb animal; also re-hanging carcasses by both hind legs on a gambrel/spreader before hide removal. 150-400 head/hour.

Poultry plant live-hang (or post-CAS hang) area: workers pull birds from a dump conveyor or module and press both legs into the moving overhead shackles of the kill line, ~25-30 birds per minute per hanger, in dim/dusty red-light conditions; birds are live and flapping in most US plants.

Sheep/lamb/goat/veal plant: after stunning, the worker shackles one hind leg of the animal on the bleed rail or restrainer exit and hoists it; later inserts a gambrel/spreader through both Achilles tendons to raise the carcass for pelt removal (legging/skinning). Smaller animals, faster manual handling, mixed sizes.

Small or very small / custom-exempt slaughter plant: multi-species (cattle one day, hogs or sheep the next), no fixed automated line. Worker stuns the animal in a pen or knock area, drags/rolls it, chains a hind leg, and uses an electric hoist or overhead trolley to raise it for sticking and skinning. Layout cramped, equipment general-purpose.

On-farm or mobile slaughter unit / custom field harvest: animal is stunned or shot in a paddock, corral, or trailer; the worker attaches a chain or spreader to the hind leg(s) and raises the carcass with a truck-mounted or trailer winch on uneven ground, in weather, with unrestrained carcass position and variable animal size and species (including deer/game in custom processing).

tasks.label: Slit open, eviscerate, and trim carcasses of slaughtered animals.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Large fed-cattle harvest floor (300-400 head/hour): worker at a rail station rods the weasand, drops the bung, opens the midline and brisket of a 700-900 lb hanging beef carcass, drops paunch and pluck onto the inspection table without puncturing gut, then rail-trims contamination, bruises and hide-side debris under USDA inspection.

Large hog plant clean line (400-1,300 hogs/hour): bung dropping and aitch-bone cut, belly and breast opening, removal of the intact gut set and pluck onto a parallel viscera line, then leaf-fat, jowl and neck trimming of the dressed carcass before splitting.

Broiler or turkey processing plant evisceration section: vent cutting, abdominal opening, drawing the viscera pack for inspection, crop/lung/neck cleanup, and trimming remains from the carcass before chilling; includes manual backup and salvage/trim positions on the shackle line.

Small/very small or custom-exempt red-meat plant: a few head per hour, mixed species across the day (beef, hogs, sheep, goats, occasional bison or veal), hand knives and a single rail, carcasses varying widely in size, fatness and condition, one or two people doing the whole dress-out.
Small or mid-size plant running a batch of market hogs (single species, uniform 250-300 lb animals): open the carcass, remove the viscera, trim leaf fat and contamination by hand at low line speed.
Mid-size single-species lamb/sheep/goat plant: bunging, brisket opening, evisceration of the pelted carcass onto the offal table, and trimming, at moderate chain speed.

tasks.label: Stun animals prior to slaughtering.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-speed beef plant (200-400 head/hr): knocker stands over a knock box, sizes up each animal (bulls, cull cows, horned cattle, varying head height), places a pneumatic captive bolt on the correct forehead site, fires, confirms insensibility and re-stuns misfires before the animal is released to the shackling line.

Large/mid pork plant: hogs moved from lairage in groups; worker either applies head-to-back electrical tongs to hogs held in a restrainer conveyor or small group pen, or tends a group CO2 gas stunning system (loading groups, watching the cycle) and captive-bolts any hog showing signs of return to sensibility.

Small/very small USDA-inspected multi-species plant (10-100 head/day): cattle, hogs, sheep or goats brought singly into a knock pen or chute with loose or no head restraint; worker uses a handheld cartridge/pneumatic captive bolt or electric tongs, judging placement animal by animal, then checks the stun.

Custom-exempt, on-farm or mobile slaughter unit: the animal is stunned where it stands in a farm pen, paddock or beside the trailer, unrestrained, with a rifle or handheld captive bolt; the worker must approach, wait for a clean head position and place the shot in an as-found outdoor setting.

Poultry/small-species plant: live birds are crated or shackled and passed through an electrical waterbath or controlled-atmosphere stunner; the worker hangs/handles birds, monitors stun effectiveness and manually stuns or dispatches birds that miss or survive the stunner.

sources.system: JBT Marel (Butina) CO2 Gas Stunning System
sources.title: CO2 Gas Stunning System | JBT Marel
sources.claim: Commercial group CO2 gas stunning systems (Butina/JBT Marel) stun pigs automatically in gondolas at up to 800 pigs/hour, with pigs driven to the stunner automatically; more than 800 installations worldwide.

tasks.label: Skin sections of animals or whole animals.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-speed beef kill floor: worker at a station on the moving chain opens the hide and pre-skins sections with hand and air knives (legging/hock skinning, midline belly opening, flanking, rumping/butting, tail stripping), then the hide-puller operator attaches the loosened hide to the down-puller clamps/chains and knives free any tears; carcasses vary in size, hides are dirty, contamination must be avoided.

Small or very-small licensed / custom-exempt slaughterhouse: worker skins whole animals largely by hand (beef, skinned hogs and sows, sheep, goats), often on a rail or cradle at low throughput, with a simple hydraulic dehider at most; animal size, condition and hide adhesion vary widely from carcass to carcass.

Small-stock (lamb/sheep/goat/veal) dressing chain: worker performs the Y-cut and leg opening, then fists/thumbs/punches the pelt loose and loads the free pelt edge into a shoulder puller or rotary pelt puller, clearing damage so pelt and carcass are not downgraded.

Station work skinning irregular parts and heads: hand skinning of beef and hog heads, cheeks, jowls, shanks/hocks and tails, and knife-trimming residual hide or hair from quarters; round, bony, non-uniform pieces handled one at a time on a table or hook.

Fabrication/packing room: removing skin/rind or membrane from flat carcass sections and primal cuts (pork bellies, jowls, loins, beef plates/navels, skin-on sections) before packing, either by knife on a table or by feeding pieces to a skinner/derinder.

Mobile slaughter unit, on-farm custom harvest, or game (deer/feral hog) processing: whole animal skinned in a trailer, farm shed or outdoors, hung from a portable hoist or laid on a rack, with variable footing, lighting, weather and animal presentation.

tasks.label: Cut, trim, skin, sort, and wash viscera of slaughtered animals to separate edible portions from offal.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Large broiler/turkey plant, evisceration department: birds hang legs-up on a moving shackle line; the worker opens the vent, draws the viscera pack, separates edible giblets (liver, heart, gizzard) from intestines/gall bladder, peels and washes gizzards, trims hearts and livers, and rails inedible offal to the by-product chute, at line speeds of thousands of birds per hour.

Hog slaughter plant, clean side: worker eviscerates carcasses on the rail (drops paunch and intestines onto the viscera pan/conveyor), pulls the pluck set, separates and trims liver, heart, lungs, tongue; other workers on the offal table sort edible stomachs and chitterlings, strip fat, and flush/wash them for the edible-offal cooler, matching each set to its carcass for inspection.

Beef plant, gut table and tripe/offal room: worker opens the carcass and drops the viscera onto the moving inspection table, separates paunch/omasum from intestines, cuts open and dumps the paunch, trims and loads it for scald/wash, and cuts, trims and washes liver, heart, tongue and tripe, discarding condemned or inedible portions.

Lamb, goat or veal plant: smaller, softer carcasses on a lower-speed chain; the worker eviscerates, removes and separates the pluck (heart, liver, lungs), pulls and strips the intestines for casings, and trims and washes the edible offal by hand with knives at a table.

Small or very small (custom/state-inspected) slaughterhouse or custom-exempt harvest unit: mixed species (beef, hogs, sheep, sometimes deer), a handful of animals per day, hand tools, no dedicated offal line; one worker eviscerates, saves the liver/heart/tongue the customer asked for, trims and rinses them at a sink, and discards the rest.

tasks.label: Shave or singe and defeather carcasses, and wash them in preparation for further processing or packaging.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-speed broiler/turkey plant, defeathering section: worker tends the scald–pick–singe–wash sequence as shackled birds pass at 100–175 birds/min, setting picker fingers and plates, clearing jams, and ensuring carcasses leave feather-free and washed for evisceration.

Poultry line touch-up/pinning station: worker standing at the shackle line pulls residual pin feathers, hairs and feather stragglers off individual carcasses by hand (pinning knife/fingers), hand-singes stray hairs, and rinses before the bird enters evisceration.

Hog slaughter unclean line: worker tends the dehairing machine, gambrels/rehangs carcasses, operates the flame singer and whipping/polishing machines, hand-scrapes residual bristles and scorch from problem carcasses, and washes the carcass before it enters the clean side.

Beef/veal/lamb kill floor: carcass washing before chill — carcasses on the rail pass through a hot-water/organic-acid wash cabinet, with the worker running spray wands or vacuum-steam on visible hair, bone dust and contamination spots.

Small state-inspected, custom-exempt or on-farm/mobile plant: worker hand-dunks birds or hogs in a scald tank, runs a drum or small inline plucker, hand-pins remaining feathers, torch-singes hair, and hoses the carcass; species and sizes vary day to day.

Waterfowl/specialty birds (ducks, geese) in a dedicated plant: after rough plucking, carcasses are wax-dipped, cooled, the hardened wax with down and pin feathers is stripped, and the carcass is washed and inspected for skin damage.

tasks.label: Saw, split, or scribe carcasses into smaller portions to facilitate handling.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-speed hog plant, clean side of the kill floor: splitting scalded, eviscerated pork carcasses lengthwise through the spine as they hang on the moving dressing-line rail, 600-1,300 head/hour, wet and cold, tight tolerance on the loin/feather bones.

Large beef packing plant kill floor: splitting 600-1,400 lb dressed cattle carcasses into two sides with a heavy band splitting saw, operator riding a moving hydraulic platform, cut must stay centered on the vertebral column for spinal-cord removal and inspection.
Beef chiller/boning room: scribing chilled sides (rib cuts to set depth defining chuck/short-rib and cube-roll lines) with a circular scribe saw on the hanging, swaying side before boning.
Beef chiller/load-out: quartering chilled sides with a saw between the 12th and 13th rib (and cutting off shanks/necks) so quarters can be handled, railed out or loaded for shipment.
Lamb, mutton or veal plant: sawing/splitting small-stock carcasses and separating them into forequarter, middle and hindquarter sections on the rail for further processing.

Small custom-exempt or locker abattoir: one worker uses a handheld band or reciprocating splitting saw to halve beef, hog and lamb carcasses and saw them into quarters/pieces, mixed species and sizes in one shift, low throughput, cramped multi-use kill room.

tasks.label: Trim head meat, and sever or remove parts of animals' heads or skulls.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-speed hog dressing line (700-1,200 carcasses/hour): severing the head from the scalded, dehaired carcass hanging on the moving overhead rail — the neck cut just below the atlas so the head stays attached or drops for inspection.

Hog dressing/clean line: trimming the jowl and neck region on the hanging carcass — removing glands, jugular veins and bloody ... up to the jaw chop, and cutting off ears/snout tips as required by the cut spec.

Hog head-boning area: whole heads presented on a table or hook line; worker splits the skull/lower jaw, pulls the mask, and harvests cheek meat, temple and occipital head meat with a hand knife, sorting by product grade.

Beef kill floor: after hiding, severing the head from the carcass with knife/hydraulic shears, cutting horns, and hanging the head on the head rail; carcass and head size vary widely across steers, heifers, cows and bulls.

Beef head table/head rail: washing the head, removing the tongue, and harvesting cheek meat and head meat with hand and Whizard knives under USDA inspection, avoiding lymph nodes, tonsils and contamination on heads of varying size and condition.

Small or very small custom-exempt plant, mixed species (cattle, hogs, lambs, goats): heads removed, skinned, sometimes split for brains, and head meat trimmed at a bench; low volume, one animal at a time, layout and species vary day to day.

tasks.label: Grind meat into hamburger, and into trimmings used to prepare sausages, luncheon meats, and other meat products.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume industrial ground beef/patty plant: 2,000-3,000 lb combos of lean and fat trim are brought to the grind line, dumped, coarse-ground, checked for bone/hard tissue, blended to a target lean point, final-ground and sent to formers or chub packers. Cold (35-45F), wet, high throughput, continuous shifts.

Further-processing/sausage plant: worker grinds pork and beef trim through coarse then fine plates into mixer-grinders for sausage, bologna and luncheon-meat batches; recipe-specific fat/lean ratios, plate and knife changes between batches, output pumped or dumped to stuffers/emulsifiers.

Small or mid-size slaughter/locker/custom-exempt plant: operator hand-feeds trim from lugs and carts into a floor-standing grinder, small mixed batches (beef, pork, venison, lamb), per-customer orders, adds fat to lean game meat, output panned, bagged or run to a stuffer; frequent changeovers and cleanup between customers.

Retail/wholesale meat room (supermarket back room, butcher shop, meat wholesaler): daily grinding of accumulated trimmings and chucks into hamburger on a bench or floor grinder, judging fat content, regrinding for finer texture, output trayed or bulk-packed for the case.

Cut/boning floor of a packing plant: trim collected from boning tables is coarse-ground into trimmings destined for sausage, luncheon meat and further processing, with removal of bone chips, cartilage and foreign material before the material moves downstream.

tasks.label: Trim, clean, or cure animal hides.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Knife trimming of green hides at a packing plant hide-trim station (any plant size): hide arrives off the hide puller/skinning cradle, worker trims tail bone, ear/lip/snout remnants, ragged edges, dewclaw skirt, heavy fat and flesh chunks, and knocks off manure tags with a hand knife, at line pace (up to a few hundred hides/hour in large beef plants), on a slick, wet floor and with hides weighing 30-50 kg.

Cleaning green hides at a large beef plant or attached hide-processing house: hides washed to remove manure, blood and dirt and run through a fleshing/demanuring machine to strip fat, flesh and hair-side manure before cure; worker feeds/oversees machines and hoses down hides and equipment.

Curing at a large beef plant / hide processor: trimmed, washed hides loaded into agitated brine raceways (or salt-spread on a line), held overnight, pulled, drained or wrung, then folded, bundled and palletized by grade for shipment to tanneries; hundreds of hides per shift.

Curing at a small or mid-size federally inspected plant or custom-exempt slaughterhouse: worker spreads each fresh hide flesh-side up on the hide-room floor, pallet or table, shovels/hand-spreads salt over the whole flesh side to the edges, stacks the hide on the pack, and later loads packs for the hide buyer; a handful to a few dozen hides a day, mixed sizes (beef, veal).

Curing outside a fixed plant: mobile/on-farm harvest units, very small custom shops and seasonal deer/game processing - hide salted, rolled or barreled in a barn, shed, trailer bay or on an outdoor pad for pickup by a hide buyer or taxidermist; layout, lighting, footing and hide condition differ site to site.

tasks.label: Observe, feel, taste, or otherwise examine products during and after processing to ensure conformance to standards.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Industrial/commercial bakery: tunnel-oven tender watches loaves, buns, cookies or crackers coming off the band, judges crust color, height, shape, split and degree of bake, pulls occasional units off the belt to feel/cut them and check internal temperature or moisture, and removes or flags nonconforming product.

Coffee, cocoa or nut roasting plant: operator pulls trier samples during the roast to look at bean color and cracks, compares the finished batch color against the house standard, checks cooled product for scorched, under-roasted or defective pieces, and holds or reworks batches that miss spec.

Dehydrator, kiln or drier tender (dried fruit, vegetables, grain, malt, pet food): grabs handfuls of product off the belt or from the kiln floor, feels for pliability/brittleness and residual moisture, looks for scorching, case-hardening and color drift, and confirms against a moisture spec before discharge.

Tobacco redrying/curing plant: operator checks lamina or stem leaving the drier for moisture ('order') by feel, judges color and leaf condition, and watches for foreign material and over-dried or wet spots, adjusting or holding product that is out of spec.

Organoleptic checks across all of the above: cupping or tasting roasted coffee, tasting a baked or dried sample for flavor, mouthfeel and crunch, smelling for scorch, smoke taint or off-notes, and signing off the batch on that sensory judgment.

Small-batch or artisan operation (craft micro-roastery, retail/wholesale artisan bakery with hearth or rack oven, small dryer): hand-formed or small-lot product on peels, racks and trays; operator judges doneness by crust color, feel and sound, with no conveyor and frequent product changes.

tasks.label: Set temperature and time controls, light ovens, burners, driers, or roasters, and start equipment, such as conveyors, cylinders, blowers, driers, or pumps.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Industrial/wholesale bakery, start of shift or product run: operator enters zone temperatures, band speed and bake time at the oven HMI, initiates burner light-off on a gas-fired tray or continuous oven, and starts the band conveyor, proofer and exhaust/circulation blowers in sequence.

Coffee, cocoa or nut roasting plant: operator selects/enters the roast profile (charge temperature, gas/burner setting, airflow, roast time), lights the roaster burner, starts drum rotation, destoner/blower, afterburner and cooling-tray agitator before charging the batch.

Drying operations (spray dryer, belt/tunnel dryer, vacuum dryer, kiln drier, tobacco redryer): operator sets inlet/outlet air temperature, humidity and dwell time, then starts feed pumps, atomizer, fans and conveyors in the required interlocked sequence and brings the unit up to temperature.

In-store or small commercial bakery: at shift start the worker switches on and preheats rack, deck or convection ovens and the proofer, dials in temperature, steam and bake-time settings on each unit, and starts the proofer fan/humidifier.

Older or partly manual equipment: hand-lighting pilots/burners with a torch or spark igniter, opening manual gas cocks and dampers, then walking the line to press local start buttons for conveyors, blowers and pumps and visually confirming flames and rotation.

Mid-run changes: resetting temperature and time controls between products or after a hold, restarting conveyors/blowers after an idle period, and re-initiating burner light-off following a lockout, on a modern PLC-controlled line.

tasks.label: Observe temperature, humidity, pressure gauges, and product samples and adjust controls, such as thermostats and valves, to maintain prescribed operating conditions for specific stages.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Large commercial bakery: operator tends a multi-zone travelling/tunnel oven on a continuous line, watching zone temperature, steam/humidity and damper readings, pulling biscuits, buns or tortillas off the discharge to check bake color, crust and moisture, and trimming zone thermostats, burner settings, steam valves and belt speed to hold the bake spec across the run.

Industrial coffee, nut or cocoa roasting plant: operator runs batch or continuous roasters, follows bean/inlet temperature and pressure gauges against a roast profile, pulls trier samples to judge color, crack and smell, and adjusts gas/burner, airflow and damper controls stage by stage, deciding drop point.

Commercial drying operation (grain/seed dryer at an elevator or mill, or belt/rotary/vacuum dryer for fruit, vegetables, spices or snack pieces in a food plant): operator monitors inlet/outlet temperature and humidity, takes samples for moisture checks, and adjusts burner temperature, fan/airflow and discharge or belt speed to hit target moisture.

Tobacco curing barn or leaf redrying/conditioning line: operator follows dry-bulb/wet-bulb temperature and humidity through yellowing, leaf-drying and stem-drying stages, inspects leaf samples for color and feel, and adjusts thermostats, dampers, humidification and burner settings to the cure schedule.

Café-scale or small artisan roastery: operator loads small batches into a shop roaster, watches bean temperature and time, judges samples by color and sound, and adjusts heat and airflow to hold the profile and end the roast.

Small craft bakery or specialty batch operation: hand-loaded deck/rack ovens and small dryers running many different products per day, operator judges crust color, oven spring and doneness by eye, touch and probe on varying dough lots and adjusts deck temperature, steam and damper by hand.

tasks.label: Observe flow of materials and listen for machine malfunctions, such as jamming or spillage, and notify supervisors if corrective actions fail.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Coffee or nut roasting plant: operator stands at the roaster and cooling tray, watches green beans feed from the hopper and product discharge to the destoner/cooler, listens for auger or chaff-cyclone jamming and grinding noises, and calls the shift supervisor when the abnormal condition persists after the usual reset.

Commercial bakery tunnel-oven line: operator walks the proofer-to-oven-to-cooler run every few minutes, watches dough pieces and pans flow evenly on the conveyor, listens for belt slipping, pan pile-ups, or dough dropping onto the floor, and reports to the line supervisor or maintenance when the jam recurs.

Grain, fruit, or vegetable drying operation (kiln drier, belt or drum dehydrator): tender monitors infeed conveyors, elevators and transfer chutes for plugging, bridging, or spillage of product, watches product depth/flow across the dryer bed, and escalates to the supervisor when plugging cannot be cleared.

Large snack-food or cocoa/peanut roasting line run partly from a control room: operator alternates between HMI/SCADA screens showing flow rates, bed depth and amperage alarms and periodic floor rounds to look and listen at the machine, notifying the supervisor when alarms and floor checks indicate an unresolved fault.

Tobacco processing/char kiln or redrying line: operator observes leaf flow across conveyors and into the drying cylinder, listens for abnormal drive or fan noise and for material spilling at transfer points, and reports persistent faults up the chain.

Small artisanal roastery or retail bakery: a single operator tends a small drum roaster or deck oven, judges flow and machine condition largely by sound and sight while doing other work, and tells the owner/manager when a problem cannot be fixed.

tasks.label: Weigh or measure products, using scale hoppers or scale conveyors.

instances.label: Industrial coffee or nut roasting plant: operator sets the batch recipe, green product is drawn from silos through weigh belts/scale hoppers ahead of the roaster, operator verifies each batch weight against the recipe target, corrects deviations (bridging, feeder drift), and logs batch weights for traceability.

Bakery, snack or cereal plant supplying ovens/dryers: majors (flour, sugar, grain) are dropped into mixer scale hoppers while minor/micro ingredients are scaled at a bench or floor scale; operator confirms weights against the batch sheet and records them before the batch goes to the oven.

Discharge / pack-off weighing of roasted or dried product: product runs across a scale conveyor (checkweigher) or through a weigh hopper/multihead weigher to fixed target weights; the operator monitors readouts, pulls off-weight units, and adjusts fill to control giveaway.

Grain, nut or fruit drying facility: bulk lots weighed in and out on automatic bulk weigh hoppers or belt scales during dryer loading/load-out; operator watches the scale, records net weights on tickets, and reconciles wet vs. dry weights (shrink).

Small artisan roastery or small commercial bakery back room: operator scoops green beans or ingredients from burlap sacks/bins into a bucket on a bench or floor scale, tops off to hit a target weight, dumps it into the roaster/oven hopper, then weighs the finished product to compute shrinkage and logs it by hand.

tasks.label: Test products for moisture content, using moisture meters.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Grain/oilseed drying at a commercial elevator, feed mill or seed plant: operator catches a sample of hot grain from the dryer discharge spout or wet-holding leg, cools it, pours it into a benchtop capacitance moisture meter (GAC/Perten-type) at the scale house or dryer control shack, reads %moisture and adjusts dryer discharge rate; repeated every 30-60 minutes through the drying campaign.

Peanut or tree-nut drying at a buying point/huller: operator probes or scoops in-shell peanuts or nuts from a drying wagon, semi trailer or bin, runs the sample through an in-shell/kernel moisture meter (sometimes after shelling a subsample), and decides when to shut the burner off; hot, dusty outdoor-covered drying shed conditions.

Coffee, cocoa or nut roasting plant: after roast and cooling, operator draws a sample of beans from the cooling tray or discharge chute, tests residual moisture on a benchtop capacitance analyzer or grinds and runs a loss-on-drying moisture balance, and records the result against the batch roast profile.

Commercial bakery / snack / cereal / pet-food plant: operator takes crackers, cookies, cereal or kibble off the belt at the oven or dryer exit, grinds or crumbles the sample, weighs it into a halogen moisture balance or LOD analyzer at the QC bench, and adjusts oven/dryer settings from the reading.

Dehydrated fruit, vegetable, spice or herb drying plant: operator collects product from tray-dryer trays or a belt-dryer discharge bin, tests moisture with a benchtop moisture analyzer or loss-on-drying unit in the plant QC room, and logs the result for the lot before packing.

Tobacco curing/redrying: operator checks moisture of cured or redried leaf at a bulk curing barn or on a redrying line, using a handheld pin/probe meter on the leaf or taking a sample to an oven-loss/LOD determination to confirm order (moisture) before baling.

tasks.label: Clear or dislodge blockages in bins, screens, or other equipment, using poles, brushes, or mallets.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Mid-run bridging or plugging at a roaster/dryer discharge chute or surge hopper in a coffee, nut, grain or snack plant: product (beans, nuts, kernels, sticky dried fruit) arches over the outlet and flow stops. The operator raps the chute wall with a rubber mallet or pokes a pole through an access port to break the arch and restore flow, then confirms flow and restarts the cycle, usually within minutes to avoid scorching product.

Blinded or clogged screens and perforated surfaces: destoner/aspiration screens, sifter decks, cyclone and dust-collector screens, perforated dryer trays or belts caked with fines, chaff, oil or product residue. Worker brushes, scrapes and blows the mesh clear (often after pulling the deck), inspects for damage and refits it during a changeover or scheduled cleanout.

Bulk storage bin/silo above or below a dryer or roaster holding crusted, bridged or rat-holed product (moist grain, flour, meal, tobacco). Worker works from the top hatch or an access door with a long pole, bar or bin whip under confined-space rules, breaking the crust or arch and watching for sudden collapse of material.

Baked-on or caked buildup on an oven/dryer conveyor band, drum interior, or discharge lip: scorched dough, sugar, batter, fines. Worker scrapes and brushes the band or drum surface so buildup stops catching product, typically at a break or shutdown while surfaces are still warm.

A hard jam at an oven or dryer transfer point: a pan tipped and wedged, a clump of product jammed under a guide or in a transition, a belt lacing snagged. Worker must reach in, judge how the item is trapped, free it with a pole or bar without damaging equipment or product, and clear spilled product before restarting.

Plugged aspiration ducting, cyclone downspout, rotary airlock or bucket-elevator boot on a drying/roasting line. Worker knocks the duct with a mallet, rods out the plug from a clean-out port, sometimes removes an inspection cover or airlock cover, clears packed material and reassembles.

tasks.label: Start conveyors to move roasted grain to cooling pans and agitate grain with rakes as blowers force air through perforated bottoms of pans.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Craft/specialty roastery (5-35 kg drum roaster) on an open shop production floor: at the end of the roast the operator opens the drop door, the batch falls into the perforated cooling tray, the stirring arms and cooling-tray blower are started, and after 3-4 minutes the cooled beans are gated out to a destoner/bin; operator occasionally hand-rakes tray corners and picks defects.

Mid/large coffee, cocoa or nut plant, batch roasting line on the plant floor: operator starts feed and discharge conveyors from a panel, the roaster discharges to a cooling tray/car with a rotating rake arm while a blower pulls ambient air through the perforated floor, then conveyors/pneumatics carry cooled product to destoner, weigher and silos; operator patrols the line and samples.

Malthouse or grain/cereal drying plant: kilned or roasted grain is discharged to a cooling vessel or kiln/germination floor where a powered turner rakes the bed as blowers force air through the mesh/perforated bottom; operator starts the legs, augers and belts routing the cooled grain to collecting bins and checks flow on the floor.

Fully automated continuous roasting/drying line (RTE cereal, nuts, cocoa, large coffee plant) supervised from an HMI/control room: product runs on a perforated slat/belt conveyor through heat and cooling zones with forced airflow through the bed and discharge conveyors under PLC recipe control; the operator starts the sequence and watches trends.

Less-automated shop: roasted grain, nuts or malt is spread on a plain perforated cooling pan or cooling floor with fans running underneath, and the operator hand-rakes and turns the bed with a rake or hoe to level it and speed cooling, then shovels/sweeps it into totes or a conveyor hopper.

Upset during the transfer-and-cool cycle: product clumps or scorches in the pan, the chute or drag conveyor to the cooling pan plugs or the bin bridges, or product spills on the floor; the operator rakes out hot material, breaks the bridge, clears the plug, cleans up and restarts the conveyors.

tasks.label: Open valves, gates, or chutes or use shovels to load or remove products from ovens or other equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Batch roasting operation (coffee, nuts, cocoa) in a roasting plant: operator opens the charge hopper gate to drop green beans into the hot drum, then opens the roaster drop door at end of roast to discharge into the cooling tray, then opens the cooling-tray gate/chute to send product to destoner or bin. Indoor production floor, fixed equipment, hot and dusty.

Wholesale/industrial bakery: loading pans, trays or dough pieces into deck, rack or tunnel ovens and removing baked product at the end of the bake — opening oven doors, running loaders/peels, pushing racks in and out, dumping product into chutes onto cooling conveyors. Institution-run production room, standard oven line, fast cycle times.

Grain, seed, nut or fruit/vegetable drying facility: opening valves, slide gates and chutes on dryers, wet/dry hoppers and augers to load wet product into the dryer and unload dried product to bins or conveyors, adjusting discharge rate to hit moisture targets. Fixed dryer battery at an elevator or processing plant, dusty outdoor/indoor equipment.

In-store/retail bakery or café-scale roastery: a small deck or convection oven and a shop roaster; operator scoops or pours green beans into the hopper, loads trays by hand, opens the oven door and pulls out finished goods, dumps roasted beans to the cooling tray. Tight quarters shared with staff and, nearby, customers.

Tobacco curing barn / on-farm kiln or drying shed: loading racks, boxes or sticks of green leaf into the barn, opening and closing barn doors, vents and dampers, then unloading cured leaf after the cure. Farm-site structure whose layout, access and clutter vary from barn to barn; weather and field mud present.

Cleanout and jam clearing: shoveling stuck, bridged or spilled product out of dryer plenums, roaster coolers, chutes and oven hearths during changeover, blockage or sanitation, often reaching into confined or awkward spaces in the as-built plant.

tasks.label: Clean equipment with steam, hot water, and hoses.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: End-of-shift open washdown in a wet-process food plant (meat/poultry cookhouse, dehydrator line, vegetable dryer): operator hoses down the exterior of the oven/roaster/dryer, its frame, hoods, guards, conveyors and the surrounding floor and drains with hot water, applies foam detergent, rinses and sanitizes. Light-to-moderate soil, wet slippery floor, other crew members present.

Interior chamber cleaning of the oven, smokehouse, roaster or drying cabinet: hot water/steam and caustic applied to interior walls, racks channels, fan cabinet, supply/return ducting to remove baked-on grease and carbonized residue; chamber must be opened, sprayed out and rinsed before the next production day.

Removable parts washing: operator strips trays, sheet pans, screens, oven racks, smoke trucks/buggies, belts and nozzle assemblies off the machine and cleans them with hot water, detergent and steam at a wash station or sink, then rinses, sanitizes and reinstalls them.

Cleaning of enclosed drying/liquid-side systems: spray dryer chambers, evaporators, feed tanks, casing/conditioning cylinders and pipework flushed with hot water and caustic on a circulation (CIP) cycle, with the operator setting up the circuit, running the cycle, draining and verifying.

Awkward-access cleaning around the drying/roasting line: steam and hot-water hosing behind and under fixed equipment, inside cyclones, chaff/dust collectors, elevator legs, exhaust ducts, elevated catwalks and hoods; requires ladders, partial disassembly, scraping tools and confined-space entry in a cluttered, poorly reachable space.

tasks.label: Smooth out products in bins, pans, trays, or conveyors, using rakes or shovels.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Continuous roasting/drying line in a nut, coffee, cocoa, cereal or pet-food plant: product mounds unevenly on the infeed belt or in the roaster/dryer bed, and the tender rakes or pushes it to a uniform depth across the conveyor width so the roast/dry is even. Hot, dusty, running line, product moving past continuously.

Bakery or prepared-foods plant pan-up/tray station: batter, dough pieces, granola mix or diced product is deposited into sheet pans, molds or dryer trays and the worker spreads and smooths it level with a scraper, spatula or small rake before the pans go into the oven/dryer. Repetitive, hand-scale, quality-critical (even bake).

Malt house or grain drying plant: raking/leveling the grain bed in a kiln floor, germination box or dryer to uniform depth, breaking up clumps and evening the surface so drying air passes uniformly. Large bed area, bulk grain, shovel and rake work.

Storage or holding bin at an elevator, roasting plant or dehydration plant: shoveling and raking dried product or grain inside the bin to knock down peaks, break surface crust and level the pile for aeration/airflow. Confined, dusty, uneven as-found surface.

Cooling stage after roasting: spreading and stirring hot roasted coffee, nuts or cocoa in a cooling tray, cooling bin or cooling conveyor with a rake or paddle so the layer is even and cools uniformly within minutes.

Off-normal cleanup during a run: shoveling spilled or overflowed product off the floor back onto the conveyor, digging out clumped/bridged product in a hopper or under a chute, clearing a plugged spout — product location and condition unpredictable, done under time pressure while the line waits.

tasks.label: Install equipment, such as spray units, cutting blades, or screens, using hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Roaster/dryer operator changes out screens, sieve panels, perforated trays or mesh decks on a rotary dryer, sifter or destoner: unbolt or unclamp the worn panel inside the machine housing, clean the seating surface, seat the new panel square, and re-torque clamp bolts with wrenches — done kneeling/reaching into a warm, dusty machine on the plant floor during changeover.

Operator installs or replaces spray units on a coating drum, flavor applicator or dryer humidification header: unthread worn nozzles/tips from the spray bar, fit new nozzles and gaskets, reconnect hoses/fittings with hand wrenches, then test the spray pattern and check for leaks before restart.

Operator installs cutting blades/knives on a cutter, granulator, slicer or dicer feeding the roaster or dryer: remove bolted-in dull blades, fit and align sharp blades, set the blade-to-bed-knife clearance with feeler gauges, and torque the retaining bolts — heavy, sharp parts in a confined blade housing.

Operator re-installs machine components stripped for sanitation or maintenance — guards, discharge chutes, ducting sections, agitator paddles, screens' hold-down bars, thermocouple probes — bolting each back onto the roaster/dryer in place with hand tools, in awkward, confined positions on the plant floor.

Operator fits a new accessory or kit onto existing equipment (e.g., a new spray-unit assembly, sensor, or blade holder): drill/align mounting brackets, adapt hardware to fit the machine, connect tubing and electrical leads, align the unit to the product path, and run a trial to verify function.

tasks.label: Push racks or carts to transfer products to storage, cooling stations, or the next stage of processing.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Industrial/wholesale bakery plant: operator pushes loaded rolling racks or oven trolleys (roughly 300–800 lb of pans, bread, buns) from the oven/proofer/depanning area across the plant floor to a cooling area, spiral cooler, blast freezer, or staging for packaging. Sealed level floors, wide aisles shared with coworkers and forklifts, occasional flour dust and wet spots.

Supermarket in-store bake-off or small artisan bakery: short moves (a few feet up to ~50 ft) of a rack of hot pans from a rack oven or proofer to a cooling station, then to a cooler or display staging. Cramped back-of-house, clutter, thresholds and swinging doors, staff working shoulder to shoulder.

Coffee, nut, or cocoa roasting plant: wheeled totes, bins, or carts of just-roasted product moved from the roaster cooling tray/discharge to degassing bins, storage, or the packaging line; warm, dusty, narrow aisles, occasional floor ramps and doorways.

Dehydration/drying facility (fruit, vegetable, jerky, pet food, grain, herbs): loaded tray trolleys or dryer trucks pushed out of tunnel/cabinet dryers to cooling racks and then to storage or the next stage; heat and humidity at the dryer mouth, floor rails or guides, heavy multi-shelf carts.

Tobacco curing/drying operation: racks, boxes, or trolleys of leaf moved between the kiln/curing barn and holding or storage areas, either in a leaf-processing/redrying plant or at a farm bulk-barn site with uneven packed ground, thresholds and outdoor weather.

Institutional or commissary bakery kitchen (hospital, school district central kitchen, hotel, correctional facility): rack of baked goods pushed from oven to a cooling station, then down shared corridors and through doors into a walk-in cooler or storage room.

tasks.label: Clean and sterilize vats and factory processing areas.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Mid/large plant (dairy-cheese, sauce, beverage, candy syrup): clean and sanitize closed vats, tanks, pipelines and heat exchangers by CIP — set up the circuit/valve matrix, run pre-rinse, caustic, rinse, acid, sanitize cycle at prescribed time/temp/concentration, verify with conductivity/temperature records and ATP swabs before the next batch.

Open or open-top process vessels with water-soluble soils (open cheese vats, syrup/sauce cook kettles, mix tanks, silos): flush residue, apply detergent to full interior surface including agitator and walls, rinse, apply sanitizer, drain and inspect. Done inside the plant between batches or at end of run.

Open-plant washdown of the processing area after the shift: pick up debris, pre-rinse floors, drains, walls, tables, conveyor frames and equipment exteriors, apply foam chemical, dwell, high-pressure rinse, apply no-rinse sanitizer, squeegee floors. Wet, slippery, chemical-heavy work over several hours.

Removable-part route: break down pumps, valves, fittings, hoses, screens, augers and filler parts; carry to the wash room; wash and sanitize them in a COP tank / parts or rack washer or by hand; dry, inspect and return them for reassembly.

Heavy detail work: scraping burnt-on sugar, caramelized product, dried dough or cooked-on protein from kettle walls, agitator blades and baffles; hand-brushing hard-to-reach nooks, gaskets and dead legs; dry-cleaning chocolate/panning equipment where no water is permitted.

Small artisan operation (farmstead creamery, small candy kitchen or commissary): hand-wash the small vat/kettle, hoops, molds and utensils in a three-compartment sink, wipe and sanitize tables and food-contact surfaces, hose and squeegee the floor and drains, log the sanitation check.

tasks.label: Set up, operate, and tend equipment that cooks, mixes, blends, or processes ingredients in the manufacturing of food products, according to formulas or recipes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Wholesale bakery / tortilla / snack plant: batchmaker scales flour, water, sugar, oil, yeast and minor ingredients per a dough formula, charges a horizontal or spiral mixer, runs it to target time/temperature/energy, checks dough temperature and feel, then discharges to a trough or divider. Ingredients arrive as bulk silo material plus 50-lb bags hand-added at a dump station.

Liquid/semi-liquid batch room (sauces, dressings, soups, syrups, beverage bases, dairy blends): operator follows a batch sheet to charge water, oils, purees, sugars, gums and dry minors into a jacketed mix tank or steam kettle, heats/cooks with agitation, pulls samples for brix/pH/viscosity, adjusts, then transfers to the filler and runs CIP between batches.

Dry blending of seasonings, spice mixes, drink mixes and bakery dry mixes: staging and dumping bagged/bulk ingredients into a ribbon or paddle blender in formula order, blending for a set time, sampling, and discharging to totes or a packaging line; frequent recipe changes across dozens of SKUs.

Cheese/dairy make room: fill vat with standardized milk, add culture, color and rennet on schedule, monitor pH and temperature, cut and cook the curd, drain whey, cheddar/stir/salt, and hoop or feed the block former; timing driven by acid development rather than the clock.

Confectionery kitchen: cook sugar/glucose/water batches in kettles or a continuous cooker to a target temperature or solids, add flavor, color and acid, temper or agitate as required, and feed a depositor or forming line; monitor cook temperature, brix and mass consistency.

Small craft plant, co-packer or commissary: small batches on largely manual equipment (tilt kettles, planetary mixers, bench scales), hand-scaled ingredients, several formula changeovers per shift, heavy reliance on sensory checks (taste, color, texture) and manual washdown between products.

tasks.label: Mix or blend ingredients, according to recipes, using a paddle or an agitator, or by controlling vats that heat and mix ingredients.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Large prepared-foods/dairy/beverage plant: operator runs recipe-driven jacketed vats and cook kettles that heat and agitate (sauces, soups, syrups, dressings, dairy blends). Bulk ingredients arrive by pipe/silo, minors are scaled and added, agitation speed/temperature/hold times are set and monitored on an HMI until the batch meets spec and is discharged.

Commercial/industrial bakery: scaling flour, water, yeast, fats, sugar and minors into a horizontal or spiral mixer bowl, running the mix stages, checking dough temperature and consistency by feel, adjusting water/time, then discharging dough to a trough or conveyor.

Cheese plant: filling the vat with pasteurized milk, dosing starter culture, rennet, calcium chloride and salt per recipe, running heating and agitation, watching for coagulation, cutting the curd, and stirring/cooking curd to the target firmness before draining.

Confectionery: cooking sugar/glucose batches in a steam-jacketed kettle or vacuum batch cooker with stirrers, adding flavors, colors, acids, chocolate or inclusions at the right temperature, checking cook temperature/moisture, then transferring the mass for depositing, pulling, or panning.

Small artisanal/craft producer (small commercial kitchen making sauces, granola, fudge, ice cream mixes): hand-weighing ingredients from bags and totes into a floor mixer or steam kettle, hand-paddling and scraping, tasting and adjusting seasoning or texture, working small variable batches with frequent recipe changeovers.

Meat/prepared-foods blending: loading meat, water/ice and pre-weighed spice or cure premix into a ribbon blender, paddle mixer or mixer-grinder, running the blend cycle for a set time, checking distribution, and dumping to totes or the next stage.

tasks.label: Follow recipes to produce food products of specified flavor, texture, clarity, bouquet, or color.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Industrial food/beverage plant: batchmaker follows a formula sheet to produce a batch of sauce, dressing, beverage, syrup or dry seasoning blend — stages and weighs major, minor and micro ingredients, charges the mixer/kettle, runs the mix and heat cycle, then checks Brix, pH, viscosity and color against spec and adjusts (adds water, acid, color, thickener) before release.

Wholesale/commercial bakery: mixer operator scales flour, water, yeast, fats and minor ingredients per recipe, mixes dough or batter in spiral/horizontal/vertical mixers to a target dough temperature and degree of development, judges feel and extensibility, adjusts water or ice and mix time, and discharges the dough to troughs or dividers.

Cheese plant: cheesemaker fills the vat with standardized milk, doses starter culture, rennet, color and salt per recipe, watches coagulum firmness to pick cutting time, cuts and cooks the curd to target texture/moisture, drains whey and checks pH and body at each step.

Confectionery plant: candy maker cooks a sugar/glucose syrup batch to a specified temperature and moisture, adds colors, flavors and acids, and works the mass (deposit, pull, form) to hit specified color, clarity and texture, checking each batch against a standard.

Brewery/winery/fermented-beverage facility: batchmaker mills and mashes grain or preps juice/base per recipe, controls temperature rests, hop or additive additions, gravity, pH and clarity, transfers to fermenter, and makes blending or finings adjustments to hit specified flavor, clarity and bouquet.

Small artisan/craft operation (chocolatier, gelato shop commissary, small-batch jam/sauce or specialty candy kitchen): worker makes small batches on general-purpose equipment — tempering chocolate, freezing a gelato batch, cooking a kettle of jam — with recipes adjusted batch-to-batch by taste, feel and eye, and hand transfers between vessels.

tasks.label: Press switches and turn knobs to start, adjust, and regulate equipment, such as beaters, extruders, discharge pipes, and salt pumps.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Large modern food plant (dairy, snack, prepared foods): at line start-up and shutdown the batchmaker presses start buttons and sets speeds/setpoints for mixers/beaters, transfer and salt/brine pumps, discharge valves and extruders, sequencing the line up in the right order, then shutting it down for CIP/sanitation. Conditions are predictable and recipe-driven.

Mid-run regulation in a commercial plant: the worker watches product condition (viscosity, curd firmness, dough consistency, moisture, texture, color) and downstream demand, and makes frequent small corrections — bumping agitator/beater speed, extruder screw speed and barrel temperature, throttling a discharge pipe valve, trimming a salt or brine pump rate.

Confectionery/candy production: operator starts and regulates a cooker/kettle, beater or pulling machine, and depositor or rope extruder on semi-automatic equipment — setting cook temperature and vacuum, beater speed, deposit rate — with frequent product changeovers between batches on a plant floor.

Small artisanal creamery, bakery, or candy shop with older, largely manual equipment: local switches and hand-set knobs on a cheese vat agitator, curd pump, brine/salt pump, steam valve, or dough mixer; cramped, varied layout, frequent changeovers and hand cleaning between small batches.

instances.label: Large/medium food plant, walkable process or packaging area (dry blending, syrup/beverage room, oilseed or ingredient processing, confectionery lines): while a batch runs, the operator watches and listens to the mixer/blender, pumps, motors, valves, hoses and conveyors for air/steam/product leaks, overheating bearings and abnormal noise, and reports what is found to the supervisor or maintenance.

Scheduled/periodic checks and walk-arounds of the batch area and its utilities in a plant: gauges and readouts on tanks, heat exchangers, compressors, CIP skids and transfer lines; note drips, hissing, hot spots, unusual vibration; record findings on a check sheet and report anomalies up the line.

Wet, hot, open-product make room or cramped small/specialty plant (cheese vat room, candy cooking kitchen, sauce/dressing kettles, bakery mixing room): the batchmaker stands at the kettle or mixer while charging and running it, watching for seal/gasket leaks, plugged discharge valves, screens or nozzles, product bridging in the hopper, boil-over and scorching, amid steam, splashes and frequent washdown.

Sensory check of the in-process product during the batch (candy syrup, cheese curd/brine, sauce, seasoning slurry): take a small sample, taste and smell it, judge whether the flavor is off - burnt, rancid, over-salted, sour - and report the undesirable taste to the supervisor.

tasks.label: Observe gauges and thermometers to determine if the mixing chamber temperature is within specified limits, and turn valves to control the temperature.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Large automated food/dairy/beverage plant: batchmaker oversees a blending/pasteurizing line, watches in-line temperature indicators and HMI trends on mix tanks and heat exchangers, and adjusts steam / hot-water / chilled-water valves (or their setpoints) to hold the mixing chamber inside spec through the run. Sanitary stainless equipment, fixed piping, continuous shifts.

Mid-size batch operation with jacketed vats and kettles (cheese vats, sauce/soup kettles, caramel and candy cookers): worker reads a dial thermometer or digital readout at the vessel and opens, throttles, or closes the steam valve and cooling-water valve repeatedly through the cook to follow the batch temperature profile.

Bakery, snack, or ice-cream mix operation: worker monitors dough/batter temperature in a jacketed mixer bowl and opens or throttles the chilled-water or glycol valve (and ice/water blend) to land the finished batch at target temperature; short batches, frequent changeovers.

Artisan or small-batch confectionery / craft cheese room: gas- or steam-heated copper kettle or small vat, hand-held or clip-on thermometer, manual gas or steam valve turned by feel and experience; recipe and vessel change batch to batch in a small commercial kitchen.

Older or partly manual plant: worker walks rounds past several cook vessels and mixing chambers, reads analog gauges and chart recorders, logs readings, and throttles manual handwheel valves on steam and cooling-water headers to correct drift.

Small artisanal/craft operation (farmstead creamery, craft chocolate, small-batch sauce or kettle shop): manual hand valves on jacketed kettles and small vats; operator starts steam/water flow and adjusts by frequent sensory and hand-instrument checks on non-standard, mixed-vintage equipment.

Line startup, product changeover and CIP: operator sets valve routing to start up or flush a line, starts the CIP circuit, watches pressures, flows and conductivity, and adjusts valves so the first product off the line meets quality.

tasks.label: Modify cooking and forming operations based on the results of sampling processes, adjusting time cycles and ingredients to achieve desired qualities, such as firmness or texture.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Cheese plant vat operation: the cheesemaker follows a coagulating/cooking vat, checks gel firmness (clean-break test, hand-feel of cooked curd), checks pH and curd moisture, and adjusts cut time, cook temperature ramp and hold time, stir/drain timing, and rennet/culture/salt dosing to hit the target curd firmness, body and moisture.

Industrial bakery/batter plant: the batchmaker samples dough during mixing (hand feel, dough temperature, consistency, occasional moisture check) and adjusts absorption (water/flour), mix time and work input, and dough temperature, so the dough forms properly downstream and the baked crumb texture meets spec.

Confectionery/chocolate plant: operator pulls cook samples (cold-water ball test, refractometer, temper meter), adjusts cooking time/temperature/vacuum, water, acid or fat/lecithin additions, and checks formed pieces (drops, chews, enrobed bars) for firmness, chew and set; re-adjusts the cooker or tempering unit accordingly.

Other processed-food batch lines (sauces, dressings, emulsified meats and sausage, snack doughs, extruded products): operator samples for viscosity, fat/moisture, bind and texture on an instrumented line and adjusts formula proportions, cook/mix cycle times and temperatures to bring the batch onto spec.

Small artisan or specialty producer (small creamery, craft candy/chocolate shop, specialty co-packer): variable raw materials, frequent product changeovers, general-purpose kettles, mixers and open vats with no inline instrumentation; quality judged largely by taste, hand feel and appearance, with ingredient and time adjustments made by hand each batch.

tasks.label: Examine, feel, and taste product samples during production to evaluate quality, color, texture, flavor, and bouquet, and document the results.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Liquid/semi-liquid batch in a food plant (sauce, dressing, syrup, beverage, ice-cream or yogurt mix): the batchmaker draws a sample from the kettle or tank at set points, looks at color and clarity, judges body/viscosity by pouring or on a spoon, tastes for seasoning/sweetness/off-notes, and records the result on the batch record before release to fill.

Cheese make room: the cheesemaker repeatedly checks vat curd and whey through the make — squeezing and breaking curd by hand to judge firmness, moisture and knitting, tasting curd for acid development and flavor, judging curd color and whey clarity — and writes observations on the make sheet in real time to time cutting, cheddaring and salting.

Confectionery batch (tempered chocolate, caramel, gummy slurry, hard-candy cook): a sample is pulled from the kettle, tempering unit or line, checked for color and gloss, for viscosity or set texture (snap/chew), and tasted for flavor and cook level; results are logged on the QC/batch sheet and the cook or tempering is adjusted.

Bakery dough/batter batch: at the end of mix the operator plunges a hand into the mixer, feels the dough for consistency, extensibility and stickiness, checks dough temperature, evaluates a scaled test piece or test bake for crumb, crust color and flavor, then records the result and adjusts water, mix time or absorption for the next batch.

Dry blend or seasoning batch (spice blend, dry mix, drink powder, bakery premix): the operator scoops a sample from the ribbon blender, inspects it for color uniformity and specks, rubs it to check for lumps and particle feel, smells it for aroma/bouquet, tastes a made-up solution, and documents in the blend log.

Fermented or cultured product in a small facility (craft brewery, kombucha, cultured dairy): a sample is drawn from the fermenter/vat during production, evaluated for bouquet, flavor development, sourness and clarity/color, and the observation is recorded to decide whether to hold, cool, or move the batch to the next step.

tasks.label: Inspect vats after cleaning to ensure that fermentable residue has been removed.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dairy/cheese plant: after a CIP cycle on a cheese vat or milk silo, the batchmaker opens the manway, shines a flashlight over walls, agitator blades, corners, outlet valve and gasket seats, feels surfaces for slippery protein film/milkstone, sometimes ATP-swabs, then records pass/fail on the pre-op sheet and calls for a re-clean if curd or milk residue remains.

Brewery, cidery, winery or kombucha plant: after CIP of a fermenter or brite tank, the worker inspects through the manway (or with mirror/light) for yeast, trub, hop matter and beerstone, checks the spray ball, dip tube, racking arm and valves, and confirms the final rinse runs clear before the vessel is released for the next fermentation.

Large industrial blending/mixing plant (sauces, syrups, dressings, sweetened beverages): pre-operational verification of several CIP'd mix tanks per shift — flashlight and mirror through the manway, checks of sugar/starch residue in dead legs and around agitator shafts, swabs on food-contact surfaces, documentation and sign-off before production starts.

Small craft or artisan operation (small cheesemaker, candy kitchen, microbrewery): open kettle or vat washed by hand, then checked visually and by touch (hand or white cloth wipe) under mediocre lighting, with older, non-standard equipment in a cramped space; scrub and re-rinse on the spot if residue is found.

Portable totes, small vats, and removable parts (agitator paddles, lids, fittings, valve seats, hoses) cleaned in a COP tank or parts washer and then inspected piece by piece on a drying rack under good light before reassembly for the next batch.

tasks.label: Fill processing or cooking containers, such as kettles, rotating cookers, pressure cookers, or vats, with ingredients, by opening valves, by starting pumps or injectors, or by hand.

instances.label: Mid/large food plant (sauce, dairy, beverage, bakery): charging liquid and bulk ingredients — water, oil, syrup, milk, slurry — into a cook kettle, vat or blend tank from bulk tanks/silos by opening valves, connecting hoses and starting transfer pumps, metering to a target weight or level on a batch sheet.

Loading bulky solids into cookers/blenders: 40 lb cheese blocks or barrels, cartons of frozen fruit or vegetables, meat chunks, IBC totes of purée — moved with hoists, bin/tote dumpers or by hand into the vessel.

tasks.label: Homogenize or pasteurize material to prevent separation or to obtain prescribed butterfat content, using a homogenizing device.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Modern high-volume dairy plant (fluid milk, cream, cheese milk, ice-cream mix): operator runs separator + in-line standardizer + high-pressure homogenizer + HTST plate pasteurizer from an HMI/control room; raw milk routed from silos through an automated mixproof valve matrix; butterfat target held to spec through the run; automated CIP at the end of the ....

Mid-size or older dairy/food plant with a semi-automated line: operator manually configures product routing (sanitary hoses, swing panels/flow plates), sets first- and second-stage homogenizing pressures by hand wheel while watching gauges, blends cream and skim in tanks to hit the butterfat target from lab results, watches the chart recorder, and hooks up CIP afterwards.

Small creamery / farmstead / artisan cheese plant: fills a batch (vat) pasteurizer by hose or by hand, agitates, holds at temperature, verifies with recording chart and indicating thermometer, cools, drains to cheese vat or bottler; occasionally runs a small homogenizer or standardizes cream by hand; hand-cleans vat and small parts.

Non-dairy and other emulsion products in a modern plant (dressings, sauces, plant-based beverages, creamer and dessert bases): in-line high-shear mixer plus high-pressure homogenizer and HTST pasteurizer run under recipe control to prevent separation of the emulsion.

Product changeover, startup and troubleshooting: switch to a new fat/formula target, change or reset the homogenizing valve and pressure for the new product, push first product through, pull samples, correct drifting butterfat or a poor emulsion, restart after a flow-diversion event.

Sensory grading of a batch for flavor and bouquet: tasting/smelling cheese plugs, chocolate liquor, syrup or candy and scoring it against grade criteria (e.g., USDA cheese grade flavor defects), with body/texture judged by hand.

tasks.label: Operate refining machines to reduce the particle size of cooked batches.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Large chocolate/compound plant, continuous line: the batchmaker runs the pre-refiner and five-roll refiner that are fed continuously from the mixer, calls up the recipe/target fineness, watches the film and roll temperatures, adjusts roll pressures and speeds, takes micrometer/Hegman fineness checks each hour, and keeps refined flake feeding the conche across a shift.

Mid-size confectionery plant, batch refining: a cooked/mixed mass (chocolate, compound, filling cream, praline paste) is charged into a ball-mill refining system via premixer and pump; the worker starts the recipe cycle, recirculates until the target ~20 micron fineness, pulls a sample for fineness testing, then discharges to the conche or holding tank.

Nut/seed paste or similar cooked-paste plant (peanut butter, tahini, halva, hazelnut paste): roasted/cooked material is milled to target fineness through a stone mill, colloid mill or ball mill in a continuous grinding line; the worker sets the gap/fineness, controls grinding temperature, and verifies fineness on samples before the paste goes to the mixing/cooling tank.

Craft/small-batch producer (bean-to-bar chocolate maker, small candy or specialty food company): a melanger, stone refiner or tabletop ball refiner sits in a small production room; the worker hand-scoops or buckets the cooked batch into the machine, scrapes down the sides, tastes and checks fineness by hand over several hours, then hand-unloads into a tempering machine or molds.

Upset and changeover handling on a refiner in a plant: the rolls run dry or band, a foreign body trips a shear pin, the mass is too thick/cold, or a product change requires opening the machine, scraping down, fat-flushing or hand-cleaning the rolls/grinding chamber and restarting to spec.

tasks.label: Clean, wash, and sterilize equipment and cooking area, using water hoses, cleaning or sterilizing solutions, or rinses.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dairy, beverage, soup/sauce or prepared-foods plant: at the end of a run the kettle/vat/pasteurizer cook loop and its connected piping are cleaned in place — operator sets up the circuit (swing bends, hose connections or valve matrix), starts the pre-rinse, caustic, intermediate rinse, acid and sanitizer steps at temperature, watches conductivity/temperature/flow and signs the cleaning record. Product-contact interiors only; no dismantling.

Continuous cook equipment with a built-in automatic wash system — spiral oven, smokehouse/thermal processing oven, industrial fryer or blancher: at shift end the operator empties the machine, loads chemical, initiates the integrated CIP/belt-wash cycle that sprays, recirculates detergent and rinses the chamber and belt, then verifies the chamber and belt are clean before release.

End-of-shift open-plant washdown in a meat, poultry, snack or bakery plant: remove guards and covers, knock down debris, high-pressure rinse the cooker/fryer/oven exteriors, frames, hoods and conveyors, apply foam, hand-scrub burned-on or protein soils, final rinse, sanitize, and wash down the surrounding cooking area — floors, walls, drains, platforms. Wet, hot, chemical-heavy; released only after visual and ATP-swab inspection.

Clean-out-of-place of removable parts: agitators, baskets, screens, nozzles, valves, sight glasses, trays, racks and smoke sticks are carried to the sanitation room, soaked/washed in a COP tank or loaded into a cabinet or tunnel washer, rinsed, sanitized, dried and returned for reassembly.

Small food plant or institutional/central kitchen with no automated cleaning: drain and filter fryer oil and boil out the fry vat, scrub the steam-jacketed kettle and tilt skillet by hand with brushes and detergent, clean retort/pressure-cooker baskets, wipe and sanitize adjacent tables and hood surfaces, hose or mop the cooking area floor and squeegee to the drain.

instances.label: Continuous fryer/oven line in a snack, bakery or prepared-foods plant: operator watches HMI trends, inline gauges and pulls samples for color, moisture and texture, then adjusts oil/air temperature, belt speed and product/oil flow to hold the product on spec through raw-material and throughput variation.

Batch cooking in steam-jacketed kettles/cookers (sauces, soups, fillings, cheese sauce, syrups) in a food plant: operator sequences ingredient additions, opens and trims the steam valve, watches temperature, viscosity/Brix and agitation, and holds the cook to the recipe endpoint.

Roasting or drying operation (coffee, nuts, cocoa, grain, seeds): operator judges degree of roast by color, smell and sample draws, and adjusts burner firing, airflow, drum speed and drop point batch to batch as green-stock moisture varies.

High-volume commercial or institutional kitchen / commissary fry-and-cook station: tending deep fryers and griddles, checking oil temperature and doneness, timing and moving baskets, and resetting fryer controls between products during a rush.

Small or legacy operation with uninstrumented equipment (artisan candy or jam cooker, kettle corn, small smokehouse, older gas-fired kettle): analog dials and hand valves, no inline sensors, doneness judged by sight, thread/feel or smell, frequent product changeovers.
