tasks.label: Measure or weigh ingredients, using scales or measuring containers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Plant batch prep for a steam kettle/cooker: operator scales major dry/bulk ingredients (flour, starch, sugar, salt, dry mix) from 25-50 lb bags, totes or bulk bins into a weigh bucket or hopper on a platform/floor scale to a recipe target, then charges the vessel. Dusty, wet-floor plant environment; bags fetched from a staging pallet, slit, poured, residue shaken out.

Scaling minor/micro ingredients for the same batch: spices, seasonings, cures, gums, colors, leavening and additives weighed to a few grams on a bench scale into small tubs or bags in a pre-weigh/scaling room, tared, labeled and staged for the cook.

Measuring liquids into the cook vessel: water, oil, brine, syrup, sauce base or vinegar measured by graduated container, bucket or metered fill into steam-jacketed kettles, fryers or pressure cookers; volumes from a few gallons to full-vessel charges.

Weighing/portioning the food product itself into the cooking equipment or its carriers: scaling batches of diced vegetables, pasta, meat or nuggets into fryer baskets, blancher carriers or kettle charges, and portioning cooked product to target weight into pans/trays at the cooker discharge.

Weight verification and record-keeping around the batch: tare/zero and test-weight checks of scales, re-weighing a charge that reads out of tolerance, topping off or removing product, and logging weights on the batch sheet or HMI for QA.

tasks.label: Tend or operate and control equipment, such as kettles, cookers, vats and tanks, and boilers, to cook ingredients or prepare products for further processing.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Food plant batch cooking: operator charges a steam-jacketed kettle or horizontal cooker with bulk ingredients (bagged powders, totes of vegetables/meat, metered liquids) for sauce, soup, chili or pie filling, sets steam and agitation per recipe, monitors temperature/viscosity/Brix, samples, then discharges to a fill line and runs cleanup.

Snack/prepared-food cook line: tending a continuous or batch fryer, blancher or cooker (potato chips, nuts, extruded snacks, par-fried products) - watching oil temperature and level, conveyor/belt speed, product color and moisture, adjusting setpoints, clearing product, filtering oil.

Cannery/pet-food retort room: loading baskets or crates of filled cans, jars or pouches into batch retorts or pressure cookers, selecting and running the validated thermal cycle, monitoring pressure/temperature charts, keeping FDA cook records, and unloading cooked product.

Dairy/beverage vat and tank work: cooking curd in cheese vats, running cook/pasteurizing tanks, syrup or brew kettles - setting temperature ramps, agitation, additions of cultures/rennet/hops, checking cook endpoint, and transferring to downstream tanks.

Foodservice/commissary kitchen: tending deep fry cookers and steam cookers - filling and dropping baskets of fries, wings, breaded items, holding cook times across simultaneous orders, shaking and dumping to holding, checking oil level/quality, all in a kitchen shared with human staff.

Small specialty plant or artisanal producer: small-batch cooking with frequent recipe changes and hands-on judgment - candy/caramel cooking to stage, jams and glazes, masa/tortilla cooking, small-batch soups - on general-purpose kettles or braising pans with manual charging and sensory checks.

tasks.label: Set temperature, pressure, and time controls, and start conveyers, machines, or pumps.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Continuous cooking line (fryer, oven, roaster, blancher) in a large food processing plant: at product changeover the tender selects the product, sets oil/zone temperatures, belt speed and dwell (cook) time on the HMI or panel, and starts the conveyor, oil circulation pumps and blowers, then verifies the line comes up to setpoint.

Batch retort / pressure cooker room in a cannery or pet-food plant: tender sets the scheduled process (come-up, cook temperature, overpressure, cook time, cool ramp) on the retort control, closes and locks the vessel, and starts the cycle, including circulation pumps and basket/shuttle movement, with FDA/USDA process records.

Batch kettle / steam vat cooking of soups, sauces, fillings or preserves in a mid-size plant with PLC/HMI controls: tender sets jacket steam temperature or pressure, agitator speed and cook time for the recipe, and starts the agitator and the transfer/discharge pump at end of cook.

Fry station, steam kettle or programmable cooker in a commercial or institutional kitchen or a small prepared-foods operation: tender sets the thermostat and cook timers, starts basket lifts/cook cycles and holds product to spec through variable order-driven demand.

Legacy or small-scale equipment (older kettles, candy cookers, batch fryers, smokehouses) with analog dials, manual steam and water valves, mechanical timers and chart recorders: tender opens valves by hand, dials in temperature/pressure, sets a mechanical timer and starts pumps or conveyors with local pushbuttons or levers, adjusting by feel and observation.

tasks.label: Remove cooked material or products from equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Continuous cook line in a food plant (spiral oven, continuous fryer, blancher/water cooker): cooked product exits the cooker onto a take-away/drain conveyor; the tender watches the discharge, frees stuck or clustered product, and fills bins, totes or the next conveyor with the cooked output.

Batch deep fryer with lift-out baskets (snack/commissary/institutional scale): when the timer ends, lift the basket(s) of fried product out of hot oil, shake/drain, and dump into a holding pan, cooling conveyor or tote, then return the empty basket for the next batch.

Steam-jacketed kettle or cook tank of soup, sauce, filling, rice or pasta: after the cook, discharge the batch out of the vessel — tilt the kettle, open the draw-off valve, or pump/scoop the hot product into totes, bags or the filler — and clear the residual product clinging in the vessel.

Bakery/oven work: pull hot trays or rack trolleys of baked product out of the oven and get the product off the pans/trays onto cooling racks or the next conveyor, without crushing or breaking the items.

Meat/poultry smokehouse, steam cabinet or cook cabinet: after the cycle, pull heavy loaded trolleys/racks or sticks of cooked sausage, ham or poultry out of the hot, humid chamber and move them to chilling, or unload the sticks/product onto a conveyor.

Retort / pressure cooker room: after the sterilizing cook, remove baskets, crates or trays of hot cans, jars or pouches from the retort and move them to the unloading/cooling station for downstream handling.

tasks.label: Collect and examine product samples during production to test them for quality, color, content, consistency, viscosity, acidity, or specific gravity.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Pumpable cooked product (sauce, soup, syrup, juice, sweetened condensed/dairy mix): mid-cook the operator opens a sample valve or dips the kettle/vat, pulls a beaker of hot product, eyeballs color and body, reads temperature and Brix/solids or specific gravity at the line, records the reading and signals a cook adjustment. Wet, hot plant floor.

At-line QA bench work in the plant: operator carries the collected sample to the bench and runs instrument tests ""acidity by pH meter or ..."" then logs results on the QC sheet and reports out-of-spec batches.

Discrete/solid cooked product (fried snacks, chips, nuggets, cooked pasta, beans, roasted nuts): operator grabs pieces off the discharge belt or from the fryer/cooker outlet, checks color and doneness, weighs the grab sample, checks moisture/oil, and adjusts cook time or temperature.

Subjective sensory and hand-feel check: tasting a batch for seasoning/flavor, smelling for scorch, candy cold-water ball-stage test, feeling curd or dough firmness ""an accept / keep-cooking decision made by the operator's senses rather than an instrument.

Hygienic sample pulled for micro testing or as a retained/hold sample: sterile bottle or swab filled at a sanitized sample port or from the batch, capped, labeled with lot and time, logged, and carried to the plant lab or cooler.

tasks.label: Pour, dump, or load prescribed quantities of ingredients or products into cooking equipment, manually or using a hoist.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Food manufacturing plant (soup, sauce, dairy, snack, pet food): per a batch sheet, the operator moves 25–50 lb bags/boxes of dry ingredients (flour, starch, sugar, milk powder, spice blends) from pallets or a staging rack, cuts and dumps them into a cooking kettle/cooker hopper or bag-dump station, verifies weight on a floor scale, and discards empty bags. Wet, warm floor with forklift and cart traffic; layout fixed by the plant.

Plant liquid charging: pumping, pouring, or metering prescribed volumes/weights of water, oil, brine, stock, tomato paste or slurry from hoses, drums, or IBC totes (sometimes with a drum lift/hoist) into steam-jacketed kettles, vats, or pressure cookers at recipe-specified points in the cook.

Plant product loading: tipping bins/totes of raw product (cut vegetables, meat pieces, pasta, potato slices) with a hoist or bin dumper into a blancher, kettle or batch fryer, or loading filled pouches/trays/baskets/racks into a retort or continuous cooker at prescribed batch quantities.

Small or specialty plant with frequent recipe changes (confectionery cooker, cheese vat, small-batch soup/sauce kettle, ethnic-foods co-packer): the operator scoops and pours pre-weighed buckets, cases, and blocks of varied ingredients into the vessel at staged times during the cook, adjusting per batch and product changeovers.

Quick-service / chain restaurant or commissary fry station: loading prescribed portions of frozen product (fries, rings, tenders) from bins into fry baskets and dropping the baskets into deep fryers, repeated through a shift alongside human crew in the kitchen.

Institutional central kitchen (school district, hospital, prison commissary): dumping cases of vegetables, bags of rice/pasta, and buckets of stock or sauce base into 60–100 gal steam-jacketed tilting kettles per a production sheet, using a hand cart or small hoist in a human-scaled kitchen.

tasks.label: Listen for malfunction alarms, and shut down equipment and notify supervisors when necessary.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Snack/prepared-food plant, continuous fryer or cooker line: the panel/annunciator raises a malfunction alarm (over-temperature, low oil or water level, conveyor jam, motor fault) while the tender watches several machines; the tender acknowledges, stops the line or hits the e-stop, and calls maintenance/the shift supervisor.

Cannery retort/pressure-cooker room: a process-deviation alarm (temperature, pressure, or come-up-time out of the scheduled process) fires mid-cycle; the operator halts or holds the cycle, segregates the batch, and notifies the supervisor/QA for a process-authority decision.

Steam-jacketed kettle, cook vat, or the boiler/steam supply serving the cook line: burner flame failure, low-water, or high-pressure alarm sounds; the operator shuts off heat/steam and the equipment and notifies the supervisor or maintenance.

Dairy or liquid-food plant, HTST pasteurizer or aseptic cooker: a temperature/flow deviation alarm sounds and the unit diverts; the operator stops the run, notifies the supervisor, and the affected product is held pending review.

No formal alarm: while tending kettles/fryers/ovens on a noisy plant floor, the worker hears an unusual noise (bearing squeal, jammed agitator), smells burning, or sees smoke/leaking product on equipment with little instrumentation, judges it warrants stopping, shuts the machine down manually, and finds or radios the supervisor.

sources.claim: Boston Dynamics Spot performs autonomous inspection rounds inside AB InBev's Leuven brewery (a food/beverage processing plant), detecting equipment issues and automatically alerting managers — covering the detect-abnormality-and-notify-supervisor portion of the task in a working plant.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous condition-monitoring rounds in a beverage plant. It transfers to the monitoring/notification half of this task — the robot senses abnormal equipment behaviour in a food-industry facility and escalates it to supervisors without a human in the ....

tasks.label: Notify or signal other workers to operate equipment or when processing is complete.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Turn valves or start pumps to add ingredients or drain products from equipment and to transfer products for storage, cooling, or further processing.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Liquid-food plant (fluid dairy, juice, syrup, liquid egg, brewery): after the cook/pasteurization step the tender routes finished product through a valve manifold or flow panel to a holding silo or storage tank, starts the transfer pump, watches level/flow/pressure, then switches the line over to flush/CIP when the tank is emptied.

Batch cook kettle in a soup/sauce/prepared-foods or meat plant: at end of cook cycle the operator opens the bottom draw-off/discharge valve and starts a positive-displacement transfer pump to move hot product to a chiller, filler or holding tank; watches for clogging of particulate product, closes the valve and flushes the line.

Charging liquid ingredients from plumbed bulk supply: operator opens valves or starts metering pumps to add measured water, oil, brine, syrup or slurry into the cooker/kettle per the batch recipe, verifying volume by meter or tank level.

Charging a liquid ingredient from a drum or IBC tote parked next to the kettle: operator drags a flexible hose or drop wand, clamps it to the tote and the pump inlet, primes and starts the pump, watches the tote empty, then breaks the connection and moves the empty container.

Older or mid-size plant with a manual flow panel: operator makes up the flow path with swing bends or flexible hoses between kettles, tanks, pumps and filler lines, hand-cranks butterfly/ball valves, starts the transfer pump and stands by, then breaks the path down after transfer.

Fryer/oil systems in a snack, potato or par-fry plant: operator opens valves and starts pumps to top up fresh oil from bulk storage, drain used oil from the fryer to a waste/storage tank, and circulate oil through filtration and heat exchangers during the run.

tasks.label: Admit required amounts of water, steam, cooking oils, or compressed air into equipment, such as by opening water valves to cool mixtures to the desired consistency.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Mid/large food plant batch cook line (soups, sauces, fillings, ready meals): operator admits metered water and steam (jacket or direct injection) into a plumbed steam-jacketed kettle or cooker per recipe, then opens cooling water/coolant to the jacket to bring the batch down to target temperature and consistency before pumping out. Sanitary plant floor, fixed piping, standard vessels, people working nearby.

Snack/protein/potato plant fryer line or large commissary fryers: operator adds fresh cooking oil to the fryer and maintains oil level during the run, admits steam/hot oil to heat exchangers and compressed air to pneumatic controls. Fixed fryer line, oil supply piping or drum/jug handling, plant floor.

Bakery, dough, or beverage/syrup batching: operator admits an exact quantity of water at an exact temperature into a mixer, cooker, or blend tank per formula, plus steam to heat the batch. Mixing room in a bakery or beverage plant with standard equipment.

Cannery / pet food / ready-meal retort room: operator admits steam into batch retorts or pressure cookers per the validated schedule, then admits cooling water and compressed air for counter-pressure cooling, venting the vessel at the prescribed points. Institutionally controlled retort room with fixed vessels and headers.

Small, artisanal, or legacy operation (small sauce/candy/deli plant, older kettles, portable vats): operator drags a water hose or opens a manual handwheel/gate valve to add water to an unplumbed or portable vessel, hand-pours cooking oil from jugs into an open fryer, and judges by eye/feel when the mixture has reached the desired consistency. Cluttered, variable floor but still an institution-controlled facility.

tasks.label: Activate agitators and paddles to mix or stir ingredients, stopping machines when ingredients are thoroughly mixed.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Food processing plant, batch cook room: operator charges a steam-jacketed or horizontal kettle with sauce/soup/filling ingredients, starts the agitator/scraper at a set speed, watches for uniform blending and no scorching during the cook, then stops agitation at the end of the batch before discharge.

Commercial bakery or snack plant: operator charges a horizontal/vertical dough or batter mixer, starts mixing, judges dough development or batter uniformity (look, feel, temperature, motor load), and stops the mixer at the right point before discharge to the divider or depositor.

Meat, poultry, prepared-salad or ready-meal plant: operator loads a ribbon/paddle blender, cooker-mixer or vacuum tumbler with cooked protein, dressing, seasoning and inclusions, runs the mix cycle, checks visual uniformity of the blend, and stops the machine when evenly distributed.

Confectionery, syrup, jam or dairy plant: operator runs a paddle-agitated cooker for caramel, fudge, fruit preparation, cheese sauce or syrup, holding agitation through the cook while consistency/solids build, and stopping the paddle when the mass is homogeneous and at target consistency.

Institutional or chain foodservice production kitchen (school district central kitchen, hospital, casino/commissary): operator cooks gravies, sauces, chili, beans or oatmeal in a large steam kettle or tilting braising pan, running its built-in mixer or hand-stirring with a paddle, and stopping when smooth and lump-free.

Small craft or specialty processor with older semi-manual equipment and variable inputs (small-batch sauce co-packer, masa/tortilla, specialty candy, brewery mash): operator starts an uninstrumented agitator or stirs with a hand paddle, judging by eye and feel because ingredient batches and recipes vary from run to run.

tasks.label: Measure and examine extruded products to locate defects and to check for conformance to specifications, adjusting controls as necessary to alter products.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Steady-state round plastic extrusion (PE/PVC pipe, medical and industrial tubing, hose, wire/cable insulation and jacket) in a pipe or cable plant: the tender checks outside diameter, wall thickness, ovality and concentricity, watches the running product for lumps, sags, sinks and surface blemishes, and corrects by changing haul-off speed, extruder rpm, vacuum/cooling or die centering.

Steady-state flat plastic extrusion (blown film, cast film, sheet) in a film/sheet plant: the operator reads the transverse thickness profile, pulls samples for gauge checks, looks for gels, specks, die lines, streaks and edge defects, and corrects by adjusting die bolts, air-ring/cooling zones, screw and haul-off speeds.

High-volume plastic lineal/profile extrusion (window and door profile, weatherstrip, decking trim) on long runs: the operator checks the profile cross-section against the drawing with gauges and templates, checks surface finish and straightness, and trims dimensions with haul-off speed, calibrator vacuum and zone temperatures.

Custom, short-run plastic or rubber profile extrusion in a job shop: frequent changeovers, novel cross-sections with no established reference, first-piece checks against a master sample, optical comparator or drawing, and corrections that are largely tooling-side (calibrator, die land, vacuum, take-off tension) made by feel between short orders.

Metal extrusion and drawing: aluminum press run-out and stretcher, where the operator inspects profiles for die lines, pickup, blisters, twist and bow and gauges dimensions, adjusting ram speed, billet/die temperature and puller settings; and metal wire/bar/tube drawing lines, where the operator micrometers drawn diameter, checks surface for scratches, scoring and neckdowns, and adjusts speed, tension and lubrication or calls a die change.

Non-steady-state episodes across all variants: line start-up and product changeover, first-article approval, and troubleshooting a defect outbreak — pulling and cutting samples, taking multiple manual measurements, diagnosing root cause (contamination, moisture, degraded melt, worn die), and making coordinated multi-variable adjustments, sometimes pulling or reworking tooling.

tasks.label: Start machines and set controls to regulate vacuum, air pressure, sizing rings, and temperature, and to synchronize speed of extrusion.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Modern plastic pipe/tubing line (PE, PVC, PP) in a producer's plant: operator starts extruder and downstream units from the line HMI, calls up a recipe, sets barrel/die heat zones, sets vacuum level in the calibration/sizing tank, internal pipe air pressure, positions the sizing sleeve/calibration basket for the diameter, and synchronizes haul-off speed with screw speed until the in-line gauge shows wall thickness and diameter in spec.

Older or low-automation plastic profile, tube or rubber hose line: dial/thermocouple heat controllers, hand-set water and vacuum valves on the sizing tank, manual air-pressure regulators, operator physically swaps or shims the sizing ring/calibrator plate in the tank, then feathers puller speed by eye and caliper checks until product gauges in tolerance.

Small-diameter, tight-tolerance line (medical tubing, small-bore hose, wire and cable insulation): start-up with laser/X-ray gauging, vacuum sizing and air pressure dialed in to hold concentricity and ID/OD, capstan or haul-off speed trimmed against extruder rpm, frequent short runs and setup trials.

Aluminum/metal extrusion press start-up: set container, die and billet furnace temperatures, load the ram speed profile, set puller and run-out table speed synchronized to exit speed, set quench air/water and burp pressure, then start the press cycle and correct until profile exit temperature and dimensions hold.

Wire or rod drawing machine setup and start: set drawing speeds of successive capstan blocks in synchronized ratio, tension/accumulator settings, die cooling water and lubricant flow, air pressure for die boxes and wipers, thread the wire, soft-start and ramp the line to running speed without breaks.

instances.label: Shift/daily preventive-maintenance round on an extrusion or wire-drawing line in a plant: check and top off hydraulic/gear oil and drawing lubricant, grease bearings and guides, inspect belts, hoses, water lines and air/oil filters, blow out and wipe down buildup and scrap around the machine, log findings. Machine is fixed in place, partly hot, with people working nearby.

In-run troubleshooting of a process/quality fault: diameter or wall drift, surface defects, melt-pressure spike, wire breaks, uneven cooling. Operator inspects the line, isolates the root cause (worn tooling, plugged screen, failed heater band or thermocouple, misaligned guide/capstan, bad feedstock), corrects it, and verifies the product is back in tolerance.

Melt-filtration and die-cleaning servicing: cleaning or replacing clogged screen packs/breaker plates on a plastics extruder when pressure rises, and caustic or blast cleaning of extrusion dies/tooling in the die area of the plant.

Hands-on tooling change and melt-path cleaning: pull and swap dies, tips, mandrels or drawing dies; scrape and brass-brush the screw and barrel during a screw pull; clean die lips, die holders and drawing die blocks of degraded polymer or metal pickup, then reassemble and restart.

Minor mechanical/electrical repairs on the line: replace a burned heater band or failed thermocouple, a worn drive belt, hose, seal, bearing or cutter blade; retighten or reseal a leaking hydraulic/pneumatic fitting; reseat a loose connector or reset/replace a drive component, then test-run the machine.

Clearing jams and faults on downstream/auxiliary equipment: puller/haul-off, cutter, coiler or spooler, vacuum sizing tank, chiller, hopper loader — untangle broken wire or product, unclog lines, clear scrap, reset the fault and restart the line.

tasks.label: Change dies on extruding machines, according to production line changes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Plastic profile/tubing/hose line changeover in a custom extrusion shop: shut down and purge the line, unbolt the hot die and tip from the extruder adapter/breaker plate with hand and torque tools, scrape carbonized polymer off die faces, bolt on the new profile die and mandrel, reconnect heater bands/thermocouples, re-set downstream calibration/vacuum tooling, then start up and dial in dimensions to print.

Large die-head change on a plastic pipe, sheet or blown-film line: crane or hoist the heavy die head/spiral mandrel off the extruder, break and remake a bolted flange joint on hot tooling, swap sizing sleeve/lip set, purge resin, re-center the die for wall-thickness uniformity, and restart the line to gauge spec.

Crosshead tooling change on a wire-coating, jacketing or medical-tubing line: replace tip and die inserts in the crosshead, set concentricity/draw-down ratio to tight tolerance, re-thread the conductor or mandrel, and requalify wall thickness and eccentricity on start-up.

Die-stack change on a horizontal metal extrusion press (aluminum profile press, copper/brass tube press) between orders: pull the preheated die stack (die, backer, bolster, ring) from the die oven or die storage, index the die slide/cassette out, extract the used hot die stack, load the new stack, lock up, clean the container, and run the first billet, then send the used die for cleaning.

Die change on a drawing machine or draw bench (wire, rod, bar or tube): stop the machine, open the die box/holder, remove the worn drawing die and nib, clean soap/lubricant residue, install the correct-size die, re-point the wire or tube and thread it through the die and capstan, and restart to size.

Charging the blender/feed section with a mixed recipe: virgin pellets plus regrind, color masterbatch and additives measured into blender bins or auger/loss-in-weight feeders on a compounding or profile line, verifying the recipe and topping off small components during the run.

Rubber/plastic 'dough': feeding slabs, strips or rolls of unvulcanized compound from the batch-off rack into the feed opening of a hot-feed or cold-feed extruder, keeping the throat fed continuously and working the stock down with a stuffing tool.

Ram/paste extrusion: stuffing a preformed billet or roll of putty-like compound (PTFE paste, rubber preform) into the cylinder of a ram extruder, seating it and closing the barrel before the ram stroke.

Metal side: charging the extrusion press or drawing line — placing logs/billets into the heater and press container, or loading wire coils on the pay-off and filling the drawing machine's soap/lubricant boxes and powder hoppers.

Aluminum/copper extrusion press: pull the preheated die stack (die, backer, bolster, tool carrier) from the die oven, load it into the die slide/holder at the press platen, secure/lock it, run the shift-in cycle, and take the first billet — hot, heavy tooling handled with hoist or manipulator on the press floor.

instances.label: Metal drawing/straightening line in a wire or bar mill: operator enters the required length and count at the line control, the coil is drawn/straightened and an inline (flying) shear cuts rod to length continuously; operator watches the length readout, spot-checks pieces, and lets cut bars discharge to a run-out/bundling table. Metal extrusion press feedline: operator sets billet/product length on the press PLC; the hot log shear/saw cuts heated log stock to the exact billet length for the press, and the extruded rod/bar is cut to specified length at the cut-off saw/shear with a servo length gauge before stacking. Plastic extrusion line making rod, tube or solid profile: operator sets the cut length/recipe on the puller-cutter (servo cutter or guillotine), runs a first-piece length check with a tape/gauge, then the cutter cuts to length on the moving extrudate for the rest of the run while the operator monitors length drift and takes off cut pieces.

Off-line/standalone shear or cut-off station on the shop floor: operator takes drawn or extruded bars from racks or bundles, feeds them to the shear against an adjustable length stop, actuates the cut (pedal/two-hand control), and sorts, stacks or bundles the cut lengths; mixed diameters, short customer-specific runs, remnant handling.

Changeover, setup and troubleshooting of the shearing mechanism: install or rotate shear blades/knives, set blade clearance and the length gauge/stop for a new size, run and measure a first article with tape or caliper and correct for tolerance, and clear a jammed or mis-sheared rod before restarting.

Cleaning confined and awkward spots: under the machine base and between the line and the wall, behind guards, inside quench/cooling tanks, catch pans, chip pans and pits, where the operator must kneel, reach in with a brush, scraper or shop vac, and remove sludge and packed scrap.

End-of-shift housekeeping: returning hand tools, dies and gauges to racks and shadow boards, coiling air/water hoses and cords, stacking empty pallets, spools and totes, emptying trash and recycling bins, and clearing walkways and forklift lanes of clutter.

tasks.label: Replace worn dies when products vary from specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Plastics pipe, tubing, hose, profile or sheet extrusion line in a plastics plant: gauges or QC checks show wall thickness/diameter drifting out of tolerance from a worn or damaged die; the operator stops or diverts the line, pulls the hot die/tooling set, fits a refurbished die of the same size, brings it to temperature, restarts and verifies dimensions.

Wire-and-cable coating crosshead or precision small-bore/medical tubing line: worn guider tip and die insert replaced on a small extruder; the conductor or tube must be re-threaded through the head, concentricity re-set with adjusting bolts, and wall eccentricity re-qualified before running product.

Aluminum or copper extrusion press: profile dimensions drift as the die bearing wears; the die stack is sheared out and removed from the die slide, sent to the die shop for correction, and a preheated corrected die stack from the die oven is loaded and the press restarted.

Metal wire drawing machine (rod breakdown, multi-block dry drawing or multi-wire line): drawn wire diameter/finish goes out of spec as a carbide or diamond die wears oval; the operator opens the die box, swaps the worn die in its holder, re-points the wire, threads it through the new die and around the capstan, and restarts.

Cold draw bench or shaped-wire/turks-head station for tube and bar: heavy worn die ring and plug/mandrel changed out with hoist and hand tools in the die holder, bar or tube end pointed and threaded through the new die, first pieces gauged before the run resumes.

Chemical/acid-bath testing at a plant fume hood or bench: metal or plastic samples immersed in an acid or solvent bath for a set period (e.g., copper-sulfate/acid immersion for intergranular attack, pickling or mass-loss corrosion check), then rinsed, dried, weighed or bent and assessed against acceptance criteria; corrosive-chemical PPE handling.

tasks.label: Weigh and mix pelletized, granular, or powdered thermoplastic materials and coloring pigments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Running extrusion line (pipe, profile, sheet, film, tubing) in a plastics plant: operator sets and verifies recipe percentages of virgin resin, regrind, color concentrate and additive on the machine-side blender at the extruder throat, keeps bins supplied from gaylords/loaders, and checks batch weights and blend logs against the job spec.

Small or mid-size custom extrusion shop, hand batching: operator scoops and weighs a few pounds of pelletized color concentrate and additive on a bench or floor scale, combines it with weighed virgin resin and regrind in a tumble drum or directly in the machine hopper, blends for several minutes, and transfers the blend to the extruder.

Dry-blend / compounding work (e.g., PVC pipe or filled compound): weigh powdered resin, fillers, stabilizers, lubricants and dry pigments to a formula card, charge a high-intensity or ribbon mixer, run the mix and discharge to the cooler/holding bin; dusty conditions, respirator and gloves.

Material staging and charging for the blend: retrieving 25 kg sacks, gaylords or bulk bags from the staging area, cutting them open and dumping them into blender bins, a dump station or hopper loader, connecting vacuum wands, and recording lot numbers for traceability.

Color or material changeover: emptying and cleaning blender bins, weigh chamber, hoppers and conveying lines of the previous color/resin, then weighing and mixing the first batch of the new recipe and confirming the blend is free of the old color.

Wire-coating/cable insulation crosshead setup: operator picks the tip (nozzle) and die pair matched to conductor diameter and finished OD, plus wire guides, from drawers holding hundreds of small precision brass tips distinguished by stamped size codes; occasionally confirms bore with pin gauges.

Small job shop or older plant: mixed, partly unlabeled and worn tooling in bins and drawers; operator gauges candidate nozzles/guides with a micrometer or pin gauge, judges wear, stacks shims/spacers by trial, and sometimes adapts a near-size piece.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume closed-die hot forging press line in an automotive/industrial forge shop: after a die change the operator starts the induction heater, transfer and press, runs the first few pieces, watches the heater feed, transfer arms and press for misfeeds, sticking parts, off-temperature billets and abnormal tonnage, then gauges the first-off forging against the print/checking fixture and approves the setup for production.

Cold heading / upsetter / boltmaker cell in a fastener plant: operator jogs then starts the machine after a tooling change, runs sample fasteners, checks head height, length, diameter and thread with go/no-go gauges and micrometers, and watches for double hits, misfeeds, wire slippage and punch/die wear during the trial run.

Small job-shop forging: low-volume varied parts on a mechanical/hydraulic press or drop hammer, operator starts the machine, forges a sample from a heated billet, listens and watches for die shift, incomplete fill, sticking or lubrication problems, and checks the sample with calipers, templates and weight before running the lot.

Large open-die forging, ring rolling or heavy press work: operator starts press and manipulator, produces a first/sample workpiece from a large heated ingot, checks major dimensions with large calipers and templates while the piece is hot, and watches the press, manipulator and hydraulics for malfunction.

Tending during an established production run: operator observes the running forging machine and automation for abnormal noise, vibration, misfeeds, die wear or lubrication faults, periodically pulls sample workpieces to check dimensions against specification, and stops or restarts the machine when something drifts out of conformance.

instances.label: In-process check during a production run on a hot forging press/upsetter: operator pulls a sample part every so many cycles from the die or the trim conveyor and checks key dimensions (length, diameter, thickness/shut height, flash, underfill) with calipers, snap gauges and go/no-go plugs, deciding whether to keep running or adjust the press. Hot, scaly, oily parts; noise, heat and lubricant mist on the shop floor.

Visual and tactile defect inspection and sorting of forged/formed parts at a bench, trim station or sorting table: looking for cracks, laps, seams, die shift, underfill, scale pits, burrs, flash remnants and plastic flash/short shots, culling non-conforming parts into scrap/rework bins and tagging the lot.

Bench or gauge-room dimensional inspection of cooled parts: micrometers, height gauge, bore gauges, dedicated check fixtures and hardness checks on a sample from the run, with readings written on a check sheet or entered into an SPC system and out-of-tolerance trends reported to the setter/QC.

First-piece / setup approval after a die change or new job, plus periodic layout inspection: the first parts are measured feature-by-feature against the print, sometimes on a shop-floor CMM or optical scanner in the QC room, and signed off before the run is released.

Large or awkward work: open-die/heavy forgings, rings and shafts measured hot at the press with large calipers, tapes, templates and gauges, or odd one-off jobs where the part is too heavy to carry to a bench and must be checked where it sits.

tasks.label: Turn handles or knobs to set pressures and depths of ram strokes and to synchronize machine operations.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Initial run setup on a press with programmable/CNC control (servo or PLC-controlled mechanical or hydraulic forging press): operator calls up the job, sets shut height / ram bottom position, tonnage or hydraulic pressure setpoints, dwell and speed, then runs trial forgings and confirms part height before releasing the run. Plant press bay, dies staged, standard gauges.

Setup on legacy manually adjusted equipment (older mechanical forging press or upsetter with hand-cranked wedge/screw slide adjustment, board or air hammer with throttle and regulator knobs, hydraulic press with a hand-set relief valve): operator turns handwheels and valve knobs by feel, watches a dial indicator or pressure gauge, strikes trial pieces, measures, and re-adjusts. Hot, dirty, noisy forge shop floor.

Mid-run correction on a machine with programmable controls: parts drift out of tolerance as dies wear or the press heats up, so ram bottom position/tonnage is nudged a few thousandths and pressure trimmed, with part checks between adjustments.

Setting blow energy, stroke and air/hydraulic pressure on a forging hammer equipped with programmable energy control (CNC hydraulic die forging hammer), including number and force of blows per die impression.

Synchronizing machine operations in a forging cell: timing the press stroke with billet heater, feed/transfer or manipulator, knockout/ejector and trim press so the sequence interlocks correctly; adjusting timing setpoints and limit switch angles.
Plastic-side work: setting clamp pressure, mold/platen height, and ram/injection stroke and pressure profile on a plastics compression or injection press before and during a run.

tasks.label: Set up, operate, or tend presses and forging machines to perform hot or cold forging by flattening, straightening, bending, cutting, piercing, or other operations to taper, shape, or form metal.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production run of hot closed-die forging in a forge shop: take a glowing billet (1000-1250°C) off the induction heater conveyor with tongs/manipulator, place it in the bust, blocker and finish impressions of a mechanical press, screw press or hammer, cycle the machine, spray die lube, remove the forging and set it on the cooling conveyor; watch billet temperature, flash formation and die filling for the whole shift.

Secondary press work on forgings in the same shop: tending trim, pierce, coin, restrike and straightening presses — feeding the forging into the die, cycling the press, clearing flash/slugs into chutes, checking parts against a gauge and stacking or containerizing accepted output.

Cold forging / cold heading production: tending multi-station cold headers, cold-forming and coining presses — keeping wire coil or blanks fed, running the machine, pulling and gauging sample parts for SPC, replenishing lubricant, sorting rejects and clearing occasional mis-feeds.

Setup and changeover for a new job: pull the previous die set, install and align the new upper/lower dies or trim tooling in the press, set shut height, stroke and ejectors, set heater and lubrication parameters, run trial pieces, measure the first article against the print, shim/adjust until in tolerance, and release the job to run.

Low-volume / job-shop and heavy work: short runs of varied part numbers with frequent size changes, hand-tong or manipulator work on open-die and upset forging of bars and rings, straightening and bending odd-shaped stock, with the operator judging each piece by eye and adjusting between hits.

tasks.label: Trim and compress finished forgings to specified tolerances.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume hot closed-die forging line (automotive/hardware parts under ~25 kg): after the forging press/hammer, each hot part is placed in the trim (and pierce) die, the press is cycled to shear off flash, and the part is restruck/coined to bring it into print tolerance; operator tends the presses, clears flash, gauges sample parts, and adjusts shut height. Indoor forge plant floor, hot scaly parts, oil smoke, noise.

Medium-volume job-shop forge: operator uses tongs to place hot forgings one at a time into a stand-alone trim press die, cycles it, separates flash from part, stacks parts on a cooling conveyor or tub; short runs, frequent part number and die changes (dozens of part numbers), part-specific handling.

Cold coining / sizing / restrike of cooled forgings on a press to bring dimensions (thickness, flatness, bore, hub height) into specified tolerance; operator loads part into the sizing die, cycles press, checks with go/no-go gauges, calipers or a fixture gauge, adjusts press setting when drift appears.

Large/heavy closed-die forgings (>100 kg — truck crankshafts, front axle beams, steering knuckles, large aerospace parts): part moved by manipulator, hoist or crane into a heavy trim/deburr press and then a calibrating (sizing) press; occasional hot saw or torch removal of large flash; dimensional checks on a layout fixture.

Plastic and small-lot finishing: removing flash/gates from molded or forged plastic and small metal parts with a bench trim press, router, knife or grinder, and pressing parts in a sizing fixture to bring them to tolerance; mixed part families, bench-level work at a finishing station.

tasks.label: Install, adjust, and remove dies, synchronizing cams, forging hammers, and stop guides, using overhead cranes or other hoisting devices, and hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Closed-die change on a mechanical, screw or hydraulic forging press in a forge shop: die setter slings a multi-ton die set with the overhead crane, lands it on the bolster/master die holder, keys or clamps upper and lower halves, sets shut height, checks match with a trial forging, and removes the outgoing hot die set.

Die installation/removal on a drop, board or counterblow forging hammer: dies seated in dovetails and locked with tapered keys driven home with a sledge, shims added to correct match and impression depth, ram/anvil alignment checked by lead or first-hit impression, with the crane and hand tools.

Tooling changeover on an upsetter/horizontal forging machine or similar multi-station machine: gripper dies, heading tools and punches installed and wedged in, stop guides set for stock length, and synchronizing cams timed so gripper, header and transfer motions coincide.

Die change on a forging trim press, coining press or smaller forming press equipped with quick-die-change hardware (subplates, die lifters, hydraulic clamps, die cart): outgoing die rolled out, staged die rolled in, clamped, located, shut height set.

Mid-run machine adjustment on a press setup: correcting slide/shut-height, stroke position, stop-guide position and cam/transfer timing from the press control after first-piece inspection or drift in forging dimensions.

Mid-run physical tooling fixes on the machine: re-torquing keys, wedges or clamp bolts after break-in, adding or removing shims under a die, swapping a cracked insert or worn stop guide with hand tools, cleaning scale from die seats.

tasks.label: Select, align, and bolt positioning fixtures, stops, and specified dies to rams and anvils, forging rolls, or presses and hammers.

instances.label: Closed-die (impression-die) hot forging press in a captive or job forge shop: setter selects the specified die set from the die storage area, cranes the several-hundred- to several-thousand-pound die blocks/holders onto bolster and ram, aligns them with keys and locating pins, bolts or wedge-clamps them, shims and sets shut height, and proves match with a first-piece forging. Hot, scaly, oily press bay.

Forging hammer (board, air, or counterblow) die setting: dovetailed upper and lower die blocks slid into ram and sow block, tapered keys driven home with a sledge, dies matched and packed/shimmed until impressions register, then re-tightened after a few blows. Heavy manual craft work at the hammer.

Trim/clip press or restrike press setup: mount trim die and punch, install positioning fixtures, gauges and stops so the hot forging seats correctly, bolt or hydraulically clamp, and adjust stops after trial parts. Lighter tooling than the forge press, alongside the forging line.

Upsetter (horizontal forging machine), forging roll, or ring-rolling mill tooling: gripper die halves, heading tool holders, or roll die segments selected and bolted to the rolls/rams and anvils, aligned to the pass line, and gap/stop settings dialed in.

Smaller press with standardized quick-change die sets/subplates (cold heading blanks, warm-formed or plastic-forming presses, secondary sizing presses): die set rolled in on lifters or a cart, located on pins, clamped, and stops set for a short high-mix run.

Open-die/hydraulic forging press: flat, V, or swage dies and die tracks changed on ram and anvil between jobs, using in-plant die handling equipment, then verified for parallelism before the next heat.

tasks.label: Repair, maintain, and replace parts on dies.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Die-room reclamation of a worn or heat-checked hot-forging die block: gouge/mill out cracked and worn impression areas, preheat, build the impression back up with specialty weld alloys layer by layer, then machine/grind the deposit back to print and inspect. Die blocks of hundreds of pounds to several tons, moved by crane to a welding bench or positioner.

Finish work on a repaired or reworked die: blending and grinding weld build-up to the impression contour, deburring flash lands and edges, polishing working surfaces, and checking the restored geometry against templates, CMM or 3D scan data in the tool room.

Routine die maintenance while the die is mounted in a running press or hammer: air-blasting scale and debris out of the cavities each cycle, applying graphite/water die lubricant, keeping impressions clear so parts release, watching for pickup and sticking. Hot, scale-laden press area.

Replacing worn or broken quick-change tooling components in the forming machine — punch and die cassettes, holder-mounted inserts, knockout pins in cassettes — by unclamping, withdrawing the worn unit, loading the replacement, clamping and confirming seating/alignment before restarting.

Replacing press-fit, keyed or bolted die components on the die assembly at the bench: driving out seized inserts, ejector pins and wear plates (sometimes with heat, gouging or a hydraulic press), cleaning bores, hand-fitting and shimming the new part, torquing keepers, and blue-checking fit.

Unplanned in-place repair and troubleshooting at the press: dressing a chipped, galled or built-up die edge with a hand grinder in the press, freeing a stuck forging, re-tightening loosened wedges, keys and clamps, laying a temporary weld patch on a hot die, all in tight access around a production line.

tasks.label: Monitor machine cycles and mill operation to detect jamming and to ensure that products conform to specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Hot or cold strip rolling mill at an integrated or mini-mill: operator works from the pulpit and walks the line, watching stands, loopers and coilers for cobbles and strip jams, tracking gauge/width/flatness and surface-inspection readouts, and pulling and gauging coil samples to confirm the strip meets order specification.

Roll forming or tube/pipe mill line in a metal products plant: tender watches entry uncoiler, forming stands, welder and cutoff for misfeeds, scrap wrap-ups and jams, and checks each bundle of profiles with go/no-go gauges, tape and calipers for length, diameter, straightness and bow.

Plate or section bending rolls in a fabrication or job shop: short runs of varied parts, operator watches the plate for slipping, skewing or binding in the rolls, and checks curvature each pass against a radius template or gauge until the rolled shape is accepted.

Plastic sheet/film extrusion-and-roll or calender line: operator monitors nip rolls, chill rolls and winder for wraps, web breaks and jams, watches thickness scanner and takes handheld micrometer readings across the web, and inspects for gels, streaks and edge defects.

Thread rolling, knurling, ring rolling or slip-roll machine tending in a machine shop: short cycles with semi-automatic feeding, operator listens and watches for parts jamming in the feeder or dies, and periodically gauges parts with micrometers, thread ring gauges or fixtures.

Coil processing line (temper mill, leveler, slitter) at a mill or service center: operator monitors payoff, looping pit, rolls and recoiler for jams, cobbles and telescoping, and verifies gauge, width, flatness and surface of the running strip against the order.

tasks.label: Adjust and correct machine set-ups to reduce thicknesses, reshape products, and eliminate product defects.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Hot/cold strip or plate rolling mill: operator watches gauge, profile and flatness readouts and corrects the mill set-up mid-schedule — roll gap/screwdown, tilt, roll bending and shifting, interstand tension, speed and coolant sprays — to hold thickness tolerance and eliminate crown, edge wave, centre buckle and wedge. Work occurs in a steel/aluminium plant on a guarded mill line with an operator pulpit.

Roll-forming or tube mill on a modern automatic-setup line: changing over to a new profile/gauge and correcting dimensional deviations (width, gauge, hole and length position, end flare) by repositioning servo-adjusted stands from a stored recipe and re-running test parts to measurement. Fabrication plant floor, coil-fed line.

Roll-forming or tube mill on a conventional line: operator diagnoses a geometry defect in the run-out part (bow, camber, twist, scoring/scratch marks, seam roll marks) and corrects it by shimming or repositioning individual roll stands and Turk's-head/straightener rolls with hand tools, checking each iteration against templates and gauges. Fabrication plant floor.

Plastic sheet/film extrusion or calender line: adjusting die-lip bolts, nip/roll-stack gaps, roll temperatures and take-off speed to bring cross-web thickness profile into tolerance, reduce gauge, and eliminate gauge bands, lines and thickness defects. Indoor extrusion hall with scanning gauge.

Job-shop three/four-roll plate or angle bending machine: adjusting side/pinch roll positions between passes to hit the specified radius against springback, correcting flat spots, barrelling and out-of-round on short-run or one-off parts. Metal fabrication shop floor, crane-fed plate.

Precision roller leveler, temper/skin-pass mill, or cut-to-length/slitting line: adjusting leveler roll penetration, backup flight positions, tension and elongation to remove coil set, crossbow, edge wave and centre buckle and to hold gauge on the outgoing sheet. Coil-processing plant floor.

tasks.label: Start operation of rolling and milling machines to flatten, temper, form, and reduce sheet metal sections and to produce steel strips.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Integrated steel plant hot strip or plate mill: operator in the pulpit starts the mill line for a slab sequence — engages roughing/finishing stand drives, initiates the rolling pass schedule, watches thread-up onto the down coiler, ramps line speed. Tandem, reversing, or temper mill in a cold-rolling / strip-processing plant or service center: coil set on the payoff reel, strip head threaded through the stand(s) and tension reel, mill started at threading speed with gauge/flatness control engaged, then accelerated to rolling speed to reduce gauge or temper the strip.

Roll-forming or ERW tube mill line in a fabrication / building-products plant: coil loaded on the decoiler, strip end fed into the first forming stands, line started to form bends and beads into a profile, run continuously with cut-off, with occasional stop/restart for coil changes.

Job shop / fab shop plate and sheet rolling: operator moves varied plate or sheet (crane or by hand) into a 3- or 4-roll plate bender, slip roll, or angle roll on an open shop floor, sets the rolls, starts the machine with pedal or CNC start, rolls a cylinder or cone, checks radius against a template, and adjusts — mostly one-offs and small batches.

Specialty narrow-strip / foil mill or plastic calendering-laminating roll stack in a dedicated plant: material threaded through the roll stack, machine started at controlled speed and temperature to reduce gauge or produce sheet/film, run under closed-loop thickness control.

tasks.label: Examine, inspect, and measure raw materials and finished products to verify conformance to specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-process dimensional check during a rolling/forming run: operator pulls a just-rolled part or strip sample off the machine, measures thickness, width, bend radius or diameter with micrometer, caliper or go/no-go gauge against the job spec, and decides whether to adjust rolls. Occurs on an open shop floor next to the running machine; parts often oily, warm and burred.

Continuous verification of strip/sheet gauge, width and flatness while a mill or calender runs: watching inline thickness/width readouts and trend charts, taking confirming hand measurements at coil head and tail, flagging out-of-tolerance material. Mill pulpit and mill line in a steel or plastics plant.

Incoming raw material verification before a run: inspecting coils, plate, bar or plastic sheet for scale, scratches, edge damage, camber or wrong gauge; checking thickness/width; matching heat number, grade and ID tag/label to the order and mill certificate. At storage racks, coil yard or uncoiler.

Final inspection of large finished rolled products: rolled cylinders, cones, plate, tubes and structural sections checked for diameter, roundness, straightness and fit to a radius template or contour gauge; parts heavy and awkward, moved by crane or forklift, checked on the floor or on stands.

First-article and batch QC of small formed/rolled parts at a bench or QC station: gauging several dimensions per part with calipers, micrometers, thread/profile gauges or a shop-floor CMM, comparing to the print, and recording results on inspection sheets or into SPC software.

sources.claim: The same robotic measurement cell runs unattended, performing inspections overnight after operators load pallets and leave, i.e. autonomous operation rather than step-by-step human control.

instances.label: Work-roll / roll-set change on a large mill stand in an integrated steel, stainless or aluminium rolling plant (hot strip, cold mill, plate, skin-pass): uncouple spindles, pull the chocked roll set with the roll-change car or crane, insert the new set, secure keeper plates and bolts, re-set the mill. Heavy (hundreds of kg to tonnes) rolls, hot/oily mill-floor conditions, done on a scheduled changeover window.

Product / size changeover of tooling on a smaller mill or forming line — tube-and-pipe mill roll cassettes, roll-forming line rolls and spacers, plate/section bending rolls, or a plastics calender/embossing roll stack: lift the roll or cassette onto the shaft or arbor, torque retaining nuts and keys with wrenches and impact tools, set roll gaps. Job shop or line-side, crane or hoist assist.

Install and align guides: entry/exit roller guides and guide boxes on a bar/rod stand, strip edge guides, troughs, side guides and feed guides — bolt the holder to the stand or bracket, shim it, and set it to the pass with a gauge or feeler, verifying alignment to the roll groove.

Install or refit guards, covers, splash shields, scale/chip shields and interlocked panels on the machine with hand tools after maintenance or a changeover: lift the panel or bracket into place on the frame, start and torque bolts, often in awkward, tight in-situ positions.

Install cooling and lubrication equipment: coolant spray headers and nozzle bars, air wipes, hoses, quick couplings and fittings — mount the header with brackets and bolts, connect and route lines, then check for leaks and correct spray pattern.

Install gears, drive components and couplings on the machine's drive train — pinion/change gears, spindle carriers, gear couplings, sprockets and chains, bearings — fitting them on shafts, aligning, and securing with keys, nuts and set screws.

instances.label: Coil change on a steel coil processing line (slitting, cut-to-length or rollforming line) at a service center or mill: retrieve the next 2–25 t master coil from staging with an overhead crane or coil car, set it on the uncoiler/payoff mandrel, center it on the pass line, expand the mandrel/clamp it, and secure the outer wrap before threading. Happens every coil.

Slitter tooling setup: to a slit plan, build knife / spacer / stripper-ring stacks on the two slitter arbors (spacers in 0.02 mm increments), set horizontal clearance and vertical overlap, torque the arbor nuts, install the arbors or slitter head into the stand, and set the separator/tension shafts.

Roll change on a hot, cold, temper or 20Hi mill stand: withdraw worn work/intermediate rolls with their chocks, position and secure the new rolls in the housing, couple drive spindles, and set roll gap and alignment before restart.

Rollformer or ERW tube-mill changeover in a fabrication shop: pull roll sets or cassettes off cantilevered shafts/spindles with a hoist, key and stack the new forming rolls with shims and spacers, align stands, and position breakdown/fin pass mandrels.
Die setup on a bending/forming machine (press-brake-type die segments, plate-roll or bender dies): select tooling to a setup sheet, position and align it in the machine, and clamp it.

Plastic film, foil or laminate slitter-rewinder setup in a converting plant: position each razor or score knifeholder on the knife beam/spindle to the ordered slit widths, lock them, and set blade penetration/overlap against the anvil.

instances.label: Lube round on a hot/cold rolling mill or roll-forming line in a steel plant: operator walks the machine at shift start, opens and fills oil cups and small reservoirs, tops up gearbox/bearing oilers, and hits grease points, working around guards, hot surfaces, scale and oil-slick floors.

Setting and adjusting coolant/lubricant flow at a mill stand: opening/closing header and nozzle valves, setting emulsion or roll-coolant flow rates for the pass and material, aiming or throttling spray headers across roll width during setup and while the mill runs.

Production round during rolling: watching pressure, flow and level gauges/sight glasses for the coolant and lube systems, and correcting a deviation on the spot (throttle a valve, clear or swap a plugged nozzle, restore flow to a starved zone).

Small job shop / light fabrication: operator oiling workpieces and rolls by hand between parts on a plate roll, tube bender, roll former or knurling setup — oil can, brush or spray bottle, varying part sizes, materials and batch sizes on a shared shop floor.
Coolant/lubricant supply service: checking emulsion or coolant tank level and concentration, topping up with water/concentrate, adjusting mixing valves to bring the mix back to spec for the job.

Documented monitoring-only round: reading and logging coolant pressure, flow and lube-system gauges on a checksheet or into the shift log and flagging out-of-range readings to the control room/maintenance, with no physical correction required.

tasks.label: Activate shears and grinders to trim workpieces.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Hot/cold rolling line (bar, rod, strip): operator at the mill pulpit/HMI activates the in-line crop or flying shear to trim head and tail ends of the rolled product as it travels on roller tables, adjusting crop length for cobbles or off-gauge ends; scrap goes to a chute.

Coil/plate finishing line at a mill finishing end or steel service center: operator threads the coil and activates side trimmers/rotary slitters and the cut-to-length or dividing shear to trim edges and crop plate/sheet to size, with automatic stacking of the trimmed product.

Roll-forming / tube-and-pipe mill line: operator activates the flying cutoff shear to sever formed sections to length and an in-line grinder/deburrer to knock down the burr and trim scrap ends on continuously running stock.

Job-shop / fabrication floor: after plate rolling, bead rolling or knurling, the operator carries the workpiece to a squaring shear to trim excess and to a pedestal belt/wheel grinder (or hand angle grinder) to remove burrs, tabs and sharp edges; part mix changes several times a shift, parts up to ~50 lb.

Large/heavy rolled work (large shells, heavy plate, rolled rings, thousands of pounds) moved by crane or manipulator; operator trims excess with a heavy shear or hand-held/pedestal grinder, dressing seams and edges on parts with part-to-part dimensional variation.
Plastics work: operator trims flash and edge scrap from rolled/calendered plastic sheet and formed plastic parts at a bench, using shears, trim knives and a grinder/sander to bring edges to spec.

instances.label: Steel mill / metal service center: operator hand-signals an overhead crane or forklift driver to bring a coil, plate bundle, or tooling to the rolling machine, then guides, steadies and lands the load on the uncoiler mandrel, saddle, or machine table; loads up to 20-30 tons, hot or oily stock, shared aisles.

Roll or tooling changeover: helper works with a setup operator or millwright to unbolt and sling worn work/backup rolls or forming dies out of the mill stand, position and align the replacements, shim and torque fasteners; heavy (100 lb to 1 ton) tooling, tight stand clearances.

Plastics rolling/calendering or extrusion-fed line: worker fills machine hoppers with resin — cutting and dumping 50 lb bags, tipping gaylords/octabins, adding regrind and colorant, hooking up vacuum loader lines, climbing a mezzanine or platform to the hopper.

Feeding stock into the machine at the infeed with a coworker: two people lift and guide a sheet, plate, strip, or blank squarely into the pinch rolls or feed table of a plate roll, slip roll, roll former, or flattener, keeping it aligned, and catching/stacking the formed part at the exit.

Miscellaneous helper work around the mill: repositioning auxiliary equipment (entry guides, run-out stands, carts, guards, conveyors), assisting a millwright by holding or steadying parts while adjustments are made, moving scrap and dunnage, working in cramped or awkward spots beside a running line.

instances.label: Rolling mill lead operator verbally directs a two- or three-person crew during a scheduled roll change on a cold rolling mill: assigning who removes the old work rolls, who stages the new set, calling out sequence and timing, and confirming lockout/tagout steps before the crew acts.

Experienced operator trains a new hire on mill operation over a shift: explaining the pulpit controls, gauge and tension setpoints, what the readouts mean, and coaching the trainee through their first passes by watching and giving corrective instruction rather than doing the work.

Operator instructs crew members on clearing a cobble (tangled/misrouted strip) after a mill wreck: explaining the safe sequence for de-energizing, cutting and pulling scrap, warning about spring tension and sharp edges, and directing torch/crane use by the crew.

Operator directs coil handling downstream: telling the crane or coil-car operator where to set coils, instructing banders on strap count and placement, and directing loaders on stacking and securing coils on trucks or rail cars per the shipping list.

Toolbox talk / shift-turnover briefing: the senior operator reviews the day's schedule, quality holds, near-misses and standard work instructions with the crew, and signs off training records or job-safety checklists for workers newly qualified on a task.

tasks.label: Thread or feed sheets or rods through rolling mechanisms, or start and control mechanisms that automatically feed steel into rollers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Integrated or mini-mill hot rolling line (slab/bloom/billet to strip, bar or section): from a pulpit the operator starts and controls the automatic feed — reheat-furnace discharge, roller tables, motorized entry guides, pinch rolls and loopers — that threads the hot stock through successive roll stands, watching for cobbles and mis-threads. Mill floor is fenced/interlocked during rolling.

Cold mill, temper mill or coil processing line (service-center slitter, cut-to-length, pickling/tandem line): coil car loads the coil to the uncoiler, straps are cut, the head end is peeled/straightened and threaded through pinch rolls, straightener, mill stands and onto the coiler; operator then runs the line at speed.

Job-shop / fabrication-shop plate or sheet roll bending: operator (often with a crane or by hand) loads a varying plate or sheet onto a 3- or 4-roll bender or slip roll, feeds it between the rolls, pre-bends the edge, rolls to radius, checks with a template or radius gauge and removes the shell.

Feeding bars, rods, tube or strip into rod/thread-rolling machines, roll formers, tube mills or straightener rolls: loading a bundle or coil, setting the hopper/bar feeder or servo feed, starting the automatic feed and hand-feeding short runs or first pieces in a production machine shop.

Plastics: threading plastic sheet or film web through a calender/polishing roll stack or laminating nip rolls at line start-up, then starting and controlling the automatic feed (haul-off, nips, winder) for the run in an extrusion or calendering plant.

tasks.label: Remove scratches and polish roll surfaces, using polishing stones and electric buffers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Hot/cold strip or plate mill: operator dresses minor pickup, nicks and scratches on work rolls while the rolls are still in the mill stand during a short stop or roll change - hand polishing stone, emery and a portable electric buffer, in a hot, oily, cramped stand with hoses, guards and crew nearby, under pressure to resume rolling.

Plant roll shop / roll-change bay: rolls pulled from the mill are mounted between centers on a roll grinder or lathe; after grinding the operator stones out remaining scratches and polishes the barrel with abrasive belt/buffer, checking the surface before the roll goes back into roll stock.

Job shop or fabrication shop with plate-bending rolls, roll formers or tube-mill rolls: operator polishes scratches, weld spatter marks and rust off the forming rolls, either in the machine (jogging the rolls) or by pulling small rolls to a bench/lathe, so the rolls stop marking the product.

Plastics processing (calender, laminator, embosser, cast-film stack): chrome-plated rolls are scuffed or scratched and transfer marks to the sheet/film; operator removes the defect with fine stones/compound and an electric buffer, usually with the roll still in the stack during a changeover, aiming for a mark-free gloss surface.

Precision return-to-service finishing: a localized scratch, dent or heat check must be blended into the roll body and the whole barrel polished to a specified finish (fine Ra / mirror), with visual and surface-roughness inspection before the roll is released, in the roll shop finishing bay.

tasks.label: Disassemble sizing mills removed from rolling lines, and sort and store parts.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Steel long-product or tube sizing-mill stand pulled from the line is craned into the mill's stand/roll shop, set on stands or a fixture, and torn down: guards and housing covers unbolted with impact and hydraulic wrenches, spindles and couplings pulled, roll shafts pressed out, bearings, sleeves, seals and spacers removed; parts are washed, inspected, then racked, binned and logged.

Roll/chock stripping cycle in the roll shop: roll assemblies from the sizing mill are placed on dechocking equipment, retaining rings and bearing housings pulled off the necks, rolls routed to grinding, chocks to the washer, and rolls and spare chocks returned to storage racks with location and inventory records updated.

Small cassette or cantilever sizing head torn down at a bench with hand and power tools: dozens of small parts (roll rings, keys, spacers, shims, seals, guide pieces, fasteners) removed, cleaned, matched into sets and sorted into labeled trays, bins and shelves by pass and size.

Teardown of a seized, worn or heat-damaged unit: rusted or galled fasteners, interference-fit bearings and scored shafts requiring heat, torch, jacks and improvised pullers; worker judges reusable versus scrap parts, segregates scrap and tags damaged components for repair.

Partial disassembly performed on the mill floor beside the running line: cramped access, hot, oily and noisy, other trades present; guides, guards, water headers, couplings and spindles stripped off the removed mill before it is carted to the shop, with removed parts staged on pallets and carted to storage.

Plastic extrusion sizing/calibration unit teardown in the plant tool room: calibrator sleeves, sizing plates, vacuum-tank tooling and mounting hardware unbolted, cleaned of melt and water scale, sorted by product size and stored on labeled tooling racks.

tasks.label: Measure completed workpieces to verify conformance to specifications, using micrometers, gauges, calipers, templates, or rulers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume stamping/punch press or plastic press line: operator pulls a sample part every N pieces to a bench beside the press, checks 2-5 critical dimensions with digital calipers, a micrometer and go/no-go pin gauges, logs values into an SPC terminal, and adjusts or flags the run. Small metal or plastic parts, oily, warm, produced continuously.

First-piece/setup verification in a high-mix fab shop after setting up a shear, cold saw, turret punch or press brake: operator measures overall length/width, hole locations, and bend angle of the first part against the drawing using a tape measure, calipers, square and angle gauge, before the job is released. New part number several times per shift.

Large or long workpieces (sheared plate, cut structural sections, long extrusions/tube) checked for length, squareness, straightness and flatness with tape, straightedge and square; parts are heavy, handled with a hoist or cart, and measured on a table or the floor beside the machine.

Formed/notched/punched sheet parts checked against a template, profile gauge or check fixture (hole pattern, flange profile, bend angle) in a fabrication shop; pass/fail plus a few dimensional readings recorded on a router or inspection sheet.

Tight-tolerance small precision parts (stamped contacts, machined/punched inserts, precision plastic parts) measured to a few thousandths with micrometers, bore gauges or an optical comparator, often 100% or high-rate sampling, results recorded to a quality system.

tasks.label: Examine completed workpieces for defects, such as chipped edges or marred surfaces and sort defective pieces according to types of flaws.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume progressive-die stamping/punching press: operator pulls parts periodically from the die exit chute or catch bin, examines them for burrs, chipped edges, cracks and marred/scratched surfaces, keeps good parts in the tote and drops rejects into segregated bins (die-mark, burr, dent) on the plant floor next to the press.

Bench sort of a suspect lot: a tub of a few thousand small stamped/punched metal parts is 100%-inspected at an inspection table under a lamp; the operator picks each piece, turns it in the light, and sorts into good, rework and scrap bins according to flaw type.

Plastic parts (die-cut, punched, trimmed sheet or molded blanks): operator checks a running batch for chipped/ragged edges, flash, scuffs and scratches, and separates defective pieces by flaw category for rework or regrind.

Large workpieces: sheared blanks, laser/plasma-cut plates or big stamped panels; operator inspects each piece for edge chips/burrs, dents and scuffed surfaces, then stacks accepted parts and moves defective sheets/panels to a rework rack or scrap skid.

Short-run / high-mix job-shop work: a batch of a dozen or fewer custom parts of a geometry never run before, inspected against the print and a customer cosmetic standard, defects judged and pieces tagged and separated as rework vs. scrap.

tasks.label: Start machines, monitor their operations, and record operational data.

instances.label: High-mix job shop / sheet metal fabricator: operator starts a CNC turret punch, fiber laser, shear or press brake for a short-run job, watches the first pieces and subsequent cycles for misfeeds, tool wear, jams and alarms, and records piece counts, run/downtime and cause codes on a paper traveler or shop-floor terminal; several different jobs per shift.

High-volume coil-fed stamping pressroom: operator starts the press and feed line at shift start after safety checks, monitors ram, feed, part flow and sound for slug jams, misfeeds and tonnage drift, clears faults, and records stroke counts, scrap and downtime in an MES or on a production log.

Plastics cutting/forming: operator starts a cutoff saw, die-cutting press or trim press on an extrusion/thermoforming line, monitors temperatures, feed speeds, blade/die condition and part flow, and logs process parameters, counts and SPC readings on log sheets each hour.

Tending several machines at once in a larger plant: operator starts and oversees 3-6 saws, shears or small presses spread over an area, walks rounds listening and looking for trouble, tops off stock, restarts after stops, and records hourly production and downtime data for each machine.

Older/manual equipment in a small shop: mechanical punch press, ironworker or foot-pedal shear with no digital controls; operator initiates each cycle with pedal or palm buttons, monitors piece by piece for slug pull, hangups and part quality, and tallies counts by hand on a sheet.
