instances.label: High-volume metal stamping/punch press tending in a production plant: feed coil or hand-load blanks into the press, cycle it, remove and stack formed parts, watch for misfeeds, slugs and burrs, clear jams, keep the die lubricated and the run on schedule.

Press brake bending in a sheet metal fab/job shop: pick a laser-cut blank from a cart, position it against the backgauge, cycle the brake while following the flange up, check the bend angle and flange length, and stack the finished part; small-to-medium batches of varied part geometries.

Cutting stock to length on a horizontal band saw, cold saw or shear: load bar, tube, plate or plastic pipe/sheet onto the feed table, set length stop, cut, deburr/clean chips, sort good parts from trim and remnants, and stack on pallets.

Running a CNC turret punch, punch-laser or laser/plasma cutting machine: load raw sheet, run the nest program, break out parts from the skeleton, remove slugs, sort and stack cut parts, dispose of skeleton and restock material.

Setup and changeover plus first-piece qualification: install and align dies/punches or press brake tooling, set gauges, stops and stroke, run the first article, measure it with calipers/gauges/angle protractor, adjust offsets, and release the job for production.

tasks.label: Test and adjust machine speeds or actions, according to product specifications, using gauges and hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Fab-shop CNC cutting machine (laser, plasma, waterjet, or turret punch): operator runs a test cut/first article, checks part dimensions, hole sizes, kerf and edge/burr quality with calipers and gauges, then adjusts cutting speed/feed rate, gas pressure, focus and kerf offsets at the control, re-cuts and re-measures until the part meets print.

Press brake / bending press: operator makes a test bend, checks the angle with an angle gauge or protractor and flange dimensions with a caliper/tape, then adjusts ram depth, bend speed, crowning and backgauge offsets to correct springback and material variation before releasing the job.

High-volume stamping or punch press with modern controls: after die installation, single-stroke test parts are pulled and measured with calipers/gauges, and shut height, stroke speed (SPM), feed length and timing, and cushion/stripper pressures are adjusted at the press control until parts are in tolerance and the press runs at rated speed.

Shear, coil slitter, or cut-to-length line: operator sets blade clearance/gap and rake angle for the material, runs a test cut, checks burr, camber, width/length with feeler gauges, calipers and tape, and readjusts knife clearance, gap and line speed.

Sawing / cutoff work (horizontal bandsaw, cold saw, plastic profile or pipe saw): operator sets and then tunes blade speed and downfeed/feed rate for the material and blade condition, checks cut length and squareness with gauges, and readjusts speed and feed as the blade wears or material changes.

Small job shop with older or general-purpose machinery (manual punch presses, ironworkers, notchers, older hydraulic presses, plastic cutters): trial-and-error adjustment of stroke, stops, speed and clearances by feel, using wrenches, shims, hand-set regulators and mechanical stops, on varied one-off jobs with no machine-side sensing.

tasks.label: Load workpieces, plastic material, or chemical solutions into machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Fabrication shop: operator destacks sheet-metal blanks from a pallet/skid and loads them into a turret punch press, shear, or press brake, squaring each blank against gauges/backgauge before the cycle.

Repetitive machine tending: operator loads small-to-medium metal workpieces (brackets, blanks, tube ends, crimp parts) into a fixture/nest on a cutting, punching, notching or crimping machine, cycle after cycle across a shift.

Heavy/long stock handling: loading bar, tube, structural or plate stock (and coils on slitters) into cold saws, band saws, shears or slitting lines, often with crane/hoist assistance because of weight and length.
Plastic stock: loading plastic/composite sheet, panel or extruded stock into a cutting, routing, die-cutting or punching machine and locating it on the bed or fixture.
Bulk plastic material: loading resin pellets/regrind from sacks or gaylords into hoppers/feeders that supply a forming or cutting machine.
Chemical solutions: filling machine reservoirs and tanks with coolant/cutting fluid, lubricant, quench or etch solution, mixing to concentration and topping up as levels drop.

tasks.label: Turn controls to set cutting speeds, feed rates, or table angles for specified operations.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Job/fab shop, CNC cutting machine (fiber laser, plasma, waterjet, turret punch). Before running a nest, the operator works at the machine's HMI/control to set or confirm cutting speed, feed rate, power/amperage and gas settings for the specified material grade and thickness, then starts the cycle.

Saw bay of a metal shop or service center. On a horizontal bandsaw or cold saw the operator sets blade speed and downfeed rate/cutting pressure for the alloy and cross-section, and swivels the saw head/table to a specified miter angle (e.g., 45 deg) before cutting stock to length.

Older, manually adjusted equipment on a shop floor: mechanical/hydraulic punch press, ironworker, shear or press brake. Operator turns hand dials, hydraulic flow valves, or changes belt/pulley positions to set stroke rate, ram speed and stock-feed rate, and loosens/tilts a table or head by hand to a marked angle.

Plastics processing plant: extrusion cut-off saw, tube cutter, slitter or trim station. Operator sets line/haul-off speed, cutter or blade speed, and feed/cut-length rates at the line HMI for the specified product size, then trims them as output rate changes.

In-process correction on any of the above: after first cuts/parts the operator inspects burr, dross, blade drift, chatter or length drift and re-adjusts cutting speed and feed rate mid-run as material grade, cross-section or tool wear vary.

tasks.label: Clean work area.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: End-of-shift floor cleanup immediately around a press, shear, or saw in a metal fab shop: sweeping steel slugs, chips, punch-outs, dust and small offcuts from around machine legs, foot pedals, pallets and skids into a dustpan or scrap pan; floor often has a thin film of oil or coolant and is cluttered with carts, stock and cords.
Periodic sweeping/scrubbing of the open floor and aisles of the department (larger clear spans between machines and along traffic lanes) to remove dust, fine debris and oil residue.

Cleaning the machine itself: blowing/brushing chips, slugs and slitter dust off the bed, die, bolster, table, ram and guard area; clearing scrap from chutes and chip pans; wiping down surfaces, guarding and the control panel.

Clearing scrap between jobs: gathering offcuts, skeletons and slugs into scrap bins/hoppers, emptying chip pans and small totes, and hauling full bins or containers to the scrap/recycling area, returning empties.

Wiping up coolant/oil spills and leaks with absorbent granules or rags, degreasing a work bench, returning hand tools, gauges and small dies to their storage locations, and disposing of used rags and consumables in the proper containers.

tasks.label: Lubricate workpieces with oil.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Hand-fed or blank-fed punch/stamping press in a pressroom: operator applies stamping oil to flat sheet-metal blanks (or to the die face) before each forming or punching stroke, using a spray bottle, brush, roller or oiled pad. Standard rectangular blanks, repetitive cycle, ordinary shop conditions.

Coil-fed progressive-die press line: lubricant must be put on the strip stock before it enters the die; the operator oils the strip, sets and tops up the stock oiler, and checks film coverage as the coil runs continuously at press speed.

Sawing, cutoff or shearing machine (horizontal band saw, circular cold saw, ironworker): operator applies cutting oil to the workpiece and blade at the cut, by squirt can, brush or by running the machine's fluid delivery, on bar, tube and plate clamped in the machine vise.

Job shop / low-volume work: operator brushes, swabs or wipes oil onto varied, irregular, sometimes heavy or awkward workpieces staged on benches, carts or pallets beside the machine before punching, notching or bending. Part shapes, oil coverage and staging locations change job to job.
Deep-draw or heavy forming press: operator applies viscous drawing compound to blanks and/or die surfaces before drawing, needing heavy, targeted coverage on the areas that stretch most.
Post-cut rust-preventative oiling: operator wipes, sprays or dips finished cut/punched parts in preservative oil before racking, storage or shipment.

tasks.label: Install, align, and lock specified punches, dies, cutting blades, or other fixtures in rams or beds of machines, using gauges, templates, feelers, shims, and hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Sheet-metal job shop, CNC press brake changeover: operator pulls the punch and die segments called for by the job from the tool rack, loads them into the ram clamps and bed rails, seats and squares the segments, locks the clamps, sets stage positions and verifies the setup on a test bend.

Stamping plant, mechanical/hydraulic press: die setter installs a single-station or progressive die (several hundred pounds to several tons) — rolls or hoists it onto the bolster, locates it against keys/locators, clamps upper half to the ram and lower to the bed, sets shut height and parallelism, checks with feelers/shims, runs a tryout hit.

CNC turret punch press setup: loading punches, dies and strippers into turret stations, matching die clearance to material thickness, keying angular orientation of shaped tools, setting stripper height, checking first-hit quality.

Guillotine/plate shear blade replacement: unbolting and lifting out worn upper and lower blade sections from ram and bed, installing new/rotated blades, shimming, setting blade clearance with feeler gauges along the length, torquing blade bolts, test cut.

Cut-off saw area: changing a bimetal band saw blade or a carbide-tipped circular cold-saw blade — removing the worn blade, mounting the new one on wheels/spindle flange, tracking and tensioning, resetting guides/guards, test cut for squareness.

Coil slitting line / rotary shear tooling build: assembling circular knives, spacers, shims and rubber strippers on the arbors to a slit schedule, setting horizontal knife clearance and vertical overlap, locking the heads, threading and test slit.

tasks.label: Adjust ram strokes of presses to specified lengths, using hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Metal stamping shop, die change on a mechanical gap-frame or straight-side press: setter brings the slide to bottom dead center, loosens the ram-adjustment locknut and turns the connection/adjusting screw with a wrench (or jogs a motorized adjust) until shut height matches the die's specified height, verifies against the die-height indicator or set blocks, then re-locks and test-strokes.

High-volume automotive/appliance stamping plant with modern servo or CNC-controlled mechanical presses and transfer press lines: stroke length, slide position and die height are set to the job's stored specification for the die being run, verified against the linear scale/indicator readout, and confirmed by a test stroke before the line runs.

Hydraulic press or press brake setup: stroke length is limited by repositioning adjustable retract/down-stop limit-switch dogs, stop rods or trip collars on the ram with hand tools (or by entering stroke limits at the control), followed by slow test strokes to confirm the ram travels only the specified distance.

Small job shop with older bench/OBI punch presses and arbor presses that have no powered slide adjust: the operator cranks or wrenches the adjusting screw against a locknut, measures the stroke/shut height with a scale, set blocks or feeler stock, and repeats trial strokes on a worn machine until the specified length is reached.

Mid-run corrective adjustment during production: after checking sample parts (burr height, punch penetration, formed depth or flatness), the operator makes a small ram/shut-height correction with hand tools, re-locks the adjustment, and re-runs parts to confirm the specification is met.

tasks.label: Position, align, and secure workpieces against fixtures or stops on machine beds or on dies.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Press brake bending in a job shop: operator takes flat sheet-metal blanks off a cart or skid, slides each against the backgauge stops/fingers, holds and supports it during each bend, repositions for the next hit; batches of tens to hundreds, part sizes and gauges vary through the day.

Punch/stamping press work: operator places a small-to-medium blank onto locating pins or a nest in the die (or against stops on the bolster), seats it, holds/secures it and trips the cycle with two-hand controls, repeating at high cadence for a production run.

Cut-off saw or shear: operator feeds bar, tube, angle or plate against a length stop or fence, squares it, clamps it in the vise or under hold-downs, and cuts; stock is often long, oily, heavy, and hand-loaded from a rack.

Flat-bed cutting machine (laser, plasma, waterjet, CNC punch): a full sheet or heavy plate is lifted onto the machine table with a hoist or vacuum lifter, squared against locating pins/corner stops, and secured with clamps, magnets or vacuum before the program is run.

Setup / first-piece work: setter installs the die or fixture, positions and aligns a trial workpiece against stops and gauges, checks it with scale, square or indicator, shims and readjusts the stops, re-clamps and re-runs until the dimensions are in tolerance, then releases the job to production.

instances.label: High-mix job/fab shop press brake: operator stages punch and die segments for a staged multi-bend layout, sets the back-gauge stops for each successive bend, and adjusts ram depth/crowning between passes. Tooling is standard segmented press-brake tooling kept at the machine.

Stamping plant, large mechanical or hydraulic power press: die setter removes a multi-ton die set with crane/bolster, brings the next die in, clamps it, sets shut height and counterbalance, adjusts ram and stops, and runs tryout hits before release to production.

Small/medium punch press, OBI press, ironworker or notcher in a job shop: operator swaps a punch-and-die set weighing tens to a few hundred pounds, sets stops/gauges on the machine bed, and adjusts ram stroke and shut height for successive punching or notching passes.

CNC turret punch or punch/laser combination machine in a fabrication shop: operator loads punch, die and stripper tooling into turret stations or a tool magazine, sets die clearance for the material gauge, and the machine indexes tooling for successive punching operations.

CNC guillotine shear or cut-to-length station in a fab shop: operator sets the back-gauge stop positions for a series of successive cut lengths and adjusts blade gap, rake angle and stroke for the material and thickness.

Coil slitting line at a steel/aluminum service center: setter builds the knife tooling arrangement (circular knives, spacers, stripper rings) on the arbors for a new slit pattern, sets spacing and knife clearance for successive passes.

tasks.label: Clean and lubricate machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: End-of-cycle / end-of-shift chip and scrap cleanup on a CNC saw, shear, punch press or machining center in a job shop or fab shop: blow or brush swarf, slugs and offcuts off the table, bed, fixtures/vise and work zone, squeegee coolant, empty chip pan or scrap bin. Repetitive, done many times per shift in a fixed spot at the machine.

Scheduled PM lubrication of the machine: shooting grease into zerk fittings on press slides, gibs, bushings and bearings with a grease gun; checking sight glasses and topping way-oil, hydraulic and air-line lubricator reservoirs; verifying the lube system pumps and lines are delivering oil. Points are scattered around and inside the machine frame, some in awkward positions.

Cleaning and lubricating the tooling on the machine between runs: wiping die faces, punches, dies and shear blades free of slugs, fines, plastic residue and burrs, and applying die lube / protective oil to the tooling before the next run.

Periodic deep-clean maintenance: draining and scrubbing the coolant sump/tank, cleaning or changing coolant and lube filters, clearing chip conveyor and pans, cleaning way covers and telescoping guards, flushing and refilling fluids per the maintenance schedule. Confined access, mixed tools, dirty fluids.

Wiping down the machine exterior and surroundings: cleaning oil and coolant film from guards, sheet-metal panels, control pendant, window/lexan shields, ladder rails, and mopping oil spills and swarf from the operator station area on an open shop floor with pallets, carts and stock nearby.

tasks.label: Position guides, stops, holding blocks, or other fixtures to secure and direct workpieces, using hand tools and measuring devices.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Press brake setup in a high-mix sheet metal fab shop: operator selects punch and die segments from a tool rack, seats and clamps them in the ram and bed at the programmed stations, sets/verifies backgauge fingers and side stops with a scale or tape, and test-bends a first piece.

Stamping/punch press die setup on a mechanical or hydraulic press: rigging and locating the die on the bolster to locating pins, clamping it with hand tools or clamps, setting stock guides, feed/pilot stops and passline, and gauging strip position before running the job.

Cutoff saw setup (band saw, cold saw, or plastic-extrusion saw) in a shop or service center: setting vise jaw position and pressure, placing V-blocks/work supports for round or odd stock, setting the length stop or shuttle feed, and checking the first cut length with tape or caliper.

Turret punch press or punch/laser combo setup: loading punch, die and forming tools into the turret/linear magazine at assigned stations, positioning sheet clamps and the locating squaring stops on the table for the blank size, and verifying part location on the first hit.

Shear/guillotine or plate-processing setup: positioning the powered back gauge to the cut dimension, setting front gauge stop arms and the squaring arm, adjusting hold-downs and blade gap for material thickness, and verifying with a tape measure on the first cut.

One-off or custom workholding: building or adapting a jig for an irregular, large or previously unseen fabricated part — clamping holding blocks and angle stops to a table or bed, shimming, occasionally tack-welding a stop, and dialing in position with an indicator, square and calipers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Fab/job shop: horizontal or vertical metal-cutting band saw has a dull or broken blade. Operator locks out the saw, releases blade tension, opens wheel covers, pulls the looped blade off the wheels, threads a new welded loop through the carbide guides and brush, re-tensions, tracks it and test-cuts.

Circular cold saw / carbide disc saw or slitting-saw blade on a cutoff or CNC sawing machine: operator unbolts the arbor nut and outer flange with hand tools, lifts off the worn disc blade, seats a sharp blade on the pin-drive flange, re-torques, and checks runout before restarting.

CNC turret punch press / press machine: a punch, die or shear-blade insert has gone dull or chipped. Operator removes the tool from the turret station or tool cartridge with hand tools, installs a reground/replacement tool from the tool rack, sets die clearance and verifies the first hit.

Coil slitting line or rotary shear at a steel/aluminum service center: worn circular slitter knives on the arbors are swapped out; operator strips knives, spacers and rubber strippers from the shaft, checks edges, rebuilds the tooling set to the cut program, and reloads the arbor.

Heavy bolted straight-blade change: guillotine/plate shear knife sections or plastics granulator/rotary-cutter knives. Dozens of socket bolts, blade segments weighing tens of pounds handled in confined space under the ram or in the cutting chamber, then blade gap/clearance shimmed and set with feeler gauges.

Abrasive cutoff wheel or grinding/deburring wheel on a cutoff saw or wheel head is worn or cracked: operator locks the spindle, removes the flange nut with a wrench, replaces the bonded wheel, re-torques the flange and ring-tests/spins it up per safety procedure.

Odd, high-mix items: nicked plastic-cutting knives, notching/crimping tooling, die-cutting rule, irregularly shaped cutters at various machines; quick touch-up under production pressure while the machine is down, quality judged by feel of the edge and by the appearance of the next cut.

tasks.label: Remove housings, feed tubes, tool holders, or other accessories to replace worn or broken parts, such as springs or bushings.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Punch press tooling teardown: at the press or tool bench, the operator pulls a punch holder/guide assembly out of the turret or ram, breaks it down (retaining ring, jam nut, keyed punch, stripper), replaces a broken stripper spring, worn guide bushing or galled punch, reassembles to the correct tool length, reinstalls and test-hits. Chips, coolant film, occasional seized threads.

Straight tooling swap at the machine's tool station: a chipped or worn punch/die segment (press brake or turret punch equipped with a tool rack or automatic tool changer) is pulled out of the clamp/station and a fresh identical tool is installed from the magazine; no internal teardown of the holder.

Feed-system accessories: remove feed tubes/bar-feeder liners, feed rollers, pusher fingers, collets or guide bushings on cutoff saws, tube cutters, bar feeders or automatic screw machines; replace worn liners, feed springs and bushings; realign and re-time the feed before restarting production.

Guard/housing removal for internal wear parts: unbolt side housings, covers or access panels on shears, press brakes or extrusion cutters (sometimes with a hoist), reach in to replace return springs, gibs, bushings or seals, reassemble and check clearance/adjustment.

Unplanned mid-shift breakdown: operator diagnoses which part failed (spring fragments, sheared bushing, deformed stripper), tears down the affected accessory in place in a partly obstructed machine, digs out broken pieces, installs replacements or swaps in a rebuilt accessory, then requalifies the first parts.

Bench/tool-room rebuild of a holder-mounted consumable: the worn cutting tool or insert is removed from its tool holder assembly, a new one installed, the assembly measured/preset and returned to the machine.

tasks.label: Sharpen dulled blades, using bench grinders, abrasive wheels, or lathes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Tool room of a metal fabrication plant: operator pulls the dull straight blades from a guillotine shear, slitter, or trim press, mounts them on a magnetic chuck of a surface grinder / straight-knife grinder, dresses the wheel, grinds the bevel to the spec angle and height, deburrs/stones the edge, and checks with a gauge before reinstalling.

Sharpening round blades: circular slitter knives, rotary trim wheels, and carbide-tipped or HSS circular saw blades used on the cut-off saws. Blade is mounted on an arbor/spindle on a knife grinder, saw sharpener, or lathe, and the periphery, side bevel, or tooth faces are ground to spec, then checked for runout and edge quality.

Regrinding punch-press tooling and die components — turret punches, dies, and small progressive-die sections — on a punch/die grinder or tool-and-cutter grinder: hold in a universal fixture, grind the face down by a few thousandths, stone/deburr the edge, re-measure length, and re-shim before returning it to the turret.

Quick freehand touch-up between production runs: operator takes a small dulled blade or cutter (nibbler blade, scrap chopper knife, hand shear blade, deburring tool) to a pedestal bench grinder, holds it by hand against the abrasive wheel, judges the bevel by eye, dips it in coolant to avoid burning, and tests the edge by feel. Blade shapes vary widely and there is no fixture or written spec.

In-place touch-up on the production machine: the blade stays mounted in the shear, slitting line, or granulator, and the operator dresses or grinds the exposed edge with a portable grinder or hand stone in cramped access alongside the machine, then resets blade clearance/gap and runs a test cut to verify.

Production sawing in a steel service center, structural fab shop or extrusion cut-off line: automatic/CNC saws run repeat job programs; per job the setter dials in band tension, guide-arm position for the section being cut and the programmed cut angle, then verifies the first cut to print tolerance.

Metal coil slitting line / rotary shear: build the knife and spacer stack on the arbors to the ordered strip widths, set horizontal knife clearance and vertical penetration (overlap) for the gauge, torque arbor locknuts with wrenches, and prove out on the leading edge of the coil.

Plastic film / sheet or narrow-web slitting and converting line: position razor, score or shear knives across the web to the ordered widths, set blade overlap depth and side load, lock knifeholders down, and confirm clean edges on a trial run.

Heating plastic or composite stock before forming/punching: operator places sheet, tube, or blank in an oven, strip heater, or uses a heat gun until pliable, monitors it, and transfers it quickly to the press or forming die inside a plant.

Large in-situ preheat: a big weldment, large-diameter pipe, or long structural member preheated with multiple torches or induction blankets in an outdoor yard or erection site, the worker walking around the piece, maintaining and re-checking temperature while forming/straightening proceeds.

Small-batch/prototype bench work: operator warms small, varying parts with a hand torch or heat gun for a few seconds each to soften them before punching or bending a handful of pieces, judging heat by color/feel, in a job shop.

tasks.label: Verify conformance of machined work to specifications, using measuring instruments, such as calipers, micrometers, or fixed or telescoping gauges.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-process spot check during a production run on a CNC drill/bore machine: every Nth part is pulled at the machine, hole diameters checked with plug/bore gauges, depths with a drop gauge or depth mic, ODs/locations with calipers; results logged and tool offsets tweaked. Parts are identical, gauges are already set up.

Near-100% gauging of small, high-volume machined parts (medical/aerospace/instrument work) at a bench or QC station: multiple gauge types per part (robotic caliper-type ODs, bore gauge, drop gauge for depth, thread go/no-go on tapped holes), accept/reject sorting and data recorded for SPC and traceability.

First-piece/setup verification on a repeat job: after setting up the drilling or boring machine, the operator measures the first part's key features (hole diameter, position, depth, counterbore) against an existing, known inspection routine and a familiar print before releasing the run.

Large or heavy workpiece on a horizontal boring mill or radial drill: bores, hole locations and depths verified while the part stays clamped on the table, using inside micrometers, telescoping/bore gauges and a height gauge; the part is too heavy to move to a gauging station.

Job-shop one-off/first-article inspection of a novel part: operator reads a paper print, decides which of 10-20 features to check, selects instruments (telescoping gauge + micrometer for a bore, depth mic for a blind hole, thread plug gauge, radius/pin gauges), measures on the bench and fills in an inspection report, all in minutes while the machine waits.

Verification of parts straight off the machine as-found: chips and coolant on the workpiece, burrs to be knocked off first, plus visual/tactile judgment of hole quality, chatter, or finish alongside the dimensional check on odd-shaped or fragile pieces.

instances.label: Job/fab shop, manual or radial-arm drill press: one-off and small-lot parts hand-clamped in a vise or strapped to the table, holes located from layout lines/punch marks; operator pulls the quill lever down to the work, feels the cut and breakthrough, sets the depth stop, engages power downfeed where the machine has one, retracts to clear chips.

tasks.label: Verify that workpiece reference lines are parallel to the axis of table rotation, using dial indicators mounted in spindles.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Setup on a CNC machining center (VMC/HMC) in a job or production shop: a new job's part is clamped in a vise or fixture on the table (often on a 4th-axis rotary table). The setter chucks a dial indicator in the spindle, sweeps a machined reference edge/face over 6-12 in., checks that it is parallel to table travel / the axis of table rotation within ~0.0005-0.002 in., taps the part and re-checks, then records the setup.

Horizontal boring mill or large HMC with a rotary (B-axis) table: a large machined housing, gearbox or weldment (hundreds of pounds to several tons) is craned onto the table and clamped. The operator sweeps an indicator mounted in the spindle along a machined reference face, rotates the table 90/180 degrees to confirm the face is parallel to the axis of rotation, and adjusts with jack screws or soft blows until within a few tenths.

Conventional/manual equipment: radial arm drill, manual mill/drill or jig borer with a rotary table or angle plate. A medium-size part is clamped, an indicator is held in the spindle or chuck, and the reference edge is swept and re-clamped until parallel to the table rotation axis. No CNC control, no probe interface; judgment and feel with hand tools.

Repeat/production setups in a dedicated cell: identical parts loaded into a dedicated fixture on a rotary table; alignment is verified at first article, after a fixture change, or at start of shift, with the indicator swept over the fixture datum or the part's reference face and the result logged on a setup sheet.

Rough job-shop verification on an as-cast or as-welded workpiece where the reference is a scribed layout line or punch-marked centerline on a painted/rough surface: the part overhangs the table, access is awkward, chips and coolant are present, and the worker combines indicator sweeps on rough surfaces with visual pickup of the scribed line using a wiggler or edge finder.

tasks.label: Establish zero reference points on workpieces, such as at the intersections of two edges or over hole locations.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Job-shop CNC drilling/tapping or vertical machining centre, low-volume mixed work: operator clamps a small-to-medium metal part in a vise on the machine table, then establishes the X/Y zero at a corner (intersection of two machined edges) with an edge finder or spindle touch probe and the Z zero on the top face, storing it as the G54 work offset.

Repeat production run on a dedicated fixture or pallet, often in a pallet-fed or robot-tended cell: the zero reference is re-established or verified at each lot, pallet or fixture change, typically by a probing routine embedded in the part program so the machine keeps running with little operator attention.

Manual drill press or radial-arm drill, one-off or small lot: part is laid out with scribed lines and centre-punch marks from a print; the operator clamps it and aligns the spindle over the punched hole locations or off two edges using a wiggler/centre finder, then sets table stops as the reference for the hole pattern.

Large crane-loaded casting or weldment clamped on a horizontal boring mill or large gantry drill: operator sweeps an existing bore with a dial indicator or probes two machined faces to set the datum, checks squareness/alignment of the part, and sets the rotary-table centreline as the zero.

Second-operation or delicate work: datum taken from an existing feature rather than an edge - a coaxial indicator or probe centred over a previously drilled hole, or a thin-walled/plastic component where light touch and judgement are needed to avoid deflecting the part while picking up the reference.

tasks.label: Change worn cutting tools, using wrenches.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production machine shop, CNC drilling/machining center: tool-life alarm or bad hole finish flags a worn drill. Operator pulls the tool assembly from the magazine, clamps the holder in a bench fixture, loosens the collet/chuck nut with two wrenches, removes the dull drill, installs a fresh one, torques, presets length/diameter, and returns the assembly to the magazine with offsets updated.

High-volume production drilling machine (gang drill, multi-spindle head, or drilling station on a transfer line): several worn drills/reamers/taps replaced mid-shift in adjacent spindles, machine stopped, chips and coolant present, tool depths and lengths reset so hole depth stays in spec.

Job shop / maintenance shop manual drill press or radial arm drill: change a dulled twist drill held in a Jacobs chuck (chuck key) or a Morse-taper drill knocked out with a drift wedge, sometimes an arbor nut loosened with a wrench; tool sizes vary job to job and part often stays clamped on the table.

Indexable tooling: replace worn carbide inserts in an indexable drill body, spade drill, or boring head using a Torx/hex wrench — blow out and clean the pocket, seat the insert, torque the screw, and re-adjust the boring head to diameter before restarting.

Large-part / aerospace or heavy-fabrication drilling: replace heavy drills, reamers, countersinks in a horizontal boring mill or big drilling machine spindle, using spanner/hook wrenches and a hoist for large tools, then verify runout and length before resuming the cut.

tasks.label: Select and set cutting speeds, feed rates, depths of cuts, and cutting tools, according to machining instructions or knowledge of metal properties.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: CNC drilling/machining-center job setup in a production machine shop: operator reads the traveler/setup sheet or NC program, pulls the specified drills, reamers, taps and boring bars from the tool crib, assembles them into holders, presets lengths/diameters, loads them into the machine's tool magazine, and enters or verifies spindle RPM, feed rates and peck/depth-of-cut values at the control before the first part.

Manual or semi-automatic drill press / radial arm drill setup in a job or fabrication shop: chuck the correct drill, countersink or reamer, set spindle RPM by shifting a belt or gear range per a speed chart for the material, set the depth stop and the power-feed rate (or plan hand feed), then drill the part.

In-process adjustment during a run: the operator hears chatter, sees discolored chips, burrs, a poor finish or a dulling drill, and dials the feed/speed override, reduces depth of cut or peck increment, or swaps in a fresh identical tool mid-job, then confirms the corrected condition on the next part.

High-volume repetitive production drilling of metal or plastic parts on gang, multi-spindle or dedicated drilling machines: parameters chosen for the material (e.g., slower speed and controlled feed to avoid melting/grabbing in acrylic or nylon), drill point geometry selected, depth stops set once and held across a long run.

Large-part work on a horizontal boring mill or deep-hole/gun drilling machine: select the boring bar/head or gun drill, set the reduced cutting speed and feed appropriate to overhang, hole depth and coolant pressure, and set roughing versus finishing depths of cut on a heavy fixtured weldment or casting.

Unfamiliar or exotic job: no complete machining instructions, so the operator applies knowledge of metal properties (SFM/chip-load charts, tool-material match, hardness, work-hardening behavior) to pick a tool grade and geometry and derive speeds, feeds and depths from scratch, proving them out with trial cuts and adjusting.

sources.date: 2026-01 (product page); system marketed and installed since ~2015

tasks.label: Position and secure workpieces on tables, using bolts, jigs, clamps, shims, or other holding devices.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Repeat production run in a machine shop: operator repeatedly loads identical small/medium metal blanks (shafts, blocks, brackets, 1-20 kg) from totes or racks into a dedicated fixture or vise on a drill press / CNC drilling or boring machine table, clamps them (crank vise, quick clamp, or air clamp), and cycles the machine.

New-job setup in a job shop: setter mounts a jig, fixture plate, angle plate or vise onto the machine table, bolts it into T-slots, taps it true with a dial indicator, shims it level/parallel, then positions and clamps the first workpiece and proves out the location.

Medium-heavy workpieces (castings, housings, pump bodies roughly 25-250 kg) hoisted with a jib crane or balancer onto a large drill/boring mill table, seated in a locating fixture or against stops, and clamped with hydraulic or strap clamps.

Very large one-off weldments, plates or multi-ton castings craned onto a horizontal boring mill or large radial drill table, blocked up on parallels, shimmed for flatness, secured with T-bolts and step clamps, then dialed in over several feet of travel.

Short-run / prototype work: a different part every few hours, including thin sheet, irregular or plastic parts that need soft jaws, backing blocks, shims or toe clamps to avoid marring, deflection or breakout damage.

Re-fixturing between operations on the same part: unclamp after first-side drilling, blow off chips, flip or reposition the part into a second fixture or rotary/4th-axis holder on the table, re-clamp maintaining location for the second-side holes.

tasks.label: Observe drilling or boring machine operations to detect any problems.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Job-shop CNC drilling/boring center: operator tends 2-3 machines, watching through the guard window and listening during the cycle for chatter, squealing, tool dulling or breakage, checking coolant flow and chip color/formation, and glancing at the control's load/alarm readouts.

Manual or radial drill press / bench boring work on one-off or small-lot parts: operator watches drill engagement and chip curl, listens and feels for the bit grabbing, walking out, or burning, and notices smoke, discoloration, or part movement in the vise.

High-volume production drilling/boring line (e.g., automotive or fastener parts), multi-spindle or transfer machine: operator monitors cycle timing, spindle load and gauge readouts, alarm lights, coolant delivery, and looks for broken taps/drills or chip packing between cycles.

Drilling plastic or composite workpieces: operator watches for melting, smearing, delamination, burr formation, chips wrapping the flutes, and part shifting or grabbing, adjusting attention as material heats up.

Large-part or deep-hole boring on castings/weldments with long cycle times: operator monitors feed pressure and vibration, swarf evacuation from the bore, coolant-through-tool pressure, and sound changes indicating drift or tool wear over a long unattended-looking cut.

tasks.label: Lift workpieces onto work tables either manually or with hoists or direct crane operators to lift and position workpieces.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production run on a CNC drilling/tapping machine or drill press: operator repeatedly lifts small blanks (under ~25 lb) out of bins, totes or trays on a cart and sets them into the vise/fixture on the machine table, seating them against locators, cycle after cycle through the shift.

Job-shop one-off or small batch: operator hand-lifts a medium part (roughly 25-75 lb) - a bracket, flange, housing or plate - off a bench, pallet or cart onto the table of a radial arm drill or boring mill, positions it to layout lines/parallels/stops, sometimes wrestling an awkward shape into place.

Part of roughly 100-1,000 lb (casting, weldment, thick plate) moved from a pallet to the machine table with a jib crane, chain hoist, vacuum lifter or manipulator; operator slings it, swings it over the table, guides it down onto parallels or an existing fixture and nudges it into location.

Long or awkward stock - bar, long plate, fabricated weldment - handled with a hoist and strap or by two people onto a large drill/boring mill table, laid flat and aligned to stops or scribed lines before setup.

Multi-ton workpiece for a horizontal boring mill: operator rigs slings/shackles, hand-signals or radios the overhead crane operator, walks the load in, lands it on the table or angle plate, and guides fine positioning before it is indicated in and bolted down.

tasks.label: Turn valves and direct flow of coolants or cutting oil over cutting areas.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Job-shop CNC drilling/boring machining center: at setup the operator aims the flexible flood-coolant nozzle(s) at the drill point for each tool length, opens the coolant valve (or commands it from the control), and re-aims/adjusts flow between tools and during the run to keep chips flushed from the hole.

High-volume production drilling cell or multi-spindle/transfer machine: operator opens manifold and through-spindle/high-pressure coolant valves at shift start, verifies flow and pressure at each cutting station, and adjusts pressure/flow per operation for peck drilling and chip evacuation.

Toolroom/maintenance shop manual or semi-automatic drill press or radial-arm drill: operator opens a hand petcock or ball valve, bends a Loc-Line hose over the drill point, or squirts/brushes cutting oil from a can onto the bit, adjusting continually as the hole deepens.

Large horizontal boring mill or deep-hole drilling of big weldments/forgings: operator repositions hoses and nozzles around a large, varied workpiece, opens high-pressure coolant valves, and adjusts flow mid-cycle for chip evacuation and to keep the tool cool on long bores.

Drilling plastics, thin stock or dry-sensitive materials: operator sets a mist/air or MQL valve, adjusts the oil-air mix and aims the mist nozzle over the cutting area to avoid melting or flooding the part, cutting flow on and off between holes.

tasks.label: Install tools in spindles.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: CNC drilling/machining center setup in a job or production shop: the operator picks the tooling called for by the program, seats each holder (CAT/BT/HSK taper) into the spindle or loads it into the tool magazine pockets, checks the taper is clean and the retention knob seated, and records tool numbers/offsets.

Manual or radial drill press / tapping machine: the operator chucks a bare twist drill, reamer, tap or countersink in a keyed Jacobs chuck, or drives a Morse-taper drill or taper sleeve into the spindle and knocks it out later with a drift key, checking runout before drilling.

Mid-run tool replacement at the machine: a drill, reamer or tap dulls or breaks during a run, so the operator stops the cycle and swaps the worn tool for a fresh one amid chips, coolant and a hot spindle, then re-touches the tool length before restarting.

Gang-drill or multi-spindle head setup: several drills, countersinks and taps are installed in adjacent spindles or quick-change adapters/collets, each set to the correct projection and spacing for a sequential drilling operation.

Large/heavy tooling on a horizontal boring mill or large machining center: installing a boring bar, angle/attachment head or oversized taper tool weighing tens of pounds, often with a hoist or two-person assist, then indicating it in.

tasks.label: Perform minor assembly, such as fastening parts with nuts, bolts, or screws, using power tools or hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bench-top small-fastener work in a machine/fab shop: after drilling and tapping, the operator joins covers, plates, or brackets on small metal or plastic parts by driving 4-12 machine screws with a pneumatic or DC electric driver; parts staged in totes at the bench, batch of a few dozen.

Medium bolt-and-nut assembly at the bench or on the shop floor: mating two drilled parts (brackets, plates, sub-frames up to ~20 lb), inserting hex bolts with washers through the drilled holes, threading and torquing nuts with a torque or impact wrench, aligning the parts by hand while starting fasteners.

Bolting hardware onto large fabricated weldments or machine frames on the shop floor: flanges, guards, brackets or plates fastened with 1/2-inch-and-up bolts, awkward reach (overhead, inside cavities, blind side), part moved by hoist or cart, impact wrench used.

Attaching hardware to workpieces or tooling at the machine in high-mix small batches: press-fit/threaded inserts, standoffs, locating pins, handles, adapter plates and clamp hardware bolted on right after the drilling operation, with the job changing from batch to batch.

Fit-up problem cases: holes misaligned between mating parts, burrs or chips in the hole, a fastener that starts to cross-thread or a stripped thread; the operator diagnoses, deburrs/reams/re-drills, shims or re-clocks the part, then completes the fastening.

tasks.label: Operate single- or multiple-spindle drill presses to bore holes so that machining operations can be performed on metal or plastic workpieces.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume repetitive production drilling of small/medium metal parts on a single- or multiple-spindle (gang) drill press in a production shop: operator takes blanks from a tote or rack, clamps each in a vise/drill jig, feeds the spindle(s) through the hole pattern, clears chips, deburrs, unloads to a tray, and gauges every nth part. Same part number for hours or days.

Tending a CNC drilling/boring machine or drill-tap center in a production or job shop: load a blank into the machine fixture, close door, cycle start, unload, air-blast chips, run first-article and periodic dimensional checks, replace dull drills when the tool monitor or hole quality calls for it.

Small-batch or one-off job-shop drilling on a manual or radial-arm drill press: read the print, lay out and center-punch or set up a jig, clamp the part in a vise or to the table, pick and change drills, spot/drill/ream/countersink, apply cutting fluid, check hole size and location with gages, deburr. Changeover several times a shift.

Large, heavy workpieces - weldments, thick plate, beams, castings - drilled on a radial-arm drill press or heavy drill line: the part is craned or rolled into place, clamped or strapped to the table, large-diameter holes drilled with flood coolant, the arm or part repositioned for each hole, chips cleared, hole locations verified.

Plastic and soft-material workpieces (acrylic, UHMW, glass-filled nylon, molded or extruded parts): peck-drilling holes to avoid melting, grabbing or cracking, backing the part to prevent breakout, deburring and handling without marring surfaces; often thin or flexible parts needing careful clamping.

tasks.label: Lay out reference lines and machining locations on work, using layout tools, and applying knowledge of shop math and layout techniques.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Small/medium machined part at a bench or surface plate in a job shop: operator applies layout fluid, uses height gauge, scriber, dividers and combination square to scribe reference lines and hole centers from a print, then center-punches each location before drilling/boring.

Flat plate, sheet or bar stock: operator computes hole-pattern coordinates from a drawing (bolt circles, edge distances), scribes datum edges and hole centers with rule/square/scriber, and punches centers before drilling.

Structural shapes / long stock (beam, angle, channel, tube) in a fabrication shop: layout of hole locations and part marks along the length from an end datum, marked with soapstone/scribe and punched for drilling.

Large weldment or fabricated assembly on a layout table or floor plate: establish datums by indicating/squaring the piece, scribe centerlines and machining locations for boring/drilling, punch or paint the marks; CAD/print geometry available.

Rough casting or forging: operator indicates as-cast surfaces, judges where stock will clean up, distributes machining allowance, then scribes reference lines and bore/hole locations on a dyed surface and punches them.

Transfer layout: hole locations taken from an existing mating part, template or used component with existing holes, transferred onto a new workpiece (spot through, prick-punch, scribe/punch to size) with no CAD model available.

instances.label: Mid-job touch-up of a dull standard twist drill (HSS or carbide, ~1/8"-3/4") at the shop's pedestal/bench grinder: operator walks the bit to the grinder, freehand grinds the two lips to the correct point and clearance angles, dips in coolant, checks with a drill point gauge, returns to the machine and proves the cut.

Regrinding other rotary tooling used at the drilling machine - countersinks, center drills, step drills, spade-drill blades, counterbores, small reamers and end mills - on the bench grinder, often with a drill-sharpening attachment or shop-made jig to hold the angle.

Grinding HSS single-point tooling used alongside the drilling work - boring-bar bits, lathe/shaper tool bits, flat form cutters - freehand on the bench grinder to establish rake, side and end relief angles, then honing the edge.

Restoring a badly worn, burned or chipped tool, or grinding a non-standard geometry for a specific job (split point, altered point angle, thinned web, custom step point): significant stock removal plus judgment about the geometry to produce.

Bench-grinder work on miscellaneous shop items and grinder upkeep: dressing chisels, punches, scribers, deburring blades and screwdriver tips, plus truing/dressing the grinding wheel and setting the tool rest before sharpening.

tasks.label: Operate tracing attachments to duplicate contours from templates or models.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Batch production on a tracer/duplicating machine that is already set up (hydraulic tracer lathe, profiler, or duplicating mill): operator loads a metal blank in the chuck/fixture, engages the stylus on the template and starts the trace cycle, watches for chatter, stylus lift and chip build-up, unloads the finished part, checks the contour with a template/gauge, and repeats through a batch on a production floor.

Re-setting a recurring job on a duplicating machine: pull the stored template/master from the tool crib, mount it in the standard template holder/rail, clamp the standard workholding, set trace feed and stylus pressure to the documented values, cut and gauge a first article, and correct offsets before releasing the run. Job shop with standard tooling and written setup sheets.

Setting up a new or unfamiliar duplicating job: deciding how to hold an odd blank, mounting a shop-made template or a customer's model, establishing the stylus-to-cutter relationship and compensating for stylus/cutter radius difference, trial cutting, diagnosing why the copied contour is off, and reworking the setup until the part is accepted. Toolroom of a job shop.

Large workpiece on a horizontal boring mill or planer-type mill using a template/model with a tracer head: casting or weldment is crane-loaded and indicated in, template is bolted to the table or template rail, contour bore/profile traced in one or more passes, feeds adjusted for heavy interrupted cuts, part gauged in place. Heavy-machining bay of a plant.

Die/mold shop three-dimensional copy milling: a pattern or model is traced to rough and finish a cavity in a die block over long cycles, with stylus/cutter pairs changed between roughing and finishing, step-over and feed adjusted, and the operator monitoring cut load and surface finish over hours of running in a tool-and-die shop.

One-off repair duplication in a small shop: a worn or broken customer sample is used as the model, holding is improvised with angle plates, clamps and shims on an older manual machine fitted with a tracer attachment, the operator compensates by feel for the worn model and hand-blends the result to fit the mating part.

tasks.label: Measure workpieces and lay out work, using precision measuring devices.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-process check during a grinding run on a production floor: operator stops the cycle (or checks between passes) and measures the ground diameter, thickness or bore of a small/medium metal part with a micrometer, snap gauge or bore gauge against a print tolerance of a few ten-thousandths, then decides whether to adjust infeed or dress the wheel.

First-article / final dimensional inspection of finished ground or honed parts in a shop QC area: caliper, micrometer, height gauge and indicator on a surface plate, or a CMM run, checking multiple print features, recording results and accepting/rejecting or sorting the batch.

Layout of rough or repair work before grinding: measuring stock allowance on a casting, weldment, forging or worn part, establishing datums, and marking/scribing lines or otherwise defining where and how much material must be removed so the finished feature will clean up within print.

Surface-finish and geometry verification after lapping, honing, polishing or buffing: profilometer Ra/Rz readings at specified locations, flatness with optical flat or indicator, roundness/taper checks, on standard shop or lab equipment.

Measuring large or heavy workpieces where the part stays in place: mill rolls, long shafts, large dies or molds — diameter/taper/crown checked with large micrometers, bore gauges or in-machine measuring devices, often with crane handling in a roll shop or heavy machine shop.

tasks.label: Inspect or measure finished workpieces to determine conformance to specifications, using measuring instruments, such as gauges or micrometers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume production grinding (e.g., centerless, cylindrical, or surface grinding of bearing races, pins, shafts). Operator pulls a finished part every few pieces at the machine, checks OD/ID/length/thickness with micrometer, snap gauge, air/bore gauge, records readings on an SPC chart, and adjusts or stops the machine if drifting out of tolerance. Shop floor, oily parts, ambient temperature.

Setup / first-article inspection after a new job or wheel dress: operator takes the first ground piece to a nearby bench or surface plate and checks all print features — diameters, lengths, squareness, concentricity, radii — with micrometers, indicators, height gauge or a shop-floor CMM, against a drawing, then signs off before running production.

Polishing/buffing/honing/lapping finish checks: operator verifies surface finish (Ra with a profilometer or by comparison specimen) and inspects visually and by touch for scratches, swirl marks, burns, remaining burrs and edge break on the finished part under shop lighting, deciding cosmetic acceptability.

Large or heavy ground workpieces (mill rolls, large rings and gears, dies, machine ways) measured in place on or near the machine with C-frame calipers, large micrometers, indicators, or a large-part CMM/portable metrology; crane or fixture handling; roll shop or heavy machine shop.

Job-shop / low-volume mixed work: operator grinds and then measures a handful of non-repeating parts of varied geometry with handheld hand tools and gauge blocks, interprets the drawing, sorts conforming from nonconforming pieces, and tags/records results.

tasks.label: Set and adjust machine controls according to product specifications, using knowledge of machine operation.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Job-shop CNC grinder (cylindrical/surface) setup for a new part: operator loads/edits the part program at the control, sets wheel speed, infeed/feed rates, spark-out, dress amount and work offsets from the print and traveler, runs a first article, measures it, and re-adjusts offsets until in tolerance. Ordinary machine-shop floor, mixed jobs, human-facing HMI and handwheels.

Tending a production run on a semi-automatic or CNC grinder: watching part size on the gauge/SPC chart and periodically adjusting size compensation, infeed rate, dwell/spark-out, dress frequency and coolant at the machine's controls as the wheel wears and the process drifts. Shop floor, standard equipment.

Manual or hand-operated surface/tool-and-cutter grinder in a toolroom: setting table travel stops, downfeed increment per pass, crossfeed, spindle/wheel speed and coolant by lever, dial and handwheel for a one-off or small-lot part, adjusting by feel and by micrometer checks between passes.

Centerless grinder setup and adjustment for a production run: setting regulating-wheel speed and angle, work-blade height, infeed/thrufeed rate and dwell, dresser settings, then trimming size compensation during the run to hold diameter. Production floor of a parts plant.

Polishing, buffing, belt-sanding or deburring machine: setting belt/wheel speed, contact pressure or force, oscillation and cycle timers on the machine controls per the finish specification, and adjusting them as abrasive wears or finish quality drifts. Finishing department of a metal-goods plant.

Honing/lapping machine setup: setting stroke length and position, tool expansion/pressure, spindle and stroking speeds and cycle timers to the bore size and finish spec, then adjusting to hold size and crosshatch as stones wear. Shop floor of a precision-parts producer.

tasks.label: Observe machine operations to detect any problems, making necessary adjustments to correct problems.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production shop: operator tends a CNC cylindrical, centerless or surface grinder running a job of similar parts. Watches the cycle, checks part size with a gauge/mic, notices size drift and wheel wear, and corrects by editing wheel offsets, changing dress compensation or triggering a dress cycle.

Production grinder in a plant: operator watches/listens for process anomalies during the cycle - wheel rubbing or crashing on approach, chatter, wheel loading or unbalance, grinding burn/discoloration, a dull dresser - then stops the machine or changes feed, speed, dress or coolant parameters to bring the process back in control.

Toolroom/job shop: operator runs a manual or semi-automatic surface, tool-and-cutter or cylindrical grinder on short-run precision work. Judges the spark pattern, sound and feel, adjusts the infeed handwheel and crossfeed, redresses the wheel and re-aims coolant to hold tolerance and finish.

Finishing department: operator tends a belt grinder, polishing/buffing lathe, honing or deburring machine. Watches surface finish and burr removal on each piece, adjusts contact pressure, belt/wheel speed and dwell as the abrasive belt, brush or buff wears, and changes worn media.

Non-routine fault at any of the above machines: unusual noise or vibration, coolant flow loss or leak, chips/swarf packing, a part slipping or misloaded in the fixture, a machine alarm. Operator investigates the root cause and makes a physical correction (re-seat part, adjust workrest blade or steady rest, clear chips, re-aim nozzle, swap wheel) or calls maintenance.

tasks.label: Activate machine start-up switches to grind, lap, hone, debar, shear, or cut workpieces, according to specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume production grinding: operator in a production machine shop tends a CNC surface, cylindrical or centerless grinder running one part number; part is placed in chuck/fixture, guard closed, cycle-start pressed, repeated hundreds of times per shift; standard-size metal parts, coolant mist, machine already set up to the spec sheet.

High-mix job shop grinding: after a setup, the operator runs small batches (25-500 pieces) of varied metal parts on a surface, tool or cylindrical grinder, activating the start switch for each cycle, checking sizes against the traveler, and changing jobs several times per shift.

Bench/manual finishing: operator switches on a pedestal grinder, belt sander, wire brush or buffing wheel and hand-holds varied parts against the wheel to deburr edges, break corners or polish to a specified finish, judging by eye and feel; parts change frequently.

Secondary-operation machines: operator loads and starts honing machines, tube/bar cut-off saws, small shears, or dedicated deburring machines on standard metal or plastic parts; short repeated cycles, hard-tooled fixtures, output gauged to print.

Large/heavy workpieces: castings, plates or long shafts brought by hoist, crane or roller cart to a Blanchard/rotary surface grinder or a large shear; operator clamps or magnetizes the piece, checks clearances and coolant, then activates the machine start switch for a long cycle.

tasks.label: Lift and position workpieces, manually or with hoists, and secure them in hoppers or on machine tables, faceplates, or chucks, using clamps.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production run on a centerless, cylindrical, or rotary surface grinder in a manufacturing plant: operator repeatedly lifts small-to-medium metal parts (shafts, fittings, bearing races, blades, 0.1–15 kg) out of totes/bins/trays and seats them in the machine's chuck, workrest, or fixture, cycling every 20–120 seconds for the whole shift.

Job-shop / low-volume setup on a manual or CNC surface, tool, or cylindrical grinder: several times a shift the operator sets a different workpiece (varied geometry, sometimes a casting or weldment) on the magnetic chuck, faceplate, or table, selects parallels, blocks, strap clamps and vises, indicates it true, and torques the clamps by hand.

Heavy or bulky workpiece (mill roll, die block, large gear, casting, 50–2,500 kg) slung with an overhead crane, jib hoist, or chain fall, walked into position over the grinder table or between centers, lowered, seated, and secured with strap clamps, T-bolts, steadies, or drive dogs.

Bulk loading of small parts: scooping or dumping totes of parts into hoppers, vibratory feeders, thru-feed centerless feed tracks, or vibratory/tumbling deburring and polishing bowls, then leveling the charge and monitoring feed.

Precision small-part work in a tool room or polishing/buffing department: mounting cutting tools, inserts, or small delicate metal/plastic parts into collets, arbors, holders, or buffing fixtures, checking runout and tightening the holder before grinding, honing, or buffing.

tasks.label: Move machine controls to index workpieces, and to adjust machines for pre-selected operational settings.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: CNC cylindrical/surface/tool-and-cutter grinder in a production machine shop: operator calls up the stored part program at the control, jogs axes to position the wheel, indexes the workpiece (table swivel, rotary index, part flip) between features, keys in wheel/dress offsets from the setup sheet, and starts the cycle.

Manual or semi-automatic surface/cylindrical grinder in a job shop or tool room: operator turns handwheels, levers and dial stops to traverse and index the table/workpiece, dials in downfeed increments, sets table dogs and wheel speed and coolant to the pre-selected values on the job sheet, for varied one-off or small-lot parts.

High-volume automatic grinder tender (centerless, double-disc, Blanchard, thread grinder): between and during batches the tender moves controls to set feed rates, infeed stops and size-compensation increments to pre-selected settings, indexes fixtures/loader positions, and re-runs the cycle after checking part size.

Deburring/polishing/buffing machine operator in a finishing shop: sets belt/wheel speed, contact pressure and oscillation to pre-selected settings, indexes the part in a fixture or rotary table between faces or features, and cycles the machine.

Job changeover/setup on a semi-automatic grinder: operator sets stops and dogs, positions an index or dividing head to the required positions, dials in all pre-selected operational settings from the setup sheet, and runs a first article before releasing the job.

instances.label: Routine wear-part replacement on a grinder/polisher standing on the shop floor: operator finds a leaking coolant hose, clogged nozzle, torn way wiper, worn centerless work-rest blade, loose or sheared fastener, damaged guard, or worn drive belt; fetches a spare from the crib and swaps it using wrenches, screwdrivers, hex keys; re-checks alignment and runs a test part.

Replacing worn tooling-side machine components: swapping a worn or damaged wheel pack/wheel hub assembly, abrasive belt, contact wheel or buffing wheel, or a spent diamond dresser nib, then re-tensioning/tracking and verifying run-out before resuming production.

Escalation on equipment condition: operator notices abnormal spindle noise, vibration, overheating, a hydraulic/coolant leak or a recurring machine alarm, decides the fix is beyond the operator's scope, and notifies maintenance/engineering with a description of the symptoms and the affected machine.

Escalation driven by workpiece quality: ground parts show chatter, burn, taper or dimensional drift that the operator traces to a machine problem (spindle bearing play, slide wear, out-of-square table) and reports to engineering for corrective action.

Larger component repair, usually alongside maintenance: replacing spindle drive belts or a motor, bearings, hydraulic hose/valve, limit switch or sensor, way covers or a ballscrew component - requires guarded disassembly, lockout, re-alignment, and test grinding to prove the machine back in.

tasks.label: Adjust air cylinders and setting stops to set traverse lengths and feed arm strokes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Job changeover on a semi-automatic reciprocating/surface grinder in a production machine shop: operator loosens the table reversing dogs/trip stops, slides them along the table slot to set the traverse length for the new part, locks them with the clamp screws, then dry-cycles the table and checks overtravel at each end, nudging a stop if needed.

Automatic buffing/polishing lathe or centerless grinder feed arm: operator sets the air-cylinder stroke stops and tunes the cylinder's regulator and flow-control needle valves so the feed arm advances the right distance at the right speed and dwell, judging contact pressure and finish by feel and from test pieces.

Honing or lapping machine setup: set stroke length and reversal points of the honing head with adjustable stops/limit switches and set air-cylinder pressure for tool expansion, then run a test bore, measure taper, and reposition the stops to correct.

Mid-run correction on a running job: after first-article inspection or when a stop has drifted or worn, loosen the lock nut, move the stop a few thousandths, retighten to spec, re-cycle and re-measure the part until within tolerance.

Older or mixed-make manual/semi-automatic machines in a small job shop: awkward access behind guards, worn threads and unmarked scales, no setup documentation; the setter positions stops with a rule or indicator largely by experience and trial-and-error, sometimes with guards removed.

tasks.label: Slide spacers between buffs on spindles to set spacing.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Job-shop / small finishing shop: operator sets up a pedestal or bench buffing lathe. Removes the retaining nut, slides cloth buffs (loose-fold, spiral-sewn, sisal) and metal spacer washers onto the tapered or threaded spindle in a chosen order so the buff face sits where the part contour needs it, re-tightens the nut, spins up and checks runout. Shop floor, compound-coated tooling, hand tools.

Production changeover on a multi-spindle automatic buffing/polishing machine (cookware, faucets, wheels, hardware): per a setup sheet, stacks buff sections and steel/fiber spacers along long arbors on several spindles so each buff lines up with a specific feature of the new part number, spacing set to fractions of an inch, then locks the stacks down.

Offline buff-pack build at a setup bench or tool crib in the plant: assembles buff-and-spacer stacks onto spare arbors/mandrels to a written spacing spec while the machine keeps running, then the pack is carried to the machine and mounted.

Mid-run correction: finish is streaked or the buffs have worn/glazed at one band, so the operator loosens the nut, adds, removes or swaps a thin spacer to shift a buff a fraction of an inch, reassembles, and re-runs a sample part to confirm the finish.

Heavy or awkward setup: large-diameter, heavy buff packs on big arbors, or older machines with gummed-up compound buildup, worn threads and mismatched/improvised spacers, requiring force, cleaning and improvisation in confined access.

tasks.label: Adjust machine controls and change tool settings to keep dimensions within specified tolerances.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Repeat production run on a CNC turning center in a job/production shop: operator gauges parts periodically with mic/bore gage or a shop-floor gauge, sees the diameter drifting from tool wear and thermal growth, and keys wear offsets into the control to hold roughly ±0.001 in.

Bar-fed CNC Swiss-type or multi-spindle running long, largely unattended cycles on small precision parts (±0.0002–0.0005 in): operator trims offsets, tweaks feed/speed overrides and coolant in response to drift, chip problems and tool loading.

Mid-run tool problem: a worn or chipped insert is detected, the operator indexes or replaces the insert in the turret tool holder (or swaps the whole tool block), re-touches off / resets the tool offset, cuts and gauges a trial part, then resumes production.

First-article / post-setup correction on a CNC lathe: the first piece is measured (bench gage or CMM), the operator corrects tool geometry and wear offsets and tweaks program parameters (finish pass, feed, spring cut), and re-runs until every dimension is inside print tolerance.

Manual engine/turret lathe or older cam-operated automatic in a toolroom, repair or short-run shop: operator adjusts cross-slide/compound handwheels, speed and feed levers, tool-post position or stops between successive cuts, measuring with a micrometer to sneak up on the finished size.

tasks.label: Move controls to set cutting speeds and depths and feed rates, and to position tools in relation to workpieces.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Setting up a CNC turning center for a new or changed job in a production/job machine shop: jogging the turret to touch off each tool and enter geometry offsets, setting the Z work offset on the part face, and entering/editing spindle speed (S), feed rate (F) and depth-of-cut values at the control before proving out the first part.

In-process control while running a CNC lathe production job in a machine shop: using feed/spindle override dials, tweaking tool-wear offsets to hold diameters as inserts dull, and backing off speed or feed when chatter, chip control or finish problems appear.

Conventional (manual) engine lathe or turret lathe work on a one-off, repair or short-run part in a job/maintenance shop: selecting spindle speed with belt/gear levers or a variable-speed dial, setting feed rate on the quick-change gearbox, and advancing cross-slide/compound handwheels by dial graduations to position the tool and set depth of cut.

Setting up and tending a bar-fed CNC Swiss-type or multi-spindle screw machine in a high-volume production shop: setting speeds and feeds for many tool stations, positioning/indexing the many tools relative to the bar stock, and adjusting offsets during the run.

Large, heavy work on a vertical turret lathe or large engine lathe in a heavy machine shop: crane-loaded castings/forgings, jogging the ram/rail to position the tool against an irregular as-cast surface, indicating the part, and dialing in conservative speeds and feeds for interrupted roughing cuts.

tasks.label: Inspect sample workpieces to verify conformance with specifications, using instruments such as gauges, micrometers, and dial indicators.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production CNC turning center in a job/production shop: operator stops the cycle after a first-off or after a tool change, pulls the turned part from the chuck or catcher, deburrs it, and checks OD, ID, length and shoulder positions with micrometer, caliper and bore gauge against the print, then dials in tool wear offsets. Coolant-wet parts, chips on the bench, quick turnaround required.

Periodic SPC sampling during a running lot (every 10th-25th part) at a bench beside the lathe or screw machine: check a handful of key characteristics with snap gauges, go/no-go plug and thread ring gauges, air gauge and micrometer; log readings on a control chart and flag drift.

Geometry/form check of a turned shaft or bushing at a bench or surface plate: part set in V-blocks or between centers, dial indicator used for runout/TIR, concentricity, taper and squareness; also thread pitch and groove checks on the same part.

First-article or final inspection of a complex turned part in the shop's quality/inspection room: CMM, optical comparator, height gauge and gauge pins used to verify all print dimensions and GD&T and produce a documented inspection report before the lot ships.

Toolroom / manual engine-lathe or repair work on a one-off or unique part with no CAD model: operator measures repeatedly during machining with micrometers, telescoping gauges and hand-held indicators, interpreting a sketch or worn print and judging fit against a mating part.

Operator opens the door, reaches into the chip- and coolant-filled work zone, loosens a Torx clamp screw on a turret-mounted holder, indexes or swaps the carbide insert, blows out the pocket, re-torques, then re-touches off / adjusts the wear offset and runs a check part.

Swapping a complete worn or broken tool assembly on a lathe: boring bar in its sleeve, drill in a holder, parting-blade holder, live/driven tool unit or a whole VDI/BMT turret station. Includes bolting up, setting center height/orientation, presetting or probing to establish the new tool offset.

Freehand sharpening at the shop's pedestal/bench grinder: HSS single-point lathe bits, drills, center drills and small custom tools reground by eye to the needed rake/relief angles, wheel dressed as needed, tool quenched, checked against a gage or by test cut.

Toolroom regrinding on a tool-and-cutter grinder: dull drills, end mills, reamers and similar rotary tools fixtured in collets/holders and reground to standard geometry in batches, then inspected before returning to service.

Regrinding low-volume, special-geometry tooling on a cutter/surface grinder with dedicated fixtures: form tools, cutoff/parting blades, thread chasers and dies, often one-off geometry judged from a print or from the worn tool itself.
