instances.label: High-volume production run on a bar-fed CNC turning center or Swiss-type lathe in a production machine shop: bar stock is presented by the bar feeder, the operator engages the automatic cycle and the turret/gang tools are fed to and along the rotating stock (face, turn, drill, thread, cut-off); operator monitors chips and tool wear, nudges feed override, restarts after each bar. Repeat parts to +/-0.001-0.005 in.

Job-shop chuck work on a CNC lathe, small batches (1-200 pieces): operator loads a billet, casting or sawn slug into the chuck, closes the door and engages the automatic feed cycle so tools rough, finish, bore and thread the part; unloads, deburrs, gauges and repeats, occasionally adjusting feed for chip control.

Setup and first-article on a CNC lathe: operator jogs the toolholder with the manual pulse handwheel to touch each tool off the face and diameter, takes a light trial cut under manual feed, measures with a micrometer and enters offsets before releasing the job to the automatic cycle.

Manual engine or toolroom lathe: operator advances the carriage and cross-slide by handwheel and engages the power-feed lever or half-nut for threading, taking successive cuts on a one-off, repair or salvage part (worn shaft, bushing, fitted pin), measuring between cuts and sneaking up on a fit to a mating component.

Large or heavy turning in a heavy machine shop: big chucker, vertical turning lathe or long shaft between centers; operator engages power feeds for long roughing and finishing passes and adjusts feed and speed mid-cut when chatter, poor chip formation or tool load appears, over cycles lasting an hour or more.

tasks.label: Crank machines through cycles, stopping to adjust tool positions and machine controls to ensure specified timing, clearances, and tolerances.

instances.label: Repeat job on a CNC turning center (chucker or bar-fed) in a job shop: setup sheet and proven program exist; setter loads tools, touches off/sets offsets, single-blocks the first cycle at reduced rapid to confirm turret-to-chuck/tailstock clearance, runs a first part, then stops and tweaks offsets until the part is on print.

New or revised program proveout on a CNC turning center: unproven toolpath, new workholding or new tool stack-up. Setter crawls the machine through the cycle in single block with feed/rapid override, hand on feed hold, stopping repeatedly to correct tool positions, offsets, approach moves and control parameters before the first good part is accepted.

During a production run on a CNC lathe: operator stops the cycle after gauging parts (or after indexing a worn insert) and adjusts wear offsets, speeds/feeds and tool positions to bring drifting diameters, lengths and threads back within tolerance, then proves the correction on the next part.

Swiss-type or multi-spindle CNC lathe setup: gang and opposed tooling around a guide bushing, main-to-sub spindle handoff. Setter cycles the machine in single block, physically adjusts tool height/position in the holders and edits synchronization/timing codes to obtain tool-to-tool and tool-to-bushing clearance and part tolerance.

Manual engine lathe or turret lathe in a shop or maintenance/toolroom: operator cranks the carriage, cross-slide and turret by hand through the cutting cycle, sets turret stops and feed trip dogs, shims and repositions tool holders on center, checking clearance and size with indicator and micrometer between passes.

Cam-operated automatic screw machine (Davenport, Brown & Sharpe, Acme multi-spindle) setup: setter bars the machine over by hand through the full cam cycle, times cams and trip dogs, adjusts cross-slide and end-tool positions and stops so tools clear each other and the stock, and sizes come in on print.

instances.label: Job setup on a 2-axis CNC turning center in a production/job shop: operator installs 6-12 VDI/BMT toolholders (OD turning, boring bars, grooving, drills) into the turret, torques clamping screws with hex keys/wrenches, then touches off each tool or uses an on-machine tool-setting arm to establish and record X/Z tool offsets, confirming with a first-article measurement.

Turn-mill / multitasking turning center with a tool magazine: preassembled Capto/HSK toolholders (turning and rotating tools) are loaded into the magazine and transferred into the B-axis spindle, clamped, and their length/diameter offsets verified with an in-machine tool-setting probe before the cycle runs.

Off-machine tool build and presetting in the shop's tool crib: assemble the cutting tool into its holder/adapter (boring bar or round-shank tool in a sleeve, insert holder), tighten to spec with hand tools at a set stickout, measure the assembly on a presetter and transfer the offsets to the lathe control.

Manual engine lathe or toolroom lathe: mount a HSS tool bit or quick-change tool-post holder, shim/adjust it to exact spindle center height using a center gauge, scale or tailstock center, tighten the post with a wrench, and indicate a boring bar or facing tool square with a dial indicator.

Swiss-type, gang-tooled or multi-spindle screw machine setup: bolt gang tool blocks, cut-off blades and cross-drilling units onto the tool plate, align them with a dial indicator and shims to a few thousandths, and verify positions before running tight-tolerance parts.

Mid-run tool replacement at the machine: index or swap a worn insert / replace a dulled preset tool in the turret during a production run, re-seat and secure it, and re-verify the offset with the tool setter or a test-part measurement before resuming.

instances.label: High-volume production run on a CNC turning center or Swiss-type lathe in a production machine shop: proven job, bar feeder or loader supplying stock. Worker presses cycle start, watches the first pieces, then monitors several machines at once for chip control, tool wear, coolant and dimensional drift, adjusting offsets and swapping tools as trends move.

Job-shop repeat job, lot of roughly 10-300 parts on a CNC chucker: worker starts each cycle, watches the cut and listens for chatter or tool failure, gauges parts periodically and tweaks wear offsets to hold print tolerances until the lot is accepted.

New job or new program proveout on a CNC lathe: worker runs the first part in single block with feed/rapid override low, hand on feed hold, watching toolpaths, approach clearances, chip formation and cut sound, then verifies the first article and edits offsets/program before releasing the job.

Conventional engine lathe or turret lathe work in a shop: worker engages spindle and power feed by hand, hand-feeds cuts, watches and listens to the cut, stops the machine to measure and re-sets depth for one-off or maintenance parts.

Repeat production of large/heavy turned parts (vertical turret lathe or big chucker; oilfield, energy, rolls, aerospace forgings): crane- or gantry-loaded single parts, long cycles, worker starts the cycle and periodically observes for chatter, tool wear and coolant, checking dimensions with on-machine probing or hand gauges.

Field/portable turning work at a customer site (portable flange facer or line-boring/turning head clamped to installed equipment at a plant, shipyard or utility): worker starts the head and watches the cut in a cramped, non-standard setting, adjusting feed as conditions change.

instances.label: Routine shift check and top-off of cutting-fluid level on CNC turning centers in a production machine shop: operator eyes the sump sight glass/level, hauls a bucket or drags a hose of premixed coolant, and fills the tank to the mark between cycles.

Weekly/periodic coolant condition check on lathes: read concentration with a refractometer (and pH/tramp-oil check), then adjust by adding concentrate or water to bring the sump back into the specified range, and log the reading.

Reacting to a low-fluid condition during a run or a lights-out shift: machine alarms or coolant flow drops, operator locates the machine, verifies level, tops it up, clears the alarm and restarts the cycle so the job is not scrapped.

Full coolant change-out on a lathe: evacuate the sump with a sump sucker, shovel/vacuum chips and sludge out of the tank, wipe or pressure-clean the tank, mix fresh coolant to ratio and refill; done every few months or between jobs.

Checking and topping off machine lubricant reservoirs on turning machines: way-lube/spindle-oil reservoir and hydraulic tank sight glasses on Swiss lathes, screw machines and turning centers, filled from a jug or pump can on a scheduled PM route.

Scheduled oil change on an older engine lathe, turret lathe or screw machine: drain the headstock/gearbox or hydraulic reservoir into a pan, dispose of used oil, replace filter, refill to sight glass with the specified oil.

instances.label: End-of-run/end-of-shift chip cleanout of the lathe's work zone: brushing, hooking and air-blasting stringy swarf off the chuck/collet, turret, tailstock, way covers and chip pan, and washing the work zone down with the coolant gun so the next setup seats correctly.
Sweeping and scrubbing the general shop floor and aisle bay serving the lathe (open floor, dust, coolant film, loose debris) at shift change or during weekly housekeeping.

Cleaning the congested floor immediately around and under the machine: piles of oily swarf, coolant/oil puddles treated with absorbent, hoses, pallets of bar stock and a chip cart in the way; chips shoveled/swept into a chip barrel.
Wiping down the machine exterior and operator station: rag-and-solvent wipe of the control panel, doors, windows, chuck and tailstock, plus wiping oil film off the bench top and machine sheet metal.

Clearing and putting away the work area's loose items between jobs: returning turning tools, inserts, boring bars, chuck keys, micrometers and gauges to the tool cart/cabinet, stowing leftover bar stock and finished parts, tossing rags, packaging and scrap offcuts.
Removing accumulated waste from the station: swapping/hauling the full chip hopper or scrap barrel to the scrap/recycling area, returning an empty, and emptying the trash bin near the machine.

tasks.label: Lift metal stock or workpieces manually or using hoists, and position and secure them in machines, using fasteners and hand tools.

instances.label: Repetitive production turning in a shop or plant: operator takes saw-cut blanks, billets or castings of 1-10 kg from a tote, bin or pallet at the machine, sets each into the hydraulic 3-jaw chuck or collet of a CNC turning center, clamps with the foot pedal, closes the door, starts the cycle, repeats for hundreds of pieces.

High-mix, low-volume job shop work: batches of 5-100 pieces of constantly changing geometry (shafts, flanges, fittings, forgings), loaded into soft jaws or special jaws on a CNC lathe; part must be seated against a stop or tapped home, occasional wrench/chuck-key work and second-op re-chucking, new part type every few hours.

Manual engine lathe / toolroom setup: irregular or odd-shaped stock mounted in a 4-jaw independent chuck, on a faceplate with bolted clamps and angle plates, or between centers with a lathe dog; operator tightens with chuck key and wrenches and dials the part in with a dial indicator to a few thousandths of runout.

Heavier chuck work, roughly 25-150 kg: casting, forging or bar section lifted with a jib crane or air hoist and sling, swung into the chuck or on the table of a large horizontal lathe or VTL, seated and clamped, sling removed.

Very heavy workpieces over ~250 kg (rolls, large housings, weldments, ring forgings) rigged with overhead crane and slings/eyebolts, landed on a vertical boring mill table or big faceplate, secured with bolted clamps, T-nuts and studs using hand tools, then trammed in; setup takes 30+ minutes.

Bar stock handling: lifting 3-4 m mill-length bars or bundles onto the magazine bar feeder rack of a CNC lathe or screw machine, or pushing bar through the spindle and clamping in the collet, plus removing remnants.

tasks.label: Install holding fixtures, cams, gears, and stops to control stock and tool movement, using hand tools, power tools, and measuring instruments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-mix job shop, CNC turning center: for the next job the setter changes the chuck top jaws (unbolts serrated soft/hard jaws with a hex wrench, mounts and torques the new set), bores the soft jaws, checks runout with a dial indicator, and sets clamping pressure. Shop floor with people, forklifts, coolant, chip carts.

Production turning shop: installing or swapping the workholding device itself on the spindle — collet chuck/clamping head with end stop, mandrel, or a part-specific holding fixture — plus setting the workstop depth and tailstock/part stop, verified with gauges and a test part.

Tool-side and stock-side setup on a CNC or turret lathe: mounting tool blocks/holders in the turret, seating and clamping them, setting turret/carriage stops and bar-feeder or bar stop position that limit stock and tool travel; presetting/measuring tool offsets.

Automated/lights-out turning cell or FMS inside a production plant: changing over the workholding (jaw pallets, zero-point fixture pallets, gripper jaws) between jobs so the fenced robot-tended cell can run the next part family unattended.

Cam-operated automatic screw machine (Davenport, Acme-Gridley, Brown & Sharpe) or older geared lathe: installing/filing lobe cams on the camshaft, swapping feed/speed change gears, setting trip dogs and slide stops, then dialing in by trial cuts.

Toolroom or large-capacity lathe: hoisting on a heavy 4-jaw chuck or faceplate, bolting a one-off custom fixture or steady rest, and indicating it true to within a few tenths with a dial indicator on a machine and fixture combination that is unique to that job.

instances.label: Toolroom/job shop, conventional engine lathe: operator bolts a hydraulic tracer (duplicating) attachment to the carriage/cross-slide, plumbs or connects its hydraulic unit, mounts the template in the template holder at the correct offset, sets the stylus contact and feed rate, then takes trial cuts and adjusts until the turned contour matches the template within print tolerance.

Manual or CNC lathe, shaft/spindle work: operator mounts and sets a taper attachment (bolt the guide bar bracket to the bed, disconnect/reconnect the cross-slide screw, set the angle from the part print or a master), dials it in with an indicator and test cut, then turns the taper.

Turret lathe or CNC turning center in a production shop: operator installs a cut-off/trimming or form-tool unit into the turret or toolpost (correct block, center height, torqued clamping), sets the tool offset, and trims workpieces to length as the operation runs.

Lathe running long slender stock: operator mounts a steady rest or follower rest (or other support attachment) on the bed ways or saddle, clamps it, and adjusts the fingers/rollers with a dial indicator to run the workpiece true before turning or trimming.

CNC turn-mill / multi-task machine: operator mounts a driven (live) tooling attachment — milling or cross-drilling head — into a turret station, clocks and torques it, verifies with probing or a test feature, and runs the added operation.

Specialty toolroom work: operator mounts a relieving (backing-off) attachment with its cams and change gears to relieve hob or tap teeth, or a knurling/spherical-turning/grinding attachment on the cross slide; sets cam throw, timing and drive, and runs a trial piece.

tasks.label: Turn valve handles to direct the flow of coolant onto work areas or to coat disks with spinning compounds.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production run on an enclosed CNC turning center in a job shop: before and during the cycle the operator opens the coolant manifold valve and bends/aims the flexible (Loc-Line) nozzles at the tool-workpiece interface for each turret station, adjusting flow so chips clear and the insert stays cooled.

Manual engine lathe or turret lathe in a general machine shop: operator opens the coolant petcock/valve and repositions the flexible nozzle onto the cut while turning, threading or facing bar stock, throttling flow up or down by hand as the cut proceeds.

Setup on a multi-spindle automatic screw machine or Swiss-type lathe: setter opens and balances a bank of coolant valves, one per tool station, and aims individual nozzles/toolholder jets at each cutting position during setup and first-piece runoff.

Metal spinning lathe: operator applies spinning compound/forming lubricant to the rotating disk blank and mandrel (valve-fed drip, spray unit, or by hand) before and during the spinning passes so the roller does not gall or tear the disk.

Troubleshooting mid-cut: operator sees smoke, discolored chips, chip nesting or a plugged/knocked-off nozzle, and by eye re-aims the nozzle, cranks the valve open, clears the blockage and verifies coolant is landing on the cutting zone.

roles.description: Set up, operate, or tend milling or planing machines to mill, plane, shape, groove, or profile metal or plastic work pieces.

tasks.label: Remove workpieces from machines, and check to ensure that they conform to specifications, using measuring instruments such as microscopes, gauges, calipers, and micrometers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production run on a CNC vertical/horizontal machining center in a job or production shop: operator opens the door, unclamps and lifts the finished metal part (0.5-20 kg) out of a vise or fixture, blows off chips/coolant, and checks key dimensions (bore, width, depth, hole positions) with calipers, micrometers and plug gauges every part or every nth part, setting aside out-of-tolerance parts.

High-mix, low-volume job shop batch (5-50 pieces) of varied metal or plastic parts: unload from the mill, quick deburr, then check several drawing dimensions with calipers, micrometers, thread and pin gauges; part geometry changes with every job and the fixture and handling differ each time.

First-article / setup piece: after the first part off a new setup, the operator removes it and verifies most drawing characteristics - many dimensions, GD&T callouts, sometimes on a surface plate or shop CMM - and records results before releasing the run.

Large or heavy workpiece on a planer mill, large gantry/bridge mill, or big horizontal boring mill: unclamping a several-hundred-kilogram to multi-ton weldment or casting, rigging and removing it with a hoist or overhead crane, then checking squareness, flatness and large dimensions with big micrometers, indicators and layout tools.

Small precision parts (medical, aerospace, electronic, and machined plastics): careful removal to avoid marring, then inspection of fine features, edge/burr condition and small dimensions under a toolmaker's microscope or optical comparator at micron-level tolerances.

tasks.label: Verify alignment of workpieces on machines, using measuring instruments such as rules, gauges, or calipers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Job-shop CNC vertical machining centre: operator clamps a small/medium prismatic metal part in a vise or fixture and verifies its location and squareness (edge find X/Y, top-face Z, check part is square to the vise jaws / not tilted) with edge finder, dial indicator, rule and calipers before starting the cut.

Production run tending several CNC mills: between parts the operator confirms each workpiece is seated correctly in its dedicated fixture (no chips under the part, clamps down, stops contacted), spot-checks position with an indicator, gauge or calipers, and reworks the setup if a part shifted.

Large casting, plate or weldment on a horizontal boring mill, planer mill or gantry machining centre: worker indicates the part in over long spans, checks parallelism to the table, squareness to the axes and available stock on a near-net-shape casting, using dial indicators, height gauge, squares and rules, often taking a long time on a heavy, awkward workpiece.

Manual knee mill or older non-CNC machine: operator sweeps/trams the head, indicates the vise parallel to the table travel, picks up edges with an edge finder and checks part position with a rule and calipers before machining.

Plastic, soft or thin-walled workpieces: worker verifies alignment and seating in soft-jaw or vacuum fixturing, checking with gauges and calipers that clamping has not distorted or lifted the part and that the datum faces are true.

tasks.label: Move controls to set cutting specifications, to position cutting tools and workpieces in relation to each other, and to start machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Contract/job-shop CNC vertical machining center, small-to-medium batches (5-200 pieces): operator calls up the program, clamps the blank in a vise or fixture on the table, establishes the work offset with an edge finder or spindle probe, measures and enters tool length/diameter offsets, jogs the axes with the handwheel to verify clearances, sets the feed and spindle overrides, and presses cycle start; adjusts offsets after the first article.

Repeat production milling in a manufacturing plant or high-volume shop: fixture already set, operator loads the blank, closes the guard door, presses cycle start, repeats every cycle across a shift while tending one to three machines, tweaks tool-wear offsets and speed/feed overrides as inserts wear, restarts after tool changes.

Manual knee mill / toolroom or maintenance shop work on one-off or repair parts: operator indicates the workpiece in a vise or on the table, sets spindle rpm with belt or variable-speed dial, sets feed rate, cranks the handwheels to bring cutter and work into relation, takes a trial cut and dials in depth, engages the power feed.

Large-part milling on a bridge/gantry mill, horizontal boring mill, or planer: crane-loaded weldment or casting on the table or a heavy pallet, operator uses the pendant to jog axes and pick up edges on the big part, sets depths of cut, speeds and feeds for long roughing passes, and starts the machine.

Plastic/composite profiling and routing in a fabrication shop: operator loads sheet or slab onto a vacuum table or fixture on a CNC router/profiler, selects and sets the cutter in the ATC or collet, sets spindle rpm and feed for the plastic being cut, positions the tool to the sheet zero, and starts the nesting/profiling cycle.

tasks.label: Observe milling or planing machine operation, and adjust controls to ensure conformance with specified tolerances.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: CNC vertical/horizontal machining center in a job or contract shop, small-to-medium batches of metal parts at ±0.001–0.002 in. The operator watches the cut (sound, chip color, spindle load), gauge-checks features between parts, and adjusts feed/speed overrides, tool-wear offsets and coolant, and swaps worn cutters, to keep dimensions in tolerance through the run.

High-volume production milling cell (automotive, appliance, medical) with repeat fixtures, automated or semi-automated part loading and in-process/post-process gauging. Operator tends several machines, watches SPC trends and machine load, trims tool offsets to re-center dimensions, and reacts to tool wear or breakage alarms.

Manual milling machine (knee mill / bed mill) or manual planer-shaper in a shop or maintenance department. Operator watches and hears the cut while hand-feeding or with power feed engaged, adjusts feed rate, depth of cut and coolant on the fly, stops to measure, and re-adjusts the dials to reach the specified size.

Milling/profiling plastic, acrylic, UHMW or composite stock on a CNC mill or router. Operator watches for melting, chip welding, burring, delamination and part deflection, adjusts spindle speed, feed and air blast/coolant, and corrects offsets for thermal growth and springback to hold print tolerance.

Large gantry mill / planer-mill machining big weldments, castings or die blocks with long, sometimes interrupted cuts. Operator observes the cut over hours, adjusts feed and depth for hard spots and scale, watches insert wear, re-indicates and re-measures the surface and compensates before the finish pass.

On-site field machining with a portable/clamp-on milling or flange-facing machine (pipe flange, pump base, in-place equipment) at a plant, ship or construction site. Operator observes the cut in a cramped, uncontrolled position and adjusts feed and depth to bring the surface within flatness/thickness tolerance.

tasks.label: Select and install cutting tools and other accessories according to specifications, using hand tools or power tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: CNC machining-center job setup in a job shop: operator reads the setup sheet/tool list, pulls end mills, shell mills, drills and holders from the tool crib, assembles cutters into collet chucks or shrink-fit holders to specified stick-out and torque, presets lengths, then loads the assembled holders into the machine's spindle/tool magazine and enters offsets.

Conventional knee or turret mill (Bridgeport-type) tooling changes: select the correct end mill, R8/collet chuck, drill chuck or boring head for the print, insert it in the spindle and tighten the drawbar with a wrench, swapping tooling several times over the course of a job in a small shop.

Large horizontal mill, planer or gantry/bed mill: mount an arbor with spacers, keys and slab/side-milling cutters and set the overarm support, or bolt a heavy face-mill body or adapter to the spindle nose using a hoist, wrenches and torque tools.

Replace worn, chipped or broken indexable inserts and clamp screws on face mills and shell mills at the bench or at the machine, indexing/rotating inserts and torquing screws to the tool manufacturer's spec before returning the cutter to service.
Install other machine accessories on the mill table: vise and soft/hard jaws, rotary table or indexer, angle plate, subplate or dedicated fixture; bolt down, then indicate in square/parallel to spec.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Job shop / high-mix small batch: operator loads small-to-medium prismatic metal blanks (0.5–15 kg) into a machine vise on a CNC vertical machining center, seats the part on parallels, taps it down, torques the vise, and verifies location on the first piece with an edge finder, indicator or spindle probe; repeats for a batch of 20–200 parts.

Higher-volume production milling: identical blanks (metal or plastic) loaded cycle after cycle into a dedicated fixture or pneumatic/hydraulic vise on a machining center; operator indexes parts against stops/locating pins, clears chips, confirms seating, and starts the cycle, tending one or more machines.

One-off / first-article setup on a manual knee mill or CNC mill: the setter improvises the workholding for a new, odd-shaped part — angle plate, strap clamps and T-bolts, shims, soft jaws, parallels — then dial-indicates the part true within thousandths, adjusts with mallet taps and re-torques clamps before releasing the job.

Very large / awkward workpieces (weldments, frames, mold bases, hundreds of kg to several tons) rigged with slings on an overhead crane onto a horizontal boring mill, planer or gantry mill table; the worker blocks, levels and sweeps the part with a dial indicator over a long table, then bolts it down with T-slot clamps and re-checks alignment.

tasks.label: Replace worn tools, using hand tools, and sharpen dull tools, using bench grinders.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: CNC machining center in a job/production shop: a solid-carbide end mill or drill is worn or chipped, so the operator pulls the toolholder, releases the cutter (ER collet nut with wrenches, Weldon set screw with hex key, or shrink-fit heater), installs a fresh cutter, cleans the taper, and re-presets length/diameter offsets before returning it to service.

Indexable tooling: worn edges on a face mill, shell mill or indexable end mill. Operator unscrews tiny Torx/Plus screws, indexes/rotates/flips or replaces each insert, cleans and inspects the pockets, replaces fatigued screws, and torques to spec at a bench or on the machine.

Tool magazine/ATC service on a machining center: pulling worn toolholder assemblies from carousel or chain pockets, loading replacement assemblies into the correct pockets, and updating the tool table/offsets so production can resume (often between jobs or during a lights-out run).

Bench/pedestal grinder work: freehand sharpening of dull tooling — twist drills, HSS end mills or single-point fly-cutter/tool bits, countersinks, deburring scrapers — judging point angle, relief and lip length by eye and gauge, dipping to avoid burning, and dressing the wheel as needed.

Manual knee mill / older planer or shaper in a toolroom or small shop: loosening the drawbar with a wrench, swapping an R8 collet or quick-change holder and cutter (or unbolting and re-shimming a planer/shaper tool bit), then re-tramming or re-touching off the tool.

Production shop, tending two to four CNC mills on repetitive high-volume jobs: engaging the automatic feed cycle over and over on standard fixtures or pallets, keeping spindles cutting through the shift, reacting to alarms and tool-life prompts.

Job shop or toolroom, conventional knee/bed mill (Bridgeport-type) or manual mode on a CNC: one-off or prototype part machined to a drawing — cranking handwheels or engaging power feed, taking roughing and finishing passes, measuring between passes to hit the dimension.

Maintenance/repair or fit-up milling: cutting a keyway, facing a boss, or milling a weldment or worn assembly to fit a mating part, cut-and-try by feel with no model or program, hand-feeding light passes and checking fit repeatedly.

Plastics/composites fabrication shop, CNC mill or 3-/5-axis router: profiling, grooving and trimming acrylic, UHMW, GRP or thermoformed parts — light cuts, watching for melting, deflection and chip/dust build-up, holding profile to spec.

Large-part shop, gantry, planer-type, floor-type boring or big five-axis mill: crane-loaded weldment, casting or assembly tool; long heavy roughing passes at engaged automatic feed, monitoring load and chip evacuation over multi-hour cycles, periodic tool changes and finishing passes.

instances.label: Production run on an enclosed CNC vertical/horizontal machining center in a job shop: flood coolant is started at the beginning of the cut and shut off at retract, coolant volume/pressure raised or lowered for different tools and the nozzle aim kept on the cutting edge as tool lengths change, part after part.

Setup of a new job on a CNC mill: operator physically bends/aims the flexible (Loc-Line style) coolant lines at the new fixture and cutter, cracks open or closes the manual ball valves/petcocks on the coolant manifold, then watches the first-article cut and throttles flow to get chip evacuation without flooding the fixture or spraying out the door.

Conventional/manual equipment (Bridgeport-type knee mill, older planer or profiler): operator flips the coolant pump switch, opens the petcock/ball valve on the flood line, aims the nozzle at the cutter by hand, pulls the one-shot way-oiler lever, and throttles the valve up or down while watching the cut and the chips.

Machine lubrication on CNC equipment: starting/verifying the way-lube and spindle lube supply at shift start, setting or checking lube cycle intervals and drip/metering rates, opening supply valves and running a purge/prime so lubricant reaches the slides and screws before cutting.

High-pressure / through-tool coolant or air-mist (MQL) work on production CNC machines: bringing up the high-pressure unit, selecting through-spindle vs. flood, and dialing pressure/flow or mist rate up and down per operation (deep pockets, drilling, plastics that melt or load up).

Machinist reworks an existing template or cutting tool at the machine to make it fit: blue-fits the template against the actual part, files/stones or regrinds a relief by hand, re-tries the fit, and iterates until the tool or template produces an acceptable part. instances.label: In-process check at the CNC or manual machine during setup and cutting: machinist stops the cycle, wipes chips, measures the just-cut diameter, bore, length or depth with a micrometer, caliper or depth mic, compares to the print, computes the deviation and the offset correction needed. Shop floor, part still in the chuck/vise, coolant and chips present.

Repeat gauging during a production run: same one to five features checked on parts every nth piece with mics/calipers/bore gauges, values recorded for SPC, trend computed and the machine adjusted when drift approaches the tolerance limit. Batch of identical parts staged in bins/trays at the machine or a nearby gauging bench.

First-article or final inspection at a bench, surface plate or inspection room: many features on one part measured with micrometers, vernier/dial calipers, bore and height gauges, gauge pins, thread mics; derived values calculated (pitch diameter over wires, taper angle by trig, true position from coordinates) and written up as an inspection report against the print's tolerances.

Verification of incoming material or a rough casting/forging before machining: measure stock diameter, thickness or casting envelope with caliper/mic, calculate available machining allowance and whether the print dimensions can be cleaned up. Done at a receiving bench or on the shop floor.

Measuring a worn, broken or undocumented component brought in for repair or duplication: machinist decides which dimensions matter, measures shaft journals, bores, threads and mating features with mics and calipers, and calculates the intended nominal dimensions and fits (allowing for wear) for the replacement part. Shop bench, no complete drawing.

In-situ measurement outside the shop: maintenance machinist takes mic/caliper/telescoping-gauge measurements of an installed bore, shaft, keyway or mating hardware on machinery in a plant or at a job site, and calculates the dimensions of the replacement part or shim. Cramped, dirty, variable access; part cannot be removed to a bench.

instances.label: Established CNC production batch (mill or lathe) in a job/production shop: machinist stands at or near the machine during the run, watches the spindle-load meter and feed/speed override displays, listens for chatter and tool squeal, checks chip color/formation and coolant flow, and nudges the feed and speed overrides as tools wear or stock varies.

First-article / new-program proveout: machinist runs a freshly posted program at 10-50% feed override, often single-block, hand on the override and feed-hold, watching the first cuts for crashes, heavy engagement, chatter and poor finish, then dials feed and speed up to production values.

Manual machining (engine lathe, knee mill, surface grinder, drill press): machinist controls and monitors feed by handwheel feel and power-feed setting and speed by belt/gear/VFD, judging cut load by sound, vibration and chip formation, and changing rpm or feed mid-cut.

Multi-machine oversight in a production shop: machinist tends 3-6 CNC machines at once, walking between them, glancing at load meters, cycle displays and finished parts, listening for abnormal noise, responding to alarms, and adjusting feed/speed overrides on each machine.

Chatter-prone or difficult-material cutting: thin-wall, long-reach, deep-hole, titanium/Inconel or heavy roughing work where the machinist continuously trims spindle rpm and feed rate during the cut to kill chatter, control heat and protect the tool and part.

Field/portable machining or in-plant maintenance machining (line boring, flange facing, on-site repair with portable machine tools at a customer plant, ship or construction site) where feed and speed are watched and trimmed by hand in an uncontrolled setting.

tasks.label: Maintain machine tools in proper operational condition.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Daily/shift upkeep of a CNC machining center or turning center in a production machine shop: clear chips out of the work zone, off fixtures/vises and out of the pan, wash down the chamber, empty or check the chip conveyor bin, top up coolant, check way-lube reservoir level, wipe doors and windows so the machine can keep running the schedule.

Metalworking-fluid care across the machines the machinist runs: checking concentration with a refractometer, adding water/concentrate to hit target, skimming tramp oil, changing coolant filters/bags, and periodic sump pump-out and clean-out with a sump vacuum before recharging.

Tooling upkeep on the machine: tracking tool wear/tool life, pulling and replacing worn cutters and indexable inserts, cleaning and inspecting toolholder tapers and the spindle taper, checking runout, and keeping the magazine/turret loaded with correct, presetted tooling.

Scheduled mechanical PM and mechanical adjustment per the builder's schedule: grease points not on auto-lube, hydraulic/gearbox/spindle-chiller oil and filter changes, air filter/regulator and coolant-pump service, replacing belts, way wipers and worn hoses, adjusting gibs and backlash, re-leveling and tightening fasteners.

Accuracy verification and compensation: running warm-up cycles, indicating spindle/table, probing a datum sphere or running ballbar/kinematics checks, checking rotary-axis pivot points, and updating compensation values so the machine holds tolerance.

Upkeep of conventional/manual machines in a job shop or toolroom (Bridgeport-type mill, engine lathe, surface grinder, saw): oil-can and one-shot lubrication, brushing/blowing chips off ways and tables, cleaning coolant trays, checking and tensioning belts, dressing and truing grinding wheels, waxing tables.

tasks.label: Fit and assemble parts to make or repair machine tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bench assembly of a machined mechanical subassembly in a job or maintenance shop (spindle cartridge, small gear/worm reducer, tool holder, indexer, fixture): press bushings/bearings onto shafts, fit keys, seals, spacers and dowel pins, torque fasteners, then indicate runout/clearance before the unit goes into a machine tool. Parts are clean and made to print.

Fitting mating machined parts to size: deburr, file, stone, lap, ream or grind a few thousandths from a bore, key slot, gib or mating face, test-fit repeatedly against the mating component until the specified slip or press fit is obtained, then assemble the pair.

Repairing an in-service machine tool on the shop floor: diagnosing the fault, breaking loose seized/dirty fasteners, stripping the affected assembly (way covers, gibs, ball screw, bearings, drive belts), replacing worn parts and reassembling and re-adjusting inside the machine's own cramped, oily geometry.

Machine-tool rebuild fitting: hand-scraping ways, gibs and dovetails to a blue contact pattern against a master straightedge or the mating part, shimming, then leveling and aligning the reassembled slides/spindle with precision levels, test bar and indicators to tenths.

Assembling large, heavy machine-tool structures with hoist or crane in an assembly bay: setting a headstock, column, turret, gearbox or drive motor onto the base, aligning and doweling, torquing structural fasteners, connecting drive trains and covers.
Off-site field repair: fitting and assembling replacement parts into installed machinery at a customer plant, mill or jobsite, in as-found conditions with portable tools and awkward access.

instances.label: Production run on a CNC lathe/mill in a job or production shop: repeatedly loading raw blanks/bar stock into the vise, chuck or collet, seating them against stops, closing the workholding, and removing finished parts, cycle after cycle for hours.

One-off toolroom, repair or maintenance setup: clamping an odd-shaped casting, weldment or worn machine part with strap clamps, parallels, shims and jacks on a manual mill, lathe or surface grinder, or indicating a unique part true in a four-jaw chuck.

tasks.label: Operate equipment to verify operational efficiency.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production machine shop, repeat CNC job: after setup, the machinist runs the machine through a trial cycle and first article, watching spindle load, coolant, tool engagement and cycle time, then keeps the machine running through the job, checking tool wear and part conformance and tweaking offsets/feeds so the machine keeps producing good parts at rate.

Job shop / prototype work, new or one-off program: machinist dry-runs and single-blocks an unproven program on a CNC mill or lathe with a novel fixture, listens for chatter and watches for interference, checks that axes, coolant and tooling behave as intended, then cuts and measures the first part and adjusts speeds, feeds and offsets before releasing the job.

Toolroom / instrument shop: after fabricating, modifying or repairing an assembly (gearbox, spindle cartridge, pump, die set, mechanical instrument, fixture), the machinist powers or cycles it on a bench or test setup and runs it through its motions to verify smooth running, correct speeds/torque and absence of binding or abnormal noise, then adjusts and re-tests.

Plant floor / maintenance shop: after repairing or rebuilding an industrial machine or machine tool in place (bearings, ways, ballscrew, hydraulics, drives), the maintenance machinist starts the machine, runs it unloaded then under load, and checks noise, vibration, heat, pressures and backlash against how the machine should run before returning it to service.

Conventional/manual equipment: machinist runs an engine lathe, knee mill, surface grinder, saw or drill press through its feeds and speeds after setup, adjustment or servicing, feeling and listening for spindle roughness, backlash, slipping belts or wheel imbalance, and takes a test cut to confirm the machine runs true.

tasks.label: Evaluate machining procedures and recommend changes or modifications for improved efficiency or adaptability.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production job shop: after running a first article or an initial lot on a CNC mill or lathe, the machinist reviews the program, tooling list, and setup sheet against actual cycle time and tool life, then recommends changes (different insert grade, higher feed/speed, fewer tool changes, revised toolpath) to the CNC programmer or manufacturing engineer, verbally and via marked-up setup documentation.

Mid-run problem diagnosis: while a job is running, the machinist observes chatter, poor surface finish, premature tool wear, or dimensional drift, forms a judgment about the cause (rigidity, workholding, coolant delivery, depth of cut strategy), and recommends a process modification to the lead/supervisor or logs it as a corrective action.

Continuous-improvement or production meeting: the machinist reviews routings, standard work, and quoted times for a family of parts with engineering and scheduling, and proposes consolidating operations, changing the machine assignment, or adopting new workholding to cut setup time.

Toolroom/maintenance machinist evaluates how a repair or replacement part is currently made or how a machine is currently set up, and recommends a modification for adaptability, e.g., making a fixture adjustable to cover several part sizes or changing a bushing design so it can be replaced without disassembly.

New job review before setup: the machinist reads the drawing, model, traveler, and prior job history for an incoming part, and recommends changes to operation sequence, datum/locating scheme, stock size, or tolerance interpretation back to engineering or the customer contact so the part runs more efficiently.

tasks.label: Diagnose machine tool malfunctions to determine need for adjustments or repairs.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Job-shop/production machine shop: parts from a running CNC mill or lathe start drifting out of tolerance or accuracy degrades over time. Machinist gauges parts, checks insert/tool condition, indicates spindle runout, checks backlash, thermal growth, workholding and chip contamination, and determines whether an offset/tool change fixes it or the machine needs alignment or repair.

Machine shop: an alarm or fault code halts the machine mid-cycle (servo overload, tool-changer/carousel fault, probe or pallet fault, coolant/chip-conveyor alarm). Machinist reads the alarm, opens guards, jogs axes, inspects the mechanism, tests, and determines whether an adjustment/reset suffices or a service repair is needed.

Machine shop, machine cutting: chatter or excessive vibration during a cut produces poor surface finish; machinist judges whether the cause is speeds/feeds, tool overhang, toolholder or fixture rigidity, and decides on the parameter change or machine service.

Machine shop: abnormal noise, heat, or smell from the machine outside the cutting process (growling spindle bearing, squealing belt, hot motor, way-lube starvation). Machinist locates the source by listening, touching, and inspecting, and determines whether adjustment, lubrication, or a component repair is needed.

Machine shop: fluid/mechanical subsystem symptoms — coolant or hydraulic leaks, low lube or air pressure, chip conveyor jam, sticky or worn ways, loose gibs. Machinist inspects lines, levels, filters and slides under and inside the machine and diagnoses the cause and remedy.

Machine shop: intermittent or electrical/control faults (failing encoder, limit switch, drive, wiring, solenoid). Machinist troubleshoots systematically across subsystems, opening electrical cabinets and panels, taking meter readings, and swapping suspect components to isolate the fault.

instances.label: End-of-run chip handling at a CNC lathe/mill in a job shop: rake wet, stringy swarf off way covers and out of the chip pan, empty the chip-conveyor discharge bucket, and drop the chips into the scrap hopper beside the machine without contaminating other alloys.

Segregating solid scrap by material: cutoffs, bar remnants, drops, and rejected parts of aluminum, mild steel, stainless, brass and titanium placed in the correct labeled gaylord/bin so the recycler's streams stay clean; occasional mixed pile must be re-sorted by hand.

Liquid and hazardous waste: pumping out a machine sump of spent water-soluble coolant and tramp oil, transferring it to labeled waste drums in the shop's satellite accumulation area, disposing of used filters, and completing the waste log for the disposal contractor.

Moving full scrap containers: pushing/towing or forking a full chip hopper, cart, or gaylord from the machine to the shop's scrap collection area or dumpster bay and bringing back an empty container so production can continue.
Routine housekeeping of the shop floor and aisles: sweeping or vacuuming up loose chips and grinding dust from open floor areas and depositing the debris in the scrap container.

Spill and residue cleanup at the machine: soaking up a coolant/oil spill with absorbent, wiping down the machine, and disposing of oily rags, spent absorbent, and small hazardous items (broken carbide inserts, grinding sludge) into the correct designated containers.

tasks.label: Lay out, measure, and mark metal stock to display placement of cuts.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Toolroom/job-shop bench layout of a small-to-medium workpiece (bar, block, plate blank up to ~50 lb): clean and coat with layout dye, establish datum edges on a surface plate, scribe cut lines and hole centers with height gauge/combination square/dividers to ~0.005-0.010 in, prick-punch centers, verify against the print.

Marking cut-off locations on raw stock at the material rack or cut-off saw: measure length of round/square bar, tube, angle or plate with tape or rule, allow for kerf and cleanup stock, and mark the cut line with soapstone, marker or scribe (often several cuts per stick, nested to minimize drop).

Layout of a large plate, weldment or fabricated blank on a layout table or shop floor: snap or scribe full-size contour and cut lines, square from reference edges, mark hole and burn locations, punch witness marks; part is moved by hoist or crane.

Repeat production/CNC setup work: check incoming stock size on a batch of blanks, mark the placement of cuts/trim lines and reference (witness) lines on each piece before rough sawing or machining, same geometry piece after piece.

Maintenance/repair layout: laying out cuts on a worn, broken or non-standard part, or on machinery installed in place (marking a keyway, a section to be cut away, or a repair patch) with no CAD model, working from measurements taken off the assembly in awkward positions.

sources.transferJustification: Related task is structural-steel layout marking rather than machinist bench layout, but the act is the same — measure the metal stock, compute where the cuts/parts fall from the drawing, and inscribe lines and centerpoints on the metal — at comparable or tighter accuracy on the same class of steel stock.

tasks.label: Separate scrap waste and related materials for reuse, recycling, or disposal.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production machinist clearing chips/swarf generated by a CNC mill or lathe: raking chip nests off fixtures and the table, blowing/washing down the enclosure, emptying the chip pan or conveyor discharge into the correct alloy-segregated hopper (aluminum vs. steel vs. stainless) at the machine on a shop floor with people and forklifts moving nearby.

Sorting solid pieces after a job: bar-end drops, plate cut-offs, scrapped/reject parts, saw slugs. Machinist judges which remnants go back to the stock rack tagged with alloy/size for reuse and puts the rest in the correct scrap bin by material (6061 vs. 4140 vs. 304 vs. brass/titanium).

Separating cutting fluid from scrap: draining/wringing coolant out of wet chips before they go to the scrap container, skimming tramp oil, and returning recovered coolant to the sump for reuse rather than sending it out as waste.

Regulated and mixed shop waste: used coolant filters, grinding sludge cakes, oily rags, spent abrasive wheels, aerosol/solvent cans and absorbent, placed into the correct labeled satellite-accumulation containers per the shop's EHS/hazmat procedure and staged for pickup.

Consolidating and moving full scrap containers: pallet-mounted chip hoppers, gaylords and drums are moved by pallet jack/forklift from the machine to the central scrap staging area or dock, empties returned to the machines.

Small job shop / toolroom with manual machines: sweeping up mixed floor debris after a job (chips, coolant-soaked sweepings, cardboard, banding, cut-off stubs, shop trash) and dividing it between the metal scrap bins and the general trash dumpster.

tasks.label: Check work pieces to ensure that they are properly lubricated or cooled.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production run on an enclosed CNC machining center or lathe in a job/production shop: between cycles and through the window the machinist verifies flood and through-spindle coolant is actually reaching the cut, watches for smoke, chip discoloration or a hot part, and re-aims Loc-Line nozzles or bumps coolant pressure when the stream is blocked by the part or fixture.

Coolant-supply condition check on the shop floor: sump level, concentration by refractometer, temperature, foam/tramp oil and smell; topping up with correctly mixed fluid so parts and tools are properly cooled on the machines the worker is running.

Manual / bench operations (engine lathe, knee mill, drill press, tapping, sawing, reaming): machinist brushes or squirts cutting oil onto the workpiece, watches and listens for smoke, chatter or squeal, touches the part to judge heat, and re-applies or pauses the cut.

Grinding and other heat-sensitive precision work (surface/cylindrical grinding, hard turning, tight-tolerance finishing): verify coolant nozzles are aimed at the wheel–work contact and delivering flow, inspect the part for burn, discoloration or thermal cracking, and let the part cool to gage temperature before measuring.

Oversize, on-site or maintenance work: portable line boring / in-situ machining of a mounted component, or machining a large weldment where coolant is hand-applied or hose-fed; worker checks by eye and touch that the cutting zone is being flooded and the part is not heating up, in a plant bay, field site or customer facility taken as found.

tasks.label: Support metalworking projects from planning and fabrication through assembly, inspection, and testing, using knowledge of machine functions, metal properties, and mathematics.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Contract/job shop: machinist receives an engineering print or 3D model for a small batch (5-50) of precision metal parts, plans the process (stock, fixturing, tooling, speeds/feeds, trig/offset calculations), programs and sets up a CNC mill or lathe, machines the parts, deburrs them, dimensionally inspects to print with micrometers/gauges/CMM, and releases inspected parts with documentation to the customer's assembly stage.

Prototype / toolroom support of an engineering project: one-off or few-off parts, often on manual mill, lathe and surface grinder; machinist selects material, works from sketches, hand-fits mating parts (stoning, lapping, scraping, reaming to fit), assembles the mechanism or fixture, checks that it functions, and iterates with the design engineer.

Production support inside a manufacturing plant: setting up and proving out a job on a CNC cell, running first-article inspection, in-process gauging and tool-offset adjustment, monitoring tool wear and part quality across a shift, segregating out-of-tolerance parts and keeping the run within print tolerance.

In-plant maintenance/repair machining: machinist measures or reverse-engineers a worn or broken machine component (shaft, bushing, gear, die detail), plans and fabricates a replacement (turning, milling, grinding, sometimes weld build-up or heat treat), then fits and installs it on the industrial machine in place and tests operation.

Precision instrument maker: fabricates small, tight-tolerance components, then assembles, aligns, adjusts and calibrates the instrument or gage (lapping, fitting, setting clearances, functional/metrological test) in an instrument shop.

Field/on-site metalworking support: shipyard, refinery, mine or construction site; machinist measures in place on existing structures or equipment, fabricates or modifies parts with portable equipment, fits them on site and verifies the result under as-found conditions.

tasks.label: Install repaired parts into equipment or install new equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bench reinstall of a repaired or newly machined component into a subassembly in the machine/maintenance shop: press-fitting bearings or bushings, seating gears, shafts and seals into a gearbox, spindle cartridge or pump end, torquing fasteners, checking fits and clearances, and turning it over by hand before release.

In-situ installation of a repaired part into a production machine on the shop or plant floor: machine stays where it stands, access is cramped and overhead or below-deck, worker refits the component, shims and indicates for alignment, torques bolts in sequence, reconnects guards/lines, and runs the machine to verify.

Mounting a new mechanical accessory or tooling onto an existing machine tool: vise, tombstone, chuck or soft jaws, rotary table, fixture plate; locate on tee-slots or zero-point interface, bolt down, indicate true, verify runout/squareness.

Installing new auxiliary equipment that requires positioning plus utility hookup: bar feeder, chip conveyor, coolant/filtration unit, tool presetter; set in place relative to the machine, align, anchor, connect power, air, coolant and signal lines, and commission.

Installing a new machine tool or large equipment in the shop: uncrate, rig and skate into position, set on leveling pads/isolators, level and anchor to the floor, connect power/air/coolant, run-in and check geometry/accuracy before handoff.

Off-site or field installation of repaired parts into a customer's equipment: mill, mine, ship, pump station or construction site; unfamiliar layout, weather or confined space, improvised rigging, fit-up problems solved on the spot with hand tools and portable machining.

tasks.label: Dismantle machines or equipment, using hand tools or power tools to examine parts for defects and replace defective parts where needed.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Machine-tool subassembly teardown in the job shop: pulling apart a lathe headstock/gear train or a mill spindle head, draining oil, breaking loose high-torque and sometimes seized fasteners in tight quarters, pulling gears and bearings with pullers/heat, inspecting races, journals and gear teeth for scoring, pitting and cracks, measuring wear with micrometers and indicators, replacing bearings/seals/gears and reassembling to clearance spec.

Bench overhaul of a removed mechanical component in the maintenance shop (centrifugal pump, gear reducer, hydraulic cylinder, valve, spindle cartridge): clamped in a vise or press, disassembled with wrenches, impact tools, pullers and heat; parts cleaned, visually and dimensionally inspected against wear limits; defective bearings, seals, wear rings, shafts replaced; unit reassembled and torqued to spec.

In-place teardown of production machinery on the plant floor (packaging machine, press, conveyor drive unit, CNC machine): lockout/tagout, removing guards and shrouds, working overhead or in awkward positions, diagnosing which component has failed, dismantling that section, replacing the defective part, and re-timing/aligning before restart.

Tooling, fixture and workholding teardown at the bench: stripping cutter bodies, toolholders, chucks, dies and fixtures; inspecting indexable inserts, jaws, locating pins, bushings, springs and screws for wear, chipping or damage; replacing the defective items and reassembling with correct torque and setting.

Precision instrument and small-mechanism teardown (dial indicators, gauges, small pneumatic tools, delicate mechanical assemblies): removing tiny screws, retaining rings and springs at a clean bench, examining parts for burrs, wear and distortion under magnification, replacing defective components and reassembling/calibrating.

sources.system: Molg robotic microfactory (with ABB Robotics)
sources.title: ABB Robotics and US start-up Molg tackle data center e-waste with robotic microfactories
sources.claim: Molg's robotic microfactory, built with ABB robots and installed at ITAD/recycling facilities, autonomously disassembles (and assembles) standardized electronic products such as servers and laptops inside a purpose-built robotic cell; it recovers components but is not documented performing wear inspection and selective replacement of mechanical parts.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic dismantling of equipment with fasteners in a fixtured cell. It marks the frontier of autonomous disassembly, but the objects are standardized low-torque electronics without corrosion, press fits or dimensional wear judgment, so it does not carry over to machinist teardown-inspect-replace work.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated unbolting/dismantling of a used assembly in a fixtured cell. Shows autonomous fastener removal is feasible at E1 for one product family, but no defect inspection of parts or replacement/reassembly is demonstrated.

sources.system: DeMoBat robot-based demonstration platform

sources.transferJustification: Related task: dismantling used equipment with powered tooling. Confirms maturity level (demonstrator) and the difficulty of perceiving aged parts, both relevant to whether machinist teardown could be automated even in a purpose-built cell.

tasks.label: Test experimental models under simulated operating conditions, for purposes such as development, standardization, or feasibility of design.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Instrumented bench/rig test of a prototype machined component or subassembly to a defined protocol in the shop's test area or a development lab: the model is clamped in a test fixture, driven/pressurized/heated to simulate service duty (speed, load, pressure, temperature), and performance data (leak rate, switching time, torque, pressure drop, temperature rise) is measured and logged for engineering. Test article and protocol are supplied; the machinist runs the rig and reports the results.

Hands-on fit-and-function trial of a one-off experimental model in the shop: the machinist assembles the prototype, turns it over by hand and then under power, listens and feels for binding, chatter, backlash or leaks, checks clearances with indicators and feeler gauges, then hand-fits, stones, shims or remachines and retries until it operates as intended.

Tryout of newly built prototype tooling, fixture, die or workholding on the machine tool under production-like conditions: mount the new tooling, run trial parts, watch for interference, part shift, chatter and burrs, inspect the trial parts, adjust setup/offsets/tooling by hand, and judge whether the design is workable.

Standardized or qualification test of prototype parts or machined test specimens per a written standard (tensile, hardness, impact, pressure/burst, leak, or dimensional acceptance) for standardization or material/design acceptance; specimens are prepared, run on lab testing machines, and results recorded on a report.

In-situ or simulated-field trial: the experimental model is installed on the host machine, vehicle or production line and operated under realistic conditions (plant floor, yard, or customer site), with the machinist rigging temporary instrumentation, observing behavior over the run, and adjusting the model between runs.

tasks.label: Set up or operate metalworking, brazing, heat-treating, welding, or cutting equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Set up and run a CNC mill or lathe for a production job in a job shop: install vise/fixture or soft jaws, load and touch off tooling, set work offsets, prove out the program, cut a first article, gauge it, tweak offsets, then run the lot.

Tend an already-set-up CNC job through a shift: load raw blanks and unload finished parts, blow off chips, deburr, gauge every nth part, correct for tool wear, change inserts, keep the machine cutting (sometimes staged for unattended overnight running).

Manual machining and one-off rework: indicate a part in on a Bridgeport, engine lathe or surface grinder to modify, salvage or fit a component to an existing mating assembly, working by feel and by measurement to a drawing or to the broken original.

Welding or brazing in the shop: MIG/TIG-weld a weldment, fixture or bracket, or repair-weld a cracked/worn part and braze a carbide tip, with fit-up, tacking and finish welds on varied, often one-off parts.

Operate cutting equipment: saw bar stock and plate to length on a horizontal bandsaw or cold saw, or cut blanks and profiles on a CNC plasma/laser/waterjet table, then unload and deslag/stack the pieces.
Heat-treat parts: load parts into a furnace or induction unit, run the harden/anneal/stress-relief/temper cycle, quench, and verify with a hardness check before release.

tasks.label: Establish work procedures for fabricating new structural products, using a variety of metalworking machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Contract/job shop: machinist receives a print or 3D model for a new machined structural component (bracket, mounting plate, frame member) in low volume, and determines the stock size, the operation sequence across saw/mill/lathe/drill, the workholding and tooling to be used, and records it as a routing and setup sheet for the job packet.

Production/OEM shop: a new structural part is entering repeat production, and the machinist establishes a repeatable procedure — machine assignments, fixture requirements, tool list, feeds and speeds, deburr and in-process inspection steps — documented so other operators can run it consistently.

Fabrication shop: a new welded or formed structural product (weldment frame, sheet-metal enclosure, formed panel assembly) requires the worker to determine flat patterns, cut/form/bend sequence, weld fixturing, and the follow-on machining operations, and to set that sequence out as the work procedure.

Plant maintenance/repair shop: a new support, guard, or structural member is needed from a rough sketch, a verbal description, or a broken sample; the machinist works out on the spot how to make it with the manual and CNC machines on hand and notes the method for future repeats.

Aerospace/defense or other regulated first-article context: the worker determines and documents the full process plan for a new structural component — machine selection, fixture concept, multi-setup sequence, and the inspection sequence required by customer quality standards (e.g., first-article documentation).

tasks.label: Install experimental parts or assemblies, such as hydraulic systems, electrical wiring, lubricants, or batteries into machines or mechanisms.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: R&D / prototype machine shop bench: machinist installs a freshly machined experimental mechanical subassembly (bracket, bearing housing, linkage, gear pack) into a test machine or rig — locate, align, shim, insert pins/dowels, install and torque threaded fasteners, check fit and free movement.

Prototype shop: wiring an experimental rig's control panel / terminal strip — cut, strip, ferrule/crimp leads and land them on screw or spring terminals on a flat mounting plate, route in ducts, label per the wiring diagram.

Prototype shop: routing and installing sensor leads and a wiring harness inside an experimental mechanism — feeding cable through frame members and confined spaces, clipping/tying, plugging connectors that require a positive click, grounding and strain relief.

Prototype shop / test cell: installing an experimental hydraulic or pneumatic system into a machine — mounting pump, valve manifold or cylinder, cutting and routing flexible hoses and rigid tube runs, starting and torquing JIC/ORFS fittings, filling reservoir, bleeding, leak-checking under pressure.

Prototype shop: service and power items before a test run — filling/greasing bearings, gearboxes and ways with specified lubricants through fittings and fill ports, and installing battery packs, power modules or accumulators plus their terminal connections.

Plant floor or customer/field site: installing an experimental part or assembly into an existing in-service machine — partial disassembly and removal of the incumbent component, working around guarding in confined access, fitting up (sometimes with on-the-spot rework), reassembly and function check.

roles.title: Metal-Refining Furnace Operators and Tenders
aliases: Arc and Argon Oxygen Decarburization Melter (ARC and AOD Melter)
roles.description: Operate or tend furnaces, such as gas, oil, coal, electric-arc or electric induction, open-hearth, or oxygen furnaces, to melt and refine metal before casting or to produce specified types of steel.

tasks.label: Regulate supplies of fuel and air, or control flow of electric current and water coolant to heat furnaces and adjust temperatures.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Steel mini-mill melt shop, AC electric-arc furnace heat: operator in the pulpit sets transformer taps/electrode regulation to drive power input, ramps oxy-fuel burners and oxygen/carbon injection through bore-in, melt-down and refining, watches water-cooled panel and roof coolant flow/temperature, and drives the bath to a target tap temperature over a ~40-60 min tap-to-tap cycle.

Foundry coreless induction furnace (gray iron, steel or non-ferrous): operator sets and trims power on the solid-state power supply as the charge sinters and melts, keeps coil cooling water flow/temperature in band, and holds the bath at pouring temperature for the day's molds, adjusting for charge additions and holding periods.

Gas- or oil-fired melting/holding furnace (crucible, reverberatory, shaft) in an aluminum, brass or secondary-smelting shop: operator lights off burners, adjusts fuel and combustion-air valves and flue dampers (or setpoints on a burner controller), and brings the bath to and holds it at temperature, judging flame and stack conditions and reacting to charge additions.

Secondary refining / oxygen steelmaking vessel: BOF blow (oxygen flow rate and lance height regulated to hit endpoint carbon and temperature) or ladle furnace / AOD / VOD (arc power, argon and oxygen flows, cooling water) reheating and trimming a heat to a narrow temperature window before casting.

Abnormal condition during a heat: water leak into a panel or induction coil, burner flameout or unstable flame, failed thermocouple or off-gas sensor, erratic arc/electrode breakage, or utility interruption. Operator inspects at the furnace, diagnoses, and intervenes by hand - backing off power, isolating and valving off a circuit, re-lighting burners, switching to manual control - to save the heat and the lining.

tasks.label: Draw smelted metal samples from furnaces or kettles for analysis, and calculate types and amounts of materials needed to ensure that materials meet specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: EAF mini-mill melt shop: near the end of melting the operator takes a bath sample and temperature with a lance through the slag door/EBT area, dispatches the disc sample to the lab (pneumatic tube), and from the returned chemistry calculates carbon and ferroalloy amounts for tap. Hot, dusty, fixed furnace position, plant-controlled premises.

Ladle metallurgy / secondary refining station: with the ladle spotted under the LF roof, the operator dips a temperature/sample probe into the ladle, gets the analysis, and calculates trim additions (FeMn, FeSi, Al, carbon) to bring the heat into grade specification before casting.

Integrated mill BOF/converter: at turndown a probe/sublance sample and temperature are taken from the converter bath; from the analysis the operator computes coolant, lime or alloy amounts needed and whether a reblow is required.

Foundry melt deck (gray/ductile iron, steel or aluminum; coreless induction furnace or cupola): the melter dips a sample cup or pours a chill coupon from the furnace, runs it on the bench spectrometer/thermal-analysis unit near the melt deck, and calculates trim alloy, carbon and inoculant additions per heat.

Nonferrous casthouse/refinery (aluminum remelt or holding furnace, copper anode furnace): the operator skims and dips a spoon or ladle sample from the furnace or transport crucible, casts a spectro disc, sends it to the plant lab, and computes alloying/hardener additions to hit the alloy spec.

instances.label: Steel mini-mill EAF: charge buckets are built to a heat recipe in the scrap bay. Steel melt shop bulk additions: lime, dolomite, carbon, DRI/HBI, pig iron and bulk ferroalloys weighed out in specified amounts (from silos, day bins, big bags or drums) ahead of charging the EAF/BOF; operator sets or verifies target weights per heat and confirms the weighed batch against the charge sheet.

instances.label: Electric arc furnace melting at a scrap-based steel mini-mill: operator works from the pulpit watching power/off-gas and bath-temperature readings, calls for immersion temperature probes at the slag door, and adjusts electrode power profile, oxy-fuel burner gas and oxygen/carbon injection to bring the heat to tap temperature.

Ladle refining furnace / AOD / holding station in the same melt shop: operator arcs and stirs the ladle to hold or raise steel temperature to the caster's aim, taking immersion temperature and sample readings between arcing steps and trimming power accordingly.

Coreless induction furnace melting iron, steel or aluminum in a production foundry: operator watches power/energy readout, checks bath with an immersion pyrometer, judges melt color and fluidity, and raises or backs off power (hold power) to keep metal at pouring temperature until the ladle is taken.

Gas- or oil-fired melting/holding furnace at a die caster, secondary aluminum plant or brass/bronze shop: operator reads bath and flue thermocouples, watches flame and metal surface, and turns fuel valves or adjusts burner controls to hold the metal within the required temperature band during charging and dosing.

Cupola furnace melting iron in a jobbing or captive iron foundry: operator watches blast pressure/volume, coke bed condition and the color and fluidity of the tapped iron, and adjusts blast, oxygen enrichment and charge to keep iron temperature on aim over a long campaign.

Small jobbing, specialty or art shop with an older manually valved crucible/pot furnace and little instrumentation: frequently changing alloys and charge sizes, operator judges readiness mainly by metal color and fluidity plus an occasional hand-held pyrometer and cracks the gas valve up or down by feel.

tasks.label: Inspect furnaces and equipment to locate defects and wear.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Between-heats condition check of the hot vessel's refractory lining and hot face at a steel mill or large melter (EAF hearth/banks/slag line, BOF, ladle, torpedo): the operator looks into the open vessel from the deck or through the slag door to find erosion, thin spots, cracked or spalled brick, and hot spots, and decides whether gunning or repair is needed before the next heat. Hot (1,400-1,700 C), dusty, time-boxed to the tap-to-tap window.

Routine shift round of the furnace exterior and auxiliary equipment in a melt shop or foundry: walking fixed routes and platforms to look and listen for water/steam leaks in cooled panels and spray rings, hydraulic and oil leaks, damaged hoses, cables and bus tubes, shell hot spots, cracked ducting and fume hood, drive and gauge condition; anomalies noted and reported. Non-contact observation, radiant heat, dust, noise.

Hands-on periodic check of wearing hardware and mechanisms on and around the furnace: electrode clamps and contact pads, burner and lance tips, tuyeres, slide-gate/stopper hardware, porous plugs, door seals and gaskets, wear plates and fasteners, play in tilt and swing mechanisms. Requires reaching in, opening covers, wiping soot, touching and moving parts, sometimes gauging with a rule or feeler.

Foundry melt-deck lining check on an induction or crucible furnace: after pour-out the operator looks into the emptied crucible for cracks, slag-line erosion, metal penetration and thin spots at the wall/floor joint, logs the observation, and judges whether the lining is good for further heats or must be pushed out. Cramped deck, sand and dust, small crew.

Scheduled downtime or pre-relining inspection of the cooled vessel and structure: entering or reaching into the furnace, sounding refractory with a hammer for loose or delaminated brick, checking shell welds, cooling-panel tubes, bottom and tap-hole area, and mapping defects to scope the repair. Confined, debris-strewn, lit by portable lamps.

Fault-finding inspection triggered by abnormal indications (suspected water leak into the bath, sudden shell hot spot, unusual arcing or vibration, pressure loss): the operator searches the area, isolates and confirms the source, judges severity, and decides whether to keep running. Unpredictable location, time pressure, sometimes partial disassembly.

instances.label: Electric-arc or basic-oxygen melt shop: operator sequences and directs (or radio-guides the crane operator for) the overhead charging crane that lifts a loaded scrap bucket from the charging aisle, positions it over the open furnace with the roof/doghouse swung clear, and drops the charge; repeated for second and third buckets each heat, in heat, dust and poor visibility.

Melt deck of a steel shop: operator adds weighed fluxes, lime, carbon, ferroalloys and slag conditioners to the furnace or ladle each heat — dumping bags or shoveling from a barrow through the slag door/ladle top, or loading day bins and hoppers that chute the additions in, adjusting quantities to the heat chemistry.

Foundry melt department: operator makes up charges of returns, pig iron, scrap, coke and limestone — weighing them and loading charge buckets, skips or conveyors by hand, with a hoist or a small loader — and feeds them into a coreless induction furnace or cupola, keeping the charge level topped up during the melt.

Non-ferrous cast house or secondary smelter: operator charges sows, ingots, T-bars and baled scrap into a reverberatory/rotary melting furnace using a charge machine, forklift or hoist, and adds salt/cover flux and alloying metal to the bath.

Start-up and light-off: operator kindles the fire — lighting burners or a pilot torch on a gas- or oil-fired melting furnace, ladle preheater or dryer, or firing up a cupola coke bed — verifying flame before bringing the unit up to temperature.
