instances.label: EAF mini-mill / scrap processing yard: operator works the scrap bay with a magnet or grab crane, segregating incoming scrap by grade, picking out contaminants (copper meatballs, wire, sealed containers, non-conforming pieces) and building charge buckets to a melt recipe; dusty bay, trucks and railcars moving in and out.

Foundry / cast house melt deck: selecting, weighing and staging charge material - ingot and sows, foundry returns, ferroalloys, carbon and lime - into charge buckets, vibratory chargers or charge cars ahead of the melt; includes hand-opening alloy bags and shoveling carbon/flux into the charge.

Applying chemicals: spraying refractory wash/coating onto ladles, launders and charge boxes, metering covering fluxes, dross-treatment or refining agents onto/into the melt, spraying wetting agents on dusty charge; done with hand lance or sprayer close to hot equipment.

Crushing/sizing: running a jaw crusher, shredder or breaker to size oversize returns, slag, skulls and lumpy alloys down to chargeable size; hopper fed by loader, shovel or crane, bridging and jams cleared by hand.

Cleaning the charge area: shoveling and raking spilled charge material, fines, sand and slag debris around the furnace and charging deck so material can be staged and loaded; hot, congested, cluttered floor with hoses, tools and traffic.
Raking/skimming dross, slag and skulls off the bath and furnace sill so the next charge can be loaded cleanly; long-handled rake or paddle at an open furnace door.

tasks.label: Remove impurities from the surface of molten metal, using strainers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Aluminium cast house / secondary smelter: operator opens the door of a melting or holding reverberatory furnace and skims dross off several tonnes of molten aluminium with a rake/paddle (hand tool or machine-mounted boom) before alloying and casting; heat, fume, dross dumped to a bin.

Iron or steel foundry melt deck: coreless induction furnace bath is dusted with coagulant and the slag is raked off the open bath surface with a hand rake or skimmer into a slag pot before tapping into the pour ladle; also a quick skim of the transfer ladle.

Steel mill: hot-metal or steel ladle deslagging at a desulfurization / EAF-BOF station — ladle tilted on a car, slag raked off the bath surface with a skimmer paddle into a slag pot, endpoint judged by appearance to limit iron loss.

Die casting or permanent-mold shop: dross skimmed each cycle/shift from the small bath of a holding furnace or dip well beside the machine with a perforated ladle or skimmer, dross dropped into a dross pan next to the furnace.

Small jobbing / nonferrous / precious-metal shop: crucible or pot furnaces (brass, bronze, zinc, lead, silver) of varied size and position; flux added and impurities lifted off with a hand strainer or perforated ladle, small batches, frequent alloy and vessel changes.

instances.label: Aluminium casthouse / secondary-aluminium plant: tender spreads measured granular drossing or cover flux over the bath of a reverberatory melting or holding furnace through the charge door (shovel, chute or lance) before stirring and skimming; hot, fume-filled furnace bay, fixed furnace positions, rail/forklift traffic.

Aluminium or copper-alloy foundry melt deck: operator treats a 200-1,000 lb transfer ladle or crucible, adding a weighed dose of cleaning/drossing flux (plus degasser) to the melt, working it into the bath, then letting the dross float for skimming before pour.

Iron/steel foundry coreless induction melt deck: operator sprinkles slag coagulant/fluxing agent over the bath of a 2-12 t induction furnace after melt-down or trim additions, so slag gathers on the surface for raking; furnace lid open, standard melt-deck layout and tools.

Steel mini-mill EAF or ladle-metallurgy furnace: lime, dolomitic lime and spar charged onto the bath to build and condition slag for desulfurization/deoxidation, either through the roof chute/fifth hole hoppers or hand-added bags at the ladle during tap or heating.

Small non-ferrous jobbing shop: gas-fired crucible furnace, varied alloys and crucible sizes, low volume; operator scoops flux powder from a bucket, sprinkles it over a small bath, stirs with a rod, waits for dross to rise; cramped, ad hoc melt area.

Secondary lead / zinc kettle refining: operator sprinkles sulfur, caustic soda or other reagents over a stirred kettle of molten lead to bring copper and other impurities up as dross; fixed kettle line, heavy fume/lead-exposure controls.

Periodic clean-out of a crucible, holding furnace or ladle after draining: chipping and scraping hardened oxide/corundum skulls and adhered metal off the walls, bottom and lip. Irregular, hard, unpredictably located deposits; confined access; hot or cooled vessel.

Scraping and cleaning accumulated oxide, coating residue and metal build-up off ingot molds, sow molds and permanent molds/dies, either between cycles at the casting station or during a scheduled off-line mold cleaning.

Shoveling, sweeping and scraping oxide, dross fines and frozen metal splash off the shop floor around the furnace front, charge door, pouring aisle and under ladle/launder positions, and moving the material into a collection bin. Congested area with hoses, pans, tooling, forklift and crane traffic.

Processing the collected skimmings and sweepings for reclamation: cooling and breaking the dross, sifting/screening it to separate recoverable metal from oxide fines, and binning, labeling and storing the fractions for remelt or sale.

roles.title: Pourers and Casters, Metal

tasks.label: Pour and regulate the flow of molten metal into molds and forms to produce ingots or other castings, using ladles or hand-controlled mechanisms.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume iron foundry: operator at a fixed pouring station on a horizontal or vertical green-sand molding line uses a pendant/joystick-controlled tilting or bottom-pour ladle (or pouring furnace) to fill molds indexing past on a conveyor; same pattern for long runs, controlled fill weight and pour time, in-stream inoculation.

Jobbing/short-run iron or steel foundry mold line: many different patterns per shift, pour weights, cup sizes and pour times change frequently; operator adjusts flow by eye and by ladle tilt/stopper as flasks index past the pouring station.

Hand-ladle work on the foundry floor: worker carries or shares a hand/bull ladle (or uses a monorail ladle) and pours a series of bench molds, floor molds, permanent molds or investment shells set out on the shop floor in positions that change job to job; nonferrous, jobbing and art/bronze shops.

Large castings: ladle of 1-20 t carried by overhead crane or monorail to floor/pit molds; operator regulates flow with a stopper rod, slide gate or tilt control, sometimes moving between multiple pouring basins on one mold, with slag skimming between pours.

Die casting / gravity permanent-mold shop: worker hand-ladles or operates a ladling mechanism to dip aluminum or brass from a holding furnace and pour a metered charge into a shot sleeve or open metal mold at a fixed machine, cycle after cycle.

Ingot, anode, pig or sow casting at a primary/secondary metals plant: operator regulates the stream from a tilting furnace, launder gate or teeming ladle into ingot molds carried on a casting wheel or chain conveyor, watching fill level and weight.

tasks.label: Read temperature gauges and observe color changes, adjusting furnace flames, torches, or electrical heating units as necessary to melt metal to specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Iron/steel jobbing or production foundry melt deck: operator melts a charge in a coreless induction furnace, dips an immersion thermocouple / watches bath color and panel gauges, and raises or cuts furnace power (hold power) to bring the heat to the specified tap temperature before pouring.

Nonferrous (aluminum, zinc, brass) die-casting or foundry melting and holding furnaces, gas-fired shaft/reverberatory or electric crucible/dosing units: operator reads bath thermocouple/pyrometer gauges and trims burner gas-air or heating-element settings to keep metal within a narrow pouring-temperature band all shift.

Steel melt shop / large melt facility: operator in a pulpit follows EAF or ladle-furnace bath temperature probes and off-gas data and adjusts the electrical power profile, burners and oxygen to reach the required tap/casting temperature; tundish temperature checked before the cast.

Small job shop or art/bronze foundry: gas-fired crucible or small induction furnace, varied alloys and small heats, readiness judged by melt color plus a hand pyrometer, operator manually adjusts gas/air valves or the power dial to reach pouring temperature.

Precision small-melt casting (jewelry, dental, investment/vacuum casting lab): a few hundred grams to a few kilograms of gold, silver or alloy melted in an induction or torch unit, watched for the correct color/mirror surface and held at a set casting temperature.

Hand-torch heating work around the pour: preheating ladles, tundishes, molds, runners or small melts with gas torches, judged largely by color of the refractory or metal, sometimes at a nonstandard or temporary work location outside the fixed melt deck layout.

tasks.label: Remove solidified steel or slag from pouring nozzles, using long bars or oxygen burners.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Continuous caster, steel mill: the ladle slide gate fails to free-open when the ladle is set on the turret over the tundish. The pourer brings an oxygen lance to the collector nozzle under the ladle and burns out the solidified steel/sand plug so the heat can start, working on the casting platform amid heat, fume and possible steel spray, under time pressure.

Between heats on the caster: removing the skull of frozen steel and slag from the ladle shroud / collector nozzle bore and the tundish nozzle seat, using an oxygen burner or bar in the ladle area so the next shroud can be coupled and flow is unobstructed.

Ladle preparation / relining bay: an emptied steel ladle is set down and the worker burns solidified steel out of the slide-gate plates, inner nozzle and well block with an oxygen lance and long bars before refractory pieces are changed. Off-line, at a fixed stand, not time-critical.

Steel or iron foundry pouring floor: a bottom-pour (stopper-rod) or teapot ladle nozzle skulls or slags over between molds. The pourer rods the nozzle with a long bar, or burns it open with an oxygen torch, between pours on a molding line or floor-pour bay, with ladles of varying size parked in varying positions.

Mid-cast blockage: the tundish nozzle / submerged entry nozzle partially clogs with alumina or a chilled skull while steel is flowing; the caster rods it from the platform with a long bar down through the hot tundish bath, judging by flow and stream shape when it is clear, without breaking refractory.

Ingot teeming or specialty shop: clearing slag and frozen steel from a bottom-pour teeming ladle nozzle, trumpet or runner nozzle between ingot sets, and chipping/burning skull from pouring spouts of smaller ladles, in a teeming aisle with varied equipment.

tasks.label: Examine molds to ensure they are clean, smooth, and properly coated.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume iron/steel foundry, automatic green-sand molding line: before each pour at the autopour station, the caster checks molds moving on the conveyor for broken cope/drag edges, loose or crumbled sand in the cavity, and that cores, filters and inoculant are in place; bad molds are pulled or the line is stopped.

Jobbing/floor foundry: no-bake or hand-rammed sand molds of varying size staged on the pour floor in varied positions; before pouring, the worker walks the line of molds, looks into each cavity, blows or brushes out loose sand, checks the refractory mold wash for even coverage and smooth finish, and patches or re-coats where needed.

Aluminum/brass die-casting or gravity permanent-mold cell: between shots the operator checks the open die faces for stuck metal, flash, soldering and residue, verifies that the die coat / release agent has been applied evenly over the cavity, and blows off or re-sprays before the die closes for the next pour.

Investment casting foundry: ceramic shell molds staged at the pouring station; the caster examines each shell for cracks, spalled coating layers, debris in the pour cup and general surface condition before molten metal is poured.

Steel mill or nonferrous plant casting bay: large cast-iron ingot molds, anode molds or ingot-chain molds; before teeming, the worker inspects mold interiors for scale, metal build-up, cracks and correct mold dressing/wash, often at a distance and with the molds hot.

sources.transferJustification: Directly the same task (examining moulds for surface integrity and cleanliness before pouring). For the investment-casting instance the transfer is to ceramic shell moulds: the same friable refractory mould bodies, the same crack/break-off defect classes and the same foundry line environment and cycle-time constraints.

tasks.label: Collect samples, or signal workers to sample metal for analysis.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Steel melt shop (EAF/BOF/ladle furnace/tundish): during the heat the caster/pourer takes a combined temperature-and-chemistry immersion sample, fitting a cartridge on a lance, dipping it to a set depth in the bath or ladle at the furnace or LF station, then withdrawing and passing the sampler on. Heat, spatter, fume; ladle arrives on a ladle car or turret.

Iron/steel foundry melt deck: operator at a coreless induction (or cupola) furnace dips a thermocouple lance and a spoon or immersion sampler into the bath, pours the metal into a thermal-analysis quick cup / chill wedge or coin mold, and carries the solidified sample to the melt-lab spectrometer before tapping.

Jobbing/production foundry pouring floor: pourer samples molten iron from a treatment or pouring ladle hanging from a crane or monorail at whatever position it happens to stop, between magnesium treatment and pouring molds; congested floor, moving ladles, sand, variable ladle height and slag cover, tight time window before the metal cools.

Non-ferrous casthouse / die-cast melt shop (aluminum, brass, zinc): caster takes a sample from a holding, dosing or transport crucible, or from the launder, pouring a disc/coupon sample mold, and delivers it to the spectrometer before the cast is released.

No handling by the pourer: at the right point in ... tap or cast the pourer signals (hand signal, horn, radio, or call to the pulpit) a sampler, lab technician or furnace operator to take the sample, and confirms timing and heat identity.

Sample retrieval and dispatch: after the immersion sampler or cup solidifies, the pourer breaks out the sample coin/lollipop, labels it with the heat number, loads it into a pneumatic-tube carrier or tray and sends it to the lab, then holds the pour until the analysis returns.

tasks.label: Load specified amounts of metal and flux into furnaces or clay crucibles.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Iron/steel foundry melt deck: charging a coreless induction furnace for a heat — weighed scrap, pig iron, borings and internal returns brought to the furnace (crane/magnet, charge bucket or vibratory charge feeder), plus weighed ferroalloy and slag-coagulant/flux additions to the bath. Hot, dusty, fume-laden melt deck; charge weights specified by the melt recipe.

Aluminium casthouse or secondary/recycling plant: charging a melting or holding furnace with sows, T-bars, baled and loose scrap and internal returns delivered in charge boxes/bins, with salt or cover flux added with the charge; each charge weight logged against the furnace recipe.

Die-casting or permanent-mold shop: keeping a crucible/stack melting or holding furnace topped up by loading standard alloy ingots (pallets or racks of ~10-25 lb bars) into the melt pot on a level-driven cycle, several times per shift.

Melt-treatment additions: weighing out and adding measured flux, degassing/cover flux, grain refiner, inoculant or nodulizer into a crucible, holding furnace or treatment ladle before pouring, per a written charge/treatment sheet.

Small non-ferrous job shop (brass/bronze/aluminium): hand-charging a lift-out or tilting crucible furnace with mixed, irregular material — cut-up gates, sprues, biscuits, odd ingot and customer scrap — weighed on a floor scale, then hand-fluxing with a powder cover flux and a plunger bell.

Art-bronze, investment-casting or precious-metal shop: weighing a small heat (a few kg to ~100 kg) of a specific alloy plus borax/flux into a clay-graphite crucible in a bench or tilting furnace; alloys, crucible sizes and charge recipes change from job to job.

tasks.label: Position equipment such as ladles, grinding wheels, pouring nozzles, or crucibles, or signal other workers to position equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume iron/steel foundry molding line: the pourer positions the lip-pour or bottom-pour ladle (on a monorail, trolley, or pouring furnace carriage) so its nozzle sits over the sprue cup of each mold as the mold string indexes past, adjusting nozzle height and lateral alignment for 100-500 molds/hour, and repositions it to refill from the holding furnace.

Jobbing or small sand foundry: molds of varying size are laid out on the floor or on a bench; the worker positions a shank, hand, or crane-hung ladle over each sprue, sets crucibles into and out of the melting furnace with tongs/shanks, and re-aims the pouring lip between differing jobs each heat.

Non-ferrous die casting / permanent mold cell: position the ladle into the holding furnace bath and then over the shot sleeve or mold cavity at the machine; set the crucible in the melter and position the pouring spout/nozzle for each shot.

Steel mill continuous caster: position the ladle on the turret arm, align and connect the ladle shroud/collector nozzle, set the tundish submerged entry nozzle and stopper, and signal the turret/crane operator for final alignment before opening the pour.

Signal and guide other workers: hand-signal a crane or transfer-car operator to lift, swing, and lower a filled ladle onto the pouring stand, treatment station, or skip, guiding it into position in a hot melt-shop bay with the pouring crew nearby.
Cleaning/finishing area: position grinding wheels, cut-off wheels, or the casting against them to remove gates, sprues, and flash after pouring; set the wheel/tool standoff for the casting at hand.

tasks.label: Skim slag or remove excess metal from ingots or equipment, using hand tools, strainers, rakes, or burners, collecting scrap for recycling.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Aluminium/non-ferrous cast house or remelt plant: caster skims dross off the bath of a large melting or holding furnace through the furnace door with a rake/skim plate before and between casts, pulling the dross into a dross pan that is taken to recycling. Radiant heat, fume, standard reverb furnace geometry, fixed casthouse layout.

Iron/steel melt shop or foundry: a filled ladle (tap, treatment or pouring ladle) is set on a stand or tilter at a deslagging/treatment station and the worker rakes floating slag off the metal surface with a rake or strainer into a slag pot before the metal is poured; slag/skull sent to recycling.

Jobbing iron/brass foundry floor: worker skims slag with a hand skimmer from a small hand or monorail ladle while moving down a row of floor molds, wiping the lip clean between pours, and drops the skimmings into a scrap bucket. Ladle position and pour sequence vary shot to shot.

Die-cast or permanent-mold shop: worker skims dross off the crucible/holding furnace bath before each hand ladle, scrapes the ladle clean, and returns the skim to the remelt bin, several times an hour at a machine-side furnace.

Ingot/pig handling: after stripping, worker removes excess metal — fins, flash, overpour lugs, frozen dribble — from ingots, pigs or sows using hand tools, chisels, grinders or a cutting torch, and throws the pieces into a remelt scrap bin.

Equipment cleaning: worker burns or chips solidified skulls and metal build-up off ladle lips, spouts, launders, pouring troughs, furnace door sills, tundishes and ingot molds using an oxygen lance/burner, bar or air hammer, then collects the scrap for remelt. Build-up shape and location differ every time.

tasks.label: Transport metal ingots to storage areas, using forklifts.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Primary/secondary aluminum or ingot plant cast house: strapped ingot bundles, sow stacks or T-bars (roughly 1–3 t) are picked with ingot forks from a fixed take-off/staging station at the end of the casting line and driven down marked plant aisles to indoor warehouse floor rows; repetitive cycles on flat concrete, mixed forklift and pedestrian traffic, WMS-recorded lot locations.

Small job-shop foundry (iron, brass/bronze, specialty alloys): after a pour the caster stacks pigs, small ingots or remelt returns onto pallets, into tubs or as loose stacks and forklifts them to whatever open floor space is free in the storage bay; floor cluttered with sand, hoses, flasks and pattern boxes; load shapes vary and drop spots are chosen by eye.

Hot-end move: warm/freshly demolded ingots or sows are carried clear of the casting machine or furnace area to a cooling or storage area; radiant heat, occasional spatter and scale, water and debris on the floor, close work around the caster and other mobile equipment.

Outdoor plant yard: bundles are carried out of the cast house across the yard to outdoor storage rows, or loaded onto flatbed trucks or rail cars; asphalt or concrete pad, rain/snow/glare, sloping ramps, other yard traffic.

Storage-area housekeeping and retrieval: locating and pulling a specific ingot lot from block stacks or racking, restacking and consolidating rows, weighing/tagging and staging bundles for shipment inside the plant warehouse.

tasks.label: Assemble and embed cores in casting frames, using hand tools and equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume automated green-sand line (DISAMATIC vertical, matchplate, or horizontal flask): every cycle the worker takes cored parts' sand cores from a rack or core mask station beside the moulding machine, blows off loose sand, and sets one or several cores into the mould cavity (or into the core mask) within a 9-30 second window, repeat parts, cores of a few kg.

Medium-volume repeat production in a conventional iron/steel foundry: mould halves (drag) arrive on a roller/trolley line, worker lifts cores of 5-100 kg (sometimes with a pneumatic balancer), seats them into core prints, checks fit and clearance, tapes or pastes joints, blows out loose sand, and signals the mould to close.

Core assembly at a bench or assembly jig in the core room: gluing/pasting core halves and several sub-cores into a core package or core stack using hot-melt or core paste, deflashing edges with hand tools, checking with gauges/fixtures, before the package goes to the moulding line.

Jobbing / one-off or very short-run large castings: floor or pit moulds, heavy cores (hundreds of kg to tons) rigged with hoist or overhead crane, hand-fitted into prints, shimmed and levelled, chaplets set, vents cut, joints sealed with mud/daubing, each job a different geometry.

Permanent-mold, semi-permanent-mold or low-pressure casting: fragile sand cores placed into hot metal dies each machine cycle (turntable or shuttle machines), with tight seating tolerances, blow-off of loose sand, and hot, radiant working conditions.

tasks.label: Turn valves to circulate water through cores, or spray water on filled molds to cool and solidify metal.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Steel mill continuous caster: operator opens/sets secondary-cooling spray water valves and mold water flows for each cooling zone, then adjusts them as casting speed, section size or steel grade change during the heat; hot, steamy caster floor under pulpit oversight.

Aluminum or copper direct-chill cast house: operator turns on and ramps mold cooling water to the casting table at the start of a drop, adjusts flow per casting recipe through the drop, and shuts water off at the end; casting pit with standard tooling.

Die casting or gravity permanent-mold foundry: operator turns valves to circulate cooling water through die cooling lines and core cooling circuits, throttling flow between shots to hold die and core temperature so the casting solidifies correctly.

Ingot or pig casting machine line in a cast house: operator turns on and trims the water spray headers that spray cooling water onto filled molds (and mold undersides) travelling on the chain conveyor so ingots solidify before discharge.

Jobbing sand or investment foundry floor: worker hand-hoses or sprays water onto filled molds, flasks, chills, or freshly shaken-out castings set out on the floor in varying positions to speed cooling before shakeout; heat, steam, clutter, no fixed presentation.

sources.system: DynaJet Flex spray cooling + Dynacs 3D secondary-cooling model
sources.title: A New Strategy for Secondary Cooling in Continuous Casting
sources.claim: Primetals' DynaJet Flex secondary cooling system with the Dynacs 3D model automatically computes and controls spray-water setpoints along a continuously cast strand as a function of casting speed, format and grade - the valve/spray-water regulation that cools and solidifies the metal.

sources.claim: The automatic spray-cooling system was started up industrially on an operating two-strand slab caster at Hyundai Steel's Dangjin plant, i.e., running in a working steel mill rather than a laboratory.

tasks.label: Pull levers to lift ladle stoppers and to allow molten steel to flow into ingot molds to specified heights.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume iron/steel foundry: bottom-pour ladle or pressure-pour vessel with stopper rod parked over molds indexed past a fixed pouring station on a molding-line conveyor. The pourer works the stopper lever to choke the sprue, hold a full cup, and cut off at the specified level, dozens of molds per hour.

Jobbing / medium-volume foundry: crane- or monorail-carried bottom-pour ladle with stopper rod teemed into flask molds and floor molds laid out around the pour aisle in arrangements that change heat to heat; worker pulls the stopper lever, walks the ladle mold to mold, and fills each downsprue/riser to a marked height judged by eye.

Specialty-steel / forging shop ingot teeming: ladle on a crane or casting car over a trumpet (uphill teeming) or over open ingot molds; teemer opens the stopper/slide gate, regulates the stream against splash and skulling, fills each mold to the hot-top mark, closes, and indexes to the next mold of the set.

Continuous / semi-continuous casting platform in a steel mill: caster operator opens the ladle stopper or slide gate to fill the tundish to the set level, then works the tundish stopper to hold the metal level in the mold at the specified height for the whole heat, including start-of-cast filling and ladle changes.

Off-normal pours in any of the above shops: nozzle oxide build-up or clogging, cold or skulled ladle, sticking or leaking stopper, mid-pour ladle change, mold that will not take metal or runs out. Worker must re-throttle the flow, lance the nozzle open, or abort and divert the heat while still delivering a sound casting.

tasks.label: Remove metal ingots or cores from molds, using hand tools, cranes, and chain hoists.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-pressure die casting / gravity permanent-mold shop: after the die opens and ejector pins push the part out, the caster pulls the shot (casting plus sprue and runners) from the die half with tongs or by hand, checks that no slug or flash remains in the cavity, and sets the part on a conveyor or quench; cycle repeats every 30-120 seconds in a hot, oily cell.

Green-sand production foundry shakeout: flasks of poured, cooled sand molds arrive from the molding line; the worker knocks or pries the casting and sand lump out of the flask, uses a bar, hook or air chisel to free stuck castings, separates gating, and moves castings to a conveyor or pallet box, occasionally slinging heavier ones with a chain hoist.

Ingot/pig casting in a primary or secondary metals plant (aluminum, zinc, lead, copper, iron): solidified ingots are stripped from chill molds on a chain or wheel caster, rapped free with hammers or bars when they stick, and lifted or tipped clear of the molds; larger ingots and mold trains are handled with an overhead crane and tongs, then stacked and bundled.

Core knockout on cooled castings: cylinder heads, blocks, valve bodies, pumps and pipe fittings are rapped with pneumatic hammers, chisels and hand tools, or loaded into a vibrating/hammering decore unit, to break out and shake free the sand or ceramic cores that formed internal passages, then checked that cavities are clean.

Jobbing or art foundry, one-off or heavy work: a floor/pit sand mold or an investment shell holding a unique casting is broken away with sledge, chisel and air hammer; the caster rigs the casting with chain hoist and overhead crane, works it loose from the mold or flask, and lands it in the cleaning area; geometry and mold layout differ from job to job.

tasks.label: Repair and maintain metal forms and equipment, using hand tools, sledges, and bars.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Ladle preparation station in a melt shop: after a heat the caster services the ladle's pouring hardware - burns/scrapes solidified metal out of the nozzle bore with a lance and bar, inspects the slide-gate or stopper for wear, replaces worn refractory plates/nozzles and gaskets, tightens the mechanism and refills the well with sand so the ladle is ready for the next pour.

Hot, dirty de-skulling and patching: knocking accumulated slag, dross and frozen metal off ladle lips, shells, pouring spouts, troughs and tundish/mould rims with a sledge, bar and chipping hammer, then chipping out damaged refractory and patching it with ram mix or gunning material before the next cast.

Mechanised casting line or die-casting cell: routine conditioning of the metal form between casts - blowing/scraping residue and flash out of the cavity, wire-brushing or cleaning the faces, and applying mould wash or release coating so the form keeps producing sound castings.

Foundry floor / maintenance bay: mechanical repair of metal moulds, permanent-mould halves, flasks, jackets and mould frames - prying seized sections apart with bars, driving and straightening bent bars, pins and clamps with a sledge, replacing pins, bushings and bolts, and tack-welding or grinding cracked and worn areas.

Servicing pouring equipment and auxiliaries between shifts: ladle tilt gear and trunnions, pouring furnace spouts, launders and runners, mould conveyor components and shanks - inspecting for wear, breaking out solidified metal, lubricating, tightening fasteners and swapping worn liners and consumable parts using hand tools and bars.

sources.system: INTERSTOP LPA (Ladle Preparation Area automation) robotic cell
sources.title: INTERSTOP Automation, Robotics and Digitalisation Solutions for Flow Control Technology | RHI Magnesita
sources.claim: RHI Magnesita's INTERSTOP LPA robotic cell performs ladle-preparation-area maintenance work: hydraulic cylinder handling and oxygen lancing, ... (exchange) of ladle slide-gate refractory parts, and cleaning of the inner nozzle surface, with the worker's role changed to supervisor of the robotic operation.
sources.transferJustification: Slide-gate plate exchange and nozzle-bore cleaning is precisely the 'repair and maintain equipment' work a caster does at the ladle prep station: removing solidified metal, judging wear and replacing worn refractory hardware.

sources.transferJustification: Same task: periodic maintenance of the ladle slide ... - cleaning solidified steel from the nozzle, assessing wear and replacing 20 kg refractory plates - carried out at a dedicated maintenance station.

sources.claim: Danieli's Q-Robot Cast Ladle is a robotic cell on the continuous-casting floor (demonstrated at ABS in Italy, ordered for Ma'anshan) that performs ladle-area operations including shroud handling with automatic cleaning and automatic detection of the ladle nozzle position, supervised autonomously by its own control system.
sources.transferJustification: Handling and cleaning of ladle pouring hardware (shroud, nozzle) in a fixed robotic cell is the mechanised equivalent of a caster servicing pouring equipment at the ladle station.

sources.system: Laserax Robot Laser Cleaning Machine / Robot Cell
sources.title: Robot Laser Cleaning Machine | Laserax
sources.claim: Laserax sells an enclosed robot laser-cleaning cell in which a robot arm carries the laser head over complex shapes and multiple surfaces to strip residue and contaminants from metal parts, running continuously in industrial plants.

sources.claim: Primetals supplies a single-purpose automatic device that opens the EAF slag door and cleans the door and slag channel, removing slag build-up that operators otherwise clear by hand.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (automatic removal of solidified slag from fixed furnace equipment) shows the limit of what is automated: a dedicated device on one fixed geometry, not general de-skulling of ladles, spouts and moulds.

tasks.label: Add metal to molds to compensate for shrinkage.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume iron foundry, horizontal or vertical green-sand molding line: molds index past a pouring station and the pourer fills each mold, holding the sprue/pouring cup full and adding metal as the level sinks so the sprue and riser feed solidification shrinkage; cycle times 10-30 s per mold, hot and smoky but the mold presentation is fixed and repetitive.

Jobbing/floor foundry (gray iron, ductile, brass): after the main pour the worker walks the rows of bench or floor molds with a hand or bull ladle and tops off sprues and open risers as they sink, judging by eye which molds need metal and how much, in a cluttered, variable pouring bay.

Nonferrous permanent-mold/gravity-die or investment casting station: worker hand-ladles into a die or shell tree on a carousel or bench and then adds metal to the sprue/riser cup to keep it full while the casting solidifies; repeated part geometry, standard dies, several stations per operator.

Large casting work (multi-ton steel or iron) poured on the floor or in a pit from a crane-carried bottom-pour ladle: after filling, the crew adds metal to several open risers/hot tops and applies exothermic topping compound, judging the sink of each riser individually over minutes.

Steel melt shop ingot casting: teeming into ingot molds from a bottom-pour ladle, then slowly filling and topping up the hot top so head metal feeds shrinkage in the ingot body before the exothermic/insulating cover is applied.

sources.system: Sinto America P-Series Auto Pouring System
sources.title: Auto Pouring Systems: P-Series - Sinto America
sources.claim: Sinto America's P-Series is a fully automatic ... ladles up to 5 tons that uses optical sensors and cameras to regulate pouring speed to match mold intake and control the metal level in the sprue cup on a pouring line, i.e. it keeps adding metal as the cup level falls.
sources.transferJustification: The cited function is closed-loop mold filling with sprue-cup level control. Keeping the cup/riser topped as the level sinks is the same act as the worker's shrinkage top-off: same molten metal, same cup target, same accepted output (a fed, shrink-free casting).

sources.system: Inductotherm Visipour
sources.title: Pouring Systems: Vision vs. Laser Control | Foundry Management & Technology
sources.claim: Inductotherm's Visipour vision-controlled stopper-rod pouring system fills molds on flask and flaskless lines mold after mold without operator intervention; the article also notes that anything less than a full sprue cup leads to shrink defects, so the level the system maintains is the shrinkage-feeding level.
sources.transferJustification: Substantiates unattended automatic pouring to a controlled sprue-cup level on production mold lines; the same closed loop supplies the extra metal that would otherwise be hand-added to compensate shrinkage.

sources.system: pourTECH 3D Laser System / closed-loop bottom-pouring systems
sources.title: Vision, Laser Technologies Combine for High-Performance Pouring | Foundry Management & Technology
sources.claim: Closed-loop automatic bottom-pouring systems with pour-cup metal-level feedback are widely installed in high-volume foundries worldwide, several hundred systems as of 2016.
sources.transferJustification: Establishes deployment scale and autonomy of pour-cup level-controlled pouring, the mechanism that keeps the sprue/riser full to feed shrinkage on molding lines.

sources.system: pourTECH automatic pouring system
sources.title: Automatic pouring – pour-tech AB
sources.claim: The pourTECH automatic pouring system runs on horizontal and vertical mold lines, with a PLC opening and closing the stopper rod using laser level feedback and positioning the nozzle over the pouring ... automatically; the operator is released from the pouring work.
sources.transferJustification: Same transfer as above: laser-fed closed-loop control of the metal level in the pouring cup performs the top-up-to-level function that the hand pourer performs to compensate shrinkage.

sources.system: Roberts Sinto Econo-Pour automatic pouring units
sources.title: Dotson Orders Two Roberts Sinto Pouring Systems | Foundry Management & Technology
sources.claim: A US ductile/gray iron jobbing foundry (Dotson, Mankato MN) converted to all-automatic pouring with Roberts Sinto Econo-Pour units using PLC proportional control, load cells and vision, showing automatic pouring is used for job-shop work when molds are presented on a line.
sources.transferJustification: Shows the E1 counterfactual is real for jobbing work: when molds are conveyed to the machine, an automatic pouring unit fills and levels every mold, including the varied patterns a hand pourer would top off.

sources.system: Robotic ladling pouring cells (industry practice, per Inductotherm/Roberts Sinto/Stotek sources)
sources.developer: Various (robot integrators; e.g., KUKA, Comau, Roberts Sinto)
sources.title: Controlling Pouring Through Automation | Modern Casting
sources.claim: Permanent mold and diecasting plants in North America routinely use robotic ladling cells in which pouring profiles are programmed into ... the required weight into each mold.

sources.system: Comau robotic gravity casting cell
sources.title: Automated Aluminum Casting with Comau Robots - Comau
sources.claim: Robotic pouring of molten aluminum into gravity dies is delivered as a production cell by a major integrator, with repeatable pouring executed inside a fully customized, fenced casting cell.
sources.transferJustification: Gravity-die pouring with a robot ladle is the same handling problem as topping the die's riser cup with additional metal; the cell is purpose-built, fixing the environment at E1.

sources.system: INTECO ICAST casting-rate controller / Advanced Teeming System (ATS)
sources.developer: INTECO melting and casting technologies GmbH
sources.title: Ingot Casting - INTECO
sources.claim: INTECO's ICAST controller performs fully automated ingot teeming by algorithmically driving the ladle slide gate through a defined casting profile with ..., used with casting cranes or INTECO ingot casting cars; installed at Ovako (two 100 t casting cars) and Buderus Edelstahl (two 200 t casting cars with the Advanced Teeming System).
sources.transferJustification: Ingot teeming's final process phase is the slow filling/topping of the hot top, the reservoir that feeds ingot shrinkage; automating the slide-gate profile through that phase is the machine equivalent of the teemer's shrinkage top-up.

tasks.label: Stencil identifying information on ingots and pigs, using special hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Primary/secondary aluminium cast house: worker applies alloy, lot and heat identification to ingots and to strapped ingot bundles as they come off the casting/stacking conveyor, using stencil plates and spray paint or marking stamps. High volume, standard ingot geometry, warm metal, fixed line layout.

Steel melt shop / steel foundry: worker stamps or stencils heat number and grade on ingots after stripping from the molds, in the pouring/stripping bay. Pieces still hot (hundreds of degrees C), sitting on ingot cars or the pit floor, with scale, radiant heat and fume.

Remelt sows, pigs and skulls: worker stencils identifying codes with paint on rough, irregular, oxidized blocks stacked on pallets or set on the plant floor or an adjacent covered yard; surface flatness and orientation vary piece to piece.

Small non-ferrous job foundry (brass, bronze, zinc, specialty alloys): worker hand-stamps small ingots with steel letter/number punches and a hammer, or sprays a stencil, after each pour. Short runs, codes change heat to heat, work done at a bench or on a cooling rack.

Shipping/storage bay: re-marking ingots and pigs whose original identification is smeared, illegible or wrong, and marking odd or partial pieces before shipment; identity supplied from the plant's heat records or an existing tag.

instances.label: Model shop at a manufacturer or R&D lab: a one-off prototype metal part (aluminum or steel block, a few inches). Worker saws a blank, fixtures it in a vise on a mill or chucks it in a lathe, selects and sets tools and work offsets, proves out the cuts, machines features to about ±0.001 in., then deburrs and inspects.

Small batch of 5-50 prototype or pre-production parts run on a shop CNC mill or lathe: repeated loading and unloading of blanks, tool changes, chip and coolant management, periodic in-process gauging and offset adjustments across a shift.

Stock preparation and simple hole work in the shop: cutting bar, plate and tube to length on a horizontal bandsaw, and drilling, reaming and tapping holes on a drill press in brackets, plates and shop fixtures, often from hand layout.

Prototype plastic and soft-material parts and templates: acrylic, Delrin, ABS or tooling board cut, milled or engraved on a router, mill or engraving machine; sheet stock held on a vacuum table or tape, light cuts, watching for melting and chatter.
Sheet-metal prototype components for a model: blanking and piercing panels on a turret punch press and forming them, producing a handful of pieces per design iteration in the shop's fabrication area.

Reworking or modifying an existing model, casting or fixture: dialing an irregular, previously machined part in on a four-jaw chuck or rotary table, then taking cut-and-try cuts and hand-measuring repeatedly until it fits its mating part.

tasks.label: Inspect and test products to verify conformance to specifications, using precision measuring instruments or circuit testers.

instances.label: Bench gauging in a model/prototype shop: the model maker takes a just-machined one-off or few-off metal or plastic part to the inspection bench and checks a handful of critical dimensions against a print or CAD-derived dimension list using digital calipers, micrometers, gauge pins, thread and radius gauges, and a surface plate/height gauge; records results and accepts, reworks, or scraps the part.

At-machine, in-process verification during setup and cutting on a lathe, mill, or jig borer: with the workpiece still held in the chuck/vise/fixture, measure bores, steps, and depths, compare to the tolerance on the drawing, adjust tool offsets, re-cut, and re-measure until the feature conforms.

Formal dimensional inspection of a complex prototype part in the shop's inspection room or QC area: fixture the part on a CMM or scanner, align to datums, measure GD&T features (position, profile, flatness, hole patterns) against the CAD model, and issue an inspection report for the engineering customer.

Conformance check of a finished model, mockup, pattern, or template: verify freeform contours and profiles against CAD or a master template, check trim edges and hole locations, gap-and-flush of mating panels, and inspect surface finish/cosmetic appearance before delivery.

Fit-and-function check of an assembled working model: bolt or press mating parts together, verify clearances and fits by feel, exercise the mechanism (slides, hinges, linkages) through its range, and confirm the assembly behaves as specified before sign-off.

Electrical/electronic verification of a working model containing wiring or a circuit board: continuity, resistance, and isolation checks with a circuit tester or multimeter, then power-up and functional check of the instrumented model against the electrical specification.

tasks.label: Rework or alter component model or parts as required to ensure that products meet standards.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: A machined metal model component comes back from inspection out of tolerance (bore undersize, boss too tall, flatness/position off). The model maker re-fixtures it on a mill, lathe or grinder in the model shop, indicates it in, takes a light corrective cut, and re-inspects until the dimension is within print tolerance.

Bench rework of machined metal model parts to finish standard: deburring, breaking edges, blending tool witness marks, stoning and polishing surfaces on a bench or with hand/pneumatic tools in the model shop until the part passes visual and finish inspection.

Trial fit and adjust of mating parts in a working model assembly: the parts bind or the mechanism does not function, so the maker assembles, finds the interference by feel/marking compound, disassembles, files or scrapes the offending area, and reassembles, iterating until the model fits and operates.

Rework of a plastic, composite or painted appearance model: scratches, mold/tool marks, blemishes or a damaged surface must be sanded out, feathered and blended, then re-polished, buffed or resprayed so the model meets the appearance standard.

Material must be added back to a metal part that was cut undersize or damaged: weld, braze or laser-clad build-up on the affected area, then re-machine and blend the added material back into the surrounding surface to restore or alter the geometry to print.

Altering an existing model part to an engineering change: add or relocate holes, slots or pockets, shorten or trim a feature per the revised drawing, which requires a new setup, program/toolpath and verification of the changed feature.

tasks.label: Drill, countersink, and ream holes in parts and assemblies for bolts, screws, and other fasteners, using power tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Model shop bench/drill-press work: a small-to-medium metal component (aluminum, steel, brass) is clamped in a vise or simple fixture and a pattern of clearance/tap holes is drilled from layout marks or a drawing, then countersunk for flat-head screws and reamed to size for dowel pins or close-fit bolts. One-off or few-off parts, tolerances of a few thousandths of an inch, deburring included.

Match-drilling on a partially assembled model or mockup at the bench: hand-held power drill or right-angle drill used to drill through mating parts in place (using a drill template, transfer punches, or scribed layout), then countersink and deburr so fasteners seat flush. Access is awkward, the assembly is only lightly clamped, and the drill must not break through into adjacent detail.

Precision hole work on the shop's CNC mill or jig borer: a one-off part is fixtured on the table and a program drills, countersinks and reams hole locations to tight positional tolerance (+/-0.001 to 0.002 in) with an automatic tool changer, for bolted joints and dowelled interfaces of the model.

Drilling and countersinking holes in plastic, acrylic, resin-cast or composite model parts and thin sheet stock: soft, grabby or brittle material, thin walls, risk of melting, chipping or star-cracking; holes must be clean and correctly sized for self-tapping screws, inserts or machine screws.

Large model, full-scale mockup, tooling template or weldment on the shop floor: holes drilled and reamed in a bulky assembly with a portable magnetic-base drill or heavy hand drill, working from a template or scribed layout, sometimes in awkward or overhead positions, then countersunk and deburred for bolts.

tasks.label: Devise and construct tools, dies, molds, jigs, and fixtures, or modify existing tools and equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In a prototype/model shop, devise and machine a metal workholding fixture or jig so a model part can be held for machining or inspection: pick datums, model it in CAD, saw stock, mill the plate and locators, drill/tap, deburr, add dowels/clamps, prove it out on the first part. Tolerances of a few thousandths of an inch.

Devise and build a mold or form tool for producing a plastic model part (aluminum injection-mold insert, vacuum-forming buck, or casting cavity block): mold layout with draft/shrink, CNC cavity machining, EDM detail where needed, cavity polishing, fit of the two halves, and a tryout shot or pull.

Modify, repair, or adapt existing tooling or shop equipment: rework a worn or mis-sized die or mold detail (weld/laser build-up then re-machine), add locating features to an existing fixture, or adapt a machine attachment to a new part. Requires diagnosis on a used, non-nominal tool, disassembly, re-fitting, and re-check.

Fabricate a welded or bolted holding fixture, stand, or assembly buck from bar/plate/tube: cut members on saw or laser, lay out and clamp, tack, weld, straighten for distortion, drill and hand-fit the locating details, verify with indicator or CMM.

Quick-turn soft tooling and aids: design and 3D print (or laser-cut) drill guides, templates, assembly/inspection jigs and support fixtures for the model, then remove supports and hand-finish/verify fit.

tasks.label: Align, fit, and join parts, using bolts and screws or by welding or gluing.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bench assembly of a one-off machined metal or plastic prototype subassembly in the model shop: the maker aligns 3-15 unique machined parts to a drawing, clamps or locates them, and joins them with machine screws, socket-head bolts and dowel pins, torquing to spec and checking squareness/flush fit before sign-off.

Welding/tack-welding a one-off fabricated metal model, fixture or template: sheet, plate and tube pieces are set on a welding table or in a simple jig, tacked, checked for alignment and distortion, then finish-welded (MIG/TIG) in the shop's weld bay.

Bonding plastic (and some metal) model/pattern components with epoxy, solvent cement or CA: the maker applies adhesive along mating faces, aligns the parts to scribe lines or locating features, clamps or holds them while curing, and cleans squeeze-out on a one-off appearance model or pattern.

Assembling a large one-off model/mockup or tooling structure: heavy panels, frames and castings moved with a hoist or cart, aligned with indicators, squares or laser measurement against a base frame in the shop, shimmed, then bolted/pinned together.

Trial fit-up where parts do not mate as machined: the maker assembles, measures interference or gaps, then hand-fits - filing, scraping, reaming holes, elongating slots, adding shims - and re-checks, repeating until the fit is right before final bolting, welding or gluing.

tasks.label: Lay out and mark reference points and dimensions on materials, using measuring instruments and drawing or scribing tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bench/surface-plate layout on a flat metal blank or plate for a prototype part: apply layout dye, use height gauge, combination square, surface gauge and scriber to lay out centerlines, edge datums, hole centers and the profile outline, then center-punch hole locations to machine-shop tolerances (a few thousandths of an inch).

Layout on plastic or thin sheet stock for a template, gage or model panel: transfer the outline and reference points from a drawing or master template onto the blank with dividers, scale, scribe or fine marker, including index/orientation marks and identification.

Layout on a three-dimensional workpiece (casting, weldment, machined block) set up on an angle plate or V-blocks: indicate/establish datums, scribe reference lines and bore centerlines around several faces with a height gauge, and prick-punch bore and hole centers.

Transfer layout on a partially finished model or mock-up: mark hole locations, trim lines or fit lines onto a part using the as-built geometry of a mating component or the existing assembly rather than nominal drawing dimensions, done at the bench or on the mock-up in the shop.

Quick shop-floor marking of raw stock at the saw or material rack: measure and mark cut-off lines, stock allowance, orientation arrows and job/part identification on bar, tube or plate with rule, square, soapstone, scribe or marker.

instances.label: Prototype/model shop: fabricate a one-off metal or plastic model part of moderate complexity on a 3-axis CNC mill from a solid model — build/adjust the CAD, generate CAM toolpaths and post the program, fixture stock in a vise or soft jaws, set tool and work offsets, cut, probe/measure, deburr and hand off an inspected part.

Model shop with additive equipment: fabricate a plastic model part by 3D printing (FDM or SLA) from the CAD file — orient and slice, set supports, run the printer, remove the part from the plate, remove supports and do light finishing, verify dimensions.

Turn a small round model component (bushing, shaft, pin, threaded fitting) on a CNC lathe from bar or slug stock — program the turning cycles, set up chuck/collet and tooling, run, part off, inspect to print tolerances.

Cut flat stock for templates and model components on a CNC router, laser, waterjet or engraving machine — import/derive the 2D profile from CAD, nest and program the cut, load the sheet or plate, cut, unload, deburr edges and mark/engrave identification.

Complex one-off model: multi-setup or 5-axis machining of an intricate component (contoured surfaces, thin walls, mating fits) requiring the maker to devise and build custom fixtures/soft jaws, plan and re-datum several setups, then bench-fit, polish and assemble the model to the designer's intent.

tasks.label: Assemble mechanical, electrical, and electronic components into models or prototypes, using hand tools, power tools, and fabricating machines.

instances.label: Bench build-up of a one-off mechanical prototype in a company model shop: press/insert bearings, bushings, dowel pins and shafts into freshly machined metal parts, stack brackets and plates, drive fasteners to spec with hand and power drivers, then check clearance and motion.

Fit-up rework during assembly in the shop: parts interfere or holes mis-locate, so the model maker diagnoses the misfit, deburrs, files, reams, taps, shims or re-drills on the drill press/mill, then reassembles and re-checks fit and function, iterating until the prototype goes together.

Installing simple electrical/electronic content in a prototype: screw-mounting a PCB, motor, switch or sensor to machined standoffs, soldering leads and pins, and mating/seating connectors, then a functional power-up check.

Building and dressing a multi-branch wire harness into a bespoke prototype enclosure: cutting and routing wires around obstacles, crimping and inserting terminals, clamping, tying, strain-relieving and labeling, then continuity/functional test.

Joining plastic/machined model parts for an appearance or scale model: applying adhesive or solvent bead, aligning and clamping mating halves, setting threaded inserts, and fastening panels to a finished cosmetic standard.

Building up a large one-off prototype, mockup or test fixture on the shop floor: rigging and hoisting subassemblies, aligning to layout lines, bolting structural members, and installing purchased components (motors, cylinders, panels) with hand and power tools.

roles.title: Patternmakers, Metal and Plastic
roles.description: Lay out, machine, fit, and assemble castings and parts to metal or plastic foundry patterns, core boxes, or match plates.

tasks.label: Read and interpret blueprints or drawings of parts to be cast or patterns to be made, compute dimensions, and plan operational sequences.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Verify conformance of patterns or template dimensions to specifications, using measuring instruments such as calipers, scales, and micrometers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-process check while machining/fitting a pattern component in the pattern shop: worker stops at the mill or lathe (or steps to the bench) and checks two to six features — bore diameters, boss heights, wall thickness — with a caliper or micrometer against the drawing, then decides whether to take another cut. Part is typically still clamped in the machine or just off it.

Final dimensional verification of a completed core box or match plate assembly (roughly 300–900 mm, aluminum, plastic/urethane or wood) against the drawing before release to the foundry: dozens of features, core print sizes, parting-line alignment, hole locations, checked on a surface plate with height gauge, calipers, scale and shrink rule; results recorded on an inspection sheet.

Verification of a large pattern or cope/drag pattern half (1.5–4 m, mounted on a board or sitting on the shop floor) for a heavy casting: overall length/width, key feature locations and shrink allowance checked with steel tape, long scales, squares and calipers, often with the pattern needing to be moved or turned.

Verification of a small, tight-tolerance detail: loose pieces, core print inserts, machined plastic or metal pattern details held to ±0.002–0.005 in, checked with micrometers, gauge pins and a bench comparator in the pattern shop.

Verification of a flat template, profile gauge, sweep or layout template against specification: 2-D outline, edge profile, hole spacing, thickness, checked with scale, calipers and profile comparison to the drawing or master.

tasks.label: Assemble pattern sections, using hand tools, bolts, screws, rivets, glue, or welding equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Pattern shop bench work: fitting and fastening the two halves/sections of a one-off foundry pattern (wood, plastic or aluminum) - aligning on dowel pins, clamping, drilling pilot holes and driving screws/bolts, then checking parting-line registration with rule, square and indicator before the pattern is accepted.

Mounting pattern halves onto a match plate or mounting board: locating each half on opposite faces of the plate so the two register within a few thousandths of an inch, drilling and countersinking through the plate, and bolting or riveting the halves down at a bench or drill press.

Welding/brazing metal pattern work: tacking and welding aluminum or steel pattern sections, attaching gating (sprues, runners, risers, ingates) and pattern hardware onto a metal pattern or match plate, then grinding welds flush; done at a weld bench with MIG/TIG equipment.

Core box assembly: doweling, clamping and screwing/bolting core box sections (metal, plastic or wood) together so the mating faces close tight and the halves align; includes fitting vents, hardware and clamps at the bench.

Adhesive bonding of rigid pattern sections in a fixture: applying epoxy/urethane or resin glue to plastic, epoxy-board or aluminum sections, mating and clamping them in a jig, and curing to a dimensionally accepted joint.

Hand-craft finishing of the assembly: forming wax/leather/plastic fillets in inside corners, attaching loose pieces, lifting eyes, alignment pins and rapping plates, and repairing or re-gluing damaged returned patterns - highly variable freehand work with hand tools.

tasks.label: Repair and rework templates and patterns.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In the pattern/tool room, an aluminum or iron foundry pattern, match plate or core box comes back from the molding line worn, gouged or nicked on a working surface. The patternmaker mills out the damaged area, builds it back up by welding/deposition, and re-cuts and blends the surface to the nominal contour and draft, checking against the model or template.

An engineering change or casting-defect fix requires reworking an existing metal pattern, match plate or core box: stock added or removed, features re-machined to revised dimensions, gates/runners/core prints re-cut. The workpiece is indicated in on a mill or CNC machining center in the shop and machined to the revised model.

A metal or plastic pattern's working surfaces are scuffed, rough or dulled from production (or freshly welded/filled). The worker restores the finish over broad contoured surfaces: sanding, blending, polishing and re-coating with sealer/release so the sand strips cleanly.

A urethane/epoxy or filled-plastic pattern or core box has chips, dings and worn edges. At the bench, the worker mixes and applies epoxy/body filler into the damage, lets it cure, then carves, files and sands it back to contour, restoring parting lines, fillets, lettering and draft by eye and feel.

Assembly-level repair: broken pattern sections re-glued/re-fastened, worn or sheared alignment dowels, bushings, vents and hardware removed and replaced, loose pattern halves re-mounted and shimmed on a match plate, and cope/drag halves trial-fitted and adjusted until they register within tolerance.

Reactive repair in the plant: a pattern is damaged mid-run and is worked on at or beside the molding machine on the foundry floor, or a sheet-metal template is checked against the pattern and tweaked in place, amid sand, traffic and no fixed setup.

Same workpiece class as metal foundry patterns, match plates and core boxes (hard metal tooling of similar size and tolerance), and the same repair sequence the task requires: cut out damage, add metal, re-machine to nominal.

tasks.label: Clean and finish patterns or templates, using emery cloths, files, scrapers, and power grinders.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bench finishing of a freshly machined aluminum pattern plate, match plate, or core box in the pattern shop: break and deburr edges left by milling, clear burrs from drilled/tapped holes and slots, blend tool marks, and rub the draw surfaces with emery cloth to a smooth finish. One-off or few-off work, part sized to be handled on a bench.

Sanding and smoothing contoured wood, urethane-board, or plastic pattern and core-box surfaces after machining: progressive grits over broad curved faces, feathering parting lines and draft surfaces, prior to sealing, filling, and painting. Pattern shop bench or sanding station.

Heavier power-grinding on metal patterns and templates: blending weld build-up or added stock after a modification, grinding down gate/sprue and riser attachment areas and high spots on a match plate, then working the ground area back to a finished surface with abrasives. Done at a grinder stand or with a die grinder, with sparks and dust.

Intricate detail finishing by hand: filing and scraping fillets, undercuts, raised lettering, deep narrow core-box pockets and sharp internal corners; iteratively checking by feel and by fit of the mating pattern halves and loose pieces, removing a few thousandths at a time so draft and fit are preserved.

Cleaning a used pattern returned from the foundry before repair/reuse: scraping and brushing off baked-on sand, resin and binder residue, rust and old coating from the entire pattern, then re-finishing the working surfaces so the pattern draws cleanly again. Shop or blast-room work on a dirty, variable-condition workpiece.

tasks.label: Set up and operate machine tools, such as milling machines, lathes, drill presses, and grinders, to machine castings or patterns.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In a foundry pattern shop / tool room, the patternmaker sets up a vertical milling machine (manual or CNC) to machine an aluminum match plate or metal pattern body: squares and clamps the blank in a vise or on the table, indicates it in, sets tool and work offsets, then mills the parting face, contours and locating features to layout dimensions, checking with indicators and micrometers.

Lathe work on a casting or round pattern component: chucking a rough casting or bar, truing it up, then facing, turning, boring and threading features such as bushing bores, core prints or sprue bushings; typically one-off or a few pieces, with in-process measurement and re-cuts to size.

Drill press / hole work on pattern plates and core boxes: laying out and drilling clearance and dowel holes, reaming, counterboring and tapping for pattern hardware, alignment pins, ejector pins and mounting bolts on match plates and core box halves.

Grinding and finishing operations on castings and pattern parts: surface grinding a plate or slide flat and parallel, pedestal/die grinding to remove gates, risers, parting-line flash and burrs from a casting, and blending machined surfaces to a required finish.

Machining plastic and composite pattern stock: setting up a CNC router or machining center to cut urethane/epoxy tooling board or foam patterns, core boxes and loose pieces to 3D CAD geometry, including roughing and finishing passes and trimming to the parting line.

tasks.label: Mark identification numbers or symbols onto patterns or templates.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In the pattern shop, the patternmaker finishes a wood, RenShape/urethane or composite pattern or core box and hand-marks its identification on it - pattern number, customer/part number, revision, plus symbols such as cope/drag arrows, core-print letters and parting-line marks - using a paint marker, stencil or stamp, on an irregular 3-D surface with the piece sitting loose on a bench or cart.

Identification is stamped or engraved into metal tooling - an aluminum match plate, metal pattern or core box - using steel character punches and a hammer, a pneumatic/electric engraving pencil, or a bench engraver, with the heavy plate lying on the bench or clamped in a vise.

The identification text is cut into the pattern, match plate or mold insert as part of the CNC machining job: the workpiece is fixtured on the CNC router or mill and an engraving toolpath mills the pattern number into a boss or flat pad while the piece is still on the machine.

Flat templates, loose pieces, layout gauges and sheet-metal or plastic check fixtures are marked with numbers and reference symbols (etched, scribed, stamped or engraved) so they can be matched to the parent pattern and returned to the right rack.

Out in the foundry or the pattern storage building, an existing large pattern or match plate (heavy, sitting on the floor, a pallet or a storage rack) is re-identified after repair or rework: the worker locates it, verifies which tool it is, and re-marks or refreshes the ID number with paint, chalk or an engraver in a dusty aisle.
An engraved metal or plastic ID nameplate/barcode tag is produced and then affixed to the pattern or core box with screws or adhesive, in a chosen spot that will survive foundry handling.

tasks.label: Lay out and draw or scribe patterns onto material, using compasses, protractors, rulers, scribes, or other instruments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bench/surface-plate layout on flat stock in a pattern shop: aluminum or steel plate, plastic sheet or polyurethane tooling board is coated with layout dye and the patternmaker transfers dimensions from the print, scribing centerlines, hole centers, saw lines and part outlines with scriber, dividers, combination square and height gauge before cutting/machining.

Layout marks applied onto a three-dimensional pattern or core box body (machined aluminum, plastic or tooling board): scribing parting-line traces, core-print outlines, draft reference lines and centerlines onto curved and stepped surfaces of the pattern under construction.

Layout on a rough casting, cast pattern blank or weldment set on the surface plate or shop floor: indicating/measuring the as-cast form, balancing the machining stock across irregular surfaces, establishing datum planes and scribing machining and datum lines with a height gauge and scriber.

Match plate / mounting board layout: scribing the plate centerline and part positions, locating dowel and bushing hole centers, gate, runner and riser positions, and center-punching hole locations on a metal match plate or mounting board before drilling and mounting the pattern halves.

Reverse-engineering layout with no usable CAD or drawing: taking dimensions off a customer's worn or damaged pattern, a sample casting or an obsolete print, deciding how the modification/repair should sit on the existing part, and scribing the new layout lines directly onto that used part.

tasks.label: Design and create templates, patterns, or coreboxes according to work orders, sample parts, or mockups.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Pattern shop receives a work order with a customer 3D CAD model for a small/medium casting; patternmaker builds the tooling model (shrink, draft, parting, core prints), programs CAM, and machines a matchplate or core box from aluminum plate or urethane tooling board on a 3- to 5-axis mill/router, then deburrs, finishes and checks it to print.

Large or one-off pattern built up by hand in wood/composite from 2D drawings, a sketch or a customer mockup with no digital model: layout and lofting on stock, sawing, glue-ups, turning, hand-shaping of fillets and draft, sanding, sealing/painting, hand-fitting of loose pieces and core prints.

Pattern or core box produced additively from the CAD model on a large-format pellet-extrusion or binder-jet machine (sometimes hybrid print-and-mill), followed by depowdering/support removal, surface finishing and dimensional check before shipment to the foundry.

Duplicate or replacement tooling created from a customer's sample part or an old pattern: digitize the sample (3D scan/CMM), rebuild the geometry with allowances, then machine or print the new pattern/core box and verify it against the sample.
Flat templates, sweeps, strickle boards, layout gauges and loose pieces cut from sheet/plate or board to a drawing or DXF nest (laser, waterjet, router), plus edge cleanup and marking.

Bench work on existing tooling: mounting cope/drag halves and gating on match plates with dowels and bushings, aligning and shimming core box halves, trial-fitting cores, and repairing or modifying worn or engineering-changed patterns by filling, welding, re-machining and refitting at the bench.

tasks.label: Construct platforms, fixtures, and jigs for holding and placing patterns.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In the pattern shop's machine shop, machining the metal (aluminum/steel) mounting plates, sub-plates and fixture components for a new pattern-holding fixture: squaring stock, milling locating pads and pockets, drilling/reaming dowel holes and tapping fastener holes to a CAD/CAM print, deburring and dimensional inspection.

At the bench, mounting pattern halves/segments onto a match plate or platform: laying out and locating them to the parting line within a few thousandths, drilling and pressing dowel pins, screwing down, sealing and blending fillets, then checking cope/drag registration against the mating half and hand-adjusting (filing, shimming, scraping) until it registers.

Fabricating and welding a steel frame, bolster or handling platform for a large or heavy pattern: cutting members to size, fitting and tacking the frame square, welding out, then machining the mounting face flat and drilling the mounting holes.

Building wood, plastic or composite platforms, follow boards, locating templates and simple drill jigs: cutting sheet/board stock to the pattern contour on a saw or CNC router, boring guide-bushing holes, and fastening/gluing the pieces into a board assembly.

Trying out and installing the finished platform/jig on the molding machine, match-plate machine or CNC table: bolting it down, indicating alignment, shimming and adjusting, running a trial mold or trial cut, and reworking the fixture until the pattern seats and locates correctly in production.

sources.claim: Hadrian operates automated, software-driven factories in which robotic arms hold and move material for CNC machining of high-tolerance aerospace/defense metal components, with machines running unattended overnight.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated production of precision machined metal parts. Fixture and jig plates for patterns are the same class of workpiece (aluminum/steel plates and blocks, milled pockets, drilled/reamed dowel and tapped holes, thousandths-level tolerances), so machining them in a robot-tended CNC cell carries over.

tasks.label: Clean and smooth molds, cores, and core boxes, and repair surface imperfections.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Jobbing/short-run foundry, floor or bench molding: after the pattern is drawn from a green-sand or no-bake mold, the molder inspects the cavity of a one-off mold (often several feet across), blows and brushes out loose sand, patches broken edges, sand drops and gouges with sand/patching compound by hand, and slicks the repaired surfaces and gates smooth with trowels, slicks and lifters before coating and closing. Geometry, size and defect location differ job to job.

Production core room: cores of a repeating type stripped from core boxes or a cold-box/shell shooter carry parting-line flash and loose sand; the coremaker rubs or files the fins off, blows/brushes the core clean, checks it, and rejects or sets aside cores with broken sections. Repetitive, known geometry, high cycle rate.

Tooling cleaning: core boxes, blow plates and pattern plates are pulled periodically and cleaned of baked-on resin/binder buildup and packed sand, with vents cleared and cavity surfaces wiped, scraped, solvent-washed or dry-ice blasted, then checked and the surface touched up so the next cores strip clean.

Molding-line station in a production foundry: between cycles the worker blows loose sand and nubs out of the mold cavity, cleans pouring cup, breather/vent holes and the pattern plate, and preps the cope/drag surfaces before the mold is closed; molds with real defects are rejected rather than patched.

Investment-casting wax room: wax patterns pulled from injection dies are trimmed of parting-line flash and gate witness, seams and blemishes smoothed with a heated tool or solvent, small surface defects filled, and the wax die cavity wiped clean between shots. Delicate, easily marred surfaces, judged visually.
