tasks.label: Sift and pack sand into mold sections, core boxes, and pattern contours, using hand or pneumatic ramming tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production green-sand foundry: molder works a jolt-squeeze/matchplate molding machine, riddles facing sand over the mounted pattern, fills cope and drag flasks from an overhead hopper, compacts by squeeze/jolt or pneumatic rammer, strikes off and vents; repetitive, dozens to hundreds of molds per shift on standard flask sizes.

Core room: coremaker packs and rams sand into core boxes — hand-ramming or bench-rammed small odd-shaped boxes and loading/operating core blowers — sets vents and reinforcing wires, strikes off the box and draws the green core.

Jobbing foundry floor molding of medium-to-large molds: pattern set in a flask on the floor or a molding station, no-bake or green sand shoveled/delivered from a mixer, tucked and pneumatically rammed around pattern contours, gaggers set, surface struck off; a few molds per shift with frequent job changes.

Very large one-off pit or floor molds for heavy castings: multi-ton flasks or a floor pit, sand delivered by mixer or crane bucket, packed and pneumatically rammed in layers around a large pattern with reinforcement and venting over hours; layout and pattern differ job to job.

Small jobbing, art or prototype foundry: bench molding one or a few molds — riddling facing sand over a loose pattern in a small flask, hand-ramming with peen and butt rammer, rapping and drawing the pattern, repairing and finishing the mold cavity; a different pattern almost every job.

tasks.label: Position patterns inside mold sections, and clamp sections together.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume green sand production foundry running an automatic molding line (vertical flaskless DISAMATIC-type or horizontal matchplate): at each job change the molder positions/locks the pattern plate set into the molding chamber, and the line forms, indexes and presses/closes the mold halves together into a clamped mold string ahead of pouring. Fenced/light-curtained machine line, standardized flask or mold block sizes, hundreds of molds per hour.

Mid-size jobbing/production foundry, semi-automatic squeeze or jolt-squeeze machine with a flask conveyor: molder sets the pattern plate into cope and drag flasks, rams, draws the pattern, sets cores, then closes the cope onto the drag on alignment pins and secures with mold clamps, jackets or weights. Repeat patterns of modest size, done on an open shop floor with people and forklifts moving around.

Heavy-section jobbing work with large flasks (roughly 1-2 m): pattern/pattern plate positioned in a large flask with a hoist or overhead crane, mold halves rolled over, cores set, cope lowered onto drag and bolted or clamped with weights. Standard flask sizes, crane-served bays.

Floor and pit molding of very large one-off castings (multi-ton loose patterns, custom gating and rigging, molds built in the foundry floor pit): pattern sections positioned and aligned by crane and hand, mold sections closed and secured with tie bars, bolts and heavy weights. Every job different, no standard flask.

Small job shop, prototype or art foundry bench molding with loose (non-matchplate) patterns: pattern halves positioned in cope and drag by hand, rammed, drawn, mold sections mated on pins and clamped or weighted. One-off or very short runs, irregular geometry, frequent hand repair of the mold cavity.

Investment casting wax room: ceramic cores positioned in the wax injection die halves, die closed and clamped for injection, wax pattern removed and set; patterns then positioned/assembled on the sprue. Climate-controlled wax room in a casting plant, standard tooling.

tasks.label: Position cores into lower sections of molds, and reassemble molds for pouring.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume automatic green-sand molding line (vertical DISAMATIC-type or high-pressure flask line) in a production foundry: as molds index every 5-15 s, the worker sets one or a few cold-box cores into the mold/drag pocket, seats them on the core prints and blows off loose sand; the machine pushes the mold string together or closes cope onto drag for pouring.

Medium-volume flaskless matchplate or horizontal flask line running short-to-medium jobs of small castings (brass, iron): worker sets several small cores into the drag half, checks seating, closes the cope onto the drag (machine or hoist), applies jackets/weights; patterns change several times per shift.

Large no-bake / floor-molded jobbing casting, one-off or very short run: worker rigs heavy cores with hoist or overhead crane, lowers them into the drag, shims and pastes/mudds core prints, checks clearances with gauges and a closing trial, then closes the cope with the crane and bolts, clamps or weights the mold.

Small bench / hand molding for prototype, repair, art or very small lot work with loose or unique patterns: worker hand-sets small fragile cores into the drag, sometimes trimming or shimming them to fit, closes the cope by hand and clamps or weights the mold.

Permanent-mold / semi-permanent-mold (aluminum) casting station: each cycle the worker places one or more sand cores into the open steel mold half on an indexing tilt-pour machine, seats them accurately, blows out loose sand, and the mold is closed for pouring.

tasks.label: Sprinkle or spray parting agents onto patterns and mold sections to facilitate removal of patterns from molds.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Machine/matchplate green sand molding in a production foundry: for every mold cycle, parting agent is applied to both cope and drag faces of the matchplate pattern before sand fill, at a molding machine station with a fixed pattern plate.

Bench/floor hand molding of small-to-medium green sand molds in a jobbing foundry: worker dusts parting powder from a bag and hand-sprays aerosol pattern spray over a loose or mounted wood/aluminum pattern and on the drag joint face before turning over and ramming the cope.

No-bake (chemically bonded) molding of medium patterns in flasks at a molding station: worker sprays liquid release agent evenly over the pattern surface, pockets and undercuts, and over flask/joint faces, before the mixer fills and the sand sets; pattern geometry changes job to job.

Coremaking: applying release agent to core box cavities (hand-rammed boxes, shell/hot boxes, cold-box tooling) every few shots so cores strip cleanly, with the box mounted at a bench or clamped in a core shooter.
Permanent mold/gravity die and wax injection tooling: spraying release agent or die coat onto heated metal mold halves or a wax injection die cavity between cycles, in a fixed press/machine position.

Very large floor or pit molding: crane-handled multi-ton patterns and large cope/drag mold sections; worker walks around and over the mold spraying parting agent on broad pattern surfaces and joint faces in place, on the foundry floor.

tasks.label: Form and assemble slab cores around patterns, and position wire in mold sections to reinforce molds, using hand tools and glue.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production foundry core room, repeat part: worker assembles a multi-piece core package (slab/plate cores) into a metal assembly jig around the core prints/pattern, applies hot-melt or paste glue at the joints, presses and checks fit, sets the finished package on a rack; same part run hundreds of times per shift.

Jobbing / medium-volume foundry bench work: worker pastes and glues core halves and slab core sections together and assembles them around a pattern in the mold section, rasping and fitting with hand tools; several different jobs per shift, core sizes and shapes change with the order.

Core bench with reinforcement: worker lays reinforcing wires or rods into the core box or into the green core before/after ramming, bends and cuts wire to fit the core contour with pliers and cutters, then glues the core halves together.

Floor/pit molding of large castings: worker positions reinforcing wires, rods, gaggers and lifters in large cope and drag mold sections as the sand is rammed, bending wire by hand to hook under flask bars, reaching into deep sections; mold size and layout differ job to job on the foundry floor.

Small art/specialty or short-run non-ferrous shop: one-off or few-off patterns, worker improvises slab-core assembly around the pattern with glue and hand tools and adds wire reinforcement where the mold is weak; no dedicated tooling exists for the job.

tasks.label: Move and position workpieces, such as mold sections, patterns, and bottom boards, using cranes, or signal others to move workpieces.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Machine molding on a green-sand line (matchplate, flaskless or flask): the molder places empty flasks and bottom boards, takes cope/drag mold halves off the machine, squares them up and positions them onto the roller/conveyor line or pouring track. Standard flask sizes, repetitive cycle, hoists and roller decks at hand.

Jobbing/production foundry, medium-to-heavy flask molds (roughly 1x1 m up to 2x1.6 m, a few hundred kg to a couple of tonnes): the molder slings the cope with an overhead crane or jib hoist, rolls it over, guides it by hand and lands it on the drag on a bottom board, aligning flask pins before closing.

Large one-off floor or pit molding in a jobbing iron/steel foundry: unique multi-tonne mold sections, patterns and bottom boards rigged with chains and shackles on a bridge crane, walked across a sand floor with variable clearances, tipped, hand-guided into a pit and closed to tight mismatch on a casting that may never be repeated.

Core room work: lifting green cores out of the core box (by hand, hoist or takeout), setting them on core plates and dryer racks, gluing/assembling multi-piece core packages, and setting cores into mold cavities on the core prints. In investment-casting shops, the equivalent handling and positioning of wax patterns and assembled trees between wax room, dip line and racks.

Acting as rigger/spotter: the molder hooks up and then signals a crane operator or lift-truck driver by hand signal or radio to bring a pattern plate, pattern, stack of flasks or a finished mold from storage to the molding station and to lower it into an exact position, calling stops and inches as the load lands.

Intra-plant transport: moving pallets and racks of finished cores, stacks of bottom boards, empty flasks and pattern boxes between the core room, storage racks and the molding stations across the shop floor, in aisles shared with people and lift trucks.

tasks.label: Lift upper mold sections from lower sections, and remove molded patterns.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-production green sand line: operator tends an automatic flaskless/matchplate molding machine (100-200 molds/hr). Each cycle the machine squeezes cope and drag against the pattern plate, strips the mold halves off the pattern, withdraws the plate and closes the mold; the worker monitors, sets cores, changes patterns and clears misdraws.

Job-shop machine molding on a semi-automatic jolt-squeeze/matchplate machine: worker rams sand in flasks on the machine, operates vibrator and draw pins, lifts the cope flask off the drag by hoist or hand, lifts out the matchplate/pattern, inspects and patches the parting face, then closes the mold. Mixed short runs, frequent pattern changes.

No-bake (airset) chemically bonded molding of medium castings in a job-shop loop or carousel: box filled and vibrated, sand cures, box rolled over, mold drawn off the pattern, pattern and mold faces blown off, mold coated and set aside for closing. Mold weights a few hundred to a couple thousand pounds.

Hand bench/floor molding of small one-off, repair or prototype castings with loose or split patterns: worker rams cope and drag, rapps the pattern, lifts the cope half off, draws the pattern (and loose pieces) with a draw spike, then repairs broken sand edges and vents before closing.

Large flask no-bake or green sand molds for heavy castings (roughly 1-10 tons of mold): flask handled by overhead crane or heavy rollover, pattern vibrated and drawn, cope half turned over and set aside, parting face cleaned and repaired.

Very large floor/pit molds for heavy one-off castings (multi-ton, several meters): cope flask lifted by overhead crane with riggers guiding, multi-piece loose and skeleton patterns rapped and withdrawn piece by piece, extensive hand repair of the cavity.

tasks.label: Cut spouts, runner holes, and sprue holes into molds.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bench hand molding of small/medium green-sand molds in a jobbing or captive foundry: after ramming the cope the molder cuts the downsprue with a sprue cutter, cuts the pouring basin, and cuts gates/runner channels into the parting face with a gate cutter, then blows the mold clean. Molds sit on a bench or rollover; geometry varies job to job.

Floor/pit molding of large one-off molds for heavy iron or steel castings: cutting one or several downsprue holes through a large cope, forming a pouring basin or seating a ceramic cup, and cutting large runner and ingate channels, often working on top of or inside the mold in awkward positions.

No-bake / chemically bonded (furan, phenolic urethane) sand molds in a mold-assembly area: drilling or cutting sprue and pour-cup openings and runner passages into hardened resin-sand cope sections with hand drills, routers and rasps before close-up.

Production green-sand molding line or squeeze/jolt machine: repetitive cutting/punching of the pouring cup and clearing of sprue and runner passages on standard flasks or flaskless molds coming off the machine on a conveyor, plus setting ceramic pour cups and filters.
Investment casting / wax work: forming or cutting the pour cup, sprue and gate passages on wax patterns and pattern trees (or opening the pour cup on shell molds) in a foundry wax room.

tasks.label: Tend machines that bond cope and drag together to form completed shell molds.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume shell foundry with an integrated shell molding line: cope and drag shells index out of heated pattern machines onto a conveyor, a glue applicator/closing press bonds and clamps them. The worker tends the line — watching the closer cycle, straightening or feeding shell halves at the closer, taking bonded molds off to the pouring jacket/shot-fill station, clearing broken shells. One or two part numbers per shift.

Semi-automatic bench station in a production shell foundry: worker takes cope and drag shell halves from a rack or the adjacent shell machine, sets a core, runs the hot-melt/resin glue applicator or dispenses adhesive, loads the pair into a pin-type shell mould closer/clamp press, cycles it, and unloads the completed mold. Moderate part mix, several patterns per shift.

Jobbing or low-volume shell foundry: mold sizes and shapes vary widely, batches are small. Worker inspects each shell half for cracks, warp and parting-line flash, breaks off flash, sets the closer's pressure pins for that pattern, glues and clamps the halves, checks mismatch, and sets aside or patches defective molds before releasing the completed mold.

Setup, changeover and troubleshooting around the bonding machine: adjusting pressure-pin plates and clamp pressure for a new pattern, setting glue temperature and bead, cleaning cured adhesive and sand debris off the closer, clearing crushed shells jammed in the fixture, and running first-off checks before the run restarts.

tasks.label: Rotate sweep boards around spindles to make symmetrical molds for convex impressions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Jobbing/steel foundry floor or pit molding: the molder plumbs a spindle in a floor plate or pit bottom, rams green or dry sand around it, and rotates a profiled sweep board through 360 degrees to strike a symmetrical cavity for a large round casting (kettle, gear blank, roll, large valve body, 1-3 m diameter); then slicks, vents, patches and blacks the swept surface before the cope is set.

Bench/flask work: a portable spindle-and-sweep rig is set in a flask on the molding bench to strike a smaller symmetrical convex impression (pulley, handwheel, pot, bowl, bearing boss) in green or bonded sand; the molder sweeps, finishes the profile by hand, cuts gates and closes the mold.

Swept cylindrical/round cores: loam or bonded sand built up on a core barrel or spindle and struck to a circular profile with a sweep/strickle board (pipe cores, cylinder liners, bushings, tapered round cores), then vented, oven-dried, coated and set in the mold.

Art, ornamental or bell foundry loam sweeping: successive sweep boards rotated on a spindle to form the core, false shape and cope of a bell, urn, fountain bowl or ornamental column base; heavy hand finishing and craft judgement on profile and surface, one-off pieces.

Setup and rework: truing and plumbing the spindle, fitting and shimming the sweep board to the drawing profile and checking with gauges, then re-sweeping, cutting back and patching a swept surface that is damaged or out of tolerance so the mold can be accepted and closed.

tasks.label: Pour molten metal into molds, manually or with crane ladles.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-production mechanized green-sand line (iron): molds index past a fixed pouring station at 100-500 molds/hour; the worker fills the pouring cup of each mold from a bottom-pour ladle or pressure-pour/channel furnace, watching cup level, pour time, temperature and in-stream inoculation, and rejecting short/over-poured molds.

Medium-volume flask or matchplate line in a mid-size jobbing foundry: molds carried on a roller/conveyor line, poured with a monorail or driven bull ladle (or two-man shank) with frequent pattern and alloy changes during a shift; pour weights tens to a few hundred pounds; skimming slag and topping risers by hand.

Job-shop floor/no-bake work: one-off or small-lot molds of varying size set out on the foundry floor or in a pouring bay, sprue and riser positions differing mold to mold; poured from hand shanks or a small crane ladle, with the pourer judging fill rate, keeping the cup full and topping risers.

Non-ferrous work (aluminum, bronze, brass) into permanent/tilt-pour metal molds, small sand molds, or preheated investment shells: worker hand-ladles metered dips from a holding furnace at a fixed station or turntable, with tight temperature and fill-rate control on repeat parts.

Heavy castings in a steel/iron jobbing foundry: multi-ton one-off molds in pits or big flasks, poured from a crane-carried bottom-pour bull ladle by a two-person crew, sometimes with more than one ladle or basin, plus slag control, hot-topping and exothermic riser feeding.

tasks.label: Operate ovens or furnaces to bake cores or to melt, skim, and flux metal.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production sand foundry core room: coated sand cores are placed on trays/racks and run through a gas- or electric-fired core drying/baking oven; the worker loads and unloads the oven, sets temperature and dwell time, monitors the cycle, and inspects baked cores for cracking or scorching before they go to the mold line.

Hot-box / shell (Croning) coremaking: the worker sets and monitors heated core-box platen temperature and cure time on the core machine (the 'oven' is the heated tooling), cycles the machine, strips and inspects cured cores, and corrects for under- or over-baked cores through the shift.

Iron or steel jobbing foundry melt deck: charging a coreless induction furnace with scrap, returns and pig, watching bath temperature and power, raking/skimming slag off the bath into a slag pot, taking samples, adding alloy trim, ladle flux and cover material, and holding metal on spec for tapping.

Aluminum or other non-ferrous foundry/casthouse: charging ingot, sow and returns into a melting or holding furnace, holding at temperature, degassing/fluxing the bath, skimming dross into a dross pan, and delivering clean metal to a dosing furnace, ladle or die-cast machine.

Small art/bronze or investment-casting shop: firing a wax burnout kiln with shells or flasks of varied size on hand-loaded shelves, and melting small heats of bronze/aluminum in a crucible furnace — hand-charging ingot, adding degasser/flux tablets, skimming dross with a hand skimmer, and pulling the crucible for pouring; layout and job mix change constantly.

roles.description: Set up, operate, or tend metal or plastic molding, casting, or coremaking machines to mold or cast metal or thermoplastic parts or products.

tasks.label: Measure and visually inspect products for surface and dimension defects to ensure conformance to specifications, using precision measuring instruments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume injection molding plant: operator pulls sample shots at set intervals from the take-out robot/conveyor at press-side, checks visually for flash, short shots, sink marks, splay and knit lines, measures 2-5 key dimensions with calipers/micrometer/pin gauges, records SPC data and flags the press if drifting.

Bench or packing-station 100% check of small molded parts (medical, electrical, consumer): operator works through trays/bins, inspects each part for cosmetic and dimensional defects, gauges critical features, sorts good from scrap, high repetition on a standard running part.

Die casting / permanent mold cell: operator inspects hot, oily aluminum or zinc castings after ejection and trim for flash, cold shuts, misruns, soldering/drag marks and gate porosity, gauges critical dimensions with fixed gauges and calipers, and rejects or routes suspect parts.

Setup / first-piece qualification after a mold or die change in a high-mix custom shop: operator measures many dimensions on the first shots against the print using calipers, micrometers, gauges, optical comparator or QC-lab CMM, documents first-article approval and adjusts the process before running.

Coremaking / sand molding: operator inspects cores and green-sand molds coming off the core machine or molding line for cracks, breakouts, loose sand, incomplete vents and print fit, checks dimensions against templates and gauges before the core is set.

Large or awkward parts (rotational molding, structural foam, large castings): operator inspects large surfaces for warpage, voids, wall-thickness variation and surface blemishes, measures with tape, large gauges or thickness gauge, often walking around the part on the floor.

tasks.label: Observe continuous operation of automatic machines to ensure that products meet specifications and to detect jams or malfunctions, making adjustments as necessary.

instances.label: Plastics plant, stable high-volume injection molding job on a modern press with take-out robot and conveyor. Operator watches several presses cycle, pulls periodic parts to check for short shots/flash/sink and dimensions, trims hold pressure, cooling time or barrel temperature at the HMI, and responds to alarms.

High-speed packaging line (PET stretch-blow bottles, caps/closures, thin-wall containers) running hundreds of parts per minute. Operator monitors weight/wall-thickness/appearance drift, keeps defective product out of the good stream, and adjusts blowmolder or press settings to hold spec.

Foundry high-pressure die casting cell (aluminum/zinc) with ladler, die sprayer and extractor. Operator observes shot-to-shot consistency, inspects castings for short fill/cold shut/flash, watches die temperature and spray coverage, and adjusts shot profile, spray or cycle timing.

Jam and malfunction recovery during a run: a part hangs up in the cavity, a sprue sticks, the take-out robot mis-picks, parts pile up at a conveyor or chute, or resin bridges in the hopper. Operator must open the guard, physically dislodge and remove the obstruction, clean the cavity/vent, spray release, then reset and restart automatic operation.

Foundry coremaking line with automatic core shooters/cold-box machines. Operator watches shot after shot for broken or incomplete cores, sand buildup, clogged vents and gassing problems, and adjusts shoot pressure/time, gassing and blow-tube cleaning as needed.

Small custom/job shop with short runs, frequent mold changes and older semi-automatic presses. Operator watches a newly hung, not-yet-proven tool, judges by eye whether parts are acceptable, and tunes the process by feel while conditions (resin lot, regrind, ambient) shift.

instances.label: Tending running injection molding presses on a plastics plant floor: watching cycles, taking parts from the mold or chute, degating/sprue removal, visual inspection, packing into cartons, keeping the hopper/dryer fed, clearing short shots and stuck parts.

Setting up an injection press for a new job: hanging/clamping the mold, connecting water, hydraulic core-pull and electrical services, purging and changing resin/color, entering or dialing in temperatures, pressures, shot size and cycle time, running first shots and correcting flash/short shots until first-article parts are accepted.

Operating a die casting machine in a metal foundry: ladling molten aluminum/zinc into the shot sleeve, spraying die lubricant and skimming dross, extracting the hot casting, quench, and loading the trim press, in heat, spatter and fumes.

Insert/overmolding work: placing metal inserts, terminals or labels into mold cavities each cycle without damaging the tool, verifying seating, then removing the overmolded part and staging it for secondary operations.

Foundry coremaking: tending a core shooter/core blower, extracting fragile sand cores from the core box, deburring the parting line, gluing/assembling core packages and racking them for the molding line.

Blow molding, rotational molding or compression molding tending: charging resin powder or SMC/BMC charges, closing and running the press or arm, unloading finished parts, deflashing/trimming and inspecting.

tasks.label: Turn valves and dials of machines to regulate pressure, temperature, and speed and feed rates, and to set cycle times.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine job startup / mold change on a modern digitally controlled injection molding press in a plastics plant: the operator calls up or keys in the parameter set at the machine HMI (barrel zone temperatures, injection velocity and pressure limits, hold pressure/time, screw speed and back pressure, clamp force, cooling and cycle timers), brings the machine to setpoint, and trims the first shots until parts pass inspection.

Mid-run process correction on an injection molding press: responding to short shots, flash, sink or dimensional drift by nudging hold pressure, switchover point, melt and mold temperatures, injection speed and cycle/cooling timers, then verifying the following shots hold spec.

High-pressure die casting cell: setting and trimming the shot velocity profile, intensification pressure, accumulator/hydraulic pressures, die temperature-control units, die-lube spray and dwell timers and overall cycle time, in a hot, oily foundry cell.

Hand-operated controls on and around presses, dies and auxiliaries: water manifold needle valves, air pressure regulators, hydraulic relief/flow valves, thermolator knobs and analog gauges on assorted, often older equipment scattered around the press; the operator walks the machine, reads gauges and turns each control by hand.

Foundry coremaking / sand molding machine: setting blow and squeeze pressures, gas-catalyst cure and purge times, sand feed rate and cycle timing on a core shooter, with frequent recipe changes between core boxes in dusty, hot conditions.

Other processes - extrusion blow molding, rotational molding, thermoforming, compression/transfer molding of rubber or thermoset: setting oven or platen temperatures, arm or screw speeds, air pressure regulators and cycle timers on mixed digital-and-analog control panels.

tasks.label: Connect water hoses to cooling systems of dies, using hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Plastics injection molding plant, mold changeover: after the mold is hung and clamped in the press, the setter connects cooling-water supply and return hoses between the machine-side manifold/temperature control unit and the mold's cooling circuits (quick-disconnect couplers or NPT fittings tightened with pliers/wrenches), then opens valves and checks each circuit for leaks. Hot platen area, cramped access, several to a dozen circuits.

Die casting or permanent-mold cell, die change: water/coolant lines connected to cover and ejector die halves and to cooling manifolds with threaded fittings and hoses tightened by wrench; higher pressure and temperature, cramped access around platens and shot end, die may still be warm.

Tool room or mold staging cart: pre-plumbing a die before it goes to the press - routing and installing jumper hoses between cooling circuit ports, threading and torquing fittings, adding clamps, labeling in/out, and pressure/flow testing the circuits on the bench.

Mid-run intervention on a running job: a hose is leaking, blown, kinked or a circuit is plugged; operator shuts isolation valves, drains, disconnects the offending hose/fitting with hand tools, fits a replacement, reconnects and verifies flow and no leaks so the machine restarts quickly.

Small or older shop with non-standard plumbing: rubber hose cut to length, pushed onto barbed fittings and secured with worm-drive clamps using a nut driver/screwdriver, hoses routed by hand behind and under the machine; layouts and fitting sizes vary machine to machine.

instances.label: Mid-size injection molding plant, 100–700 ton press: at end of a run the operator shuts down, purges, disconnects water/oil/air hoses and the ejector coupling, breaks loose and removes platen clamps or bolts, hooks an overhead hoist or rolls a mold cart in, lifts the 300–4,000 lb mold out of the platens, sets it on a rack and wipes the platens. General plant floor with cranes, aisles and people.

High-changeover molding line with quick-mold-change equipment: multi-ton mold (up to ~15 t) on a machine fitted with hydraulic or magnetic clamps, ejector coupler, automatic multi-couplers, driven rollers and side mold-change tables/carts on rails; operator initiates and supervises the unload sequence at the end of the ....

Die casting cell: after the run the die (1–20 t) must come out of a hot- or cold-chamber machine — cooling water and hydraulic core-pull lines disconnected, ejector plate detached, clamps released, die pulled with crane or die cart, in a hot, oily, lubricant-spattered foundry environment.

Small tooling on small machines: removing small dies, mold inserts, sprue bushings, nozzle tips, or core boxes (typically under ~100 lb) by hand with wrenches or a small hoist from small injection, rubber/thermoset compression, or core-shooting machines in a job shop or foundry core room.

Nonstandard/legacy removals: die or mold stuck or galled in the platens, seized or rounded-off bolts, damaged tooling, cramped or obstructed older machines, one-off fixtures in a mixed job shop — requires prying, heating, improvised rigging and judgment about what to disassemble.

tasks.label: Perform maintenance work such as cleaning and oiling machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Injection/blow molding press: cleaning the mold — wiping cavity and parting-line surfaces of residue, gas/plate-out deposits and release-agent buildup, clearing vents, air-blowing the cavity, applying rust preventative — during a run, at shift end, or at mold change on the shop floor.

Routine lubrication per the machine's PM schedule: greasing/oiling tie bars, toggle links and pins, platen guides, ejector and mold-height mechanism; checking and topping hydraulic and gearbox oil on presses and die-casting machines.

Die-casting / metal casting cell: applying die release lubricant and coolant to the die faces and blowing off residue between shots, lubricating the plunger tip and shot sleeve, and clearing flash and soldering from die faces.

Housekeeping around the press: sweeping/scrubbing spilled resin pellets, regrind, sand, oil, hydraulic drips and water from the floor of the machine's work area, and removing scrap and purge chunks from around the machine base.

Wiping down machine exteriors, guards, platens and tie bars; cleaning oil and grease leaks off the frame; cleaning material handling ancillaries — hoppers, feed throats, dryers, loaders, granulator chambers and mold water manifolds — between material or color changes.

Scheduled deeper preventive maintenance: changing or cleaning hydraulic and air filters and screen packs, descaling/flushing mold cooling channels, purging and cleaning the screw, barrel and nozzle at material change, cleaning heater bands, thermocouples and cooling-water strainers.

tasks.label: Smooth and clean inner surfaces of molds, using brushes, scrapers, air hoses, or grinding wheels, and fill imperfections with refractory material.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-pressure die casting: between shots the operator/automation blows flash, loose metal and residual water off the open die faces and cavity with air, and applies release agent, with the die mounted in the machine platens; hot, fast cycle, cavity in a fixed known position.

Plastic injection molding: cleaning resin residue, gas/off-gassing deposits and vents from the cavity and cores, either with the mold still in the press (brushes, cloths, cleaner spray, dry ice) or on a bench, to restore part surface quality before restarting a run.

Sand foundry production molding/coremaking line: blowing loose sand out of cope/drag cavities and core boxes, wiping tooling, and applying refractory coating/wash to the mold cavity surface before mold closing, at line rate.

Hand repair of sand molds and cores: brushing loose sand, scraping and slicking damaged edges, and filling broken spots, pits and imperfections with refractory paste/mold daub, judged by eye and touch on a finishing bench or at the mold line.

Permanent mold / gravity or low-pressure die casting: scraping and wire-brushing metal buildup and burnt-on coating off the hot die faces, blowing out the cavity, then spraying refractory die coat (e.g. DYCOTE-type) evenly over the mold surfaces before returning the mold to production.

Tool-room heavy mold maintenance: mold pulled and opened, cavity surfaces ground and stoned with grinding wheels/abrasives to remove burrs, washout and heat-check, pits and worn spots filled (weld/refractory) and the surface blended back to the original finish.

tasks.label: Operate hoists to position dies or patterns on foundry floors.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Injection molding plant, scheduled job change: operator rigs a 0.5–5 ton mold on the overhead crane or jib hoist, lifts it off the tooling rack, walks it to the press, guides it between the platens onto the locating ring, seats and clamps it, then connects water/hydraulic lines. Plant floor with other operators, forklifts and running machines nearby.

Die-casting shop die change: operator uses the bay crane to lift die halves (often several tons) from the die rack or preheat oven, guides them into the machine platens against locating pins, sets clamps, and hoists out the old die. Hot, oily floor; standardized die lifting eyes and stops.

Automated/semi-automated foundry molding line: hoisting a match plate or pattern plate set from the pattern rack onto the molding machine's pattern carrier, aligning to the dowels/registers and bolting it down, at a scheduled pattern change.

End-of-run teardown and staging: unclamping the die or pattern, hoisting it out of the machine, setting it on a cart or on blocks on the shop floor for cleaning/inspection, then craning it back into its numbered storage rack or to the die-repair area.

Jobbing/floor-molding foundry: hoisting large one-off wood or metal patterns, core boxes and flasks with chain slings and tag lines, hand-guiding them into a floor flask or pit mold, rolling over and adjusting the seat in loose sand. Non-standard lifting points, cluttered sand floor, riggers assisting.

tasks.label: Cool products after processing to prevent distortion.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Small-to-medium injection molded parts in a custom/captive plastics plant: each shot's parts are taken from the press (or off the takeout conveyor) while still hot and set on cooling racks, in nests, in a water/air-cooled fixture or a quench bath so they hold dimension; operator checks a sample for warp/shrink before packing. High-cycle, repetitive, plant floor with people moving around.

Large injection molded parts (automotive fascia, seat shells, totes, appliance panels) from 500-2500 ton presses: the hot, floppy part must be lifted without marking or bending and set into a dedicated cooling jig/fixture that holds its geometry for a fixed hold time before degating, trimming and inspection.

Die casting (aluminum/zinc/magnesium): hot shot is pulled from the die and immediately quenched in a water tank or set on a cooling conveyor/rack to stabilize the casting before trim press and inspection; hot metal, spray lubricant, splash and steam.

Sand / permanent-mold foundry: poured molds and shaken-out castings must cool in a controlled way — cooling line or cooling drum with metered water, cooling conveyors, or moving hot castings by hoist/cart to a cooling bay or yard and letting/spraying them down before shakeout, gate removal and blasting; mixed casting sizes, dust, heat.

Other molding processes (blow molding, heavy-gauge thermoforming, rotational molding, compression molding): parts held on cooling stations, blown with fans/air rings, water-sprayed on the mold, or racked in cooling fixtures until dimensionally stable before demolding and trimming.

tasks.label: Install dies onto machines or presses and coat dies with parting agents, according to work order specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Plastics injection molding plant: per the work order, the operator changes the mold on a horizontal injection press (a few hundred to several thousand pounds), rigging it with crane or mold cart, aligning the locating ring on the platens, clamping, hooking up water, hydraulic core and ejector connections, and wiping/spraying release agent on the cavity before first shot.

High-pressure die casting shop: installing cover and ejector die halves into a hot die casting machine, setting ejector rods and cooling lines, verifying alignment, then setting up and applying the die lubricant/parting agent coating to the die faces before and between shots, per the job's die-spray program.

Compression/transfer molding or rubber molding: bolting or clamping smaller heated dies into press platens per work order, setting shut height and heat, and coating cavity surfaces with parting/release agent before and during the run.

Foundry core room: mounting the core box/tooling set into a core shooter (cold box or shell), clamping it, connecting blow plate and gassing plate, and applying release/parting agent to the core box surfaces before shooting cores.

Permanent mold / gravity or low-pressure casting: mounting a metal mold (die) onto a tilt-pour or LPPM machine platen, connecting cooling/actuators, then spraying refractory die coat / parting compound to specified thickness and touching up worn areas per work order.

tasks.label: Unload finished products from conveyor belts, pack them in containers, and place containers in warehouses.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume run of one small/medium injection-molded part number: parts tumble onto a takeaway conveyor at the press, operator watches for obvious defects, bulk- or count-packs them into cartons or a gaylord, tapes and labels the container, stacks cartons on a pallet, stretch-wraps, and moves the pallet by pallet jack/forklift to a floor or rack location in the plant's finished-goods warehouse.

Large molded products (plastic pallets, crates, totes, bins, large automotive/appliance parts) come off the line one at a time; the operator trims/degates, stacks them directly on a pallet or in a rack cart, banding or wrapping the stack, then transports the load off the production floor to the warehouse or staging lane.

High-mix custom molding shop: several job changes per shift, many part numbers, each with its own pack-out spec (poly bags, layer pads, dividers, foam trays, specific counts, job-specific labels and travelers); operator degates, checks cosmetics, packs to the work-order spec, and carts/forklifts mixed small containers into warehouse locations.

Metal die casting/foundry: hot, oily, heavy castings arrive on a conveyor after quench and trim; operator inspects for flash, cold shuts and drags, packs them into returnable steel bins or part-specific dunnage racks, and a full bin is forklifted to warehouse storage.

Cosmetic or critical parts (medical device components, optical parts, Class A automotive trim) in clean or controlled conditions: each part individually inspected, handled without touching cosmetic surfaces, bagged or nested in a tray with interleaves, cartoned with count/lot documentation, then palletized and placed in the finished-goods warehouse.

tasks.label: Remove finished or cured products from dies or molds, using hand tools, air hoses, and other equipment, stamping identifying information on products when necessary.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Thermoplastic injection molding: each cycle the operator opens the gate or waits for ejection, takes molded parts and sprues out of the open mold, blows off/degates as needed and sets parts in a bin, tote or on a conveyor; plant floor, hot parts, fast cycles.

Die casting: operator/extractor pulls the hot casting (aluminum/zinc matrix with biscuit and runners) out of the open die with tongs or hand tools, quenches it, blows off quench fluid with an air hose and places it in the trim press or rack.

Rubber, silicone or compression/transfer molding: prying cured flexible parts out of multi-cavity heated molds with picks, brushes and air blast, separating parts from flash, placing them in trays; parts stick and tear easily.

Large-part processes (industrial blow molding, structural foam, rotational molding): demolding bulky parts such as tanks, cases or kayaks, sometimes with pry bars, air wedges, hoists or a second worker, then setting them on racks or trim fixtures.
Coremaking: removing cured sand cores from core boxes on a core shooter, blowing loose sand off, deburring lightly and setting fragile cores in racks or assembling them into core packages.

Stamping/marking identifying information on the removed part — pressing a hand stamp or date-code insert, pad printing a logo, dot-peen or laser marking a part/serial number — then racking the marked parts.

tasks.label: Obtain and move specified patterns to work stations, manually or using hoists, and secure patterns to machines, using wrenches.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Injection molding shop: operator gets the scheduled mold from the tool rack, moves it with an overhead crane or mold cart to the press, sets it on the platen, bolts/clamps it with wrenches, and hooks up water and hydraulic lines. Molds 200 lb to several tons; plant floor with aisles, cranes, other workers.

Green-sand foundry: operator pulls the specified match plate or pattern plate set from pattern storage, moves it manually or by hoist to a squeeze/vertical molding machine, and bolts or clamps the pattern plate to the machine's pattern carrier, checking alignment before restarting the line.

Die casting cell: die change on a cold-chamber machine — crane the die halves out of the rack and into the platens, bolt/clamp them, connect cooling and ejector hookups, tighten with wrenches, and verify die closure. Heavy hot tooling, standardized machine mounting.

Small tooling: hand-carried molds, core boxes, or die inserts under ~50 lb moved from a shelf to a bench-top press, shell-core machine, or small compression/rubber press and secured with clamps and hand wrenches, often several changeovers per shift.

Jobbing shop with large or non-standard tooling: oversized or one-off patterns, cope-and-drag pattern rigging, or odd-sized core boxes rigged with crane and slings, shimmed and aligned by feel, and bolted with improvised clamping to a machine that was not built for that tool family.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Injection molding shop floor: for a new job, the setter pulls the specified mold from the tool rack, brings it to the press by crane or mold cart, aligns it on the platens, clamps it, hooks up water/hydraulic/electrical connections and ejector, and verifies fit before startup.

Small hand-fitted tooling and consumables at the machine: swapping nozzle tips, screw tips and check rings, sprue bushings, hot-runner tips, interchangeable cavity/date inserts, and sprue-cutter or trim blades - usually hot, cramped work with hand tools at the injection unit or in the open mold.

Die casting cell: changing a hot die on a cold- or hot-chamber machine (crane or die cart, clamping, hose and core-slide connections) plus shot-end tooling - plunger tip, shot sleeve, and die-spray head nozzles/attachments.
Blow molding: changing the blow mould set/mould package (and associated blow pins or neck tooling) on a stretch-blow or extrusion blow molder for a different container size.
Foundry core room: changing the core box, blow plate, gassing plate and vents on a core shooter for the next core job, then clamping and proving the tool.

tasks.label: Repair or replace damaged molds, pipes, belts, chains, or other equipment, using hand tools, hand-powered presses, or jib cranes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Damaged mold/die must come out of the press: operator unbolts or unclamps the tool, disconnects water and hydraulic lines and electrical, slings it with the jib crane or overhead hoist, pulls it, sets a spare or repaired tool in the platens, re-clamps, re-connects lines and requalifies first shots. Injection press or die-cast machine on the plant floor.

On-machine minor mold/die repair while the tool is still in the press: freeing or replacing a broken ejector or core pin, swapping an O-ring or leaking water fitting, digging out a stuck slug or flash, stoning a nicked parting line, retightening loose plates. Hot tool, cramped access between tie bars, hand tools only.

Bench repair of a mold removed to the tool crib: split the mold halves, press worn bushings, leader pins or sprue bushings in and out with the arbor/hand press, replace broken return springs and seals, reassemble, check that ejection and slides work by hand before the tool goes back.

Replace damaged or leaking pipes, water lines, hydraulic hoses and fittings on the machine, mold manifolds, temperature controllers and chillers: shut down and drain, cut and route new hose, thread and torque fittings, purge and leak-check under pressure.

Replace worn belts, chains, sprockets and rollers on parts conveyors, granulators, dryers, sprue pickers and material-handling equipment: remove guards, slack the tensioner, strip the failed belt or break the chain, fit and tension the new one, re-guard and run a test cycle.

Replace other damaged machine components with hand tools and a hoist: heater bands and thermocouples on the barrel, nozzle tips, limit switches, gaskets, worn plunger tips/shot-sleeve hardware on a die-casting machine, damaged guarding.

instances.label: Injection/thermoplastic press setup: operator picks the cooling medium and circuits for the mold being run (chilled water, tower water, or hot oil), connects the mold's temperature-control hoses to the manifold/TCU, purges air, opens the valves and verifies flow in each circuit before start-up. High-pressure die casting cell start-up: operator selects the die release agent and its dilution ratio for the die and alloy, charges or primes the lube supply, then starts the die-lube spray and the die cooling-water flow at cycle start, checking spray coverage and water lines. In-cycle release-agent/lubricant application on semi-automatic or smaller presses (small injection shops, permanent-mold/gravity casting, rubber and thermoset compression molding): starting and timing the per-cycle release spray or applying it between shots, adjusting the amount to part quality.

Machine lubrication: operator selects the correct grease or hydraulic/way oil per the machine's spec sheet, fills the reservoir or hooks up the bulk supply, starts the automatic lube pump for tie bars, toggles and ejectors, and confirms lubricant is reaching the points.

Plant coolant/fluid management: mixing water-glycol or emulsion to the prescribed concentration, topping off central coolant tanks or machine sumps, and starting the chiller/cooling-tower circulation pumps and checking flow to the presses. Utility area and shop floor.

tasks.label: Adjust equipment and workpiece holding fixtures, such as mold frames, tubs, and cutting tables, to ensure proper functioning.

instances.label: Plastics injection molding plant: after a mold is hung in the press, the setter adjusts the workpiece-holding fixture and machine — clamp plates/clamps on the platens, mold height (daylight), clamp tonnage, ejector stroke and couplings — then closes the press and verifies the mold seats, seals and ejects properly before the run.

High-pressure die casting cell: setter adjusts die clamping and positioning on the platens, die height/locking force, tie-bar and ejector-plate attachment, and spray/extractor position so the die closes square and functions correctly at temperature.

Iron/steel foundry green-sand molding line: operator adjusts the pattern plate/mold frame (flask) mounting and alignment on the molding machine, mold thickness and squeeze settings, and mismatch/alignment so molds form and strip properly.
Core room: operator mounts and adjusts the core box (tool) on a core shooter — clamping, alignment of blow plate and gassing head, vents and ejection — and verifies cores shoot and release cleanly.
Thermoforming/trim station in a plastics plant: operator adjusts the forming and cutting tables (parallelism, height, tool block position) and the trim/punch tooling so parts form and cut to size.

Corrective and auxiliary adjustments on the shop floor during production: repositioning part tubs, chutes, guards and conveyor guides; shimming, realigning or re-torquing a loose fixture, mold frame or table with hand tools after flash, mismatch or a drop-out problem appears mid-run, on mixed-vintage, non-standardized equipment.

tasks.label: Maintain inventories of materials.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Injection molding floor: operator walks the press line at shift start, checks resin/regrind/masterbatch on hand at machine side (gaylords, boxes, hopper and loader levels), counts what remains, records quantities on a sheet or in the ERP and flags low items for reorder. Indoor plant aisle, standard racking and pallet positions, institution-controlled.

Replenishment of palletized material: pull a gaylord/pallet of resin or masterbatch from warehouse racking with a forklift or pallet jack, move it to the designated press-side position, connect it to the vacuum loader/central conveying line, and update the stock record for the consumed pallet.

Replenishment of bagged material: retrieve 25-50 lb bags of resin, colorant or additive from the stockroom, cut and dump them into the press-side hopper or blender, dispose of the empty bags, and record the bags consumed against the job.

Die casting / foundry: verify stock of aluminum or zinc ingot bundles, core sand, binder, flux, die lubricant and release agent; move ingot pallets from the storage bay to furnace-side staging in a hot, dusty aisle; log usage and reorder points.

Stockroom cycle count: count consumables and small items on shelves and in bins (metal inserts, packaging cartons, labels, purge compound, mold release, spare nozzle tips), reconcile counts against ERP records, and correct discrepancies.

Receiving: a truck delivers resin, ingot or packaging; worker checks pallets against the packing slip, looks for damaged/wet bags or crushed cartons, moves the pallets into rack or floor storage, and receipts them into the inventory system.

tasks.label: Position and secure workpieces on machines, and start feeding mechanisms.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume plastics injection molding at a molding plant: for a job that runs for weeks, the operator loads a carrier/'book' frame or a set of inserts into the open mold, verifies seating, closes the guard gate and presses cycle start; material feed (hopper/dryer/auger) is engaged at start of shift. Standard press, plant floor shared with other operators.

Precision insert molding: small stamped metal terminals, pins or threaded bushings (thousandths-of-an-inch tolerance) must be seated in each cavity of a multi-cavity mold within a 20-40 second window, with checks that cavities are clear of debris before the mold closes; scrap or mold damage results from misplacement.

Custom/job-shop molder (high mix, low volume): several changeovers a week across older horizontal and vertical presses; each job has different inserts, carriers, drop locations and manual gate/clamp routines, and the operator also positions the workpiece, starts the feed and handles secondary work between shots.

Metal die casting cell: operator/setter places steel inserts, cores or liners into the die, confirms clamping, then starts the automatic ladle or metal feed and the shot; hot die faces, lubricant mist, molten aluminum or zinc spatter.

Sand or permanent-mold foundry: setting fragile sand cores or chills into mold halves on a molding machine or a turntable of casting machines, positioning pattern plates/flasks, then starting the sand blow/feed or pour cycle; heat, dust, and cores that break if mishandled.

Other press molding (compression, transfer, rubber, or SMC/composite): weighing and positioning a charge, preform or insert into heated press cavities, securing it, closing the platens and starting the press feed cycle; heavy tools, hot platens, tacky material.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume injection molding plant: operator at a press-side bench cuts sprues, gates and parting-line flash off small-to-medium thermoplastic parts with a hook knife or nippers, visually checks the trimmed edge, and boxes the parts while the press cycles.

Scrap/regrind duty in a molding shop: operator gathers runners, sprues, and reject parts from bins around the presses, feeds them into a beside-the-press or central granulator, clears jams, and returns the ground regrind to the material feed or a gaylord for reuse.

Blow molding line: operator strips tail/moil and neck or bottom flash from containers, jugs or industrial drums with knives and hand deflashers as parts come off the machine, then throws the flash into a grinder.

Large-part molding (rotational molding, structural foam, heavy-gauge thermoforming): operator trims parting-line flash and cuts openings on large plastic parts with utility knives and hand tools, working around a part too big to hold.

Die casting / metal casting cell: operator removes gates, biscuits and flash from castings using nippers, hand knives/scrapers or a trim press, inspects the parting line, and sends the trimmed scrap back to remelt.

Custom / short-run job shop: operator hand-trims a small mixed batch of unfamiliar molded parts with a knife, judging where flash is heavy or thin on parts that have no dedicated trim tooling or program.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Injection/blow molding plant: operator weighs or proportions virgin pellets, regrind and color concentrate per a job recipe, lifts 25-50 lb bags or scoops from gaylords, and dumps the blend into the press hopper/tub at the machine throat; dusty, mixed pedestrian and forklift traffic, several presses per operator.

tasks.label: Spray, smoke, or coat molds with compounds to lubricate or insulate molds, using acetylene torches or sprayers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-pressure die-casting cell (aluminum/zinc): between shots the operator sprays water-based die lubricant/release onto both hot die halves and the plunger area, then blows off excess, on a fixed cycle; die is in a known open position at the machine.

Injection or compression molding machine (plastics/rubber): operator periodically opens the mold and hand-sprays mold release or an anti-stick/lubricating compound on cavity and core, wiping/cleaning first, to cure sticking parts before restarting the cycle.

Gravity/tilt-pour or low-pressure permanent mold casting: operator sprays refractory die coat (mold wash) onto preheated steel/iron mold cavities and cores, building insulating/lubricating thickness, and touches up the coating every few hours as it wears.

Smoking molds, cores, ingot/permanent molds, or ladle tooling with an acetylene torch to lay a carbon soot film for release and insulation; operator plays the flame over the hot surface by hand until coverage looks right.

Large tooling at floor level: spraying release or refractory coating on oversized core boxes, patterns, sand molds, or large dies staged off the machine, working around the tooling with a hand gun or pressure pot.

tasks.label: Preheat tools, dies, plastic materials, or patterns, using blowtorches or other equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Plastics plant: before a molding run, the operator brings resin up to temperature — setting and starting a hopper/central dryer, loading pellets or regrind, verifying material temperature/dryness (including reheating of preforms/sheet in blow-molding or thermoforming lines). Standard drying equipment on a production floor.

Injection molding shop: at cold start or after a mold change, the operator preheats the mould — connecting hot water/oil temperature-control unit hoses or energizing cartridge/band heaters and hot runners, waiting for the tool to reach set temperature before the first shots.

Die casting cell: at cold start the operator preheats the die (and often the ladle, gooseneck or plunger tip) with a hand blowtorch/gas burner and/or a hot-oil die temperature unit, checking surface temperature with a pyrometer before first casts.

Foundry floor (permanent-mold, gravity die, sand or investment casting): the worker torch-preheats or burner-dries pouring ladles, mold halves, core boxes and patterns at various locations, with hot metal, smoke, and variable tooling positions.

tasks.label: Inspect workpieces for defects, and measure workpieces to determine accuracy of machine operation, using rules, templates, or other measuring instruments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-process sampling check at the machine: every Nth part the operator pulls a turned/milled/ground metal part out of the machine, wipes off coolant and chips, checks one to four key dimensions with digital calipers, a micrometer, a bore gauge or go/no-go gauges, logs the SPC reading and tweaks a tool offset if size is drifting. Shop floor, coolant and swarf present, parts typically fist-sized or smaller.

First-piece / setup inspection after a job changeover on one of the machines the operator tends: the first part is taken to a bench and every dimension on the print is verified with calipers, micrometers, height gauge, radius and thread gauges, then signed off before production is released. High-mix job-shop work, a new part number every few hours to few days.

Visual and tactile defect inspection of parts coming off the machines: burrs, chatter and tool witness marks, scratches, incomplete cuts, chipped edges on metal parts; flash, short shots, sink marks and splay on molded/formed plastic parts. Operator eyeballs and feels each part or a sample and sorts good from scrap while machines keep running.

Off-line measurement of a complex or critical part in the shop's QC area: the operator carries the part to a CMM, optical comparator or surface-finish tester, sets it up, runs or follows the measurement routine and produces a dimensional report for a customer or internal sign-off.

Checking large or awkward workpieces against templates, straightedges, rules and radius/contour gauges: press-braked or roll-formed sheet parts, bent tube, weldments, large castings. Part is handled on a layout table or on the floor next to the machine; contour and profile conformance, angles and overall size are checked.

tasks.label: Observe machine operation to detect workpiece defects or machine malfunctions, adjusting machines as necessary.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Job-shop/production machining department: operator tends 3–6 CNC mills, lathes, screw machines or grinders and watches for dimensional drift and tool wear — gauges parts periodically, updates tool offsets, indexes to a redundant/replacement tool when a cutter wears or breaks, and stops a machine that is making out-of-tolerance parts. Open shop floor, aisles, coolant mist, other workers present.

Same machining floor, process-signature anomalies: operator hears chatter, sees a spindle-load spike, smoke, or an impending crash / overload on one of the machines and reacts by overriding feed, changing spindle speed, or feed-holding the machine before scrap or damage occurs.

Injection molding / extrusion plant: operator tends 4–8 molding machines, inspects shots for short shots, flash, sinks, splay, burn marks and weight drift, and adjusts switchover point, hold pressure, barrel temperatures or cycle time; segregates suspect parts. Climate-controlled plant floor with conveyors and part bins.

Stamping / punch press line with coil feed: operator watches for misfeeds, buckled stock, slug pulls, parts not ejecting, burrs and die wear; stops the press, corrects feed length, shut height, tonnage or lubrication, and restarts. Noisy press room, guarded presses, scrap conveyors.

Fabrication shop laser/plasma cutting machine or robotic welding cell: operator monitors cut or weld quality (dross, incomplete cuts, part tip-ups, spatter, burn-through, seam wander) and adjusts feed rate, focus, gas or weld parameters, or stops the cycle. Guarded cell on a shop floor.

Hands-on mechanical troubleshooting after an anomaly is noticed, across all machine types: reaching into the work zone to clear a chip nest or jammed slug, freeing a part stuck in the mold, wiping/reaiming a coolant nozzle, replacing a chipped insert by hand, re-seating a slipped workpiece or re-shimming a die, then verifying the fix. Ad-hoc, varies with each fault.

tasks.label: Set up and operate machines, such as lathes, cutters, shears, borers, millers, grinders, presses, drills, or auxiliary machines, to make metallic and plastic workpieces.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production run on CNC turning/milling machines in a metalworking shop: operator keeps two to four machines running - loads bar/blanks or castings into chucks and vises, cycle-starts, unloads, deburrs edges, gauges sample parts with micrometers/gages, swaps worn inserts, and keeps the batch moving to the next operation.

Job changeover/setup on a CNC lathe or machining center between jobs: mount the fixture, vise or soft jaws, load and preset the required cutting tools, call up the program, set work and tool offsets, run and inspect a first article, and adjust offsets until the part is in ....

Forming/cutting press work in a fabrication shop: set dies or press-brake tooling and back gauges on a punch press, press brake or shear, then feed blanks, form or shear the metal or plastic workpieces, check angles/dimensions, and stack finished parts.

Conventional/manual machine work in a toolroom or small job shop: engine lathe, knee mill, drill press, surface grinder and band saw used for one-off, repair or prototype pieces - layout and indicating, hand-feeding cuts, dialing in by feel, measuring and reworking to fit.

Grinding operations: set up and tend surface, cylindrical or centerless grinders - mount and dress the wheel, set stops/size control, load and unload shafts or small precision parts, gauge size, and compensate for wheel wear.

Plastic workpieces: sawing, routing, trimming, drilling and tapping plastic or composite stock and molded parts on routers, saws and drilling machines (plus light forming presses), holding edges clean and dimensions within print.

tasks.label: Change worn machine accessories, such as cutting tools or brushes, using hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Job shop / production machine shop: a CNC machining center's tool assembly holds a dull or chipped solid round tool (end mill, drill, reamer). The operator pulls the holder from the magazine or bench rack, loosens a collet nut / presses the tool out of a powRgrip or shrink-fit holder with hand tools, installs a fresh tool, presets length, and returns the assembly to the magazine.

Turning center or indexable milling cutter: the operator stops the cycle, unscrews a small torx clamp screw at the machine or at a bench, blows chips and coolant out of the insert pocket, indexes or replaces the worn carbide insert, retorques the screw, and re-touches the tool offset. Chip- and coolant-covered, tight access.

Grinding, deburring or finishing machine: the operator changes a worn grinding wheel or wheel pack, an abrasive belt/disc, or a wire brush — unbolting a flange nut with a spanner, mounting the new accessory, then dressing/balancing it and checking runout before restart.

Punch press, turret punch or press brake: the operator replaces worn punches, dies or forming tools in the tool station/turret using hand tools and shims, checks alignment and clearance, and test-runs a part before resuming production.

Sawing and miscellaneous machine accessories: change a dull band saw or cold saw blade (de-tension, thread through guides and wheels, re-tension and track), or swap worn brushes, wipers, chip guards and similar consumables, often in cramped positions with hand tools.

tasks.label: Set machine stops or guides to specified lengths as indicated by scales, rules, or templates.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Sheet-metal fab shop: operator sets the back gauge stops/fingers (and shear stops) on a press brake or shear to specified flange lengths from a drawing, checking with a rule or tape and repositioning fingers/tooling for each job change.

Cutoff saw or lathe: operator sets a length stop on a horizontal band/cold saw, or a bar-feed/turret stock stop on a lathe, to a specified cut length using a scale or tape, for repetitive cut-to-length production runs.

Mill, drill press, or grinder: operator sets travel stops, trip dogs, depth stops, table dogs or fences to specified positions using dials, scales, gauge blocks or a template so the machine stops at the specified dimension.

Roll former, slitter, or plastic extrusion/downstream line: operator positions guide rails, guide rolls, knives or spacers to specified widths using scales or spacer templates during a size changeover.
Punch press or coil/press feed line: operator sets stock guides, edge guides, passline height and gauge pins/stops to specified locations from a setup sheet or template before starting the run.

Mid-run correction: operator gauges the first piece (or a periodic sample) against a template, scale or gauge, then nudges the stop/guide a few thousandths and re-locks it to bring parts back to print.

instances.label: Setting up a CNC machining/turning center (often one of several the operator tends) in a job or production shop: confirming the sump holds the right coolant at the right concentration, choosing the delivery mode for each tool (flood, through-spindle/high-pressure, air blast), aiming the nozzles at the cut, and starting flow at cycle start.

Tending a group of manual or semi-automatic machines (band saws, drill presses, surface grinders, engine lathes, screw machines) on a shop floor: switching on the coolant pump or opening the valve, hand-directing a flexible nozzle at the cutting zone for each new setup, and adjusting flow by eye during the run.

Routine fluid service across a bank of machines: checking sump concentration with a refractometer, mixing concentrate and water to the specified ratio, topping off or recharging sumps, refilling way-lube/oiler reservoirs, and greasing fittings before or between shifts.

Forming work on presses, die-casting machines, or roll formers: selecting the drawing compound/die lubricant for the job, filling and starting roller-coater or spray lubrication on the coil or blanks, setting spray/flow rates, and keeping die lube flowing each cycle.

Changeover or exception cases: a new material or process demands a different fluid (straight cutting oil for a tough alloy, dry or air-only for plastics, a portable mist/MQL unit), requiring the old fluid to be drained, the tank cleaned, drums fetched, and the machine charged with the newly selected fluid.

tasks.label: Make minor electrical and mechanical repairs and adjustments to machines and notify supervisors when major service is required.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: During a production run, the operator services the work zone of one of the machines: clearing packed chips/swarf off the fixture and part, wiping or blowing coolant and residue off locating surfaces, and clearing the coolant spray path so the next part loads and cuts correctly. Routine, repetitive, same machine and fixture each cycle.

Parts start drifting out of tolerance because a cutting edge has worn or chipped. The operator gauges the part, adjusts tool wear/length offsets on the control, swaps in a fresh insert or a duplicate tool, re-verifies dimensions, and resumes the run.

A jam, misfeed, or mechanical misalignment stops a machine: a part hangs in the chute, a feeder or guide has drifted, gibs/ways are loose, a belt has gone slack, or a press shut height/stop needs resetting. The operator frees the obstruction and readjusts the mechanism by feel and measurement so it does not recur.

A small worn or broken mechanical part must be replaced with hand tools: a coolant hose or nozzle, an air fitting, a drive or timing belt, a seal/O-ring, a way wiper, a worn gripper pad or clamp. Requires opening guards or panels in a cramped machine interior, removing fasteners, fitting the new part, and re-checking operation.

A minor electrical fault: blown fuse or tripped breaker, a failed proximity/limit switch or photo-eye, a loose or damaged connector or wire, a burned-out indicator lamp. The operator locks out the machine, checks continuity/voltage with a meter, replaces or reseats the component, restores power, and confirms the machine cycles.

The operator notices an abnormality beyond their scope while tending machines — spindle noise or vibration, a hydraulic/air leak, an overheating motor or drive, a recurring servo alarm — verifies it, and reports it to the supervisor/maintenance so the machine is scheduled for major service.

instances.label: Production machine shop floor: operator stands at the control panel/pendant of a CNC lathe or machining center and moves controls to set cutting parameters — keying in or editing spindle speed (S) and feed (F) values, setting tool/work offsets that fix depth of cut, jogging with the MPG handwheel to touch off, and trimming feed/rapid override dials during the first cut. Chips, coolant mist and varying job setups; several machines run in parallel.

Shop with conventional/manual secondary machines (engine lathe, knee mill, drill press, turret lathe): operator shifts geared-head speed-change levers or moves the belt on step pulleys, selects a feed lever position from the feed chart, sets a depth stop/micrometer stop and swivels the head or vise to an indicated angle, then locks it with a wrench.

Fabrication shop press brake or other forming press: setter mounts the punch and die, sets ram depth/bottoming position and target bend angle, sets backgauge stops and stroke, then test-bends and adjusts the depth to correct for springback.

Grinding, sawing and drilling machines: operator sets infeed/downfeed rate dials and wheel speed on a surface or cylindrical grinder, dials in dress depth, sets blade speed and feed pressure and the miter angle on a saw head, or sets drill depth stops — mostly dials, levers and clamped angular adjustments, verified by trial cut and gauge.

Older gear/cam driven machines: mounting change gears on a lathe quadrant or hobber for a required feed/thread ratio, fitting cams and stop dogs on a multi-spindle screw machine or automatic, or mounting a template/tracer pattern — sliding gears on studs, setting mesh/backlash by feel, and tightening the quadrant or cam-drum fasteners.

instances.label: Experienced machine operator walks a newly hired operator through setup of a CNC mill or lathe on the shop floor: explaining tooling and fixture selection, how to load the program, set work and tool offsets, and verify first-piece dimensions — conveying the procedure step by step while the trainee performs it.

Operator coaches a peer through a job changeover across a different machine type in the cell (e.g., moving a trained lathe operator onto a press brake or screw machine), explaining differences in controls, cycle sequencing, and part handling between the machines.

Operator briefs a temp or entry-level tender on safe operation of the machines they will tend: guarding and interlocks, lockout/tagout, emergency stops, chip and coolant handling, and shop rules, before the worker is released to run the machines.

During a running shift, operator answers a coworker's questions and corrects technique on the fly — advising on feed and speed adjustments, offset corrections for tool wear, gauge/micrometer use, and diagnosing why a part is out of tolerance.

Operator explains setup sheets, travelers, and revised work instructions to the crew at a shift handoff or toolbox meeting, including documenting or annotating the procedure so the next shift can repeat the setup.

tasks.label: Extract or lift jammed pieces from machines, using fingers, wire hooks, or lift bars.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: CNC lathe/mill jam: a finished or partly machined workpiece hangs up — welded to the chuck jaws, wedged in the parts catcher, or stuck in the unload chute. Operator halts the cycle, opens the door, reaches into a coolant- and chip-filled chamber and frees the piece with fingers, a wire hook, a mallet or a small bar, then re-references and restarts.

Feed/transfer jam in an automated line between machines: a misfed blank in a press feeder, a scrap slug stuck in the die, or a part wedged in a bowl-feeder track, chute or transfer conveyor. Operator e-stops/locks out, works a wire hook, magnet or pliers into the pinch point, extracts the piece, checks for damage and restarts.

Plastics jam: a molded part or sprue sticks in the mold cavity/runner, or material bridges and jams the feed throat, hopper or granulator. Operator extracts it with a brass hook or pick, working hot, close to mold surfaces that must not be scratched, under cycle-time pressure.

Chip/swarf jam: long stringy chips form a bird's nest wound around the tool, bar stock or spindle and jam the work zone or chip conveyor. Operator pulls the tangle clear with a hook and gloved hands, sometimes cutting it, then clears the chamber before restarting.

Heavy jam needing leverage: bar stock jammed in a bar feeder or saw, or a heavy stamping/casting stuck in a die or extractor. Operator uses a lift bar, pry bar, wedge or hoist — often with a second worker — to break the piece free without damaging tooling.
