instances.label: Flat sheet/plate layout: at a layout table in a fab or machine shop, the operator measures from the stock edge with rule/square/straightedge and scribes or soapstone-marks cut lines and part outlines on steel, aluminum or plastic sheet before shearing, sawing, plasma or router cutting. Large or heavy pieces marked where they sit: on the shop floor, on rollers or at the machine, the operator uses tape measure, chalk line, square and soapstone to mark reference lines, hole/fitting locations and cut lines on beams, large plate, or partly assembled weldments too heavy to move to a bench.

tasks.label: Verify dimensions, alignments, and clearances of finished parts for conformance to specifications, using measuring instruments such as calipers, gauge blocks, micrometers, or dial indicators.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-process / first-off check of a machined die detail (block, punch, insert, plate) at the machine or bench in the tool room: wipe the part, check diameters, thicknesses and step depths with micrometers, calipers and a height gauge against the print, decide accept/rework before the next operation.

Formal final inspection of a finished precision detail on the surface plate or in the inspection room: hole locations, flatness, parallelism, squareness and tight-tolerance features checked with gauge blocks, dial indicators, gauge pins and a height gauge (or CMM), producing a documented conformance result.

Verifying fits, clearances and alignment during die/mold build-up: punch-to-die cutting clearance, insert-to-pocket fit, gib and slide clearance, guide pin/bushing alignment, shut height and parallelism of shoes, using feeler gauges, gauge pins, dial indicator sweeps and blue spotting on the partly assembled tool at the bench.

Inspecting first-article / tryout parts produced by the finished die or mold (stampings, moldings) against the part print with calipers, micrometers, gauges, optical comparator or CMM, to confirm the tool holds the specified dimensions.

Press-side or in-service verification during die repair/maintenance in the stamping plant: measuring wear, punch protrusion, clearances and alignment on a die mounted in the press or sitting on a bolster, with restricted access, feeler gauges and indicators.

Setting up and running a repeat batch of standardized tooling details or spare die components (dozens of pieces) on a mill, lathe or grinder in a shop with standardized workholding and an existing proven program; operator loads blanks, monitors, gauges and compensates for tool wear across the run.

tasks.label: Fit and assemble parts to make, repair, or modify dies, jigs, gauges, and tools, using machine tools, hand tools, or welders.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: New die build: in the tool room, bench-assemble a one-off progressive or compound stamping die — set punches, die buttons and retainers, springs, guide pins and bushings; hand-fit with stones and files; blue and spot mating faces; shim and adjust punch-to-die clearances to tenths; dowel and bolt the shoes; check shut height and hand-prove the tool.

Die repair in the die-repair bay or at the press line: strip a worn or crashed die, diagnose the failure, TIG/micro-weld build-up on cracked or washed-out die sections and punch tips, dress and re-grind, replace broken details and springs, refit the section into its pocket, reassemble and prove out under the press.

Engineering-change modification of an existing die or mold in the tool room: machine or EDM a new detail or insert, open a pocket, weld and re-cut a form, then fit the new detail into the existing tool, re-dowel, reassemble and verify the change against the revised print.

Jig and fixture build: fit and assemble locating pins, rest pads, drill bushings, clamps and toggle assemblies onto a machined base plate; ream and press dowels; torque fasteners; align and adjust with indicator/CMM to hold part location to print for a one-off custom fixture.

Gauges and machinists' hand tools: fit and lap gauge members, assemble go/no-go plug, ring and snap gauges to size, certify with gauge blocks; rebuild or repair shop hand tools, arbors and holders (press, fit, adjust, test).

Assemble cutting-tool and holder packages in the tool crib/toolroom: shrink-fit or collet-mount cutters into holders, add coolant fittings and set screws, set assembly to length and check runout on a presetter.

tasks.label: Inspect finished dies for smoothness, contour conformity, and defects.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Finish-machined/ground die and mold components (die buttons, trim steels, inserts, mold cores and cavities) brought to a bench or inspection room in a tool room: verify profile/contour against CAD or print, check dimensions and radii, check surface finish, and look for tool marks, burrs and nicks before the part goes to assembly.

Blanking/piercing punch and die cutting edges on a finished progressive-die station: inspect edge condition and sharpness for chipping, rollover, burr and micro-cracks, verify edge radius/profile and clearance, under magnification at the bench or on a comparator/measuring machine.

Large assembled stamping die (draw/form die, one to many tons) on the die bench or in the tryout press: spot the die faces with blueing to judge contact, run hands over draw radii and binder surfaces for smoothness, look for scratches, galling, weld-repair marks and low spots, and confirm the form matches the die model before sign-off.

Polished or textured injection-mold cavity/core: inspect the full shape-giving surface under strong light and magnification for scratches, pits, swirl and orange peel, verify polish grade (e.g., SPI finish) and texture uniformity, and check parting-line and shutoff surfaces for damage.

In-process verification at the machine: after 5-axis milling, hard-milling or EDM of a die block, check the contour and surface condition while the workpiece is still clamped on the machine table, to confirm conformity and finish before unclamping.

tasks.label: Lift, position, and secure machined parts on surface plates or worktables, using hoists, vises, v-blocks, or angle plates.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Tool room bench/machine table: small machined workpiece (under ~25 lb) — a punch, die block, gauge blank or mold insert — set on parallels or v-blocks in a precision vise on a mill, grinder or bench, tapped down, indicated true to a few thousandths and clamped before the next operation.

Die/mold shop: medium component (roughly 50–300 lb) — a die section, shoe segment or mold plate — lifted off a cart with a jib crane or chain hoist, set on a machine table or surface plate against an angle plate or stops, strap-clamped and dialed in.

Die shop bay: large die shoe, bolster or mold base (1,000–20,000 lb) rigged with eyebolts/slings on an overhead bridge crane, landed on a die bench, boring-mill table or large surface plate, blocked, leveled and clamped down.

Granite surface plate for layout/inspection: machined part set in v-blocks or bolted to an angle plate, squared and indicated to tenths with a height gauge/indicator, then secured so lines can be scribed or dimensions checked.

Die tryout, fitting and repair: die halves or fixture components repeatedly positioned, shimmed and re-secured on a worktable or bench beside a press while the toolmaker spots, blues and fits mating parts, with frequent unclamping and repositioning.

tasks.label: File, grind, shim, and adjust different parts to properly fit them together.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Toolroom bench fitting of new, mostly prismatic/cylindrical die and mold details (punches, die buttons, retainers, heel/wear plates, gibs, strippers): stone and file mating faces and edges to remove burrs and heat-treat scale, grind or lap to size for a specified slip or press fit (0.005-0.03 mm), shim gib/wear-plate clearance, trial-assemble and re-check with mic, gauge pins and feeler stock.

Die spotting / tryout of contoured draw, form and flange dies: apply spotting blue, close the die in a spotting press under load, read the contact pattern, hand-grind and stone high spots on the freeform die face, add or remove shims under pads and pressure pins, and repeat until contact and panel quality are accepted.

Injection-mold benching: fitting cavity/core inserts, slides, lifters and shutoff surfaces so the mold seals steel-safe and shuts off without flash - hand stoning and grinding parting-line and shutoff faces, shimming inserts to height, blue-checking and reworking until the mold closes correctly.

Building and adjusting jigs, fixtures, checking gauges: grinding or lapping locator pads and rest buttons, shimming locators and clamps to bring dimensions into tolerance, indicating the assembly in, tapping and re-shimming, torquing fasteners and re-verifying with indicators or CMM.

Die/mold repair and adjustment on as-found tooling in the die shop or at the press line: disassembling a section of the tool, fitting a replacement punch, button or trim steel to the surrounding worn geometry, regrinding and adding shims equal to the stock removed to restore cutting clearance and timing, reassembling and trying the tool out, often under production-downtime pressure.

tasks.label: Smooth and polish flat and contoured surfaces of parts or tools, using scrapers, abrasive stones, files, emery cloths, or power grinders.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Tool room bench work: deburring, stoning and filing flat and simple machined/ground/EDM'd die and mold detail components (die plates, shoes, blocks, spacers) — breaking edges, removing burrs and grind/EDM marks, stoning flats before assembly. Fine polishing of injection-mold cavities and cores to a specified finish (SPI B/C prep through A-series mirror), on hardened tool steel with freeform geometry, ribs, corners and parting-line detail, using progressive diamond stones/paste, felt bobs and hand-held rotary tools at the polishing bench.

Finishing small precision items — punches, pins, gauges, small inserts and machinists' hand tools — with emery cloth, fine stones and buffing to remove marks and produce a smooth or mirror surface without altering size beyond tolerance.

Blending and polishing a repaired area on a die or mold section at the bench: dressing down TIG/laser-clad weld build-up on a worn edge or radius with grinders, stones and abrasives until it blends into the surrounding surface and matches the original contour.

In-place touch-up during die tryout or a production run: stoning high spots revealed by spotting blue, polishing out galling, pickup, scoring or burrs on a die mounted in a press or spotting press, working overhead/into pockets in the press shop under time pressure.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bench layout in the tool room: a squared-up steel die block or plate (a few inches to ~24 in) is set on a surface plate/angle plate, coated with layout dye, and lines for pockets, slots and edges are scribed with a vernier height gauge, combination square and scribe to ±0.005–0.010 in, then referenced during subsequent milling/grinding.

Layout done at the machine: workpiece clamped in a vise or bolted to a mill/EDM/grinder table, edges found with an edge finder or indicator, datums established and reference lines scribed or witness marks placed before machining.

Layout on large or irregular workpieces — multi-ton die blocks, castings, forgings or weldments craned onto the shop floor or a large machine table — using straightedges, squares, tape, surface gauge and soapstone/scriber (sometimes a portable arm/laser tracker) to distribute stock and mark machining lines.

tasks.label: Conduct test runs with completed tools or dies to ensure that parts meet specifications, making adjustments as necessary.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: First tryout of a new sheet-metal stamping die (draw/form/trim) in a tryout or production press at a die shop or stamping plant: die is set, blanks are run, panels are checked for splits, wrinkles, burrs and springback on a checking fixture or CMM, then the toolmaker blue-spots the die, hand-grinds/stones high spots, welds and recuts relief, alters draw beads, pads and shims, and re-runs until panels are accepted.

Tryout of a progressive, compound or small stamping die in a toolroom press: strip stock fed, sample hits run, parts gauged with micrometers, pin gauges, optical comparator for hole location, burr and flatness; toolmaker then adjusts punch-to-die clearance, shims, sharpens punches, tunes strippers, pilots and feed length, and re-runs.

T1/T2 sampling of a completed injection mold or die-cast die at a molding/casting machine: mold hung, process set, shots run, parts judged for short shots, flash, sink, warp and dimensions; corrections made to the tool — vent, polish, bench a parting line, adjust gate/ejectors/cooling — then resample until parts are approved.

Tryout of a completed jig, fixture, checking gauge or welding fixture: fixture mounted on a machine or bench, test parts loaded and machined/checked, repeatability and fit verified against the master or print; locators, pins, clamps and rest pads are adjusted, filed, lapped or re-dowelled until the fixture holds parts to spec.

Test cut with a newly made or reground special cutting tool (form tool, boring/insert tooling) in a CNC machine where acceptance turns on part dimensions: run a trial part in test stock, measure the controlled features, and bring the part into spec by correcting tool offsets/setting position, then re-cut to confirm.

Test cut with a newly made special cutting tool where the trial part shows a geometry, finish or edge problem (chatter, poor finish, wrong form profile, burr) and the toolmaker must rework the tool itself — regrind relief or the form, hone the edge, adjust rake — then re-cut and re-measure.

instances.label: Toolroom: drill and tap the screw/dowel hole pattern in a die shoe, backing plate or fixture plate (steel or aluminum, up to a few hundred pounds). Worker clamps the plate to the drill press table, picks up layout/edge coordinates, spot-drills, drills clearance and tap-drill holes, taps 1/4-20 to 1/2-13, chamfers/deburrs and checks fit with screws.

Bench drill press in a machine shop: small die/fixture details (punch retainers, spacers, gib blocks, gauge bodies) held in a drill-press vise; spot, drill, countersink or ream, then power- or hand-tap small threads (#6-32 to 1/4-20) in tool steel or aluminum without breaking taps; deburr and thread-check.

Repeat work: a small batch (5-50) of identical plates or blocks drilled and tapped using a drill jig or stops for repeatable location; the same setup run part after part, with periodic hole-size and thread checks.

Fitting/assembly stage: holes located off the actual as-built parts - transfer-drilling through one plate into its mate, picking up an existing hole or dowel with an indicator/probe, adding or relocating a mounting hole in a partly assembled die or fixture, then tapping it.

Salvage/repair: a stripped or damaged threaded hole or a broken screw/tap in an existing (often hardened) die component - pick out or drill out the broken fastener, drill oversize and tap for a larger screw or thread insert, working around the surrounding assembly.

tasks.label: Set pyrometer controls of heat-treating furnaces and feed or place parts, tools, or assemblies into furnaces to harden.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine batch hardening of small tool-steel workpieces (punches, die inserts, form tools, gauges) in the shop's in-house heat-treat area: worker sets the furnace temperature controller/pyrometer to the spec for the steel grade, racks parts in a basket or on a tray, places the load into a box or atmosphere furnace with tongs, soaks, then transfers to the quench.

Tempering / stress-relief runs after quench: worker sets the tempering oven controller to the required temperature and time, places quenched tool components on trays or racks into the oven, and repeats for double or triple tempers, unloading between cycles.

Vacuum-furnace hardening of die and mold sections and cutting tools: parts are wired or racked on a grid fixture, the load is transferred into the vacuum furnace, the cycle recipe (ramp, soak temperature, gas-quench pressure) is set on the furnace controller, and the load is gas-quenched and then tempered.

Heavy work: a large die block, die-cast die insert or mold plate (100 kg to over 1,000 kg) is slung with a hoist or moved on a charge car/fork into a large batch furnace; the toolmaker sets the ramp and soak setpoints on the pyrometer/controller, soaks the load, and quenches or air-cools it.

One-off or rush job with a mixed, unfamiliar load: the toolmaker works out the cycle from the steel supplier's data sheet, attaches load thermocouples, watches the pyrometer trace, manipulates hot parts with tongs from furnace to oil/salt quench by feel and color, then checks hardness and re-runs or adjusts if the result is off.

roles.title: Welders, Cutters, Solderers, and Brazers
roles.description: Use hand-welding, flame-cutting, hand-soldering, or brazing equipment to weld or join metal components or to fill holes, indentations, or seams of fabricated metal products.

tasks.label: Operate safety equipment and use safe work habits.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Fabrication/manufacturing shop, pre-weld setup at a bench or station: don PPE (auto-darkening hood, leathers, gloves, respirator), swing the local fume-extraction arm into position, hang welding curtains/screens to shield co-workers from arc flash, confirm ventilation is running, attach the ground clamp correctly.

Shop equipment safety checks and shutdown: verify gas cylinders are capped and chained upright, leak-check regulators/hoses, inspect leads, electrode holders and cable insulation, confirm machine grounding, then purge lines and shut off gas and power at end of job/shift.

Maintaining safe conditions during a weld in a shop: keeping combustibles and rags clear of spatter, safe stinger/torch handling and parking, screening the arc from passersby, controlling hot metal and slag, housekeeping of the work area between joints.

Field/construction hot work (structural steel, plant maintenance, occupied building renovation): obtain hot-work permit, survey and clear or blanket as-found combustibles, rig spark containment, station an extinguisher, and hold a post-weld fire watch on an uncontrolled site.

Confined-space or elevated field welding (tank, pressure vessel, ship compartment, pipe rack): test the atmosphere with a gas monitor, set up forced-air ventilation blower, don harness/retrieval line and supplied-air respirator, coordinate with an attendant, maintain continuous monitoring while welding.

sources.transferJustification: The welder's safety task (arc-flash screening, guarding bystanders, safe shielding-gas connection) is discharged inside the cell by machine-monitored guarding and integrated gas supply rather than by human PPE and screens.

tasks.label: Examine workpieces for defects and measure workpieces with straightedges or templates to ensure conformance with specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: General fabrication / job shop: after running fillet and groove welds on a steel weldment at the booth, the welder visually examines each bead for cracks, porosity, undercut, burn-through and overlap, checks leg size and profile with fillet/weld gauges, and lays a straightedge or square across the assembly to check flatness, distortion and squareness before it moves on.

Production manufacturing plant (automotive, ag/heavy equipment, sheet-metal OEM): repetitive weldments checked against go/no-go templates, check fixtures and prints — verifying weld presence/length/location, hole and mount positions, and post-weld distortion, at line rate on every part or a sampling plan.

Pipe and pressure-vessel shop: welder checks joint fit-up (root gap, hi-lo/internal misalignment, bevel angle) with gauges and templates before welding, then examines the completed root and cap of the girth/longitudinal weld for undercut, incomplete fusion, reinforcement height and alignment against code acceptance criteria.

Field/site work (structural erection, pipeline, plant maintenance shutdown): welds made in place on erected steel, tanks or pipe in a ditch; the welder inspects the joint in situ — often overhead, in confined or elevated positions, in weather, with grinding dust and variable light — and uses a straightedge, square or template to check alignment and fit of members already in place.

Repair/maintenance shop: a used, dirty or damaged part (truck frame, bucket, cracked casting, worn shaft) is examined for cracks and prior-weld defects before repair, then re-checked after welding with a straightedge for warp/flatness and against a template or the mating part for dimensional conformance.

tasks.label: Weld components in flat, vertical, or overhead positions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production/repetitive arc welding of small-to-medium parts in a job shop or OEM fabrication shop: brackets, weldments, tubing and plate assemblies tacked and clamped on a bench or fixture, mostly flat and horizontal fillet and groove welds, repeated across a batch, subject to visual/weld-size inspection.

Heavy and structural fabrication of large weldments in a shop or fabrication yard: beams, frames, tanks, machine bases, ship hull blocks. Work is crane-positioned; the welder climbs on and into the assembly and runs long fillet and multi-pass groove welds in flat, vertical and overhead positions, often to code (AWS D1.1) with NDE.

Pipe and spool welding in a pipe fabrication shop: root, hot, fill and cap passes on carbon/stainless spools, rolled on a positioner or fixed-position (5G/6G), to ASME code with radiographic acceptance.

Field welding of standardized structural or pipe joints at a construction, pipeline or plant erection site: steel column splices, girth welds on line pipe, repeated joints of known geometry welded in place, outdoors or under temporary cover, with weather, wind and access constraints and code inspection.

Field/site welding of varied, non-standard joints under access constraints: retrofits, brackets and attachments, miscellaneous metals, work aboard ships afloat, at height or in confined spaces, one-off joints with improvised fit-up and no repeat geometry.

Maintenance and repair welding to rebuild worn or cracked components: hardfacing and build-up of mining/agricultural/industrial wear parts, rolls, dies and buckets, typically brought into a plant maintenance or repair shop, where the worn geometry differs part to part.

tasks.label: Detect faulty operation of equipment or defective materials and notify supervisors.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production welder in a metal fabrication shop notices mid-weld that the equipment is misbehaving — erratic arc, wire feeder slipping or birdnesting, shielding gas flow dropping, worn contact tip or bad ground — stops, diagnoses that it is a machine fault rather than technique, and reports it to the lead/supervisor so the machine can be serviced or swapped.

Before or during setup, the welder finds the incoming material is defective or wrong: mill scale/laminations, rust pitting, cracks, warped or out-of-tolerance parts, wrong alloy or wrong thickness versus the traveler, bad fit-up from the cutting/forming station; the welder judges it unweldable to spec and notifies the supervisor or QC rather than proceeding.

During production the welder sees recurring weld discontinuities in their own or a neighbor's work (porosity, undercut, burn-through, inconsistent bead) and traces the cause to a faulty machine, bad consumable lot, or contaminated gas, then reports the pattern to the supervisor so the lot or machine can be pulled.

Field work — construction site, pipeline, shipyard, or plant shutdown — where the engine-driven welder output fluctuates, leads or cables are damaged, or delivered consumables are wet/damaged; the welder identifies the fault under outdoor and confined-space conditions and notifies the foreman or safety supervisor.

Start-of-shift or periodic equipment check: cylinders, regulators, hoses, torch, cables, fume extraction, PPE; the welder finds a leak, damaged hose, or failed extraction unit, tags the equipment out and reports it to the supervisor or maintenance.

tasks.label: Recognize, set up, and operate hand and power tools common to the welding trade, such as shielded metal arc and gas metal arc welding equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production welding in a manufacturing plant: welder sets up a GMAW/FCAW machine (wire, shielding gas, voltage/wire-feed), loads repeat steel parts into jigs on a bench or positioner, runs fillet/lap welds on batches, then de-slags, grinds and wire-brushes with hand and power tools.

Custom job-shop fabrication, high-mix low-volume: welder reads the print, selects and sets up the right process and machine (MIG, stick, or TIG), tacks up a one-off assembly on the bench, welds varied joints and positions, and grinds/cleans to finish.

Heavy plate / structural / shipyard fabrication inside a large facility: big weldments and hull or frame blocks set by cranes; welder carries the gun and leads to the work, runs multipass fillet and groove welds on thick plate, gouges and grinds between passes.

Pipe spool / pressure-piping shop: welder sets up on a positioner or turning rolls, tunes the machine for root and fill passes, runs girth welds on carbon or stainless spools to code, cleans and grinds between passes.

Field, maintenance and mobile repair welding: in-situ work on installed equipment, structures and piping at plants, yards, farms and jobsites; welder hauls an engine-driven or portable machine, judges the damage, gouges or grinds out cracks, fits patches and welds out-of-position in confined or elevated spots.

Jobsite erection welding of standardized heavy structural joints: full-penetration groove welds on steel column splices set by crane at a building site, welder sets up the machine, preheats, and runs multipass welds in the prepared groove.

tasks.label: Select and install torches, torch tips, filler rods, and flux, according to welding chart specifications or types and thicknesses of metals.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production/fab shop, GMAW or FCAW: welder reads the WPS/welding chart for the alloy and plate thickness, picks the matching wire type and diameter, and installs the correct contact tip, gas diffuser, nozzle and liner on the MIG gun; loads/changes the wire spool or drum and trims the stickout.

Manufacturing shop, GTAW (TIG) on stainless/aluminum sheet and tube: welder selects tungsten type and diameter, collet, collet body and gas cup per the chart for the metal and thickness, installs them in the torch, and selects the matching filler rod alloy and diameter from the rod rack.

Fab shop or plate yard, oxy-fuel cutting/heating: welder consults the manufacturer's tip chart for fuel gas and plate thickness, selects the cutting tip (or rosebud heating tip), seats and tightens it in the torch head, attaches the correct cutting attachment/torch handle, and checks seating for leaks.

Bench work in a shop, torch brazing/soldering of tubing, fittings or assemblies: welder selects the filler alloy rod (e.g., BAg/BCuP or solder) and the compatible flux for the base-metal combination, installs the appropriate torch tip for the joint size, and applies/coats flux on rod and joint before heating.

Field or site work (construction erection, pipeline, mobile repair, shipboard): welder selects stick electrodes, filler rods or cutting tips per the procedure and the metal type/thickness from a truck or gang box, and installs them on a handheld torch, electrode holder or cutting attachment in weather and on varied, unfixtured work.

tasks.label: Mark or tag material with proper job number, piece marks, and other identifying marks as required.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Structural steel fab shop: after cutting/fitting, the welder writes the piece mark and job/shop-order number on beams, angles, plates and sub-assemblies with soapstone or paint marker, so pieces route correctly to fit-up, paint and shipment. Pieces of many sizes sit on tables, racks and carts as found; marks must be legible after blasting/painting.

Production/job-shop welding: welder stamps, etches or laser/dot-peen marks identifying marks on finished weldments, small parts and test coupons at a bench — part number, heat/lot number, welder ID stamp — for traceability before parts go to inspection.

Tagging and labeling: attaching wire-tied metal or plastic tags to bundles and racks of like parts, applying adhesive barcode labels to parts, skids and pallets, and tagging remnant stock with heat/job numbers before it is returned to the rack or shipped.

instances.label: Production/job fabrication shop: welder preps small-to-medium sheet and plate parts at a bench or welding table — grinds mill scale and rust off the joint edges, knocks dross/slag off plasma- or laser-cut edges, wipes cutting oil and grease off with solvent, wire-brushes the weld zone before MIG/TIG welding.

instances.label: Job/fab shop bench work: welder wheels an oxy-acetylene cart to a bench, threads oxygen and fuel regulators onto cylinder valves and wrench-tightens, cracks cylinder valves, sets working pressures on both regulators, purges hoses, opens torch valves, strikes the torch and tunes to a neutral flame for cutting, welding or heating.

CNC oxy-fuel burn table / mechanized cutting station in a plate shop: operator hooks the machine to the piped oxygen/fuel supply and station outlet regulators, then sets preheat oxygen, fuel and cutting-oxygen pressures for the plate thickness, ignites the torch(es) and trims the preheat flames before the burn program runs.

Field work (construction, demolition, scrap, farm/heavy-equipment repair): portable rig hauled to an as-found site, regulators connected to bottles on a cart or truck rack, pressures set and flame lit and adjusted outdoors in wind, cold or confined access, often re-adjusted through the job.

HVAC/refrigeration/plumbing brazing and soldering in buildings and residences: connect regulator to a B-tank or MAPP/oxygen kit in a mechanical room, crawlspace or occupied space, set low delivery pressure/flow, light the torch and set a soft brazing or soldering flame at the joint.

Shipyard, heavy structural fab or pipe shop with manifolded gas: welder couples hoses to a station manifold outlet, opens the station valves, sets regulator pressures for cutting, gouging or preheating, lights the torch and adjusts the preheat flame, working from staging or inside assemblies in a controlled yard/shop.

tasks.label: Monitor the fitting, burning, and welding processes to avoid overheating of parts or warping, shrinking, distortion, or expansion of material.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production/repeat-part welding in a metal fabrication shop: welder runs a batch of identical brackets, frames, or weldments held in jigs on a bench, watching heat build up over the run, adjusting travel speed/current, skipping around the part and letting it cool, and checking parts against the jig for warp before releasing them.

Heavy/structural thick-section work in a fabrication shop, yard, or shipyard: multi-pass groove and fillet welds on plate, beams, girders and stiffened panels; welder checks preheat and interpass temperature (temp sticks/pyrometer), sequences and back-steps welds, balances passes side-to-side, and watches for pull-in and camber change.

Thin-gauge and precision work: 16-24 ga sheet, tubing, stainless and aluminum, exhaust and auto-body panels; TIG/short-arc MIG where burn-through and oil-canning are the risk. Welder tacks a sequence, stitches/skip-welds, uses heat sinks and purge, pauses for cooling, and watches color and puddle size continuously.

Pipe spool / pressure piping welding in a fab shop: root, hot, fill and cap passes on carbon and stainless spools per a WPS with preheat and interpass temperature limits; welder monitors heat between passes and controls bead placement so the spool stays in tolerance and passes RT.

Site welding of structures on a construction site, plant, or vessel under outfitting: column splices, pipe racks, tank shells, ship hull seams; weather, wind, awkward positions and restricted access, with the welder monitoring heat input and distortion of already-erected steel.

Cutting and burning operations in a shop or yard: hand and track oxyfuel/plasma cutting of plate and shapes, bevelling and air-arc gouging; the worker watches kerf, speed and heat accumulation and orders the cuts so the plate or part does not warp or shrink out of size.

tasks.label: Grind, cut, buff, or bend edges of workpieces to be joined to ensure snug fit, using power grinders and hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production fabrication shop, repetitive parts: welder grinds mill scale, dross and burrs off the edges of standard laser/plasma-cut parts and grinds bevels at a bench or fixture so the joint closes tight before tacking. Same part family all shift, parts arrive on carts from cutting.

Custom/job-shop fabrication, one-off or low-volume parts: welder torch- or plasma-cuts the member to length, grinds a bevel or land, dresses the cut edge, and hammers or jacks a lip flat to close a gap so mating pieces sit snug; geometry differs job to job.

Heavy fabrication / shipyard / structural shop: edge prep on large weldments and heavy sections (plate 25-70 mm, nodes, rings, girders) staged on the shop floor by crane — grinding, arc-gouging and back-gouging joints, often reaching into awkward positions on a big assembly.

Field construction / pipeline site, work on loose members before erection: beveling pipe ends and plate edges, grinding bevels and removing coating at a laydown area or field shop trailer, weather and dust present but the piece can be handled and set on stands.

Field construction / erection, in-situ prep on already-installed or immovable structure: grinding and gouging the edges of a beam, column or tank shell in place at height or in a trench, cutting out a section, and bending/persuading the joint edges to line up for a snug fit.

Mobile repair and maintenance (farm equipment, truck frames, plant machinery): grinding out cracked or corroded edges to a V, cutting a patch plate to match an irregular hole, bending it to the contour, and fitting it — usually on the damaged machine itself or on a bench in a small repair bay.

tasks.label: Weld separately or in combination, using aluminum, stainless steel, cast iron, and other alloys.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Shop fabrication welding in a manufacturing plant or job shop: welder works at a bench/jig station or positioner, running GMAW/GTAW/FCAW on mild steel, stainless, and aluminum weldments — brackets, frames, tanks, trailer and equipment subassemblies, wear-part rebuild — either repetitive batches or one-off/small-batch high-mix parts with imperfect fit-up. Parts are staged, tacked, clamped, welded, and visually/dimensionally inspected.

Heavy/large-structure welding inside a shipyard or heavy-fabrication facility: long fillet and butt seams on thick steel plate panels, ship hull blocks, pressure parts, and large weldments; the welder carries the machine to the workpiece, works in and around the block, positions of weld vary, welds are inspected to class/Navy standards.

Pipe and tube welding in a pipe/spool fabrication shop: carbon, stainless, and alloy pipe joints rolled on positioners, root-fill-cap passes to ASME/X-ray quality, fit-up gaps and mixed diameters, plus small pressure vessels.

On-site welding of heavy structural steel joints during building erection: column-to-column splices and thick-plate groove welds on erected frames, multi-pass, at height, with preheat and weather/wind conditions, inspected by UT.

Miscellaneous field welding away from any shop: pipe tie-ins, tanks, structural add-ons, handrails, bracketry and equipment modifications at plants, farms, mines, and job sites; awkward access, out-of-position welds, dirty/painted base metal, varied alloys, work performed from a welding truck.

Maintenance and repair welding of damaged or worn components: cracked cast iron housings, engine blocks and machine bases, broken machinery parts and dissimilar-metal joints; the welder must judge the damage, gouge/drill out the crack, choose electrode and preheat/interpass regime, weld and peen, in a repair shop or at the customer's site.

tasks.label: Chip or grind off excess weld, slag, or spatter, using hand scrapers or power chippers, portable grinders, or arc-cutting equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production manufacturing plant: welder grinds spatter off and dresses/blends weld beads flush on repeat medium-size weldments (brackets, frames, exhaust or body parts) held on a bench, table or positioner in a weld booth; standard parts, known joint locations, cosmetic/pre-paint quality bar.

High-mix job shop / custom fabrication: one-off or small-lot parts of varying geometry; chipping slag from FCAW/SMAW passes with a hand chipper and wire brush, grinding stops/starts, spatter and excess reinforcement before paint or fit-up; parts moved by hand or hoist to a grinding bench or laid on the shop floor.

Heavy/large weldments in a fab shop or shipyard: girders, tanks, pressure vessels, ship blocks, heavy-equipment frames; welder works around and inside a large assembly, gouges out a defective or tacked weld with air-carbon-arc or plasma and grinds the cavity clean, dresses long multi-pass welds out of position.

Field construction / erection / pipeline site: chipping slag between passes and grinding welds on erected steel, pipe joints or bridge members, outdoors at heights, in trenches or on scaffolds, with weather, dirt and changing access.

Maintenance and repair welding on equipment in place: removing old weld, slag and spatter on machinery, truck frames, mine or mill equipment, ship interiors; confined or awkward access, unpredictable part condition and orientation.

tasks.label: Develop templates and models for welding projects, using mathematical calculations based on blueprint information.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Custom/job-shop fabrication: welder reads a blueprint for a repeated part (gusset, bracket, base plate, hole pattern), works out the dimensions and hole centers arithmetically/trigonometrically, then lays out and cuts a reusable pattern from cardboard, hardboard or thin sheet, which is used to trace and cut the production parts. Indoor fab shop, shop-standard steel stock.

Plate/sheet development work: welder-fabricator develops a flat pattern for a curved or non-planar shape (cone or truncated cone reducer, square-to-round transition, gored elbow, pipe branch) by radial-line or triangulation calculation from blueprint dimensions, then marks the development full-size on plate or paper as the template. Indoor shop, layout table or floor.

Pipe/vessel spool shop: welder calculates miter, saddle, lateral and branch intersection developments from isometric drawings and pipe OD/wall data, makes wrap-around templates or marks cut/bevel lines directly on pipe and vessel heads before cutting and fitting. Indoor pipe shop, standard schedule pipe.

Field work (construction site, plant shutdown, ship or heavy-equipment repair): welder measures as-found geometry of an existing structure or damaged component, combines it with blueprint information and calculated allowances, and makes a cardboard/sheet template on the spot for a patch plate, brace, handrail return or replacement section. Weather, access restrictions, distorted and out-of-square existing steel.

Building a physical model, mock-up or welding jig/fixture to blueprint dimensions: welder computes part positions and angles from the drawing and fabricates a jig, layout board or full-size mock-up used to hold and check the weldment. Indoor shop with standard bench, table and stock.

tasks.label: Repair products by dismantling, straightening, reshaping, and reassembling parts, using cutting torches, straightening presses, and hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Heavy fabrication/repair shop: a damaged excavator bucket, dozer blade, boom, or trailer frame comes in bent and cracked. Welder assesses damage, torches/gouges off the deformed or broken section, heat- and press-straightens members, refits with clamps and hand tools, then rewelds and grinds to fit.

Field repair at a customer site (construction site, farm, quarry, mine, roadside): welder works from a service truck on equipment as found — cuts off a bent tooth adapter, cracked bracket, or damaged rail/guard, straightens with heat and a porta-power, refits and welds in place, often overhead or in awkward positions.

Plant maintenance shop: damaged machinery components (conveyor frames, chutes, brackets, guards, dies, mezzanine steel) are dismantled, bent members straightened on a shop press or with heat, reshaped, and reassembled/rewelded during a maintenance window.

Auto/truck body and frame shop: collision-damaged frame rails, bumpers, subframes, or box/bed structures are dismantled, pulled/straightened on a frame rack or press, sectioned with a torch or plasma, and reassembled by welding to factory dimensions.
Shop bench work: press-straightening simple, repeat-geometry bent parts (shafts, rods, bars, small profiles) — check runout/deflection, press to tolerance, recheck; no cutting or rewelding required.
Shop bench work: small weldment repair — cut/gouge off a broken tab, lug, or bracket from a small part, dress the surface, fit a replacement piece and weld it back on.

tasks.label: Clean or degrease parts, using wire brushes, portable grinders, or chemical baths.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Fabrication job shop, pre-weld prep: welder uses an angle grinder with grinding disc or wire wheel/cup brush to strip mill scale, rust, paint, oil and cutting oxide from plate, pipe, and structural members staged on benches, carts, or the shop floor before fit-up.

Fabrication/production shop, post-weld cleanup: chipping and wire-brushing slag, grinding weld spatter, dressing and blending weld beads on fabricated assemblies of varying size and geometry so the part is clean for inspection, paint, or the next pass.

Field/site work: cleaning joint areas and adjacent surfaces on pipe, structural steel, tanks, or installed equipment at construction sites, pipeline right-of-ways, or outdoor yards with a portable grinder or power wire brush, in variable weather, access, and body positions.

Production shop batch degreasing: repetitive small and medium parts run through a solvent or aqueous parts washer, vapor degreaser, or chemical dip tank — load, soak/spray, rinse, dry, unload — before brazing, soldering, or welding.

Repair/maintenance bay: cleaning greasy, painted, corroded or mud-caked used components (heavy equipment buckets and frames, truck chassis, farm machinery) with wire brush, grinder, and solvent to expose sound metal before weld repair.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic deburring/grinding of cut steel. tasks.label: Hammer out bulges or bends in metal workpieces.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Fabrication shop bench/plate table: flat plate or sheet parts (laser-, plasma- or flame-cut blanks, or plates bowed and waved by cutting/welding heat) are hammered flat on an anvil or table, checked with a straightedge, so they will fit up and weld correctly.

Fabrication shop: bent long stock and simple round/flat parts — round bar, rod, shaft, pipe/tube, angle, flat bar — straightened by hammering on an anvil or in an arbor/hydraulic press before or after welding, checked for straightness/runout.

Structural steel shop: welded beams and girders (H-beams, T-sections, plate girders) whose flanges have pulled in/out and whose webs have bowed from submerged-arc or MIG welding; the welder hammers/presses the flanges and web back to flatness and camber tolerance.

Job shop bench: a one-off three-dimensional weldment (machine frame, bracket assembly, box/tank weldment, chute) with local bulges and bows from welding; the welder judges by eye and straightedge where to strike, uses hammer with dolly/backing block, clamps and sometimes localized heat, and re-checks with square and tape.

Repair/maintenance shop: bent or bulged sheet and plate on large assembled equipment — truck bodies, trailers, dump beds, buckets, hoppers, tanks — hammered out in place on the machine with sledge, dolly and torch heat before or after weld repair.

Field work (construction site, shipyard erection, plant maintenance): straightening bent flanges, buckled plate, misaligned members in place on the structure, often at height, in confined spaces or outdoors in weather, using sledge and heat, checked by eye/level.

tasks.label: Check grooves, angles, or gap allowances, using micrometers, calipers, and precision measuring instruments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Plate/structural fabrication shop: before and during welding, the welder checks root opening, bevel/groove angle, root face and plate misalignment on tacked groove joints using a welding gauge (Hi-Lo/Cambridge), caliper and rule; parts sit on benches or the shop floor.

Pipe/tube fabrication shop: welder checks root gap, land, bevel angle and hi-lo on pipe or tube butt joints held in stands/rollers before and between passes, adjusting fit-up or tacks when out of tolerance.

Heavy/large weldment shop (shipyard block, rail car, pressure vessel, heavy equipment): welder checks gap and alignment along long groove seams on large assemblies, working from ladders/platforms and in awkward positions with gauges and tape.

Production shop bench check: repeated micrometer/caliper measurement of material thickness, machined weld-prep dimensions, groove depth and finished weld/part dimensions on repeat parts, recorded against a check sheet for QC.
Field structural erection: welder checks groove gap, bevel and alignment on column splices and beam-to-column joints in place at a construction site, at height, outdoors in variable weather.
Field maintenance/repair (plant shutdown, mobile welding rig, mine/farm equipment): welder checks fit and gap on irregular repair joints on worn or cracked in-service parts, in situ with hand gauges.

tasks.label: Melt and apply solder to fill holes, indentations, or seams of fabricated metal products, using soldering equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Sheet-metal / architectural metal shop: worker solders seams and joints on fabricated galvanized, copper or stainless assemblies (duct sections, pans, gutter and flashing sections, hoods, tanks) at a bench or on a shop table, using torch or soldering copper, flux and solder wire; parts vary in size and shape, fit-up gaps must be bridged, joint must be leak-tight and reasonably cosmetic.

Production or repeat-part soldering of copper/brass/steel assemblies in a manufacturing plant: heat-exchanger and radiator joints, plumbing fittings, valve bodies, electrical components; same part over and over, filler applied to seal seams and fill gaps, leak test follows.

Rework/cosmetic fill: after weld or fabrication inspection, worker fills pinholes, porosity, gouges and low spots (indentations) on fabricated products (food-service stainless, ornamental metalwork, body/lead filling) with solder, then dresses the fill flush; defect number and location differ part to part.

Field, in-place work: soldering copper roofing pans, gutter and downspout joints, flashing corners on a building, or sealing a hole/leak on installed piping or equipment at a customer site; awkward positions, weather, ladders/roofs, work cannot be moved.

In-plant maintenance soldering inside a controlled facility (factory, shipyard, utility): a leaking cooler, tank, tubing bundle or fixture is removed to the maintenance shop bench, the hole or seam is cleaned, fluxed and filled with solder, then leak-checked and returned to service.

tasks.label: Ignite torches or start power supplies and strike arcs by touching electrodes to metals being welded, completing electrical circuits.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production manufacturing shop (fabricated metal, machinery, transport equipment): welder at a bench/positioner station repeatedly starts the wire feeder/power supply and strikes GMAW or FCAW arcs on tacked steel parts, dozens to hundreds of arc starts per shift, on a shop floor shared with other workers.

Custom/high-mix job shop or in-plant maintenance shop: one-off or small-batch weldments and repairs; welder hand-positions varied parts, sets the machine, scratch- or lift-starts TIG, strikes stick electrodes, or starts MIG on differing joints, materials and thicknesses, often re-striking after grinding.

Field construction on prepared, repeatable joints on large structures: striking arcs on steel column splices/moment connections at an erection site, or pipeline girth welds on the right-of-way; outdoors, weather and wind, access by scaffold, band or track.

Mobile/field repair welding from a welding truck at a plant, mine, ranch, bridge or roadside: starting the engine-drive power supply and striking arcs on broken equipment welded in place, unknown steels, awkward out-of-position joints, no fixturing.

Shipyard or heavy-fabrication plant on very large weldments: welder (or robot) travels to the joint inside ship blocks, tanks and structural assemblies and strikes arcs at each seam, repeatedly repositioning across a block.
Torch work in a shop: igniting an oxy-fuel cutting/gouging/heating torch or a brazing torch (striker or auto-ignitor), setting preheat, and initiating plasma pilot arcs for cutting operations.

tasks.label: Guide and direct flames or electrodes on or across workpieces to straighten, bend, melt, or build up metal.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Repair/fabrication shop: building up metal on worn or undersized parts brought into the shop — hardfacing bucket lips and teeth, rebuilding shafts, rolls and dies, filling gouges, holes and low spots in castings and weldments. One-off or small-batch parts of varied geometry, craned onto a bench or positioner, MIG/TIG/PTA/laser deposition, then ground or machined back to size.

Structural steel / general fabrication shop: flame (or induction) heat straightening of welding distortion — spot, line and vee heats on plate panels, beams and weldments to pull out bow, angular distortion and buckling, checked iteratively with straightedge and square until within tolerance. Shop floor, overhead crane, standard equipment.

Shipyard / heavy plate shop: line heating with gas torches to form and fair curved shell plates and stiffened panels to template or design curvature, alternating heating passes with measurement, sometimes with jacks or water cooling.

On-site inside a customer facility (power plant boiler, paper mill, refinery, factory floor): building up eroded or worn surfaces on equipment that cannot be moved — boiler waterwall tube wastage, turbine/pump shaft journals, mill roll surfaces — during an outage, working from scaffolding or staging inside an institution-controlled plant.

Outdoor field work at a mine, quarry, farm, yard or construction site: hardfacing and build-up on heavy equipment as found — dozer blades, bucket edges, ground-engaging tools, crusher or rail parts — engine-driven welder, weather and dirt, no fixed layout.

Field straightening/bending of structure in place: heat-straightening a bridge girder or truss member bent by vehicle impact, pulling bows out of erected steel, straightening bent equipment frames or trailer rails, with torch heat patterns combined with jacking, judged by measurement on site.

sources.system: IHIMU-α (IHI-α) automated steel plate bending / line heating system

sources.claim: IHI Marine United's IHIMU-α is a fully automated line-heating (gas flame) plate bending system that measures the plate, plans heating lines and heats it to target curvature including finishing heats; used on plates for actual ships since the 1997 IHI-α predecessor.
sources.transferJustification: Line heating is literally guiding flames across a workpiece to bend metal; heat straightening of weld distortion is the same operation with flatness rather than curvature as the target, using the same torches, heat patterns and measurement feedback on comparable steel plate.

tasks.label: Use fire suppression methods in industrial emergencies.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Incipient fire at the point of work in a fabrication/manufacturing shop: slag, sparks or hot metal ignite rags, cardboard, wood dunnage, oily debris or insulation, often under a bench, behind stock or inside a scrap bin. Welder stops the arc, secures the torch/gun, grabs the nearest ABC extinguisher or fire blanket, knocks the fire down, then checks the area for re-ignition and reports it.

Fire-watch / suppression duty during and after permitted hot work in an industrial plant, refinery or shipyard: welder or designated fire watch monitors the work zone and adjacent spaces (other side of a bulkhead, deck below, behind walls), wets down combustibles, and extinguishes sparks and smoldering material with an extinguisher or hose during work and for 30-60 minutes afterward.

Field / outdoor hot work on a construction site, pipeline right-of-way, farm or erection job: cutting or welding sparks ignite dry grass, tarps, insulation, spilled fuel or debris with no fixed protection nearby. Welder uses the truck-mounted extinguisher, water can, shovel/dirt or a hose to put it out before it spreads.

Fire that has grown beyond incipient inside a large plant space (stored combustibles, pallets, coatings, or a fuel spill alight after cutting). Welder shuts down equipment, pulls the alarm, evacuates the area and applies a wheeled extinguisher, standpipe hose stream or plant fire monitor / hands off to the emergency response team.

Oxy-fuel or gas equipment emergency: hose fire, flashback/backfire into the torch, burning regulator or cylinder valve, or a burning welding machine. Welder must instantly shut fuel and oxygen valves, cool the cylinder with water, apply an extinguisher and move cylinders clear.

Hot work ignites material inside process equipment: slag or sparks fall into a dust-collection duct, filter, conveyor or pit and smolder. Welder shuts down the collector/ventilation and extinguishes the embers before a flash or deep-seated fire develops.

sources.system: Unifire FlameRanger / Force 50 & 80 robotic nozzles

sources.claim: Unifire's FlameRanger autonomous robotic fire suppression system (robotic nozzles plus IR3 flame detection) is installed in waste-to-energy plants and recycling facilities, where it detects and suppresses fires fully automatically, at the fire's source, within seconds and without human intervention.
sources.transferJustification: Same task family — applying a suppression agent to an industrial fire — but performed by a fixed installation covering a defined, unobstructed volume rather than by a person carrying an extinguisher to an arbitrary point of ignition.

sources.claim: FlameRanger has been third-party tested and shown to detect, locate and accurately suppress ... on ro-ro passenger ship weather decks, replacing the 5-12 minutes crew normally take to respond; it is fully autonomous with optional remote control.
sources.transferJustification: Substantiates autonomous suppression of a real fire in an institution-controlled, fixed-layout work space (a vehicle deck), i.e. the emergency-suppression action itself, validated by third-party fire tests.

sources.transferJustification: Directly covers suppression of fires in industrial facilities, the setting of the task; limited to fires within the monitor's line of sight in a large open volume.

sources.claim: Mitsubishi Heavy Industries' Firefighting Robot System (water cannon robot, hose-laying robot, reconnaissance robots and a command vehicle) was deployed to the Ichihara City ... for petroleum-complex fires; the robots move, lay hose and adjust water discharge autonomously while an operator selects the plan.

sources.claim: GreCon spark detection and extinguishing systems mount infrared spark sensors and extinguishing nozzles directly on industrial exhaust ducts and automatically quench sparks and ignition sources in ... with water mist, protecting filters and silos while production continues.

sources.claim: Firetrace automatic fire suppression systems are fitted to CNC/EDM and automated machinery; on fire the detection tubing bursts, the cylinder valve discharges agent directly onto the fire, and an integrated switch automatically stops the machine.

sources.transferJustification: Supports the negative judgment that mobile firefighting robots that would have to find and attack a fire amid shop clutter or on a jobsite are teleoperated today.

tasks.label: Preheat workpieces prior to welding or bending, using torches or heating furnaces.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Structural/heavy-plate fabrication shop: welder applies an oxy-fuel rosebud or gas heating torch to thick steel weldments, beams, base plates or castings to bring the joint area to the WPS-required preheat (e.g., 150-400F), verifies with temp sticks/IR gun, then welds and maintains interpass temperature. Parts sit on tables, positioners or the shop floor in a controlled industrial facility.

Pipe/pressure-vessel or spool shop: preheating pipe joints and vessel seams (carbon, chrome-moly, high-strength steels) with torch, resistance heating pads or induction cables to a code-specified temperature, thermocouple- or crayon-verified, before root and fill passes; pipe held on rollers or positioners in a controlled shop.

Field or in-situ work: pipeline right-of-way, structural steel erection, plant shutdown or mobile repair. Welder preheats joints outdoors or inside installed equipment with a torch or portable induction/resistance heater, in wind, cold and awkward positions, on structures that cannot be moved; layout differs at every site.

Production brazing/soldering of small assemblies (HVAC copper tube joints, carbide-tipped tools, fittings, electrical assemblies): repetitive preheating of parts with a bench torch, induction coil or heating furnace before applying filler, at a fixed bench or line in a manufacturing plant.

Heating prior to bending/forming or flame straightening: torch or induction heating of plate, bar, pipe or a distorted weldment to forming temperature in a fab shop or shipyard (line heating of hull plate, hot bending of bar stock, straightening a warped frame), guided by temperature indicators and shape checks.

Maintenance/repair shop one-offs: preheating a cracked cast-iron or cast-steel component, a worn bucket tooth or a heavy machine part before repair welding, using a rosebud torch or by soaking the part in a heating furnace/oven; geometry differs part to part and volumes are one or two pieces.

sources.claim: Wolf Robotics (Lincoln Electric Automation, Fort Collins CO) supplies robotic cells in which the robot performs gas preheating of workpieces (natural gas, propylene, propane) with an infrared sensor monitoring interpass temperature, sold to heavy-fabrication customers.

sources.system: Motoman / gantry robot induction-heater tending cells (Grant Prideco pipe upsetting; Tier-1 crankshaft forging)

sources.claim: In deployed US industrial cells, Motoman and gantry robots tend automated induction heating systems: robots unload 2250F billets from an induction heater into a forging press, and a gantry robot moves pipe whose end has been heated to forging temperature in ... into the upsetting press.

sources.system: Turntable-type automatic flame brazing machine with preheating (KETCHAN)
sources.title: Turntable-Type Automatic Flame Brazing Machine with Preheating - KETCHAN Induction
sources.claim: Commercial automatic flame-brazing machines integrate a controlled preheating stage ahead of the brazing torches on a PLC-sequenced rotary indexing table, with robot loading/unloading variants offered for high-throughput production.
sources.transferJustification: Directly the brazing-preheat variant of the task: the machine raises workpiece temperature with a gas flame under program control before filler metal is applied.

sources.system: TESI induction pipeline construction preheating equipment
sources.title: Induction heating for welding and coating of pipeline field joints - TESI
sources.claim: Induction equipment makers supply automatic and semi-automatic machines for weld preheating in pipeline construction, but the field units are positioned and supervised by the crew rather than by a robot.
sources.transferJustification: Same task (weld preheat) in the field, but autonomy of placement and operation is not established, so it is treated as human-operated and does not support a positive field judgment.

tasks.label: Set up and use ladders and scaffolding as necessary to complete work.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Fabrication/structural steel shop: welder drags over a step ladder, rolling scaffold tower or platform to reach the upper welds of a tall weldment, tank, frame or trailer sitting on the shop floor, climbs with stinger/torch and leads, and completes the elevated fillet or groove welds to shop standard.

Shipyard or heavy fabrication yard: welder rigs or climbs staging, ladders and platforms inside hull blocks, tanks or around large vessels to reach overhead and vertical seams in confined, congested steel structures, then welds from that staging.

Industrial plant maintenance/turnaround (refinery, power plant, mill): welder works from erected tube-and-clamp or system scaffold, or a secured ladder, to cut and weld in-place piping, ductwork and structural repairs at height under permits and hot-work controls.

Commercial/industrial construction site: welder sets an extension ladder or moves a mobile scaffold to weld structural connections, embeds, stair stringers, joists or handrails at height in a partially built structure, amid other trades, changing layout and weather.

Mobile field service/repair: welder at a customer site (farm, warehouse, mine, bridge, rooftop) carries and foots a ladder against an as-found surface, or builds a small scaffold, to weld or cut a bracket, rail or cracked member overhead in a one-off configuration.

sources.transferJustification: Same task family (arc welding of steel weldments); establishes that autonomous welding to production quality is routine when the workpiece is presented in a purpose-built cell.

sources.system: Gantry-, track- and pedestal-mounted adaptive robotic welding systems (trade-press survey of commercial installations)

sources.transferJustification: Directly substitutes for the access function of the task: in a purpose-built cell, elevated weld locations are reached by the machine's own gantry/track rather than by a worker on a ladder.

sources.claim: LadderMan is a research system in which a Unitree G1 humanoid autonomously climbs ladders of varying geometry on real hardware; manipulation while on the ladder was performed by teleoperation, and no welding work was performed.

sources.system: Robo-Welder (Shimz Smart Site)

sources.claim: Shimizu's Robo-Welder autonomously welds large steel building columns and was used on the Toranomon-Azabudai construction project, but it is placed at each column joint by workers/lifting equipment and works at the deck level rather than providing its own elevated access.

sources.system: Hilti Jaibot

sources.claim: Hilti's Jaibot is a commercially deployed semi-autonomous construction robot that drills overhead holes from its own mast after being driven into position by a worker, i.e. overhead jobsite work done without ladders, but for drilling rather than welding and with an operator moving the machine.
sources.transferJustification: Related task = overhead work at height on an active jobsite; shows only low-height (slab-soffit) reach from an integral mast, with no seam-tracking welding and no ladder or scaffold use, so it does not carry over to welding at scaffold heights.

tasks.label: Operate metal shaping, straightening, and bending machines, such as brakes and shears.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Job/fab shop press brake work: welder-fabricator pulls laser-cut or sheared blanks off a cart, selects and loads punch/die tooling, sets backgauge from a print, bends flanges/hems on short runs (1–50 pieces), checks angle with a protractor and adjusts for springback.

Shearing stock to size: squaring sheet or light plate on a power shear, and cutting flat bar/angle to length on a shear or ironworker station, positioning against the backgauge and stacking cut blanks.

Rolling plate into cylinders/cones on a 3- or 4-roll plate roll, and bending heavier plate or structural shapes (angle, channel, flat bar) on rolls, ironworker benders, or a hydraulic press, checking the radius against a template.
Tube/pipe bending on a rotary-draw, mandrel, or CNC bender for handrails, frames, exhaust, roll cages: loading the tube, setting bend angle/rotation, and checking spring-back and ovality.
Straightening/flattening repeatable production parts: bars, shafts, and cut or punched blanks run through a straightening press or roller leveler to bring runout/flatness within tolerance.

Correcting distortion in one-off weldments and bent structural members on the shop floor: shimming into a press or porta-power, applying heat or press strokes iteratively, and re-checking against a straightedge or fixture until the piece meets the print.

instances.label: Robotic arc-welding cell in an auto-parts or heavy-fabrication plant: during a production run the weld drifts out of spec (joint gap/part tolerance variation, seam wander, spatter loading the nozzle, marginal arc starts). The operator corrects it by adjusting weld parameters/torch offsets at the controller or by triggering torch service, then resumes the run.

Hard fault in an automated arc-welding cell: wire birdnest, part tacked to the fixture, torch collision, or a part that slipped/misloaded in the clamps. The operator stops the machine, opens the holding devices, frees, repositions or scraps the part, clears spatter/slag by hand, re-references and restarts.

Automated resistance spot/projection welding line or cell: expulsion, undersized nuggets, sticking or mushroomed electrodes. Corrected by changing current/force/time schedule at the weld control, dressing or replacing electrode caps, and releasing the clamped workpiece.

Laser cutting machine on a sheet-metal shop floor: dross, burn marks, cut interruptions, worn or spatter-damaged nozzle. The operator adjusts feed rate/focus/assist-gas at the control, cleans or swaps the nozzle, and re-cuts the affected parts.

Physical trouble that halts a laser cutter or an automated solder/braze line: part tipped up and jamming the head, part fallen into the slats, board jammed on the conveyor, fixture that will not release. The operator stops the machine, opens guards and holding devices, clears it by hand with tools, and restarts.

Automated soldering or brazing machine (wave, selective, reflow oven, induction or furnace brazing): bridging, cold or dull joints, insufficient fill, over- or under-temperature. Corrected by adjusting zone temperatures, conveyor speed, preheat, flux volume or coil power at the machine controls.

instances.label: Production plant, medium-to-high volume: tend an existing fenced robotic arc- or spot-welding cell. Load stamped/cut steel parts into the cell's fixtures at the load station, clamp, hit cycle start, watch the cycle, unload welded assemblies to a rack, visually check welds, change contact tips/dress electrodes, clear spatter. Same part family all shift.

Open shop floor bench station: operate/tend a resistance spot, projection, or seam welding machine (pedestal welder, press-type welder). Hand-place small stampings, brackets, weld nuts or wire assemblies between the electrodes or in a nest, actuate, remove and stack finished parts, spot-check nuggets/peel tests. Parts arrive in totes on carts; people work all around.

Job setup/changeover in a high-mix fabrication shop: mount or swap fixtures and tooling on the welder or robot cell, load or teach the program, set current/voltage/wire feed/travel speed/gas flow, run test coupons or a first article, inspect and measure, adjust parameters until welds are in spec, then release the job to run.

Mechanized welding of large weldments in a fab shop: pipe spools, pressure vessels, tanks, structural beams. Workpiece staged by overhead crane onto positioners or turning rolls, machine (submerged-arc column-and-boom, seam welder, spool welding cobot) aligned to the joint, multi-pass welding run and monitored, wire/flux replenished, weld inspected.

Machine taken to the work outside a fixed workstation: portable/orbital or track-mounted welding equipment set on a joint at a construction site, erected structure, pipeline right-of-way, or inside a ship hull. Variable joint fit-up and access, weather and staging vary, equipment rigged into place, multi-pass weld run and checked.

Same factory/fab shop: operator selects the correct small consumables for the machine and job — contact tips of the right bore, gas nozzles, liners, diffusers — from labeled boxes in the shop's consumables cabinet or crib, matching part numbers to the wire size and process data chart, and carries them to the cell.

Laser cutting machine operator: for each new job the machine's technology table specifies a cutting nozzle type/diameter for the material and sheet thickness (e.g., 2.0 mm single vs. bi-flow for stainless); operator selects that nozzle from the rack at the machine and confirms it matches the program.

Resistance spot/seam welding line: tender selects electrode caps, tips or wheels of the right alloy class, face geometry and diameter per the weld schedule for the metal type and gauge, drawn from cap stock kept at the line.

Job-shop brazing/soldering setup: operator consults data charts to choose the braze filler alloy (rod, ring, paste), the matching flux, torch tip size or solder alloy for the base metals and joint, pulling similar-looking items from mixed bins in the tool crib/chemical cabinet.

Field or site work with portable automatic/semi-automatic welding equipment (pipeline spread, shipyard erection, plant maintenance): consumables (wire, flux, rods from a rod oven, tips) are chosen per the welding procedure from a job trailer or gang box, outdoors, with variable weather, layout and storage.

tasks.label: Prepare metal surfaces or workpieces, using hand-operated equipment, such as grinders, cutters, or drills.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Metal fabrication/production shop: batches of flame-, plasma-, or laser-cut steel parts arrive on pallets or carts; operator uses an angle grinder, belt sander, or wire wheel to knock off slag, lead-ins, burrs and sharp edges and to round edges before the parts go to the welding machine or robot cell.

Joint preparation before machine welding/brazing: grinding or torch/plasma beveling of plate and pipe edges, cutting stock to length, and grinding mill scale, paint, rust or oxide off the faying surfaces so the machine weld will pass inspection. Work at a bench, saw, or on a layout table in the shop.

Post-weld dressing of machine-welded assemblies in the shop: grinding weld beads flush or blending them, chipping/grinding spatter and slag, removing tack-weld remnants and dressing fixtures, using handheld grinders and burrs on parts held on a bench or positioner.

Hole-making and secondary machining on workpieces before welding/brazing: drilling, reaming, countersinking or tapping holes with a hand drill, mag drill or drill press, and punching, on parts clamped at a bench in the shop.

Large weldments and assemblies (equipment frames, tanks, truck/vehicle bodies, ship foundations) prepped on the open shop floor: the operator walks around and climbs on the part with a grinder, needle scaler or sander to clean scale, spatter and weld seams over large, one-off, variable geometry.

Off-site/field repair prep: cleaning rust, paint, scale and corrosion off in-place steel structures or installed equipment (bridge members, tanks, machinery) with hand-held power tools before repair welding, at a site taken as found with awkward access and weather.

tasks.label: Mark weld points and positions of components on workpieces, using rules, squares, templates, or scribes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production fab shop, layout/bench area: operator reads a shop drawing and uses rule, square and scribe/soapstone to mark centerlines, component footprints and weld points on flat sheet or plate parts (brackets, stiffeners, gussets) before they go to a welding machine or robot cell. Batch of like parts, clean mill-finish steel, indoor.

Repetitive template work: operator lays a sheet-metal or plywood template/jig over each blank and scribes or punch-marks component positions and tack points for a repeat production run feeding a resistance or MIG welding machine. High volume, tight tolerance (~1/16 in.), indoor bench.

Structural/heavy fabrication shop: marking fitting and weld positions on beams, columns, channels and angles laid on skids or roller stands, using tape, framing square and soapstone/center punch, on several faces of the member, before fit-up and machine/robot welding.

Round and tubular work: marking saddle/fitment locations, seam and clocking centerlines, and flange/fitting positions on pipe and tube for spool or tube-frame welding; wrap-arounds, squares and scribes used on curved surfaces.

Large three-dimensional weldment already tacked together (tank shell, machine frame, trailer chassis) sitting on the shop floor or a positioner: worker measures from datum features and marks positions for the next brackets/attachments and their weld points.

Repair, retrofit or field job: marking weld points and component positions on an in-service, rusted, painted or previously fabricated assembly with no reliable model, sometimes at a customer site or in the yard, working from measurements taken off the as-found part.
