tasks.label: Set dials and timing controls to regulate electrical current, gas flow pressure, heating or cooling cycles, or shut-off.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Robotic or mechanized arc-welding cell (MIG/TIG/submerged-arc, robot or column-and-boom) in a fabrication plant: before and during a production run the operator selects/sets the weld schedule at the power source or teach pendant - current/voltage, wire feed and travel speed, shielding-gas flow, arc-start/crater-fill and weld/cool timing - runs a coupon and tweaks values until welds pass.

Resistance welding machine (pedestal spot welder, projection press, seam welder, hanging weld gun) in an automotive-supplier, appliance or fab plant: operator sets weld current or heat percentage, squeeze/weld/hold/off cycle counts and electrode air pressure on the weld timer/controller, and re-adjusts as electrodes wear or fit-up varies.

Soldering/brazing machine on a production line (SMT reflow oven, wave/selective solder machine, induction or furnace brazing line) in an electronics or HVAC/appliance plant: operator sets zone temperatures, conveyor speed, preheat and cooling cycle times, nitrogen or fuel-gas flow and shut-off, then verifies the thermal profile and adjusts.

Laser cutting or laser-welding machine on a sheet-metal shop floor: operator loads the job and sets/confirms laser power, pulse and duty timing, assist-gas type and pressure, focus/standoff and beam shut-off for the material and thickness, then corrects for plate-to-plate variation.

Legacy or lightly instrumented equipment in a job shop: analog rheostat/heat dials, mechanical cam timers, cylinder-mounted pressure regulators and rotameter flowmeters with needle valves - the operator physically turns knobs, cracks valves and reads a float or gauge to hit a target, re-checking during the run.

Mechanized welding away from a plant floor: pipeline welding tractors/bugs on a right-of-way, field-fabrication or shipyard-block orbital tube welding - operator sets current, gas flow and timing on the weather-exposed control unit at the site, with wind, dust and temperature affecting settings.

tasks.label: Turn and press knobs and buttons or enter operating instructions into computers to adjust and start welding machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Robotic arc-welding cell on a plant floor: operator stands at the cell HMI/teach pendant outside the fence, calls up or loads the weld program for the part running, tweaks weld parameters (voltage, wire feed speed, travel speed, weave), then presses the cycle-start/palm buttons after each part is loaded, repeating all shift.

Resistance spot, projection, or seam welding machine tender in a metal-goods plant: keys weld current, weld time, squeeze and hold settings into the weld controller keypad or turns dials on the machine, presses start / steps the initiation pedal for each part, and steps up current as electrodes wear.

Laser cutting or laser welding machine operator at a CNC console in a sheet-metal fabrication plant: selects or types in the part program, sets power, focus, assist-gas and feed parameters on the control, then presses cycle start and re-starts after each sheet or nest.

Soldering/brazing machine operator (wave solder line, induction brazing machine, or continuous brazing furnace) in an electronics or HVAC plant: sets temperatures, conveyor speed, preheat and flux settings on the machine's touchscreen HMI or knobs, starts the machine, and nudges settings during the run.

Small job shop / custom fabrication shop: worker sets up an assortment of semi-automatic welding power supplies and small automated welders (turns voltage and wire-feed knobs, sets gas flow, selects a stored program) on machines parked at varying spots on the shop floor, then starts the machine for a short run.

Field or heavy-site work: operator sets up a portable welding tractor, submerged-arc unit, or orbital pipe welding machine at a construction site, shipyard hull, or pipeline spread — dialing in current/voltage/travel speed on the weather-exposed controller and starting the pass.

tasks.label: Assemble, align, and clamp workpieces into holding fixtures to bond, heat-treat, or solder fabricated metal components.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume production plant: operator takes stamped sheet-metal or tubular parts from racks/bins at a load station of an automated weld cell (or spot-weld line), drops them onto locating pins in a holding fixture, closes clamps and cycles the machine; same part repeated all shift.

Bench/pedestal resistance, projection or small laser welding machine: operator places small stamped or machined parts (and weld nuts/inserts) into a nest fixture, aligns them by eye/locators, holds/clamps and actuates; parts arrive loose in bins or tote trays.

Brazing/soldering prep: assembling mating metal components with braze rings, preforms or paste into graphite/stainless holding fixtures and loading them onto a conveyor-belt, vacuum or induction brazing station; small clearances, flux/preform placement matters.

Heat-treat department: loading machined parts (shafts, gears, small castings) onto fixtures, racks or baskets in a set pattern and charging them into a furnace or induction hardening station, then unloading after quench.

High-mix fabrication shop: fitting up multi-piece weldments (brackets, frames, suspension parts) — assembling several components, aligning to the print, clamping in a fixture for a welding machine, with frequent part changeovers and part-to-part variation.

Large or one-off custom weldment setup: crane- or hoist-set heavy sections onto a fixture table, shim and adjust for part variation, measure squareness/diagonals, clamp and tack to hold alignment before machine welding or heat treatment.

instances.label: Robotic arc-welding cell in a production plant: operator loads a first-article weldment into the fixture, dry-runs the program at reduced speed, checks torch-to-work alignment/TCP, runs a trial weld, inspects the bead for undercut/porosity/penetration, then tweaks voltage, wire feed, travel speed and touch-up points before releasing the job to production.

Resistance spot or seam welding machine/robot line setup (auto parts, appliance, stamping plant): operator runs test coupons of the production stack-up, performs peel/chisel or ultrasonic nugget checks, then adjusts weld current, weld time, squeeze/electrode force, dresses or changes caps, and re-tests until nuggets meet the schedule.

Laser cutting or laser welding machine: operator runs a trial cut/weld on scrap or a lead-in coupon, checks kerf quality, dross, focus position, nozzle condition and assist-gas pressure, then adjusts focus, feed rate, power and gas and re-runs before the nest or production part is released.

Automated soldering line (reflow oven, wave, or selective solder machine): operator runs a test/profile board, checks joints and thermal profile against the paste and joint spec, then adjusts zone temperatures, conveyor speed, preheat, flux volume, solder wave height or nozzle before production boards run.

High-mix job shop or small fabrication shop: operator sets a semi-automatic or hard-automation welding/brazing machine for a short-run, often one-off part, burns a trial weld on scrap or a sacrificial coupon, bends/breaks it at the bench, and adjusts machine settings, fixturing and torch position by hand.

Field or on-site mechanized welding (pipeline right-of-way bug-and-band or orbital welding, shipyard block, plant shutdown): operator sets the track/head on a practice coupon or pup joint, runs a trial pass in ambient site conditions, has it visually/NDE checked, and adjusts procedure parameters and head alignment before the production joint.

instances.label: Robotic arc (GMAW) welding cell in a fab shop or auto supplier: between cycles/at shift change, remove spatter build-up from the gun's gas nozzle, contact tip and diffuser, apply anti-spatter liquid, cut the wire to stick-out, and swap worn front-end consumables/torch body so the cell keeps welding to quality.

Resistance spot/projection welding machine or robot gun: dress (re-face) the mushroomed copper electrode caps, remove dressing chips, replace worn caps, and clean spatter off the electrodes and holders so weld current and nugget quality stay in spec.

Laser cutting/laser welding machine: service the consumable at the head - clean or exchange the cutting nozzle, verify nozzle condition, re-center the beam/focus after the change - to stop burring and dross on parts.

Laser or plasma machine housekeeping: scrape slag and dross off the bed slats, empty the scrap/slag drawer, wipe or replace the protective cover glass and lens, and blow out the cutting head area and enclosure with an air hose and cleaning fluid.
Selective/wave soldering machine: clean and change the solder nozzle and clean the flux nozzles/spray head on an electronics line so solder joints and flux deposition stay consistent.

General preventive-maintenance round on the shop floor: wipe down the machine and fixtures, blow chips/dust/spatter off tooling with an air hose, grease slides, positioner bearings and clamps, check coolant/hydraulic levels, change filters, skim dross from a solder pot, and make small adjustments or replace worn liners, hoses and clamps with hand tools per a PM checklist.

instances.label: High-volume plant, robotic arc/spot welding cell changeover: operator pulls the standard weld fixture for the next part number from the tooling rack, hoists it onto the positioner faceplate or table, drops it onto locating dowels, bolts it down with T-slot bolts and wrenches, then checks position with scale/square/dial indicator and touches off the robot program.

Laser cutting / laser welding machine setup: installing a fixture plate, nest, or stops on the machine bed or shuttle pallet, squaring it to the machine axes, bolting it down, and verifying origin/alignment before the program runs.

Job-shop or prototype one-off setup: a non-standard or shop-made jig is adapted, shimmed, and located by layout to the drawing (tacking stops in place, iterative indicator/tape checks and rework of the fit) because no repeatable, standardized tooling interface exists for the job.

Brazing or soldering machine / conveyor or induction furnace: operator removes hot brazed or soldered assemblies (tube joints, HVAC fittings, carbide tips) from fixtures or the conveyor with tongs or pliers and places them in a cooling rack, quench, or tote.

Large/heavy weldment (roughly 500-4,000 lb structural assembly, tank, frame) in a fabrication bay: operator unclamps the tooling, rigs chains or slings to an overhead hoist or jib crane, pries or taps the weldment free where it has stuck to the fixture, and lands it on a stand or trailer.

Modify, repair, or re-qualify an existing fixture in service at the machine: replace a worn locating pin, re-weld a broken stop, add a clamp for a revised part number, shim or grind to bring welded parts back into tolerance, and prove it out with trial parts on the production line.

instances.label: Robotic/automatic arc-welding cell in a metal fabrication or automotive plant: keep the torch-side auxiliaries running through the shift - cycle the torch through the nozzle-cleaning/reamer station, apply anti-spatter, cut the wire stickout, replace burned-back contact tips and spattered nozzles, re-verify tool center point.

Operate and monitor the workpiece-positioning auxiliaries feeding an automatic welder: servo positioner, turning rolls/headstock-tailstock, column-and-boom manipulator or seamer. Index and rotate the weldment between passes and trim rotation/travel speed so the joint stays under the torch at the right angle.

Submerged-arc station on heavy plate, pipe or beam fabrication: tend the flux hopper and the vacuum flux-recovery unit - keep flux flowing over the joint, recover unfused flux, separate fused slag and fines, empty the dust bag, refill the hopper.

Shielding-gas supply for the welding machine: monitor manifold/cylinder pressures, change out depleted cylinders or cylinder packs, reconnect and leak-check regulators/pigtails, and set flow rate for the process.

Wire-supply auxiliaries: watch spool/drum level, hoist and mount a fresh 44 lb spool or 500 lb bulk drum, thread the wire through conduit, drive rolls and liner, set drive-roll tension, and clear birdnests or liner jams after a feed fault.

Material-transfer auxiliaries around the welding machine: run the infeed/outfeed conveyor or transfer table, use the hoist/manipulator to place parts into the welding fixture, actuate clamps, and move finished weldments off to the next station.

tasks.label: Anneal finished workpieces to relieve internal stress.

instances.label: Batch stress-relief in a fabrication/heat-treat shop: operator racks welded weldments (brackets, frames, subassemblies) into baskets or on a load base, charges a batch or car-bottom furnace, selects the ramp/soak/cool recipe per spec, watches the chart recorder, and unloads and stages the cooled parts.

High-volume small welded/brazed/soldered assemblies run through a continuous mesh-belt or conveyor furnace for anneal/stress relief: operator feeds parts or trays onto the belt, sets belt speed and zone temperatures, tends the line and takes off finished parts.

Inline post-weld seam annealing on a tube/pipe mill or continuous welding line: operator sets the induction annealer power/pyrometer recipe for the diameter and wall, monitors weld-seam temperature and coil alignment as product runs continuously, and adjusts to keep the anneal in spec.

Localized induction stress relief of a welded part at a station in or beside the welding cell (welded shafts, axle housings, tanks): part is loaded into the fixture/coil, the timed heating cycle runs, part is unloaded and identified.

Shop PWHT of a large fabrication (pressure vessel section, pipe spool, heavy weldment): attach thermocouples, wrap flexible ceramic pad or induction heaters and insulation around the weld, program the heat-treat console, run and log the coded cycle, strip the setup.

Field/on-site PWHT of welds on installed piping, tanks or structures at a jobsite or during a plant turnaround: rig heaters and insulation in place at height or in congested space, run and document the cycle in outdoor/variable conditions.

tasks.label: Start, monitor, and adjust robotic welding production lines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Shift or job start-up of a robotic arc-welding cell/line: verify wire, gas and coolant, select/load the correct weld program for the part number, home the robots, confirm torch tool-center-point and consumable condition, run a warm-up/test piece before releasing the line to production.

Monitoring a running line of one or more welding stations: watching arc stability, spatter and cycle indicators, tracking weld-data/alarm screens, and checking finished weldments for bead size, undercut, burn-through or missed welds so bad parts do not travel downstream.

Adjusting the process for drift and part-to-part variation: tweaking voltage, wire-feed speed and travel speed, shifting torch angle/position or touching up program points when joints sit off nominal, fit-up gaps vary, or bead appearance drifts.

Recovering from routine process faults that stop the cycle: stubbed/burned-back wire, arc-start failure, spatter-clogged nozzle, worn contact tip, TCP drift; clean or change consumables, cut the wire, re-establish the arc and restart the cycle with minimal downtime.

Hands-on intervention inside the cell: a weldment tacked or jammed in the fixture, a crashed/bent torch neck, damaged cable or liner, spatter build-up and loose locating pins/clamps on the tooling that must be cleaned, shimmed or re-adjusted before the line can run to quality again.

tasks.label: Dress electrodes, using tip dressers, files, emery cloths, or dressing wheels.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume robotic resistance spot welding (automotive body shop, tier-1 supplier, appliance line): the operator/tender keeps the weld guns' copper caps to spec — running or verifying tip-dress cycles at the cell's dresser, checking dressed face diameter and alignment, swapping worn cutter blades, hand-dressing during setup and troubleshooting.

Pedestal, rocker-arm or press spot/projection welder in a job shop or fabrication plant: the operator stops the machine every few hundred welds and restores the mushroomed electrode faces with a hand file, emery cloth or hand-held pneumatic tip dresser, then checks face diameter and upper/lower alignment before resuming.

Resistance seam / roll-spot welder on a production line (fuel tanks, drums, tubing, cans): the operator dresses the electrode wheels — knurl or dressing wheel, file or emery cloth — to restore the contact face and remove pickup, during scheduled stops or continuously as the machine runs.

Automated GTAW/plasma work (orbital tube welding, robotic TIG cell): the operator dresses the tungsten electrode — grinding the taper and truncation on a dedicated tungsten grinder or dressing wheel to a specified angle — and reinstalls it in the torch with correct stick-out.

In-situ hand dressing during setup, troubleshooting or field/maintenance service: filing and emery-clothing non-standard or damaged electrode faces, offset/special-shaped electrodes, multi-gun fixtures and projection-welding platens/dies with restricted access, at varying machines and sites.

tasks.label: Immerse completed workpieces into water or acid baths to cool and clean components.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume production floor: operator lifts small brazed/soldered assemblies (copper fittings, HVAC tubes, contacts, 0.5-10 lb) hot off the brazing station with tongs and immerses them in a water quench tank at the workstation for a few seconds, then racks them to drain/dry. Repetitive, same part family all shift.

Pickling/cleaning room in the plant: operator loads batches of brazed or soldered parts into wire baskets and immerses them in a heated acid pickle bath (sulfuric/nitric/citric) to strip flux and oxide for a timed soak, then transfers through rinse tanks and dries. PPE, fume ventilation, corrosive chemicals.

Heat-treat/fabrication bay: larger welded or brazed weldments and hardened components (25-150 lb) are moved from the furnace or welding fixture into a water/polymer quench tank using a hoist, manipulator, or basket; transfer time and agitation must meet spec; steam, heat, and heavy loads.

High-mix job shop: low-volume, varied one-off pieces of different geometry arriving from several stations; operator judges which bath (water quench vs. acid pickle) and dwell time per piece, may re-dip or re-clean, and handles unfixtured parts of unfamiliar shape.

Electronics/precision soldering line: small, delicate soldered assemblies or boards are dipped in aqueous cleaning/rinse baths after soldering to remove flux and cool, with careful handling to avoid damaging joints and components.

roles.description: Set up, operate, or tend heating equipment, such as heat-treating furnaces, flame-hardening machines, induction machines, soaking pits, or vacuum equipment to temper, harden, anneal, or heat treat metal or plastic objects.

tasks.label: Read production schedules and work orders to determine processing sequences, furnace temperatures, and heat cycle requirements for objects to be heat-treated.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Adjust controls to maintain temperatures and heating times, using thermal instruments and charts, dials and gauges of furnaces, and color of stock in furnaces to make setting determinations.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Modern computer-controlled batch furnace (vacuum, sealed-quench atmosphere, or tempering furnace) in a commercial heat-treat plant or captive shop: operator selects/edits the recipe, watches control and load thermocouple readouts, chart/SCADA trends and vacuum/atmosphere gauges, and adjusts setpoints, ramp rates and soak times so the load meets spec and AMS2750/CQI-9 uniformity requirements.

Continuous production heating equipment and induction/flame hardening machines: operator sets zone temperatures, belt or scan speed, and coil power, then trims settings during the run using pyrometer readings, zone thermocouples and part appearance as part size, alloy or throughput changes.

Older or lightly instrumented equipment in a job shop, forge or tool room: box, pit, salt-bath or forge furnace with dial controls, a single indicating controller and a strip-chart recorder; operator judges readiness partly by the color of the stock seen through the door, adjusts gas/power by hand and estimates soak time.

Off-normal conditions on any furnace: an unusually heavy or dense load lagging the setpoint, thermocouple drift or failure alarm, power interruption or restart after downtime, or QC hardness/case-depth feedback that requires changing temperature or soak time mid-campaign.

Plastics heating equipment: thermoforming sheet ovens and annealing/curing ovens where the operator adjusts zone heater outputs and dwell time based on infrared/pyrometer readings and part or sheet appearance (sag, gloss) to hold forming temperature.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Commercial or captive heat-treat shop, batch atmosphere/integral-quench furnace: operator opens the furnace door (hydraulic/push-button, sometimes latched) and pushes or places steel baskets and trays of mixed parts (gears, fasteners, castings) onto the hearth using a charge car or forklift; loads vary by work order, shop aisle shared with people and lift trucks.

Continuous line (mesh-belt, roller-hearth, pusher, or shaker-hearth): operator starts the conveyor/belt drive and feeds bins or trays of small parts (fasteners, stampings, bearings) at the charge end, keeping flow steady and clearing jams; high volume, repetitive, standard product mix.

Captive aerospace/tool-room department with vacuum or small batch furnaces: operator opens the chamber or hinged door, slides a fixtured load or grid onto the hearth rails, closes the door and starts the cycle; moderate weights, standard fixtures, low-volume varied work.

Forge shop or mill reheat: charging cold or hot billets, bars, and large forgings into slot, rotary, or car-bottom furnaces via roller table, charging machine, manipulator, or by signaling an overhead crane; heavy hot stock, radiant heat, scale on the floor.

Steel or aluminum mill soaking pit / large pit furnace: operator signals the crane operator to lift and set aside pit covers and to lower multi-ton ingots into the pit with tongs at spaced positions, then signals when the pit is recovered; heavy loads, extreme heat, mill pit bay.

Small job shop or maintenance heat-treating: manual box furnace or salt bath, operator swings open a hinged door and places small odd parts on the hearth with tongs or a fork, one-off jobs with no standard fixturing.

Batch furnace operation in a production plant (integral-quench batch furnaces, car-bottom or vacuum furnaces): build and stage the load on grids or fixtures, move it with a charge car, hoist or load table, select and start the recipe, run the transfer through oil/polymer quench, washer and temper furnace, then unload the finished load.

Commercial job-shop heat treat department, high mix: several customer lots per shift of varied parts (tool steel dies, shafts, fittings, aerospace hardware) racked or wired onto trays and baskets by hand, hoisted into batch/vacuum/salt-bath equipment, recipe chosen per the customer's spec, quenched and tempered, with tongs and hooks around hot work.

Induction hardening machine operation: load shafts, gears, pins or crankshafts into the coil/centers or chuck, start the scan or single-shot cycle, monitor power, scan rate and spray quench, unload hot parts to a temper oven or conveyor, and pull periodic parts for hardness/pattern checks.

Flame hardening work: setting and running flame-hardening equipment on gear teeth, sprockets, rings, races or machine ways - regulating oxygen/fuel and flame heads, scanning the surface with torch and water quench, then moving parts to a holding temper.

Set-up and changeover for a new job: swap induction coils/quench heads, fixtures, baskets or grids, attach load thermocouples, enter or edit the recipe in the controller, run a first piece or test coupon, check hardness/case depth and adjust power, time, temperature or quench before releasing the job to production.

instances.label: Commercial or captive heat treat shop, batch integral/sealed-quench furnace: operator watches the cycle timer, opens the vestibule, indexes the basket or tray of gears/fasteners off the load table into the integral oil quench, then pulls the drained load with a load car, hoist or forklift and moves it to the washer and temper. Mixed customer lots, oil smoke, 1,550-1,750 F loads up to a few thousand pounds.

Small job shop, tool room, or captive shop with a manual box, pit, or salt-bath furnace: at the specified time the operator opens the door, pulls individual parts (dies, punches, blades, springs, castings) with tongs, immerses and agitates them in a water, oil or brine tank, then racks them to air-dry/cool. Part mix changes lot to lot; no fixturing.

Continuous line (mesh belt, shaker hearth, rotary retort, pusher) running fasteners or small parts: the furnace discharges into an integral oil quench and the operator tends the line, watching belt speed and quench level, breaking out and inspecting the quenched parts as they exit the wash/temper conveyor into bins.

Induction or flame hardening station with integral spray/immersion quench: operator loads a shaft, gear, or ring into the machine chuck/scanner, the part is heated and quenched in place on the specified cycle, and the operator removes the hot part and racks or conveys it to cool.

Aluminum solution heat treating: operator runs a drop-bottom or horizontal furnace with a basket of castings/forgings, and at the end of soak the load must be transferred into the water/polymer quench within a few seconds' quench delay, then racked to air-dry before aging.

Large or heavy work: long shafts, large gears or forgings removed from a rotary hearth or car-bottom furnace and moved by hoist, manipulator or press-quench fixture into oil, then straightened/tempered. Heavy, awkward, radiant-hot pieces requiring careful positioning and short transfer times.

instances.label: Heat-treat shop floor: experienced operator walks a new hire through furnace startup, control-panel navigation, recipe/setpoint entry, and shutdown, explaining what each control and readout means while the trainee does the keying.

Coaching during the trainee's first supervised runs: answering questions, pointing out abnormal readings or scale/discoloration on parts, explaining hardness-test checks and paperwork, and correcting mistakes as they occur.

In-process hot-color observation: operator watches the incandescent color of the load through a furnace sight port, or the glow of a part during flame/induction hardening or forging preheat, to confirm the correct temperature and uniform heating, and adjusts settings or flags a bad part.

Lot-level final color/shade inspection of finished batches (black oxide, blued, nitrided, or plated after heat treat) for uniformity across the lot before release, with sign-off paperwork and nonconformance documentation.

instances.label: High-volume mesh-belt hardening/tempering line (fasteners, bearings, stampings) in a captive or commercial heat treat plant: at a job change the operator sets belt speed (and feeder/loading rate) from the process spec so parts get the prescribed time at temperature, then verifies part spacing and discharge.

Roller-hearth, pusher, rotary-retort or walking-beam continuous furnace: operator sets index/push rate and the speeds of charge, quench and temper conveyors so trays/baskets get the prescribed soak time, and keeps the cadence synchronized with quench and downstream equipment.

Continuous strip or wire annealing line with payoff and take-up reels: operator sets line/reel speeds and tension for the prescribed thermal cycle for the coil gauge and grade, and re-sets speed at coil (weld) changes.

Mid-run corrections on a running continuous furnace: hardness/temperature checks or discharge appearance come back off target, load weight or part spacing varies, the furnace lags on recovery, or a jam/line stop occurs, and the operator trims conveyor/reel speed to restore the prescribed cycle.

Small-lot custom work in a job shop on an older continuous belt or draw furnace with a manual speed dial/tachometer: operator computes belt speed from the customer spec and section thickness, sets it by hand, times the belt with a stopwatch, and re-sets for the next mixed lot.

tasks.label: Test parts for hardness, using hardness testing equipment, or by examining and feeling samples.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Commercial heat-treat shop / captive heat-treat department: after quench and temper, the operator pulls a sample of small-to-medium parts (fasteners, pins, gears, stampings, PM parts) from a basket or fixture, wipes/deburrs the test spot, seats each part on the anvil of a bench Rockwell tester, runs HRC/HRB readings at specified locations, compares to the spec, and logs results on the load traveler/SPC chart.

Forge, foundry or large-part heat-treat plant: Brinell test on large annealed/normalized/quenched-and-tempered forgings, castings, bar or wheels — spot must be ground or milled flat, indent applied at high load, indentation measured optically, result recorded against the load certification.

Shop-floor check on parts too large or awkward to bring to a bench tester (shafts, dies, rings, weldments, parts still on the rack or in the fixture): operator uses a portable Leeb/UCI/Telebrineller-type tester, takes several readings at accessible spots, averages and records them.

Quick qualitative go/no-go check at the furnace: operator draws a file across the part edge, scratches or taps it, and examines/feels the surface (scale, color, temper color, softness) to confirm the load hardened or annealed as intended before committing the batch.

Metallurgical/QC lab of the heat-treat facility: a test coupon or sacrificial part is sectioned, mounted and polished, and the operator runs a microhardness (Vickers/Knoop) traverse from the surface inward to verify effective case depth and core hardness on a carburized/nitrided/induction-hardened load.

instances.label: High-volume production plant (automotive, bearing, fastener): operator repeatedly mounts similar shafts, pins or gears (roughly 1-15 kg) on arbors, in chucks, or between centers of an induction hardening scanner or single-shot machine. Commercial heat-treat job shop or low-volume in-house work: mixed part numbers, lots of 5-50. Operator selects and installs the correct fixture/arbor/holding station, adjusts tailstock centers, mounts each odd-shaped workpiece and verifies alignment/runout relative to the coil or flame head; frequent changeovers.

Large, heavy workpieces - long shafts, large ring gears, dies, weldments (50 to 1,000+ kg) - slung with hoist, jib crane or manipulator and set between centers, onto a mandrel, or onto press-quench die tooling; rigging, alignment and hot-part handling dominate.

Small, delicate or plastic parts: operator places small precision components or plastic parts into nests, trays or masking fixtures for controlled heating/annealing, where part-to-part contact, damage or wrong orientation would scrap the load.

tasks.label: Reduce heat when processing is complete to allow parts to cool in furnaces or machinery.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Commercial or captive heat treat shop, batch atmosphere/box/integral-quench or draw (temper) furnace: at the end of the soak the operator cuts the burners/heating elements back or drops the setpoint, shuts atmosphere gas, and leaves the load to cool in the furnace at a controlled rate before unloading. Plant floor with forklifts, other operators, standard PLC/HMI-equipped furnaces.

Aerospace/medical/tool-steel vacuum or controlled-atmosphere furnace: at cycle completion the operator ends the heating segment and starts the cool-down (backfill and gas-quench/blower cool or slow vacuum cool) to a specified cooling rate, with load thermocouples logged for AMS 2750 pyrometry compliance.

Continuous mesh-belt/pusher furnace line or robot-tended induction-hardening/quench-and-temper cell: at end of run or shift the operator reduces zone temperatures/power and lets remaining parts cool in the equipment; the line is fenced/conveyorized and built around the machinery.

Plastics or composites plant annealing/curing/stress-relieving oven: after the hold, heat is reduced and the parts are allowed to cool slowly in the oven at a controlled rate (fresh-air/fan cooling) to avoid warping or new stresses, then unloaded.

Older shop with legacy, largely manual equipment (gas-fired pit or box furnace with hand gas cocks and dial pyrometers, salt bath, forge furnace): the operator manually turns down valves/rheostats, cracks or closes the door or damper, and judges the cool-down by gauge and experience.

Field/portable heat treatment (post-weld heat treat, stress relief) on a pipeline spread, construction site, or plant turnaround: after the soak the technician brings the power console down at the specified degrees-per-hour cooling rate and lets the joint cool under the insulation blankets.

tasks.label: Mount fixtures and industrial coils on machines, using hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Scheduled product changeover on an induction hardening machine (scanner or single-shot): operator unclamps and removes the existing standardized quick-change inductor/coil from the coil head, lifts the next repeat-run coil out of the tool crib rack, bolts/clamps it onto the head with wrenches and hex keys, makes the water and bus-bar (fishtail) connections, and checks the coil-to-part air gap before running a trial part. Shop floor of a captive or commercial heat treat plant.

Mounting and removing workholding fixtures and tooling on heat-treating machines between jobs: centers, drive chucks, locating plates, spinners, quench rings and tool plates bolted to a machine table, spindle or quench-press platen with hand tools, then shimmed/aligned and checked for runout and clearance. Standard shop equipment, hoist available for heavier plates.

Furnace-side fixturing: installing and swapping grids, racks, trays, jigs and basket assemblies on furnace hearths, charge tables, charge cars and quench-press platens; heavy, sometimes warm or scaled hardware, bolted or pinned in place with hand tools, hoist- or crane-assisted, in a hot and dirty aisle.

Non-routine first-article or repair setup: fitting a newly built, modified or repaired inductor or a custom fixture that has no pre-qualified mounting interface — fabricating or shimming mounts, hand-fitting and dressing bus-bar contact faces, leak-checking water circuits, and iteratively adjusting position/coupling until trial pieces pass hardness and case-depth checks.

Light, bench-scale mounts: attaching flame-hardening torch heads/tips, small induction coils, thermocouple and part-locating fixtures on small or bench-mounted heat-treating machines using screwdrivers, small wrenches and clamps.

tasks.label: Heat billets, bars, plates, rods, and other stock to specified temperatures preparatory to forging, rolling, or processing, using oil, gas, or electrical furnaces.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume forge shop: operator tends an induction billet heating line ahead of a forging press — dumps cut billets into a hopper/feeder, sets the recipe (diameter, exit temperature, feed rate), watches the pyrometer, kicks out under/over-heated billets, and keeps heated billets flowing to the press. Stock is uniform, cut to length, and arrives by conveyor.

Gas-fired forge furnace (slot, box or rotary hearth) in a forge shop built for people: operator charges assorted billets and bar ends by hand tongs or a small charging device, sets zone temperatures, judges soak by color/pyrometer, then pulls the hot stock and carries or passes it to the hammer or press. Sizes and lots change through the shift.

Rolling mill / bar mill reheat furnace (walking beam, pusher or rotary hearth): billets, blooms or slabs are charged from a roller table, heated to rolling temperature through zoned burners, and discharged to the mill. The tender sets zone setpoints and charge/discharge rates from a pulpit and handles cobbles and delays.

Batch furnace in a job shop or captive heat-treat department: operator racks bars, rods and plates onto trays, baskets or fixtures, charges them into a gas or electric box/car-bottom furnace (by hand, cart or fork truck), sets the recipe on the controller, soaks to a specified temperature, and unloads for the downstream forming/rolling operation. Mixed lots, frequent changeovers.

One-off or short-run heating of oversized or odd-shaped stock — a large ingot or heavy bar for open-die forging, a thick plate or a weldment section — charged with an overhead crane, tongs or a rail manipulator into a general-purpose furnace; the operator judges placement, soak time and heat by eye and pyrometer, and the workpiece differs every time.

tasks.label: Position stock in furnaces, using tongs, chain hoists, or pry bars.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Commercial or captive batch heat-treat department: operator loads a repeating set of part SKUs (gears, fasteners, shafts, castings) into steel baskets/trays or onto fixtures and charges a batch integral-quench, atmosphere or vacuum furnace, using tongs for placement and a chain hoist/load table or charge car for the basket. Shop floor with forklifts and other operators; parts arrive on pallets or conveyors.

Heavy single workpieces (large shafts, rolls, dies, ingots, forged rings) charged into a car-bottom, pit or box furnace using an overhead crane, jib or chain hoist and slings, then positioned on the hearth/blocks with tongs or pry bars for correct spacing and support. Forge shop or foundry heat-treat bay.

Inline heating ahead of forming: bar, billet or blank stock fed into an induction heater, rotary hearth or roller-hearth furnace at a forge or hot-stamping plant; operator positions stock on the feed table/coil entry with tongs and keeps the furnace charged at press cadence.

Hot-side corrections at an operating furnace: stock that has shifted, tipped, jammed the pusher, or crowded neighboring pieces is nudged, re-spaced or freed with a pry bar and long tongs through the door of a hot chamber; occasional repositioning of fixtures/racks inside the hot furnace.

High-mix tool room, small job shop or lab heat treat: one-off or very small lots of unique geometries wired, hung, or set on stools/plates in a box furnace or salt bath, positioned by hand with tongs; part shape, mass and required orientation change with every job.

tasks.label: Repair, replace, and maintain furnace equipment as needed, using hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Scheduled preventive-maintenance round on a batch or continuous heat-treat furnace and its auxiliaries during a planned shutdown in the shop: clean burners/nozzles and blow out dust, change quench-oil or filter elements, lubricate chains and bearings, tighten loose fittings and terminal connections, check and adjust door seals and belt/chain tension, using wrenches, screwdrivers, grease gun and shop vac; hot, oily, cramped access around and under equipment.

Replace a failed process/control thermocouple, sensor, or damaged wiring at the furnace: lock out power, unscrew the fitting and protection tube, pull the burnt-out element, fit and land the new one on the terminal block, then verify the temperature reading matches the controller before restart.

Replace hot-zone hardware inside a partially cooled furnace chamber: electric heating elements, radiant tubes, burner assemblies, retort/muffle parts, graphite or moly hot-zone components; involves crawling into or reaching inside the chamber, freeing heat-scaled and seized fasteners, handling brittle ceramic and fiber, and working overhead in awkward postures.

Refractory, insulation and door repair: chip out spalled brick or damaged ceramic-fiber module, patch with castable or mortar, re-anchor insulation, and replace door gaskets, seals, sand seals or heat curtains, using hammer, chisel, trowel and hand tools; the damage is different every time and is judged by eye.

Mechanical repair of furnace auxiliaries: conveyor chains and belts, quench elevators and pushers, circulation fans, pumps, hydraulic/pneumatic hoses, valves and couplings; replace worn links, bearings, hoses or actuators in place, or pull the component to a shop bench and rebuild it before reinstalling and testing.

Unplanned mid-shift breakdown: a load jams, a fixture or basket breaks, an element trips out or a line leaks; the operator diagnoses the fault, makes a quick hand-tool repair or part swap with the load still in process, and returns the furnace to the cycle under time pressure.

tasks.label: Clean oxides and scales from parts or fittings, using steam sprays or chemical and water baths.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Batch chemical descaling/pickling in a heat-treat or finishing shop's tank line: operator loads scaled parts and fittings into baskets, lowers them into acid pickle, then rinse/neutralize/passivate tanks with timed immersion, and dries the load.

Aqueous spray/dunk washer: operator loads oil-quenched and scaled parts into a cabinet or belt washer basket, selects the cycle, runs wash-rinse-dry, unloads and inspects for residual scale or oil before tempering/shipping.

Hand-held steam or high-pressure water spray at a wash-down station: operator sprays larger parts, fixtures, grids and baskets, rotating and re-spraying areas until scale, salt and quench residue are gone.

Small job shop, high mix: mixed one-off parts and fittings of varied geometry cleaned in water/chemical baths, agitated with tongs or hooks, with brush or spot re-treatment of stubborn scale after visual check.

Tending the descale/wash section of an automated (fenced) heat-treat or pickling line: parts move continuously through spray and bath stations; operator monitors, checks output cleanliness, adjusts nozzles/concentrations.

tasks.label: Stamp heat-treatment identification marks on parts, using hammers and punches.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Captive heat-treat department of a manufacturing plant (automotive, bearing, fastener): a repeat-run lot of identical small/medium parts arrives in totes or on a conveyor after quench/temper; operator stamps the same heat-lot/process code in the same designated spot on each piece with hand hammer and steel character punch or a bench stamping press, hundreds of pieces per lot.

Heavy work in a forge/mill/heat-treat bay: bars, billets, plates, shafts or large forgings, often still hot, sitting on roller tables, cooling beds, racks or the floor; operator strikes a heat/grade/lot number into a designated face with a heavy hand hammer and steel type, working around scale and awkward orientations.

Aerospace/defense/medical spec work: heat-treated rings, disks, shafts, fittings that must carry low-stress identification marks at drawing-specified locations (heat lot, process code, inspector stamp), applied per AS9132-type specs and checked for legibility and correct placement before the lot is released with its traceability paperwork.

Commercial job-shop heat treater: mixed customer lots of 1-20 pieces, unfamiliar geometries arriving all day in baskets and on carts around the shop; the operator reads the work order/customer print for which mark and where, finds a suitable flat area on each odd part, and hand-stamps it, then returns it to the basket.

Occasional marking at the inspection or shipping bench: a handful of finished pieces get a hardness/heat-treat certification or inspector code stamped on them after testing, content varying piece to piece, done between other duties.

roles.title: Layout Workers, Metal and Plastic
roles.description: Lay out reference points and dimensions on metal or plastic stock or workpieces, such as sheets, plates, tubes, structural shapes, castings, or machine parts, for further processing. Includes shipfitters.

tasks.label: Mark curves, lines, holes, dimensions, and welding symbols onto workpieces, using scribes, soapstones, punches, and hand drills.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Structural steel fabrication shop: from shop drawings/Tekla model, mark a beam, column or angle with connection/fitting locations, hole centers, part numbers and weld data using soapstone, scribe and center punch so fitters and welders can place clips and plates.

Fab shop plate and sheet layout: mark cut contours, curves, bend lines, dimensions and center-punch hole locations on steel/aluminum plate or sheet laid on a layout table, using square, tape, scribe, soapstone and punch, sometimes drilling small pilot indents.

Shipyard fabrication shop: mark hull plates, brackets and stiffener profiles with frame/stiffener lines, joint and trim lines, hole locations, piece marks and welding symbols before cutting and panel assembly.

Shipfitting in the erection area or drydock: mark cut, trim and fit-up lines, bulkhead/stiffener positions and weld symbols directly on a partly assembled block or on the vessel in place, working around obstructions, on vertical and curved surfaces, from reference points transferred on site.

Machine/job shop layout on castings, forgings and machine parts: apply layout dye, establish datums on a rough part, scribe centerlines and reference lines with height gauge on a surface plate or with combination square, then center-punch hole locations for drilling.

sources.claim: Voortman V704 is a commercial CNC beam layout marking machine that carbide-scribes/mills layout onto all four sides of a profile in one pass, marking contours, welding information and part numbers from the CAD/DSTV file, within an automated in-line production system.

sources.system: Aerospace Rotative Component Robotic Marking Cell (dot peen)
sources.title: Dot peen marking machine - MCYTR21330E - Pryor Marking Technology - robotic
sources.claim: Pryor's robotic marking cell uses a multi-axis robot with integrated vision and rotary-table fixturing to apply dot-peen marks to specified positions on large metal components inside an enclosed cell.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: permanent identification marking of fixtured metal parts in a robotic cell. It transfers to punch/scribe layout marking of castings and machine parts because the objects (rigid metal parts held in fixtures), the actuation (impact/peen marks at programmed coordinates on the part surface), and the environment (enclosed, fixtured robotic cell) are the same; only the content of the marks differs.

tasks.label: Plan locations and sequences of cutting, drilling, bending, rolling, punching, and welding operations, using compasses, protractors, dividers, and rules.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Structural steel / plate fabrication shop: worker studies a shop drawing for a plate or angle part and works out, with rule and protractor on the print and the stock, where cuts, holes, and bend lines fall and the order of burn, punch, drill, and bend so that dimensions hold after forming. Output is a marked-up print or routing decision handed to the burner/press operator.

Shipyard/shipfitting: planning the layout and operation sequence for a bulkhead, frame, or shell plate assembly - deciding roll and cut order, joint fit-up order, and weld sequence to control heat distortion - using dividers, protractors, and rules against full-scale layout templates and lofted dimensions.

Job shop / machine parts and castings: determining datums and the order in which features are laid out and machined on a casting or weldment set up on a surface plate, deciding which reference lines are established first and where drilling and milling operations will be located given stock allowance found on the part.

Sheet metal work: developing a flat pattern with compass and rule, then planning the punch/notch/bend sequence on the brake, including bend allowances and which flanges must be formed first to avoid tool interference.

Field, repair, or one-off work (maintenance shop, on-site fabrication): planning where to cut and in what order to cut, drill, and weld on an as-found or damaged part with no drawing, sizing off the existing assembly with rule and dividers.

tasks.label: Fit and align fabricated parts to be welded or assembled.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Structural steel fabrication shop: working from detail drawings/BIM, the layout worker locates, squares and clamps clips, gussets, stiffeners, base plates and end plates onto rolled beams and columns on horses or a layout table, checks dimensions with tape and square, and tack welds them for the welder; mill tolerances and camber make each piece slightly different.

Production weldment shop (trailer frames, equipment bases, cabs, sheet-metal enclosures): the worker loads laser-cut and formed parts, brackets, tubes and machined pieces into jigs and fixtures, checks fit and gap, clamps and tack welds a repeat-run assembly.

Shipyard panel/sub-assembly shop: shipfitter positions stiffeners, webs, collars and brackets on flat plate panels and bulkheads, pulls them down with magnets, wedges and hydraulic dogs, checks spacing to layout marks, and tacks for welding.

Ship erection and on-board fit-up: aligning curved shell plates and multi-ton blocks/sub-assemblies on the ways or in dry dock, and fitting foundations, brackets and pipe hangers inside hull compartments, using come-alongs, chain falls, dogs, wedges, jacks and heat, in confined and overhead positions.

Pipe spool / pressure-vessel fabrication shop: fitting flanges, elbows, tees and nozzles to pipe on rollers and stands, setting root gap and land, squaring the flange face and orienting bolt holes, then tacking the joint.

Field erection, retrofit or repair site (building frame, bridge, plant, ship afloat): fitting new members, patch plates, stair stringers or replacement parts to existing structure hung from a crane, using drift pins, spud wrenches, come-alongs and torch/grinder trimming, with weather, access and as-built variation.

instances.label: Job/machine shop: a machined casting, forging or weldment is set up on a granite surface plate or layout bench; the worker establishes datums with parallels/V-blocks, then locates bore and boss centre lines and hole centres using a height gauge, gauge blocks and a dial indicator, verifying the layout against the print before machining.

Sheet/plate fabrication shop: a flat template (pattern or drill template) is laid on sheet or plate stock on a layout table; the worker checks the template's position relative to stock edges and struck centre lines with scale, square, height gauge and indicator, adjusting until within tolerance before scribing or punching.

Shipyard fabrication/panel shop: locating frame and butt centre lines on a large steel plate or stiffened panel and verifying the positions of templates or marked part locations (stiffeners, penetrations, brackets) before cutting and fitting; large heavy workpiece handled by crane inside the shop.

Shipfitter on an erected hull block or in the building dock: verifying a template's or structural member's position against the ship's reference centre line and frame lines in a confined, curved, weather-exposed structure, using tape, plumb/level, straightedge and indicators.

Machine shop: a large weldment or casting is craned onto the table of a horizontal boring mill or layout table; the worker sweeps the part with a dial indicator to pick up an existing bore/edge, locates the centre line, and verifies marked or templated positions before machining begins.

QC/inspection area of a metal or plastic parts plant: verifying centre-line location and template/fixture-derived feature positions on finished parts using gauge blocks, height gauge and dial indicator on a granite plate, producing an accepted inspection record.

instances.label: Structural steel / shipfitting shop: worker studies blueprints and existing templates for a plate assembly (bulkhead, frame, gusset), computes trigonometric dimensions, bevel and joint geometry, and plans the layout sequence including allowances for weld shrinkage and heat distortion, producing marked-up prints, cut lists and layout plans for the fitters.

Sheet metal fabrication shop: worker develops flat-pattern layouts (parallel-line, radial-line, triangulation development) for ducts, transitions, hoppers and enclosures from blueprints, calculating bend allowances and material stretch for the specific gauge and alloy, and plans how patterns nest on the stock sheet.

Machine shop precision layout: worker plans the layout of castings, forgings or machine parts from engineering drawings, choosing datums and reference points, verifying enough stock remains on all machined faces, and computing hole-center coordinates and angular dimensions by trigonometry before any scribing occurs.

Boiler, tank and pipe shop: worker plans layouts for tube and pipe intersections, miters, nozzle penetrations and rolled shell courses, applying trigonometry and knowledge of how plate behaves when rolled, formed and heated, and specifies the layout/fit-up sequence to control distortion.

Plastics and composite fabrication: worker plans cut and forming layouts on plastic sheet or stock from prints and templates, allowing for thermal expansion, forming shrinkage and grain/extrusion direction, and documents the layout plan for downstream cutting and forming.

General job/weldment shop: one-off or small-batch custom frames and skids from tube, angle and plate — lay out on stock, cut to length, fit members in a jig or on a layout table, square up and tack the frame for welding.

instances.label: Structural steel fabrication shop: worker takes dimensions off shop drawings/3D model and marks a wide-flange beam, channel or angle with fit-up locations for clip angles and stiffeners, hole centers, cut/cope lines and piece marks using tape, square, soapstone and punch; stock is craned onto layout tables/roller stands.

Machine shop layout on castings, forgings and machine parts: setting the part on a surface/angle plate, applying layout dye, and scribing/center-punching datum lines and hole centers with a height gauge so stock is balanced for subsequent machining and assembly.

Field / in-situ layout: shipfitter marking reference points inside an erected block or on board, or a field crew marking hole and fit-up locations on already-erected structural steel or large installed equipment at a jobsite.

instances.label: Machine-shop layout/inspection area: worker hand-lifts a machined part or small casting (5-35 lb) onto a granite surface plate, seats it on parallel blocks (or clamps it to an angle plate), squares and shims it so the reference face is true, then transfers heights for scribing. Fabrication/machine shop: a production casting or weldment of 100-1,500 lb is rigged with slings on a jib or overhead hoist, landed on a cast-iron surface plate or layout platen, set on parallels/jack screws, leveled and indicated true before layout. Shipyard or structural steel fabrication hall: plates and structural shapes (stiffeners, webs, brackets) are craned onto a layout platen or fitting jig, blocked and squared to marked reference lines for layout and fit-up. Institution-controlled indoor fab hall, repeating panel/stiffener geometry.

One-off or oversized workpiece: a large irregular casting, machine base, or custom weldment is set on a floor plate/large surface plate using multiple blocks, wedges, jacks and chain falls, then iteratively jacked, shimmed and indicated with a height gage/level to establish datums on a part the shop has never seen before.

instances.label: Job/fab shop: from an engineering drawing or 3D CAD model of a part, develop the flat pattern and prepare a sheet-metal (or plastic) template — a profile template or hole-location drilling template — cut to size, holes and reference marks added, edges deburred, template stamped/labelled with the job number for reuse on the layout bench.

Shop pattern/template of wood (plywood, MDF) or plastic used for repeatedly tracing a part contour onto plate or sheet stock: shape cut to the developed outline, locating holes bored, edges trued so a scriber can follow, then hung on the template rack.

Paper, cardboard, or mylar template produced on the layout table or loft floor: dimensions transferred from the drawing or full-scale layout, arcs struck, outline cut with knife or shears, bend/reference lines and part identification marked on the face.

Copying/reverse-engineering: a customer sample, a worn-out template, or an existing flat part is on the bench; the worker picks up its outline and hole pattern by measurement or tracing and prepares a fresh template in metal, plastic, or board that reproduces it within layout tolerance.

Field/in-situ templating: a shipfitter or field layout worker goes to the erected structure (curved hull frame, existing weldment, penetration in an installed panel) and makes a template from paper, wood strips, or light sheet, fitting and trimming it to the as-built geometry before returning it to the shop.

tasks.label: Install doors, hatches, brackets, and clips.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Shipyard panel/sub-assembly shop: shipfitter picks brackets, clips, collar plates and small lugs from a parts cart, sets them to chalk/laser layout marks on a flat steel panel or sub-assembly, squares them with dogs/wedges, and tack welds them for later final welding.

Shipyard block/unit assembly bay: fitting a watertight door frame or hatch coaming into a cut opening in a bulkhead or deck of a large steel block — rigging the assembly with a crane, aligning and shimming to fair the frame, checking squareness/gap, tack welding, then hanging the door leaf and dogging hardware.

Aboard an erected hull or a vessel in drydock/repair: installing doors, hatch covers, brackets and clips inside compartments and on decks — confined spaces, overhead and vertical positions, staging/scaffold access, existing structure and coatings, layout varying vessel to vessel.

General metal/plastic fabrication shop (non-ship): laying out and installing access doors, hinges, hasps, mounting brackets and spring clips on enclosures, tanks, ductwork, machine frames or structural members — drilling/punching, bolting, clinch-fastener or clip insertion, and tack welding at the bench or on a layout table.

Field/site installation at a customer location or open yard: fitting brackets, clips and access hatches onto already-erected structures (storage tanks, silos, bridge girders, platforms) using portable layout tools, temporary supports and field welding under outdoor conditions.

tasks.label: Inspect machined parts to verify conformance to specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Job-shop inspection bench / surface plate: the worker takes a machined part (roughly 2-30 cm) from a tote, reads the print, and checks 5-30 features with digital calipers, micrometers, bore and thread gauges and a height gauge on a granite plate, plus a visual burr/finish check, then records results and accepts or rejects.

Quality-lab first-article or batch inspection: part is clamped on a DCC coordinate measuring machine or optical comparator, a program is run against the CAD/print, and a full GD&T dimensional report is produced for an aerospace/medical customer requiring documented 100% or FAI inspection.

In-process check at the machine on the shop floor: a part still in the vise/chuck or just off the CNC mill or lathe is checked for critical bore diameters, hole positions and depths, and the worker decides accept, rework, or offset adjustment while the machine sits idle.

Fabrication-shop check of larger workpieces - weldments, plate, structural shapes, castings roughly 0.5-3 m - verifying overall size, hole patterns, squareness, flatness and layout lines against the print with tape, square, height gauge or portable arm/scanner, with the piece on a layout table or the shop floor.

Shipyard / heavy structural fit-up verification: a shipfitter checks a hull block or large assembly tens of feet across in the assembly hall or on the ways - frame spacing, plate alignment, bulkhead squareness, weld gaps - against the drawing, working around scaffolding, cranes and other trades.

tasks.label: Apply pigment to layout surfaces, using paint brushes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Machine shop bench work: layout worker brushes Steel Blue layout fluid (Dykem) from a brush-in-cap bottle onto the faces of small-to-medium one-off or small-batch parts, castings, brackets and plate pieces set on the layout bench or surface plate, covering only the areas that will be scribed, then lets it flash off before scribing with height gage or surface gage. Parts vary shape to shape; the bench is shared, with other machinists and traffic nearby.

Fabrication shop: coating larger steel plates, weldments and structural shapes (angle, channel, beam sections) lying on a layout table or shop floor with layout fluid or whitewash over the region to be marked, before snapping/scribing lines for burning and hole locations. Overhead crane moves the stock in and out; coating must be uniform and glare-free over a large area.

Shipyard panel/plate shop before assembly: shipfitter or layout worker applies marking pigment (layout fluid, whitewash, paint) to plate and profile stock as it comes off the blast/prime line, so frame, cutout and stiffener locations can be scribed; work is done on flat stock at the platen or roller conveyor in an institution-controlled yard shop.

On already-assembled or installed work: applying pigment to layout surfaces of erected hull blocks, tanks, or machinery frames in the erection area, on staging, or at a customer plant — the workpiece cannot be moved, access is awkward (overhead, vertical, confined), the area to coat is a small designated patch of a large structure, and conditions vary with weather and staging.

Toolroom / precision layout: applying a thin, even, glare-free coat of layout blue to precision surfaces (die blocks, gage-quality machined faces, mating surfaces) where film build must add practically no thickness and coverage must be complete for high-accuracy scribing and inspection.

instances.label: Job-shop rack plating: worker racks a mixed daily batch of small/medium metal parts (brackets, castings, machined components) and uses a manual or air hoist to lower the rack into a sequence of clean/acid/plate/rinse tanks, holding each for the specified time, agitating, then lifting and draining. Part mix and process sequence change job to job.

High-volume production plating in a captive plant: barrels or racks of a repeating part (fasteners, stampings, connectors) are immersed through a fixed tank sequence with standard dwell times, shift after shift, with the operator loading, starting the cycle and monitoring.

Hot-dip galvanizing: steel fabrications or baskets of small parts hung on jigs are lifted by crane and immersed in a ~450 °C molten zinc kettle for the specified dwell, then withdrawn at a controlled rate/angle with skimming and draining, in hot, fume-laden conditions.

Precision anodizing/plating of aerospace, defense or medical parts: masked and racked components immersed for tightly specified times and controlled withdrawal, with process parameters logged to spec (e.g., MIL-A-8625, Nadcap), scrap tolerance near zero.

Dip coating in liquid plastic or paint: parts or molds immersed in plastisol, solid-film lubricant, or an immersion paint/e-coat bath for a specified dwell with controlled immersion and withdrawal rate, then drained/spun before cure.

Bench-scale hand dipping of small or delicate items (jewelry, electronic contacts, decorative hardware) held on wires, tweezers or small racks and immersed for short timed dips in a series of small beakers/tanks at a workbench line.

instances.label: Manual/semi-automatic rack plating line in a small metal-finishing job shop: for each rack of parts the operator figures the required amperage from part surface area and the spec's current density, turns the rectifier's voltage/current dials (or keys a digital setpoint), watches the ammeter/voltmeter through the 15-60 minute cycle and trims the setting as the load plates. Work occurs on an open shop floor beside the tanks.

Barrel plating (zinc, zinc-nickel, tin) in a job or captive shop: operator sets and adjusts rectifier voltage/current for each barrel load, ramping up at the start, changing amperage for load weight/part mix, and holding amp-hours to meet thickness. Recipe-driven automated hoist line: operator selects/scans the job at the line's HMI, confirms or edits the rectifier setpoints for each plating cell, then monitors amp/volt readouts on several cells at once and corrects drift or an out-of-range cell during the run.

Precision/spec-controlled work - hard chrome, Type II/III anodize, aerospace or Nadcap-audited plating: current is stepped or ramped on a defined schedule (current density per square foot, ramp, dwell, pulse/periodic reverse), voltage watched for contact problems, and every setpoint logged for the certification package.

Abnormal or first-run conditions: burnt or dull deposit, poor rack contact, low bath conductivity, an unfamiliar part geometry with no established recipe. Operator inspects a trial rack, reasons about what the readings and the deposit appearance mean, and changes current/voltage by judgment, repeating until the finish is acceptable.

instances.label: High-volume production plating plant (barrel, reel-to-reel or automated hoist line) running small metal parts — fasteners, connectors, stampings, terminals. tasks.label: Set up, operate, or tend plating or coating machines to coat metal or plastic products with chromium, zinc, copper, cadmium, nickel, or other metal to protect or decorate surfaces.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Tending an automated barrel or rack electroplating line (acid/alkaline zinc, zinc-nickel, tin, electroless nickel) in a captive or job shop: loading barrels/racks at a fixed load station, calling up the part's recipe on the PLC/HMI, monitoring rectifier amps, bath temperature and hoist cycle, making chemical additions, unloading and spot-checking coverage and thickness. Guarded tank line, fixed station spacing, programmable hoists.

Manual or semi-automatic rack/barrel plating of small-lot, mixed job-shop work in an open shop bay: hand-racking assorted parts (some awkward or heavy) on hooks and wire, moving racks tank to tank on an air hoist or by hand, timing dips, watching for gassing/burning, rinsing, drying, inspecting. Hundreds of part numbers, frequent changeovers.

Hot-dip galvanizing of fabricated steel (brackets, gratings, poles, weldments): wiring and jigging parts on racks, running the load through degrease/pickle/flux tanks and the molten zinc kettle on an overhead crane, controlling immersion and withdrawal rate, skimming ash/dross, quenching, then inspecting and touching up runs. Hot, fume-laden kettle hall inside a galvanizing plant.

Operating a continuous coating line — steel strip hot-dip galvanizing or continuous strip/wire electroplating: threading the coil or wire, setting line speed, current density and air-knife pressure/position, holding coating weight to order spec, watching gauges and edge quality from a pulpit and trimming setpoints. Purpose-built continuous line.

Routine in-shift bath tending and chemistry maintenance: drawing bath samples and titrating or analyzing them, adding brighteners, salts and makeup chemicals, keeping levels, pH and temperature in range, backwashing filters, replenishing anode baskets or zinc, and logging results so the line stays in spec.

New-part setup and defect troubleshooting: working out how to rack or barrel an unfamiliar part, masking threads/bearing surfaces with plugs, tape or lacquer, placing anodes, thieves and shields, computing current from surface area, running a first article, measuring thickness, and diagnosing and correcting burning, staining, poor coverage or adhesion problems.

High-volume captive plating in a large manufacturer or a continuous strip/coil plating-galvanizing line: operator watches coating thickness/weight gauges, line speed, cell currents and solution levels, adjusts wiping or current to hold coating weight, and stops the line when readings go out of spec.

Electronics plating (PCB or semiconductor wafer plating tool) in a controlled fab/clean bay: operator monitors tool status screens, bath analyzer alarms, flow and filter pressure gauges and rectifier/pulse readings; changes setpoints and aborts or holds the tool when parameters drift.

Anodizing or electroless nickel line: operator watches bath temperature, pH, MTO/turnover and rectifier readings, adjusts heating/cooling and replenishment, and stops processing when the bath drifts outside the process window.

Precision/critical work (aerospace hard chrome, electroless nickel, medical or electronic gold plating): parts and test coupons are withdrawn from the bath at set intervals, examined under magnification and measured for thickness against a written spec, results logged, and parts returned to solution if under thickness.

Batch hot-dip galvanizing of fabricated steel: the crane withdraws the jig of fabrications from the molten zinc kettle after the timed dip; the operator watches the withdrawal and looks the whole fabrication over for bare spots, ash inclusions, drips and dross pimples, marking pieces for touch-up.

instances.label: Barrel-plated small parts (fasteners, stampings, small hardware) in a plating job shop: after the final rinse the operator brings the barrel to the unload station, dumps the wet load into a centrifugal spin dryer or drum dryer, runs the drying cycle, and containerizes dry parts. Decorative/cosmetic work (bright chrome, nickel, brass hardware, plated plastics): after rinsing, the operator hand-wipes each piece with clean cloths to remove water spots, streaks and drag-out from crevices; the acceptance standard is a visually spot-free, unmarked finish.

Small delicate precision items (jewelry findings, electronic connectors, medical components) rinsed in DI/cleansing liquid and dried by tumbling in sawdust or corn-cob-media barrels, or gently spun, then separated from the media without nicking, tangling or staining the parts.

Low-volume job-shop work: one-off, large or awkward customer parts (frames, castings, long extrusions, repair/restoration items) rinsed with spray or a dip in a manual tank, tilted to drain trapped solution, and hand-dried with cloths or air before packing.

tasks.label: Test machinery to ensure that it is operating properly.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Pre-run functional check of an automatic/manual plating line in a job-shop or captive finishing department: energize the line, start pumps, filtration, air/eductor agitation and heaters, run the hoist/transporter through a dry cycle to confirm travel, indexing and dwell, confirm rectifiers energize and hold set amperage/voltage, verify ventilation and alarms/interlocks, and watch and listen for anything abnormal before parts are loaded.

Test run to prove the machine is plating correctly: hang a test panel, test rack or first-piece parts, run the plating cycle, then examine and measure the deposit (appearance, coverage, thickness by XRF or Hull-cell/panel check) and confirm the bath, anodes and current are delivering the specified coating; re-run after any correction.

In-process and support-equipment checks while the line runs: read rectifier ammeters/voltmeters and panel displays, verify tank temperatures and levels, confirm filter pumps, blowers, chillers and scrubber/waste-treatment pumps are running, check for leaks, hot motors, cavitation or unusual noise, and flag anything out of range.

Test after maintenance, repair or changeover: jog the hoist or barrel drive, verify limit switches, proximity sensors, timers and safety interlocks, re-run one or more cycles empty or with a dummy load, and confirm the equipment returns to proper operation before production restarts.

Diagnostic testing when something appears wrong during production (burnt or dull deposits, rectifier tripping, slow cycle, low flow): check suspect components with meters and by observation—bus bar and rack contacts, anode condition, pump output, heater/controller—to determine whether the machinery is operating properly and what is at fault.

tasks.label: Measure, mark, and mask areas to be excluded from plating.

instances.label: Repeat-production job in a plating job shop: operator at a masking bench works through a batch of familiar metal parts (shafts, brackets, fittings), reading the job traveler/print, checking dimensions with rule or calipers, and applying masking tape, dots, caps and plugs to threaded holes, bores and faces that must stay bare. High-precision masking of a large or complex high-value component (aerospace landing-gear part, engine component, hydraulic rod, blisk): layout lines measured and marked from the drawing, then tape plus lacquer applied to a tight-tolerance boundary; the part is heavy and handled with a hoist or fixture.

High-volume repetitive masking of many identical small parts for selective plating (e.g., connectors, contacts, small hardware for gold or silver plating): the same few masking operations applied hundreds of times over a shift on trays or racks.

One-off, first-article, or repair/MRO job: an unfamiliar or worn part arrives with a drawing or customer note; the operator decides the masking method, measures and scribes layout marks on irregular or damaged geometry, then masks it, improvising around features that vary part to part.

High-volume captive line (automotive fastener zinc barrel line, tin/copper strip or PCB line): scheduled replenishment of soluble anode metal into fixed-position anode baskets or feeder rails along an engineered line; standard ball/pellet anode stock, standard basket positions, work done on a set maintenance schedule.

Hard chrome or anodizing shop: heavy lead/lead-tin or conforming anodes are hung from the busbar, centered or inserted into bores of the fixtured workpiece with insulators and spacers, connected to the positive terminal and lowered into the hot acid tank; anode geometry is part-specific and repeated for production parts.

Small-tank decorative, jewelry, electronics or lab-scale plating: small sticks, strips or pieces of gold, silver, nickel or platinized titanium anode metal are hooked onto anode rods over small tanks and immersed; frequent changeovers between metals and bath types, small parts, tight tank-side space.

Anode maintenance work: slipping cloth/polypropylene anode bags over new anode bars or baskets, tying or clipping them, brushing off anode film and corrosion products from hooks and contacts, then re-hanging the bagged anode assemblies in the tank.

Large-part plating (industrial rolls, aerospace/heavy components) in deep tanks: heavy anode plates or bars, often several hundred pounds, are rigged to a hoist or crane, set on the busbar at a set spacing from the workpiece and lowered into the plating solution.
