instances.label: Automated barrel or rack plating line in a job shop or captive finishing plant: at the start of a load the operator calls up the part recipe at the line's PC/HMI station and sets or verifies bath temperature setpoints, rectifier settings, barrel rotation/oscillation speed and hoist transfer speeds before the load is released to the line.

Manual or semi-automatic plating line in a small shop: operator sets each tank's thermostat/temperature controller (immersion heater or steam valve), turns the rectifier voltage/current dials, and sets barrel rotation and hoist/agitation speeds using panel-mounted knobs and switches, checking a tank thermometer as the bath comes up to temperature.

Hot-dip galvanizing / molten-metal immersion work: operator sets the kettle burner or immersion-heater controls to hold the molten zinc (or tin/solder) bath at the specified temperature, and sets dip, withdrawal and conveyor/centrifuge speeds for the load.

Continuous strip, wire or coil coating line (electrogalvanizing, hot-dip strip galvanizing, tinning): pulpit operator enters line speed and pot/furnace temperature setpoints for the coming coil grade and coating weight and ramps the line to speed.

Mid-run corrective adjustment: after seeing thin or heavy coating, burning, dull deposit or slow drainage on inspected parts or a gauge reading out of range, the operator raises or lowers the bath temperature setpoint and/or slows the line, barrel or hoist to bring the coating back into specification.

tasks.label: Monitor and measure thicknesses of electroplating on component parts to verify conformance to specifications, using micrometers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume rack or barrel plating shop (zinc, nickel, tin): after a load comes out of the tanks the operator pulls one or more sample parts from the rack/basket, rinses and dries them, measures plating thickness at 3-5 designated points with a micrometer, magnetic/eddy-current gauge or bench XRF, compares to the spec on the traveler, logs the readings and adjusts immersion time or current if drifting.

Job shop running a repeat, established part number (known geometry, standing measurement points): operator measures a sample before and after plating with a micrometer on critical diameters/threaded features, or uses a probe/XRF at the spec'd locations, and records conformance on the job traveler.

Job shop running a first-time or one-off custom part from a customer print: operator interprets the drawing, decides where the critical/significant surfaces are, chooses the measurement method (micrometer differential vs. gauge), measures and documents; part geometry has never been seen in the shop before.

Precision electronics plating (connector strip, lead frames, contacts, PCB) on reel-to-reel or automated selective plating lines: sub-micron gold/nickel/tin thickness monitored continuously in the running line and by sampling coupons; readings used to trim the line so precious-metal thickness stays just inside tolerance.

Hard chrome / heavy engineered plating on large parts (hydraulic cylinder rods, rolls, molds): operator measures diameters at several stations along the part with large micrometers before plating, after plating and after grinding, computing deposit thickness on the diameter; parts are heavy and moved with hoists.

Final QC / first-article bench inspection with documentation: sample parts from a finished lot are taken to the QC bench, measured with micrometer and XRF at the specified points, results entered against the specification for the certificate of conformance, with occasional cross-section backup.

instances.label: Higher-volume production plating/anodizing line: operator runs the line hoist or overhead crane to lift a loaded rack, flight bar, or barrel from the load station and set it on the line's feed carriage/cradle at the start of the cycle. Job-shop rack plating: operator uses a jib or bridge hoist with chain slings and hooks to lift heavy or awkward castings, weldments, or bundled parts off a pallet or cart and place them on the plating rack/flight bar or feed carriage. Part mix changes job to job; rigging points, balance, and clearances judged by the worker; wet, crowded aisles.

Hard chrome / cylindrical work: hoist a long shaft, hydraulic rod, roll, or cylinder (often 6-20 ft, several hundred to several thousand pounds) and lower it onto rotating spindles or contact fixtures on the carriage, aligning to spindle centers and electrical contacts, sometimes with a second worker steadying the load.

Hot-dip galvanizing or large-immersion work: overhead crane used to lift a hand-jigged bundle, beam, or fabrication from the jigging area and hang it on the dipping carriage or kettle crane beam. Heavy loads, hot and fume-laden bay, partly open building, jig make-up varies with each fabrication.

Barrel plating in a small/older shop: hoist a loaded plating barrel or basket from the loading stand and set it onto the machine's carriage/spindle drive so drive dogs and contacts engage, then repeat for successive barrels. Standard barrels, worn equipment, manual hoist pendant, tight floor space.

Occasional oversized or one-off workpiece: multi-point rigging with spreader bar or lifting beam, two workers guiding, careful maneuvering past other racks and tank edges to seat the piece on the carriage or fixture; unique geometry with no established lifting fixture.

instances.label: Plating job-shop floor: operator works a manual glove-box blast cabinet, holding small-to-medium high-mix parts (fittings, castings, brackets, tooling) by hand or on a turntable, aiming the nozzle to strip oxide/old plating and raise an anchor profile, visually checking and re-blasting missed spots, then racking parts for the plating line. Part types change many times per shift.

Batch blasting in semi-automatic equipment on the shop floor: operator loads baskets/hooks of similar parts into a tumble-belt or spinner-hanger blast machine, selects the cycle (media, time, pressure), runs it, unloads, blows off residual media, inspects a sample and re-runs rejects.

Walk-in blast room/booth: large workpieces (frames, shafts, rolls, tanks, weldments) set on carts or hung from a monorail; suited operator uses a hand-held nozzle with a portable pot to blast the whole surface to a specified cleanliness/profile (e.g., SSPC SP-10) before plating or thermal spray, then checks coverage.

Selective/masked roughening: operator masks threads, bores, bearing journals or sealing faces, then blasts only the bond areas of a part to a specified roughness for coating adhesion, verifies profile/appearance, removes masking and hands off to the plating or spray line within a short time window.

Occasional oversized or rework blasting outside the booth: a large fabricated assembly or a returned part is spot-blasted in an open shop bay or the yard with a portable blast pot and containment, under variable lighting, layout and weather.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: End-of-shift / weekly washdown of the plating line area in a job shop: hosing down floors, walkways, grating and catch basins around the tanks, flushing drag-out and spilled solution to the trench drain. Wet, chemically splashed floor with hoses, carts and totes present.

Cleaning plating racks, hooks, tip contacts, baskets and barrels: scraping and wire-brushing plated-metal buildup off rack tips and contacts, knocking debris out of barrel perforations, chemically stripping and then hosing the racks clean at a wash station before returning them to service.

Periodic tank cleanout: pumping down a plating or rinse tank, scraping sludge, hard salt and scale off tank walls, heaters, coils and anode bars, hosing the residue to the waste-treatment drain, cleaning or replacing anode bags and filter media, then refilling. Confined, awkward access, hazardous chemicals.

Cleaning removable ancillary equipment at a sink or wash station: filter chambers and cartridges, pump strainers, spray-rinse nozzle manifolds, drip pans and small parts baskets — knocked/scraped free of hydroxide sludge and scale, then hosed and rinsed.

In-place cleaning of installed machinery and structures: hosing and scraping crystallized salts and drag-out off tank rims and flight bars, hoist rails, bus bars and cathode contacts, rectifier cabinets, guards, dryer/oven interiors and conveyor chain, working around live line equipment in a cluttered wet aisle.

tasks.label: Clean workpieces, using wire brushes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Pre-plating bench cleaning of batches of small/medium metal parts in a job-shop plating facility: operator holds each part against a bench-mounted wire wheel (or uses a hand/power wire brush) to remove rust, oxide scale, weld slag and light corrosion before racking for the plating line; repetitive batches of like parts.

Post-plating/post-pickle touch-up at a bench: wire-brushing plated or pickled parts to remove smut, burnt or rough deposits, contact marks and loose residue, inspecting by eye and re-brushing until the surface is acceptable, then setting parts aside for rinse/inspection.
Between loads, wire-brushing plating racks, hooks and rack contact tips at a bench or rack table to strip metal buildup and restore electrical contact before the rack is reloaded.

Large or heavy workpieces (weldments, castings, structural pieces going to galvanizing/hard chrome) brushed with a handheld power wire brush while sitting on a cart, buggy or rack beside the line; variable geometry, awkward reach, part often too heavy to hand-manipulate.

In-place cleaning of line hardware around the tanks: hand wire-brushing bus bars, anode/cathode contact bars, clamps, saddles and hooks where they hang, in cramped wet aisles between tanks, without removing the hardware from the line.

One-off, high-mix items: a few odd customer parts (repair or prototype pieces, mixed and delicate geometries, plastic-on-metal assemblies) needing ad-hoc spot wire-brushing before plating, each set up and judged individually in a minute or two.

tasks.label: Mix and test solutions, and turn valves to fill tanks with solutions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine replenishment of a running production plating bath (zinc, nickel, chrome, copper) in a job-shop plating line: after the shift's analysis, the operator measures out metal salts, acid and proprietary brightener/carrier concentrates from carboys or 55-gal drums, meters them into the tank by pump or hand-pour, and lets agitation/circulation mix them in.

Drawing samples from several hot, fuming process tanks with a dipper/sample bottle and testing them at the shop bench: acid-base or EDTA titrations, pH, specific gravity, sometimes a Hull-cell panel; results logged and required additions calculated.

Turning valves to bring tanks back to working level and volume: opening DI/city-water and solution supply valves to top off process tanks after evaporation and drag-out, refilling rinse tanks, watching the level and closing the valve without overflowing.

Complete new-bath make-up or bath change-over: charging a make-up/process tank with a measured volume of water, adding liquid concentrates and bagged dry salts to a recipe, heating and mixing until dissolved, then testing and adjusting before releasing the bath to production.

Mixing and filling ancillary solutions in the same shop: alkaline cleaners and pretreatment/conversion-coating baths, sealers and dyes, and batch chemical solutions for the wastewater treatment system - diluting to label ratio, filling the tank, and spot-testing concentration/pH.

tasks.label: Replace worn parts and adjust equipment components, using hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Anode/electrode consumable maintenance on a plating line: operator shuts down a tank section, pulls spent or eroded anodes and corroded anode hooks off the anode bar, replenishes titanium baskets with nickel/zinc/copper pellets, wire-brushes and re-torques the anode-bar contacts with wrenches, and replaces split anode bags. Wet, corrosive, hot tank-side work in a plating shop.

Rack, barrel and fixture refurbishment at the shop bench: replacing worn or burnt rack tips, hooks and spring clips, re-tipping and re-coating racks with plastisol, swapping worn barrel danglers, perforated panels and barrel contact cables, using pliers, screwdrivers, wrenches and a crimping tool.

Fluid-system component replacement in the process area: changing fouled filter cartridges/bags in filter chambers, replacing worn pump seals, impellers, hoses, unions, valves, immersion heaters and thermocouples on tanks; involves draining, unbolting wet chemical plumbing, re-sealing, refilling and leak-checking.

Mechanical repair and adjustment of the transport equipment: replacing worn hoist chains, cables, sprockets, bearings, drive belts, cam followers and contact shoes on the automated hoist/conveyor or barrel drive, then adjusting limit switches, stops, chain tension and flight-bar alignment and test-running the line until motion is correct.

Bolted hardware and electrical contact maintenance: replacing worn bus-bar contacts, jumper cables, saddle clamps and brackets, cleaning oxidized rectifier and bus connections, replacing worn agitation nozzles/eductors, and re-torquing loose hardware found on the daily walk-around, using wrenches, socket sets and a wire brush.

tasks.label: Place plated or coated materials on racks and transfer them to ovens to dry for specified periods of time.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume rack plating line in a captive/production plating shop: after the plating and rinse sequence, the operator transfers freshly plated medium-sized parts (brackets, trim, connectors) onto drying racks or trays at a fixed unload station and moves the loaded rack into a hot-air dryer/bake oven, running a set dwell time. Fixed part mix, repetitive cycle, wet parts, drainage orientation matters.

Barrel-plated small hardware (zinc-plated fasteners, stampings, clips): operator moves the plated/chromated load into baskets or trays, sets them on multi-tier oven racks or carts, and rolls the rack into a batch bake oven for hydrogen-embrittlement relief (e.g., ~4 hours at 375-425 F) per a written spec, logging start time.

High-mix job shop: dozens of different customer part numbers per shift, low volume each. Operator lays or hangs assorted wet plated/coated parts on drying racks and trays, orienting each for drainage and to avoid contact marks, wheels the cart across the shop floor to a batch oven, and sets the timer to the customer's specified bake period.

Large/heavy plated components (hard-chrome piston rods, hydraulic cylinders, landing-gear parts, large castings): operator uses a jib hoist or overhead crane to place parts on oven racks or a bake fixture and load a walk-in/batch oven, then closes the door and runs the specified bake cycle.

Delicate or critical parts (aerospace, medical, electronic connectors) plated to spec: parts must be placed on racks or trays without contact marks or nesting, oriented per process sheet, and baked for a documented period with recorded temperature for Nadcap/ISO traceability; damage or missed bake means scrap.

tasks.label: Measure and set stops, rolls, brushes, and guides on automatic feeders and conveying equipment or coating machines, using micrometers, rules, and hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Changeover on a conveyorized automatic plating/coating line in a job-shop plating facility: operator measures the new part width with a rule/tape, loosens guide-rail clamps and stop brackets with wrenches, slides side guides and part stops on the feeder and conveyor to the measured dimension, retightens, and runs test parts until parts track without jamming.

Setting nip/gap and pressure on the rolls of a coating machine (roll coater, wringer/squeegee or applicator rolls on a strip or sheet line): micrometer/feeler-gauge measurement across the roll face, adjusting jackscrews and mechanical stops to a spec gap, then verifying coating thickness on a trial run.

Setting mechanical stops, travel dogs and limit-switch positions on the automatic hoists/loaders of a barrel or rack plating line so racks index and lower correctly over each tank: measuring positions with a rule, loosening and sliding switch brackets and stop blocks with hand tools in a hot, humid, fume-laden tank room with tight access.

Setting brushes on a brush/scrub, brush-plating or brush-deburring unit feeding the plating line: measuring and adjusting brush height/penetration and contact pressure against the workpiece with hand tools and a rule, checking contact witness marks on test parts.

Removing worn brushes from a scrub/brush unit and installing new ones (unbolting hubs/shafts, seating new brush sections, torquing fasteners), then re-measuring and re-setting brush height and pressure.

Air-knife / wiping-die setup on a continuous hot-dip coating line: measuring and setting knife-to-strip distance, lip gap and tilt with gauges and hand tools at line speed changes or coating-weight changes, verifying with coating-weight readings.

tasks.label: Position containers to receive parts, and load or unload materials in containers, using dollies or handtrucks.

instances.label: Transporting loaded containers — tubs, steel baskets, plastic totes, skids of parts — between receiving/staging, the plating line, and inspection/packing/shipping inside the plating plant, using carts, dollies, hand trucks or pallet jacks; marked aisles shared with forklifts and people, damp floors near tank rows.

Staging and swapping containers at the line's load and unload stations: bringing an empty tote/bin/cart, positioning it to receive plated parts as they come off a barrel dump, dryer or unload table, then pulling the full container away and staging it for the next operation.

Hand-transferring parts into and out of containers: tipping baskets, scooping or picking loose plated parts and placing them into tubs, partitioned boxes or dunnage, handling wet, oily or warm parts and mixed part types in a job shop, taking care not to scratch plated surfaces.

Moving heavy or awkward material: 55-gallon chemical drums, gaylords, anode boxes, heavy racks/fixtures and long bar stock, using drum dollies and two-wheel hand trucks between the dock, chemical storage and the line; tight aisles, thresholds and uneven or wet floor.

Ad hoc/irregular handling: customer-supplied odd containers and cardboard boxes, one-off small lots, staging wherever floor space allows in a cramped older job shop with no fixed container positions or standard tote sizes.

instances.label: Scheduled lubrication PM on an automatic plating line: greasing/oiling the overhead hoist and conveyor chains, trolley bearings, drive units, gearboxes and rails, using grease gun and oil can at marked points, some overhead above process tanks in a wet, fume-laden aisle.

Routine wash-out of rinse tanks and process tank interiors between solution changes or at shift/weekly intervals: drain or pump down the tank, spray and scrub the interior walls and bottom, flush residues to treatment, refill with water/solution.

Periodic full clean-out of a plating bath tank: pump the bath to a holding tank, shovel/vacuum settled metallic sludge and dropped parts, descale walls, heating coils and anode bar, clean or replace anode bags and baskets, inspect the tank liner, then refill and re-balance.

Fluid-system maintenance: change bag/cartridge filters and clean filter chambers, clean pump strainers and inlets, replace seals, hoses and fittings, clear plugged spray nozzles and rinse headers, clean exhaust hoods and ductwork over the tanks.

Cleaning plating racks, barrels, anode hooks and electrical contacts: strip metallic buildup from rack tips, wire-brush/abrade bus-bar and saddle contact surfaces, wash out barrels and check perforations, inspect plastisol rack coatings.

Minor mechanical repair and adjustment during PM: replace worn conveyor chain links, belts, hoses and gaskets, tighten loose fittings, re-align guides, adjust hoist limit switches and clean up leaks found during the round.

tasks.label: Preheat workpieces in ovens.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Job-shop plating/finishing plant: operator wheels a cart or carries racks and baskets of cleaned parts to a walk-in batch oven on the shop floor, opens the door, positions loads on shelves or a rolling cart, sets temperature and soak time on the oven HMI, and pulls the hot load out on schedule for the plating line. Mixed part types and load sizes, coworkers and fork trucks moving about, no fixturing.

Automated/conveyorized plating or coating line with an in-line dry-off / preheat oven: parts are hung on racks or loaded in barrels at a load station, programmable hoists or an overhead conveyor carry each load through the oven per a stored recipe, and the operator sets oven setpoints and monitors temperatures and line faults. Purpose-built line with guarded work zones.

Hot-dip galvanizing plant: jigged steel fabrications are lifted by overhead crane out of the flux tank into a drying/preheat oven (100-130 C) and then to the kettle; heavy loads, radiant heat, drips, timing tied to kettle availability.

Small parts and small ovens: trays or wire baskets of fasteners, connectors, or plastic components are dried/preheated in a cabinet oven beside the plating tanks; operator loads trays, dials in temperature and time, times the soak, and unloads with gloves or tongs to the plating rack or barrel.

Large or awkward workpieces (structural steel, castings, tooling, large plastic housings) preheated in a large oven: hoist, fork truck, or crane places the piece on an oven cart, careful placement to avoid contact marks, sometimes a thermocouple attached, then withdrawal and transfer to the coating station while hot.

tasks.label: Monitor machine operations to determine whether adjustments are necessary, stopping machines when problems occur.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: CNC tool & cutter grinder in a cutting-tool shop or toolroom: the worker watches a grind cycle on end mills, drills or reamers — wheel loading and dressing, coolant flow, chatter/burn, size drift — and pauses the cycle, tweaks offsets or dresses the wheel when the process drifts; stops the machine on a crash or alarm.

Production grinding of parts in a plant or job shop (cylindrical, centerless, surface, thread grinders): the worker monitors size drift against in-process gauge readings, dress frequency, wheel wear and surface burn across long runs, stopping the machine when parts go out of tolerance or the wheel/dresser faults.

Saw-blade, knife and industrial-blade sharpening service shop: automatic/CNC sharpening machines with blade loaders; the worker watches tooth indexing, blade feed, grinding wheel condition and stops the machine on a misfeed, jam or off-spec grind.

Manual or hand-fed equipment in the same shop (pedestal/bench grinder, manual surface grinder, hand-fed blade or drill sharpener): the worker judges by spark pattern, sound, vibration and part heat while feeding the work by hand, backing off the feed or shutting the machine down when the wheel glazes, loads, or the part burns.

Mobile/on-site sharpening service (van-mounted or portable sharpening machine at a restaurant, butcher shop, mill or customer jobsite): the worker monitors a portable grinding/sharpening unit in an uncontrolled setting and stops it if the blade slips, the wheel loads, or the machine sounds wrong.

tasks.label: Select and mount grinding wheels on machines, according to specifications, using hand tools and applying knowledge of abrasives and grinding procedures.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Job/machine shop: worker selects a specified vitrified wheel (abrasive type, grit, grade, bond) from the wheel rack for a manual or semi-automatic surface or tool-and-cutter grinder, visually inspects and ring-tests it, mounts it on the arbor with blotters and flanges, torques the spindle nut, replaces the guard, then trues, dresses and balances the wheel before running the job.

Cutting-tool production or regrind plant: setup on a 5-axis CNC tool grinder. Operator builds/selects the wheel pack called for by the grinding program (several wheels and spacers on an HSK adapter), balances it, mounts it to the grinding spindle or loads it into the machine's wheel magazine, and qualifies wheel diameter and face positions before grinding.

Saw and tool sharpening service shop: mounting CBN/diamond or resin-bond wheels on circular-saw, band-saw, router-bit or knife sharpening machines, matching wheel spec and profile to the tooth geometry and blade material, setting wheel position, then dressing/aligning to the tooth face.

Production plant, heavy grinding: changing a large, heavy wheel (cylindrical, centerless, gear or roll grinder) using a hoist or wheel cart, seating it on the flange/adapter, bolting and torquing to spec, then truing/dressing and dynamically balancing it on the spindle.

Mobile/on-site sharpening service: in a van or on a customer's shop or kitchen floor, fitting or replacing the abrasive wheel, belt or disc on portable sharpening equipment, selecting the grade for the tools being serviced, in a space taken as found.

Small shop or maintenance department: replacing a worn or wrong-grade wheel on a bench/pedestal grinder or an abrasive belt on a belt grinder - remove guard and spindle nut, fit new wheel with blotters and flanges, reassemble, dress and true.

instances.label: Production/regrind shop: set up and run a CNC tool & cutter grinder (e.g., ANCA/Walter type) to manufacture or resharpen solid-carbide end mills, drills and step tools — select/mount wheel packs and collets, load the program, set coolant nozzles, probe the blank, run and gauge the batch.

Die/mold finishing bench or cell: polishing hardened steel die and mold surfaces with abrasive wheels, belts, or hand-held polishers to a specified surface finish without altering geometry.

Maintenance/tool crib: offhand bench and pedestal grinding, ad-hoc touch-up sharpening of assorted worn tooling (drill bits, lathe tool bits, chisels, mower/shear blades) judged largely by eye and feel, one item at a time, high mix and unpredictable condition.

tasks.label: Inspect, feel, and measure workpieces to ensure that surfaces and dimensions meet specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-process dimensional check during a production grinding run in a tool/regrind shop: operator stops the cycle, checks diameter, length, flute depth or corner radius of a carbide endmill/drill with micrometer, snap gage or indicator, decides whether to adjust wheel compensation. Batch work, repeated part type, at the machine.

Final geometry inspection of a finished or reground cutting tool against the print: rake/relief angles, concentricity/runout, radius profile, flute form, checked on an optical comparator, tool projector or bench measuring device before the tool is packed or returned to the customer.

Visual and tactile inspection of the ground surface and cutting edge: looking for grinding burn, chatter marks, wheel scratches, edge chipping or micro-burrs, running a thumb or finger over the edge and surface to judge sharpness and smoothness, flagging pieces for rework.

Verification of surface finish and form after precision grinding/honing/polishing: roughness measured with a profilometer or compared against roughness standards, plus flatness/parallelism checked on a surface plate with indicator and gage blocks.

Inspection of large or heavy sharpened items: circular saw blades, band saw teeth, planer/industrial knives and slitter blades — checking tooth height and set, side clearance, runout, blade flatness and straightness; heavy, awkward handling in a saw-service shop.

High-mix one-off work: a worn, unusual or customer-supplied item (custom form cutter, broach, obsolete blade, damaged tool) with no drawing or fixture, inspected by comparison to a sample, by fit with a mating part, or checked in situ at a customer's plant on a mobile sharpening call.

tasks.label: Perform basic maintenance, such as cleaning and lubricating machine parts.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: End-of-shift cleaning of the tool/cutter or surface grinder itself: clearing grinding swarf, sludge and abrasive dust from the table, magnetic chuck, wheel guard and inside the machine enclosure; blowing off with an air gun and wiping surfaces and way covers with rags in a tool room or job-shop grinding department.

Routine lubrication per the machine's lube chart: oiling slideways and ballscrews, pumping grease into fittings on the wheelhead, table drive and dresser, checking sight glasses and topping up oil reservoirs on grinders of several makes and ages in the shop.

Grinding-fluid service: checking coolant level and concentration, topping off the sump, keeping ferrous swarf and fines out of the fluid (filter media / magnetic separator), skimming tramp oil, and periodic sump attention on the grinder.
Housekeeping around the machines: sweeping, vacuuming or scrubbing abrasive and metal dust, chips and coolant drips off the shop floor and aisles near the grinders at shift change.

Periodic deeper service: removing guards and covers to clean way wipers, coolant nozzles and the wheel dresser, cleaning or changing dust-collector and air filters, emptying swarf/sludge bins, and cleaning belts and drive components.

tasks.label: Remove finished workpieces from machines and place them in boxes or on racks, setting aside pieces that are defective.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume production grinding plant (centerless, cylindrical, rotary surface grinders) running batches of small precision metal parts (pins, bushings, inserts, blanks). Operator opens the machine, takes finished parts off the chuck/fixture or output chute, blows off coolant/chips, spot-gauges or eyeballs them, packs them into layered trays, boxes or totes, and drops chipped, burned or out-of-tolerance pieces into a reject bin. Repetitive, same part family for a whole shift.

Cutting-tool manufacturing or regrind shop with CNC tool & cutter grinders (end mills, drills, taps, reamers, carbide inserts). Worker removes the finished tool from the collet or pallet, inspects cutting edges under magnification / checks measured report, places tools in labeled boxes, plastic tubes or carrier pallets and racks by customer job, and sets aside tools with chipped edges, grinding burn or geometry out of spec.

Saw sharpening service shop: carbide-tipped circular saw blades and band saws sharpened on dedicated CNC sharpening machines. Worker unloads the blade from the machine spindle/clamp, hangs it on a rack or returns it to the customer's crate/box, and sets aside blades with cracked plates, missing or fractured tips that cannot be reused.

General high-mix sharpening/filing shop or service counter: one-off customer items each day — kitchen and industrial knives, scissors, planer/jointer knives, chisels, mower blades, drill bits, hand tools. Machines are hand-loaded and hand-unloaded; the finished piece is wiped, checked by feel and eye, put into the customer's bag/box or hung on the pick-up rack, and items too worn, warped or damaged to sharpen are set aside for return.

Toolroom / job shop precision grinding of dies, punches, gauges and mold components on surface and cylindrical grinders. Low volume, high mix, tight tolerances. Worker releases the magnetic chuck or centers, lifts the finished workpiece out, deburrs and wipes it, sets it on a rack, cart or in a padded/oiled box for the next operation, and quarantines pieces that failed the final inspection.

Large/heavy finished items — long guillotine and industrial slitting knives, large planer blades, big saw blades, large tooling — removed from the grinder with hoist or two-person handling, placed on pallets, A-frames or heavy racks, with damaged or scrapped pieces set aside separately.

tasks.label: Dress grinding wheels, according to specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Cutting-tool production/regrind shop: conditioning and dressing resin- or vitrified-bonded CBN/diamond wheel packs on a CNC tool-and-cutter grinder (e.g., 5-axis machine) between grinding cycles — sticking to remove glazing/loading and truing the pack so tool geometry stays within microns of print.

Precision form/profile dressing on a CNC cylindrical, surface, or gear grinder: putting a specified radius, angle, or gear-worm profile into the wheel with a single-point diamond, CNC form roll, or diamond dressing disc, then checking the resulting form on a test part and compensating.

Toolroom/job shop: routine truing and dressing of a conventional vitrified wheel on a manual or semi-automatic surface or cylindrical grinder — mounting the diamond dresser on the chuck/table, taking dressing passes to square and open the wheel face, and resetting the wheel-height offset.

Sharpening service shop (saw blades, knives, milling cutters, drills): conditioning wheels on semi-automatic sharpening machines between varied jobs — applying a dressing stick or mounted dresser to CBN/diamond wheels whose profile must be restored before the next blade type is run.

Off-hand/pedestal or bench grinder in the shop: hand-dressing a glazed or out-of-round aluminum-oxide wheel with a star or diamond dresser on a tool rest to restore a square, free-cutting face, judged by eye, sound, and spark.

Field or mobile service (customer plant, sawmill filing room, maintenance shop): truing/dressing a newly mounted or worn wheel on whatever grinder is installed, with non-standard machines, no dedicated dressing attachment, and dust/coolant conditions taken as found.

tasks.label: Remove and replace worn or broken machine parts, using hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Sharpening shop / tool room: a grinding wheel (or wheel pack, abrasive belt, sanding disc) on a tool & cutter grinder, saw sharpener or pedestal/belt grinder is worn out. Worker locks out the machine, unbolts the guard with a spanner/hex key, backs off the flange nut, dismounts the worn wheel, ring-tests and fits the replacement with blotters and flanges, torques it, refits the guard, then trues/dresses and test-runs it.

Shop: worn workholding and fluid-delivery items on the grinder are swapped with hand tools — collets, chuck/base jaws, wheel adapters and hubs, worn coolant nozzles/distributor blocks, tool-holder bushings. Fasteners are accessible, parts are catalogued standard items, and fit must be clean and repeatable.

Shop: worn mechanical components inside the machine are replaced — drive/timing belts, spindle or slide bearings, cam followers and index pawls, gibs, wipers, worn workrest blades and guides. Requires removing covers and guards, pullers and torque wrenches, cleaning/anti-seize, then re-shimming and realigning to restore accuracy.

Shop, mid-job breakdown: something has broken (cracked bracket, sheared cap screw, snapped spring, damaged limit switch or wiring, smashed guard). Worker diagnoses the failure, disassembles only as far as needed in a cluttered machine interior, extracts the broken fastener/part, fits a replacement (sometimes improvised or fabricated), and verifies the machine grinds to spec before resuming.

Sawmill filing room / large-machine setting: replace worn saw guides, guide pads and inserts, band-wheel wear components, tensioning and clamp parts on bandmills, gang saws or chipper equipment — heavy parts, awkward overhead or in-frame access, wet and chip-laden conditions, working in place on the machine.

Field / mobile service: at a customer's premises or from a sharpening van — a landscaper's yard, food plant, print shop or jobsite — replace worn parts on the customer's sharpening or cutting equipment in whatever space and lighting is found, with only the tools carried on the truck.

tasks.label: Fit parts together in pre-assembly to ensure that dimensions are accurate.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Toolroom / production machine shop bench: after grinding a pin, punch, plug gauge or bushing to size, the grinder trial-fits it into its mating bore, retainer or die button to confirm the slip or press fit — feeling for shake or tightness — and returns it to the grinder for a few tenths if it will not enter or is loose. Small parts (<5 kg), clearances of a few hundredths of a millimeter, repeated over a lot of like parts.

Cutting-tool / blade sharpening shop: fitting a resharpened blade, knife or indexable insert back into its holder — a planer or chipper head, slitter shaft, cutter-body pocket, or a saw blade onto its arbor — and checking seating, projection and runout before the tool assembly goes back to the customer or into the machine.

Bench or surface-plate pre-assembly of multi-piece ground tooling: stacking ground die shoe plates, sliding guide pins into bushings, seating punches in retainers, then verifying with feeler gauges and an indicator that faces are parallel, square and fully seated. Parts 5–50 kg, some handled with a jib hoist.

Die/mold shut-off spotting and hand-fitting: coat mating ground faces with layout blue, close the halves or seat an insert in its pocket, read the contact pattern, stone or grind the high spots, and repeat until contact is uniform — an iterative judgment-driven fit on large, one-off tooling.

In-machine / in-assembly fit-up: carrying a reground component (machine slide gib, spindle sleeve, large fixture element, sharpened blade bar) to the machine or assembly it belongs to and fitting it in place to verify clearance, often in a cramped position, using shims, taps and a pry bar, with the surrounding machine as found.

tasks.label: Inspect dies to detect defects, assess wear, and verify specifications, using micrometers, steel gauge pins, and loupes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Tool room / grinding department of a manufacturing plant: after regrinding, the worker inspects small punch-and-die components and die inserts at a bench — micrometer over OD and land widths, steel gauge pins in bores, 10x loupe over cutting edges for chips, burrs and burn — and accepts or rejects against the print.

Die shop handling small-bore dies (wire-drawing, extrusion, tablet-press dies): the worker gauges the bore with pin gauges, checks bearing length/angles, and examines the bore and face under a loupe or microscope for ring wear, scoring and cracks before deciding whether the die is re-polished or scrapped.

Die shop or press-shop bench: a large stamping/forming die section or shoe is set on a bench or die cart; the worker checks profile and critical dimensions with micrometers, gauges and templates and scans the working surface with a loupe for galling, chipping, and edge breakdown, writing up findings.

At-press inspection in a stamping/forging plant: the die stays installed in the press or is opened in place; the worker reaches into a cramped, oily, poorly lit die space with a light and loupe, checks clearances and wear with feeler gauges and pins, and reports whether the die must be pulled.

Job-shop / commercial sharpening service receiving-inspection: a mixed batch of used, unfamiliar customer dies and tooling arrives with no CAD or measuring program; the worker measures whatever features matter, assesses wear and damage under a loupe, and judges salvageability and regrind stock to quote the job.

tasks.label: Compute numbers, widths, and angles of cutting tools, micrometers, scales, and gauges, and adjust tools to produce specified cuts.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Job shop / regrind service: worker takes a dull HSS or carbide end mill, drill or reamer, determines OD, flute count and index, relief and rake angles from the print or the worn tool, checks size with a micrometer and angle gauges, then sets the tool-and-cutter grinder (wheelhead angle, tooth rest, infeed) to restore the specified cutting geometry. Mixed one-offs and small lots.

Cutting-tool production plant or large corporate toolroom: operator running CNC tool grinders measures ground tools on an optical/laser measuring machine, computes diameter, land width, helix and clearance-angle deviations caused by wheel wear, and enters compensation offsets in the grinding program to hold tolerances of a few microns across a batch.

Saw sharpening shop or sawmill filing room: worker computes hook, top-clearance and side-clearance angles, tooth pitch and gullet dimensions for carbide-tipped circular blades or band saws, sets the sharpener's angle stops / CNC tooth-geometry parameters and feed pawl, and gauges the resulting teeth before running the blade.

Industrial machine-knife and blade sharpening (meat and food processing, paper converting, planer and slitter knives): worker computes the bevel angle and land width for the blade type, sets the grinder table/wheel angle and depth of cut, and verifies edge geometry with angle gauges and a micrometer.

Precision toolroom grinding of gauges, dies, form tools and inserts to size: worker reads micrometers, indicators and gauge blocks, computes remaining stock and wheel-wear allowance, and adjusts downfeed/crossfeed and dress compensation on a surface or profile grinder to hold tenths on the specified cut.

Mobile / on-site sharpening service: worker travels to a restaurant, butcher shop or customer plant with portable belt and wheel equipment, judges the required bevel angle for each knife or blade, sets the guide angle, and sharpens on the customer's premises with variable space, power and lighting.

tasks.label: Turn valves to direct flow of coolant against cutting wheels and workpieces during grinding.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: CNC tool-and-cutter grinder (e.g., resharpening end mills/drills) in a production tool-grinding or regrind shop: during setup and cycle start the operator opens the coolant valves for the active nozzle bank, checks that each jet strikes the correct wheel in the wheel pack and the tool, and sets flow/pressure; coolant runs through the automatic cycle.

Manual or semi-automatic surface / cylindrical / cutter grinder in a job-shop toolroom: operator opens the petcock or ball valve on the coolant line, bends the loc-line nozzle to aim at the wheel-work contact, throttles the flow so it wets the zone without flooding the operator or the gage, and shuts it off before dressing, gaging, or unloading.

Saw/blade sharpening shop or sawmill filing room: carbide circular-saw, band-saw, or industrial knife sharpening machines; operator turns coolant on for each blade, redirects the nozzle for different tooth geometries or blade diameters, and maintains flow through long automatic grinding runs.

Mid-cycle intervention on any grinder: worker sees sparking, burn/discoloration, wheel loading, or splashing, and opens the valve wider, throttles it back, or redirects the nozzle during the grind; also cuts coolant momentarily to inspect or measure a hot workpiece.

Small-shop, portable, or on-site sharpening (mobile knife/saw sharpening truck, ag or mower blade grinding in a barn or customer's shop): water or coolant delivered by a hand valve, gravity drip, or squeeze bottle onto a bench or portable grinder, with no fixed layout and varying fixtures.

Field/on-site work: repairing or rebuilding cutting edges and cracked components at a customer site or on installed equipment (sawmill, plant floor, jobsite) with portable welding/brazing gear and hand-held or portable grinders, in whatever access and lighting exist.

General/retail sharpening shop: bent flat-bar items such as lawn-mower blades, brush-cutter blades and hedge-trimmer bars are straightened on a small hydraulic/arbor press or over an anvil before grinding, to plain flatness checked by eye and straightedge.

General/retail sharpening shop: one-off, oddly shaped items brought in dented or bent (scissors and shear blades, dented cutter bodies, clipper heads, small castings and tool bodies) that must be judged individually and worked with hammer, dolly and vise on the bench, each different from the last.

tasks.label: Place workpieces in electroplating solutions or apply pigments to surfaces of workpieces to highlight ridges and grooves.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Tool room / job shop bench: grinder brushes or daubs layout fluid (e.g., Dykem Steel Blue) onto the relief, flute or land of a one-off or small-lot cutting tool, reamer, form die or gauge held in the hand or a vise, covering only the area of interest so ridges, grooves and scribed lines stand out before and during grinding; part is picked up, coated, set to dry, then returned to the grinder.

Batch spray application of layout/marking pigment: a lot of similar tool blanks, saw plates, hobs or die sections is hung or laid out in the shop's spray/finishing booth and given an even thin pigment coat (aerosol or spray gun), then dried before grinding or scribing.

Plating/finishing area of the shop: sharpened tools or small parts are hung on racks or loaded in barrels and immersed in a sequence of electroplating / black-oxide / copper-flash and rinse tanks with controlled dwell times, then dried and unloaded.

Large workpiece on shop floor or bench: marking blue / Prussian blue spread thinly over a large die face, gear teeth, broach or machine way to reveal high spots and contact pattern, sometimes on a piece too large to move easily, followed by mating or inspection.

Inspection bench: dye penetrant or contrast pigment sprayed/dipped onto a reground tool, blade or carbide-tipped cutter, dwelled, excess removed and developer applied so cracks, grinding marks and grooves are highlighted for inspection.

tasks.label: Duplicate workpiece contours, using tracer attachments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Cutting-tool plant / tool-grinding department: reproducing a form or profile (step drill, form cutter, profile end mill, radius or corner geometry) on cylindrical tool blanks so each piece matches a master profile or template. Batches of standard blanks held in collets/chucks; operator sets the template or profile, runs the copy cycle, gauges the profile and adjusts wheel/stylus offsets.

Job shop: duplicating a contour on a shaft, roll, spindle or similar turned part using a hydraulic/mechanical tracer (duplicating) attachment on a lathe or cylindrical grinder from a template or master part; short runs, part chucked between centers, operator dials in the trace, checks with gauges and repeats for the batch.

Tool-and-die shop: profile/form grinding a die insert, punch, or form tool to a template or magnified layout on an optical profile grinder or pantograph-type contour grinder; one or a few pieces, workpiece on a magnetic chuck or precision pallet, frequent stop-and-check against the template with comparators.

Production plant, repetitive contour copying: running an established duplicating job (cam/lobe profiles, blade or airfoil contours, ratchet/serration forms) where the master contour is already proven; the worker loads pieces, runs cycles, dresses the wheel, gauges to keep the copied contour in tolerance across a shift.

Tool room one-off: customer brings a worn, broken or obsolete part with no drawing; the worker mounts the sample as the master, sets up the tracer, produces a duplicate contour on a blank, then hand-fits, stones and iterates against the sample until it matches and functions.

tasks.label: Generate prepress proofs in digital or other format to approximate the appearance of the final printed piece.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Commercial print/prepress department: after files are normalized and imposed, the technician generates a soft proof (PDF/JPEG or virtual color proof) from the workflow and posts it to an online approval portal or emails it to the client/CSR for content, layout and color review. No physical artifact is produced.

Print shop proofing room: technician RIPs a color-critical job (commercial or packaging) to a calibrated large-format inkjet contract proofer with an ISO 12647-7 control strip, prints on proofing stock, verifies the wedge with a spectrophotometer, applies the verification label/date, and places the proof with the job ticket for the press or for shipment to the client.

Full-size imposition/plotter proof for a sheetfed or web job: technician outputs the imposed signature(s) on a wide-format plotter with registration, fold and trim marks, checks pagination and marks against the job ticket, and delivers the proof to the pressroom for makeready/press check.

Packaging/label converter: technician prints a proof of the carton artwork on proofing substrate, cuts and creases it on a digital sample-making table to the dieline, then folds and glues it into a 3D structural mockup for client sign-off.

Small in-plant, quick-print or label shop: technician outputs a quick proof of a business card, form or flyer on the digital press or office-grade color device, checks it against the job envelope/ticket, and leaves it at the counter or with the job for the customer or CSR to review.

instances.label: Commercial sheetfed/web print plant plateroom: technician releases an imposed job to the thermal platesetter, plates are imaged, processed (or run process-free), punched/bent, then verified as the correct job/color/press and staged on the right plate trolley or rack for the pressroom. Standard plate sizes, climate-controlled plateroom, many such jobs per shift.

Keeping the platesetter supplied: fetching plate cartons or pallets from stock, removing shrinkwrap/protective boards, separating interleaf slip sheets, and loading plates into the single/multi-cassette autoloader or onto the pallet loader without scratching or fingerprinting the emulsion.

Plate quality control and calibration: imaging a control target/UGRA strip, measuring dot area on the plate with a plate reader, comparing to shop aim curves, updating linearization/tone-reproduction curves in the workflow, checking punch register and plate-to-plate consistency, and signing off the device as in tolerance.

Scheduled preventive maintenance and consumables: cleaning processor rollers and brushes, changing developer/finisher chemistry and filters, cleaning the gum section, wiping the imaging drum, vacuuming laser optics and dust filters, clearing the punch die area, and disposing of spent chemistry.

Fault clearing and minor repair: a plate misfeeds or jams in the loader, imaging drum, bender or processor; the technician opens the machine, removes the damaged plate, re-registers the punch or replaces a worn belt/roller/vacuum cup, reruns the plate, and escalates to a service engineer if needed.

tasks.label: Maintain, adjust, and clean equipment, and perform minor repairs.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine upkeep round on a computer-to-plate platesetter/imagesetter in a commercial printing plant's prepress/plate room: vacuum plate dust and coating debris from the plate path, wipe the imaging drum, clamps and transport rollers with lint-free cloth and cleaner, clean the optics window, clean and lubricate the punch and registration pins, check/replace air and dust filters, wipe the machine exterior and control panel, then image a test plate to confirm the machine is clean and in register.

Plate/film processor upkeep: check developer level, temperature and conductivity, top up or change chemistry, drain and flush the tank, pull the roller rack and scrub rollers and brushes free of gum and coating sludge, clean the gum and dryer sections, replace filters, refill and dispose of spent chemistry per plant procedure, then run a control plate/strip to verify.

Daily/weekly upkeep of digital proofing devices and wide-format or desktop inkjet output units: run nozzle checks, run and verify head-cleaning cycles, swab the printhead and capping/wiper station, replace ink cartridges and the waste-ink tank, clear paper jams and misfeeds from the paper path, clean feed and pinch rollers, load a new media roll, and print and measure a verification target.

Diagnose-and-fix minor faults on prepress equipment: an error code, streaking or scumming plates, a misregistering punch, a jammed transport or a stalled loader; remove covers, trace the cause, adjust or replace a small part (sensor, belt, spring, fuse, worn roller), reassemble, recalibrate with test targets/densitometer, verify, and log the repair or escalate to the service vendor.

Scheduled wear-part or consumable swap at a documented service interval on a known machine: pull and replace a worn feed roller, squeegee/cleaning blade, exposure lamp, or filter cartridge in the location the service manual specifies, seat and secure it, and run a confirming cycle.

Housekeeping of the plate room floor and work area around the equipment: sweep and mop plate dust, paper trim, slip-sheet scrap and chemistry drips from the floor around the platesetter and processor so debris does not get into the machines.

tasks.label: Operate presses to print proofs of plates, monitoring printing quality to ensure that it is adequate.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Commercial sheetfed offset shop: prepress tech takes freshly imaged plates to the press, hangs/loads them, runs the press up, pulls proof sheets, reads the color bar with a spectrodensitometer, compares register, density and dot gain against the contract proof, adjusts ink keys/register until an acceptable OK sheet is produced.

Small commercial or in-plant shop, short-run work: tech who both plates and runs the press pulls a quick proof of a newly imaged plate (small offset press/duplicator) on the job stock, checks image position, register, type legibility and scumming/toning, corrects and re-pulls before the run.

Web offset newspaper/publication/business-forms plant: plates hung in the printing towers, press run up to speed, tech/operator checks running-web color bars, side-lay and circumferential register and ink density on the first copies, adjusts to the OK copy before the run is counted.

Flexo packaging/label prepress room: plates mounted on sleeves or cylinders, then a paste-ink or wet proof pulled on a mounter-proofer or dedicated flexo proof press with production ink, anilox and substrate; tech inspects register, dot reproduction, text and impression, remounts or re-images if inadequate.

Prepress department contract proofing: tech outputs a color-managed halftone/contract proof of the plate-ready imposition on an inkjet proofing device with a control wedge, then measures the wedge and verifies conformance (e.g., ISO 12647-7 tolerances) before plates are released or as the reference for the press proof.

Specialty/legacy proofing: letterpress or engraving proof press, gravure or screen test print — tech mixes and hand-rolls ink, positions the plate/screen and substrate, pulls a one-off proof on an old hand-fed proof press, and judges it by eye under a light booth.

instances.label: Commercial sheetfed offset plant prepress: technician takes each imaged and processed aluminum plate off the CTP processor, examines it on the light table for scratches, dirt, incomplete imaging or scumming, then reads the exposed control wedge with a plate scope/microscope to verify dot area at highlight, midtone and shadow patches against the target curve, and confirms the plate matches the job proof and imposition before release to press.

Newspaper or commercial web plant: plates flow at high volume from CTP and processor onto a punch/bend and conveyor line; the technician checks imaging quality plate by plate, measures the wedge at intervals, verifies each plate's page/colour identity, and pulls plates with imaging or development flaws for remake, under deadline pressure.

Flexo/packaging plate room (trade shop or converter in-house): verifying that finished photopolymer plates conform to the master file/proof - correct plate for the job and colour, all image elements present, no washout damage, torn edges or missing type - before the plates go to mounting and press.

Flexo/packaging plate room: microscope/plate-scope measurement of dot size, dot shape and minimum holding dot (1-2% highlights) plus dot centre/screen-ruling checks on finished photopolymer plates, compared against the platemaking spec and the previous plate set.

Small commercial or quick-print shop: a handful of polyester or thermal aluminum plates per job, examined quickly under a light table with a loupe against the client proof for content, register marks and imaging completeness, with an occasional plate-reader check of dot percentage; no plate conveyor or bending line.

Legacy/specialty work: comparing a newly made, duplicated or repaired plate against a retained master plate or master film on a light box - overlaying and checking register marks, trim marks and image content - in specialty shops (screen stencils, letterpress/engraving, large-format) where plate types and formats vary job to job.

tasks.label: Examine unexposed photographic plates to detect flaws or foreign particles prior to printing.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Commercial sheetfed offset prepress department: technician opens a pallet/box of unexposed thermal or violet aluminum plates, lifts each plate (or spot-checks the top of the stack), and examines the coated face and edges under room light for scratches, dents, coating streaks and dust or foreign particles before loading the platesetter cassette; flawed plates are set aside and the vendor lot is flagged.

High-volume newspaper/web offset plant: plates are drawn from cassettes by a CTP autoloader; the technician inspects incoming plate stock and pulled samples of unexposed plates for coating flaws, edge damage and airborne particles/paper dust that cause pinholes, deciding whether a lot or pallet is usable before it is fed to the imaging line.

Flexo/packaging prepress: technician examines unexposed photopolymer plate sheets (and the protective slip film) for embedded specks, gels, nicks, dirt and coating/thickness irregularities on a light table or bench before imaging and exposure.

Small commercial, quick-print or in-plant shop: a handful of plates per job, mixed sizes and vendors, partly used boxes stored open on a shelf; the operator takes each plate out, glances over it under ambient shop lighting for dust, fingerprints, scratches or coating faults, and rejects or wipes it before hand-feeding the platesetter.

Darkroom/safelight work: examining unexposed graphic-arts film or photosensitive plates for fog, base scratches, emulsion defects and foreign particles under safelight conditions before exposure/imaging.

Lithographic printing plates are coated aluminum sheet, and the flaw classes the prepress worker looks for (scratches, dents, inclusions, coating streaks, dirt) are exactly the defect classes these brightfield/darkfield line scanners are built to detect, at comparable or finer resolution, with material conveyed past fixed sensors.

tasks.label: Start presses and pull proofs to check for ink coverage and density, alignment, and registration.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Commercial or packaging print plant: operator starts a 4–8 colour sheetfed offset press (Heidelberg Speedmaster / Koenig & Bauer Rapida / Komori Lithrone class) after plate change, runs sheets up to colour, pulls press sheets to check solid ink density, dot gain, colour-to-colour registration and image position, and adjusts ink keys and register until the sheet matches the OK sheet. Press is a recent model with inline measuring bar and automated makeready.

Mid-size sheetfed offset shop with an older or mid-generation press that has no inline measuring bar: operator starts the press, physically pulls sheets from the delivery, carries them to a scanning spectrophotometer console (e.g. Komori PDC-SX / Prinect Axis Control) or reads them with a handheld densitometer and loupe, then adjusts ink keys, circumferential/lateral register and sets the sheet aside as the approved proof.

Digital production press (toner or cut-sheet/continuous-feed inkjet: Xerox Iridesse/Versant, Canon varioPRINT iX, Ricoh, HP Indigo) in a commercial or in-plant print shop: operator starts the press, runs a test/calibration print, checks colour density and uniformity, front-to-back and image-to-media alignment/registration and streaking, then runs calibration/alignment routines before releasing the job.

Web-fed packaging, label or publication press (CI flexo, narrow-web flexo, rotogravure, web offset): operator threads substrate, brings the press up to speed, uses register marks and a colour bar under a strobe/inspection camera to check colour-to-colour and print-to-die registration, impression pressure and ink density on the running web, and trims the first good copy as the proof.

Small commercial or in-plant shop running a legacy one- or two-colour offset duplicator, envelope or business-forms press: operator starts the press manually, pulls sheets by hand, eyeballs coverage, ink density and image position against a job ticket or ruler, tweaks ink fountain keys and image position, often on short runs of a few hundred sheets.

Specialty press work — textile/graphic screen printing carousel, pad printing or letterpress/foiling: operator loads screens or plates, runs a test print on scrap stock, inspects opacity/coverage, colour and multi-colour registration by eye, then micro-adjusts screens, off-contact or plate position and pulls another test print until approved.

instances.label: Mainstream commercial sheetfed offset shop: press (e.g., Speedmaster/Komori/RMGT) with motorized ink keys at a remote console but no inline spectrophotometer. During makeready and the run the operator pulls sheets, reads a densitometer or judges by eye against the OK sheet, and opens/closes individual ink-zone keys and ink fountain roller/ductor speed to bring each zone to target density.

Industrialized sheetfed shop whose press carries inline or scanning closed-loop color measurement; ink-key openings and fountain speed are driven from measured densities/Lab values while the operator monitors, sets targets, and intervenes on exceptions (spot colors, ghosting, ink/water balance).

Web offset plant (newspaper, commercial heatset, business forms): long runs on a multi-unit web press with a remote inking desk; operator trims ink-zone keys and fountain feed rates per unit/side as density drifts with speed, paper roll changes, and dampening.

Flexographic or gravure packaging/label plant: ink is fed to the chamber/fountain by pumps; operator adjusts pump flow rate, chamber pressure and ink feed (plus solvent/water addition affecting flow) to hold ink film and density on target through the run.

Small commercial shop, in-plant, or quick-print operation with an older or small-format press (duplicator, Heidelberg GTO, small letterpress or narrow-web unit) whose ink fountain keys are hand-turned thumbscrews and whose fountain roller/ductor sweep is a manual dial; operator adjusts by eye at the machine.

tasks.label: Verify that paper and ink meet the specifications for a given job.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Commercial sheetfed offset shop: before makeready the operator takes the job ticket to the skid of stock at the press (or in the paper store), reads the pallet/wrapper label to confirm brand, grade, basis weight, sheet size, grain and count, riffles and eyeballs sheets for curl, damage or moisture problems, and confirms the ink cans/pails on the cart carry the correct process and PMS numbers and ink chemistry (conventional vs UV) for the job.

On-press verification during makeready and run in an offset pressroom: pull a press sheet, read the color bar with a densitometer/spectrophotometer against the job's density/Lab targets (ISO 12647/G7) or compare spot colors to the approved proof or drawdown, and confirm the inks in the fountains are delivering to the job specification.

Narrow-web flexo label / flexible-packaging press: verify the substrate roll on the unwind matches the job (material, width, caliper, coating/treatment) from the roll tag, and verify the inks — correct PMS/base inks in the pans, viscosity within the job's cup-second/cP window, and printed color within tolerance of the approved sample.

Digital toner/inkjet production press (short-run/in-plant): confirm the stock loaded in the tray or feeder is the media the job specifies and is within the press's certified weight/coating limits, and verify the machine's colorant output conforms — run a calibration/verification target and check it against the job's color target before releasing the run.

Specialty work (gravure, screen, UV/metallic, large-format): verify an unusual substrate (board, film, synthetic, vinyl) against the supplier certificate and job spec, and verify specialty ink against an approved customer sample — hand drawdown or proof press pull, tack/viscosity check, cure or adhesion test — before the job is allowed to run.

tasks.label: Collect and inspect random samples during print runs to identify any necessary adjustments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Commercial sheetfed offset shop: on a 4–8 color press running 5,000–50,000 sheets, the operator pulls a sheet from the delivery at intervals, scans the color bar with a spectro/densitometer at the console, checks register with a loupe and looks over the sheet under D50 light for hickeys, scumming, streaks and setoff, then corrects ink keys, dampening and register.

Digital production press (toner or sheetfed/continuous-feed inkjet) in a commercial or in-plant shop: during a run the operator pulls prints, compares them to the approved proof/target, looks for color drift, banding, streaks, missing jets, and image placement/duplex registration, and triggers calibration or head/registration adjustments.

Narrow-web flexo label/packaging press: operator takes a label or web sample at the rewinder or inspection station, checks it on a light table and with a loupe for print-to-die register, streaks, voids and dirty print, measures spot colors to a ΔE tolerance, verifies barcode readability, and adjusts impression, register, ink viscosity or anilox settings.

Web offset commercial/newspaper press: operator takes a copy off the folder delivery or conveyor every so often, checks color-to-color and front-to-back register, cut-off, ink density and ink/water balance, and fold/ribbon position, then makes corrections remotely from the press console while the web keeps running.

Wide-web flexo/gravure packaging or corrugated printing: a sample is cut from the running web or a printed board is taken from the stacker, compared against the approved retained sample for color, doctor-blade streaks, pinholes and register, measured with a handheld spectrophotometer, and settings (impression, viscosity, register, blade) are adjusted.

Small commercial/in-plant shop with older or small-format equipment and very short runs: operator eyeballs pulled samples against an approved proof under a desk lamp, without measuring instruments, judging color, register and defects by eye and adjusting by feel.

tasks.label: Feed paper through press cylinders and adjust feed and tension controls.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Medium/large-format sheetfed offset press in a commercial or folding-carton plant: pallets of stock staged at the feeder, feeder head/suckers/blast-and-suction air/sheet separators and side lay set for the stock, sheets run through the cylinders at 15,000-21,000 sph, piles changed during the run, doubles and misfeeds corrected.

Web offset press (coldset newspaper or heatset commercial): ~1-tonne paper reels loaded into reelstands, new reel spliced/pasted to the running web, web threaded through printing units, dryer/chill rolls and folder at start-up or after a break, infeed/outfeed draw rolls and tension zones set and trimmed during the run.

Roll-fed flexo/gravure packaging or narrow-web label press: roll mounted on the unwind, web threaded through print stations, dryers and die station, unwind/inter-station/rewind tension set for paper, board, label stock or film, splices made at roll change.

Digital production press (cut-sheet toner/inkjet, or roll-fed inkjet) in a commercial shop or in-plant: stock loaded into trays or high-capacity feeder, media profile selected and feed parameters (air/vacuum, tray guides, registration) set for varied short-run stocks, misfeeds cleared.

Small shop with a small-format or older press (single/two-colour duplicator, hand-fed platen/letterpress, envelope or heavy-board work): pile jogged and loaded by hand, sucker height and separators fiddled with sheet by sheet, awkward or static-prone stock coaxed through, frequent hand intervention.

tasks.label: Monitor automated press operation systems and respond to fault, error, or alert messages.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-run print-quality alert on a production press in a commercial pressroom: the console or inline measurement system flags color density/ΔE drift, register deviation, a detected sheet defect, or a nozzle-out. The operator interprets the alert, corrects ink zones/register/head compensation, verifies with a sheet or scan, and lets the run continue.

Material- or consumable-supply alert on an automated web or sheetfed line: reel/roll running low, ink low in the fountain or chamber, plate or coating-plate change due, blanket wash-up interval reached. The operator responds by splicing the new reel, refilling/cleaning the ink system, changing plates, or launching the wash program, then resumes production.

Jam, misfeed, or web-break fault: a digital production press signals a paper-path jam, a sheetfed press stops on double/late sheets or a delivery pile jam, or a web press signals a web break. The operator opens covers/guards, locates and pulls out damaged substrate, re-threads or re-webs, fans the pile, resets the fault, and restarts.

Machine/system fault code requiring on-press diagnosis and hands-on remedy in the pressroom: dirty or misaligned sensor, dryer/UV or chill-roll alarm, ink pump or circulation fault, vacuum/air fault, damaged blanket or plate, drive interlock. The operator walks the press, diagnoses the cause, fixes or replaces the part, clears the alarm, and verifies output.

Digital production press consumable/service alert: toner or ink container empty, waste toner bottle full, developer/fuser or printhead-wiper service prompt, calibration/registration prompt after the swap. The operator swaps the physical module, disposes of waste, and runs the calibration routine before resuming the queue.

Small commercial or in-plant shop with older short-run offset, small-format digital, or wide-format devices lacking inline closed-loop control; one operator watches several machines. Alerts (media feed error, ink/water balance, printhead warning, sheet count mismatch) are answered by pulling and eyeballing sheets, hand-measuring, and tweaking the machine by feel.

instances.label: Large-format sheetfed offset press (B1/Rapida/Speedmaster XL class) in a folding-carton or packaging plant, long runs: pallets of board/paper are brought to the feeder, the pile is set on the feeder table (often with non-stop rack), and feeder head, side lays, sucker/blower and pile height are set for the sheet size and caliper.

Medium- or small-format sheetfed offset press in a general commercial or quick-print/in-plant shop: frequent short runs with mixed stocks (text, cover, carbonless, envelopes), reams or part-pallets hand-loaded into the feeder, side guides, sucker feet, feed table and pile height adjusted for each new sheet size.

Roll-fed web offset press (newspaper, heatset commercial, business forms): 500-1,500 kg paper reels retrieved from the reel store, unwrapped and splice-prepared, mounted on the reelstand/unwind chucks, centered for roll width and webbed up or set for the autopaster.

Flexographic or gravure packaging web press (CI flexo, wide-web film/board, label converting): substrate roll lifted onto the unwind shaft/chucks, core and web width aligned, web guides and edge sensors set for the roll width, spliced to the running web.

Production digital cut-sheet press (toner/inkjet, e.g. iGen/Indigo/AccurioPress class) in a digital print or in-plant shop: reams or stacks loaded into feed trays/high-capacity feeder modules, tray guides set and paper size/weight profile selected for each stock change; many small loads per shift.

tasks.label: Secure printing plates to printing units and adjust tolerances.

instances.label: Commercial/packaging sheetfed offset pressroom (4-10 unit B2/B1 press, e.g. Speedmaster XL 106, Rapida 106, Lithrone). At each job change the operator collects register-punched plates from the prepress trolley, feeds/hangs them in the plate cylinder clamps of each unit, confirms correct plate-to-unit assignment, then trues up circumferential, lateral and diagonal (cocking) register and checks plate-to-blanket packing before the run.

Web offset tower press (newspaper, heatset commercial, business forms). Operator climbs the tower decks, hooks pre-bent plates onto the plate cylinder lock-up bars of multiple couples, tensions them, and sets circumferential/side register and compensator settings; plates change many times per production day.

Wide-web CI flexo packaging plant. Photopolymer plates are taped to sticky-back on sleeves/cylinders offline in the plate room using a mounter-proofer to hit registration marks within a few tens of microns; sleeves are then slid onto the mandrels of the print decks and impression/register set at the press.

Narrow-web label/tag flexo press (Mark Andy, Nilpeter, Bobst M-series). Small plates hand-taped to light plate cylinders or sleeves on a bench mounter, cylinders dropped into the print stations, then register and impression dialed in on press at low speed against a running web.

Short-run/small-format offset: quick-print, in-plant or mailing shop with a duplicator or B3 press (Ryobi/RMGT 9-series, AB Dick, SM 52). Operator clamps a polyester or aluminum plate by hand into head and tail clamps, tightens/tensions it, and adjusts register screws and image position by trial sheets.

Gravure and specialty processes (rotogravure cylinders, screen frames, letterpress/flexo dies). Heavy engraved cylinders are hoisted or trolleyed into the printing unit bearings, or screens/plates clamped into frames, then pre-register and impression set before the run.

tasks.label: Clean ink fountains, plates, or printing unit cylinders when press runs are completed.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Commercial sheetfed offset shop, modern multi-color press (e.g., Speedmaster/Komori Lithrone): at end of a run the operator washes blanket and impression cylinders and the ink roller train, wipes out the ink fountain/duct and fountain roller ends, and pulls the plates for storage or scrap. Press has program-controlled washup devices; residual hand-wiping around the units.

Small commercial/in-plant shop with an older or small-format press or duplicator (1-2 color, no automatic washup): operator scrapes leftover ink out of the fountain with a knife, hand-washes rollers, blanket and impression cylinders with solvent and rags, wipes and gums plates for reuse, in a cluttered but shop-controlled pressroom.

Flexographic label/flexible-packaging press: at job end the operator flushes or empties chambered doctor-blade systems and ink trays, pulls anilox rolls/sleeves and doctor blades, washes plates and sleeves, and cleans ink pumps and hoses — using on-press wash circuits and/or carrying parts to wash-room cabinets.

Heatset commercial web or coldset newspaper press hall: end-of-run cleaning of blanket cylinders across multiple units and towers, cleaning ink fountains/rails and pans, wiping plate cylinders and removing plates; presses typically equipped with automatic blanket/roller cleaning systems plus manual touch-up at height on catwalks.

Rotogravure packaging/publication press: after the run the operator drains and cleans solvent ink pans and circulation systems, cleans doctor blades and chambers, and cleans the engraved gravure cylinders before they are removed and returned to storage; solvent-controlled area with ventilation.

Digital press (electrophotographic or inkjet) operator: end-of-run cleaning of the imaging plate/blanket or printhead faces, wiping transfer/impression cylinders, emptying and cleaning ink/toner waste trays, running the press's cleaning routines in a climate-controlled digital print room.
