tasks.label: Change press plates, blankets, or cylinders, as required.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Commercial/in-plant sheetfed offset shop: between jobs the operator pulls 4–8 exposed plates from the CtP output cart, hangs them on the plate cylinders of a multi-unit press (or feeds them to the press's plate-change device), removes and discards the old plates, and checks register before the makeready sheets run.

Web offset plant (newspaper, insert, book or business-forms web press): operator plates up multiple towers/couples, matching colour and page order, on a tall press with catwalks; plates arrive punched and bent from the platesetter and must be loaded and locked, with old plates pulled and binned, under tight edition deadlines.

Flexographic label/flexible-packaging or corrugated plant: operator mounts photopolymer plates with stickyback tape onto sleeves/print cylinders to register marks, then loads the sleeves/cylinders (and matching anilox) into the print decks and removes the previous job's tooling.

Offset press (sheetfed or web): a worn, smashed or ink-swollen rubber blanket must be replaced — unbolt/loosen the blanket bar reel rods inside the unit, pull the old blanket and packing, insert and align a new blanket, torque to spec, and re-tension after a short run.

Digital press (toner or liquid electrophotographic, e.g. HP Indigo/Xerox iGen-class): operator swaps imaging consumables that stand in for plates/blankets/cylinders — photoconductor foil, transfer blanket, drum or imaging unit — following the press's guided replacement procedure and recalibrating.

Rotogravure packaging or publication press: heavy engraved cylinders (often 100+ kg, shafted or hollow) are moved from the cylinder store by hoist/trolley, loaded into each printing unit with its ink pan, chucked and pre-registered, and the finished job's cylinders removed for cleaning.

tasks.label: Obtain or mix inks and fill ink fountains.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Commercial/packaging sheetfed offset pressroom, makeready and run: operator fetches cans or cartridges of process inks (K/C/M/Y plus varnish) from the ink store, charges the ink fountains/ducts of a 4- to 10-unit press with an ink knife or cartridge, and tops up fountains as ink is consumed during the run.

Sheetfed offset custom spot color: operator obtains a PMS/brand-color formula, weighs base inks on a scale, blends the batch, pulls a drawdown to check the match against the customer standard, corrects, then fills the corresponding ink fountain and keeps it topped up.

Web offset / newspaper or heatset commercial web plant: ink is drawn from drums, totes or bulk tanks; operator connects and monitors the pumping supply to each fountain, swaps drums, and keeps fountains supplied over long continuous runs.

Flexographic or gravure packaging/label plant: operator obtains or mixes solvent-, water- or UV-based inks to a spot formula in the ink kitchen, adjusts viscosity with solvent/additives, and charges ink pans, trays, fountains or chambered doctor-blade circulation systems, replenishing during the run.

Small quick-print, in-plant or specialty shop with legacy small-format equipment (offset duplicator, letterpress, small screen press): operator hand-mixes a small quantity of custom ink on a slab from a formula book or by eye, and scoops it into a small ink fountain with a knife.

Digital press (electrophotographic or production inkjet): operator obtains and loads ink canisters, cartridges or bulk ink containers and toner, connects them to the press ink system, and keeps supplies replenished.

instances.label: Commercial sheetfed offset shop: at shift start and periodically during the run, the operator checks pressroom thermometer/hygrometer readings against spec (roughly 72°F, 45-55% RH), logs them, and adjusts the humidifier/HVAC setpoint or damper, or calls maintenance, when readings drift (dry winter air causing static and misregister, humid summer air causing curl).

Press-side compensation on a sheetfed litho press: temperature/humidity drift shows up as ink/water balance, tack, static or register problems, so the operator adjusts dampening-solution temperature, conductivity/alcohol dosing, ink-unit temperature control, static eliminators and ink keys to bring the sheet back to standard.

Heatset web offset or production inkjet web: operator monitors web temperature, dryer and chill-roll temperatures and paper moisture, and adjusts dryer setpoints, chill-roll temperature or the remoistening unit to keep paper moisture and web behavior within spec as ambient conditions change.

Flexo/gravure packaging plant: operator monitors ink temperature and viscosity, drying-oven temperature and ambient humidity (solvent evaporation, static on film, board warp), and adjusts solvent/water addition, ink chiller and dryer temperature accordingly.

Substrate storage/laydown area: operator verifies that skids or rolls delivered from the warehouse have acclimated to pressroom temperature before unwrapping, checks storage-area temperature/RH, and moves or holds stock (or adjusts store humidification) so paper enters the press at equilibrium moisture.

Small in-plant or short-run digital shop with no dedicated pressroom climate control: operator diagnoses jams, static, curl or condensation as weather-driven, then improvises — repositioning or wheeling in a portable humidifier/dehumidifier, moving stock away from an HVAC vent, closing a dock door, wiping condensation, changing media settings.

instances.label: Saddle-stitching line in a commercial bindery: operator pulls booklets/magazines off the stitcher-trimmer delivery every few minutes and checks for missing or malformed staples, missed or out-of-order signatures, loose/torn pages, ink spots and trim quality; line runs 10,000-25,000 copies/hour.

Perfect-binding (softcover) line: operator pulls a bound book from the binder/three-knife trimmer, checks spine glue coverage and adhesion, cover-to-block match and alignment, hinge score, page order, loose or torn pages, ink spots and trim edges.

Hardcover/case-binding bookline: operator samples cased-in books for case fit and squares, joint/hinge formation, headband and endsheet gluing, spine appearance, jacket placement, plus sewn or glued block integrity including loose or uncut threads.

Unbound work at folders, cutters, gatherers and collators: operator examines folded signatures, gathered book blocks and trimmed flat sheets for wrinkles, off-fold, torn corners, ink spots/hickeys, missing or doubled sheets before the work moves downstream.

Short-run digital finishing shop: operator checks booklets from a bookletmaker or single-clamp perfect binder against the job ticket for correct page sequence, staple/glue quality, torn pages and marking, on jobs of a few hundred copies that change several times a day.

Specialty hand-finishing bench: operator inspects wire-o and spiral-bound books, laminated and mounted pieces, pocket folders, tabbed/index work and pop-up or hand-assembled items for loose pages, skewed punching, lamination bubbles, glue squeeze-out and surface marking; product mix varies job to job.

tasks.label: Monitor machine operations to detect malfunctions or to determine whether adjustments are needed.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Attending a perfect binding line (gatherer, binder, three-knife trimmer) during a production run in a commercial bindery: watching for missed or out-of-sequence signatures, jams in the pockets, glue temperature/bead behavior, book thickness deviations, and judging when the line must be stopped or adjusted.

Attending a high-speed folding machine (buckle/knife folder) in a print finishing plant: watching for double feeds, misfeeds, jams, sheet skew and out-of-tolerance folds while the machine runs, and determining when folding rollers/plates need adjustment.

Attending a saddle stitcher or collating/booklet line: watching pocket feeders for misfeeds and missing signatures, monitoring stitch formation and caliper/thickness rejects, watching the trimmer and delivery for jams, and calling for adjustment when faults recur.

Attending a guillotine cutter or three-knife trimmer: watching cutting cycles for squareness, draw/knife marks, uncut or double-cut product, stack shifting and clamp behavior, judging when the knife is dull or the machine needs adjustment.

Attending a roll-fed laminating, coating or web finishing line: watching web tension and tracking, looking for wrinkles, bubbles, delamination, register drift and splice faults, and deciding when to stop or adjust.

Small in-plant or quick-print shop finishing: tending a tabletop booklet maker, collator, creaser or small binder while doing other work, reacting to jam/misfeed alarms, unusual noise, overheating or counters, and judging whether adjustment is needed.

tasks.label: Lubricate, clean, or make minor repairs to machine parts to keep machines in working condition.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine in-machine cleaning on the bindery floor after a run or at shift end: blowing/vacuuming paper dust, lint and trim chips out of a folder, saddle stitcher, three-knife trimmer or gatherer; wiping ink, wax and adhesive film off rollers, belts, feed wheels, guides and photo-eye sensors with solvent rags; emptying waste. Guards opened, machine locked out, cramped access around in-place mechanisms.

Scheduled lubrication per the machine's PM chart in the plant: oiling chains, cams and slides, greasing zerk fittings on folder shafts and stitcher heads, topping up oil reservoirs and mist lubricators, jogging the machine to reach points behind guards, then wiping excess.

Minor repairs and adjustments prompted by a symptom (misfeeds, double sheets, crooked folds, skipped stitches): diagnosing the cause, then replacing a worn belt, vacuum sucker, spring, wire guide, bearing or dull blade, tightening loose fasteners, and re-aligning guides before test-running the machine.

Servicing the adhesive/coating system of a perfect binder, gluer or laminator: purging and scraping carbonized hot-melt from the glue pot, application rollers and nozzles, clearing spine-prep milling/roughing tooling and dust extraction, then refilling and re-priming the system.

Off-machine deep cleaning of removable components at the parts sink or wash tank: folding rollers, gripper bars, perf/score tooling, chain sections and stitcher parts are pulled off, soaked/degreased, brushed clean of dried adhesive and paper fiber, dried, and returned for refitting.

Job setup on a modern electronically controlled binding line: recalling stored job settings or entering format on the touchscreen, motorized size adjustment, running a test book, checking hole-to-edge register and closure, and releasing the job to run.

Physical changeover and troubleshooting: swapping punch dies or pitch, changing closing bars for a different wire diameter, disabling punch pins for an odd trim size, threading a new wire/coil spool, and clearing paper jams or mis-inserted coils mid-run.

tasks.label: Prepare finished books for shipping by wrapping or packing books and stacking boxes on pallets.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume book manufacturing plant: stacks of finished perfect-bound books come off the binding/trimming line; worker bundles or shrink-wraps piles of a uniform title and stacks the wrapped bundles onto pallets to a set pattern, with slip sheets, on the bindery production floor.

Packing station in the bindery shipping area: worker counts standard trade-size books into corrugated cartons, adds a protective board/void fill and packing slip, closes and tapes the carton, and labels it for a bulk trade or wholesaler order.

Shipping area of a commercial printer/bindery: worker stacks sealed cartons of finished books into a stable pallet load to a stacking pattern with slip sheets, then stretch-wraps the completed pallet for truck shipment.

Short-run / print-on-demand book operation: single copies or a few copies per order, many different trim sizes and weights; worker wraps each book to size in a mailer or right-sized wrap, encloses a packing slip, applies the shipping label and verifies label-to-product match.

Small trade bindery or specialty finishing shop: odd, fragile or oversize items (large-format art books, boxed sets, spiral-bound kits, poster tubes, mixed-content shipments), hand-wrapped in kraft paper/bubble with corner protection, boxes hand-built to fit, small counts and constant changeover.

tasks.label: Set up or operate glue machines by filling glue reservoirs, turning switches to activate heating elements, or adjusting glue flow or conveyor speed.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Commercial book/magazine bindery, high-speed perfect binding line (Müller Martini, Kolbus, Bourg): at shift start the operator switches on the EVA hot-melt pre-melters and side-glue units, keeps the melter reservoirs supplied with granulate, sets spine glue film length/thickness and nozzle width for the job, matches glue delivery to clamp/conveyor speed, and makes mid-run corrections when spine glue runs thin or squeezes out.

Digital/short-run print shop, one- to four-clamp perfect binder (Horizon BQ-470/BQ-500, Duplo DPB-500, CP Bourg): pour EVA pellets into the machine's glue tank, flip the heater switch and wait for warm-up, set glue thickness/temperature and clamp (conveyor) speed from a job template, top up the tank during a 25-500 book run.

PUR adhesive work on a melt-on-demand binder or premelter: load a foil-encased 2-4 kg PUR cartridge/slug or swap the interchangeable PUR tank, prime/purge the circulation and nozzle, set application width and glue volume, and clean the application head at shift end; moisture-sensitive material handled in sealed form.

Inline gluing heads on finishing equipment other than binders — folder-gluers, envelope/mailing lines, tipping-on and spot-glue stations fitted with Nordson/Robatech/Valco applicators: fill the hot-melt reservoir, energize heaters and wait for setpoint, set bead pattern and glue flow, and synchronize application to the conveyor/line speed for the run.

Cold-glue (PVA/dextrin) machines in the bindery — casemaker/cover-maker glue rollers, mounting/laminating gluer, padding press trough: fill the glue pot or trough from a pail, set roller gap/glue film weight, adjust conveyor speed for the board and cover stock, keep the pot topped up and wipe rollers during the run.

tasks.label: Train workers to set up, operate, and use automatic bindery machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Commercial trade bindery: an experienced finishing operator trains a new hire on a perfect binder — explaining and demonstrating clamp/spine-prep and glue-temperature settings, then watching the trainee run makeready and correcting technique until the trainee can produce saleable books.

Print finishing department: trainer teaches a worker to set up and run a continuous folder or saddle stitcher — fold-plate and pocket adjustments, stitcher head timing, jam clearing and guard/safety rules — at the machine during a live production job.

Small in-plant or digital-print shop: lead operator cross-trains an existing employee onto a second machine (three-knife trimmer, laminator, or booklet maker), walking through the OEM manual, job ticket specs, and quality checks over a shift or two.

Formal onboarding session in a training room or at a workstation: reviewing standard operating procedures, lockout/tagout and machine-guarding safety, quality standards, and signing off training documentation for new bindery operators.

OEM/vendor installation training after new automated bindery equipment is purchased: the plant's lead trainer, having been trained by the vendor, then instructs the crew on programmable setups, recipes, and changeover procedures over several days.

tasks.label: Insert book bodies in devices that form back edges of books into convex shapes and produce grooves that facilitate cover attachment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume hardcover trade/textbook production in a commercial bindery: sewn or adhesive-bound book blocks of one format arrive by pallet or inline conveyor from the block line; the worker keeps the rounding-and-backing station of a hardcover bookline supplied with blocks (loading the pile feeder/infeed channel), sets format and clears jams so each block gets a convex spine and joints.

Mid-volume job-shop hardcover work: worker hand-feeds book blocks one at a time, fore-edge down, into a standalone or short-line rounding-and-backing machine, with several format changeovers per shift and stacks of blocks arriving on carts/pallets from the previous operation.

Short-run digital, print-on-demand and library rebinding: runs of 1-50 copies, each block a different trim size and thickness; blocks must be rounded and backed with essentially per-book setup before casing-in.

Specialty products in a commercial bindery: diaries, notebooks, photo books, albums, board and padded-case books with unusual paper, thickness or swell; rounding/backing of blocks that need extra care and non-standard settings.

Hand bindery / conservation and repair work: a unique or fragile hand-sewn text block is rounded with a backing hammer and set up in a laying press or backing boards to form the shoulders, judged by feel on a one-off basis.

tasks.label: Cut cover material to specified dimensions, fitting and gluing material to binder boards by hand or machine.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Edition/long-run casemaking in a book manufacturing plant: worker tends an automatic casemaker (e.g. Kolbus DA-class or Smyth) that takes cloth/printed paper from piles or a reel, cuts it to size, applies glue, registers front/back boards and spine strip onto it, and turns in the edges at 40-65 cases/min; worker sets format, loads magazines, and pulls samples for squareness and turn-in checks.

Short-run/on-demand hardcover and photobook cases in a digital book plant: run sizes from one copy upward, format and spine width changing case to case; cover material cut per cover, boards fed and glued on a digital casemaking line integrated with the print workflow.

Small trade or in-plant bindery: modest quantities of standard rectangular cases, ring-binder covers, menus, diplomas, presentation covers. Worker cuts cloth/vinyl/paper on a board shear or guillotine to a spec sheet, spreads glue, lays boards to a marked jig with correct joint gaps, cuts corners and turns in edges by hand or with a semi-automatic case maker, then nips in a press.

Library binding/rebinding: existing text blocks of mixed sizes measured individually, buckram cut to the measured dimensions, boards positioned and glued to build a case for each volume, worked through a bench/machine mix in batches of differing sizes.

Fine, custom and restoration work in a hand bindery or conservation studio: leather or specialty material pared and cut to shape, corners mitred, material fitted around rounded spines, raised bands, existing damaged covers rebacked or patched, one-off slipcases; fit judged and adjusted by feel while the paste is open.

Fine/craft bindery studio: one-off full-leather binding — paring leather with a knife, hand sewing on cords, backcornering, covering with mitred corners and turn-ins over the boards, then bespoke gold tooling with heated brass fillets and pallets on the curved leather spine.

instances.label: Trade/commercial bindery or print-finishing shop: hand foil-stamp lettering of hardcover cases and spines for short runs and one-offs (theses, diplomas, presentation volumes, library titles, personalized Bibles/journals). Worker sets brass type or a die in a hot-stamp/blocking press, squares the case against stops or a jig, sets temperature/dwell/pressure, and pulls the impression; title must sit square and centered on the spine with clean, unbroken foil.

Book manufacturing plant / edition binding: blocking and embossing of cloth, leather and paper cases with foil and blind dies on production stamping presses; makeready, register to pre-printed cover art, foil and dwell adjustment, quality checking of lettering and spine copy across long runs of identical cases.

Grooving and joint work: cutting or scoring grooves in binder's board for hinges on cases, and forming the groove/joint of cased-in books with bone folder, hand press, backing boards or heated forming jaws, on stock of varying board and cover-material thickness until the joint is tight and even.

Fine/bespoke binding studio: hand gold tooling and hand lettering with heated pallets and handle letters on a covered, rounded leather spine with raised bands - laying glaire and gold leaf, spacing letters by eye between the bands, judging tool heat and dwell on a unique skin, plus blind tooling and decorative fillets to a design fitted to the individual book.

Conservation/restoration lab (library, archive or rare-book shop): finishing work on unique, fragile volumes - stamping and adhering a replacement leather lettering piece, re-tooling gold on a rebacked spine, matching existing historic lettering style, size and placement without damaging the original binding.

instances.label: High-volume book manufacturing plant: sewn book blocks coming off Smyth-type sewing machines must be nipped/smashed to crush the fold swell before gluing, lining and casing-in; thousands of identical blocks per shift, uniform stock and format, machine runs at line speed with an operator monitoring.

Short-run / digital book production (photobooks, yearbooks, book-of-one): sewn or glued blocks of continually varying format and thickness must be compressed immediately after sewing/gluing, job changing on the fly, quality checked per copy.

Mid-size trade or in-plant bindery with a standalone smashing/nipping press: worker takes lifts of folded, sewn or glued signatures off skids parked wherever there is floor space, jogs them square, feeds them into the smasher, cycles it, and restacks the compressed blocks on a skid; several different jobs a day.

Small custom/craft or library bindery: sewn or glued text blocks of contemporary materials placed between pressing boards in a hand nipping press or standing press and left under pressure for minutes to overnight; sizes vary job to job, operator sets pressure by feel.

Conservation / rare-book repair shop: fragile, damaged or oversize text blocks (brittle paper, vellum, warped older sewn sections) pressed in a hand press with tins, blotters and shaped boards, with pressure and duration judged item by item to avoid damage.

tasks.label: Form book bodies by folding and sewing printed sheets to form signatures and assembling signatures in numerical order.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume book manufacturing plant: printed offset sheets are folded on a buckle/knife folder into 16- or 32-page signatures, stacked, then fed to a multi-station gathering machine that assembles signatures in numerical order and hands the collated block to Smyth/thread sewing heads. Worker sets up the folder and sewer, loads feeder piles, watches collation marks, clears misfeeds and doubles.

Short-run / medium trade bindery with frequent job changeovers: many different trim sizes and page counts per shift; operator makes ready the folder for varied fold patterns and stock weights, loads signature hoppers or the sewing machine feeder, checks back-marks and signature sequence, and hand-feeds odd items (fold-outs, tipped sheets).

Small craft / edition bindery: printed sheets folded by hand or on a small folder with a bone folder for creasing, signatures knocked up, punched and sewn on tapes or cords at a sewing frame or on a small sewing machine, then collated in numerical order for a short edition of hardcovers, albums or blank books.

Library, archive or museum conservation/repair bench: a damaged or disbound volume is pulled, leaves are guarded and refolded into new signatures, and the book body is resewn by hand to match the original structure (sewing supports, kettle stitches), with signatures reassembled in original order on fragile, non-uniform paper.

Digital book-on-demand production: sheets or a web from a digital press are scored, folded and collated inline, sequence verified by barcode/image, and the block thread-sewn, run-length often one to a few copies with job changes on the fly; worker loads paper and unloads finished book blocks.

tasks.label: Design original or special bindings for limited editions or other custom binding projects.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Edition bindery / trade finishing shop: developing the special cover treatment for a limited-edition print run — choosing cloth, leather or specialty paper, laying out foil-stamp or blind-tooling die artwork, specifying endpapers, headbands, ribbon and slipcase — and issuing a spec sheet plus a comp/sketch for publisher approval.

One-off fine 'design binding' commission for a collector or private client: reviewing the text, developing concept sketches for the cover imagery, deciding sewing structure, board attachment, onlay/inlay scheme and titling, and presenting drawings and material swatches for client approval before execution begins.

Custom presentation work in a small bindery or print-finishing shop: designing a bespoke award portfolio, corporate presentation binder, guest book or photo album — stamping layout, material and closure choices, sized to the client's supplied content — communicated as a proof/drawing and quote.

Institutional/library or conservation bindery: specifying an appropriate special binding or protective enclosure for a rare or damaged item — period-appropriate style, structure and materials — recorded as a written treatment/design proposal for curator sign-off.
Exhibition or competition design binding by an artisan binder: iterative concept development, thumbnail drawings, colour and tooling studies, and a written design rationale submitted with the entry.

tasks.label: Punch holes in and fasten paper sheets, signatures, or other material, using hand or machine punches and staplers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

Bindery floor: saddle-stitching signatures/sections into booklets and magazines on a stitching line — signatures fed to the saddle, wire stitches driven through the spine, book delivered to trimmer; runs of hundreds to hundreds of thousands.

Finishing bench or small-shop station: hand or foot-operated stapling of small collated sets, short-run booklets, NCR sets and covers — corner or side stapling with a manual/electric stapler or flat-book stitcher, short runs with frequent job changes.

Specialty finishing: punching and fastening non-paper or mixed materials — plastic/chipboard covers, index tabs, tags, door hangers, calendar hangers — and fastening with eyelets, rivets, binder posts or brads; short runs, varied stock thickness and hole patterns.

tasks.label: Repair, restore, or rebind old, rare, or damaged books, using hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-house library/school collection repair: at a workroom bench, a worker triages worn circulating volumes — reattaching loose covers and hinges, replacing a torn spine with book cloth and PVA, mending page tears, tightening a shaken text block — using bone folder, knife, brushes, and a nipping press; each book's damage differs.

Commercial library/textbook rebinding in a production bindery: worker pulls the old case off a used volume, judges recase vs. oversew vs. double-fan adhesive binding by paper and margin condition, mends damaged leaves, adds new endsheets, fits and stamps a new case, and cases in — machines assist each step but the worker inspects, hand-feeds, and finishes.

Conservation lab treatment of a rare/antiquarian book: leather or cloth rebacking with original spine retained, corner and board repair, consolidation of degraded leather, resewing broken sewing on cords or tapes, all while preserving original material to documented conservation standards.

Full hand rebind in a craft/fine bindery: text block pulled and cleaned, guarded and resewn on tapes, rounded and backed, boards laced or attached, covered in leather or cloth, headbands sewn, title gold-tooled or stamped, endpapers pasted down for a customer's damaged heirloom or antiquarian volume.

Paper/text-block repair at a conservation bench: mending tears with Japanese tissue and wheat starch paste, removing old pressure-sensitive tape and adhesive residue, guarding and tipping in loose plates and detached leaves, flattening and filling losses (e.g., leaf casting), then reassembling the text block.

sources.system: Treventus ScanRobot (2.0 MDS)
sources.title: Automatic Book Scanner or the ScanRobot developed by Treventus
sources.claim: The Treventus ScanRobot automatically turns pages of bound volumes in a purpose-built V-cradle for digitization — the closest deployed automated manipulation of book pages — but it only turns and images pages; it performs no repair, gluing, sewing, or tool work on the book.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated handling of the pages of fragile bound books. It shows machine page handling is feasible in a purpose-built cradle, but the system neither diagnoses damage nor applies adhesives, tissue, thread, or hand tools, so it does not substantiate completion of any repair or rebinding instance.

sources.system: RePAIR robotic reassembly system
sources.developer: Ca' Foscari University of Venice and EU RePAIR consortium
sources.title: RePAIR: Results and Future Prospects of the Project Integrating Robotics and Artificial Intelligence in the Reassembly of Frescoes at Pompeii
sources.claim: The RePAIR project built a prototype robotic system with vision and manipulators that physically reassembles broken fresco fragments at Pompeii — the leading robotic cultural-heritage restoration demonstration — and it handles only rigid fragments in a lab, with archaeologists correcting errors.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic restoration of damaged cultural heritage objects. It is the closest robotic analogue, but works on rigid plaster fragments with pick-and-place motions in a controlled lab, not on limp paper, thread, leather and paste, and it remains a research prototype requiring expert supervision.

sources.system: Espresso Book Machine (EBM)
sources.date: deployed since 2007; library installation page current 2025
sources.title: Espresso Book Machine | Cincinnati & Hamilton County Public Library
sources.claim: The Espresso Book Machine autonomously prints, perfect-binds and trims new paperbacks on demand in library and bookstore settings; it fabricates a binding only from sheets it has just printed and cannot accept, disassemble, or repair an existing damaged volume.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated bookbinding. It shows that binding a fresh, uniform text block is fully automatable in a purpose-built machine, but the rebinding instances start from a used, warped, variably sized volume that must be pulled, cleaned, mended and matched — steps the EBM has no mechanism for.

sources.system: Kolbus Casemaker DA 260
sources.title: Kolbus: KOLBUS America
sources.claim: Kolbus casemaking machines produce hardcover book cases fully automatically at up to 40 cycles per minute in purpose-built book production lines, for new editions of uniform size.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated fabrication of hardcover cases, one component of rebinding. The machine runs on standardized board and cloth for identical new books; it cannot measure and fit a case to an individual damaged volume, retain original boards, or attach the case to a repaired text block.

sources.system: Kasemake automated box-making machine
sources.developer: Conservation By Design / AG CAD (used by Library of Congress General Collections Conservation Section)
sources.title: Box Making Activities in the General Collections Conservation Section | Guardians of Memory (Library of Congress blog)
sources.claim: In the Library of Congress conservation section, even the most automated rehousing workflow is a computer-driven Kasemake cutter that cuts and creases board while staff measure the item, operate the machine, and fold and label every box by hand.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: the most standardized, most highly automated operation in a book conservation lab. Even here the machine only cuts flat board and a human performs all measurement, folding, assembly and handling of the damaged book, indicating no robotic system performs the dexterous portions of conservation bench work.

sources.system: HF Group library binding production process
sources.title: Library Binding – HF Group, LLC
sources.claim: Commercial library rebinding is condition-dependent human judgment work: the binder decides between recasing, oversewing, sewing through the fold, or double-fan adhesive binding based on the individual volume's paper, margins, and intactness of the original sewing, with hand trimming and mending as needed.
sources.transferJustification: Not a robotic system: cited to document what the instance requires. Each used volume is assessed and routed individually and hand-fed through separate machines by workers, so no automated line performs the whole rebind of a damaged book.

roles.title: Laundry and Dry-Cleaning Workers
aliases: Fur Glazing and Polishing Machine Operator
roles.description: Operate or tend washing or dry-cleaning machines to wash or dry-clean industrial or household articles, such as cloth garments, suede, leather, furs, blankets, draperies, linens, rugs, and carpets. Includes spotters and dyers of these articles.

tasks.label: Operate extractors and driers, or direct their operation.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Industrial laundry plant (linen supply, healthcare co-op, uniform rental): worker charges large washer-extractors or a tunnel/press extraction line from carts, slings or conveyors, selects the wash/extract formula for the classification, moves extracted 'cakes' or wet loads to large tumble dryers, sets dry time/temperature, monitors and discharges dried goods to carts or conveyors for finishing.

On-premises laundry in a hotel, hospital or nursing home: worker loads 60–200 lb open-pocket washer-extractors from linen carts, runs the extract cycle, transfers heavy wet linen to tumble dryers, sets cycles, cleans lint screens, and unloads dried linen into carts, often directing a helper's operation of a second machine.

Retail dry-cleaning shop: worker loads a sorted lot of garments into the dry-cleaning machine (which extracts solvent and dries inside the drum), selects the program for the fabric class, monitors the cycle and moisture/temperature, and unloads garments promptly to a cart or hanging rail for finishing.

Laundromat / wash-dry-fold or personal-laundry service: attendant runs individual customers' mixed household loads through standard washers and dryers, keeps each order segregated, picks temperature and dry settings for mixed fabrics, pulls items that must not be over-dried, and unloads to a folding table.

Rug and carpet cleaning plant: worker rolls a soaking-wet area rug into a centrifugal wringer/extractor, closes and starts the spin, unloads the extracted rug and hangs or racks it in the drying room, monitoring drying progress.

Specialty cleaner (leather, suede, fur, draperies, delicate household articles): worker loads small lots into a tumbler/dryer or drying cabinet with conservative time and temperature settings, checks items mid-cycle for shrinkage or damage, and unloads by hand.

tasks.label: Remove items from washers or dry-cleaning machines, or direct other workers to do so.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Industrial laundry plant (linen supply, uniform rental, healthcare laundry): at cycle end the worker opens a 100–450 lb open-pocket washer-extractor or takes the discharge of a tunnel washer, drags/rakes the heavy tangled wet linen cake out into a cart, sling or onto a conveyor, on a hot wet wash-aisle floor, keeping up with cycle timing.

On-premise laundry at a hotel, hospital or nursing home: worker opens a 35–75 lb front-load washer, pulls the wet sheets, towels, gowns or personal linens out by hand into a cart or directly across into the adjacent tumble dryer, several machines cycling at once through the shift.

Retail dry cleaner: worker opens the dry-to-dry cleaning machine at cycle end and removes 40–60 lb of mixed customer garments (suits, dresses, silks, coats) from the drum, keeping tags/tickets with the pieces and moving them to the pressing station or hanging rail without dropping them on the floor.

Laundromat / wash-and-fold shop: worker removes finished customer loads of mixed personal clothing from front-load or top-load washers and transfers them into dryers or carts, in a customer-facing store, checking for stray small items and stragglers left in the drum.

Lead/shift worker directs others: monitors which machines have finished, tells helpers or new employees which washers or dry-cleaning machines to empty and where the goods go, and verifies loads were pulled promptly so machines are freed up.

sources.claim: Physical Intelligence's π0 policy drove a mobile manipulator to take laundry out of a household dryer, put it in a hamper and fold it, running fully autonomously — the closest demonstrated analogue of emptying a machine by robot, but a research demo on consumer appliances in the lab.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: unloading a clothes dryer drum, mechanically the same act as emptying a washer or dry-cleaning drum. Cited to show the state of the art for machine-emptying by a general-purpose robot; it is a lab demo on a household appliance, not worker-quality output in a commercial laundry.

sources.claim: Dyna Robotics' DYNA-1 arms fold napkins and linens autonomously for 24-hour runs and a folding robot has been installed at a laundromat in Sacramento — an autonomous textile-handling robot working inside a human laundry business, but doing folding at a table, not emptying washers.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous handling and folding of laundry inside a working laundromat (E2). Cited to bound what is deployed in human laundry facilities: the deployed work is folding from a basket, not opening and emptying washer drums.

tasks.label: Load articles into washers or dry-cleaning machines, or direct other workers to perform loading.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume commercial/industrial laundry plant (hospital, hotel, linen-rental): soiled flatwork (sheets, towels, gowns) arrives in bulk carts/bags; worker classifies, weighs and loads batches of 100-500 lb into a tunnel (continuous batch) washer or large open-pocket washer-extractors, shift after shift.

Industrial laundry processing soiled garments/workwear/uniforms: worker pulls tangled garments from bulk bins one at a time, checks pockets for pens, tools and other foreign objects, sorts by customer/category/color, and loads them into washing machines or sling bags feeding the washers.

Retail or wholesale dry-cleaning plant: worker sorts tagged customer garments by color, fabric and soil level, empties pockets, and loads 30-60 lb batches into the dry-cleaning machine drum; also loads shirt washers and wet-cleaning machines, then closes door and selects the cycle.

On-premises laundry at a hotel, nursing home or hospital: worker wheels carts of soiled linen from chutes/floors, weighs loads, and hand-loads 60-200 lb washer-extractors (or several small machines), closing doors and starting cycles between other duties.

Bulky/specialty articles: comforters, duvets, blankets, draperies, mats and area rugs (occasionally leather, suede or fur pieces) inspected and carefully loaded, one or a few at a time, into large washers, rug-washing equipment or small dry-cleaning machines.

Lead worker/shift lead directs other workers on loading: assigns which classifications and batches go to which machine, instructs on correct load weight and sorting, and verbally corrects loading errors rather than loading personally.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Industrial/commercial laundry plant, terry and small pieces: bath towels, hand towels, washcloths, bath mats and napkins tumbled dry, taken from bulk carts, separated, sorted by type/size, counted, folded and stacked for the customer route.

tasks.label: Start washers, dry cleaners, driers, or extractors, and turn valves or levers to regulate machine processes and the volume of soap, detergent, water, bleach, starch, and other additives.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Industrial/commercial laundry plant (linen supply, industrial launderer, healthcare linen): wash floor with a tunnel washer or a bank of large open-pocket washer-extractors and dryers. Worker selects the wash formula for the goods category, starts washers/extractors/dryers, confirms the chemical injection pumps are delivering detergent, alkali, bleach and sour, and adjusts water levels, temperatures and dosing settings. High volume, standardized goods categories.

Worker selects the preset formula for sheets, towels, gowns or personal clothing, starts the machines and the driers, and occasionally adjusts dose rates, water temperature or extraction settings for heavily soiled or special items.

Laundromat or small wash-dry-fold / shirt shop: attendant loads vended or small commercial washers with mixed customer garments, measures and pours detergent, bleach and softener by hand or via a dispenser, selects water temperature and cycle per customer instructions, starts washers and then sets and starts the driers.

instances.label: Retail/small drycleaning plant: spotter at the spotting board takes each incoming garment (wool suit, silk blouse, rayon dress), reads the care label and judges fiber, locates and identifies the stain (beverage, grease, ink, makeup, blood, perspiration), and decides wet-side vs dry-side procedure, the specific agents (protein formula, tannin formula, POG, amyl acetate) and their order, including a colorfastness/bleed test on a hidden seam before committing.

Counter/intake marking in a drycleaning store or plant: worker inspects the customer's bagged garments item by item, asks or reads what caused the stain, judges fabric and stain type, and writes the pre-spot instruction/treatment plan on the tag or ticket for the spotter, flagging items that may not come clean.

Commercial/industrial linen or uniform plant: worker at the clean side inspects washed flatwork and garments (hotel sheets, napkins, healthcare linen, workwear) and determines which stained pieces get routed to rewash/reclaim treatment, which get spot pretreatment, and which are condemned, per the plant's quality standard for that customer and linen class.

Specialty and high-risk articles: wedding gowns, leather/suede, fur, drapery, vintage or unlabeled mixed-fiber garments, aged or unknown stains. Worker must test the fiber and dye, judge whether the stain is dye-based, tannin, oxidized or heat-set, and choose a cautious procedure and solvent (or decline treatment).

On-site or off-premise work at customer premises: rug, carpet, or upholstery/drapery cleaning, where the worker identifies fiber (wool vs olefin vs viscose) and stain (pet urine, red dye, rust, grease) in place, under variable lighting and furniture, and determines the spotting agent and procedure before treating.

Specialty items in a cleaning plant: rugs and carpets, drapery, leather/suede/fur, wedding gowns and household goods are laid out and inspected for fiber content, dye stability, sun fading and color loss, pet/urine stains and prior home-treatment damage, and the item is classified for a specialty process or refused.

tasks.label: Apply bleaching powders to spots and spray them with steam to remove stains from fabrics that do not respond to other cleaning solvents.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Retail/wholesale dry-cleaning plant spotting board: a spotter takes a shirt, blouse, dress or pair of trousers that still shows a stain after solvent cleaning, lays the stained area over the nose of the board, identifies the stain (coffee, wine, ink, fruit, perspiration), brushes or spatulas on a bleaching agent (hydrogen peroxide, sodium perborate/hydrosulfite powder), flushes with the steam gun, vacuums, inspects under lamp and repeats until the stain is gone without a ring or fabric damage.

Color- or fiber-sensitive garment at the same spotting board: silk blouse, wool suit, tie, wedding gown, printed or dark-dyed piece. Worker must test dye fastness, pick a mild reducing/oxidizing bleach, apply tiny amounts, steam-feather the edges, and stop before dye stripping, yellowing or fiber damage occurs; a mistake means a claim on a customer-owned garment.

Industrial/commercial linen-supply laundry: white cotton/poly table linens, napkins, sheets and towels pulled at inspection or as classified rewash. Worker sprays or dabs a bleach spotting solution on the residual spot at a spotting station or table, steams/flushes it, and returns the piece for rewash; high volume, standardized white goods, tolerance for an occasional reject to rag stock.

On-premises laundry at a hotel, hospital or nursing home: staff spot-bleach blood, iodine, food or ink marks on sheets, gowns, bibs and tablecloths at a sink or small spotting table with bleach solution and a steam/spray gun before rewashing; limited equipment, mixed item types, done between wash loads.

Rug, carpet, drapery and upholstery cleaning plant: after cleaning, worker locates remaining discolorations on a large flat textile spread on a wash floor or drying rack, applies bleaching agent (peroxide, reducing bleach) to the spot with brush or sprayer, applies steam or hot water to drive and flush it, then rinses and blots; large, heavy, dye-sensitive items.

Objects (garments), chemistry (oxidizing bleach) and precision (a few cm patch without damaging surrounding fabric) are comparable to spot bleaching, which supports the chemical-application step when the garment and target area are presented to the machine; it does not cover stain diagnosis, agent selection or verification of removal.

tasks.label: Operate machines that comb, dry and polish furs, clean, sterilize and fluff feathers and blankets, or roll and package towels.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Industrial/commercial laundry plant (hotel, healthcare or textile-rental): worker tends the towel finishing line — pulls dried towels from carts or the dryer conveyor, feeds the small-piece folder, clears the stacker, then bundles, rolls or bags and labels packs of towels for delivery. Hundreds of pieces per hour, mixed sizes.

Smaller structured operation (hotel on-premise laundry, gym/spa/salon linen room, small commercial laundry or dry-cleaner back room): worker runs a compact folder or table-top roller, rolls towels coming out of the dryer, and bundles or poly-bags them for the shelf or a customer order. Human-standard equipment, moderate volume, work done at a table beside the machine.

Blankets and comforters: worker loads thermal hospital blankets, hotel blankets or comforters into a washer or tunnel washer, runs the wash/thermal-disinfection cycle, transfers them to a tumbler for the drying and fluffing cycle, then unloads the fluffed goods into carts in a commercial laundry.

Fur garments at a furrier or specialty dry cleaner: worker loads fur coats into a sawdust/corncob tumbling drum, runs the cleaning cycle, removes the media in a cage drum, air-dries, then combs, glazes and polishes the pelt on a fur machine and inspects the lustre before the garment is returned.

Feather and down goods: worker runs a pillow renovation machine — opens the old ticking, blows the fill into the sterilizing chamber for UV/ozone treatment and dust sifting, fluffs it, tops it up and refills a new ticking (or tends a bulk down washing/drying line at a feather processor).

tasks.label: Pre-soak, sterilize, scrub, spot-clean, and dry contaminated or stained articles, using neutralizer solutions and portable machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dry-cleaning plant spotting board: the spotter inspects each incoming garment, identifies stain type (protein, tannin, oil, ink, dye) and fiber, selects neutralizer/acid/alkali and spotting agents, works the stain with steam gun, air, tamping brush, spatula and vacuum board, flushes and dries locally, avoiding rings, dye loss or fabric damage on silk, wool, beaded and structured garments.

Large industrial / healthcare / hospitality laundry: batches of contaminated or heavily stained linen, gowns, workwear and shop towels are classified, pre-soaked/pre-washed with break and neutralizer chemistry, disinfected, extracted and dried; stained pieces are pulled for reclaim/rewash before finishing.

On-premises laundry at a hospital, nursing home or hotel: worker pre-treats individual stained or soiled items (blood, incontinence, food, ointment) by spraying/soaking and rubbing at a sink or soak tub, then runs a disinfecting wash and dries; mixed small loads of linen and residents' personal clothing.

Rug-cleaning plant, machine-washable synthetic and standard wool area rugs: rug is dusted, soaked in the wash tub with detergent/neutralizer, scrubbed, rinsed, wrung in a centrifuge and dried in a drying room.

Rug-cleaning plant, delicate or heavily contaminated pieces: hand-knotted orientals, silk or dye-bleeding rugs and pet-urine-contaminated rugs requiring hand-applied enzyme/urine neutralizer, hand spotting of rust or dye stains, controlled hand scrubbing and careful drying.

On-site work at customer premises (home or office): spot-cleaning and extracting stains from installed carpet, upholstered furniture and draperies with a portable extractor, sprayer and neutralizer solutions; layout, furniture and soil conditions differ at every job.

tasks.label: Mix and add detergents, dyes, bleaches, starches, and other solutions and chemicals to clean, color, dry, or stiffen articles.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Industrial/commercial linen plant (hotel, healthcare, uniform rental): worker runs tunnel washers and large washer-extractors, selects the wash formula for each batch, and ensures detergent, alkali, bleach, sour and softener are delivered in the right amounts and sequence; connects/changes chemical totes and checks dosing against titration results.

On-premise laundry at a hotel, nursing home or hospital: for each washer-extractor load the worker adds measured detergent, bleach, destainer and softener, adjusting quantities for load size and soil level; chemicals are poured from jugs or delivered by an installed dispenser.

Dry-cleaning store/plant: charging the dry-cleaning machine's solvent with detergent/sizing per load, dosing wet-cleaning chemistry into the wetcleaning washer, and adding starch/sizing to shirt washers for the requested stiffness.

Spotter at the spotting board: judging fabric and stain type, selecting and mixing spotting agents (protein, tannin, oil-and-grease, rust removers), applying them by brush/tamp/steam gun to individual stains, then flushing and neutralizing without damaging the garment.

Dyeing/tinting work: mixing a dye bath to match a required color, weighing and dissolving dyes plus salt/leveling/fixing agents, and adding them to a dye machine or vat for garments or rugs, then checking and correcting the shade.

Specialty cleaning in a rug, leather or fur department: hand-mixing a cleaning or conditioning solution in a bucket/tank to a formula and applying or charging it for the specific article being processed.

tasks.label: Wash, dry-clean, or glaze delicate articles or fur garment linings by hand, using mild detergents or dry cleaning solutions.
Match sample colors, applying knowledge of bleaching agent and dye properties, and types, construction, conditions, and colors of articles.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dry-cleaning/dye plant: a customer's faded or off-color garment (wool coat, cotton dress) is to be immersion re-dyed to match its original color or a supplied swatch. The worker judges fiber type, construction and condition, formulates a dye recipe, runs a test swatch, adjusts, and dyes the article until the finished color matches within visual tolerance.

Spotting bench in a dry-clean plant: after stain removal or bleach damage a small area has lost color. The worker blends dyes on a palette or airbrush, matching the surrounding fabric's exact shade, and feathers the color into the damaged spot on a hanging or laid-out garment without leaving a halo or ring.

Commercial/industrial laundry: a lot of white or light-colored linens or uniforms comes out grayed, yellowed or with dye transfer. The worker compares the lot with the whiteness/color standard sample, selects the bleaching agent (chlorine, oxygen, reductive) and strength appropriate to the fabrics' construction and condition, and reprocesses the lot until it matches the standard.

Leather/suede/fur specialty cleaner: a worn leather jacket or suede skirt must be recolored to match its original color or a sample chip. The worker mixes leather dye/finish to the matching shade and sprays and blends it over the made-up garment, feathering into unfaded areas.

Plant with dye equipment handling household textiles: a set of draperies, blankets or table linens is dyed as a lot to match a customer's sample swatch or existing pieces already in the room; recipe formulated, lot dyed in a machine, shade checked against the sample and corrected.

tasks.label: Spray steam, water, or air over spots to flush out chemicals, dry material, raise naps, or brighten colors.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Pre-spotting at a dry-cleaning plant spotting board: worker lays a soiled garment (wool suit, cotton shirt, polyester dress) over the board nose, identifies the stain, applies a spotting agent with brush/spatula, then flushes it out with the steam gun or water gun over the vacuum grid and dries the area with the air gun before the garment goes into the cleaning machine. Fabrics, stain types and locations vary item to item; over-flushing causes rings, dye bleed or fabric damage.

Post-cleaning re-spotting at inspection: garment comes out of the dry-cleaning machine with a residual spot or a ring; worker returns it to the board, works the area with wet-side or dry-side agents, feathers the edges with steam and air, uses the vacuum and air gun to dry the spot without leaving a water ring, and checks brightness/colour match against the surrounding cloth.

Delicate and specialty articles: silk, wool crepe, velvet, suede/leather, fur, blankets and draperies. Light, distance-controlled steam or air only, brushing or air-blowing to raise the crushed nap or pile, no aggressive flushing; a mistake ruins an expensive item and the worker must judge fibre, dye stability and construction by eye and hand.

Commercial/industrial laundry spotting table: hospitality linens, chef whites, workwear pulled out of the wash for stubborn stains (grease, blood, ink, food). Durable cotton/poly-cotton, standardized items, high volume; worker sprays the stain remover, flushes with the steam/water gun and blows it dry, then returns the piece to the wash or to finishing.

Rug and carpet plant: after shampoo/cleaning chemicals are worked into an area rug laid flat on the wash floor, worker sprays water over the treated areas to flush the chemicals out of the pile, grooms/raises the nap, and works the surface until residue and detergent are gone before extraction and drying.

Targeted spot work on rugs and upholstery: pet urine spots, dye bleeds and traffic-lane marks treated individually with a chemical then flushed with a hot-water/steam wand and air-dried, either on a rug in the plant or on carpet/upholstery at a customer's premises where furniture, layout and soil conditions are as found.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Industrial/commercial laundry plant: bleaching a batch of white goods (hotel sheets and towels, healthcare linen, food-service linen) as the bleach step of a wash formula. Worker classifies/weighs the batch, sees that bleach and hot water go into the bath, and the goods soak in the bleach liquor for the programmed time before rinsing. High volume, standard textiles, fixed washroom layout.

On-premise laundry at a hospital, nursing home, or hotel: worker loads a washer-extractor with stained or dingy whites, selects the bleach formula or adds measured bleach to the hot-water bath, runs the soak/bleach cycle, checks the result, and unloads. Small staff, one or two machines, standard linens.

Manual vat/tub soak in a commercial laundry back area: heavy-soil or dingy goods (bar mops, chef coats, restaurant napkins, mop heads) placed in a vat or sink of hot water with bleach mixed in, left to soak, stirred and checked periodically, then moved to the washer or rinsed. Batch quantities of uniform goods.

Dry-cleaning shop spotting/bleaching bench: one garment or a small lot with a dye stain, yellowing, or perspiration mark. Worker chooses an oxidizing or reducing bleach, mixes a small quantity with hot water in a tub or spotting vat, immerses the item, watches closely for stain removal versus color/fiber damage, pulls it at the right moment, neutralizes and rinses. Mixed fabrics, one-off customer-owned goods.

Specialty/restoration work in a plant: whitening or bleaching wedding gowns, heirloom or yellowed table linen, draperies, and delicate or non-standard articles (leather, suede, fur trim, area rugs). Bleach bath mixed by hand to strength, item hand-immersed and supported, endpoint judged by eye, high damage liability.

Dye house / garment-finishing operation: bleaching piece goods or garments (denim, uniforms, greige fabric) in vats, kiers or dyeing machines. Bleaching agent and auxiliaries weighed and dissolved in hot water and fed to the vessel; material soaks or circulates until the required whiteness is reached, then is rinsed and neutralized.

instances.label: Retail/commercial dry-cleaning plant, spotter-dyer: a single customer garment (blouse, dress, uniform jacket) with dye transfer, color bleed, or a color to be removed before re-dyeing is immersed by hand in a heated color-stripping/bleach bath in a small dye vat or sink, agitated with a paddle, checked repeatedly for shade, then lifted out, neutralized and rinsed. Industrial/institutional laundry (linen, hospitality, healthcare): a batch of stained white linens (napkins, tablecloths, towels, gowns) is run through a programmed bleach bath step in a washer-extractor or tunnel washer to strip stains and discoloration; worker loads the batch, selects/starts the formula, monitors, and unloads to extraction and drying.

Laundry or hotel on-premise plant: badly discolored individual items are soaked by hand in an open bleach/color-stripping tub or sink, pushed under with a paddle, watched until the color lifts, then wrung out, rinsed and returned to the wash line.

Small-lot dye shop / commercial dyeing operation attached to a cleaner: lots of garments, yarn, or piece goods are loaded into baskets or onto carriers and immersed in a heated stripping/bleach liquor to standard timed formulas before re-dyeing, then rinsed and neutralized.

Rug, carpet or drapery cleaning plant: a large heavy item is immersed in a wash pit or bleach/color-stripping tub, worked by hand or brush, held for a controlled dwell, then lifted, rinsed and extracted. Bulky, water-logged, awkward to handle.

Specialty leather, suede or fur cleaning plant: garment or pelt is immersed in a bleaching bath to strip or even out color, with constant judgment about substrate damage, followed by neutralizing, rinsing and conditioning.

sources.claim: Dyna Robotics' DYNA-1 model runs stationary dual-arm robots that manipulate limp textiles (napkin folding) autonomously for more than 24 hours with no human intervention, at quality standards set by commercial customers.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: sustained autonomous manipulation of limp flatwork textiles at a fixed workstation in a commercial laundry/hospitality setting. It supports textile handling at a station but does not cover chemical-bath immersion or shade judgment.

tasks.label: Identify articles' fabrics and original dyes by sight and touch, or by testing samples with fire or chemical reagents.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Counter/intake inspection at a retail dry cleaner or plant: the worker takes in routine customer garments (shirts, trousers, suits, dresses, blouses), looks at and feels each item — checking or overriding the care label — to decide the fabric (cotton, wool, silk, rayon, acetate, polyester, blends) and note the color/dye, so the cleaning process and tagging are set correctly.

Spotter at the spotting board: before applying a stain agent, identifies the fabric of the specific garment area and tests the original dye for fastness by dabbing solvent/reagent or steam on an inconspicuous seam or hem, blotting onto a white cloth, judging color transfer, then choosing the safe chemistry.

Commercial/industrial laundry (hotel, healthcare, workwear): the worker sorts high volumes of incoming soiled linens, towels and uniforms, judging fabric type (cotton vs poly-cotton vs microfiber vs synthetic workwear) and color class by sight and touch to route each item to the right wash formula and temperature.

Unlabeled, vintage or home-sewn textile article (label missing or illegible; drapery panel, tablecloth, costume, thrift/antique garment): the worker identifies the fiber by feel and, when unsure, snips a yarn from a seam allowance and runs a burn test or chemical solubility/reagent test in the plant's testing area.

Specialty non-woven-textile article: leather, suede, fur, fur-trimmed coat, beaded or sequinned gown, or an area rug — the worker identifies the skin/pile/fiber type and the dye (aniline vs pigmented leather, fugitive rug dyes) by sight and touch and by cautious reagent testing on a hidden spot.

On-location assessment at the customer's premises: drapery takedown, rug pickup or on-site inspection in a home or office, identifying fiber and dye in the field (variable light, item hanging or installed in place) to quote and choose the cleaning method.

sources.system: Fibersort (Valvan Baling Systems)
sources.title: Fibersort brings textile recycling a step closer | Siemens
sources.claim: The Fibersort is a commercial sorting machine in which individual garments pass a scanning station where an RGB camera determines color and an infrared camera ... fiber composition, after which the machine physically blows each garment into a category bin (e.g. blue cotton, red nylon) at ~2,000 pieces/hour.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is automated sorting of post-consumer garments; it carries over because the machine performs exactly the identification act at issue — determining fiber composition and colour of an individual whole garment presented to it — on the same class of objects (apparel and household textiles).

sources.system: Fibersort
sources.developer: Interreg NWE Fibersort consortium / Valvan Baling Systems
sources.title: FIBERSORT FACT SHEET (Interreg NWE)
sources.claim: Independent laboratory (Centexbel) assessment of Fibersort output found the NIR-based fiber-composition identification reliable for most fractions, both pure and blended, with published per-fraction accuracy figures (e.g. cotton 100 fraction measured 98.5% cotton; polyamide 100 fraction only 61%).
sources.transferJustification: Quantifies the quality of the automated fabric identification used above; relevant because the task's accepted output is a correct fabric call, not a manipulation.

sources.system: Siptex (Stadler plant with TOMRA NIR sorters)
sources.title: Siptex: A pioneering textile sorting technology for increased circularity | European Circular Economy Stakeholder Platform
sources.claim: The Siptex plant in Malmö, opened 2021 and operated at industrial scale by Sysav with Stadler/Tomra equipment, is a fully automated facility that identifies and sorts mixed post-consumer textiles by fibre type and colour using NIR and visual spectroscopy.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is industrial-scale textile sorting; transfers because the identification step (fibre type plus colour of unlabeled worn garments and household textiles) is the same determination the laundry worker makes by sight and touch.

sources.system: HEIMDAL.Camera / HEIMDAL.RFID (Inwatec, JENSEN-GROUP)
sources.title: Smart automation for every laundry size | JENSEN-GROUP
sources.claim: Inwatec's HEIMDAL module, installed in working industrial laundries (e.g. bardusch Yverdon, 27 tonnes/day), identifies garments by color, pattern, ... using AI vision plus RFID, so items are sorted automatically to the correct wash process.

sources.system: THOR robot separator + HEIMDAL.Camera + BIFRÖST sorting line
sources.title: Automatic Soil Sort • Clean Show 2022 | Inwatec
sources.claim: Inwatec's automatic soil-sort line combines conveyors, the THOR robot that picks single soiled items from bulk with 3D cameras and grippers, an AI camera that assigns sorting criteria from visual appearance, and an X-ray reject stage; BIFRÖST sorts up to 2,000 pieces/hour into bins.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is singulating and classifying soiled laundry; transfers because the machine must isolate one arbitrary limp garment from a heap and make the fabric/colour call that this task requires, on the same objects in the same industry.

sources.system: Refiberd hyperspectral material-detection system
sources.title: Startup Refiberd uses AI technology to advance intelligent sorting for textile recycling
sources.claim: Refiberd pairs a hyperspectral camera ... to determine fiber composition of textiles without destructive chemical testing, with first customer deployments from 2024 and industry recognition in 2025-2026.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is fiber identification of unlabeled post-consumer textiles on a sorting line; it substitutes directly for the worker's burn/solubility test because the output is the same fiber determination on the same materials.

tasks.label: Spread soiled articles on work tables, and position stained portions over vacuum heads or on marble slabs.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Retail dry-cleaning plant spotting station: worker takes everyday customer garments (dress shirts, blouses, trousers, cotton/poly jackets) off the incoming rail or bin, shakes them out and spreads them flat on the spotting board, finds the food/ink/oil stain and lays that portion squarely over the vacuum nose before steam/chemical treatment.

Delicate and structured garments at the same spotting board: silk blouses, beaded or sequined evening dresses, wedding gowns, lined wool suits, pleated skirts, ties. Worker must spread without crushing trim or stretching bias fabric, sometimes working over a marble slab, and position a small stain precisely without abrading the fibre.

Leather, suede, shearling and fur items: heavy, stiff, non-uniform hides and garments spread on the work table or marble slab, with the soiled/stained portion positioned for careful spot work; items are bulky and easily marked by grippers or excess pressure.

Household and hospitality flatwork brought in for spotting: tablecloths, napkins, bed sheets, pillowcases, light blankets. Worker spreads the piece flat on a large work table and positions the stained section (wine, grease, blood) over the vacuum head or slab.

Oversize/bulky household articles: pinch-pleat draperies with hooks, heavy comforters and duvets, area rugs and carpet sections. Worker wrestles the article onto the table or floor slab, spreads the relevant panel, and positions the soiled region over the vacuum head.

Industrial/commercial laundry pre-spotting: work uniforms, chef coats, aprons, shop towels and hospitality linens coming from soil sort. Worker spreads the soiled garment on a table, locates grease/blood/ink marks and positions them over the vacuum board for pre-spray before washing.

sources.system: SpeedFolding (dual-arm ABB YuMi cell, UC Berkeley)
sources.developer: UC Berkeley AUTOLab (Avigal, Berscheid, Asfour, Kröger, Goldberg)
sources.title: SpeedFolding: Learning Efficient Bimanual Folding of Garments (arXiv:2208.10552)
sources.claim: SpeedFolding, a bimanual robot cell, autonomously manipulates an initially crumpled garment into a smoothed configuration on a table and then folds it along specified lines, at 93% success and 30-40 garments per hour, generalizing to unseen garments.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: smoothing a crumpled garment flat on a work table is the 'spread soiled articles on work tables' step; comparable objects (shirts, trousers), comparable precision, performed in a fixed bimanual cell over a table.

sources.system: Cloth Funnels (dual-UR5 real-world garment manipulation system)
sources.title: Cloth Funnels: Canonicalized-Alignment for Multi-Purpose Garment Manipulation (TRI)
sources.claim: Cloth Funnels learns a real-world dual-arm policy that takes arbitrarily configured garments to a predefined smoothed configuration at a specified rigid pose (canonicalized alignment), used as the first step of a real ironing and folding system.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: aligning a garment to a target pose on a table is exactly what 'position stained portions over vacuum heads' requires — placing a chosen garment region at a fixed location on the work surface — with the same deformable objects and table-top precision.

sources.system: DYNA-1
sources.title: Dyna Robotics Unveils DYNA-1: The First Commercial-Ready Robot Foundation Model Offering Fully Autonomous, Round-the-Clock Dexterity
sources.claim: DYNA-1 is a pair of stationary robotic ... that autonomously picks linens/napkins from a bin, lays them out and folds them, running over 24 hours continuously at production quality without human intervention.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: flatwork folding begins by spreading a crumpled napkin/linen flat on a work table, the same handling as spreading soiled flatwork for spotting; same objects (table linens, towels) and same table-top workspace.

sources.system: DYNA-1 folding cell at a Sacramento laundromat
sources.title: Laundry Folding Robots: What Laundromat Operators Need to Know (Cents)
sources.claim: Dyna Robotics has installed its autonomous folding arms in a working laundromat in Sacramento, one of the first commercial deployments of autonomous folding in a laundry facility; systems handle common items (t-shirts, towels, napkins, linens) at roughly 60% of human throughput.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: laying out and folding clean laundry in a laundromat shows garment spreading on a work surface inside a real laundry facility, but no deployed system locates a stain and positions that region on a spotting board.

sources.system: THOR robot separator (with ODIN X-ray / HEIMDAL camera modules)
sources.title: THOR | Robot Separator - Single Piece Separation of Laundry
sources.claim: Inwatec's THOR robot separator autonomously picks single soiled garments, towels and linen out of bulk on the soiled side of industrial laundries using 3D cameras and smart grippers, at 1,200-1,500 pieces per hour; it is installed in commercial laundries.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: singulating and picking arbitrary soiled garments from bulk in a working laundry is the pick-and-present step preceding spreading; same soiled textiles, same facility, but it does not spread items flat or position stains.

sources.system: Quantex flatwork quality-control scanner
sources.title: Quantex: Perfect Quality Control of Flat Linen
sources.claim: Kannegiesser's Quantex camera system on production ironer/folding lines automatically detects stains and holes on ... of flat linen and automatically diverts rejected items, with configurable stain-size and contrast tolerances.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: machine localization of stains on textiles in a production laundry supplies the perception half of 'position stained portions over vacuum heads'; same materials and lighting-controlled line, though the manipulation is only a divert.

sources.system: Dual-arm leather spreading system (YOLOv8-BIFPN grasp-point detection)
sources.developer: Shaanxi University of Science and Technology
sources.title: Efficient leather spreading operations by dual-arm robotic systems (Scientific Reports)
sources.claim: A dual-arm robotic system for spreading leather achieved only a 72% success rate in grasping and spreading irregular hides on a laboratory platform.
sources.transferJustification: Same physical operation (spreading a stiff, irregular hide flat on a table) as spreading leather/suede garments; the 72% success rate is well below the reliability a dry-cleaning employer would accept.

sources.system: Isaac 0
sources.title: Robot folds laundry with remote human help (New Atlas)
sources.claim: Weave Robotics' Isaac 0 laundry-folding robot, shipping in 2026, blends autonomy with remote human teleoperation, with specialists stepping in on garments it cannot handle.
sources.transferJustification: Shows that garment handling outside purpose-built cells still relies on remote human intervention, supporting negative judgments at E2/E3 for varied garment types.

sources.system: π-model-based commercial folding robots at laundry customer sites
sources.title: The Physical Intelligence Layer
sources.claim: Physical Intelligence's partner folding service, operating in laundromats and homes, reports autonomy measured as a percentage of total time with remote specialists intervening to reach presentable folds across varied garment types and fabrics.
sources.transferJustification: Garment handling in real laundry facilities is still partially teleoperated with remote intervention, which supports negative judgments for full-autonomy completion at E2.

tasks.label: Hang, fold, package, and tag finished articles for delivery to customers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Retail dry-cleaning plant: after pressing on a form finisher or utility press, the presser takes each garment (suits, dresses, blouses, pants), hangs it on a wire/plastic hanger, checks the heat-seal barcode tag, matches it to the customer's ticket, groups the pieces of an order on the assembly rack or conveyor, and slips a poly bag over the finished order for the customer counter.

Commercial/industrial laundry (linen and uniform rental): items coming off the ironer/tunnel finisher are folded (towels, sheets, napkins, table linen, scrubs, workwear), counted and stacked to a set pack count, then wrapped/bundled or bagged and labeled by customer for route delivery.

Apparel manufacturing / screen-print or textile-products plant: after final pressing, garments are folded to a spec fold, poly-bagged and sealed, hang tags, size stickers or SKU labels are applied, and units are stacked in cartons by size run for shipment to the retail customer.

On-premise laundry at a hotel, hospital or institution: pressed/finished gowns, table linen and uniforms are folded or hung, sorted by department or floor, and bagged or racked on carts for internal delivery.

Small shop / specialty and odd items: wedding-gown boxing and preservation, drapery, leather, comforters, quilts, uniforms with customer-specific name tags, alterations returns - each item packaged by hand in a non-standard way, hand-tagged and staged for pickup.

sources.claim: Metalprogetti's One Touch Assembly plus the Giulietta auto-bagger is a commercially installed dry-cleaning line that automatically assembles a customer's garments into an order on the conveyor, unloads the completed order and bags and labels it; the only human step is loading incoming garments into free conveyor slots.
