tasks.label: Operate steam, hydraulic, or other pressing machines to remove wrinkles from garments and flatwork items, or to shape, form, or patch articles.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Retail/commercial dry cleaning plant: presser takes laundered dress shirts from a cart, dresses each one onto a single- or double-buck shirt press (aligning collar, placket, yoke, sleeves), cycles the steam/air press, then removes and hangs the finished shirt. High repetition, 40-70 shirts per hour, customer-owned garments of varied size and fabric.

Dry cleaner / garment care plant: finishing trousers, skirts, jackets, coats and uniforms on utility (hot-head) presses, topper/legger units and tensioning form finishers - positioning the garment on the buck or form, setting creases, cycling steam and pressure, touching up with a steam iron before bagging.

Dry cleaner / bridal or specialty shop: hand-guided pressing of delicate or complex items - silk blouses, pleated skirts, beaded gowns, lined tailored wool, vintage garments - on a vacuum buck with iron and steam gun, judging heat, moisture and shine risk fabric by fabric.

Industrial/commercial laundry (hotel, hospital, linen rental): feeding sheets, duvet covers, tablecloths, pillowcases and napkins into flatwork ironer (mangle) lines - presenting corners/edges to the spreader-feeder clamps, running the ironer, and catching/stacking pressed items at the folder end. High volume, fixed line layout.

Apparel or textile-products manufacturing plant: production pressing at a fixed station - under-pressing seams open, fusing interlinings, blocking/shaping collars, cuffs and lapels, and final pressing of finished garments before inspection and packing, working from bundles or a hanging conveyor.

Uniform, embroidery or screen-print shop: using a heat/transfer press to apply patches, emblems, heat-transfer vinyl and name tapes, and to shape or form items (caps, molded panels) - positioning garment and applique by hand, setting time/temperature/pressure, cycling the press and checking adhesion.

sources.system: BLIZZ towel feeding robot (with JENSEN Butterfly folder)

sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic handling of limp textiles and presentation to a finishing machine in a laundry. It supports feeding folders for terry only; the vendor markets no ironer-feeding product, so it does not substantiate autonomous pressing of flatwork.

sources.claim: Even the leading laundry-robotics vendor's clean-side towel product only prepares single towels for a human operator to feed, indicating that feeding finishing/ironing machines in laundries remains an operator job.

tasks.label: Straighten, smooth, or shape materials to prepare them for pressing.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dry-cleaning plant / shirt laundry: presser takes washed shirts one at a time from a cart or conveyor, shakes them out, smooths the body, straightens the placket, aligns collar and cuffs, and positions the garment on the shirt-press buck or body form before the press cycle. High repetition (40-60 shirts/hour), damp cotton and blends, mixed sizes.

Commercial/industrial laundry flatwork: operator pulls tangled sheets, tablecloths, napkins, pillowcases and towels from carts or slings, separates single pieces, finds and squares the leading edge, spreads the piece flat and wrinkle-free, and presents it to the flatwork ironer or folder.

Apparel/textile-product manufacturing finishing department: presser aligns and smooths cut panels, seams and facings on the buck for under-pressing; shapes collars, cuffs, lapels and sleeve heads; positions parts squarely under the head so the press does not set in a crease.

Small dry cleaner or tailor shop, specialty and delicate work: pleated skirts (aligning each pleat), silk and rayon blouses, beaded/embellished pieces, drapery panels, suede and leather; hand-easing fullness, blocking and stretching to shape before hand-pressing or spot pressing. Item-by-item judgment, no two alike.

Bulk plant handling of hung outerwear and large garments: coats, jackets, uniforms, robes and gowns loaded on a form/topper; smoothing the body, squaring shoulders, pulling the hem and sleeves taut and tensioning the garment so it holds its shape for the finishing cycle.

tasks.label: Remove finished pieces from pressing machines and hang or stack them for cooling, or forward them for additional processing.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Retail/commercial dry cleaner or shirt laundry: presser lifts the finished dress shirt off a single- or double-buck shirt unit press, checks it, slides it onto a wire hanger, buttons the collar and hangs it on the assembly rail/conveyor. High cadence (60-100+ shirts/hour), mixed fabrics, sizes and colors, hot damp fabric, cluttered station shared with the press operator.

Dry cleaning / garment care plant: presser takes pants, skirts, jackets, dresses and coats off a legger, topper, utility press or form finisher, straightens them, hangs them on hangers and puts them on a rolling rack or conveyor to cool before assembly and bagging, or moves them to a second press station for touch-up.

Industrial or on-premise (hotel/hospital) laundry flatwork: worker at the discharge end of a flatwork ironer takes off sheets, duvet covers, tablecloths, napkins and pillowcases as they emerge, stacks them in counted piles on a table/cart for cooling, or feeds them onward into the folder/stacker for further processing.

Industrial uniform/workwear laundry: shirts, coveralls and gowns finished on hangers in a tunnel finisher or garment press are taken off the finisher, checked, and forwarded onto sorting/bagging conveyors or assembly rails for the customer batch.

Apparel or textile-product manufacturing plant: operator removes pressed or fused components (collars, cuffs, plackets, pockets, panels, drapery headings) from a buck press, fusing press or steam press, lays them flat to cool and stacks them in bundles or places them on a conveyor/cart for the next sewing operation.

Small dry cleaner or alterations shop, specialty and delicate work: wedding gowns, drapes, pleated skirts, leather/suede, comforters and other bulky or fragile items hand-pressed on a board or puff iron; the worker eases the item off the board, hangs it on a padded hanger or rolling rack to cool, and re-presses areas that shift.

tasks.label: Finish pleated garments, determining sizes of pleats from evidence of old pleats or from work orders, using machine presses or hand irons.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dry-cleaning / garment-care plant: a knife- or accordion-pleated skirt comes off the cleaning machine with its pleats relaxed. The presser reads the faint remaining fold lines to judge pleat width and placement, aligns and clips 15-40 pleats, and presses each with a hand iron on a padded board (often with a press cloth), producing a sharp, evenly spaced pleat set matching the garment's original.

Dry-cleaning / laundry plant: other pleated items - pleated dresses, blouses with pleated fronts, pleated-front trousers, kilts, pleated formalwear - finished on a utility press, puff iron or form plus hand iron, judging pleat size and location from old creases, working around zippers, linings and trim.

Apparel plant or pleating contractor: pleats set into cut fabric panels or yardage to the pleat type, width and depth specified on the work order (e.g., 20 mm knife pleats for a school-uniform skirt), then heat-set so they survive wear and cleaning, before the panels go to sewing.

Apparel plant final pressing: an assembled pleated garment (skirt, dress, pleated-front trouser) gets its pleats touched up and set on a machine press or with a hand iron per the work order, with pleats aligned to seams, hem and waistband before inspection and bagging.

Drapery / home-textile workroom: pinch-, box- or cartridge-pleated drapery panels and valances pressed along the pleat folds with a hand iron on a long table, pleat spacing taken from the work order or from existing fold lines of a re-made panel; heavy lined fabric, long panels.

Bridal, formalwear, costume or alterations shop: delicate or unusual pleating (chiffon, silk, sunburst/crystal pleats, historical costume) hand-pressed at low volume with careful heat control, pleat size copied from surviving pleats or a sketch/work order; every garment different.

tasks.label: Lower irons, rams, or pressing heads of machines into position over material to be pressed.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Retail/plant dry cleaner: presser places a suit jacket, skirt or dress panel on a utility or hot-head press buck and brings the heated head down over that section, repeating section by section; fabric type (wool, silk, synthetic) dictates pressure and dwell, and the head must not crush buttons or trim. Setting: dry-cleaning plant floor with other workers and equipment.

Commercial laundry / dry-cleaner shirt line: laundered shirt loaded onto a shirt-unit buck and a collar-and-cuff press; body, yoke, sleeve, collar and cuff heads and clamps come down over the shirt in sequence at 40-60+ shirts per hour. Setting: laundry finishing room, standard machines, fixed layout.

Trouser and form finishing in a laundry/dry-clean plant: pants topper or legger press heads lowered over waistband, seat and legs after the garment is positioned; also form finishers whose clamps close on the garment. Repetitive, standardized garment types.

Apparel/textile manufacturing plant: under-pressing and fusing of standardized cut parts (collars, cuffs, front panels, waistbands) — component laid on a flat-bed fusing or hot-head press table and the heated head or belt brought down over it for a timed cycle. High repetition, uniform parts.

Screen-print / DTF / heat-transfer decoration shop: garment dressed on a platen, transfer positioned, and the heat head lowered over the garment for a timed press (plus pre-press). Alignment to the print area matters; platens and garment styles change between jobs.

Specialty and detail work: puff iron, hand iron or small press lowered onto delicate or awkward items (bridal gowns, beaded or leather garments, pleats, drapery, alteration touch-ups) where the placement, pressure and dwell of the iron are judged item by item. Setting: cleaner/tailor shop workroom.

tasks.label: Identify and treat spots on garments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dry-cleaning plant spotting board: garment arrives with a stain of unknown origin (wine, grease, ink, makeup, food). Worker inspects under a spotting light, judges fiber/dye and stain class, selects among several spotting agents, tamps or brushes, flushes with the steam gun and vacuum, re-inspects for rings or dye loss before the garment goes to cleaning/pressing.

Presser at a dry-cleaner press station: while pressing shirts, trousers, jackets, spots a small mark on the garment, decides whether to apply a quick pre-spotter/steam-gun flush at the press or tag the piece and route it back to the spotter/rewash, then finishes pressing so the piece is customer-ready.

Industrial/commercial laundry finishing line (hotel linen, healthcare linen, uniform rental): items arrive from the tunnel washer onto the ironer/folder or garment finisher; worker scans each piece for remaining stains and pulls stained items out for rewash or pre-spot treatment while keeping line speed.

Apparel manufacturing / garment finishing plant: newly sewn garments carry sewing-machine oil, grease, marking chalk or handling soil; worker at a spotting table uses a solvent spot gun with air/vacuum to remove the mark, then presses the garment for shipment.

Specialty and delicate work (wedding gowns, silk blouses, wool coats, beaded or leather-trimmed items) at a dry cleaner or specialty plant: worker tests colorfastness on a hidden area, chooses mild chemistry and low-pressure application, and works the spot slowly to avoid fabric or trim damage.

tasks.label: Shrink, stretch, or block articles by hand to conform to original measurements, using forms, blocks, and steam.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dry-cleaning / wet-cleaning plant: an everyday garment (wool coat, suit jacket, dress, trousers, knit top) that has shrunk or gone limp in cleaning is revitalized back toward its original dimensions — mounted on a body form or dolly, hem/sleeve clamps set, then steamed and air-stretched until the seams and body come back to size.

Dry cleaner / garment-restoration workroom: a shrunken or stretched-out knit (cashmere sweater, hand-knit, knit dress) is hand-blocked flat on a padded board — dampened/steamed, eased and pinned out to the customer's original measurements, then left to set. Each piece differs in fiber, gauge and amount of distortion.

Hosiery mill finishing department: socks and tights are boarded — pulled over heated foot/leg forms and steam-set to the size and shape on the spec sheet before pairing and packing. High volume, standard sizes, repetitive.

Knitwear/apparel factory finishing: sweaters, knit panels and collars are steam-blocked on forms, bucks or marked blocking tables to the measurement chart for the size (chest, length, sleeve) before assembly or final packing.

Hat shop, western-wear store, millinery or hat-renovation bench: a felt or straw hat is steamed and blocked over a wooden/aluminum block, the crown pressed and the brim stretched, to bring it back to its original size and shape.

Specialty/oversized delicate work: lace curtains, tablecloths, embroidered panels, tapestries, veils and wedding-gown skirts are stretched and pinned on frames or blocking boards to their original dimensions with hand steam, worked slowly to avoid tearing or distorting the piece.

tasks.label: Finish fancy garments such as evening gowns and costumes, using hand irons to produce high quality finishes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dry-cleaning plant / garment-care shop finishing station: presser final-presses a cleaned silk, satin or crepe evening or cocktail gown with a hand iron and press cloth on a padded vacuum board — pressing lining, bodice seams, hems and pleats without leaving shine, iron marks or seam imprints, then bagging it for customer pickup.

Dry-cleaning plant: plain, unembellished long dress/evening gown in a steam-tolerant fabric (polyester, rayon, knit) that only needs wrinkles removed and shape restored to a customer-ready standard; no structured bodice, beading or pleat setting.

Bridal shop or specialty cleaner: steaming and hand-pressing a heavily embellished gown — beaded/sequined bodice, lace appliqué, multi-layer tulle skirt and train — working layer by layer, using low heat, press cloths and pressing tools around trims that cannot take direct iron contact.

Theatrical, dance or film costume shop / wardrobe room: pressing costumes of mixed and unusual fabrics (velvet, taffeta, brocade, period garments with boning and trims) before fittings or performances — pressing seams open on point pressers and hams, setting ruffles and cuffs, touching up quickly between calls.

Couture atelier or high-end apparel manufacturer: in-process and final hand pressing of an evening gown — pressing seams open over a sleeve board, shaping darts and curved seams over a ham, setting pleats and hems with a hand iron and clapper on a vacuum table before final inspection and shipping.

instances.label: Dry-clean plant / uniform finishing department: after machine pressing, the presser slides jacket, blazer and coat shoulders, sleeve caps and armhole seams back and forth over a steam-heated shoulder or sleeve puff iron to smooth the curved areas; wool and blended suiting, garments arrive on a rail in mixed sizes and styles.

Dry cleaner / laundry: mainstream blouses, dresses and skirts (polyester, rayon, cotton blends) — presser works gathered shoulder seams, sleeve caps, bust darts and curved side seams over an egg or mushroom puff form to finish areas the flat press cannot reach.

Dry cleaner / specialty finisher: delicate or detailed garments — silk blouses, chiffon overlays, heavily gathered or puffed sleeves, ruffles and soft pleats — pressed over the ball form with light contact, constant fabric shifting and heat judgment to avoid shine, scorch or crushing of the gathers.

Apparel manufacturing finishing department: production runs of the same style — the presser under-presses and finishes sleeve heads, shoulders, armholes and curved seams of jackets, coats or tailored tops over heated ball/last forms at a fixed pressing station, at line takt.

Bridal, formalwear and costume shop: one-off gowns and dresses with beading, boning, layered skirts and heavy gathers; the presser works curved bodice, shoulder and sleeve areas over the ball form, supporting the garment weight by hand and judging each area individually.

Tailor / alteration shop attached to a cleaner or retailer: post-alteration touch-up of individual customer garments — reshaping a shoulder, easing a resewn sleeve cap, pressing a dart tip or a curved yoke over the puff iron, different garment type and area on almost every piece.

tasks.label: Spray water over fabric to soften fibers when not using steam irons.

instances.label: Retail dry cleaner / neighborhood laundry: presser lays a shirt, trousers or jacket on the press buck, mists water from a hand spray bottle over stubborn wrinkles, set-in creases or dry-cleaned wool before pressing with a dry (non-steam) head; garments vary item to item, customer turnaround same-day.

Industrial laundry / linen and uniform plant: operator sprays or dampens flatwork (sheets, tablecloths, napkins) and uniform garments that have come out too dry, before feeding an ironer or press line; high volume, standardized items, fixed stations.

Garment manufacturing finishing/under-pressing department: worker mists water over wool or cotton panels, seams and lapels to relax and swell fibers before hand-iron or buck pressing during assembly and final press; repetitive, same style repeated across a run.

Alterations, tailoring, bridal or costume shop: selective, careful misting of delicate or specialty fabrics (silk, linen, wool crepe, beaded gowns) on one-off garments, judging how much water each fabric tolerates to avoid water-spotting or shrinkage before pressing.

On-location pressing: hotel back-of-house/guest room, retail sales floor, film or theatre set, or drapery pressed at a customer's site; presser dampens fabric with a spray bottle in a space taken as found, sometimes on hanging or installed fabric.

tasks.label: Position materials such as cloth garments, felt, or straw on tables, dies, or feeding mechanisms of pressing machines, or on ironing boards or work tables.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dry cleaner / laundry shirt unit: presser takes a washed dress shirt from a cart, opens it, slides the body over the buck or form, aligns placket, yoke and side seams, sets sleeves, and positions collar and cuffs in the tensioning collar-and-cuff press clamps; mixed fabrics, sizes and styles, ~30-60 shirts/hour.

Trousers, skirts and jackets on form-type presses: pulling pants over a topper form and setting the waistband, then laying each leg on the legger buck squared to the existing crease; or dressing a jacket/dress on a form finisher. Garment-specific alignment, no two garments identical.

Utility / hot-head press: laying one section of a garment at a time flat on the padded buck (jacket panel, sleeve on a sleeve board, uniform, drape, curtain), smoothing it, pressing, then repositioning for the next section through 5-15 cycles; must avoid setting false creases in tailored or delicate goods.

Ironing board / work table hand pressing and touch-up: spreading a shirt, blouse, table linen or lightly wrinkled garment flat and smooth on the board or table, then repositioning and flipping it through the ironing pass before hanging.

Commercial/industrial laundry finishing line: taking washed towels, napkins, table linens and sheets from carts or a conveyor and placing them onto the feeding conveyor or corner clamps of a flatwork ironer or folder at line speed.

Apparel/textile manufacturing: positioning cut fabric parts, interlinings, felt blanks or straw bodies on the die, table or feed conveyor of a fusing press, heat-transfer press, block or molding press, to a marked registration, then removing the pressed part.

tasks.label: Moisten materials to soften and smooth them.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dry-cleaning plant pressing station: presser takes cleaned suits, dresses, skirts and trousers from the rail, dampens them with a water spray bottle or the press's steam pedal/steam gun to relax fibers, smooths the fabric over the buck and presses. Mixed fabrics and sizes, high throughput, garments arrive on hangers.

Commercial/institutional laundry shirt line: operator moistens collars, cuffs, plackets and shirt bodies with steam spray (or works with damp-from-wash shirts) and smooths them onto a shirt press/collar-cuff unit; standardized items, hundreds per shift.

Apparel manufacturing plant, under-pressing and final pressing: operator steams/dampens fabric panels, seams and finished garments of one repeated style to soften, shape and smooth them before the next sewing step or before bagging.

Textile/piece-goods and household-textile work: dampening or conditioning yardage, drapery panels, table linen or fabric rolls with water spray/steam so the material softens and lies flat before pressing, calendering or shaping.

Small dry cleaner, tailor or alterations shop handling delicate and one-off items: hand steamer or fine mist applied by judgment to bridal gowns, pleated silks, velvet, wool coats, suede/leather and felt hats, moisture dosed to each material to avoid water spotting or shrinkage, then smoothed or blocked by hand.

sources.transferJustification: Related task is garment finishing; the steam-chamber stage is exactly this task's act of moistening material so it softens and smooths, applied to the same garments a presser handles.

tasks.label: Clean and maintain pressing machines, using cleaning solutions and lubricants.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: End-of-shift cleaning of a garment press (utility, legger, topper) in a retail dry-cleaning plant: wipe the pressing head and buck with cleaning solution, scrub off starch/soil/scorch buildup on the head, brush lint and threads from the vacuum grate and buck cover, wipe steam lines and controls, drain condensate. Cramped shop floor, hot machine, mixed press models.

Cleaning hand-iron / steam-iron equipment at a pressing station in a garment plant or laundry: clean the soleplate with iron cleaner or a cleaning stick, clear clogged steam holes, wipe the vacuum board cover and steam gun, flush/descale the condensate and water filter. Fixed workstation, standard equipment.

Scheduled lubrication per the manufacturer's manual: oil or grease press pivots, hinges, linkages, latch mechanisms, air-cylinder rods, chains and bearings at listed points; top up the air-line lubricator and check oil levels; wipe off excess. Machine locked out, points in tight or partly enclosed locations.

Cleaning and maintaining a flatwork ironer/mangle in a commercial or hotel laundry: remove lint and fiber buildup from rolls, chest and tapes, clean the chest surface, apply ironer wax, wipe and lubricate the chain drives and bearings. Large fixed machine, long working surfaces, high heat.

Deeper periodic maintenance: replace worn press pads and buck covers (fabric/felt stretched and clipped), swap air/lint filters, clean or replace steam trap screens and nozzles, tighten fasteners and replace small worn parts, requiring partial disassembly and reassembly of the press.

sources.system: Cold Jet automated/robotic dry ice blasting cells

sources.claim: Cold Jet sells fully automated dry ice cleaning ... in which a robotic arm and blaster clean production tooling and machine surfaces (molds, weld-cell fixtures and equipment) of residue inside an enclosed automated cell.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: removing baked-on residue and release agents from press tooling and machine surfaces. A garment press head/platen carries the same kind of scorched starch and soil film on a metal surface; a fixtured cleaning cell removes it without a human wiping it.

tasks.label: Press ties on small pressing machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Retail/wholesale dry cleaning plant: customer neckties returned from cleaning are pressed one at a time on a small utility press or tie press between other garments. Widths, lengths, fabrics (silk, wool, poly) and constructions vary; presser judges heat/steam, aligns the tie centered and untwisted, avoids flattening rolled edges or leaving seam impressions, then hangs/bags it.

Commercial laundry or uniform-rental plant: batches of identical uniform ties (school, hotel, restaurant, military contracts) pressed on a small press at a steady piece rate; items are uniform in size and fabric, work arrives in bundles or on a rail, output goes to a hanging rail or bagging station.

Necktie or apparel manufacturing plant: newly sewn ties are finished on small tie pressing machines (tip/edge presses, shaped forms) as a station on the production line; standard styles in known sizes, high throughput, pressed items stacked in a bin for the next station.

Nonstandard and problem items on the same small press: knit ties, bow ties, hand-rolled or vintage/damaged ties, heavily creased or previously badly pressed ties, plus small odd items (ascots, sashes). Requires per-item judgment, low heat/steam-only treatment, hand shaping and re-inspection.

Small shop or on-premise laundry (alterations shop, hotel valet department): occasional tie pressed on a small press or steam form amid other pressing work, with the worker fetching the item, setting the machine, pressing and returning it to the customer rack.

sources.system: Stiratrice NICO 4 (tie pressing machine)
sources.title: STIRATRICE NICO 4 – Frigerio e Corazza
sources.claim: Frigerio e Corazza's Nico 4 is a commercial necktie pressing machine used in tie manufacturing: independent heated plates, vacuum suction that clamps the tie to the plate, mechanical clamping for closed/two-sided ties, four adjustable laser pointers for edge alignment, microprocessor and touch-screen programs selectable by fabric, and a bin for pressed ties with an assisted discharge system; it presses two-sided, four-sided and seven-fold ties. The operator lays the tie on the plate; the clamp/steam/vacuum press cycle and discharge are machine-controlled.
sources.transferJustification: This is the exact task object and operation — pressing neckties on a small pressing machine — with the workpiece held in a known position by vacuum/mechanical clamps and the press cycle run from stored programs; only the lay-up of the tie is done by a person, which at E1 is the environment's presentation of the work.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: machine pressing of a flat garment laid out on a plate. It shows that once a textile item is presented in a fixture, transport into the press, the steam/vacuum press cycle and unloading of the finished piece run under machine control at production quality — the same sequence a tie press requires.

tasks.label: Block or shape knitted garments after cleaning.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Retail/small dry cleaner or laundry: an ordinary machine-knit wool, cotton or acrylic sweater comes off the wet-clean or dry-clean cycle and must be reshaped - laid flat on a padded blocking/vacuum table, eased to its original body and sleeve measurements, cuffs, hem ribbing and neckline smoothed, steamed with a hand iron or steam gun, then dried flat. Garments arrive one at a time in mixed fibers and sizes.

Dry-cleaning plant or laundry finishing department: knit tops, sweaters, polos and knit dresses are shaped on a steam-air form finisher/dummy or puff iron - the presser dresses the garment onto the form, sets clamps, sleeve supports and tension, runs the programmed steam/air cycle, touches up cuffs and collar, and hangs the finished piece. Steady production pace.

Delicate or high-value hand-knits: cashmere, lace shawls, open-work or beaded/embellished knits, vintage and hand-made pieces pinned out to schematic or customer-specified dimensions on a blocking board with T-pins or blocking wires, lightly steamed, and left to dry for hours; the presser judges how far each area may be stretched and where pressure or steam must be avoided.

Re-stretch/restoration job: a knit that has shrunk, felted or distorted in cleaning is dampened (sometimes with a relaxing agent) and worked back to its original measurements on a stretcher frame or blocking table, checked repeatedly against the tag size or the customer's measurements, then re-steamed and dried; a customer-complaint job with a quality bar set by the original garment.

High-volume industrial finishing: a commercial laundry or knitwear finishing plant batch-processes knit garments after washing - pieces are spread on steam/vacuum knit press tables or dummies feeding a conveyor line, pressed, blocked to size and dried at rates of hundreds of garments per hour, with standardized sizes and repetitive styles.

tasks.label: Activate and adjust machine controls to regulate temperature and pressure of rollers, ironing shoes, or plates, according to specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Commercial dry cleaning plant / shirt laundry: presser powers up utility presses, form finishers, leggers and shirt units at shift start, sets steam and air pressure, buck/head temperature and cycle timers, and re-adjusts through the day for mixed customer garments (wool suits, silk blouses, poly blends), judging by fabric type and inspection of finished pieces.

Industrial/commercial laundry (hotel, healthcare, linen supply): operator activates a flatwork ironer line and sets roll/chest temperature, ironing speed and contact pressure for the linen category being run (sheets, duvets, tablecloths, towels), adjusting during the run when linen comes off damp or over-dried.

Apparel manufacturing plant: operator sets up a fusing press or final-press machine for a production order — temperature, pressure and dwell/belt speed per the fabric-and-interlining spec sheet — runs test bonds, then adjusts settings when bond strength or fabric appearance is off.

Uniform-rental / garment-processing plant: operator activates tunnel finishers, toppers and form finishers and sets steam/air temperature, blower pressure and tension per garment program for batches of scrubs, gowns, coveralls and workwear.

Small shop (tailor/alterations, bridal, costume, boutique on-premises laundry): worker sets the hand iron or steam-generator thermostat and the buck press pressure/steam valves — often older manual equipment — for varied, one-off and delicate items (beaded gown, vintage wool, pleated skirt), adjusting by feel and test pressing.

sources.system: Kannegiesser SmartLaundry / central program control (X6, SmartConnect ironer lines)
sources.title: Step by step to SmartLaundry: Kannegiesser - Global
sources.claim: Kannegiesser SmartLaundry process control assigns finishing programs to machines from the batch database; once the program is set, the ironer itself takes the correct speed, contact pressure and temperature for the laundry category — the regulation this task describes, done by machine control in working industrial laundries.

sources.system: Kannegiesser SmartLaundry automatic program setting via ticket/barcode

sources.claim: In uniform-rental/healthcare garment plants every article is machine-identified (barcode/RFID married to its hanger) and each garment type has a defined finishing process through X-MT tunnel finishers, presses and folders on an automated transport system.

tasks.label: Use covering cloths to prevent equipment from damaging delicate fabrics.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dry-cleaning plant finishing department: presser lays a muslin/cotton press cloth over a delicate wool suit panel, silk blouse, or acetate lining laid on the buck of a hot-head/utility press, closes the head for the steam-and-press cycle, lifts the cloth, checks for shine or scorch, and repeats around the garment. Garments arrive continuously on hangers, all different, at production pace.

Hand touch-up at an ironing board or vacuum table in a dry cleaner, alterations shop, or bridal/retail workroom: worker positions a delicate item (embroidery, appliqué, sequins, lace, silk, velvet) and irons through a press cloth or Teflon shoe, repositioning the cloth repeatedly as work moves around collars, plackets, and trims.

Apparel/textile manufacturing finishing line: operator lays a Teflon or silicone-treated cover sheet over printed graphics, heat-sensitive synthetics, or fusible seams on each of hundreds of near-identical units at a fixed press station, cycles the press with a foot pedal, and removes the sheet; highly repetitive and standardized.

Specialty high-value items in a shop back room: beaded eveningwear, bridal gowns, leather/suede, vintage or heirloom textiles pressed on a table or mushroom press with selected covering cloths, with judgment about cloth type, dampness, and heat, and zero tolerance for damage to an irreplaceable item.

Equipment set-up/maintenance: fitting or replacing clean protective covering cloths and pads on press bucks, mushroom and sleeve pressers, and Teflon shoes on iron soleplates at shift start or when covers become soiled or scorched.

On-location pressing/steaming: wardrobe or drapery work at a film/event site, showroom, or client premises, where garments are pressed with covering cloths on a portable board or table in a space taken as found.

sources.system: SpeedFolding (ABB YuMi bimanual robot)
sources.developer: UC Berkeley AUTOLAB / KIT (Avigal, Berscheid, Asfour, Kröger, Goldberg)
sources.title: SpeedFolding - Learning Efficient Bimanual Folding of Garments (IROS 2022)
sources.claim: SpeedFolding (ABB YuMi bimanual cell) autonomously manipulates a crumpled garment into a smooth, flat canonical configuration and then folds it, 93% success in under 120s, generalizing to unseen garments of different color, shape and stiffness — evidence that a fixed robotic workcell can grasp a limp cloth and lay it out smoothly and reliably.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: smoothing/flattening a limp fabric on a work surface. Placing a press cloth over a garment requires the same core competence — grasp a limp cloth, lay it out wrinkle-free over a defined area — with comparable object properties (garment-weight woven fabric) in a fixed workcell.

sources.system: bullmer AWM 2000 / Compact E600 automatic spreading machines
sources.title: AWM 2000 - Automatic spreading machine by bullmer
sources.claim: Bullmer AWM 2000 automatic spreading machines lay textile plies from a roll onto a cutting table with sensor-monitored, tension-free, high-precision spreading, including sensitive fabrics; a purpose-built machine that covers a work surface with a smooth layer of cloth without human hands.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: laying a length of cloth flat and wrinkle-free over a work surface in a purpose-built cell. A press-cloth cover in an E1 press cell is the same operation — cloth fed and spread smoothly over the fixtured workpiece before the head closes — with the same fabric handling and evenness requirement.

sources.system: DRF Spreader Feeder (flatwork ironer line)
sources.title: Finishing and Folding Systems | Industrial Finishing Systems
sources.claim: Commercial spreader/feeder machines in industrial laundries automatically straighten and spread flatwork linen and feed it into a heated ironer at >1,200 large pieces per hour, demonstrating machine-controlled spreading of limp cloth immediately before a hot pressing stage.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: mechanically spreading a limp cloth flat and presenting it to a hot press. This is the mechanical core of laying a covering cloth over goods entering a press, performed at commercial reliability in purpose-built machinery.

sources.system: π0 generalist robot policy (fixed dual-arm and mobile manipulators)

sources.claim: Physical Intelligence's π0 policy autonomously folds laundry with a fixed pair of arms or a mobile manipulator, flattening and manipulating varied garments from a crumpled state in uncut, fully autonomous runs.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous manipulation of limp garments and cloths (grasp, flatten, place) in a fixed workcell — the same class of deformable-object handling required to pick a press cloth and drape it over a garment presented on a buck.

sources.system: Presso EcoRobo automated garment care machine

sources.claim: Presso's EcoRobo is a commercially deployed, purpose-built automated garment-finishing cabinet that tensions and steam-presses garments to a finished state without a skilled presser, i.e. a machine-built environment in which delicate garments are finished without contact-press damage.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: finishing/pressing garments without damaging the fabric, in a purpose-built machine cell. It shows the pressing half of the instance is achieved commercially in an E1 setting, so the remaining requirement is only the automated placement of a protective cover layer.

sources.system: Bedding/blanket manipulation systems (Puthuveetil et al., 'Bodies Uncovered' / RoBE; Berkeley bed-making)

sources.claim: A peer-reviewed review of robotic cloth manipulation reports autonomous robotic systems that grasp and smooth bedsheets and that autonomously cover and uncover a person in bed with a blanket — i.e. draping a cloth over a target region has been done autonomously by real robots.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: draping a sheet/blanket over a shaped target so that a chosen region is covered. Covering a garment area with a press cloth is the same manipulation — placing a flat cloth over a specific region of a 3D object — at similar scale and precision.

sources.system: TEO humanoid ironing robot

sources.claim: The humanoid TEO autonomously detects wrinkles with 3D perception and force feedback and reduces them using an unmodified household iron on an ironing board, but only as a laboratory research demonstration far below commercial pressing quality and speed.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: operating human pressing tools on fabric. It is the closest robotic work to hand pressing, and it shows the human-tool, human-station (E2) version remains a slow research demonstration, not worker-quality work.

tasks.label: Examine and measure finished articles to verify conformance to standards, using measuring devices such as tape measures and micrometers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Retail dry cleaner / neighborhood laundry: after pressing shirts, trousers, skirts and simple tops, the presser examines each piece under shop lighting for remaining wrinkles, scorch, spots the cleaning missed, and torn/missing hardware, occasionally checking a hem or sleeve length with a tape against the ticket before bagging; nonconforming pieces go back for re-press or re-clean.

Retail dry cleaner / bridal-formal shop: presser examines structured or delicate finished pieces on hangers or forms - suit jackets and coats, lined dresses, pleated skirts, gowns, drapery panels - judging lapel roll, crease placement, pleat spacing (sometimes measured with a tape), shine or impression marks from the press, and fabric damage.

Commercial/industrial laundry (hotel, hospital, restaurant linen): finisher inspects ironed and folded flatwork - sheets, duvet covers, tablecloths, napkins - as it leaves the ironer/folder line, checking for stains, holes, tears, creases and wrong size/fold, and pulling nonconforming pieces for rewash or discard.

Industrial laundry / uniform rental: after tunnel finishing or pressing, worker inspects workwear and uniform garments hanging on a monorail or rack - checking press finish, seams, buttons/zippers, damage, and that the garment matches the size and wearer label - before it is bagged for delivery.

Apparel manufacturing final press/finishing area: after final pressing, the worker lays the garment flat on the table and measures spec points (chest, body length, sleeve length, shoulder, waist, inseam) with a tape against the buyer's spec sheet and tolerance, records values, and passes or rejects the piece.

Textile products manufacturing (curtains, table linens, fused/laminated or molded pressed pieces): after pressing/fusing, worker measures finished panel dimensions with a tape and material thickness or bond gauge with a micrometer against the shop standard, then accepts, re-presses, or scraps the piece.

sources.system: Kannegiesser Quantex
sources.title: Quantex: Perfect Quality Control of Flat Linen: Kannegiesser - USA (EN)
sources.claim: Kannegiesser Quantex is a commercial camera scan system mounted on folding machines of industrial-laundry ironer lines that inspects every finished piece of flat linen for stains and holes on both ... and physically separates rejected items into trolleys or onto reject conveyors.

sources.system: Kannegiesser Quantex / Quantex Dry Work
sources.title: Quantex – Systematic quality control: Kannegiesser - USA (EN)
sources.claim: Quantex also detects wrinkles, creases, alignment problems and edge irregularities on flat linen at ironer speeds up to 60 m/min, with per-article tolerance settings, and automatically routes flawed items for rewash or disposal - i.e. it performs the examine-and-conformance-decision step for finished pressed textiles.

sources.system: Kannegiesser Quantex camera scanner at Royal Jersey Laundry
sources.developer: Herbert Kannegiesser GmbH / Royal Jersey Laundry
sources.title: How AI is shaping our industry’s future - Laundry & Cleaning Today
sources.claim: Quantex is deployed in a working commercial laundry (Royal Jersey Laundry, Dagenham UK), where it replaced the human end-of-line quality check on folded linen, detecting creases, damage and stains to customer-specific criteria; the operator bought two additional units.

sources.system: Yunji Zhihui garment visual inspection and measurement machine
sources.developer: Dongguan Yunji Zhihui Technology Co., Ltd.
sources.title: Finally AI in manufacturing: Garment measurement inspection in a flash
sources.claim: Dongguan Yunji Zhihui's garment visual inspection and measurement machine conveys a garment laid flat on its belt past a vision system and automatically returns all spec-point measurements plus a Pass/Fail verdict in about six seconds (15 measured dimensions on a T-shirt, claimed error within ±1 mm, 4,800 pieces per 480 minutes).

sources.system: sewts.VELUM (FANUC M-10iD robots, IDS 3D cameras)
sources.title: Intelligent robots for commercial laundries - IFR case study
sources.claim: sewts VELUM, a two-arm FANUC robot cell with 3D vision, autonomously picks crumpled laundered textiles, identifies seams and corners, and spreads/feeds them crease-free into folding machines in a commercial laundry at human-comparable throughput.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic pick-and-spread of limp finished textiles in an industrial laundry. It shows that presenting individual finished textile articles flat and wrinkle-free to an inline inspection/folding machine can be done autonomously in a purpose-built cell, which is the handling half of examine-and-measure at E1.

sources.system: Inwatec ODIN.Xray
sources.title: Fully automatic sorting of Soiled Workwear | Inwatec
sources.claim: Inwatec ODIN.Xray inspects individual garments in industrial laundries and automatically rejects nonconforming ones at up to 2,200 items per ..., but its inspection target is foreign objects inside soiled workwear, not press finish or finished-garment dimensions.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated per-garment inspection with automatic rejection inside a laundry. Cited only to show what garment-level automated inspection currently covers (foreign objects in soiled workwear); it does not cover finish quality or dimensional conformance of pressed garments.

tasks.label: Finish velvet garments by steaming them on bucks of hot-head presses or steam tables, and brushing pile (nap) with handbrushes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Commercial dry cleaning / garment care plant: after cleaning, a velvet dress, blazer or jacket is finished on a steam-air form finisher or steam table. The presser steams without letting the head or table crush the pile (needle board or steam-only, no pressure), works panel by panel and around seams, buttons and linings, then brushes the warm, damp pile with a handbrush in the nap direction, inspects for crush marks/water spotting, and hangs the garment for the customer.

Apparel manufacturing finishing department: repeated velvet styles come off the line in volume; the presser lays each garment or panel on the buck of a hot-head press or steam table (often over a needle board), applies steam with little or no pressure, repositions the garment several times to cover sleeves, fronts and seams, brushes the pile with a handbrush to set the nap uniformly in one direction, and hangs for QC and packing.

Small storefront dry cleaner or tailor shop back room: one utility press plus a hand steamer; miscellaneous velvet items (holiday dresses, velvet blazers, velvet collars/trims on wool coats, velveteen children's wear) arrive one at a time, with cramped space, varying garment construction, and touch-up steaming and hand brushing done between other pressing work.

Specialty work — costume/theatrical wardrobe, bridal or couture salon, vintage restoration: crushed, embellished or antique velvet garments needing judgment about heat and moisture, localized steaming to raise flattened pile, careful work around beading, boning and linings, and patient brushing to restore nap without abrading fibers.

Large velvet pieces in a plant: velvet drapery panels, capes, choir robes or theatrical drops laid over wide steam tables; the worker manages heavy bulky yardage, steams section by section, and brushes long runs of pile to a uniform lay before folding or hanging.

sources.system: Presso EcoRobo / StretchAI garment care machine
sources.title: Presso's EcoRobo Garment Care Technology
sources.claim: Presso's EcoRobo garment care cabinet performs a programmed finishing cycle using robotic tensioning wires and steam; it is a commercially deployed machine in hotels, apartment buildings and garment care shops. It presses/refreshes garments but there is no pile (nap) brushing function and no evidence of velvet finishing.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated steam pressing/finishing of garments. Transfer is partial only: the cycle applies steam to a garment a human has hung inside the cabinet, and the machine has no brush and no pile-direction sensing, so it cannot deliver the brushed-nap output that defines velvet finishing.

sources.system: Presso garment care machine
sources.title: Dry clean your clothes in this climate startup's vending machine
sources.claim: In the Presso machine, a human user positions the garment inside and enters fabric/size information before the automated cycle runs; the machine does not pick up, position, or reposition garments itself.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: machine garment finishing. Shows the loading/positioning and any garment-specific handling remains human, so the machine cannot substitute for the presser's manipulation of the garment on a buck.

sources.system: Figure 02 humanoid with Helix VLA
sources.title: Helix Learns to Fold Laundry
sources.claim: Figure's Helix VLA model folds towels fully autonomously from a mixed pile, described by the developer as a first for humanoids and one of the hardest dexterous manipulation problems; the demonstration is a lab/office table setup with flat towels, not garment steaming or nap brushing.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous manipulation of deformable textiles. It marks the frontier of general-purpose robot cloth handling — folding flat towels — well short of steaming a velvet garment on a press buck and brushing its pile at commercial quality.

sources.system: Robotic Assembly of Garments (Sewbo/Siemens/Bluewater Defense ARM project)
sources.title: Robotics innovation is key to reshoring the $1T apparel manufacturing industry
sources.claim: An ARM Institute-funded robotic garment assembly project found industrial robots could not handle limp apparel fabric directly and had to laminate garment pieces with a water-soluble stiffening polymer to make robotic handling possible, in a factory sewing context.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic handling of garment fabric in an apparel factory. It shows that even in a purpose-built industrial cell, limp fabric handling requires artificially stiffening the material — an option unavailable for finishing a completed velvet garment.

sources.system: Inwatec Robot Separator (THOR) / ODIN sorting line
sources.title: Fully automatic sorting of Soiled Workwear | Inwatec
sources.claim: Inwatec's robot separator, deployed in industrial laundry plants, autonomously picks and separates individual soiled garments from conveyor-fed bulk and passes them to X-ray and vision sorting. Deployed laundry-plant robotics handle sorting and feeding, not pressing, steaming or napped-fabric finishing.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous garment handling inside a structured laundry facility. It establishes what deployed plant robots actually do — grasp and singulate garments — and that no comparable deployed system performs press finishing or pile brushing.

sources.system: TEO humanoid robotic ironing
sources.developer: Universidad Carlos III de Madrid (Estevez et al.)
sources.title: Robotic ironing with a humanoid robot using human tools
sources.claim: Academic robotic ironing work with a humanoid using an ordinary iron and ironing board remains a laboratory demonstration on flat garments; no evaluation against commercial finishing quality and no handling of pile fabrics.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic pressing/ironing of garments. The demonstration is lab-scale on flat cloth with a household iron, far from steaming a velvet garment on a hot-head press buck and brushing the pile to a saleable finish.

tasks.label: Measure fabric to specifications, cut uneven edges with shears, fold material, and press it with an iron to form a heading.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Custom drapery/curtain workroom (small shop): a one-off panel of decorator fabric is spread on a long work table, measured to the customer's finished length, the uneven cut edge is trimmed square with shears, the top is folded down over buckram (double fold) and pressed with a hand iron to set the heading before stitching. Fabrics vary (sheers, linings, velvets); each order is a different size.

Curtain / home-textile manufacturing plant: batch run of panels cut from rolls. Worker measures/marks each panel to the spec sheet, trims uneven ends, folds the top heading allowance and presses it at a pressing station (hand iron or buck press) so the heading holds its crease for the sewing operators downstream.

Dry cleaner / commercial laundry drapery department: laundered or dry-cleaned drapes are re-measured to finished length, frayed or uneven edges trimmed with shears, the heading refolded and pressed with an iron/press so the panel hangs to the original specification before rehanging or delivery.

Apparel or soft-goods finishing station: a component (valance, bed-skirt, banner, shower curtain top, garment hem/waistband) is measured to spec, the uneven raw edge trimmed with shears, folded to the marked depth and pressed with an iron to form the finished heading/hem edge presented for sewing or shipment.

On-site work at a client's home, office or hotel room: drapery already hung is measured in place, a hem or heading is trimmed and re-folded, and touch-up pressing is done with a hand iron/steamer against a board or the hanging panel, working around furniture and fixtures.

sources.system: HCW SA-VC3836 Auto Vertical Curtain Trimming Machine
sources.title: SA-VC3836 Auto Vertical Curtain Trimming Machine - HCW Automated Curtain Sewing
sources.claim: Commercial automatic curtain trimming machine measures a clamped curtain panel to a preset height with servo control and trims the excess fabric with a rotary cutter, producing a precisely measured panel ready for top hemming; 35-50 panels/hour.

sources.system: HCW SB-FEC-1736 Fully Automatic End Cutting Machine

sources.claim: Fully automatic end-cutting machine pulls fabric from the roll, cuts curtain panels to an operator-set length and count, and stacks them on a conveyor for the next process at about 4 panels per minute.

sources.claim: Fully automatic curtain hemming machine with conveyor and rear fabric clamp folds and stitches curtain hems, marketed specifically for sample and made-to-order curtains produced in small batches with varying hem requirements.

sources.system: HCW S-CT450 Fully Automatic Curtain Pinch Pleating Machine
sources.title: S-CT450 Fully Automatic Curtain Pinch Pleating Machine
sources.claim: Fully automatic pinch-pleating machine uses a robotic arm to hold a whole curtain panel, forms the heading pleats automatically and feeds them to the sewing head without an operator controlling the feed.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: forming the pleated heading of a curtain. It shows automated handling of a full limp curtain panel and machine formation of the heading, the same fold-and-set operation the presser performs by hand.

sources.system: HCW S-ATS-2B-NH Automatic Dual Head Towel Sewing Machine With Heat Pressing
sources.title: S-ATS-2B-NH Automatic Dual Head Towel Sewing Machine With Heat Pressing
sources.claim: Automatic dual-head hemming machine for home textiles combines sewing with heat pressing, described as automatic ironing and shaping of the fabric, running 800-1000 pieces per hour.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: hemming flat home textiles. The machine folds the edge and heat-presses it in one automatic cycle - the same fold-and-press-to-set-a-crease operation used to form a heading, on comparable limp fabric.

sources.system: TEXPA automatic home-textile lines (e.g. FITTED C90-360)
sources.title: Home - TEXPA / World premiere: TEXPA innovation produces fitted sheets
sources.claim: Manufacturer of fully automatic production lines for home textiles that cut, sew, fold and package the goods; its fitted-sheet line runs from the roll to the finished product using robot systems for personnel-independent production.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated manufacture of flat home textiles (sheets, covers, curtains). It establishes that measuring/cutting from the roll, hemming/folding and finishing of large limp panels runs unattended in purpose-built lines.

sources.system: Chicago Dryer Edge / King Edge feeders with ironers and folders
sources.title: Products | Chicago Dryer
sources.claim: Industrial laundry finishing lines automatically spread, present, iron (press) and fold flatwork such as sheets and table linen; feeders provide automated high-volume presentation into ironing and folding equipment.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: pressing and folding laundered flat textiles. Comparable limp large-panel material and the same press/fold output; establishes that laundries already press and fold such goods by machine rather than by hand iron.

sources.system: Macpi 255 automatic pressing unit
sources.title: 255 - KNITTED CLOTHES IRONING | Macpi
sources.claim: Automatic pressing unit for knitted garments with conveyor feed presses garments in an automatic cycle after preparation on a working plate, with automatic unloading.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: machine pressing of textile articles in a factory. Demonstrates that the pressing step itself is performed to commercial quality by automatic conveyor-fed presses rather than a hand iron.

sources.system: TEO humanoid robot ironing
sources.title: Robotic ironing with a humanoid robot using human tools | IEEE Xplore
sources.claim: Research humanoid robot ironed garments autonomously with an unmodified household iron and ironing board, a laboratory demonstration rather than production-quality work.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: ironing cloth with a hand iron. It is the closest general-purpose-robot analogue to pressing a heading in a human workroom, and it remains a slow single-garment lab demonstration, not worker-quality output.

sources.system: Figure 02 with Helix policy
sources.title: Wild Video Shows Humanoid Robot Effortlessly Folding Laundry
sources.claim: Humanoid robot demonstrated autonomous laundry folding using a learned vision-language-action policy; capability is limited to folding cloth, with no measuring, shear cutting or iron pressing shown.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous folding of limp fabric by a general-purpose robot. It bounds what general-purpose robots do in human/home settings - folding only - and so does not substantiate measuring, shear-trimming and iron-pressing a heading.

tasks.label: Insert heated metal forms into ties and touch up rough places with hand irons.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume necktie factory, finishing station: presser takes sewn/turned ties from the line, slides the heated metal blade form inside the tie tube, presses it on the tie press, withdraws the form, and touches up seam, edges and tips with a hand iron on a heated vacuum board. Standard silk/polyester ties, repetitive, hundreds per shift, bundled for packing.

Same factory finishing station but mixed constructions within and between runs: wool and knit ties, heavy jacquards, differing blade widths (skinny to extra-wide) and lengths, lined and unlined. Presser swaps forms, adjusts heat/steam and pressure, and hand-irons more rough places (puckered seams, bubbled interlining, tip edges).

Small custom/sample workshop or high-end maker: short runs and one-offs (bespoke and seven-fold ties, hand-rolled edges, bow ties, ascots). Pressing done largely by hand against a blade form with an iron, frequent changeovers, no two jobs alike, quality judged by eye against a sample.

Dry cleaner or garment-care shop: pressing one customer's cleaned or wrinkled tie at a time using a tie form/padded board and a hand iron, avoiding shine, water spots and seam impressions on delicate silk, interleaved with other garment pressing work.

End-of-line inspection/packing touch-up: ties flagged by the inspector for creases, puckers or rough spots are individually spot-pressed with a hand iron (sometimes over a cloth) before boxing; the presser must locate the defect and treat only that area.

sources.system: Liba WK 10-2 Finishing Press (necktie finishing/ironing press)
sources.developer: Liba / n-tec GmbH (exclusive dealer, Krefeld, Germany)
sources.date: 2026-07 (current product page; product described as well established for many years)
sources.title: necktie machines — n-tec GmbH (Liba, Tisora, Brimato necktie machinery)
sources.claim: The Liba WK 10-2 Finishing Press, sold and serviced by n-tec GmbH for necktie factories, is a machine-controlled necktie ironing system: ties pass through the press between two textile belts, are ironed with programmable pressures at defined positions, vacuum-cooled and dehumidified, then automatically stacked into bundles (up to 2000 pieces per 8 hours). It replaces form-plate pressing ('no form plates necessary').

sources.system: Liba WK 8-2 Tie Tipping Press
sources.title: necktie machines — n-tec GmbH
sources.claim: The same necktie machinery line includes the Liba WK 8-2 tie tipping press, which presses wide and small tie tips on templates either manually or automatically, with an automatic stacker, at up to 2500 pieces per 8 hours — i.e. programmatic heat/pressure forming of tie ends in a purpose-built machine.
sources.transferJustification: Related sub-operation (tip/blade-end pressing rather than full-length form pressing) on the identical object, the necktie, at the same heat-and-pressure precision, in the same factory finishing line; it substantiates that the shaping of tie ends normally done with hand-held heated forms is achieved by machine-controlled templates.

sources.system: Nico 4EVO tie pressing machine
sources.date: 2026-07 (current product page; product line online since ~2018)
sources.title: Tie manufacturing machines – Frigerio e Corazza EN
sources.claim: Frigerio e Corazza (Italy), a supplier of tie manufacturing machines, markets the Nico 4EVO pressing machine that presses tie tips with independent pressing plates, vacuum locking and an internal steam generator; the same catalogue still lists a heated, suction professional tie ironing board (NATY) for manual work, indicating hand ironing remains standard equipment alongside the presses.
sources.transferJustification: Related operation (machine pressing of tie tips) on the identical workpiece and with comparable heat/pressure precision; shows that purpose-built tie presses handle the shaping step, while the persistence of manual heated ironing boards in the same catalogue indicates hand touch-up is not machine-substituted.

sources.system: Robotic sewing workcell (digital-twin integrated apparel automation)
sources.developer: Siemens Technology with Sewbo and partners
sources.title: A Deployment Case Study in Robotic Apparel Automation: Digital Twin Integration, Interoperability, and Workforce Enablement
sources.claim: A Siemens/Sewbo-affiliated robotic sewing system for apparel was deployed as a workcell on a denim factory floor, using temporarily stiffened garment pieces, vacuum grippers, vision-based alignment and closed-loop visual servoing for 2D pocket operations and 3D shaping seams — state-of-the-art robotic handling of limp apparel fabric still requires a dedicated cell with custom tooling.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (robotic garment-piece handling and sewing in an apparel plant) with the same class of limp silk/denim fabric; it bounds the environment tier — even the most advanced apparel fabric-handling robots operate inside purpose-built workcells with fixtured presentation, not as general operators at a human press station.

sources.system: PR2 robotic ironing system (multi-sensor surface analysis)
sources.developer: Columbia University (Li, Hu, Xu, Yue, Grinspun, Allen)
sources.title: Multi-Sensor Surface Analysis for Robotic Ironing
sources.claim: Research robots can autonomously detect wrinkles and iron flattened cloth with a hand iron, but only as laboratory demonstrations on a table/ironing board with ordinary flat cloth, not at commercial garment-finishing quality or speed.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (autonomous ironing of cloth with a hand iron) is the closest published analogue to hand-iron touch-up of rough places; its lab-only, flat-cloth scope shows the touch-up step is not demonstrated at worker quality on shaped silk neckties.

sources.system: TEO humanoid robot ironing
sources.developer: Universidad Carlos III de Madrid (Estevez, Fernandez-Fernandez, Victores, Balaguer)
sources.title: Robot Household Companion — Ironing (UC3M Robotics Lab)
sources.claim: The humanoid robot TEO autonomously located wrinkles in a garment placed on an ironing board and reduced them with an unmodified household iron using force/torque feedback — again a laboratory demonstration, not a production finishing operation.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (humanoid using a human hand iron on a garment) tests exactly the touch-up motion at issue; it is confined to a lab setup with a single flat garment on a board, so it does not carry over to worker-quality tie finishing in a shop.

tasks.label: Brush materials made of suede, leather, or felt to remove spots or to raise and smooth naps.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dry-cleaning / specialty leather-care plant: after cleaning, a one-off customer suede or leather garment (jacket, coat, skirt) is inspected and hand-brushed at a bench with suede brush/eraser to lift collar and cuff soil marks and restore an even nap; garments vary in cut, color, finish, trim and condition, and over-brushing ruins the piece.
Dry-cleaning plant or hat renovator: a fur- or wool-felt hat is cleaned, blocked on a form, then brushed/pounced to remove spots and smooth the nap before it is returned to the customer.

Apparel or leather-goods factory finishing station: uniform batches of finished suede, leather or felt garments and accessories are brushed after pressing to raise an even nap and remove press marks, chalk and dust before bagging.

Apparel/leather-goods factory, pre-assembly: cut suede or leather panels, hides and felt piece goods are brushed or buffed flat, in quantity, to raise or smooth the nap and remove dust before pressing or sewing.
Hat factory finishing department: blocked felt hat bodies on forms are pounced and brushed on production machines to a specified velour/suede surface finish.

Small shop or retail back room (shoe repair, tailor, uniform shop): a customer's suede shoes, bag or felt hat is brushed by hand at the counter to remove spots and lift the nap, often while the customer waits.

sources.system: Bahner Type 234 automatic wet brushing machine / Type 314 velour finishing machine
sources.title: New Machines - Our Portfolio - Bahner Maschinenhandels GmbH
sources.claim: Bahner Maschinenhandels sells current production hat-industry machines including an automatic wet brushing machine (234) for the surface of men's velour hats and a velour finishing machine (314) for surface finishing of hats and hat bodies; the hat is loaded on the machine and the machine performs the brushing cycle.

sources.system: Finimat head crown finishing machine 341-FK6 (with ZO/ZK tool)
sources.title: Finimat head crown finishing machine with ZO or ZK tool (341-FK6)
sources.claim: The Bahner Finimat system automatically treats the surface of the hat crown; the vendor distinguishes such automatic machines from hand-guided velour/fancy finishing machines, stating the automatic machine performs the work itself once fed and started.

sources.system: Effect pouncing machine (336)
sources.title: Effect pouncing machine (336) - Bahner Maschinenhandels GmbH
sources.claim: The Bahner effect pouncing machine works the felt surface of hats/hat bodies with a rotary grinding pad to produce suede-type nap finishes, i.e. machine surfacing of felt to a specified nap.

sources.system: Lafer raising machines / GSMI sueding machines
sources.title: Surface Finishing Gains New Precision | Textile World
sources.claim: Raising and sueding machines from Lafer are automated production machines that raise nap on woven and knitted fabric (including wool goods) as it passes through the machine.

sources.system: Industrial fabric brushing machines (textile finishing)
sources.developer: textile finishing machinery industry (e.g. Mario Crosta, Lafer)
sources.title: What is a brushing machine used for?
sources.claim: Industrial textile brushing machines remove loose fibers, lint and surface debris from goods and raise surface fibers to form a nap, e.g. on suede-type and napped fabrics.

sources.system: Bergi Kurta buffing machine (with in-line dedusting machine)
sources.title: Buffing machine with buffing roller for tannery and leathers
sources.claim: Bergi's Kurta buffing machine buffs/polishes leather with a paper-wrapped buffing roller in a single pass and can run continuously in line with a dedusting machine and automatic stacker - the industrial operation that raises and evens the nap on suede/nubuck leather.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: machine buffing/dedusting of leather in a tannery line. It is the same physical operation as the presser's flat-material work - abrading/brushing a leather surface to raise and even the nap and remove surface dust - on the same material, with the workpiece fed through a purpose-built machine.

sources.system: Robotic shoe-upper roughing cell (3D machine vision + cooperative robot control)
sources.developer: University research with shoe-industry partners (published in Robotics and Autonomous Systems)
sources.title: Automatic surface roughing with 3D machine vision and cooperative robot control - ScienceDirect
sources.claim: A robot cell with structured-light 3D vision plans and executes abrasive surface treatment paths over leather shoe uppers held on lasts, following the part contour automatically.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic abrasion of leather uppers. It shows a fixtured leather workpiece can be surface-treated along a vision-derived contour path by a robot in a purpose-built cell, supporting E1 for brushing/buffing leather parts presented in a fixture.

tasks.label: Sew ends of new material to leaders or to ends of material in pressing machines, using sewing machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Textile finishing mill, entry of a continuous press/calender/decatizing range: operator pulls the head of a new open-width woven roll to the machine entry, butts it to the tail of the piece running through, and runs a chainstitch/overlock seaming machine across the full 150-320 cm width so the range never stops.

Same machine entry, but knit, jersey or elastane-blend goods whose cut ends curl and skew; operator must decurl, hold selvedges square and sew a low-bulk seam so the joint does not bow, pucker or mark when it passes the press bed.

After a changeover or a stoppage, a leader cloth is threaded through the press/finishing machine and its trailing end brought back to the entry; the operator sews the head of the new material to the leader so the new piece can be drawn through the machine.

Heavy or technical goods - canvas/duck, coated or laminated fabric, felt, heavy nonwoven - joined with a strong flat or butted seam that must survive nip rolls and heated press beds without breaking, bulking or marking the goods.

Smaller non-mill operation (garment plant press line, commercial laundry flatwork ironer, sample or short-run finishing room): attaching a leader or joining ends with a general-purpose or portable sewing machine, non-standard leader material and an improvised, one-off setup.

sources.claim: Comatex JOIN-RAIL is a commercially sold rail-mounted automatic cut-and-sew unit installed at the entrance of textile finishing/processing lines that clamps the full fabric width, aligns the two edges, and automatically traverses and seams the head of a new roll to the tail of the previous one (~25 s per seam) on woven, warp/circular knit, non-woven and technical/laminated fabrics 180-600 cm wide.

tasks.label: Select, install, and adjust machine components, including pressing forms, rollers, and guides, using hoists and hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dry cleaner or small commercial laundry: presser replaces worn pads and covers on a utility press buck, sleeve board, or shirt-unit form - stripping the old padding, stretching a new fabric/Nomex cover over the curved form, and securing it with clips, drawstrings, or staples, then closing the head to check fit. Compliant, deformable goods; machine as installed on the shop floor; hand tools only.

Industrial shirt/garment laundry: swap the rigid pressing form or buck on a shirt unit, form finisher, or utility press when changing garment type or size - unbolt and hoist the old form off, set and align the replacement, reconnect steam/vacuum/air lines, torque fasteners, and run a test press.

Apparel manufacturing plant: set up a fusing/transfer press or die press for a new style - select and install the correct die, platen, or pressing head and belt, mount it with hand tools, then set stops and guides and run a sample to verify placement and pressure.

Commercial laundry plant flatwork ironer or roll press: install or change a roll, feed ribbons/tapes, and edge guides - using an overhead hoist or lift to handle the heavy roller, seating it in its bearings, tensioning and aligning the guide tapes with hand tools.

Mid-shift adjustment on an existing pressing machine: reposition guides, stops, and gauges with hand tools (wrenches, screwdrivers) to suit a different garment size or fabric, checking alignment on trial pieces and re-tightening.

roles.title: Sewing Machine Operators
aliases: Buttonhole and Button Sewing Machine Operator
Complete Garment Lockstitch Sewing Machine Operator
Lockstitch Armhole Sew and Trim Operator
roles.description: Operate or tend sewing machines to join, reinforce, decorate, or perform related sewing operations in the manufacture of garment or nongarment products.

tasks.label: Monitor machine operation to detect problems such as defective stitching, breaks in thread, or machine malfunctions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume apparel plant, single-needle lockstitch station: operator runs bundles of cut parts at piece rate while watching the needle zone and feeding fabric for thread breakage, skipped stitches, puckering, or uneven seam allowance, and listening for motor/timing noise on a noisy sewing floor.

Tending programmable/automatic sewing equipment (multi-head embroidery, automatic pocket setter, bartacker, pattern tacker): operator oversees one or several machines, responds to thread-break and bobbin-run-out alarms, and watches for needle breakage or misregistration during unattended cycles.

Non-garment heavy sewing (auto seat covers, upholstery, mattresses, canvas, tarps, safety gear): thick multi-ply material on walking-foot or heavy-duty machines; operator watches for skipped stitches, needle deflection or breakage, thread tension faults, and feed slippage.

Small shop, sample room, custom/alteration or short-run production: frequent material and thread changes on varied machines; operator monitors stitch formation closely on each piece and catches tension or timing problems that arise after each changeover.
High-speed overlock/serging or coverstitch operation: operator monitors chain formation, looper thread supply, edge trim quality, and cutting knife condition while feeding continuous seams.

tasks.label: Place spools of thread, cord, or other materials on spindles, insert bobbins, and thread ends through machine guides and components.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Mid-run bobbin change on an industrial lockstitch, bartack or pattern-sewing machine in a sewn-products plant: the bobbin thread runs out, the operator stops the machine, opens the hook cover, removes the empty bobbin/case, seats a full pre-wound bobbin (drawing the end under the case tension spring) or swaps in a pre-set spare case, draws the bobbin thread up through the throat plate and resumes. Pre-wound bobbins and spare cases are stocked at the station. Happens many times per shift.

Re-threading the needle (upper) thread after a thread break, needle change or thread jam on a single-needle lockstitch machine on the line: pull the end from the cone on the overhead stand, pass it through the stand eyelet, pre-tension, tension discs, check spring, take-up lever, lower guides and finally the needle eye, pull a tail under the presser foot, and test-stitch to confirm tension.

Style/colour changeover at the start of a new order: place new spools/cones of thread, cord or elastic on the machine spindles or overhead stand (sometimes tying the new end to the old and pulling it through), thread the complete upper path, fit a matching-colour bobbin, and sew test seams before production starts.

Threading a multi-thread machine in the factory — 3-5 thread overlock/serger, coverstitch, or multi-needle chainstitch: cones on the thread stand, each end routed through its own guides, tension units, loopers/spreaders in the correct sequence and one or more needles, then chain-off tested.

Threading in a small alteration/upholstery/custom workroom or home-based contract sewing: a domestic or older industrial machine on a shared table amid clutter, varied spool sizes and thread types (heavy nylon, monofilament, decorative cord), no standard station layout or tooling.

sources.system: T-NT (tactile needle-threading robot)
sources.title: Precise Robotic Needle-Threading with Tactile Perception and Reinforcement Learning
sources.claim: The state of the art for autonomous robotic needle threading — a two-arm lab rig with tactile sensing that finds a thread tail and inserts it into an eyelet held by a second robot — reaches only about 63% success, far below the reliability an employer would accept, and covers only the final eye-insertion step of machine threading.
sources.transferJustification: Closest published robotic analogue of threading a needle eye with limp thread; cited to show even this sub-step is not yet at worker reliability, let alone the full spool-to-needle path.

sources.system: Baby Lock Jet-Air Threading (Victory serger)
sources.title: Serger Threading Made Easy With Jet Air Threading | Baby Lock
