sources.transferJustification: Directly the task; shows that the only marketed 'automatic threading' still requires a human to place the spool and insert the thread end, so it cannot support a positive autonomous judgment.

sources.system: Robotic apparel sewing cell with JUKI CP-180-controlled sewing machine
sources.title: Robotic Automation in Apparel Manufacturing: A Novel Approach to Fabric Handling and Sewing
sources.claim: A 2025 research system for robotic apparel manufacturing integrates robot arms with an industrial sewing machine, but the robots handle fabric and machine control signals (presser foot, thread trimming); thread setup of the machine is not automated.
sources.transferJustification: Adjacent task (robotic sewing) in the same environment; shows current sewing-automation research delegates fabric handling to robots while thread/bobbin setup remains a manual or machine-integrated function.

tasks.label: Position items under needles, using marks on machines, clamps, templates, or cloth as guides.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume apparel/soft-goods plant: operator picks cut fabric plies from a bundle at a standard single-needle/overlock workstation and positions them under the needle for straight or gently curved seams, hems and edge serging, guiding by the cloth edge, a machine throat-plate mark or an edge guide; repetitive same-style work all shift.

Apparel plant, three-dimensional operations on partly assembled garments: positioning a shaped body under the needle to set a sleeve, attach a collar/cuff/waistband, or sew a curved seam, matching notches and chalk marks and easing fullness while the garment shape changes under the presser foot.

Operator loads an item into a clamp, template, jig or fixture-guided automatic unit (programmable pattern tacker, automatic pocket welter/setter, bartacker, automatic label or zipper unit, embroidery hoop), aligns it to the template marks and starts the cycle; the clamp/frame then indexes the piece under the needle.

Non-garment bulky flat goods: positioning large heavy pieces under heavy-duty needles — mattress covers and tape-edge closing, quilted panels, rugs and bath mats, pillow covers, tarps, flags — where the piece is big and heavy but the sewing path is a straight run or perimeter.

Shaped three-dimensional non-garment covers: automotive seat trim covers, upholstered furniture covers, boat/RV covers and tents — positioning multi-ply, pre-shaped or foam-backed assemblies under the needle, matching notches and marks while wrestling the bulk of the assembly.

Custom, small-lot or repair work in an alteration room, dry cleaner, sample room or job shop: one-off or few-off items, frequently changing garment types and materials, positioned under the needle by eye against chalk marks, pins or basted lines.

tasks.label: Guide garments or garment parts under machine needles and presser feet to sew parts together.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Apparel/textile-products plant, high-volume joining of flat cut panels on basic items: T-shirt shoulder and side seams, knit tops, pillowcases, towels, bedding, flags. A bundle of pre-cut plies sits at the station; the same seam is repeated all shift on standard fabrics in long runs.

Apparel plant making structured or tailored garments: setting sleeves into armholes with ease, joining collars, cuffs, facings and linings on jackets, dress shirts and tailored trousers; notch and plaid matching, slippery or stretch fabric, seams sewn on partly assembled three-dimensional garments.

Non-garment sewn-products plant: joining panels of automotive seat covers, airbags, furniture upholstery, mattress covers, tarps, bags and protective gear; heavy, coated or leather material, long straight and curved seams with tight seam-allowance tolerances, high volume.

Attaching one component to a garment part at a single station: patch pockets, labels, zippers, elastic, straps, binding, reinforcement stitching — small, repetitive, precisely positioned joins on flat parts.

Small shop, sample room or alteration department: one-off or very short runs, style changes several times a day, unique customer garments taken in, re-seamed or repaired; no dedicated program, template or tooling exists for the job.

sources.system: SEWBOT / LOWRY workline

sources.claim: SoftWear Automation's SEWBOT machine-vision worklines were in commercial production for customers making pillows, bath mats, car mats and towels sold in US big-box retail — autonomous sewing worklines that join and edge fabric panels.
sources.transferJustification: Pillow, mat and towel production is the same act as the rated task — panels of limp fabric guided under a needle and presser foot and joined/edged — on the same machinery class, differing only in the product sewn.

tasks.label: Remove holding devices and finished items from machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume apparel line (cut-and-sew plant): after finishing a seam on a single-needle lockstitch or overlock machine, the operator lifts the presser foot, pulls the limp sewn panel out from under the needle, clips/removes thread chains, and lays it on the finished bundle pile beside the station; cycle repeats every few seconds all shift.

Programmable automat station (pattern tacker, bartacker, buttonholer, pocket setter, template/pallet sewer): after the cycle, the operator releases and lifts the work clamp, template or sewing pallet off the machine, takes the finished component out of the clamp, sets clamp aside or reloads, and stacks the finished piece.

Non-garment / heavy goods (motor vehicle seating, upholstery, mattress panels, tarps, industrial textiles): operator unhooks jigs, frames or hold-down bars and drags or lifts a large, heavy finished item (seat cover, quilted panel, cushion cover) off the machine bed onto a cart, rack or conveyor.

Embroidery / decorative station: operator unlatches and removes the hoop, clamp or tubular frame from the multi-head embroidery machine arms, takes the embroidered garment out of the hoop, tears away excess backing/stabilizer, and places the finished item in a bin.

Small shop, sample room, alterations or custom job work: one-off or short-run items of widely varying size and material (drapes, bags, leather goods, wedding gowns, prototypes); operator removes guides/attachments, pins or clamps and lifts the finished item off a general-purpose machine, frequent style changeovers.

tasks.label: Match cloth pieces in correct sequences prior to sewing them, and verify that dye lots and patterns match.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume apparel cut-and-sew plant, solid-color knit or woven goods: operator receives a tied bundle of cut parts with a bundle ticket at the machine, breaks the bundle, separates single limp plies, checks size/lot markings, and stacks fronts, backs, sleeves, facings in the order they will be joined.

Non-garment sewn products (automotive seat covers, furniture upholstery, mattress covers, tarps, bags, medical/industrial textiles): operator draws cut panels of woven, coated fabric, vinyl or leather from carts/racks, checks hide or roll lot codes, and lays panels out in assembly sequence at the station.

Patterned goods needing plaid, stripe, engineered-print or nap matching: operator pairs pieces so the repeat lines up across the intended seam, checks nap/grain direction, and rejects or swaps pieces that will not match before sewing.

Small contract shop, sample room or short-run/custom work (uniforms, costumes, custom covers): frequent style changes, small bundles of few pieces, mixed fabrics; operator collects pieces from a cut table and orders them per the sample or work ticket.

Dye-lot/shade problem cases: bundle contains pieces cut from different lays or rolls, or with visible shade or print-registration variation; operator compares pieces side by side under light, pulls mismatches, reconciles with tickets and obtains replacement pieces.
Home-based sewing contractor or in-store alteration workroom: pieces laid out on whatever table or floor space is available, no standard layout or lighting, one-off jobs and customer-supplied fabric.

tasks.label: Fold or stretch edges or lengths of items while sewing to facilitate forming specified sections.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Apparel plant sewing floor: operator folds the hem allowance of light woven/knit garment parts (T-shirt and polo bottoms, sleeves, trouser bottoms) into a folder/guide and coverstitches or lockstitches the hem, keeping fold width even along flat or tubular edges at line rate.

Knit underwear/activewear plant: operator stretches elastic band to a specified tension ratio and feeds it with the body fabric through an overlock/coverstitch machine to form a waistband or leg opening, matching elastic length to a longer fabric length without ripples.

Textile product mill (home textiles): operator folds and sews hems or binding on flat panels — bed sheets, pillowcases, towels, bath mats, curtains, table linen — including sewing stretched elastic into fitted-sheet corners on long standard-size runs.

Heavy technical/bedding goods: operator folds binding or tape over the thick edge of mattress borders and panels, car mats, tarps, canvas bags or awnings and sews the folded edge, handling stiff, bulky material and corners.

Automotive seat trim / furniture upholstery cut-and-sew: operator eases, stretches and folds contoured cover panels of leather, vinyl or heavy cloth against one another while sewing, forming 3-D shaped sections (bolsters, listing pockets, skirt hems) where one edge must be stretched to fit a shorter mating edge.

Sample room, custom drapery workroom, or alteration/repair shop: one-off or very small-lot items in varying fabrics and sizes; operator folds hems, turns edges, or stretches trims on garments and made-to-measure goods that change style with every piece, judging fold width and ease by eye.

tasks.label: Cut excess material or thread from finished products.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume knit apparel plant (T-shirts, underwear, activewear): after each overlock/coverstitch operation the operator snips the thread chain and thread tails off the sewn piece with nippers and trims small excess fabric before passing it on; hundreds of pieces per hour, limp knit fabric.

Woven-goods plant (dress shirts, pants, jackets, uniforms): operator trims thread ends and excess seam allowance/excess fabric on sewn sub-assemblies — collar and cuff edges, pocket and welt corners, facings — using shears at the workstation before the part moves to pressing.

Heavy nongarment sewn goods (automotive seat covers, furniture upholstery covers, mattress panels/borders): operator trims excess fabric, foam-backing overhang and thread ends from bulky sewn assemblies at a heavy-duty machine station.

Industrial/technical textiles and accessories (bags, tents, awnings, harnesses, webbing goods, medical/filtration textiles): operator cuts excess webbing/material and trims thread ends from finished sewn items, often with hot knife or heavy shears.
Decorated goods (embroidered caps, logos, patches, appliqué on garments): trimming jump threads, thread tails and excess backing/appliqué material from finished decorated pieces.

Small shop, sample room, alterations department or home-based contract sewing: one-off or very short-run items of varied construction; operator snips threads and trims excess fabric by hand on whatever garment is in front of them.

tasks.label: Select supplies such as fasteners and thread, according to job requirements.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Apparel/cut-and-sew plant: operator reads the work order or bundle ticket and pulls the specified thread cones (color code, tex/ticket weight, fiber) from the thread rack or supply cabinet, staging enough cones for the machine and the run.

Apparel plant trim/notions area: operator picks fasteners and trims listed on the trim sheet — boxed buttons, polybagged zippers, snap sets, hook-and-loop, elastic, labels — from labeled bins and shelves and carries them to the workstation.

Non-garment industrial sewing (upholstery, auto seating, canvas/awning, mattresses, bags): operator draws heavy bonded thread cones, webbing rolls, buckles, grommets and hardware from a stockroom shelf per the job spec sheet.

Sample room / small custom shop: no SKU on the ticket — operator holds candidate thread cones and fastener samples against the customer's fabric swatch and judges the closest shade and weight match before selecting.

Alterations counter or home-based contract sewing: operator rummages a personal drawer, caddy or wall of assorted spools for the nearest matching thread and a suitable button/zipper from mixed loose stock.

tasks.label: Examine and measure finished articles to verify conformance to standards, using rulers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume apparel cut-and-sew line (knit tops, T-shirts, workwear): after finishing a bundle, the operator lays each garment or sewn panel flat on the worktable and checks key points (chest width, sleeve/hem length, seam allowance, stitch density) with a ruler or tape against the buyer's spec sheet, setting aside out-of-tolerance pieces.

Technical/automotive sewn components (airbag cushions, seat covers, seat belts, medical drapes, safety harnesses): standardized high-repetition parts; the operator inspects stitching and measures seam allowance and panel dimensions with ruler/gauge against tight written tolerances before the part moves on.

Home textiles and flat industrial soft goods (curtains, flags/banners, pillow shams, flat covers, tarps): the operator spreads the finished flat item on a large table and measures length, width and hem depth with a tape or yardstick against the order spec.

Bulky three-dimensional finished sewn goods (mattress covers, tents, boat/equipment covers, duffel bags, upholstered cushions): the operator wrestles a large limp assembled article into shape on the floor or a big table and measures across seams, openings and girths with a tape.

Custom, bespoke or small-lot work (alteration and uniform shops, costume and drapery workrooms, sample rooms): each finished article is unique, measured against a work order, pattern, or the customer's own measurements, with judgment about fit and workmanship as well as dimensions.

Home-based or contract piecework on standard items: an operator sewing standard garment components at home or in a small contractor's workroom measures finished pieces against the contractor's spec sheet before packing them for pickup.

tasks.label: Turn knobs, screws, and dials to adjust settings of machines, according to garment styles and equipment performance.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Style/fabric changeover on a single-needle lockstitch machine in an apparel or sewn-goods plant: operator sets needle-thread tension, stitch length (SPI), presser-foot pressure and machine speed for the new style, sews a test seam, and re-tweaks the dials until stitch balance and SPI meet the spec sheet.

In-run corrective adjustment on a lockstitch/topstitching operation responding to equipment performance: seam pucker, loose underside stitch, thread breakage, or thick cross-seam sections; operator nudges the tension nut/dial, presser-foot pressure and speed while production continues.

Overlock/serger or coverstitch setup for knit goods: differential feed ratio lever, stitch-length push-button/screw, three or four thread-tension dials, cutting width and presser-pressure screw, set by feel across test samples to stop rolling, waving or puckering.

Heavy or specialty machine (walking-foot machine for upholstery, leather goods or automotive interiors; bartacker; programmable pattern sewer): adjust foot lift/stroke, foot pressure, thread tension, stitch length and speed for thick multi-ply material and heavy thread.

Attachment and guide setup on the machine: reposition a folder, binder, hemming guide or edge guide, loosen and retighten set screws with a screwdriver, align the trimming knife or needle guard, then test-sew and re-align until the hem/binding width is right.

Small alterations/custom shop or home-based contract sewing on a domestic or light-industrial machine: dial tension, stitch length and presser pressure for a one-off garment in mixed fabrics, with no engineering or mechanic support and no standard spec sheet.

tasks.label: Repair or alter items by adding replacement parts or missing stitches.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Rework station on an apparel/sewn-goods plant floor: garments flagged by QC for skipped or broken stitches, open seams or misaligned seam allowances. Operator locates the defect on the assembled, limp garment, picks out bad stitching with a ripper when needed, re-sews the segment overlapping the existing stitch line, backtacks and trims threads. Defect type and location vary item to item across mixed styles.

Adding standard replacement components on production runs or returned/second-quality goods in a plant or contract sewing shop: sewing on replacement buttons, brand or care labels, name tapes, emblems/patches, missing bartacks or belt loops. The same part goes in the same place on many like items, high volume, standard materials.

Customer alterations on finished garments in a retail alterations room, uniform shop, bridal shop or dry cleaner: hem trousers or shorten sleeves, take in a side seam, replace a broken zipper, resize a waistband. Requires measuring/marking to the customer's fit, unpicking original stitching, re-sewing to match the original construction, pressing.

Repair of heavy or technical sewn goods and upholstery in a fabrication shop: patching a torn tarp, awning, tent or truck/boat cover, re-stitching a blown seam on a seat cushion or cover, replacing webbing, straps or hardware on bags and slings. Bulky, worn, one-off damage sewn on walking-foot or long-arm machines.

Industrial laundry / uniform-rental repair room: patching holes, burns and tears at variable positions on worn work pants and jackets, mending ripped linens and shop towels, restitching worn seams. High volume of items but item-specific damage on soiled, laundered, deformed garments.

Uniform-rental or workwear repair of a standard component: replacing a worn patch pocket, cuff, knee panel or hook-and-loop closure on a standard workwear style, the same defined operation repeated across many identical garments.

tasks.label: Perform equipment maintenance tasks such as replacing needles, sanding rough areas of needles, or cleaning and oiling sewing machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Mid-shift needle change at the operator's station on a plant sewing floor (apparel/cut-and-sew, auto trim, or industrial textiles): the needle breaks, bends or dulls; the operator raises the needle bar, loosens the needle-clamp setscrew with a small screwdriver or hex key, pulls the old needle, selects the correct system/size/point, inserts it fully to the stop with the long groove and scarf correctly oriented, retightens, rethreads and runs a test seam.

Shift or daily cleaning of the operator's machine in the plant: brushing and air-blowing lint, thread nests and fabric dust from the throat plate, feed dog, bobbin case, hook race and tension discs (often removing the needle plate and bobbin case first), clearing thread from the trimmer, and wiping down the bed and table.

Lubrication in the plant: checking the oil sight glass/reservoir on an automatic-lube industrial machine and topping it up, or hand-oiling designated oil points and the hook race on plain/older or specialty machines (bartack, blindstitch, walking-foot), then wiping excess oil and running the machine on scrap to avoid oil spots on goods.

Smoothing rough spots: fine-sanding or polishing a burred needle point/eye or a nicked throat plate, hook point, or presser foot with emery cloth or a fine abrasive after thread shredding or fabric snagging is observed, then checking with scrap fabric.

Same maintenance work performed by an operator in a small custom shop, alterations/upholstery workroom or home-based contract sewing space, on a varied assortment of old and new domestic and industrial machines in a crowded, non-standardized workspace.

tasks.label: Mount attachments, such as needles, cutting blades, or pattern plates, and adjust machine guides according to specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Apparel/soft-goods plant sewing floor: operator's single-needle lockstitch or overlock machine breaks or dulls a needle mid-run. Operator loosens the needle-clamp set screw with a small screwdriver, removes the needle, selects the correct size/point type per the style spec, inserts it fully to the stop with the long groove/scarf correctly oriented, retightens, rethreads and test-stitches on a scrap.

Style/order changeover at the station: operator bolts on or swaps a folder, binder, hemmer or edge guide, positions it relative to the needle for the specified seam allowance or hem width, tightens the mounting screws, sets the presser foot/guide, sews a test sample, measures it, and re-adjusts until the spec is met.

Blade work on a factory machine: replacing worn upper/lower knives on an overlock/safety-stitch machine or a trimming/cutting attachment, setting knife overlap and trim width to spec, then checking the trimmed edge on a test run.

Automated/pattern machine setup in the plant: loading or swapping pattern plates, clamp templates, dies or work clamps on bartack, pattern-tacker or template sewing machines per the work order, seating and bolting them, checking alignment/registration to the stitch program on a first piece.

Small workroom, sample room, alterations shop or home-based contract sewing: a single machine on a crowded, non-standardized bench; operator changes the needle and snaps or screws on an attachment (zipper foot, welting foot, guide bar), eyeballs and adjusts the guide, and tests on scrap.

sources.claim: NeedlyMat is a commercial purpose-built machine that autonomously inspects textile needle boards, identifies damaged/bent felting needles, extracts them and inserts replacement needles into the correct board positions.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: replacing textile-machine needles in a needle board rather than in a sewing-machine needle bar. Same class of object (small hardened textile needles), same required precision (seating a needle in a tight bore in the correct position), machine-controlled removal-and-insertion cycle with vision-based inspection, performed in a purpose-built machine.

tasks.label: Cut materials according to specifications, using blades, scissors, or electric knives.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Apparel/sewn-goods plant cutting room: a multi-ply lay of woven or knit fabric is spread on a long table with a paper or chalked marker; the operator cuts pattern pieces with an electric straight knife or round knife, following marker lines, adding notches and staying within tolerance so pieces bundle correctly for sewing.

At the sewing station on partly assembled goods: the operator trims excess fabric and seam allowance with scissors or snips, clips corners and curves, notches, cuts pocket/buttonhole openings, and cuts thread ends between operations, working to the spec sheet on garments held in the hands or under a clamp.

Cutting narrow goods to specified length or width: elastic, binding tape, webbing, straps, ribbon, hook-and-loop, interlining or lining strips cut with scissors, an electric knife, or a hot knife (sealing synthetic ends), in batches at a bench beside the sewing line.

Heavy or technical materials in an upholstery, marine-canvas, automotive-trim, or industrial-textiles shop: leather hides with grade/defect variation, vinyl, foam, canvas, ballistic nylon cut single-ply to pattern with an electric knife, round knife, or hand blade on a shop cutting table.

Sample room, alteration, or repair work: a one-off piece cut from a chalk-marked paper pattern laid on a remnant or on the customer's material, single ply, irregular edges, cut with shears to a spec that may be adjusted on the spot before sewing.

tasks.label: Inspect garments, and examine repair tags and markings on garments to locate defects or damage, and mark errors as necessary.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: End-of-line / in-line inspection in an apparel sewing plant: operator takes each sewn garment from a bundle or hanger, turns it, checks seams, stitching, puckering, stains, loose threads and labels, then chalks or stickers the defect and sets the piece aside for repair. Mixed styles, frequent style changes, soft limp goods handled by hand.

Operator inspects incoming cut parts/panels at the sewing station before joining: checks each ply for fabric flaws, holes, shade variation and cutter's or fabric-inspection markings, and pulls or marks bad panels for replacement.

Repair/mending station in an industrial laundry or uniform-rental plant: garments arrive tagged or diverted as damaged; operator reads the repair tag, locates the rip, hole, missing button or blown seam on the garment, and marks/flags it before sewing.

Alterations shop or dry-cleaner tailoring room: one-off customer garments (coats, dresses, jeans, uniforms) arrive with a handwritten repair ticket pinned on; the operator reads the ticket, finds the described damage or fit problem on a highly varied garment, and chalks/pins the spot.

Non-garment sewn goods plant (auto seat covers/airbags, upholstery, mattress panels, tents, bags): operator inspects large or heavy sewn assemblies for stitch defects, skipped seams and fabric flaws, and marks the defect location or tags the piece for rework.

sources.transferJustification: Same content as the inspect-and-flag step: locating damage (holes, stains) on a textile article presented at the station and segregating it for repair, in place of a chalk mark or defect sticker.

sources.transferJustification: Airbag cushions are sewn textile products inspected for stitch-level defects at precision comparable to garment seam inspection; object type, defect classes and fixtured presentation transfer to sewn-goods defect inspection.

tasks.label: Attach buttons, hooks, zippers, fasteners, or other accessories to fabric, using feeding hoppers or clamp holders.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Apparel plant, dress shirts/blouses/knit tops: attaching sew-through buttons to plackets, cuffs and collars on flat, pre-pressed panels with a button-sewing machine fed from a hopper/feeder bowl and holding the fabric in a clamp; high volume, 5-10 buttons per garment, placement within a few millimeters of marks, operator loads, cycles and stacks.

Jeans, workwear and children's wear: setting metal tack buttons, prong snaps and rivets at waistbands, pocket corners and plackets using hopper-fed attaching presses with dies and clamp holders; multi-ply denim or knit, must set fully without crushing or holing the fabric, hundreds of sets per shift.

Zipper attaching: inserting zippers into jacket fronts, pocket openings, cushion/mattress covers and bags on clamp- or template-guided sewing units; two plies plus tape must be aligned, slider kept clear, seam matched to panel edges.

Hooks, bars, hook-and-eye tape and hook-and-loop fastener attached to partly assembled, three-dimensional garments (trouser waistbands, bras, uniforms) held in a clamp or press; bulky limp pieces, frequent style changes and small runs.

Nongarment sewn products (upholstery, tarps, awnings, marine covers, bags, industrial/medical textiles): setting grommets, snaps and other fasteners along hems of heavy, large or awkward panels with hopper-fed presses and clamp holders; material weight and size dominate handling.

tasks.label: Position material or articles in clamps, templates, or hoop frames prior to automatic operation of machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Commercial embroidery/decoration shop: operator hoops flat garments (t-shirts, polos, jackets) — slides the inner ring under a single garment layer with cut-away backing, tensions the fabric in the hoop or magnetic frame, aligns to placement marks (left chest, back yoke), and mounts the hoop on the multi-head machine's frame arms before automatic stitching. Styles, sizes and fabrics change constantly across small orders.

Apparel/sewn-goods plant: operator repeatedly places small flat parts (care labels, pocket blanks, plackets, elastic tabs, webbing straps) into the clamp or template of a programmable pattern tacker, bartacker or button/buttonhole automat, closes the clamp and trips the cycle; one style runs for a long batch, parts arrive in bundles at the station.

Apparel plant: operator loads larger panels and subassemblies (jeans back-pocket on hip panel, shirt fronts, quilted panels, hood pieces) into a large sewing template/jig, smoothing the plies to registration marks and closing the template before the CNC template machine or pocket setter sews the pattern.

Industrial/technical sewn-products plant (automotive interiors and airbags, seat covers, safety harnesses and webbing, footwear uppers, medical textiles): operator positions cut pieces, layered stacks or coated/heavy fabrics in fixtures, pallets or clamps of automatic pattern-sewing or bonding machines; tolerances are tight and parts are dimensionally consistent, long production runs.

Caps, bags and already-assembled 3D items: operator mounts a finished cap on a cap-driver frame, hoops a tubular sleeve or bag panel in a specialty clamp, or clamps a shaped assembled item in a fixture for automatic embroidery/tacking, working around seams, bulk and stretch.

tasks.label: Draw markings or pin appliques on fabric to obtain variations in design.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume apparel plant: operator chalk/pen-marks placement guides on flat cut panels at the sewing station — pocket and trim placement, dart points, stitch and buttonhole lines — using a template or ruler on standard wovens/knits, repeated across a bundle.

Pinning or positioning appliques, patches, emblems, labels or decorative overlays onto flat garment panels in the correct location before topstitching (logo patches on uniforms, decorative overlays, contrast pocket/tag pieces) in a factory or contract embroidery shop.

Nongarment sewn products shop (upholstery, mattress covers, awnings, boat canvas, sails): marking reference lines, pleat/zipper/grommet placement and assembly marks on large limp panels spread on a work table.

Sample room / small-batch production: marking specified pattern marks and applique placement lines on single-ply pieces for a new style from the pattern or tech pack, quick turnaround, varied fabrics.

Design-variation work requiring the operator's own judgment: chalking or pinning applique/trim placement on an assembled or draped garment (on a form or on the finished body), matching prints/plaids, adjusting placement by eye until the look is right.

Self-employed or home-studio custom sewing and alterations: marking and pinning appliques/trim on a customer's garment in a converted room or at the client's site, one-off items, non-standard layout and lighting.

sources.system: Zund Universal Drawing Tool (UDT) on Zund cutting systems
sources.title: Universal Drawing Tool - UDT | Zund
sources.claim: Commercial CNC cutting tables carry a drawing tool that precisely draws assembly marks, symbols and text on fabric and leather held on the machine's vacuum table, executing the marks from the digital pattern file.
sources.transferJustification: Same task — drawing markings on fabric — performed by a gantry machine on material fixtured on a vacuum table; the marks are the placement/assembly marks a sewing operator would otherwise chalk.

sources.system: Industrial pen plotter marking machines and textile drills (sewn-products marking equipment)
sources.developer: Sewn Products Equipment Co. (industrial marking equipment supplier)
sources.title: Industrial Marking Solutions | Sewn Products Equipment Co
sources.claim: Industrial marking equipment for sewn-products plants includes CNC pen-plotter marking machines for drawing lines and symbols and textile drills for making placement marks through multiple plies in high-volume production.
sources.transferJustification: Same task (marking fabric for placement/design reference) executed by machine; drills produce the multi-ply placement marks operators otherwise chalk by hand.

sources.system: Digital plotter/cutter tables in marine canvas shops (e.g. Chicago Marine Canvas; Carlson Design plotter/cutter)

sources.claim: Marine canvas and upholstery shops run multi-tool CNC plotter/cutter tables that mark, cut and punch large fabric panels, replacing hand marking of patterns.
sources.transferJustification: Same task in the nongarment segment: the table draws on large limp panels the marks a fabricator would otherwise chalk by hand.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: positioning limp cut pieces onto panels and machines inside a working garment plant; shows applique-like placement in a human-work facility is still narrow, trial-stage and not yet worker-quality across styles.

tasks.label: Tape or twist together thread or cord to repair breaks.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Apparel plant, single- or multi-needle industrial lockstitch machine: needle or looper thread snaps mid-seam. Operator stops the machine, finds the broken end at the tension/take-up, twists or knots it to the end coming off the cone, pulls the joint through the guides and resumes the seam. Fine polyester/cotton thread, high piece-rate pressure.

Multi-head embroidery or automated stitching machine tending in a decorating/contract plant: a thread-break detector stops the head; the operator twists the broken thread ends together (or knots the running thread to a fresh end), draws the joint through tensioners and needle, and restarts the head. Several heads may break per shift.

Nongarment industrial sewing (mattresses, upholstery, awnings, tarps, auto trim, bags): heavy bonded thread or cord breaks or frays. Operator tapes or twists the coarse cord ends together to splice them so the run continues, sometimes joining cord from a new cone to the running cord.

Cone/creel changeover and preventive splicing on multi-thread machines (sergers, chainstitch, quilting, bag-closing machines fed from several cones): operator twists/knots the tail of a new cone to the running thread so the joint feeds itself through the guides without full re-threading.

Small alteration/custom shop or home-based contract sewing: worker at a domestic or light industrial machine in a variable, uncontrolled space; thread breaks in mid-repair, or a drawstring/trim cord parts and is twisted or taped back together; setup, lighting and thread types differ job to job.

sources.system: ROBOspin piecing robot
sources.title: ROBOspin – Piecing Robot for Ring Spinning | Rieter
sources.claim: Rieter's ROBOspin is a commercially sold piecing robot that rides on ring- and compact-spinning machines and automatically repairs broken yarn ends ('ends down') while the machine runs, guided by individual spindle monitoring.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: repairing a broken thread/yarn end on a textile machine. The robot finds the loose end of a fine spun yarn, re-threads it through a guide and rejoins it to the running strand — the same objects (fine yarn/thread), the same precision class (grasping and joining a sub-millimetre strand), and the same purpose (restore a broken thread so the machine can run) as the sewing operator's twist-together repair, performed in a purpose-built on-machine setting.

sources.system: ROBOspin piecing robot
sources.title: ROBOspin Increases Efficiency In Ring And Compact Spinning | Textile World
sources.claim: Trade press reports the whole ROBOspin piecing cycle — locating the yarn end, threading it through the traveler, and re-placing it in the drafting system — runs fully automatically, at up to 95% piecing efficiency, in mills in the US, Turkey and India.
sources.transferJustification: Same related task as above; this source establishes that the complete break-repair cycle (find both ends, thread through a guide, rejoin, restart) is done end-to-end without an operator and at production reliability, which is what 'completing the instance at worker quality' requires.

sources.system: Auto-Coner automatic winding machine with air/thermo splicers (Rieter Autoconer X6, Saurer Flexsplicer)
sources.title: Auto-Coner Winding Machine in Yarn Spinning: Technology and Sustainability - Textile School
sources.claim: Automatic winders (Auto-Coner class machines) detect yarn breaks and splice the broken ends back together with air splicers as a routine, largely unattended production function.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: joining two broken thread ends to restore a running strand. The splicing unit's suction arms retrieve both ends and join them in a splice chamber with no operator — the mechanised equivalent of the operator's twist/knot repair, on comparable thread material, in a purpose-built machine environment.

sources.system: Mesdan JOINTAIR / AQUASPLICER / HOT JOINTAIR splicers and automatic knotters
sources.title: Yarn joining solutions | Mesdan
sources.claim: Mesdan supplies a full range of automatic splicers and mechanical knotters designed to be fitted onto textile machines to join thread/yarn ends of different fibre types, structures and counts, including coarse counts.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: the mechanised replacement of the hand-tied knot used to repair a broken thread. It covers the coarse/heavy thread and cord case as well as fine thread, and shows the joining device is a standard machine-integrated (E1) component rather than a laboratory one-off.

sources.system: Robotic sewing and knot-tying system (ABB YuMi dual-arm robot + thread manipulator)
sources.developer: Hamlyn Centre, Imperial College London (Hu, Zhang, Li, Yang)
sources.title: Robotic Sewing and Knot Tying for Personalized Stent Graft Manufacturing (arXiv 1803.08478)
sources.claim: A dual-arm ABB YuMi robot with a customised sewing device and closed-loop visual servoing performed autonomous stitching and successive knot tying with surgical-grade thread at sub-millimetre accuracy in laboratory trials.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic manipulation and knotting of fine sewing thread. It shows a general-purpose robot arm pair can grasp, tension and tie thread autonomously in a fixtured cell, supporting the 'twist/knot two thread ends together' act in a purpose-built (E1) setting; it is a lab demo, so it supports E1 only.

tasks.label: Baste edges of material to align and temporarily secure parts for final assembly.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Apparel / soft-goods factory, flat cut pieces: operator aligns two or more limp cut plies (facing to shell, lining to panel, zipper tape, pocket, label) and runs a long temporary basting/tacking stitch so the parts hold position for the final seam; bundle work at a standard industrial machine, standard woven and knit fabrics, repetitive high volume.

Automotive / transportation interior plant: aligning and temporarily tacking leather, vinyl or foam-laminated cover panels (seat covers, headrests, door and airbag panels) at notch marks before the final decorative or structural seam; heavy coated material, curved edges, jigs and templates available, high volume with tight seam tolerances.

Furniture / institutional upholstery plant or shop: basting large cover panels, welt cord, boxing strips and decking of heavy upholstery fabric or leather so the curved pieces stay matched for the final closing seam; medium batch sizes, bulky pieces, frequent style changes.

Industrial and home textile products (tarps, tents, awnings, bags, mattress covers, curtains, medical textiles): tacking the long edges of large heavy panels together so they stay aligned while the final seam is stitched; awkward, heavy, oversized material handled at a long-arm or table machine.

Tailored clothing (suits, coats, uniforms): basting canvas/interlining to jacket fronts, basting sleeve heads into armholes with fullness eased in, hem and collar basting on a partly assembled three-dimensional garment; judgment about ease distribution and shaping, stitch must be removable without marking.

Sample room, custom order and alteration work: one-off or very small lot items, basting pieces together for a fit check or before a designer's approval, unfamiliar fabrics and instructions, constant changeover, often on an already partly finished garment.

sources.system: LOWRY SEWBOT workline (SoftWear Automation)
sources.title: SEWBOTS Transforming The Sewn Products Industry | Textile World
sources.claim: SoftWear Automation's gantry LOWRY Sewbot workline uses machine vision to track and steer limp cut fabric panels through sewing heads, producing home textiles and T-shirts in a purpose-built automated workline with one operator supervising several machines.
sources.transferJustification: Basting is a temporary alignment stitch on the same limp cut plies the Sewbot already aligns and permanently stitches (hems, edge serging, panel joins) under vision control; the manipulation, materials and needle placement are the same, at lower precision demand.

sources.system: SEWBOT (SoftWear Automation)
sources.title: Sewbots - Softwear Automation
sources.claim: Sewbot worklines target exactly the flat sewn-goods panels that basting operations serve (bath mats, towels, pillow and mattress covers, T-shirts), with cameras and sensors steering the fabric and compensating for textile distortion in real time.
sources.transferJustification: Same objects (cut limp panels) and same operation family (edge stitching two aligned plies); a basting pass is a longer-stitch, lower-tolerance version of the seams the machine already sews.

sources.system: Robotic apparel sewing cell (Siemens Technology with Sewbo, Levi Strauss, Bluewater Defense)
sources.title: Robotic Automation in Apparel Manufacturing: A Novel Approach to Fabric Handling and Sewing (arXiv 2503.00249)
sources.claim: A Siemens/Sewbo robotic cell with a collaborative arm, overhead camera and welding tool estimates the pose of cut fabric pieces, aligns them and temporarily joins them before sewing; validated with cotton on the Bluewater Defense production line ... at Levi's research facility.
sources.transferJustification: Temporarily joining aligned cut pieces so they hold position for the final sewing operation is precisely the purpose of basting; the cell performs it on the same garment panels, though it fuses rather than stitches the temporary join.

sources.system: KL 500 3D robot sewing unit (KSL Keilmann / PFAFF Industrial)
sources.title: KL 500 (by KSL Joining Technology GmbH) - PFAFF Industrial
sources.claim: KSL/PFAFF KL 500 robot sewing units are integrated into 3D sewing cells that stitch automotive interior covers in dashboard plants worldwide in 24/7 production, with automatic vision-based seam-path correction and minimal operator intervention.
sources.transferJustification: Robot-guided stitching of leather/vinyl cover material held in cell fixtures involves the same materials, edge alignment and seam accuracy as tacking cover panels together before final assembly.

sources.system: RoQom 6000 / RoQom 7500 robotic sewing cells
sources.title: Robotic - KMF Maschinenbau GmbH
sources.claim: KMF Maschinenbau's RoQom robotic sewing cells (Yaskawa 6-axis robots) sew curved seams on seat-cover parts with camera-based geometry correction, and a RoQom variant holds and guides textiles while applying hot-melt adhesive to fix parts, with automatic program selection by barcode.
sources.transferJustification: Holding cover textiles in alignment and fixing them with hot-melt is the industrial equivalent of basting (temporarily securing parts for the final assembly seam), on the same leather and textile cover panels.

sources.system: PFAFF 3590 Portal / PFAFF 3587 CNC sewing units
sources.title: CNC-Units and automation - PFAFF Industrial
sources.claim: PFAFF's programmable large-area CNC stitchers (up to 1200 x 2000 mm) and clamp-frame sewing units run stored seam programs on clamped panels for car interiors, seats, airbags, bags and convertible tops.
sources.transferJustification: Once large panels are clamped in the frame the unit stitches any programmed path, including a long tacking line that holds panels aligned for a later closing seam; same heavy technical textiles and panel sizes.

sources.system: Dvolu automated upholstery cell (Fanuc M-710iC)
sources.title: Fanuc-powered robotic cell automates furniture upholstery process
sources.claim: A Fanuc M-710iC vision-guided robotic work cell built by integrator Dvolu automates upholstery of chair seat linings at a Canadian furniture manufacturer, stretching, stapling, trimming and palletizing cover fabric that stretches and wrinkles.
sources.transferJustification: Stretching cover fabric into alignment and stapling it to hold position is functionally the same as basting in upholstery work (temporarily securing cover material for final assembly), on the same heavy upholstery fabrics inside a robotic cell.

sources.system: Aitu humanoid sewing robot / Ai10 AI sewing machine
sources.title: Taizhou enterprise showcases AI-powered humanoid sewing robot at 2026 WAIC
sources.claim: Aitu Technology (Jack Technology) showed a garment-specific humanoid sewing robot at WAIC 2026 that moved between workstations and did material handling, positioning and template alignment; a trade-show demonstration rather than production work at a human sewing station.
sources.transferJustification: Closest evidence to a robot working a conventional sewing workstation as a human does, but it is a staged conference demonstration with no evidence of worker-quality basting output, so it cannot support an E2 judgment.

tasks.label: Position and mark patterns on materials to prepare for sewing.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Small/mid-size sewn-goods shop doing its own cutting: operator spreads yardage on a shared cutting table, lays hard oaktag/paper pattern pieces, weights or pins them, traces the outline with tailor's chalk or marker and adds notches and dart/drill marks, then bundles for sewing. Fabric type and layout change job to job.

Production sewing floor: operator receives bundles of cut panels and, before sewing, marks internal placement points (patch-pocket location, dart point, buttonhole, label/trim position) on each panel using a perforated template or marking card with chalk or a disappearing pen at the workstation.

Non-garment / industrial sewn products (upholstery, marine canvas, awnings, automotive trim, bags): operator positions rigid templates on leather hides, heavy vinyl or coated canvas on a large table, works around hide defects, grain and nap, and marks outlines and reference points with silver pencil or soapstone.

Custom / made-to-measure or costume work from flat goods: operator positions patterns on plaid, striped, napped or printed fabric, aligning repeats across pieces, then chalk-marks outlines, notches and construction points for a one-off or very small run.

Alterations and fitting: operator marks new hem, seam or dart lines directly on an already-assembled three-dimensional garment on a dress form or on the customer, pin-folding and chalking the alteration lines before re-sewing.

Home-based or small contract sewing in a residence or a workspace taken as found: pattern pieces laid on fabric on a dining table, floor or improvised surface, pinned and chalk-marked, with variable lighting, clutter and no standard equipment.

sources.system: Eastman Eagle S125 / C125 Automatic Cutting System
sources.date: 2019 (manual revision; product line in commercial service for decades)
sources.title: Eagle C125 Automatic Cutting System Operator's Manual
sources.claim: Eastman's Eagle CNC cutting systems carry a tool head with pneumatically controlled pen and airbrush marking systems and execute a nested marker automatically, marking, cutting, drilling and punching flexible materials (fabric, upholstery, vinyl, leather, composites) held on the machine's own vacuum table/conveyor.
sources.transferJustification: The machine performs the task's purpose directly: it places the pattern set on the material and physically marks it (pen/airbrush marks, drill holes, notches) so the pieces are ready for sewing, on the same fabrics, leathers and coated goods a sewing operator would chalk-mark.

sources.system: Versalis Furniture

sources.claim: Lectra's Versalis furniture line runs as an all-in-one cutting line from ..., with a scanner that digitally maps defects and a head carrying blades and drills.

sources.developer: multiple (Gerber/Lectra, Bullmer, Morgan Tecnica, Zünd, Eastman)

tasks.label: Perform specialized or automatic sewing machine functions, such as buttonhole making or tacking.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Apparel plant, shirt/blouse line: operator runs an automatic buttonhole machine on cut front plackets — positions the panel to marks, cycles the machine for each of 5-7 buttonholes, checks cut/stitch quality, trims threads, stacks bundles, changes thread color between styles.

Denim/workwear plant: operator runs a programmable bartacker or belt-loop attaching unit — bartacks belt loops, pocket corners, fly ends and stress points on heavy indigo panels and assembled jeans, indexing the garment between tacks and inspecting placement.

Industrial/technical textiles (bags, harnesses, military gear, straps): operator runs a programmable pattern tacker or template ('automatic') sewing machine on small parts — labels, webbing straps, tabs, D-ring keepers — clamping each part in a jig, cycling the pattern, unloading.

Automotive / heavy goods plant: operator tends specialized automatic cycle-sewing units on seat covers, airbags, restraint webbing or trim — loads pre-cut panels or webbing into clamps/fixtures, runs the programmed seam or tack cycle, checks stitch integrity on safety-critical parts.

Small custom shop, sample room or alterations department: occasional buttonholes, bartacks and tacking on one-off or short-run varied garments — different fabrics, weights, thread colors and buttonhole sizes, positioned to the tailor's chalk marks on a semi-industrial buttonhole/bartack machine.

Mixed-product plant: operator runs an automatic button-sewing station or automatic embroidery/monogram machine — loads and aligns the panel or hoops the piece, selects the program, runs the automatic cycle, inspects and unloads.

sources.system: FOXSEW Automatic Shirt Front Placket Button Sewing Indexer

sources.claim: FOXSEW's automatic front-placket button indexer sews buttons on shirt fronts with a vacuum placement/alignment system, an auto-moving indexer and a motorised conveyor that feeds the shirt to the machine, so one person can tend several machines.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automatic button attaching rather than buttonholing. Same machine class, same limp shirt panels, same indexing/clamping precision and same automatic cycle, so performance carries over to automatic buttonhole/tacking stations.

sources.claim: Juki's AB-1351 is a commercially sold automatic belt-loop attaching machine that feeds, folds, cuts and bartacks belt loops to consistent dimensions, eliminating the separate loop-cutting operation; one operator can tend two units.

sources.developer: KSL Keilmann / PFAFF Industriesysteme und Maschinen GmbH
sources.date: product page retrieved 2026-07 (system in series production for years)
sources.title: KL 500 (by KSL Joining Technology GmbH)
sources.claim: KSL/PFAFF KL 500 robot sewing units are integrated into 3D sewing cells running 24/7 in automotive dashboard plants worldwide, stitching interior parts with vision-based automatic seam-path correction and minimal operator intervention.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-executed decorative/structural seams on automotive trim rather than buttonhole/tack cycles. Same fixtured limp-material workpieces, comparable stitch-placement precision and the same purpose-built cell, so it substantiates automatic specialized stitching cycles in that environment.

sources.system: SEWBOT / LOWRY autonomous sewing workline
sources.title: Softwear Automation launches Sewbots-as-a-Service
sources.claim: SoftWear Automation's SEWBOT autonomous sewing workline, which uses machine vision and robotic fabric manipulation, has been commercially deployed producing rugs, bath mats, automotive, medical and other sewn goods in dedicated worklines.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous seaming/hemming of soft goods rather than buttonholing. It substantiates machine-vision robotic handling and precise stitching of limp fabric inside a purpose-built workline, the capability the tacking/buttonhole cycle needs at E1.

sources.system: Aitu humanoid sewing robot (with Ai10 AI sewing machine)
sources.developer: Aitu Technology (subsidiary of Jack Technology), Zhejiang
sources.title: China's humanoid robots face their real test on the factory floor (Xinhua/People's Daily Online)
sources.claim: Aitu (Jack Technology) humanoid sewing robots are in production trials at Chinese garment factories doing narrow station tasks — loading/unloading fabric at template sewing machines and positioning material for pocket setters — with 97% ply-separation success on a single product/fabric type, and cannot yet run a production flow without human involvement.
sources.transferJustification: Directly related: tending automatic/template sewing machines on a garment factory floor. Cited to show the state of robot work at ordinary human sewing stations — narrow trials, single fabric type, sub-worker reliability — not to substantiate completion.

roles.title: Shoe and Leather Workers and Repairers
roles.description: Construct, decorate, or repair leather and leather-like products, such as luggage, shoes, and saddles. May use hand tools.

tasks.label: Dye, soak, polish, paint, stamp, stitch, stain, buff, or engrave leather or other materials to obtain desired effects, decorations, or shapes.

instances.label: Shoe repair shop: after resoling/reheeling a customer's pair, the worker trims and buffs the sole and heel edge on a finishing machine, applies edge dye/ink, burnishes it hot, then cleans, creams and buffs the uppers. Arbitrary footwear (dress shoes, work boots, heels, sneakers) of unknown make, worn and mismatched in color; dye shade matched by eye; one pair at a time at the bench/finisher.

Footwear recoloring/restoration service in a repair or shoe-care shop: deglaze or strip the old finish, mask soles and hardware, apply dye or stain in several coats to change or renew color, seal, then cream and buff to a shine; includes deep-clean/condition ('soak') jobs on suede, nubuck and smooth leather. Judgment on prep, coverage and blending of worn areas.

Leather goods repair/restoration in a shop: handbags, luggage, jackets, saddles and tack — touch-up dye on scuffs, re-paint cut edges, stain patches to match, hand- or post-bed-machine restitch a burst seam, then buff and condition. One-off custom craft work in a leather shop: casing (soaking) the leather, hand-tooling and stamping decorative patterns with swivel knife and stamps and a maul, antiquing/staining and highlighting, slicking and burnishing edges, saddle-stitching by hand — for a custom saddle, holster, belt or portfolio to a customer's design.

Small repeat batch of identical straps/belts in a leather workshop: edge-dye or ink dozens of pieces of the same pattern, hot-stamp or emboss a logo/initials, run a programmed decorative topstitch, and burnish. Same shape every time, jigs or clamps available, item presented to a bench machine.

Production/personalization work in a leather goods or footwear workshop or small factory: spray stain/finish on cut panels or lasted shoes of a known model, machine-buff/polish identical shoes, edge-dye components in jigged packages, laser-engrave or emboss monograms and logos, and sew programmed decorative seams — repeated over a run of identical items.

Small leather-goods jobs: shorten belts and punch holes, replace buckles and snaps, restitch straps, relace and recondition baseball gloves (threading lace through holes and knotting), replace purse feet and rivets — quick counter jobs on many different item types.

Clean, condition, re-dye touch-ups and polish/shine footwear at the bench: wash or brush soiled uppers and midsoles, treat leather with cream/conditioner, cover scuffs, buff to a finish and return the pair looking restored.

Production-line joining in a small footwear or leather-goods plant: applying cement to lasted uppers and unit soles and mating them, bonding upper components, or running seams on a bench line under standard work instructions and takt time.

tasks.label: Inspect articles for defects, and remove damaged or worn parts, using hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Shoe repair shop: customer's worn dress shoes or boots come in for new heels. Worker inspects the pair, judges heel/top-piece wear and any breakdown of the heel block, then pries off the worn rubber top-piece or stacked heel with heel pullers, pincers, knife and hammer, drawing out nails without damaging the heel seat or upper.

Shoe repair shop / resoling operation: cemented-construction shoes and sneakers needing full or half soles. Worker inspects the worn outsole, then heats and peels/pries the glued sole unit off the upper with knife, pincers and heat, cleans residual adhesive, leaving the lasting margin intact for the new sole.

Shoe repair shop: mixed component repairs — inspect boots/shoes and rip out worn insoles and linings, cut broken welt or upper stitching with a seam ripper/knife, pull damaged eyelets, hooks, shanks or a broken boot zipper, in preparation for replacement parts.

Luggage/handbag/leather goods repair bench: inspect a suitcase, briefcase or handbag for defects (broken zipper, torn handle, split gusset, damaged hardware, worn corners) and unpick stitching or cut away the damaged handle, zipper tape, feet or trim with seam ripper, knife and pliers, preserving the surrounding leather.

Saddlery/tack shop (sometimes on-site at a barn): inspect a saddle, bridle or harness for cracked or rotted leather, broken stitching and worn hardware; strip off damaged billets, stirrup leathers, worn padding or fleece and cut out old stitching with a knife, ripper and pliers before rebuilding.

Footwear/leather goods plant or brand refurbishment center: inspect in-process or finished articles for defects at a bench or line — crooked sole bond, excess cement, flash, wrinkled upper, defective hardware — and trim or strip off the offending part with knife, nippers and pliers so the article can be reworked.

tasks.label: Check the texture, color, and strength of leather to ensure that it is adequate for a particular purpose.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Cutting room of a footwear or leather-goods factory: before clicking, the worker spreads each hide/skin on the cutting table, looks over grain texture and shade uniformity, finds scars, brands, loose grain and thin or stretchy areas, and decides which zones are good enough for visible vamps versus linings or hidden parts.

Small-batch or bespoke workshop (handbags, belts, shoe uppers, orthopedic footwear): the worker pulls a hide or skin from the rack for a specific component, checks grain texture and finish, compares shade to the other panels of the article, checks substance/thickness and looks for weak spots before cutting.

Saddlery/harness work with heavy vegetable-tanned leather: the worker selects a side for skirting, straps or stirrup leathers, judging temper and firmness by flexing and pulling the piece by hand, feeling the grain and back, and deciding whether it will carry load without stretching.

Shoe repair shop: choosing patch, sole, heel or lining leather from shop stock for a customer's worn item - holding candidate pieces against the shoe to match colour and grain, bending and tugging them to judge firmness and strength, and deciding whether the piece will hold for that repair.

Material room / QC bench of a footwear or leather-goods plant: verifying an incoming lot of hides against the specification - shade against a colour standard, thickness/substance gauging, and strength checks (tensile, tear, stitch tear) on cut specimens before the lot is released to production.

Assessment away from the worker's own bench: a customer brings in their own hide or an item to be re-leathered, or the worker assesses leather in place on furniture, a car interior or a saddle at the customer's site, under whatever light and conditions are found there.

sources.system: Mindhive BlueSelect
sources.title: Mindhive BlueSelect: AI-powered wet-blue leather grading
sources.claim: Mindhive BlueSelect is an AI hide-grading machine installed inline in tanneries; it scans each wet-blue hide, detects 30+ defect classes down to hair-follicle resolution, measures cuttable area and applies the customer's grading rules automatically at line speed. Listed users include Bader, JBS Couros, Scottish Leather Group and Tasman Tanning.
sources.transferJustification: Same task content as the instance - judging a hide's surface texture/defects and quality zones against rules that define what the hide is good enough for - performed on whole hides fed through a scanner rather than by a cutter at a table.

sources.claim: Zund's Dectura workflow couples Mindhive FinishSelect, an AI quality-assessment machine for finished leather, to MindCUT nesting and Zund cutters: it maps defects at 0.17 mm, identifies 20+ defect types, applies customer-specific Natural Feature Guide grading rules and assigns quality grades used to place cut parts.

sources.claim: Trade-press launch report on Mindhive FinishSelect: the conveyor-based inspection and grading machine produces a digital hide quality map in 15 seconds versus 7-10 minutes for manual inspection, detecting defects as small as a hair follicle across 20+ types, and is built with industrial conveyors to integrate with factory workflows.

sources.transferJustification: Covers the structural/strength element of the check: the machine finds thin, weak zones that a worker finds by stretching the hide, and assigns quality zones governing downstream use.

sources.transferJustification: Machine-run measurement of the same physical property the worker judges by pulling and flexing, executed to the leather industry's own strength standards.

sources.claim: ZwickRoell's roboTest F is a commercial robotic testing system for non-rigid sheet specimens such as plastic films, foils and textiles: up to 200 specimens sit in holders on a carousel and are conveyed automatically to the testing machine, where ... without an operator.

tasks.label: Shape shoe heels with a knife, and sand them on a buffing wheel for smoothness.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Small shoe repair shop: a customer's men's leather dress shoe or work boot gets a new rubber/composite heel lift or combination heel. The cobbler nails on an oversized top-piece, pares the excess flush to the existing heel block with a knife, then sands it on the finisher's abrasive/buffing wheel to a smooth, even edge before dyeing/burnishing. One-off shoes of varied size, style and wear.

Repair shop: women's dress shoes and boots with slender, leather- or vinyl-covered heels. Worn heel tips/lifts are replaced and the heel is re-shaped and lightly sanded flush without abrading or scorching the heel covering; the finish must match the surrounding covered surface.

Repair shop / restoration: rebuilding worn stacked-leather heels on Goodyear-welted shoes and cowboy boots - adding leather lifts, cutting and paring the heel breast and sides with a knife to re-establish the pitch and profile, then sanding on the wheel to blend the layers before staining and burnishing.

Orthopedic/pedorthic shoe modification lab: heel lifts, medial/lateral heel wedges or flares of EVA/crepe are added to a patient's shoe, then knife-trimmed and ground/sanded to a prescribed height and smoothly blended into the shoe's existing sole and heel line.

Small-batch shoe or boot manufacturing / bespoke workshop: heels of newly lasted shoes are trimmed and shaped (heel breast, seat and edges) and scoured/buffed smooth on abrasive wheels as part of the bottom-finishing sequence, in runs of a given style and size.

sources.title: ABB robots are helping a small shoe factory take some big steps
sources.claim: ABB IRB 1600 robot cells at DB Shoes' factory in Rushden, UK autonomously rough lasted leather shoes by guiding a rotating abrasive disk around the bite line, running about 210 stored programs for different styles and sizes in daily production.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic abrasive material removal on assembled leather shoes held on lasts. It transfers to shaping and sanding heels because the objects (leather shoes), the tooling (rotating abrasive wheel/disk) and the required care (the article notes the wheel could tear delicate panels) are the same; only the region of the shoe differs.

sources.system: DESMA amir fc automated tooling cells / roughing robot

Pedorthic heel lifts, wedges and flares use the same materials and tolerances, so machine shaping substitutes for knife-and-buffing-wheel shaping of the build-up.

tasks.label: Place shoes on lasts to remove soles and heels, using knives or pliers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Neighborhood shoe repair shop, heel-only job: worn top lift or heel block on a woman's pump or man's dress shoe/boot. The repairer sets the shoe on a jack/last, pries the rubber top lift or stacked heel off with nippers/pliers, and pulls the residual nails without tearing the heel seat or upper. Worn, one-off customer goods of every make.

Repair shop, full resole of a Goodyear-welted or stitchdown dress shoe or work boot: shoe on the last, the outsole lockstitch is cut with a knife/channel cutter without severing the welt, the outsole is pried and peeled off the welt and midsole, and the nailed heel stack is knocked/pulled off. Welt, insole and upper must survive intact for restitching.

Repair shop, half-sole or full leather-sole removal on a welted or Blake-stitched shoe with the heel left in place: the old sole is cut across the waist, skived and peeled with knife and pliers, adhesive residue removed, feather edge left clean. Precise, judgment-driven knife work on a single worn shoe.

Repair shop, cemented/unit-sole footwear: glued rubber, EVA or wedge unit sole on a casual shoe, sneaker, or work boot where sole and heel are one piece. The shoe goes on a last/jack, the bond is heated and the whole sole pulled/cut away, leaving the lasted upper for a new unit sole.

High-volume institutional operation (brand recrafting/refurbishment center, industrial or military footwear repair contractor, take-back line): the same few models arrive in batches on carts or a conveyor, dedicated presses, ovens and pullers are on hand, and soles are stripped in bulk to a fixed procedure.

sources.transferJustification: Same physical act as the task's core step - separating an outsole from a shoe upper - on the same objects (worn, heterogeneous end-of-life footwear), but performed for material recovery rather than for resoling.

sources.claim: CETIA's tear-off line for glued shoes combines an oven that reactivates the adhesive with a robot that applies a tearing force to pull the sole off the upper - the same heat-and-pull method a cobbler uses on cemented shoes.
sources.transferJustification: Directly substantiates robotic removal of a cemented sole from a shoe; the shoe repairer's cemented-sole removal uses the identical heat-plus-pull mechanism.

sources.system: CETIA shoe de-soling machine

tasks.label: Repair or replace soles, heels, and other parts of footwear, using sewing, buffing and other shoe repair machines, materials, and equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Neighborhood shoe repair shop: replace worn heels/top-lifts on men's and women's dress shoes. Pry or grind off the worn rubber lift, level the heel base, cut/cement a new lift, nail it, trim the overhang on a finisher, then sand, dye and burnish the edge. Each pair differs in size, style, heel height and wear pattern; worker holds the shoe by hand against wheels and machines.

Repair shop: half-sole or full-sole replacement on cemented or stitched leather dress shoes. Rip off the old sole, clean adhesive and nails, roughen the bottom, cut and fit new leather/rubber sole stock, cement, press, trim excess with a knife, then edge-sand, stain and finish. Condition of the welt and insole varies pair to pair.

Repair shop: women's high-heel work — replacing snapped-off plastic heel tips/taps, re-gluing loose heel covers, reattaching or reinforcing a broken stiletto heel, replacing thin leather soles on delicate pumps. Small, fragile parts, thin material, cosmetic finish matters.

Repair shop or resole specialist: resoling work boots, hiking boots and Goodyear-welted footwear. Remove the lug sole/heel block, repair or replace the welt, cement a new Vibram unit, stitch the outsole on a sole stitcher, build and attach the heel block, then trim and finish. Heavy, stiff, often dirty and misshapen from wear.

Repair shop: athletic/sneaker and casual footwear — reattaching separated outsoles, rebuilding worn midsoles or toe caps, patching or replacing other parts (zippers, straps, elastic) on synthetic uppers. Solvent cleaning, contact cement, clamping and cosmetic cleanup.

Pedorthic/orthopedic footwear lab attached to a clinic: modify shoes to prescription — split the outsole, bond in a heel or sole lift, add a wedge or rocker, rebond and grind the added material to the prescribed shape and blend it to the existing sole. Prescription geometry differs per patient; footwear supplied by the patient.

sources.system: DESMA amir®c robotic cementing cells and lines
sources.title: DESMA automates footwear production – robot-aided solutions for cementing upper and sole with amir®c
sources.claim: DESMA's amir®c product line is a commercially deployed, robot-based cementing system for footwear factories: robots scan each sole's contour and apply primer/cement, and a roughing robot roughens uppers along a defined path. Sole laying is still performed by an operator, assisted by an automatic bottoming cell.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: attaching soles to new shoes in a factory. It is the closest industrial analogue to resoling, but it works on new, matched components lasted on precise lasts with a loaded 'production recipe'; it does not remove worn soles, cut and fit sole stock to a used shoe, nail heels, or trim/dye edges, and even sole laying remains manual.

sources.system: Robot-based shoe manufacturing automation testbed (industrial manipulator + 3-D scanner + cementing tool)

sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic roughing and adhesive application on new shoe uppers/soles in a fenced production testbed. tasks.label: Cut, insert, position, and secure paddings, cushioning, or linings, using stitches or glue.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Shoe repair shop bench: a customer brings worn shoes or boots; the repairer cuts a replacement sock lining, heel pad, tongue pad or metatarsal cushion from sheet leather/foam to fit that particular shoe, works cement into the shoe's footbed cavity, positions the pad by hand and presses it down, then trims flush. Every shoe differs in size, last shape, wear pattern and interior condition.

Small-batch footwear / leather-goods production bench (custom shoemaker, small US footwear or leather goods maker): cutting lining and padding pieces to a standard pattern from stock material, positioning them on flat uppers, vamps, wallet or case panels, and securing them by cement or by machine stitching, in repeatable runs with jigs and patterns.

Handbag, briefcase or luggage relining in a repair shop: the old lining is torn out, new lining panels and any padding are cut to the pattern of that bag, then positioned inside the bag's cavity and stitched or glued along seams reached by reaching into a floppy, partly closed interior.

Pedorthic / orthopedic shop or lab: per prescription, cutting cushioning layers (PPT, Poron, EVA, felt) and lining materials, then gluing them onto a custom orthotic shell, into a modified shoe, or onto a brace or prosthetic socket liner; each device is bespoke and hand-fit, then ground and skived to blend.

Saddlery / harness shop: replacing or adding panel flocking, felt or foam padding in a saddle panel, and cutting and hand-stitching or gluing a leather or linen lining over it; heavy, thick, curved multi-layer leather work on a stand or stitching horse.

tasks.label: Draw patterns, using measurements, designs, plaster casts, or customer specifications, and position or outline patterns on work pieces.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production cutting room of a footwear/leather-goods plant: hides or sides are laid out and the graded production pattern set is positioned (nested) on them, avoiding scars, brands and stretch-sensitive zones, and outlined/marked before cutting.

Shoe/bag repair shop: the worker traces the outline of a replacement part (half-sole, heel lift, tap, patch panel, insole, strap) from the worn part or the damaged area onto leather or rubber stock, adding allowance, then cuts it out.

Orthopedic/made-to-measure footwear shop with a digital last workflow: foot measurements or a scanned plaster cast produce a custom last, an existing style pattern is adapted to it, and the pieces are outlined on the leather.

Fully bespoke shoemaking: the maker takes a last built from a plaster cast/measurements, tapes and draws the mean form by hand, drafts new style lines to the customer's brief, and transfers the outlines to the leather.

Saddle/harness/tack shop: large hard templates for seat, skirts, flaps and billets are laid on a side of firm veg-tan leather, oriented for firmness and stretch direction, and scribed around with a scratch awl.

Custom leather goods (bag, holster, luggage, belt) made to a customer's verbal or sketched specification: the worker drafts a new paper/board pattern from measurements, then positions and outlines it on the hide.

tasks.label: Nail heel and toe cleats onto shoes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Shoe repair shop: customer's worn dress shoes get metal or rubber heel taps (heel plates/cleats). Cobbler removes the old tap, positions a plate of the right size flush with the rear edge of the worn heel top-piece, drives 3-6 brass nails or screws by hammer or bench machine, sands the edge and dresses it. Shoes vary by brand, size, heel material and wear pattern.

Shoe repair shop: recessed toe taps/toe plates on leather-soled dress shoes. Cobbler grinds or routs a shallow pocket in the worn toe of the sole matching the plate outline, checks the plate sits flush with the sole plane, fastens it with small nails/screws, then sands the edge and applies edge dressing and polish. Cosmetic quality matters to the customer.

Shoe repair shop/boot shop: metal heel cleats (horseshoe taps) and toe cleats nailed onto cowboy boots, work boots and heavy footwear. Thick leather or stacked heels, heavier nails, dirty and heavily worn uppers and soles, tall shafts that must be supported on a jack or boot column.

Production/finishing bench in a small footwear factory, custom boot shop or orthopedic footwear lab: attaching heel top-pieces, cleats or protective plates with nails on a repetitive run of the same model, shoes presented on lasts or jacks at a dedicated nailing/heel-attaching machine station.

Tap/dance and specialty shoes: screwing or nailing taps and cleats to prescribed positions on new shoes of known models (tap shoes, clogging or Irish hard shoes, specialty cleated footwear), with a consistent fastener pattern and no recess-cutting.
