tasks.label: Re-sew seams, and replace handles and linings of suitcases or handbags.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Cobbler / leather-goods repair shop: customer brings in a leather handbag with a burst side seam or a torn strap anchor. Worker inspects the damage, picks out broken thread, realigns the existing needle holes, and re-sews with a walking-foot or patcher machine plus hand stitching where the machine cannot reach; thread color and stitch length must match the original. Each job is one-off.

Repair shop: replace or rebuild a handbag handle or shoulder strap. Worker removes the old handle (cutting stitches, drilling out rivets), selects and cuts matching leather, skives and edge-finishes it, sets new hardware/rivets, and stitches the new handle to the bag body, often working inside the assembled bag.

Luggage repair depot or brand warranty service center: replace the telescoping or side carry handle on a hard/soft-side suitcase. Worker opens or partially unstitches the lining, removes rivets/screws, fits a standard replacement part for that model, then re-secures the lining and re-sews the opened seam.

Repair shop: replace a shredded lining in a handbag or suitcase. Worker removes the old lining (unpicking seams around pockets and zips), uses it as a pattern to cut new fabric, sews the lining panels, inserts it into the assembled bag, and hand slip-stitches the closing seam invisibly.

Luxury/designer bag restoration at a specialist or brand atelier: re-sew opened seams to a cosmetic standard, sometimes by hand saddle stitch matching the original stitch holes and pitch, on a valuable bag where any mark or misplaced hole is unacceptable.

Shop repair of a nylon/canvas duffel, backpack or soft suitcase: re-sew a straight blown seam or bar-tack and replace a webbing handle; materials are plainer and seams more accessible, but the article is still a finished 3D bag that must be turned and fed through the machine.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: machine sewing of seams. Cited to show the closest demonstrated capability is sewing flat cut panels in a purpose-built cell; it does not cover picking out old stitching, aligning existing holes, or working inside a finished bag.

tasks.label: Stretch shoes, dampening parts and inserting and twisting parts, using an adjustable stretcher.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Neighborhood shoe repair shop: customer's leather dress shoe or pump is a half size too tight overall. Worker inspects the material, sprays/wipes stretching liquid on the vamp and quarters, inserts a two-way adjustable wooden stretcher, twists the handle to expand width (and sometimes length), leaves it 24-48 hours, removes it and checks the result.

Spot stretching for a bunion, corn, hammertoe or bone spur: worker locates the pressure point the customer marks or indicates, dampens that spot, inserts the stretcher fitted with relief-spot plugs positioned exactly at the point (or uses a ball-and-ring stretcher with a heat gun), twists to raise a localized bulge, then re-fits and repeats until the pressure is relieved.

Boot work: tall dress boots or cowboy boots too tight in the calf shaft or instep. Worker dampens the shaft/instep leather, inserts a boot calf stretcher or instep stretcher through the boot opening, cranks it to a measured circumference, often over repeated sessions, and checks against the customer's calf measurement.

Retail shoe store / while-you-wait service: new shoes stretched on the shop's stretching machine or with spray plus heat in minutes, customer tries the shoe on, worker adjusts the amount of stretch and repeats until the fit is accepted before the customer leaves.

Orthopedic/pedorthic shop: prescription or diabetic footwear stretched to accommodate a documented foot deformity, sometimes over a modified last or cast, on delicate or synthetic-lined uppers where over-stretching or splitting would ruin an expensive shoe; iterative fitting against the patient's foot.

sources.system: Tenghong TH-739A/TH-739B intelligent automatic toe lasting machine
sources.developer: Guangdong Tenghong Machinery Technology Co., Ltd.
sources.title: Intelligent automatic toe lasting machine with memory control

sources.transferJustification: Related task: pulling-over/toe lasting. The machine performs the same physical operation as shoe stretching - forcing leather to conform to a rigid form under controlled tension without tearing it - on the same material (leather uppers), at higher precision than a hand stretcher, at a fixed machine station where the work is presented to the machine.

sources.system: DGSF QY-309 Computerized Steaming Shoe Last Inserting Machine (also QY-305/QY-307 variants)

sources.transferJustification: Related task: steaming and last-insertion in shoe finishing. It performs exactly the two mechanical steps of this task - dampening the shoe with steam and inserting/driving a rigid form into the shoe to stretch and shape it - on comparable objects (leather shoes) with machine-controlled stroke positions standing in for the stretcher's twist adjustment.

sources.claim: A robotic cell picks individual shoes off a conveyor, 3-D digitizes each one and then executes roughing and cementing along the shoe's upper surface, i.e. vision-guided application of a liquid to specified regions of a particular shoe inside a fenced industrial cell.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic roughing and cementing of shoe uppers. It substantiates machine handling of individual shoes and vision-guided application of a fluid to the correct area of a specific shoe - the 'dampening parts' element of this task - in a purpose-built cell.

sources.system: Collaborative robotic shoe-polishing cell (force-controlled manipulator with specialized polishing tool)
sources.developer: Academic-industrial project published in Int. J. Computer Integrated Manufacturing / arXiv 2411.09603
sources.title: Smart Automation in Luxury Leather Shoe Polishing: A Human Centric Robotic Approach
sources.claim: A collaborative robotic cell with a force-controlled manipulator and a dedicated tool performs polishing of finished luxury leather shoes, a delicate finishing operation on completed footwear previously done only by skilled craftsmen.

sources.system: Boot Ironing Machine V15-B / HC-777C
sources.title: Boot Ironing Machine (V15-B /HC-777C) - Shoes Making Machine and Boot Machine
sources.claim: Commercial boot ironing/shaping machines mount a boot shaft over rotating aluminium moulds and apply wet hot air and pressure to shape the boot leg over the form in footwear plants.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: boot-leg ironing/shaping. Same objects (boot shafts) and same principle as boot stretching - moisture plus heat with the leather forced over a form - though the loading appears operator-driven, so it is cited only as supporting context.

tasks.label: Read prescriptions or specifications, and take measurements to establish the type of product to be made, using calipers, tape measures, or rules.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Shoe repair shop intake/bench: cobbler reads the customer's work ticket or verbal instructions, inspects the worn shoe or boot, and measures it with a rule and calipers (heel height and pitch, sole/midsole thickness, shank length, welt width) to establish which replacement sole, heel block, lift or patch material to make or fit.

Pedorthic / orthopedic footwear work in a specialty store or clinic: worker reads a physician's or podiatrist's prescription (e.g., diabetic accommodative insoles, 12 mm sole lift for limb-length discrepancy) and measures the patient's live feet and lower limbs with a Brannock device, tape measure and calipers (length, ball width and girth, instep, arch height, lift height) to establish the device or shoe modification to be made.

Bespoke/custom shoe or boot making: maker reads the customer's order specification and takes a full set of foot measurements with tape and rule (length, joint and waist girths, heel-to-ball, ankle, calf for boots) on the seated/standing customer in the shop to establish the last size and pattern to be built.

Leather goods bench or small factory (luggage, cases, belts, straps, upholstery panels): worker reads the pattern spec sheet or work order, gauges leather thickness with calipers/thickness gauge, measures hide area and usable zones, and measures out stock with rule and tape to establish the parts and sizes to be cut.

Saddlery, harness and tack work: worker reads the customer's specification and takes measurements at a barn, arena or shop — wither and back contour of the horse with a flexible curve or tree gauge, girth line, rider seat size, or the dimensions of existing tack needing a replacement strap — to establish the saddle, harness or repair part to be made.

sources.system: Creaform MetraSCAN 3D-R / CUBE-R
sources.title: Detect Quality Issues Faster and Make Better Decisions With R-Series 3D Scanning Systems
sources.claim: Creaform's MetraSCAN 3D-R robot-mounted optical CMM and the CUBE-R turnkey measuring cell perform automated dimensional measurement of parts against CAD specifications inside an enclosed cell installed at production lines; commercially sold and installed for at-line inspection.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated dimensional inspection. It is the same act as the human step here — physically bringing a measuring instrument to a workpiece and reading out dimensions to metrology-grade precision, then comparing them with a digital specification — on objects of comparable size and with far tighter precision than calipers or a rule require.

sources.claim: Lectra's Versalis leather cutting system scans each hide as it is loaded to determine quality zones and defects, then automatically nests the ordered parts across the hides; used in automotive and luxury leather cutting rooms.

sources.system: Robot-based upper/sole manufacturing system (3-D scanner + industrial manipulators)

sources.title: Robot-Based Automation for Upper and Sole Manufacturing in Shoe Production (Machines 10(4):255)
sources.claim: A robot-based shoe manufacturing cell measured individual shoes with a 3-D scanner (gauge line on the upper, XYZ positions of the sole ...) to derive the work path, verified on a demonstrative production line with conveyor lines supplied by a shoe manufacturer.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic roughing/cementing path generation. The measuring step is identical to the one rated here — a machine measures an individual shoe held in a fixture and derives from those dimensions what work/part is required — on exactly the objects (shoes, soles) that shoe workers measure.

sources.system: Real-time 3D vision-based robotic adhesive spraying system for lasted uppers
sources.title: Real-Time 3D Vision-Based Robotic Path Planning for Automated Adhesive Spraying on Lasted Uppers in Footwear Manufacturing
sources.claim: A 3D vision-based robotic cell reconstructs each lasted shoe upper into a high-resolution point ... in real time and plans the work path from those per-item measurements.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: per-item scanning of footwear in a robotic cell. It demonstrates machine measurement of the individual shoe's geometry to sub-millimetre resolution, the same measurement act required to establish sizes and parts for a shoe.

sources.system: UPOD-S 3D Laser Full-Foot Scanner
sources.title: Validation of an Automated Optical Scanner for a ... - ProQuest
sources.claim: An automated optical full-foot laser scanner reproduced the foot and ankle anthropometrics used for custom footwear and orthoses with mean absolute error under 1 mm, i.e. at or better than hand measurement quality.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated anthropometric foot measurement. It produces the very measurements (length, widths, girths, heights) the worker takes with tape and calipers to establish the shoe, last or orthosis to be made, at accuracy exceeding manual practice, with the foot presented to the machine.

sources.system: Aetrex Albert 2 Pro / Albert 3DFit scanner
sources.title: 3D Scanning for Custom Footwear and Orthotics
sources.claim: Aetrex Albert 3D foot scanners are installed in retail stores and clinics, producing a complete 3D reconstruction of ... customer's foot with key measurements (length, width, girth, instep, arch height) that drive footwear and orthotic selection.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: in-store automated foot measurement for orthotics. The output is the same measurement set the pedorthist takes by hand to establish the product; it is a static sensing kiosk rather than an actuated machine, so it is cited as supporting quality evidence only.

sources.system: Aescape robotic massage table

sources.claim: Aescape's fully automated robotic table is deployed in Equinox gyms; it 3D-scans the client's body, maps key anatomical points, and then works on the body with force-controlled robotic arms without an operator.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous 3D scanning and physical contact with a live human body in a commercial facility. It substantiates that an actuated machine can measure and locate a person's body geometry to working precision while the person is positioned on the machine — the presentation condition assumed for taking a customer's foot measurements at E1.

sources.system: In-line automated leather thickness/area measuring machines (conveyor systems; e.g. GER Elettronica, Selin)

sources.claim: Leather thickness/substance is measured in industry either by hand gauge or by an automated measuring device built into a conveyor system, and tanneries run electronic conveyor machines that measure hide area automatically.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated measurement of leather stock. It is the same measurement (substance/thickness and area of a hide against a specification) that the leather worker makes with a gauge and rule to establish what can be cut, on identical material.

tasks.label: Attach accessories or ornamentation to decorate or protect products.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Shoe repair shop: customer brings worn dress shoes/boots; worker attaches protective heel taps, toe plates or rubber sole guards — assesses wear, pries off the old tap, selects/trims a matching piece, cements and nails it, sands and finishes flush. Every pair differs in heel shape, size and wear pattern.

Shoe/leather repair shop: one-off hardware work on customers' handbags, belts, luggage and jackets — replacing or adding buckles, snaps, rivets, studs, D-rings, metal feet and corner protectors on limp, already-assembled goods; hardware selected to match the original.

Leather goods / footwear manufacturing bench or line: attaching standardized trim and hardware (eyelets, rivets, logo plates, buckles, decorative overlays, sequins/studs) to identical cut parts in batches, using setting dies, presses and jigs, to a fixed spec.

Custom saddlery / western leather shop: setting conchos, spot studs, silver corners, nameplates and decorative trim onto saddles, tack, holsters and show gear — curved 3-D assemblies, one-off layouts, hand-fitted and often riveted or laced from both sides.

Small-batch craft leather shop: applying a repeating ornament pattern (studs, sequins, appliqué, decorative stitching) to flat belt blanks, wallet panels or bag fronts before assembly, working from a drawn or digital layout.

Orthopedic / therapeutic footwear lab: attaching protective toe caps, wear plates, reinforcement patches and metatarsal bars to prescription shoes; each pair modified to an individual prescription and shoe last, then finished so the addition is smooth and durable.

sources.system: ZSK technical embroidery machines with Vision System (OPSII)
sources.title: ZSK Embroidery Machines - Automotive
sources.claim: ZSK industrial embroidery machines used in automotive interior production place decorative elements on leather and artificial-leather cut parts, with a camera-based Optical Positioning System aligning placement on the fixtured panel.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: machine placement of decorative elements onto leather cut parts held in a frame. Same act as attaching ornamentation to a leather product, same material and comparable millimetre placement precision, but only with the panel presented flat and fixtured.

sources.system: ZSK functional sequin device (FSD) on ZSK embroidery machines

sources.claim: ZSK machines attach discrete sequins to hooped material automatically as part of the embroidery run, without a separate manual placement step.

tasks.label: Make, modify, and repair orthopedic or therapeutic footwear according to doctors' prescriptions, or modify existing footwear for people with foot problems and special needs.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Fabricating a pair of custom foot orthoses/therapeutic inserts to a physician's prescription (e.g., Medicare Therapeutic Shoe Bill diabetic inserts, accommodative or functional devices) in the shop's fabrication room: starting from a plaster/foam cast or 3D scan plus the Rx, producing the shell (vacuum-formed, milled or printed), adding posts/pads, bonding a top cover, trimming and grinding to the finished device.

External modification of an existing stock or therapeutic shoe: removing/opening the outsole, fabricating and bonding a tapered heel/sole lift for leg-length discrepancy, a rocker or metatarsal bar, a medial/lateral flare or wedge, then grinding the buildup to blend with the shoe's contour, re-attaching the outsole and refinishing/dyeing. Done at a bench with hand-held grinder, cement, press.

Internal modification/adaptation of an existing shoe for a foot problem: spot-stretching over a bunion or hammertoe on a ball-and-ring or stretching machine, skiving and cementing in met pads, tongue pads, heel lifts or relief pockets, removing/replacing a factory insole, filling a shoe for a partial-foot amputation. Small, varied, judgment-driven hand work on the customer's own worn shoes.

Repairing or refurbishing existing orthopedic/therapeutic footwear and devices: resoling worn custom or extra-depth shoes, replacing worn rocker soles and lifts while preserving the prescribed geometry, restitching split uppers, re-covering worn orthosis top covers, re-gluing delaminated buildups. Work arrives dirty, worn and one-off.

Making a pair of custom-molded orthopedic shoes from scratch over a patient-specific last: modifying/carving the last from a cast or scan, pattern making, cutting and closing the leather upper, lasting, bottoming with a prescribed sole/rocker, finishing and fitting.

tasks.label: Select materials and patterns, and trace patterns onto materials to be cut out.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Shoe repair shop bench work: repairer sizes up a customer's damaged shoe or boot, picks sheet stock (sole/rubber, lining, patch leather) matching the item's weight, color and grain from shelf scraps, then traces around the removed sole, the worn part, or a shop template with chalk/silver pen before cutting. Every job is a different, worn, three-dimensional item.

Custom/bespoke shoemaker or small footwear atelier: selects an upper hide and lining by color, temper and grain for the order, pulls the pattern set graded to the customer's last and size, lays the pieces on the hide avoiding brands, scars and loose belly, respecting stretch direction, and scribes around them for clicking.

Cutting room of a small-series leather goods / footwear manufacturer (handbags, luggage, belts, shoe uppers): selects hides from the incoming lot and the pattern pieces for the work order, nests templates on each hide to a yield target, and marks them for hand cutting or clicker-press cutting.

Custom orthopedic/therapeutic footwear and brace lab: selects glove leather, lining, plastazote/foam and reinforcement per prescription, selects the individually graded upper pattern generated for the patient's last, and marks the pieces on the material for cutting.

Saddle, harness and tack shop: selects a heavy vegetable-tanned side by thickness, firmness and area (back vs. belly) for skirts, fenders, straps and billets, chooses the pattern templates for the tree/size, positions them on the side and scribes them with an awl before cutting.

tasks.label: Inspect finished products to ensure that shoes have been completed according to specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-process check at the operator's own machine on a mass-production footwear line: after each machine cycle (cementing/spray-gluing, sole press, stitching, heel attach) the operator takes the shoe or shoe part off the machine, checks the feature just produced (glue coverage and squeeze-out, sole/upper alignment, seam quality, no machine marks) and passes it on or sets it aside for rework/adjustment.

End-of-line cosmetic inspection of every finished shoe on a high-volume, standardized line (athletic, injection-molded or direct-soled footwear, few SKUs at a time): surface scuffs, excess glue, stitching faults, sole misalignment, symmetry with the mate; defective shoes pulled off the line to rework.

End-of-line inspection on mixed-model leather, dress or work-boot production with frequent style changes: grading cosmetic issues (shade variation, wrinkles, dirt, loose threads) against limit samples, plus tactile checks — pressing the bond, feeling the inside/lining and insole seating, flexing the shoe.
Pre-packing verification station: confirm the correct left/right pair, matching sizes, correct model, intact and correct labels/SKU on shoe and box, and that both shoes are present before boxing.

Dimensional/spec conformance check of sampled shoes against the approved sample or spec sheet: heel height, sole thickness, length/girth, position of components, using gauges, templates and comparison to the golden sample.

Small-shop or custom work: orthopedic, custom-made, hand-finished or repaired shoes inspected against an individual work order in a small factory, orthotic lab or repair shop; one-off items with no golden sample and highly varied models.

It shows finished and part-finished shoes can be fixtured, located to millimetre contour accuracy and presented to a machine inside enclosed purpose-built cells, which is the presentation the E1 counterfactual for an inspection station assumes.

tasks.label: Align parts to be stitched, following seams, edges, or markings, before positioning them under needles.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Closing room of a footwear plant (work boots, dress shoes, athletic uppers): operator takes cut leather/synthetic/textile parts from a bundle, mates two flat components (vamp to quarter, backstay, lining to upper) so that edges or marked seam lines register within about a millimeter, holds the registration, and feeds the pair under the needle of a flatbed or post-bed lockstitch machine.

Attaching small components to a flat panel at marked positions before stitching: logo/brand overlays, labels, eyelet stays, foam collars, elastic gores, zipper tape. Operator positions the small piece on the larger panel by locating registration marks or notches, then slides the assembly under the needle.

Working a computerized pattern/template stitcher: operator lays cut parts into a jig or template following registration pins and marks, closes the frame, and loads it into the automatic sewing machine, which then sews the programmed path.

Three-dimensional / assembled-shoe stitching: aligning welt, insole rib and lasted upper on a Goodyear inseam or outsole stitcher, feeding a lasted upper to a Strobel sock-lining stitcher, or aligning a moccasin plug to a vamp on a moccasin machine — the workpiece is a shaped, partly built shoe that must be steered by feel around curves.

Small-lot custom, orthopedic or rework operations in a small shop or factory repair bench: aligning a patch, replacement quarter, or reinforcement onto a partly finished or returned shoe on a patcher/darner machine, with varying styles, materials and non-standard part positions.

tasks.label: Operate or tend machines to join, decorate, reinforce, or finish shoes and shoe parts.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Volume athletic/casual footwear plant, sole-attaching station: operator takes lasted uppers off the conveyor, mates the cemented outsole to the lasted upper by eye, loads the pair into a hydraulic sole press (or loads last/upper into a direct-injection mold station), cycles the machine, and removes and inspects the pairs; single model runs, high cadence.

Lasting operation: operator mounts the upper and insole on the last, positions the assembly in a toe/side/heel-seat lasting machine, aligns the back seam and toe by eye, actuates pincers/wipers and cement injection, removes the lasted shoe, and adjusts machine settings when the style or size changes.

Stitching room: operator runs post-bed, flatbed, or computer-controlled pattern stitchers to join cut upper parts, sew decorative topstitching and logos, or run a welt/outsole stitcher — guiding or loading leather/textile parts, changing thread and needles, matching seams and edge margins.

Bottoming prep: operator tends roughing/buffing machines to abrade the lasting margin along the bite line, and cementing/spray machines or brush stations to apply adhesive to uppers and soles, then passes shoes through the activation oven; must follow the sole contour accurately on each style.

Finishing room: operator tends edge trimming/setting, heel and edge burnishing, brushing/polishing wheels, and spray-finishing booths on assembled shoes; cosmetic quality judgment, varied colors and materials, shoes handled one at a time against powered wheels.

Small shop work — a resoling/recrafting operation, boot rebuilder, or custom orthopedic footwear lab: operator runs a finisher (sanding/buffing wheels), sole stitcher, press, and heel machine on one-off shoes of many different makes, sizes, and states of wear, judging each job individually.

instances.label: Stitching room of a footwear plant: operator removes sewn uppers, vamps or welted/outsole-stitched shoes from a programmable stitching machine and examines the seams — stitch count and pitch, skipped or broken stitches, thread tension, pattern alignment, and whether outsole stitches are properly seated in the channel — setting rejects aside for rework.

Cutting/component prep: operator removes die-cut or skived leather and textile parts, counters, insoles and outsoles from a clicking press or splitting machine and examines them for cuts, holes, grain flaws, thickness, dimension to pattern, and correct count per pair.

Finishing/final line: operator removes the finished shoe from a buffing, edge-inking, heat-setting or polishing machine and examines it for scuffs, burn marks, glue residue, uneven color or edge finish, left/right symmetry and pair match against the sample shoe, marking touch-ups.

Small custom, orthopedic or repair shop: operator removes a one-off or short-run shoe (custom last, modified orthopedic build, resoled/reheeled repair) from a stitcher, heel-attacher or finishing wheel and examines it against the individual order or the original shoe, with no repeated reference product.

tasks.label: Draw thread through machine guide slots, needles, and presser feet in preparation for stitching, or load rolls of wire through machine axles.

instances.label: Start-of-shift setup of a single-needle post-bed or cylinder-arm lockstitch upper-stitching machine in a footwear plant: operator mounts a thread cone on the stand, draws the limp thread through the overhead guide eyes, tension discs, check spring, take-up lever, lower guides and the presser-foot/needle-bar guide, threads the needle eye, pulls a tail through, and test-stitches a scrap to confirm balanced stitch formation.

Mid-run rethreading at the operator's station after a thread break, run-out, or a change of thread color/gauge for the next shoe model: the machine sits in place on a crowded stitching-room bench, thread may be jammed at the hook or take-up, and the rethread must be done in under a minute to keep the line moving.

Threading a multi-thread or specialty machine — double-needle decorative stitcher, zigzag/moccasin stitcher, Strobel machine, or a multi-needle ornamental/embroidery head — with several independent thread paths, differing guide layouts and multiple needle eyes to be threaded in the right order.

Threading a heavy sole/welt stitching machine (Goodyear welt or McKay/outsole stitcher) with thick waxed or bonded cord: thread is drawn from the reel through the wax pot and tension gear, along the guides, and through the awl/needle and hook, with hot wax and stiff tacky cord.

Loading a fresh roll/spool of wire (tack, staple or reinforcing wire) onto the axle/spindle of a lasting, tacking, heel-nailing or wire-stapling machine, securing the roll, and feeding the wire end through the machine's feed rolls and guide tube until it presents at the forming head.

instances.label: Shift-routine gross clean-down of the operator's machine on a footwear factory floor: blowing/brushing leather dust, buffing dust, thread lint and trimmings off accessible surfaces, feed area, table and guards of a stitcher, skiver, roughing or press machine, then wiping down.

Cleaning that requires opening or partial disassembly: pulling the needle plate/bobbin case to clear packed lint from the hook race, scraping dried cement off applicator rollers, nozzles and press pads with solvent, emptying/replacing dust-collector bags and filters on a roughing or buffing machine.

Scheduled lubrication: adding oil to a stitching machine's reservoir and drop-oiling designated oil points, greasing fittings on lasting machines, sole presses and conveyors, checking sight glasses and oil levels, wiping excess.

Replacing a broken, bent or dull needle mid-run on a post-bed, flatbed or sole-stitching machine: stopping the machine, loosening the needle-clamp setscrew, extracting the stub, seating a new needle at correct height and scarf orientation, tightening, re-threading and test-stitching a scrap.

Changing consumable tooling/wear media on finishing machines: swapping a worn abrasive disc, brush or sanding wheel on a roughing/buffing machine, replacing a skiving or trimming blade, mounting fresh media and checking run-out.

Minor adjustments and small repairs: clearing thread or material jams, tightening loosened fasteners, replacing a slipping drive belt or worn presser foot, checking air lines and reporting faults beyond operator scope.

tasks.label: Test machinery to ensure proper functioning before beginning production.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Start-of-shift test of a stitching/closing machine on the shoe factory floor: power up the head, thread needle and bobbin, run a test seam on scrap leather or upper material, judge stitch formation and thread tension, adjust tension/stitch length until the seam is acceptable, then begin production.

Test of a cutting/clicking or die press before a run: mount or verify the die/blade, check blade sharpness and cutting depth/pressure, make a trial cut in scrap stock, compare the cut part to the pattern for size and clean edges, adjust depth or pressure, then start cutting.

Test of a heat- or adhesive-process machine (cement activator, sole attaching press, heat setter, direct-injection sole molder): confirm temperature, pressure and cycle timers reach setpoints, run one trial cycle on a sample shoe or scrap, check the bond/mold output, adjust settings, then run.

Test of a finishing/preparation machine (roughing or buffing wheel, edge trimmer, skiver, eyeletter, heel nailer): run the machine empty to listen for vibration, chatter or slipping belts, check the abrasive/cutter and dust extraction, run a sample part, inspect the result, replace or adjust tooling as needed.

Pre-production walkaround readiness check of the assigned machines and their utilities without operating them: read air-pressure and temperature gauges, look for adhesive/oil leaks and worn belts, feel or listen for abnormal heat and noise on running upstream equipment, confirm guards are in place, and flag faults to maintenance.

instances.label: Mid-run bobbin change at a lockstitch upper-stitching machine (post-bed or flat-bed) in a footwear plant's stitching room: when the underthread runs out the operator opens the slide plate/shuttle race, removes the spent pre-wound bobbin, seats a matching pre-wound bobbin in the bobbin case/shuttle with the thread tail drawn under the tension spring, and closes up. Thread changeover at the start of a job: operator reads the work order or shoe-part tag, picks the specified cones/spools of thread (correct color, size, fiber) from a stock rack or cart, and places one or several cones on the spindles/pins of the machine's thread stand above the stitching head. Factory stitching room, standard machines in fixed rows.

Loading heavy waxed thread onto a sole/welt machine (Goodyear welt sewer, outsole stitcher, McKay): a large spool or ball of waxed thread is set onto the machine's spool holder/spindle and brought to the looper/awl side near the wax pot. Greasy, machine-specific, older heavy equipment in the bottoming department.

Shift-start / changeover round on a tended group of machines: operator loads pre-wound bobbins into the shuttles of several stitching machines and restocks the bobbin supply (winding bobbins on a bobbin winder and placing them at each station), moving between machines on the plant floor.

Small sample room, orthopedic/custom shoe shop, or short-run domestic plant with mixed legacy machines (Singer 29K patcher, Landis, old post-beds): operator selects thread and bobbins for a variety of non-standard machines, each with a different shuttle/spindle arrangement, in a cluttered but owner-controlled shop.

tasks.label: Cut excess thread or material from shoe parts, using scissors or knives.

instances.label: Stitching room of a footwear plant: after each seam/operation on a lockstitch or programmable sewing unit, the operator snips the needle and bobbin thread tails and any loose thread ends from the limp stitched upper with small scissors before passing it on.

Lasting/assembly bench: operator trims excess pliable upper material with a knife — surplus lining, seam allowance, Strobel/insole margin, backer or reinforcement overhang — on a partly assembled, deformable shoe.

Final finishing/inspection station: operator inspects finished shoes and snips stray threads, glue strings, and small material tags found anywhere on the shoe (inside the collar, tongue, eyestay, sole edge) before boxing.

Small-shop work: sample room, orthopedic/custom shoe shop, or repair operation where one-off or varied shoes are trimmed of excess thread and material with scissors and knives at a bench, with no fixed part presentation.

Order/color changeover: operator mounts a different thread cone (new color or size), re-routes thread through the winder tension assembly, sets tension and fill level, and winds a batch of spools for several machines in the stitching room, sorting them into labeled trays.

Specialty thread winding: waxed, monofilament, or heavy decorative thread that snarls or bites into the wind; operator hand-guides the thread while treadling, slows the wind, checks for even layering and correct fill, and rewinds when the build is bad.

tasks.label: Position dies on material in a manner that will obtain the maximum number of parts from each portion of material.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Cutting room of a footwear factory: operator lays a natural leather hide on the board of a swing-arm clicking press or beam press, then places steel-rule dies for upper parts (vamps, quarters, toe caps) one at a time, nesting them tightly while dodging scars, brands and loose flank, and respecting grain/stretch direction, to get the most parts per hide.

Factory cutting room: positioning dies on synthetic sheet or roll goods (PU, coated fabric, mesh, lining, textile) for uppers and linings, often several plies stacked; material is uniform, so dies are laid in a dense repeating grid across the width to minimize edge waste.

Sole/bottom-stock cutting: positioning dies on sheet stock (rubber, EVA, crepe, texon/fiberboard, insole board, felt) on a clicking or traveling-head press to cut outsoles, insoles, heel lifts and stiffeners, staggering left/right dies to maximize parts per sheet.

Working remnants: positioning small dies on offcuts, side pieces and leftover hide sections to recover small components (counters, tongues, straps, backstays) from irregular scrap shapes, deciding what will still fit before the piece is discarded.

Small shop setting — sample/prototype room, custom or orthopedic shoemaker, or shoe repair shop: positioning a handful of dies on a few skins or scrap pieces for one-off or very small batch work, with frequent pattern and size changes.

instances.label: High-volume footwear line, standardized run: operator takes lasted uppers / shoe bodies off a moving conveyor or tray line, loads them into an inline heat-setting, chiller or cement-activation oven, then puts them back on the conveyor for the next station. Same model and size range for the whole run, cadence a few seconds per shoe, parts semi-rigid because they sit on lasts.

Sole-attaching / molding station: operator pulls lasted uppers from a rolling rack or conveyor, seats them on the mold station or last holder of a direct-injection, vulcanizing or sole-press machine, unloads the shoe after the cycle and racks it. Requires accurate seating so the mold closes cleanly.

Component feeding: operator collects stacks of limp cut parts (linings, mesh/leather panels, counters, toe puffs) from bins, hand-staged racks or a conveyor, feeds them into a molding press, fusing press or activation oven, and returns the processed pieces to trays and racks. Pieces are floppy, stacked irregularly, and batches change often.

Small-batch / mixed-model work in domestic boot plants, orthopedic and custom shoe labs, or resoling operations: frequent style and size changeovers, hand-staged racks and carts, odd or one-off items, short runs, worker judges which part goes in which mold or oven and for how long.

Rack and trolley staging: gathering the loaded rack or cart of parts at the machine, moving it across the plant floor to the queue at the next work station, and bringing empty racks back, sharing aisles with people and hand trucks.

tasks.label: Turn setscrews on needle bars, and position required numbers of needles in stitching machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine needle replacement at the machine on a single-needle post-bed, flat-bed or cylinder-arm shoe stitching machine after a needle breaks or dulls mid-run: operator loosens the small needle-bar setscrew with a screwdriver/hex key, pulls the broken or worn needle out, inserts a new round-shank needle pushed fully up to the stop with the scarf facing the hook and long groove forward, retightens the setscrew, and test-stitches. Shoe factory production floor, machine head at the operator's station.

Job changeover setup on a single-needle stitching machine: operator fits a different needle system/size/point (e.g., leather cutting point for uppers vs round point for linings, heavier gauge for stitch-down seams), turning the setscrew, seating the needle at correct height and orientation, and verifying needle-to-hook clearance before the run. Factory floor, scheduled between production lots.

Twin-needle or multi-needle machines (double-needle lockstitch, multi-needle decorative/ornamental stitchers, zigzag or Strobel-type units): positioning the required number of needles in the specified needle-bar holes/gauge positions, each seated to depth and rotationally oriented, with all setscrews turned down so the needles run true to their respective hooks. Factory floor.

Needle change on a computerized/automatic pattern stitcher or automated shoe-upper sewing unit: reaching into a more enclosed head, loosening the clamp setscrew, replacing the needle, resetting needle-bar height per the machine's spec, and running a test pattern. Factory floor, machine stopped and guarded during service.

Bench/maintenance-area work: needle bars, needle clamps or spare machine heads set up away from the line, with needles installed and setscrews torqued in batch ahead of a production run or after a rebuild. Structured maintenance bench inside the plant.

sources.system: NeedlyMat
sources.title: NeedlyMat the champion of NEEDLE BOARDS!
sources.claim: NeedlyMat is a commercial automatic needle-changing machine for the needle boards of needle-punch machines: a board is presented to the station and the machine identifies damaged/bent needles and extracts and replaces them autonomously, seating thousands of steel needles at defined positions.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: re-needling needle boards for needle-punch machines. It handles the same class of object (small hardened steel textile needles with ~2 mm shanks), requires extracting broken/bent needles and seating replacements to depth at a defined position and crank orientation, and is performed on a needle-carrying assembly taken off the machine and brought to a purpose-built station — exactly the E1 counterfactual of positioning needles in a stitching machine's needle bar. The remaining difference (a setscrew clamp instead of a press fit) is covered by the robotic screwdriving evidence.

sources.system: OnRobot Screwdriver (with screw feeder, on UR/other industrial arms)
sources.date: product page retrieved 2025-12; product commercially available since 2020
sources.title: Multifunctional robotic screwdriver | OnRobot
sources.claim: Commercially sold robotic screwdriving end-effectors with screw feeders drive and torque very small machine screws autonomously in industrial cells, with torque control down to 0.15 Nm and built-in detection of picked, wrong-length or improperly inserted screws.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic fastening of small machine screws in assembly cells. A needle-bar setscrew is an M2–M4-class screw tightened at fractions of a Nm, within the demonstrated size and torque envelope, so the tightening half of this task transfers directly when the needle bar is fixtured.

sources.system: Robotic unscrewing system (Universal Robots UR10e + Intel RealSense D405 + custom mechatronic screwdriver)
sources.developer: authors of Robotics and Computer-Integrated Manufacturing paper (RCIM 2025, DOI 10.1016/j.rcim.2025.103032)
sources.title: Robotic system for automated disassembly of electronic waste: Unscrewing
sources.claim: A vision- and force-guided robot arm autonomously locates, identifies and loosens/removes screws of several head types on real devices, aligning the driver tip with the screw head using force sensing before unscrewing.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic unscrewing during disassembly. Turning a setscrew loose is the first half of this task; the demonstrated capability (finding a small screw head by vision, aligning by force, and backing it out under torque monitoring) is the same operation at the same screw scale.

sources.claim: Force-controlled industrial robots are commercially deployed for precise assembly and fitting, using predefined insert/search/push functions to mate close-fitting parts and seat them against stops in fenced production cells.

Pushing a needle shank up a matching bore until it bottoms on the stop is a short force-controlled insertion of the same kind, at the same clearances, when the needle bar is fixtured.

sources.system: Autonomous robotic assembly pipeline (part singulation to precise insertion)

sources.claim: Research robots autonomously singulate small parts and insert them into holes with sub-millimetre clearance, achieving submillimeter in-hand pose estimation that enables successful insertion where naive pick-and-place fails.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: precise peg-in-hole insertion of a small part picked from a feeder. Positioning a needle in a needle-bar bore demands the same grasp-pose accuracy and sub-millimetre insertion tolerance, so the capability transfers to the insertion step in a fixtured cell.

tasks.label: Turn screws to regulate size of staples.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Changeover setup on a production stapling/side-lasting machine in a footwear plant: for a new style or upper thickness, the operator turns the staple-length regulating screw to the setting on the spec sheet, fires test staples into scrap, and checks leg length before releasing the run.

Mid-run corrective adjustment: staples are coming out too long/short (crown standing proud or legs not clinching). Operator stops the machine, backs off a locknut if present, turns the regulating screw a fraction of a turn, test-fires, inspects, and repeats until staples are right.

Multi-screw setup at the same station: the staple-size screw is set together with related wire-feed/driver-depth and clamp screws per a setup chart, then the first-piece sample is inspected and signed off by the operator or a QC checker.

Older or non-standard bench stapling machines in a small plant or refurbishing shop: worn slotted screws, no current spec chart, machine-specific access; the operator sets staple size by feel and eye, iterating with test staples and hand tools.
Shift-start / preventive check across several machines on the floor: the tender walks machine to machine, fires sample staples, and tweaks the size-regulating screw on the ones that have drifted.

sources.system: ASG AX-10 assembly cell with X-PAQ torque/angle-controlled screwdriver
sources.developer: ASG, a Division of Jergens Inc.
sources.title: Robotic Cell Automates Screwdriving Process | ASSEMBLY
sources.claim: Commercially available robotic screwdriving cells (ASG AX-10 Cartesian assembly cell with the X-PAQ DC-electric driver) turn small screws at fixtured, taught locations under closed-loop torque and angle control, i.e., a robot can rotate a small screw a precisely specified amount inside a purpose-built cell.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: driving/tightening small machine screws to a commanded torque and rotation angle in a fenced tabletop cell. It transfers to regulating staple size because that adjustment is exactly the rotation of a small machine screw by a specified amount at a known location; objects (#000–#10 class screws) and required precision (angle-controlled rotation) are comparable.

sources.system: Automated robotic RF cavity filter tuning system (COBOT + multi-axis arms + Cartesian platform)
sources.developer: Yigit, Afacan et al. (published in Journal of Field Robotics)
sources.title: A Fully Automated Robotic System for Tuning Optimization of RF Cavity Filter - Journal of Field Robotics
sources.claim: A fully autonomous robotic system tunes RF cavity filters by turning miniaturized tuning screws in a closed loop against measured output, iterating until the measured response meets specification — a task previously done only by experienced human tuners by rule of thumb. The filter is fixtured in a purpose-built robotic tuning station.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: post-production tuning of a machine's output by turning small adjustment screws while measuring the result and iterating to spec. This is the same control loop as turning a screw to regulate staple size (turn, test, measure, re-turn), with comparable screw sizes and finer required resolution, in a fixtured cell.

sources.system: Autonomous robotic screwdriving system for high-mix manufacturing (physics-informed SINDy screw-tip model)
sources.developer: Manyar, Patel & Gupta, University of Southern California (Robotics and Computer-Integrated Manufacturing)
sources.title: Autonomous robotic screwdriving for high-mix manufacturing - ScienceDirect
sources.claim: An autonomous robotic screwdriving system handles high-mix, low-volume work: it localizes and drives several screw types across ten different industrial parts, tolerates pose uncertainty via active/passive compliance, and detects four failure modes with adaptive retries.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous engagement and rotation of varied screws with uncertain pose, including failure detection and retry. Transfers to worn or non-standard staple-size regulating screws presented in a cell, where the driver must find the slot, engage without camming out, and rotate a controlled amount.

sources.system: In-line machine vision gauging/measurement systems

sources.claim: In-line machine vision gauging systems perform non-contact dimensional measurement on production lines at high rates and with high repeatability, providing the automatic verification of a test staple's dimensions needed to close the adjustment loop in a robotic cell.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated dimensional inspection of small metal parts. It supplies the 'check the test staple' step of this task; staple crown/leg length is a simple backlit dimensional measurement well within demonstrated in-line gauging capability.

sources.system: Xiaomi humanoid robot (EV plant die-casting workshop trial)

sources.transferJustification: Cited to bound the E2 case, not to support it: the in-facility humanoid work substantiated to date is repetitive fastener installation on line-presented parts at ~90% success, not locating a specific adjustment screw on a legacy shoe machine and calibrating it against inspected output.

tasks.label: Hammer loose staples for proper attachment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Side/heel-seat lasting line in a footwear or work-boot plant: after the lasting machine staples or tacks the upper margin to the insole, the operator checks the lasted bottom on the last and hammers down staples that stand proud so the margin lies flat before pounding, roughing and sole attaching. Shoes arrive on racks/conveyor in production runs of one style.

Insole attaching / heel-seat tacking station: tacks or staples holding the insole to the last, or the heel-seat margin, are checked and any that are loose or standing up are hammered home on the last bottom with a small hammer at the bench.

Heel attaching station on women's shoes and boots: after nails/staples are driven through the heel seat into the heel block, the operator hammers any loose or proud fastener (often reaching into the shoe cavity or at the heel breast) so the heel is firmly attached.

Goodyear-welt / cement-lasted boot line: staples securing the upper and insole (and shank or toe box) are hammered flush on the lasted bottom before welt stitching or sole cementing, on heavy leather work boots.

Quality-check / rework bench: shoes pulled from the line or from finishing with staples flagged as loose, protruding or misdriven anywhere on the shoe — inside the shoe, under the sock lining, at the heel or sidewall — on mixed styles; operator locates each defect and hammers it, without damaging the finished surface.

Sample room / small-batch or orthopedic production: hand-lasted or short-run shoes where tacks and staples are placed in varying positions by hand; the operator hammers loose ones on a bench stand, judging placement shoe by shoe with no repeating program.

sources.system: IDEA-FOOT automated production plant (robotic cells A and B; cell B built with DESMA, lasting machines by Brustia)
sources.developer: CISAS University of Padova / ITIA-CNR with DESMA and Brustia, installed at BZ Moda
sources.title: Novel Automated Production System for the Footwear Industry (IFIP AICT 397)
sources.claim: The IDEA-FOOT automated footwear plant installed at shoe manufacturer BZ Moda includes a robotic cell in which a manipulator picks the lasted shoe from the pallet conveyor and performs shoe-bottom hammering (pounding), grinding, roughing and cementing by pressing the shoe bottom against fixed tools; a second manipulator loads/unloads the heel-seat and side lasting machine.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic hammering/pounding of the lasted shoe bottom in the same production sequence in which the heel-seat and side lasting machines fasten the upper with nails/staples. It acts on the identical object (lasted shoe on a last), applies percussive force to the same lasting margin where loose staples sit, and seats protruding fasteners flat as part of flattening the margin, so it delivers the accepted output of 'staples properly attached' without needing a hand hammer.

sources.system: Elettrotecnica B.C. heel-seat pounding machines Mod. 888 (peening, programmed) and Mod. 667/667S (lasting & pounding)

sources.title: Heel seat pounding machines | ElettrotecnicaBC

sources.transferJustification: Related task: machine peening/pounding of an assembled shoe to re-secure loose lasting. Same workpiece (lasted shoe), same corrective purpose as hammering loose staples, and the fastener-seating force is delivered by the machine rather than a hand hammer; only shoe presentation is manual, which the E1 counterfactual supplies by fixturing.

sources.system: Lasted shoe pounding machines (B03.13) / programmable-axis lasted-bottom working machines (B04)

sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated pounding of the lasted shoe bottom. The pounding cycle presses and hammers the same lasting margin in which lasting staples/tacks are set, driving proud fasteners flush; equipment operates on the same objects at the same precision as the hand-hammering step it replaces.

sources.system: Heel seat lasting machines (B03.11) and side and heel seat lasting machines (B03.12)
sources.developer: Italian footwear machinery makers listed by Assomac (e.g. Brustia-Alfameccanica, ORMAC)

It shows that setting these exact fasteners home in a fixtured lasted shoe is routine machine work, so a re-drive/seating cycle at the same station produces the same accepted output as hand-hammering a loose staple.

sources.system: DS-403 fully automatic pneumatic heel nailing machine

sources.transferJustification: Related task: automatic driving of heel fasteners through the heel seat on a shoe held on the machine's stand. sources.system: Collaborative robotic shoe-polishing cell (UR-class cobot with force control)
sources.developer: Polytechnic University of Marche (Forlini, Ciccarelli, Carbonari, Papetti, Palmieri) with a luxury footwear company

sources.system: Inline toe pounding / setting stations on automated lasting conveyor lines

sources.transferJustification: Related task: mechanical hammering of the lasted margin inline. Confirms that hammering/compaction of the exact area where lasting staples are set is delivered by conveyor-fed machines rather than by hand, at production quality and cadence.

roles.title: Sewers, Hand
roles.description: Sew, join, reinforce, or finish, usually with needle and thread, a variety of manufactured items. Includes weavers and stitchers.

tasks.label: Select thread, twine, cord, or yarn to be used, and thread needles.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Cut-and-sew / soft-goods plant, hand-finishing station: the sewer takes the thread specified on the style ticket (standard poly/cotton cone or spool) from the workstation rack, pulls and cuts a length, threads a fine hand needle (sharps/betweens) and knots it, repeating dozens of times through the shift as work bundles arrive.

Alterations / tailoring / bridal / dry-cleaner shop: the sewer holds the customer's garment up against a wall of hundreds of thread shades, judges the best match by eye and also picks fiber and weight (silk, all-purpose, topstitch or buttonhole twist), then threads a fine hand needle for hems, buttons and linings.

Upholstery, mattress or leather-goods plant: the sewer selects heavy waxed twine, nylon cord or button twine called for by the product spec and threads curved needles and long straight tufting/closing needles, often several at a time, at a bench beside the frame or panel.

Textile mill weaving/stitching work: the worker selects yarn according to the pattern repeat and threads yarn ends through small eyes — heddle eyes, drop wires and reed dents when drawing in or mending a warp, or a hand needle for linking/mending — on the mill floor.

Home-based or on-site sewing (self-employed sewer's home workroom, a client's home for drapery or slipcovers, backstage wardrobe repair): the sewer picks thread from a personal stash matched by eye to the item at hand and threads assorted needles, often in poor or variable light with no fixed workstation.

sources.system: Stäubli SAFIR S80 automatic drawing-in machine
sources.title: Automatic drawing-in machine - up to 2 warp beams - SAFIR S80 | Stäubli United States
sources.claim: Stäubli's SAFIR S80 automatic drawing-in machine selects and threads warp yarn ends through reed dents, drop wires and heald eyes fully automatically according to the pattern repeat, in a stationary purpose-built machine loaded by operators.
sources.transferJustification: Drawing-in is the weaving version of this task: yarn ends are selected per the pattern and each is threaded through a heald eye and reed dent, openings of needle-eye scale, with the same flexible fine strands a hand sewer handles.

sources.system: Stäubli SAFIR automatic drawing-in machines
sources.title: Automation: A Key To Successful Textile Production | Textile World
sources.claim: SAFIR automatic drawing-in machines are in routine use in weaving mills' drawing-in departments, supplying completely drawn-in warp beams with no crossed threads or multiple threads in a heddle.
sources.transferJustification: Same transfer as above: this documents mill deployment of machine selection and threading of yarn through heald eyes at production quality.

sources.system: Brother Entrepreneur Pro X PR1055X
sources.title: 10-Needle Wireless Enabled Home Embroidery Machine - PR1055X | Brother
sources.claim: Brother's commercial 10-needle embroidery machine carries a built-in automatic needle-threading system that draws ordinary soft embroidery/sewing thread through the eye of each needle on a button press, once the thread is routed through the fixed guides.
sources.transferJustification: The machine performs exactly the fine step of this task — hooking a soft thread and pulling it through a ~0.4 mm needle eye — with the needle held in a fixed position and ... thread presented in guides, which is how a purpose-built station would present the work.

sources.system: Tajima TMEZ-1401 multi-needle embroidery machine
sources.title: TMEZ 1401 | Hirsch Solutions
sources.claim: Tajima commercial embroidery machines change needle bars automatically at color changes coded in the design data, i.e. the machine selects which thread is used from the digital job spec without operator intervention.
sources.transferJustification: Covers the 'select thread to be used' element when the thread is specified by a job ticket/design file: the machine picks the specified thread supply itself from a presented set.

sources.system: Ethicon apparatus for forming fine gauge and monofilament armed sutures (US7185411B2)
sources.title: US7185411B2 - Method and apparatus for forming fine gauge and monofilament single and double-armed sutures
sources.claim: Ethicon's armed-suture production apparatus automatically pulls suture thread from a supply reel, cuts it and inserts the cut end into a needle held in a swaging station, with needles oriented and loaded automatically.
sources.transferJustification: Arming a suture is machine 'needle threading': a fine flexible strand is cut and inserted into the receiving opening of a (usually curved) needle held in a fixture — the same act, objects and sub-millimetre precision as threading a hand needle.

sources.system: Ethicon automatic needle-suture assembly and packaging machine (needle threading and swaging system)
sources.title: Control system for an automatic needle-suture assembly and packaging machine (US5487216)
sources.claim: Ethicon's automatic needle-suture assembly machines are high-volume production machines that thread and swage roughly sixty surgical needles per minute, with automated pull-testing of each armed needle.
sources.transferJustification: Same transfer as the previous item; this documents the throughput and reliability (with pull-testing) of purpose-built machine threading of needles in commercial production.

sources.system: T-NT (tactile perception + RL needle threading, dual-arm robot with GelSlim-like sensors)
sources.title: Precise Robotic Needle-Threading with Tactile Perception and Reinforcement Learning (CoRL 2023)
sources.claim: The strongest published autonomous general-purpose robot needle-threading system reaches only about 63% success with the needle fixed in a jig, and explicitly cannot handle soft sewing thread.

sources.system: TARS T-Series / A-Series humanoid robot
sources.title: TARS Demonstrates a Robot That Can Perform Hand Embroidery, Breaking Through a Key Automation Bottleneck in Flexible Manufacturing
sources.claim: TARS Robotics showed a humanoid robot threading a needle and stitching ... two-handed at a single live event; the release does not state whether execution was autonomous or teleoperated, and no deployment is claimed.

sources.system: Honda multi-fingered hand
sources.title: Multi-fingered Hand | Honda R&D
sources.claim: Honda's multi-fingered robotic hand is presented as precise enough to thread a needle, but Honda's system is a remote-operation (teleoperation) architecture in which a human operator makes the high-level decisions.

tasks.label: Measure and align parts, fasteners, or trimmings, following seams, edges, or markings on parts.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Cut-and-sew apparel plant: hand sewer takes cut panels/linings/facings for a style being run, matches notches, match points and seam allowances, aligns edges of two or more plies and pins/tacks them ready for stitching; repeated hundreds of times on the same style.

Fastener placement in a garment/uniform or cover plant: measuring from a placket edge or a marked point and positioning buttons, snaps, hooks-and-eyes, or hook-and-loop tape at the correct spacing on a panel or finished garment before attaching.

Trimmings and labels: aligning lace, binding, piping, emblems, appliqué patches, care/brand labels or decorative tape to a marked line or edge on garments, curtains, pillows and other sewn home textiles in a plant.

Upholstery, automotive seating and leather goods plant: aligning cut leather/vinyl/foam-backed panels and listing strips to seam lines and notches on seat covers, furniture covers or handbags, matching hide grain and following scribe/marker lines before stitching.

Specialty three-dimensional hand work on bulky or irregular finished goods: closing plush toys and cushions, hand-stitching balls, moccasins, sails or mattress panels, where parts must be aligned on an already-assembled, non-flat article.

One-off repair/alteration station (in-plant rework bench, alteration or dry-cleaner shop): a single customer garment of unknown pattern is measured, hem or patch position marked, and torn seams/parts aligned by hand for restitching.

sources.system: Robotic apparel automation system (Siemens Technology + Sewbo stiffening technique)
sources.title: [2503.00249] Robotic Automation in Apparel Manufacturing: A Novel Approach to Fabric Handling and Sewing
sources.claim: Siemens/Sewbo robotic sewing system estimates the pose of cut fabric pieces, temporarily joins (aligns and tacks) pieces together, and sews with closed-loop visual servoing; validated on the Bluewater Defense apparel production line and at a Levi's research facility.
sources.transferJustification: 'Temporarily joining fabric pieces' after vision-based pose estimation is exactly the measure-and-align-parts step: plies are registered to each other along their edges before stitching, on the same denim/cotton garment panels a hand sewer aligns.

sources.transferJustification: The deployed cell performs garment-panel handling, registration and sewing of denim parts; positioning panels to seam lines under seam monitoring is the alignment step of this task.

sources.transferJustification: Aligning templates that fix fabric patterns in register is the machine equivalent of aligning parts and trims to markings before sewing, on the same garment pieces.

tasks.label: Trim excess threads or edges of parts, using scissors or knives.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Apparel plant finishing/inspection table: worker picks each sewn garment (tee, blouse, trousers) off a bundle or hanger, turns it over, locates stray thread tails at seam ends, bartacks, buttonholes and labels, and snips them flush with small thread nippers or scissors without cutting the fabric; limp, variable garment, threads in arbitrary positions.

At or beside a sewing station in an apparel/home-textile plant: trimming excess fabric at the edge of a just-sewn part - cutting back seam allowance, clipping curves and notches, trimming overlock chain and excess material flush to the stitch line on collars, cuffs, pockets - with scissors or a knife.

Furniture/automotive upholstery shop: after a cover or seat lining is stretched, stitched or stapled over a frame or panel, trimming the excess fabric, vinyl or leather around the edges with a knife and snipping the thread ends on the stitched seams of the panel.

Footwear/leather-goods plant: trimming excess leather, lining or welt material at the edges of stitched uppers, soles, bags and belts with a knife, and clipping stitching thread ends on the stitched parts.

Custom/alteration workroom, bridal or costume shop, or home-based sewing business: a one-off or small-lot garment or drapery is held in the hand or on a form and the worker trims thread ends and excess fabric edges as the item is finished; layout, lighting and item type vary from job to job.

Industrial/technical sewn-goods plant (mattress covers, car mats, awnings, flags, medical and military textiles): trimming excess material and thread chains from the edges of large, heavy sewn panels laid out on a big table or conveyor.

sources.transferJustification: Direct: the cell performs the trimming of excess fabric at the edges of an upholstered part, the same operation the hand sewer performs with a knife on upholstery panels.

tasks.label: Sew, join, reinforce, or finish parts of articles, such as garments, books, mattresses, toys, and wigs, using needles and thread or other materials.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Hand stitching on already-assembled or customer-owned articles: at a bench in a clothing-store alteration room, repair shop or tailoring workroom, replacing buttons, closing a split seam on a finished jacket, slip-stitching a lining closed, blind-hemming, tacking shoulder pads or beadwork on high-end pieces. Every item is a one-off of unknown construction; stitches must be invisible from the face; the worker reaches inside a soft 3-D garment.

Apparel, footwear and sewn-accessory plant, production runs: hand attaching labels, emblems, patches and trims; bartacking and reinforcement stitching at stress points; tacking and joining cut parts before or after machine operations. Repeated identical work on a flat or lightly shaped workpiece at a bench in the sewing room.

Home-furnishing and technical-textile plant (textile product mills, textile furnishings, coated fabric/vinyl goods): joining and edge-finishing cut panels into pillows, bath mats, area rugs, mattress covers, curtains, cushion covers, tarps and covers. Repeat runs of standard sizes, largely flat pieces handled on a table.

Mattress, futon and bedding plant: tufting mattresses through the panel with a long needle and twine/lace, closing borders and corners, finishing the tape edge and hand-sewing handles or labels on the assembly line. Heavy, bulky standard-size units moving down a line.

Bindery / print-finishing plant: thread-sewing folded signatures into sewn book blocks, reinforcing and finishing sewn bindings, hand-sewing blank books, restoration/repair stitching. Paper signatures gathered in order; sewn book block must open flat and hold.

Miscellaneous soft-goods manufacturing (dolls and plush toys, wigs and hairpieces, novelty, medical and craft goods): closing the stuffing opening of a stuffed toy with an invisible ladder stitch, attaching features, hand-tying or sewing hair into a lace wig cap, hand-finishing short-run novelty items. Small soft 3-D objects, frequent style changes.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: machine-sewn joining of garment parts rather than needle-and-thread hand joining. Transfer holds for the joining/reinforcing part of the hand sewer's work: same articles (garment panels), same limp fabrics, same seam-quality acceptance, in a purpose-built cell.

sources.transferJustification: Directly substitutes the hand sewer's mattress tufting (long needle and twine pulled through the mattress) with an in-line machine; same article, same tuft/knot output, doubling a manual tufter's rate.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: machine closing/binding of the mattress edge seam and machine simulation of hand-stitched borders, i.e. the joining and finishing operations mattress hand sewers perform on the same article.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: programmed machine stitching of the same attachments and reinforcements (labels, emblems, patches, tacks) that hand sewers apply with needle and thread, on a workpiece held in a clamp frame as an E1 setting would present it.

tasks.label: Use different sewing techniques such as felling, tacking, basting, embroidery, and fagoting.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Cut-and-sew apparel plant, production hand-finishing station: applying thread tacks/French tacks joining lining to shell, hand-attaching labels, trim and belt loops, and basting components before machine operations, on garments flowing down a human production line at piece-rate pace.

Alterations, bespoke tailoring, bridal, costume or sample-room hand work on an individual garment: felling hems and lining edges, slip-stitching, basting for fittings, hand-only decorative work (fagoting, beading, couture embroidery) on three-dimensional garments of varied fabric and construction, often on a form or the customer's own garment.

Home-textile / mattress / sewn soft-goods plant: hand closing and finishing operations on flat goods — slip-stitch closing of pillow and cushion covers, closing stitches on quilted panels, edge tacking and finishing on mats, towels and bedding in a production facility.

Custom drapery and upholstery workroom: hand-tacking pleats and linings on made-to-measure draperies, blind-stitching closures and tacking trim on three-dimensional upholstered furniture pieces and slipcovers, with each piece a different size and fabric.

Embroidery/monogramming shop or decorating department: producing embroidered monograms, logos, appliqué and decorative stitching on hoopable garments and flat linens to a supplied design, at commercial quality.

Technical and industrial sewn-goods plant (automotive interiors, medical soft goods, safety and protective products, composite preforms): reinforcement stitching, tacking and finishing stitches on heavy, coated or technical materials to specified stitch patterns.

sources.system: SEWBOT / Lowry sewing workline
sources.title: Softwear Automation launches Sewbots-as-a-Service
sources.claim: SoftWear Automation's SEWBOT is a fully automated, vision-guided robotic sewing workline commercially deployed to produce rugs, bath mats, pillows, towels, automotive and medical sewn products — i.e. autonomous manipulation and stitching of limp fabric in a purpose-built cell.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: machine seaming, hemming and closing of flat textile goods. It transfers to the hand-sewer's closing and edge-finishing stitches on the same pillows, mats and towels — same limp materials, same stitch tolerances — with the workline supplying the fixtured presentation of each piece.

sources.system: Sewbo/Siemens robotic denim sewing workcell
sources.title: A Deployment Case Study in Robotic Apparel Automation: Digital Twin Integration, Interoperability, and Workforce Enablement (arXiv:2606.16078)

sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated placement and decorative/utility stitching of small components (tags, pockets, arcuates) on fixtured garment panels. Hand tacking and label/trim attachment in a plant involve the same fabrics, the same small-component alignment and comparable stitch precision.

sources.claim: Aitu's purpose-built humanoid sewing robot, deployed at garment factories in several countries, moves between workstations and completes fabric handling, positioning, template alignment and ... — but its work is template-machine tending on shirts and T-shirts, not hand-stitch techniques.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: tending template sewing machines on a garment factory floor. It shows what robots can do on the open factory floor (loading and template-based machine sewing), which is the ceiling relevant to judging whether hand-stitch operations could be done at E2.
