tasks.label: Fit garments on clients, altering as needed.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Neighborhood alterations shop or dry-cleaner alteration counter: a walk-in customer changes into trousers, a skirt or a dress; the sewer has the customer stand on a fitting platform, checks drape and balance, pins and chalks a hem, waist take-in, sleeve shortening or side-seam adjustment while the customer shifts and comments, then takes the garment off the customer, rips the original stitching, presses, re-sews and finishes it (often blind-hem or hand-fell), and confirms fit at pickup.

Menswear/suiting retailer or custom clothier: customer wears the jacket and trousers; the fitter assesses shoulder, collar gap, sleeve pitch and length, jacket length, trouser seat, rise and break, marks with chalk and pins, then alters - taking in the center back seam, shortening sleeves from the cuff with functional buttonholes, letting out the seat - and refits at a second appointment.

Bridal/formalwear salon: multiple fittings of a gown on the bride over weeks; pinning bust cups, side seams, straps and hem on slippery or beaded delicate fabric over crinoline; hand-tacking, re-beading over altered seams, building a bustle, adjusting corset lacing; the client moves, sits and walks to test the fit.

Theatrical, dance, or film/TV costume shop: fitting a mock-up or finished costume on a performer in the shop's fitting room; pinning and marking for movement and quick changes, checking against the designer's sketch and the performer's range of motion, then altering the costume and refitting, often under short deadlines before dress rehearsal.

Fitting away from a fixed shop: tailor makes a house call or visits a client's office, hotel room, or a wedding venue on the day; fits and pins the garment in whatever room is available, then performs hand alterations on the spot with a travel kit or takes the garment away for machine work.

sources.system: Sewbo / Siemens robotic sewing workcell (ARM Institute-funded, with follow-on RACER work)
sources.developer: Sewbo, Inc. with Siemens (ARM Institute project)
sources.title: Project Highlight: Advancing Automated Robotic Sewing - ARM Institute
sources.claim: State-of-the-art autonomous garment sewing operates on flat-cut panels inside a fixed industrial workcell feeding an assembly line; it sews shape-defining jeans seams with vision-based closed-loop correction, but works on new-garment assembly, not on garments worn by or fitted to an individual client.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic garment assembly sewing. It shows machines can sew fabric autonomously in a purpose-built cell, but it does not transfer to this task: workpieces are pre-cut panels presented by the cell, there is no live client, no fit assessment, no pinning or chalking on a body, and no ripping and re-sewing of an already-constructed garment.

sources.system: Sewbot Workline
sources.title: Sewbots® - Softwear Automation
sources.claim: Commercially offered robotic sewing is a factory 'workline' that manufactures standard T-shirts on demand from cut goods inside a purpose-built machine environment; no alteration of finished garments to an individual customer's fit is offered.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated apparel manufacture. Comparable materials (knit/woven fabric) but the environment is a vacuum-table workcell with fixtured, machine-presented panels and standard sizes; it demonstrates nothing about assessing or adjusting fit on a human client, so capability does not carry over.

sources.system: Force-Modulated Visual Policy for robot-assisted dressing
sources.title: [2509.12741] Force-Modulated Visual Policy for Robot-Assisted Dressing with Arm Motions
sources.claim: The closest robotic capability involving a garment on a live person is assistive dressing: an autonomous policy pulls a long-sleeve garment onto a participant's arm in a lab, adapting to arm motion. It handles donning only - no fit evaluation, pinning, marking, or alteration.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-assisted dressing of a person. It is the nearest demonstrated contact-rich garment-on-human manipulation, but it only slides a sleeve onto a limb in a lab; it makes no judgment of drape, balance or ease, does not pin or chalk, and performs no sewing, so it cannot substantiate completing a fitting-and-alteration instance.

tasks.label: Smooth seams with heated irons, flat bones, or rubbing sticks.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Apparel factory sewing floor, under-pressing between sewing operations: a hand sewer/finisher opens and smooths seams on shirt, trouser, skirt or jacket parts with a steam hand iron or at a buck-press station, dozens to hundreds of pieces a shift, standard fabrics and repeating part shapes, to a factory quality standard (seam flat and open, no shine or impressions).

Custom tailoring, bespoke or alterations shop: pressing seams open and flat with a hand iron, clapper, point presser or sleeve board while constructing or altering a suit, dress or uniform; one-off garments, varied wool/silk/blend fabrics, work interleaved with hand stitching at a bench.

Leather goods / footwear closing room or workshop: rubbing and beating stitched seams flat with a bone folder, rubbing stick, roller or hammer on handbags, wallets, belts, gloves or shoe uppers after stitching and gluing, so the seam lies flat before the next assembly step.

Home-furnishings, upholstery or technical-textile workroom: smoothing long straight seams open on drapery panels, slipcovers, cushion and mattress covers, vehicle seat covers or canvas goods on a large pressing table with a hand iron or seam roller; heavy or coated fabrics, large limp panels.

Delicate, embellished or irregular one-off items: pressing seams on beaded or sequined gowns, theatrical costumes, sheer or heat-sensitive synthetics, curved or three-dimensional assemblies, where the sewer presses locally over a ham or point presser with a press cloth and judges heat, moisture and pressure item by item.

Home-based piecework sewer, wardrobe/costume worker backstage or on location, or an on-site upholsterer: smoothing seams with a portable iron, steamer or rubbing stick in a room taken as found, with no fixed pressing station and variable items.

Upholstery / furniture / auto-trim shop: worker lays templates on upholstery fabric, vinyl or a leather hide, marks around them while matching nap, pattern repeat and avoiding hide defects, and cuts cushion, panel and welt pieces to the job specification.

Industrial and technical sewn-goods plant (bags, safety gear, filtration, medical/orthopedic soft goods, awnings, marine canvas, sails): worker marks heavy coated or technical textiles from templates or CAD prints and cuts panels, often thick or stiff material, to close dimensional tolerance.

On-site or in-home custom patterning: worker takes the pattern directly off the object in place — boat cockpit or bimini, an in-situ sofa, window for drapery — taping or fitting pattern material to the 3-D shape, marking it, and cutting the pattern/fabric there or in a home workroom.

tasks.label: Measure parts, such as sleeves or pant legs, and mark or pin-fold alteration lines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Alterations shop/dry-cleaner workroom bench, casual bottoms: customer's jeans, chinos or casual skirt laid flat on the worktable; worker measures up from the existing hem by the ticketed amount (or from the customer's pin), chalks the new line around each leg, folds and pins the hem ready for stitching.

Same workroom bench, tailored/structured garments: wool suit trousers, lined jacket sleeves, shirt sleeves with cuffs and plackets, lined dresses. Worker measures the sleeve from shoulder seam or cuff (or the leg from crotch), marks the alteration line with chalk or tailor's tacks around a lined, cuffed, vented or delicate part, and pin-folds it.

Fitting room of a tailor shop or department store with the customer wearing the garment: worker kneels, pin-folds each pant leg to the shoe break, chalk-marks sleeve length at the wrist bone, compares left and right, while the customer shifts stance and the garment moves on the body.

Bridal/formalwear fitting: client stands on a platform in a floor-length gown; worker measures the hem from the floor all around and pins or chalk-marks it through several layers (lining, tulle, lace), and pin-folds straps or bodice seams.

Custom/made-to-measure studio, flat work: sleeve and leg pattern pieces or cut fabric panels laid on the cutting table; worker measures them against the client's revised measurements and marks the new seam, hem and dart lines on the flat fabric, pinning folds before sewing.

Off-site fitting: client's home or office, backstage/on-set costume call, or a uniform fitting at a client workplace; worker measures the sleeve or pant leg on the wearer and pins/marks the alteration lines in a room taken as found, with variable lighting and no fixed layout.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: marking cut parts in a factory cutting room. Transfer: identical deliverable (a mark placed on apparel fabric at a measured position, to millimetre precision) on the same material, in a purpose-built fixtured table environment.

sources.system: Kuris single-ply cutter with integrated camera system
sources.title: Automated Cutting & Sewing Developments | Textile World
sources.claim: Cutting machines image the actual material and compute machine coordinates from it, i.e. they measure the workpiece and then act on it, rather than relying only on a fixed program.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: vision-derived cutting paths. Transfer: supports the 'measure the part' half of this task — the machine derives dimensions from the actual fabric presented and places its tool path accordingly.

sources.system: Garment visual inspection and measurement machine
sources.developer: Dongguan Yunji Zhihui Technology Co., Ltd.
sources.title: Finally AI in manufacturing: Garment measurement inspection in a flash
sources.claim: A commercial machine automatically measures the dimensions of finished garments laid on its bed in seconds, showing that automated measurement of garment parts is available where the garment is presented to the machine.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: QC measurement of finished garments. Transfer: the measurement step of this task (dimensions of a garment part such as a sleeve or leg) on the same objects, when the garment is presented flat in a purpose-built machine.

sources.system: Robotic sewing workcell (UR5e, suction gripper, Sewbo stiffening, digital twin)
sources.developer: Siemens Technology with Sewbo / Levi Strauss
sources.title: A Deployment Case Study in Robotic Apparel Automation: Digital Twin Integration, Interoperability, and Workforce Enablement
sources.claim: State-of-the-art robotic garment work remains a fenced factory workcell handling prepared denim panels with vacuum grippers and vision alignment, reaching roughly 90% trial success on pocket and seam operations.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic handling and sewing of denim pieces. It bounds current capability: garment manipulation is achieved only with stiffened, fixtured production panels inside a purpose-built cell, not on customers' finished garments or on people.

sources.system: Bot Couture robotic sewing system
sources.developer: Siemens Technology, ARM Institute partners (demonstrated at Levi Strauss Innovation Center)
sources.title: Project Highlight: Bot Couture & Robotic Clothing Manufacturing
sources.claim: ARM Institute's Bot Couture project demonstrated robotic machine tending and visually servoed precise sewing of denim pants in a representative factory environment.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic sewing/machine tending on garment panels. Transfer: shows the environment class in which robots handle apparel fabric today — a fixtured industrial cell with prepared pieces — and no capability on assembled consumer garments.

tasks.label: Remove stitches from garments to be altered, using rippers or razor blades.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Alterations bench in a dry cleaner / retail-store alterations department: unpicking a machine-sewn hem (blind-hem or lockstitch) on trousers, skirt or jeans so the garment can be shortened or lengthened; the tailor slides a seam ripper under each stitch, cuts thread without nicking the wool/denim/lining, pulls out all thread residue and brushes the seam clean, ready to re-press and re-sew.

Custom tailor shop: taking in or letting out side seams, waistband, seat seam or a dress bodice — unpicking the waistband/lining stitching, the seam itself and any topstitching through several layers plus interfacing and serged edges, keeping the seam allowance intact and the fabric unmarked.

Tailored suit jacket or coat at a shop workbench: unpicking the sleeve out of the armhole, opening lining stitching, removing shoulder pads or sleeve heads and pad-stitching in dense wool with curved, multi-directional stitch lines that must be undone stitch by stitch.

Bridal / formalwear / delicate garment work in a bridal shop or specialty tailor: unpicking seams in silk chiffon, lace, beaded or knit fabric, often with a razor blade under good light, where a single misplaced cut leaves a permanent hole, pull or run; also removing beading and hook-and-eye tapes.

Home-based custom sewer / small studio or costume shop: ripping out basting or a seam sewn crooked in a garment in progress, or removing an embroidered patch, name tape or applique from a customer's jacket so the fabric can be reused, working on a domestic table amid varied garments and clutter.

sources.system: RIT-GIS automated textile disassembly system (AI-guided robotic laser cutter + sorting gantry)
sources.developer: Rochester Institute of Technology, Golisano Institute for Sustainability
sources.title: New RIT technologies help minimize global textile waste | RIT
sources.claim: RIT's Golisano Institute prototype is a fully automated, conveyor-fed cell that images used garments, then uses an AI-guided robotic laser cutter to cut out logos, collars, cuffs and other non-recyclable elements, followed by a robotic sorting gantry; the garment is destroyed into recycling feedstock rather than preserved for alteration, and the system removes fabric features, not the stitching of a seam.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated garment deconstruction for recycling. It is the closest machine-controlled 'taking a garment apart' capability found, but it cuts through fabric to excise components destined for shredding; it does not sever and extract seam thread while leaving both panels, seam allowance and surface intact, which is what stitch removal for alteration requires. Cited to show the frontier, not to substantiate completion.

sources.system: TARS Robotics humanoid robot (hand-embroidery demonstration)
sources.title: TARS Demonstrates a Robot That Can Perform Hand Embroidery, Breaking Through a Key Automation Bottleneck in Flexible Manufacturing
sources.claim: A humanoid robot performed hand embroidery on stage — threading a needle and stitching ... bimanually on flexible material — the closest demonstration of fine tool work on cloth; it was a one-off live event demonstration and the release does not state whether the robot acted autonomously or was teleoperated.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: bimanual needle-and-thread work on fabric. Sub-millimetre tool use on limp cloth is the shared requirement, but the demonstration creates stitches on a presented workpiece rather than locating, severing and extracting existing stitches in an assembled garment; autonomy is unstated, so it cannot support a positive judgment.

sources.system: Robotic sewing workcell (Sewbo / Siemens, ARM Institute project)
sources.developer: Sewbo Inc. with Siemens; ARM Institute
sources.title: Project Highlight: Advancing Automated Robotic Sewing - ARM Institute
sources.claim: The Sewbo/Siemens ARM Institute robotic sewing workcell handles, aligns and sews jeans side seams and rises with closed-loop vision correction, and was integrated with an existing factory assembly line; apparel robotics at the frontier builds garments from flat panels inside a purpose-built cell and includes no capability for unpicking or removing existing stitching.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic sewing of garment seams in a purpose-built cell. It establishes what apparel robotics can do with fabric in an E1 environment — feeding and stitching flat panels — and by omission shows no fielded or demonstrated system performs the inverse operation of seam ripping on an assembled garment.

tasks.label: Sew garments, using needles and thread or sewing machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Alteration shop or dry-cleaner sewing room: machine-sew a new hem on a customer's trousers, skirt, or simple dress in stable woven or denim fabric after it has been marked and pressed e one straight/circular line matching the garment's original finish (blind hem, topstitch, or chainstitch jeans hem), one one-off garment at a time.

Shop workroom: hem or edge-finish a delicate or complex one-off garment e a chiffon or georgette rolled hem, a lined and pleated skirt, a multi-layer bridal skirt with horsehair braid e where fabric handling, curvature and layer count vary garment to garment.

Shop workroom: re-sew seams on and repair fully assembled garments e take in or let out side seams of a dress or jacket, taper trouser legs, shorten lined sleeves with vents and buttons, reset a waistband, replace a broken zipper, patch a tear, restitch a split seam e working inside a three-dimensional finished garment of unknown construction.

Self-employed custom sewer's home studio or small workroom: machine-assemble a straightforward custom garment from cut pattern pieces e a costume tunic, simple shift dress, uniform, or a small repeat run of the same simple item e joining panels with straight and gently curved seams and finishing edges.

Bespoke workroom: machine-assemble a fitted one-off garment e bridal gown, tailored suit jacket, formal dress e with curved and eased seams, set-in sleeves, interfacing, boning, invisible zipper, and a bagged lining, in fine or slippery fabric cut to one client's measurements.

Shop workroom or fitting area: hand sewing with needle and thread e hand-rolled or blind hems, slipstitching a lining closed, pad stitching a lapel, tacking, attaching buttons, hooks and eyes, and invisible mends on one-off garments.

sources.system: SEWBOT workline (SoftWear Automation)
sources.title: Sewbotsu2013 Softwear Automation
sources.claim: SoftWear Automation's Sewbot worklines use machine vision and lightweight robotics ... through conventional sewing machines and automatically sew complete T-shirts from cut panels inside a dedicated robotic workline.

sources.system: SEWBOT T-shirt workline, 3rd generation
sources.title: SoftWear Automation Secures $20M in Bestseller-Led Funding Round to Support Scaling 'Sewbots'
sources.claim: SoftWear Automation is bringing a third generation of its automated T-shirt Sewbot workline to commercial availability, indicating the autonomous garment-sewing workline is a productized system rather than a one-off demo.

sources.system: Robotic sewing workcell (Siemens Corporation + Sewbo)
sources.developer: Siemens Corporation, Sewbo, Levi Strauss, Bluewater Defense (ARM Institute funded)
sources.title: Robotic Automation in Apparel Manufacturing: A Novel Approach to Fabric Handling and Sewing
sources.claim: A Siemens/Sewbo/Levi's/Bluewater Defense robotic cell (UR5, suction gripper, temporary fabric stiffening, closed-loop visual servoing) autonomously sews straight and curved seams on trouser panels in denim, cotton and polyurethane, with seam error inside the 3 mm apparel-industry quality benchmark; validated at a Bluewater Defense production line and Levi's research facility.

sources.system: Deployed robotic sewing workcell (UR5e, digital thread from DXF, suction table, pocket hemmer/setter)
sources.developer: Siemens Corporation, Sewbo, Levi's, Bluewater Defense
sources.title: A Deployment Case Study in Robotic Apparel Automation: Digital Twin Integration, Interoperability, and Workforce Enablement
sources.claim: The same robotic sewing workcell was deployed on a denim factory floor in a production-adjacent line, autonomously performing back-pocket hemming, pocket setting, arcuate sewing ... (Stage 1) and the 3D front rise, back rise and side seams of denim shorts (Stage 2), with 90% trial success at 180 s and 360 s per trial.

sources.system: Automated Bottom Hemming through Robotic Garment Manipulation (ARM Institute project)
sources.title: Invigorating an Established Yet Fragile Textile Industry | Manufacturing USA
sources.claim: An ARM Institute project produced a bimanual robot that destacks a T-shirt, reshapes it, and loads it into an automatic bottom ..., which sews the circular hem at the garment's bottom edge e a complete robotic hemming operation inside a robotic cell.
sources.transferJustification: Same task (hemming a garment on a sewing machine); shows the load-align-sew hem cycle done autonomously on a limp garment rather than a rigid part.

sources.system: ARM Institute robotic sewing program (Bot Couture and follow-on projects)
sources.developer: ARM Institute with Siemens, Sewbo, Henderson Sewing, Bluewater Defense, Levi's
sources.title: Project Highlight: Advancing Automated Robotic Sewing - ARM Institute
sources.claim: ARM Institute reports that its robotic sewing projects demonstrated reliable handling, alignment and sewing of jeans seams, covering more than half of jeans assembly operations, and that the workcell was integrated with an existing assembly line feeding downstream processes.

tasks.label: Let out or take in seams in suits and other garments to improve fit.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Tailor shop or dry-cleaner alterations department: taking in a men's suit jacket at the center-back/side-body seams and/or trousers at the seat and inseam. Worker unpicks existing stitching (and lining, vent, waistband as needed), re-marks the pinned line, sews the tapered seam through wool plus interfacing/lining, trims, presses the seam open on a buck, and closes the lining so the alteration is invisible.

Bridal or formalwear shop alterations room: taking in a gown or cocktail dress at bodice side seams/princess seams. Delicate or beaded fabric, multiple layers (shell, lining, boning, tulle), hand-finishing of the lining, and the change must preserve the garment's designed shape; single-shot job with no room for damage.

Tailor shop: letting out seams to enlarge a garment (trouser seat/waist, jacket side seams, skirt side seams) using the available inlay. Requires ripping the old stitch line, judging whether allowance suffices, pressing out the old crease line so the original stitch holes and shine do not show, re-sewing, and re-finishing the waistband or lining.

Retail-store or dry-cleaner alterations counter: quick take-in of a simple unlined garment (blouse, shirt, casual dress) — taper one or both side seams by a known amount, sew the new line, trim/serge the allowance, press. Fast turnaround, moderate quality bar.

Self-employed dressmaker/custom sewer working out of a home workroom, with fitting done at the client's home or a temporary space: taking in or letting out seams on a variety of client garments, layout and equipment vary, garments arrive as found with unknown construction.

sources.system: Sewbo / Siemens robotic sewing workcell (ARM Institute 'Bot Couture' / Robotic 3D Sewing)
sources.developer: Sewbo Inc., Siemens Technology, with ARM Institute, Levi Strauss, Bluewater Defense
sources.title: Project Highlight: Advancing Automated Robotic Sewing - ARM Institute
sources.claim: Sewbo/Siemens robotic sewing workcell (ARM Institute projects, with Levi's and Bluewater Defense) autonomously handles, aligns and sews the three-dimensional shaping seams of jeans — side seams and front/back rises — from cut fabric panels in a factory workcell, with vision-based closed-loop seam-path correction; it was integrated into an existing assembly line for downstream finishing.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: assembling seams in new-garment manufacture. It shares sewing-machine seam formation, but the work is flat cut panels presented from a digital pattern in a purpose-built cell, not an existing finished three-dimensional garment. It includes no unpicking of existing stitching, no bespoke seam line derived from a customer fitting, no lining/waistband reassembly and no pressing of the altered seam, so it does not substantiate completion of a let-out/take-in alteration.

sources.system: SEWBOT worklines
sources.title: Materials World: Spotlight Automated Sewing - Softwear Automation
sources.claim: SoftWear Automation's SEWBOT worklines use computer vision and light robotics to steer fabric through the needle and autonomously produce sewn goods (bath mats, towels, t-shirts) at production volumes in dedicated factory worklines.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: high-volume sewing of simple new products from flat fabric in a purpose-built workline. The machine is fed standardized flat plies on its own transport surface and repeats a fixed product recipe; it has no demonstrated ability to take apart and re-sew a customer's constructed garment to a new, individually determined seam line, so it does not transfer to alterations.

sources.system: VELUM
sources.title: Intelligent Robotics for Laundries Closes Automation Gap | RoboticsTomorrow
sources.claim: sewts' VELUM robot uses AI and computer ... limp, finished textiles in commercial laundries, picking towels and terry linen and feeding them crease-free into existing folding machines; deployed in large laundry facilities.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic manipulation of finished limp textiles inside a structured human work facility (E2 laundry). It shows grasping and presenting cloth, but the accepted output is a fed/folded towel, not a re-sewn seam; no cutting, unpicking, stitching or pressing of a garment is performed, so it cannot substantiate alteration work.

sources.system: Automated garment deconstruction prototype
sources.developer: Rochester Institute of Technology (with Nike, Goodwill, Ambercycle collaborations)
sources.title: New RIT technologies help minimize global textile waste | RIT
sources.claim: RIT's automated garment deconstruction system for recycling uses machine vision and a robotic laser-cutting gantry to identify and cut away non-recyclable elements such as zippers and logos from used clothing.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated take-apart of existing finished garments. It is the closest demonstrated 'work on a garment as received', but it is destructive laser cutting for recycling feedstock, not the non-destructive seam removal, re-stitching and pressing needed to alter a garment to a wearable, saleable standard, so it does not transfer.

tasks.label: Measure customers, using tape measures, and record measurements.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Custom/made-to-measure shop: adult client stands in shirtsleeves or close-fitting clothes in the shop's fitting area while the tailor takes a full set of 20-30 body dimensions (neck, chest, waist, seat, sleeve, shoulder, outseam/inseam, posture notes) for a new suit, shirt or dress, and writes them onto an order form or into the shop's order system.

Bridal/formalwear salon: consultant/seamstress measures a bride or bridesmaid over the undergarments she will wear (bust, underbust, natural waist, hips, hollow-to-hem, girth), sometimes with shoes on, to select the gown size to order and to plan later alterations; measurements recorded on the order sheet.

Alterations counter (dry cleaner, department store, or tailor shop): the customer wears the garment to be altered over street clothes; the tailor measures/marks how much to shorten a hem or sleeve, how much to take in at the waist or side seams, and records the amounts on the alteration ticket, typically in one to three minutes at the counter or in a small fitting stall.

On-site group measuring inside an institution: tailor or uniform vendor sets up at an employer's facility, school, band/team room, or military installation and measures dozens of people in a session (chest, waist, inseam, sleeve, hat/shoe size), recording each set to a roster or order file.

Measuring away from any controlled premises: dressmaker or tailor travels to a client's home, a hotel suite for a wedding party, or a theatre dressing room, and takes body measurements in whatever space, lighting and floor surface is available, recording them in a notebook or phone.

Clients who cannot hold a standard standing pose: young children who fidget, frail or elderly clients, wheelchair users needing adaptive garments, pregnant clients, or clients with marked posture asymmetry; the worker physically positions the body, measures seated or in stages, and records both the numbers and posture observations.

sources.system: VITUS Smart XXL 3D body scanner (Human Solutions of North America)
sources.title: Machine learning prediction of combat basic training injury from 3D body shape images (PLOS One / PMC)
sources.claim: The VITUS Smart XXL 3D body scanner (Human Solutions/VITRONIC) was deployed at Fort Jackson for personalized uniform fitting: 17,680 Army basic-training recruits were scanned in 2017, each scan under 20 seconds, with the machine's software automatically producing 161 body measurements; a further 64,000 scans were run at Lackland Air Force Base.
sources.transferJustification: Same task: taking and recording a person's body measurements for garment (uniform) fitting; the machine replaces the tape-measure step and writes measurements to the sizing record.

sources.system: VITUS / VITUSsmart 3D body scanner
sources.title: VITUS 3D Body Scanner — Markus Maurer, VITRONIC GmbH
sources.claim: The VITUS body scanner is an electromechanical machine: motorized sensor units travel from top to bottom inside scanning columns to sweep the body, and the VITUSsmart variant was designed for installation in a fitting room.

sources.system: VITUS Bodyscan
sources.title: 3D Body Scanning Hardware | Humanetics
sources.claim: Humanetics markets the VITUS bodyscan commercially for professional apparel use, with ISO 20685-compliant accuracy, 6-10 second scan time and automatic extraction of more than 150 body dimensions.

sources.system: Scanatic 360 Body Scanner (TG3D Studio)
sources.title: Optimize Fit: Using a 3D Body Scanner for Made-to-Measure — TG3D Studio
sources.claim: A bespoke suit maker (Made-to-Fit) installed two Scanatic 360 body scanners in its retail fitting rooms in Copenhagen and ...; the 3-second scans standardized measurement capture and reduced the need for hand measurements before garment production.
sources.transferJustification: Same task in the occupation's own setting: capturing and recording a customer's body measurements in a tailoring shop for a bespoke garment order.

sources.system: Fit3D ProScanner
sources.title: Fit3D Proscanner: Precise Body Scanner | DexaFit
sources.claim: The Fit3D ProScanner is a commercially deployed measuring machine with a motorized rotating platform and a sensor that travels vertically; it extracts over 400 measurements, including circumferences, automatically in under a minute, and is installed in gyms, clinics and wellness facilities.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (automated anthropometric measurement of a standing client in a service facility) transfers: same object (adult standing body), same circumference/length dimensions and precision class, same indoor commercial setting as a tailor's fitting room.

sources.system: Size Stream SS20 / Size Stream booth scanner
sources.title: Size Stream | SS20 and On-Site 3D Body Scanning & Measurement Systems
sources.claim: Size Stream sells booth body scanners that capture over 240 measurements in seconds and are offered either as permanent retail/enterprise installations or as portable booths taken on site for uniform programs and made-to-measure workflows.
sources.transferJustification: Same task: automatic capture and recording of customer body measurements for sizing and made-to-measure orders, including on-site group uniform fittings.

tasks.label: Fit and study garments on customers to determine required alterations.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Alterations fitting at a tailor shop or dry-cleaner/alterations counter: the customer changes into trousers, a skirt or a jacket and stands in the fitting area; the tailor looks at how the garment hangs, kneels to pin the hem to the customer's shoe height, pinches and pins the waist/seat/side seams, marks sleeve length with chalk or pins, and confirms the alteration list with the customer.

Formalwear/bridal fitting in a salon or department store: customer on a raised fitting platform in front of three-way mirrors wearing a gown, tuxedo or suit with the intended shoes and undergarments; the fitter pins bodice and princess seams, marks the hem circumference, plans a bustle and checks strap and shoulder fit, in one of several scheduled fitting sessions.

Bespoke/made-to-measure baste fitting in a tailor's atelier: a partly assembled, hand-basted canvassed jacket or trousers is put on the client; the tailor studies balance, collar gap, shoulder slope, sleeve pitch and posture asymmetries, chalks and re-pins seams, sometimes ripping and re-pinning a shoulder or collar on the body.

Costume/uniform fitting in a costume shop or backstage wardrobe: a performer or employee tries on a costume or uniform; the cutter/draper pins and marks adjustments while the wearer moves, sits or performs a few dance/work motions to check range of motion, under time pressure before a show or shift.

Mobile or home-based custom sewer/dressmaker fitting: the fitting happens in the client's living room or bedroom, a home studio, or on location (e.g., a bride's house before the wedding); variable lighting, no fitting platform or mirror wall, clutter and pets present, the client wearing the garment while the sewer pins and marks.

sources.system: 4D Knit Dress robotic activation arm
sources.developer: MIT Self-Assembly Lab with Ministry of Supply
sources.title: MIT's 4D-Knit Dress changes shape in response to heat
sources.claim: The most advanced in-store robotic garment-shaping demonstration puts the garment on a mannequin and runs a pre-programmed robot path to heat-shrink it; the robot does not fit or assess a garment on a live customer.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotically customising a garment's fit. Transfer fails because the workpiece is a mannequin on a fixed base, the path is pre-programmed rather than derived from studying fit on a customer, and no alteration is determined, pinned or marked.

sources.system: Force-Modulated Visual Policy for Robot-Assisted Dressing (CoRL 2025)
sources.developer: Carnegie Mellon University (Hao, Wang, Ravie, Hegde, Held, Erickson)
sources.title: Force-Modulated Visual Policy for Robot-Assisted Dressing with Arm Motions
sources.claim: State-of-the-art autonomous robot manipulation of clothing on a live person is limited to advancing a sleeve of a loose everyday garment onto a participant's arm in a laboratory; no assessment of fit, pinning or marking is performed.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: manipulating a deformable garment against a human body. Transfer fails: the robot only pulls a sleeve onto an arm in a lab rig and cannot judge drape, balance or hem level, nor place pins or chalk marks on a standing customer.

sources.system: Euveka connected/robotic mannequin (Emili)
sources.title: Can a shape-shifting mannequin make the fashion industry more sustainable?
sources.claim: Commercial robotic mannequins morph to a client's measurements so that a human fitter can drape and evaluate a garment; the machine holds a body shape but does not fit or study a garment on a customer or determine the alterations.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: presenting a body form for fitting. It does not substantiate this task because the customer is absent, the garment is placed and assessed by a person, and required alterations are still judged and marked by the human fitter.

sources.system: 3D body-scanner bespoke tailoring service (English Cut)
sources.developer: bespoke tailors with commercial body-scanning vendors
sources.title: Can a Robotic Tailor Make a Bespoke Suit?
sources.claim: Automated tailoring services substitute 3D body scanning for fittings; the scanner takes measurements optically, performs no physical action on garment or customer, and reported fit results are mixed.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: deriving fit information from a customer. It cannot support a positive judgment because a scanner is not a physically embodied machine acting on the world, and the article reports mixed results still requiring tailor intervention.

tasks.label: Trim excess material, using scissors.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Tailor/dressmaker workroom, at the sewing station or bench: after stitching, trimming and grading seam allowances, clipping curves, notching corners and trimming bulk out of a partly assembled garment; light-to-medium wovens, 1-4 plies, cut close to the stitching without nicking the garment.
At the machine during construction: snipping thread tails and overlock/serger chains as each seam is finished, garment part still at the sewing station.

Finishing/pressing table before delivery: hunting down and snipping stray thread ends, whiskers, basting remnants and loose tacks all over a completed three-dimensional garment (jacket, gown, trousers).

Alteration bench in a shop or dry-cleaner's tailoring room: after marking, cutting off excess length or width from an existing garment - trouser hems, sleeve shortening, taking in side seams, cutting a bridal hem - through folded plies and sometimes existing seams, along a chalk line.

Fitting area with the garment on the client's body or on a dress form: cutting away excess from a draped or basted mock-up, trimming a hem or facing allowance in place during a couture/bridal fitting.

Cutting table: trimming excess from flat material - surplus lining, interfacing or fusible, excess fabric around a pattern piece or a repair patch, squaring up yardage - all pieces lying flat and accessible.

sources.system: ScissorBot
sources.title: ScissorBot: Learning Generalizable Scissor Skill for Paper Cutting via Simulation, Imitation, and Sim2Real
sources.claim: A learned policy drives scissors on a robot arm to autonomously cut curves drawn on a thin deformable sheet (paper) that is fixtured at its top edge, with real-robot accuracy comparable to a one-handed human operator.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: cutting a thin, limp sheet along a marked line with scissors. Same tool and comparable precision to trimming excess fabric along a marked edge; the sheet is held by a fixture, which is exactly the E1 presentation. Transfer is partial - woven cloth is limper and frays more than paper.

sources.system: Lowry SEWBOT (SoftWear Automation)
sources.title: SEWBOTS® Transforming The Sewn Products Industry | Textile World
sources.claim: The machine-vision-guided Lowry Sewbot autonomously serges the outer edges of bath mats and microfiber towels faster than a human operator, with one operator supervising up to six machines.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: serging/overlocking, in which the machine's knife trims the excess fabric off the edge as it stitches. The Sewbot performs this on textile panels under machine control, i.e. machine-controlled trimming of surplus cloth at an edge to production quality.

sources.system: SEWBOT workline
sources.title: Automated Cutting & Sewing Developments | Textile World
sources.claim: Sewbot worklines manipulate limp fabric autonomously with a four-axis robotic arm, vacuum gripper and a 360-degree conveyor under machine vision that tracks individual threads at the needle.
sources.transferJustification: Characterizes the environment in which the trimming/serging occurs: a purpose-built workline where fabric is presented to the machine by conveyor and held by vacuum, i.e. an E1 setting.

sources.system: Industrial overlock (serger) with edge knife
sources.title: Mastering Sewing with Overlocker: Essential Tips for Seamless Projects
sources.claim: On an overlock/serging machine the knife trims the surplus fabric off the seam edge while the stitch is formed - the standard mechanized way excess material is trimmed in sewn-goods production.
sources.transferJustification: Definitional support for what 'serging' does in the Sewbot evidence; operator-fed here, so not itself a basis for a positive judgment.

sources.system: Gerber Paragon
sources.title: Gerber Paragon, fabric cutting machine for garments | Lectra
sources.claim: A commercial CNC gantry knife cutter cuts garment parts from fabric on an automated conveyorized vacuum bed to programmed contours at production quality and speed.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: knife-cutting fabric along a programmed contour on a fixtured, vacuum-held bed. Physically the same act as trimming excess material from flat cloth along a line, on the same materials and at tighter tolerance than hand scissors.

sources.system: Robotic apparel sewing workcell (fabric handling + sewing machine control)
sources.title: Robotic Automation in Apparel Manufacturing: A Novel Approach to Fabric Handling and Sewing
sources.claim: A ROS-integrated robotic sewing workcell handles fabric and controls the sewing machine's presser foot and thread trimming automatically as part of the automated sewing operation.
sources.transferJustification: Directly covers the sub-instance of cutting thread ends at the machine: the trimming is executed under robot/machine control rather than by the operator's scissors.

tasks.label: Assemble garment parts and join parts with basting stitches, using needles and thread or sewing machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bespoke/custom tailoring workroom: tailor assembles a one-off jacket, coat or trouser from freshly cut wool suiting — pad-stitching/basting the canvas to the forepart, basting shoulder seams, setting and basting sleeves, closing side seams with long temporary hand or machine basting so the garment can be tried on the client and ripped apart afterward. Drapey shaped panels, unique pattern per client, fit-critical.

Bridal/eveningwear shop: dressmaker assembles bodice, skirt panels, linings, interlining and boning of a gown from cut pieces and joins them with basting for a first fitting. Slippery satin/chiffon/lace, beading, many plies, curved princess seams; each gown a unique pattern and size.

Small custom-sewing shop or home studio: simple garment (A-line skirt, elastic-waist trousers, knit top, simple shirt) in stable cotton, denim-weight or knit fabric assembled from cut panels; side seams and zipper machine-basted with a long stitch before a quick fit check and final stitching.

Small custom-sewing shop: one-off dress, blouse or lined garment in slippery, sheer, stretch or specialty fabric (silk crepe, georgette, velvet, lace) from a pattern drafted for that client; parts pinned, matched at notches and basted by hand or machine before fitting.

Costume/theatrical or sample workroom: a muslin toile or mock-up is assembled from cut cotton pieces and joined with quick basting stitches so the shaped panels, darts and armscye can be fitted on the performer and marked for correction.

Small-batch custom production: a set of identical simple garments (uniform tops, dance costumes, aprons/scrub tops, a designer's duplicate samples) in stable fabrics, all from the same graded pattern; the sewer repeatedly assembles cut parts and machine-bastes/joins the same seams.

tasks.label: Make garment style changes, such as tapering pant legs, narrowing lapels, and adding or removing padding.

Tailor shop workroom: restyling a tailored suit jacket or sport coat 	ming the body and sleeves, narrowing wide lapels. Requires opening the lining and facing, unpicking canvas and pad stitching, re-cutting the lapel line, re-taping the roll line, re-sewing and hand-finishing, then blocking and pressing the lapel roll.

Alterations/tailor workroom: adding or removing shoulder pads or bust padding in a jacket, blazer, coat or dress 	 opening the lining at the shoulder or side, extracting or inserting pads/cups, reshaping the sleeve head and armhole, re-stitching and closing the lining by hand, pressing the shoulder over a ham.

Bridal or formal salon: restyling a gown 	 changing the neckline, adding or removing sleeves or straps, inserting bra cups/padding, adding a bustle or modesty panel. Done on delicate lace, satin, beaded and layered fabrics after a fitting on the client, with hand finishing and steaming.

Theatrical, film or performance wardrobe: restyling costumes or uniforms 	 narrowing lapels, tapering trousers, adding shoulder padding for character shape 	 often worked on location in a wardrobe trailer, backstage room or borrowed space with improvised layout and tight deadlines between fittings.

Small custom/sample workroom: a custom sewer makes style modifications across a small batch of stock or sample garments (e.g., removing shoulder padding and narrowing lapels on a run of jackets, tapering a batch of uniform trousers) to a spec sheet, with garments hung on racks and worked at industrial machines and pressing stations.

tasks.label: Maintain garment drape and proportions as alterations are performed.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Alterations shop or dry-cleaner alteration counter: shortening/lengthening trousers, taking in or letting out the waist and seat, tapering legs. Worker checks the hang on the customer or a form, pins and chalks, opens the original seams, re-sews, and presses so the legs hang straight, the crease stays aligned and the break over the shoe is right.

Menswear tailor shop: suit jacket or coat alteration — shorten sleeves (often from the shoulder), take in side and center-back seams, adjust shoulders. Multi-layer wool with canvas, padding and lining; the worker must preserve balance, lapel roll, collar hug and clean drape across the chest and back after re-assembly and pressing.

Bridal salon or formal-wear shop: gown alteration — take in the bodice, adjust straps, hem multiple layers of tulle/satin/lace, add a bustle. Bias-cut and slippery or beaded fabrics; the worker fits on the client over several appointments and must keep the skirt hanging level and the proportions of the silhouette intact.

Home-based sewing/alterations business (spare room or basement studio, variable layout and lighting): everyday dresses, skirts, blouses and knitwear brought in by neighborhood clients — side-seam take-ins, dart adjustments, strap and hem shortening on stretchy or delicate fabric, checked on a form and pressed so the garment still hangs correctly.

Custom sewing/dressmaking studio: fitting adjustments made during construction of a made-to-measure garment — a muslin or partly assembled garment is tried on the client, seam lines are moved, ease is redistributed and panels re-cut so the finished garment's drape and proportions match the design.

tasks.label: Take up or let down hems to shorten or lengthen garment parts, such as sleeves.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Alteration shop or dry cleaner: shorten a customer's finished trousers/jeans to a length marked at fitting — pick out the existing hem stitching (or cut and re-attach the original jeans hem), measure and mark both legs, trim allowance, press, blind-hem or topstitch, final press, match the two legs.

Bridal/formalwear or dress shop: hem a dress, skirt, or gown pinned on the customer — multiple layers, linings, chiffon/lace/satin, uneven or circular hems, often hand-stitched or horsehair-braid finish, pressed and inspected before delivery.

Tailor shop: shorten or lengthen sleeves on a lined suit jacket or coat — open the lining, remove the cuff hem, reset the length, deal with cuff buttons/buttonholes, re-hem, hand slip-stitch the lining, press over a sleeve board.

Let a hem down to lengthen a garment (child's school or uniform trousers, growing-child dress, military/service uniform sleeves): unpick the old hem, press out the crease, judge available allowance, add a facing or false hem when short, re-hem and press.

Small production / custom-sewing operation: batch hemming of new, raw-edge garment parts to one specified length (e.g., sleeve and bottom hems on a run of uniform shirts, costumes, or made-to-order garments) — same fabric, repeated straight or circular hems, work presented in stacks at a machine.

Work performed off-premises: mobile/home-based tailor hemming at a client's house, or wardrobe alterations backstage or at a venue — garment measured on the client, portable machine or hand-sewing, variable lighting, furniture and surfaces taken as found.

tasks.label: Repair or replace defective garment parts, such as pockets, zippers, snaps, buttons, and linings.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Alterations shop or dry cleaner: customer brings trousers, a jacket or a dress with a broken or separated zipper. The tailor unpicks the old zipper from the finished 3-D garment (fly, side seam, or back of a lined dress), matches a new zipper by type/length/color, pins or bastes it, sews it in while managing bulk and lining, then hand-finishes and presses.

Shop or department-store alteration room: replace missing/broken sewn-on buttons on shirts, suits, coats or uniforms. Match the button (often the garment's spare or from a button box), snip away old thread remnants, position it against the buttonhole, sew (hand or button machine), shank/knot and trim.

Shop bench: replace non-sewn fasteners - prying off and re-setting metal snaps/rivets, hooks-and-eyes, or bar-and-hook waistband closures on jeans, workwear, bridal and uniform garments, including reinforcing torn fabric under the fastener.

Alterations shop: repair or replace worn/torn pocket bags and ripped pocket openings in trousers, jackets and coats. The worker turns the garment inside out, unpicks the damaged pocketing from inside the finished garment, cuts new pocketing from stock, restitches it into the seam, and reinforces the corners.

Tailor shop: replace or repair a shredded lining in a jacket, coat or skirt. Unpick the lining from armholes, facings and hem of the finished garment, use it as a pattern to cut new lining, machine-sew the new lining sections, insert them into the shell and hand-finish armholes and hem.

Self-employed custom sewer working from a home studio: assorted small repairs on client garments dropped off as found - reattaching belt loops and hooks, replacing worn waistband elastic, mending split seams, patching worn knees/elbows, restitching hems on varied fabrics, with no two jobs alike and no standard fixtures.

tasks.label: Press garments, using hand irons or pressing machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Under-pressing during construction or alteration in a tailoring/alterations shop: between sewing steps the worker presses seams open, sets darts, and shapes curved areas over a tailor's ham or sleeve board with a hand iron and steam, on standard garments (trousers, shirts, jackets).

Final press of a completed or altered garment (suit jacket, trousers, dress) before customer pickup, done at the shop's pressing station with a hand iron or a commercial buck/form press, to produce a crisp, presentation-quality finish.

Localized touch-up pressing after an alteration: pressing a newly turned hem, re-setting a trouser crease, flattening a resewn seam, and steaming out wrinkles picked up during handling on a customer's garment.

Pressing delicate, embellished or unusual materials in the shop: silk, velvet, sequined or beaded bodices, pleated chiffon, leather trim, vintage fabric; requires test-pressing scraps, press cloths, low heat and judgment to avoid scorching, shine or crushed pile.

Home-based dressmaker/custom sewer pressing cut pieces, seams and hems of a one-off garment on a domestic ironing board in a converted room at home, with variable layout and no institutional standard.

tasks.label: Fit, alter, repair, and make made-to-measure clothing, according to customers' and clothing manufacturers' specifications and fit, and applying principles of garment design, construction, and styling.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine alteration of ready-to-wear clothing in an alterations shop, dry cleaner, or retail alterations department: shorten trouser/skirt hems (blind-stitch, cuffed, or original-hem), shorten jacket sleeves, take in waistband and side seams, taper legs. Each garment is a different fabric, construction, and thread color; the tailor unpicks existing stitching, presses, re-sews on standard machines, and presses again to a finish the customer will inspect.

Fitting session with the customer wearing the garment: taking body measurements, evaluating drape and balance on a moving person, pinning and chalk-marking take-ins, hem lengths and sleeve lengths, sometimes over several fittings on a partly constructed garment.

Repair of worn or damaged garments brought in by customers: replacing a broken zipper in trousers/jacket/dress, restitching split seams, patching or reweaving tears, repairing linings, moving or replacing buttons, mending pockets. Damage location and garment construction differ every time.

Complex bridal or formalwear alteration and fitting: multi-layer gown with lining, tulle, boning and beading; taking in bodice side seams and princess seams, hemming multiple layers, adding a bustle, hand-finishing and re-beading, fitted on the client over multiple appointments.

Constructing a custom garment from scratch to a customer's measurements and a chosen style: drafting/adjusting the pattern, cutting fabric and interfacing, assembling a tailored jacket, dress, or costume (set sleeves, collar, canvas/interlining, zipper, lining), pressing and hand-finishing, with intermediate try-ons.

Producing a simple made-to-measure or spec garment in a shop or small production setting: a T-shirt, simple knit top, uniform piece, or simple trousers cut and sewn to specified dimensions from a manufacturer's or customer's spec sheet, with no on-body fitting required.

tasks.label: Position patterns of garment parts on fabric, and cut fabric along outlines, using scissors.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Alterations/repair shop back room: tailor lays a small pattern piece or traced template (patch, facing, cuff, pocket bag, replacement panel, lining piece) on a remnant or short length of yardage on the cutting table, weights or pins it, and cuts it out with shears. Small parts, tolerance a few millimeters, one-off, same-day turnaround.

Self-employed dressmaker's own studio (often a room in a home): a full set of paper pattern pieces for a custom dress or shirt is laid on folded or single-layer woven or knit yardage, grainline aligned, pinned/weighted, then cut with shears. Standard fabrics (cotton, linen, ponte, twill), one garment.

Bespoke/made-to-measure tailoring shop: pattern pieces for a jacket or trousers chalked onto wool suiting laid on the cutting table, with plaid, stripe or check matched across fronts, sleeves and pockets, plus nap direction respected; cut with shears, with inlays left at seams.

Bridal/formalwear atelier: pattern pieces positioned single-layer on delicate or slippery goods (silk chiffon, charmeuse, tulle, plain lace, sequined-free satin), motifs and scallop edges placed deliberately, pieces cut with shears while keeping the fabric from shifting or distorting.

Couture atelier one-off: heavily beaded, sequined or three-dimensional appliquéd lace where the maker cuts around individual motifs, works motif-by-motif to continue the lace across seams, and avoids severing beadwork; entirely judgment-driven placement and hand cutting.

Small custom workroom producing a short run (a dozen bridesmaid dresses, uniforms, or a small wholesale order): fabric spread in several plies on a long table, pattern pieces nested to conserve yardage, weighted, and cut through the stack with shears or a rotary cutter.

tasks.label: Record required alterations and instructions on tags, and attach them to garments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Department store / menswear retail alterations: after a fitting, the tailor writes the required work (hem 1.5", take in waist 1", shorten sleeves) plus customer name, ticket number and due date on a paper alteration ticket, then safety-pins or staples it to the garment (often at the waistband or lapel) and hangs it on the work rack.

Dry cleaner / alterations counter intake: garment taken in at the counter, a printed or handwritten work ticket with customer data and alteration instructions is produced and attached to the garment with a pin, tag gun, or heat-seal/adhesive ID tag before the garment goes onto the conveyor or rack.

Bridal or formalwear salon: after a multi-step gown fitting, detailed notes (hem length by station, bustle type, strap shortening, cup insertion) are written on a tag and attached to the gown, which is then bagged and stored with the tag visible for the seamstress.

Independent custom tailor / dressmaker workroom: instruction tags or slips are written for individual garments or bundles of cut components and pinned to the garment or panel, referencing chalk marks and pinned folds made during the fitting.

Mobile or home-based sewer: alterations noted at a client's home, wedding venue, or the sewer's own home workspace; the note is written and pinned to the garment on the spot, with no fixed layout or standard equipment.

tasks.label: Examine tags on garments to determine alterations that are needed.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Alterations shop or dry-cleaner workroom: the sewer takes the next garment off the ready-to-work rack, locates the fitter's ticket pinned or stapled to it (often handwritten: 'hem 1.5", taper sleeves, take in waist 1"'), and determines the sequence of operations and the customer/order number.

Bridal, formalwear or department-store alterations department: garments hang on numbered racks with printed/barcoded work-order tags; the sewer reads or scans the tag on the hanging garment to identify the order and the alterations listed on it.

During or right after a fitting: the worker checks the manufacturer's sewn-in labels (size, fiber content, care symbols) inside the collar, waistband or side seam, plus retail hangtags, to judge what alterations are feasible and record what is needed.

Uniform, workwear or costume-shop batch alterations: garments arrive in bins or on hanging conveyors carrying barcoded or RFID tags identifying the wearer and the standing alteration spec (hem length, sleeve length, patch placement); worker reads the tag and determines the work.
Mobile/on-site custom sewer at a client's home, office or event venue: examines the garment's labels and the job ticket in a space taken as found, with variable lighting and no fixed layout.

Dry-cleaner front counter / retail floor: reading tags on garments hanging on the customer conveyor or intake rack to spot which items are flagged for alteration and to check care tags for restrictions.

tasks.label: Develop, copy, or adapt designs for garments, and design patterns to fit measurements, applying knowledge of garment design, construction, styling, and fabric.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bespoke bridal/formal gown: tailor consults with the client, sketches a design concept, selects silhouette and fabric, then drafts a pattern to the client's recorded measurements (bust, waist, hip, length, posture allowances). Output is a design plus a set of pattern pieces to be cut.

Adapting a commercial or house block pattern to an individual client's measurements — full-bust adjustment, sway-back, shortening/lengthening, ease changes — for a dress, blouse or trousers in a small alterations-and-custom shop.

Copying an existing garment a client brings in (a worn-out favorite dress, a discontinued uniform jacket): measuring or rubbing off the garment's panels to reconstruct a pattern that reproduces it in new fabric.

Bespoke menswear: a tailor drafts a coat/trouser/shirt pattern from a client's measurements using a drafting system and a personalized block, marking style features (lapel shape, pocket placement, vents) per the client's order.

Costume, dance, theatrical or specialty garment: interpreting a designer's or client's concept sketch into a workable design and pattern, accounting for stretch fabrics, movement, and quick-change construction.

Small-label sample and size-set work: a custom sewer develops a pattern in CAD pattern-making software (e.g., a digital block adapted to a spec sheet), grades it to a size range, and plots the pattern for cutting.

tasks.label: Put in padding and shaping materials.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Alteration/tailor shop: inserting, replacing, or repositioning shoulder pads and sleeve heads in a customer's suit jacket, blazer, coat or dress. Worker opens the lining, positions the limp pad by eye against the customer's shoulder shape, pins and hand-tacks or basts it through the shoulder seam, then closes the lining.

Custom garment construction/repair in a shop workroom: applying fusible or sew-in interfacing to collars, cuffs, plackets, waistbands, facings and buttonhole areas of a garment being made or rebuilt — cutting the interfacing to the piece, positioning it on the flat panel, and pressing/fusing or stitching it in.

Bridal/formal workroom: building structure into a gown bodice — inserting boning into casings or seam allowances, sewing in bra/bust cups or foam, adding a built-in corselette or waist stay to a fitted or altered bodice.

Bespoke/made-to-measure tailoring workroom: basting the haircloth/canvas chest piece into a jacket forepart and pad-stitching the lapel roll and undercollar so the canvas holds the shape of the chest and lapel.

Dressmaking workroom: shaping hems and silhouettes — horsehair braid or crinoline in a gown hem, interlined/underlined hems, sleeve head rolls, bust padding in an evening gown, pads to correct a client's uneven shoulders.
Costume/theatrical shop: building foam body padding, hip pads, bustles, historical shaping and character padding into custom costumes, each piece one-off and shaped to a specific performer.

tasks.label: Weigh ingredients, such as dye, to be mixed together for use in textile processing.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production dyehouse color kitchen: operator reads the batch recipe card/terminal, retrieves the named powder dyes from drums or sacks in the dye store, and weighs each component (grams up to tens of kilograms) on a bench or floor scale into a bucket/bag for one production dye lot; several dyes per recipe, several lots per shift; dusty, must avoid cross-contamination and record weights.

Weighing/measuring bulk auxiliaries for the same batches: salt, soda ash, caustic, acids, sequestrants, leveling agents, softeners in powder or liquid form, 5-100 kg quantities into drums, kegs or dissolving tanks feeding the dyeing machine; heavy handling, PPE, delivered to the machine on schedule.

Dye lab / sample dispensary: weighing very small dye quantities (0.01-2 g, analytical balance) and making up stock solutions and chemical additions for lab dips and shade-matching trials in beakers/dyepots; dozens of small recipes per day, high precision, traceability required.

Mid-run shade correction: after a shade check on a running batch, the operator quickly weighs a small add-on quantity of one or more dyes/chemicals and prepares it for addition to the machine while it is held at temperature; time-critical, small and irregular amounts.

Small commission dyehouse, garment dyeing unit or denim wash laundry: weighing bleach/oxidizer, permanganate, enzymes, brighteners and dyes into buckets at a chemical station for varied small lots; low volume, many different recipes and products, general-purpose scales on a bench.

tasks.label: Start and control machines and equipment to wash, bleach, dye, or otherwise process and finish fabric, yarn, thread, or other textile goods.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Batch fabric dyeing/bleaching in a knit or woven commission dyehouse: operator sets the recipe on the jet/overflow/jigger controller, starts the machine, runs the temperature/time profile, admits dyes and auxiliaries at the right steps, checks shade, drains, rinses and stops the cycle.

Package, beam or hank dyeing of yarn and thread in pressure kiers: carriers of packages are placed in the vessel, the bleach/dye/rinse program is started and controlled through pressure and temperature stages, then the load is drained, hydro-extracted and dried.

Continuous ranges — bleaching/scouring range, pad-dye or indigo rope range, washing range, tenter/finishing line: operator starts the line, sets line speed, pad pressures, box temperatures and dwell, controls the running range and stops it at roll changes.

Garment or piece dyeing and wet finishing in rotary drum machines at a garment dye house or denim laundry: load garments, select and start the program, control the dye/wash cycle and chemical additions, check shade, extract and unload.

Small-lot, sample and specialty work in a small plant or on legacy equipment: hand-controlled jigs, becks or skein machines with manual valves, frequent recipe changes, operator judging shade by eye and adjusting the run.

tasks.label: Observe display screens, control panels, equipment, and cloth entering or exiting processes to determine if equipment is operating correctly.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Batch dyeing (jet, beck, jig, package) operator in a commission dye house watches the machine's PLC/HMI screen and control panel through a cycle — temperature ramp, pressure, liquor circulation, dosing steps, alarms — to judge whether the machine is running the recipe correctly.

Continuous range operator (bleach range, mercerizer, pad-steam dye range, tenter frame) stands at the entry/exit and watches cloth as it feeds and emerges — checking for creases, wrinkles, curled selvedge, roping, tears, shade streaks, off-registration — while also glancing at speed, tension, and temperature readouts to decide whether the range is operating correctly.

Operator makes walking rounds of assigned machines in the dye house: looking and listening for leaks, steam or water on the floor, abnormal pump or drive noise, vibration, jammed rolls, blocked drains, and indicator lamps, to determine whether any unit is malfunctioning.

Operator monitors a computerized central dyeing control system / alarm board covering several machines (chemical dosing, dye kitchen dispensing, effluent and utility readouts), interpreting trend curves and alarm messages to determine whether each process is on-spec.

Washing, extracting, and drying operations (continuous batch washer, dryer, or glass-fiber sizing/drying line): the tender watches exit moisture, temperature and belt-speed displays and observes the emerging web or goods to determine that the equipment is functioning correctly.

tasks.label: Notify supervisors or mechanics of equipment malfunctions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Monitor factors such as temperatures and dye flow rates to ensure that they are within specified ranges.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Add dyes, water, detergents, or chemicals to tanks to dilute or strengthen solutions, according to established formulas and solution test results.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Batch dyehouse color kitchen: for a scheduled lot on a jet/package/beam machine, the operator weighs out several powder dyes to the gram per the recipe card, dissolves them in hot water in a mixing tank, and delivers the dye solution to the dyeing machine's addition tank before the cycle step calls for it.

Bulk auxiliary additions during a batch cycle: operator draws salt, soda ash, caustic, peroxide, detergent/leveling agent from drums, bags or bulk tanks and charges the measured amount into the machine's addition/mixing tank at the programmed step, adding water to make up the specified volume.

Mid-run correction: after a shade check or a bath test (pH, concentration, strike rate), the operator adds a small extra quantity of dye or chemical to strengthen the bath, or adds water to dilute it, to bring the solution back to formula.

Continuous range (bleaching/washing range, pad-dye, denim indigo range): operator makes up and tops off the pad-bath/box mixes with caustic, peroxide, wetting agent, indigo/hydrosulfite while the range runs, keeping concentration constant as liquor is carried off with the fabric.

Small or specialty operation (garment dyer, skein/carpet dyer, sample dyeing, small commission finisher): operator hand-mixes small quantities of dye and chemicals in buckets or beakers at a bench and pours them into an open kettle or small machine, sometimes with ad-hoc or infrequently used products.

tasks.label: Examine and feel products to identify defects and variations from coloring and other processing standards.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Final/intermediate inspection of dyed-and-finished piece goods: operator mounts a roll on a lighted perch/inspection frame in the dye house or finishing department, runs the open-width woven or knit fabric past, spots shade bars, dye streaks, spots, creases, holes, marks and grades the roll (e.g., 4-point), and feels the cloth for harshness/uneven finish.

Shade approval of a dye lot: operator cuts a swatch from the batch, compares it against the customer/lab standard in a light booth or on a spectrophotometer, checks side-to-center and end-to-end uniformity, and decides pass, re-dye, or shade-sort.

In-process check at the machine: operator pulls or views a sample from a running jet/beck/jig or off the rollers of a continuous bleaching/dyeing/finishing range, judges color development and evenness against the standard, feels the wet or hot cloth for hand and finish pickup, and calls for a dye add or machine adjustment.

Dyed yarn packages, cones, skeins or loose stock: operator pulls packages from the carrier after unloading, looks for shade differences package-to-package and inside-to-outside (ring dyeing), stains and yellowing, and squeezes/handles the yarn for hardness and softener hand.

Garment-dyed, piece-washed or made-up goods (garments, hosiery, towels, small piece goods) handled item by item after wash/dye: operator turns each item, checks for streaks, crocking, seam shading and uneven wash, and feels for softness and stiffness.

tasks.label: Adjust equipment controls to maintain specified heat, tension, and speed.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Batch dyeing in a commission dyehouse: operator runs a jet/overflow, winch/beck, jigger, beam or package-dyeing machine on a recipe — holds the heating ramp (e.g. 2 °C/min), hold and cool-down temperatures, pump/nozzle pressure and reel or fabric circulation speed, adjusting steam and cooling valves and drive settings at the machine's panel through the cycle.

Stenter (tenter) frame / heat-setting and finishing range: operator sets and trims chamber temperatures, line speed, overfeed and chain width to hold specified drying, residual moisture, shrinkage and fabric tension as different fabric lots and weights run through.

Continuous pretreatment line (bleach range, desizing/washing range, mercerizer, continuous dye range): operator holds steam/box temperatures, dwell time, roller drive speeds and section-to-section web tension so the web runs wrinkle-free and to specified pickup.

Older or partly manual equipment in a small dyehouse: manual steam and cooling valves, hand-wheel or brake-band tension devices, variable-speed drives with mechanical adjusters and analog gauges; the operator judges by gauge, hand feel of the fabric and experience and trims controls by hand.

Startup and upset response: threading/leading fabric into the range, ramping speed while watching the web, reacting to creases, edge curl, a fabric break, a tension surge or a temperature excursion by slowing the line, re-threading or smoothing the goods and then dialing conditions back to specification.

tasks.label: Soak specified textile products for designated times.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Piece goods (woven/knit fabric rolls) steeped in a mill dye house: fabric is loaded as a rope into a jet/beck/jigger or wound onto a beam, submerged in a scour, bleach, or dye liquor, held for the designated soak time at set temperature, then drained, rinsed and unloaded wet.

Yarn in package (cone/bobbin) or hank form soaked in a package-dyeing kettle or hank machine: carriers are loaded with packages, lowered into the vessel, steeped/circulated for the specified time in bleach or dye bath, then lifted out and passed to extraction/drying.

Garments/denim soaked in rotary washers, paddle or garment-dye machines in a laundry/finishing plant: a lot of garments is loaded into the drum, chemicals (enzyme, bleach, softener, dye) dosed, steeped for the designated time, drained, extracted and unloaded.

Lab-dip and sample work in the plant's color lab: small swatches, skeins or package samples soaked in beaker/small-vessel dyeing units for the prescribed time to match shade before bulk production; results checked and recipes recorded.

Small-lot or specialty soaking done by hand in open vats/tubs at a custom or craft dye house: irregular items (rug sections, sample garments, technical or mixed goods) submerged, weighted or agitated by hand, judged by eye, timed and pulled out manually.

tasks.label: Inspect machinery to determine necessary adjustments and repairs.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Start-of-shift and periodic walkaround of the assigned dyeing machines (jet, beck, package or jig dyers, washers) on the dye-house floor: look for water, steam, dye and hydraulic leaks at pumps, seals, hoses and valves; check pressure/temperature gauges, sight glasses and control readouts against expected values; listen to circulating pumps, motors and blowers for abnormal noise; feel/observe for hot bearings; note what needs an operator adjustment versus a maintenance write-up. Hot, humid, fixed machine layout.

Scheduled condition checks on the auxiliary and utility equipment serving the dye machines - steam headers and traps, compressed-air lines, drive motors and gearboxes, dye/chemical dispensing pumps and metering lines - readings and condition recorded on a checklist that feeds the maintenance department.

Close mechanical inspection of the fabric path and contact parts with the machine stopped and guards open on a continuous range, padder, tenter or washer: guide rolls, nip/squeeze rolls, doctor blades, seals, belts and chains examined and felt for wear, grooving, torn rubber covering, gum/lint buildup or damage; operator decides clean/adjust versus tag the part for replacement.

Checking the machine's filters, strainers, lint screens, spray nozzles and drain valves - pulling screens and filter elements out and examining them for clogging, scale, wear or tears, and deciding whether cleaning suffices or a replacement must be ordered.

In-run troubleshooting inspection: the batch shows streaks, shade variation or the machine alarms/stops, and the operator inspects jets/nozzles, dye circulation pump and filter, level and temperature sensors, valves and drives while the machine is loaded, to determine the cause and whether an operator adjustment will fix it or maintenance must be called.
