tasks.label: Sew ends of cloth together, by hand or using machines, to form endless lengths of cloth to facilitate processing.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Continuous open-width range (bleach range, mercerizer, continuous dye range, washer/tenter) in a dye house: as one piece runs out, the operator lays the tail of the running piece over the head of the next roll across the full 1.5-3 m width, aligns the selvedges, and runs a portable/trolley chainstitch or overlock machine across to make a square, tension-even seam so the range never stops.

Batch/roll preparation station: joining many short rolls (~50-100 m) of greige knit or woven end-to-end into one large batch on an A-frame, in a plait, or on a beam to feed dyeing, printing or finishing; repeated seams, roll handling, edge alignment, defect cut-outs and rejoins.

Rope-form dyeing (jet, soft-flow, overflow, beck/winch): after the lot is loaded through the port, the operator pulls the head and tail of ... gathered, often damp rope out of the machine, flattens the bunched ends by hand and sews them into an endless loop with a hand-held bag-closer, working in the confined, wet space at the vessel port.

Sewing a leader/apron cloth (dummy cloth, canvas leader or lead-out cloth) to the head or tail of a lot so the fabric can be threaded through or pulled clear of a range, dryer or beam; the leader is a different, usually heavier cloth than the production fabric.

Hand sewing and in-process fixes: tacking or restitching a seam that burst mid-run, hand-stitching small sample lots, narrow or delicate specialty pieces, patching a tear, or sewing where a machine cannot reach (inside a J-box, at a beck rail, on a partly threaded range).

tasks.label: Ravel seams that connect cloth ends when processing is completed.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Open-width continuous range (bleach/pad-dye/tenter/finishing line) in a dye house: at the take-up batcher or inspection stand, the chain-stitch cross seam joining two dry pieces of moderate-weight woven or knit fabric (1.5-3 m wide) arrives; the operator stops the wind-up, picks and ravels the seam thread across the full width to separate the pieces without losing fabric, clears loose thread, and doffs/starts the next roll.

Rope-form batch dyeing (jet/overflow/beck) unload: several pieces sewn end-to-end (often sewn into a loop) come out of the machine soaking wet and heavy in tangled rope form; the operator finds each seam in the wet rope at the plaiter/cart and ravels it to separate the lots before extraction and drying.

Heavy or dense goods at the range exit: carpet from a continuous dye range or beck, upholstery, and industrial/technical fabrics whose ends are joined by heavy, doubled or multi-row stitching (sometimes taped or reinforced); the operator ravels or picks out these stiff seams in a cramped area beside the machine, often on stiff or coated cloth.

Short lots, narrow or sample goods, and leader/tail cloths: at a rewind or perching table the operator ravels the seam joining a leader cloth or a short fent to the processed piece, on light flat fabric laid taut on the table, and cleans off the pulled threads.

sources.system: Automatic Seam Ripping System (ASRS): Stitch Identification System + Coordinate Generation System + Laser-based Ripping System
sources.developer: Singh et al., academic research team (published in Procedia Manufacturing, Elsevier)
sources.title: Automatic Seam Ripping System - ScienceDirect
sources.claim: A research prototype, the Automatic Seam Ripping System (ASRS), autonomously images a stitched fabric seam, identifies the stitch line with a vision algorithm, generates the ripping trajectory as G-code, and rips the seam with a laser head - i.e. machine-controlled removal of a sewn seam from fabric presented flat in a purpose-built rig.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: ripping an unwanted stitched seam in an apparel plant. It transfers to raveling the seam that joins cloth ends because the object is the same (two fabric layers joined by machine stitching), the required precision is the same (remove the stitching without weakening or cutting the cloth), and the accepted output is the same (pieces separated, fabric intact).

sources.transferJustification: Same related task as above (seam ripping of stitched fabric); this item supplies the quality and cycle-time comparison against a human operator that the worker-quality test requires.

sources.claim: Commercial cross-seam detection sensors are standard on textile finishing lines: they detect the sewn cross seam in the running web and switch a machine output so the line reacts (e.g. opening calender rollers), showing that locating the seam in an open-width finishing line is already automated equipment, which is what a purpose-built ripping cell would rely on for presentation.

tasks.label: Remove dyed articles from tanks and machines for drying and further processing.

instances.label: Piece dyeing of knit/woven goods in a production dyehouse: at cycle end the operator opens the jet/soft-flow/overflow machine, threads the fabric rope over the unloading winch, plaits several hundred kg of wet rope into a trolley or onto a batcher, breaks the rope ties, and stages the lot for dewatering/slitting/drying.

Package (cheese/cone) yarn dyeing: after the cycle the operator hoists the bobbin carrier out of the kier with a crane or shuttle, moves it to the hydro-extractor, then transfers the packages to the hot-air/RF dryer and off-loads them to trolleys or pallets.

Hank/skein, loose stock, tow or top dyeing: dyed material on star-frames or perforated carriers is lifted out of vertical/horizontal machines, drained, taken to centrifuge and dryer, and staged for winding or blending.

Garment, hosiery and small-piece dyeing in rotary drum, rotary-paddle or open-pocket machines: operator opens the door and pulls tangled wet garments/socks/tees into a cart or onto a conveyor, then loads the extractor and tumble dryer; loads are bulk, wet, heavy and prone to roping.

Beam dyeing, jig dyeing, and continuous bleach/dye ranges (incl. carpet and wide-goods ranges): heavy dyed beams or batch rolls are uncoupled and doffed with hoist, crane, or lift truck at the end of the ... and moved to the next finishing step.

Small commission/specialty or sample dyehouse: mixed odd lots (rugs, trims, ropes, specialty apparel, lab and short-run dips) processed in older becks, kettles and small machines; the operator lifts, untangles and hand-carries wet goods out, with no two lots presented the same way.

tasks.label: Prepare dyeing machines for production runs, and conduct test runs of machines to ensure their proper operation.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Batch fabric dyeing machine (jet/overflow/soft-flow/beck/jig) in a fabric dyehouse: boil-out or flush the vessel from the previous shade, check nozzles, pump, valves and door gaskets, call up and set the process program (water level/liquor ratio, temperature ramp, pump and reel speeds) on the controller, charge the stock/addition tanks with the dye and chemical recipe, then fill and circulate to verify flow, heating and absence of leaks before the production batch runs.

Yarn package or hank dyeing kier in a yarn dyehouse: fit the correct spindle/hank carrier and blanking plates for the lot size, position the carrier in the vessel, seal the lid, set the program and liquor-flow parameters, verify dosing lines are connected, and run a circulation/pressure test to confirm flow direction and rate before dyeing starts.

Continuous range (bleach/scour range, pad-batch or thermosol dye range, carpet continuous dyeing range): mix and fill pad boxes and washbox chemistry, set nip pressures, line speed, box levels and steamer/oven temperatures, thread up the leader cloth, then run trial yardage and check shade, side-to-center uniformity and pick-up, adjusting before the production run is released.

Dye kitchen / dosing station preparation tied to a scheduled run: weigh the powder dyes and chemicals per the recipe card, dissolve them, charge dosing and addition tanks, and check the dosing pumps, flowmeters and delivery lines that feed the assigned dyeing machine.

Small-scale test dyeing before committing the production machine: prepare the lab or sample dyeing unit, dose the trial recipe, run the lab dip / strike-off, compare shade to the standard and adjust the production recipe and machine settings accordingly.

Start-up verification after maintenance or changeover: run the empty machine on water, check temperature, pressure, level and pH probe readings against references, watch for leaks after gasket, seal or pump work, make mechanical adjustments (belt tension, roller alignment, valve packing) and report faults that need a mechanic.

tasks.label: Test solutions used to process textile goods to detect variations from standards.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Batch dyehouse, mill floor: operator draws hot liquor from a running jet/beck/package dyeing machine through the sample cock into a beaker, checks pH (meter or strips) and temperature against the recipe window, and calls for acid/alkali correction if off standard. Hot, humid, steam, several machines per operator.

Continuous preparation/bleach range: operator samples the peroxide/caustic saturator or kier liquor each shift-hour and titrates it (permanganate/thiosulfate or acid-base) at a floor test station or the plant lab to check H2O2 and NaOH concentration against the standard, then orders make-up chemical.

Finishing/padder or size mix: operator checks the concentration of a pad-bath chemical mix, softener/resin bath, or sizing solution using hydrometer/Baume, refractometer or a solids test, and compares it with the formula spec before and during the run.

Color kitchen / dyebath strength check: operator draws a sample of a dye stock solution or of the exhausting dyebath and checks dye strength/shade against a standard with a spectrophotometer, comparator or visual standard, to confirm the solution matches the recipe.

Process water and rinse water: operator or utility tender tests softened supply water or rinse water for hardness, residual chlorine, alkalinity or conductivity against mill standards at the water-treatment area, and reports deviations.

sources.system: Metrohm Process Analytics 2035 / 2060 TI Process Analyzer (textile dye bath application)
sources.title: Online analysis of indigo, hydrosulfite, and other parameters in textile dye baths | Metrohm
sources.claim: Commercial online process analyzers (Metrohm 2035 Potentiometric / 2060 TI) monitor textile dye baths, running fully automatic titrations for dye (indigo) and hydrosulfite concentration plus pH, conductivity, redox and temperature from a plumbed plant circulation loop, so deviations are detected without an operator drawing samples.

sources.system: Metrohm 2060 Process Analyzer (H2O2 online monitoring)
sources.title: Online monitoring of hydrogen peroxide during the CMP process | Metrohm
sources.claim: The Metrohm 2060 Process Analyzer performs automated titrimetric determination of hydrogen peroxide concentration (plus pH, conductivity, temperature) in a process bath online, with results every few minutes used for dosing control.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: online peroxide titration of a semiconductor slurry bath. The analyte (H2O2), the wet-chemical titration method and the aqueous process-bath matrix are the same as testing a textile bleach/peroxide saturator liquor against a concentration standard, and the analyzer is plumbed to the process line in the same way.

sources.system: KA Industrial Engineering / Metrohm robotic analyzer (Universal Robot + OMNIS Sample Robot)
sources.developer: KA Industrial Engineering Pte Ltd with Metrohm
sources.title: Lab of the future: Automated robotic analysis of petroleum products | Metrohm
sources.claim: A commercial robotic titration cell (Universal Robots cobot arm plus Metrohm OMNIS Sample Robot) runs the complete wet-chemistry analysis of liquid samples in a QC laboratory - uncapping the vial, homogenizing, pipetting a weighed aliquot into a beaker and titrating to a result - and is designed for unattended operation.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated TAN/TBN titration of petroleum samples. The manipulation (uncapping vials, pipetting an aliquot, titrating to endpoint against a spec) is the same bench procedure a dye-house operator uses to titrate peroxide, caustic or dye liquor samples, at comparable volumes and precision.

Baume/hydrometer or refractometer checks of a pad-bath or size solution are the same measurement on the same kind of aqueous chemical solution, at the same precision, with the sample presented in a rack instead of a beaker.

tasks.label: Thread ends of cloth or twine through specified sections of equipment prior to processing.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Continuous open-width wet-processing/finishing range in a dyehouse (bleach range, washer, continuous dye range, stenter/tenter): operator brings the new roll or plaited batch to the entry, sews or clamps its leading end to the tail of the fabric already threaded through the line, and guides the cloth through entry guide rollers, padder nip and scray so the range draws it through all sections.

Open-width batch equipment (jig dyer, beam dyeing machine, padder/mangle, drying cans, batcher): operator threads the cloth end from the let-off over and under a fixed sequence of guide rollers, through the immersion trough/nip, and fastens it to the take-up roll before starting the run.

Rope-form batch dyeing (jet, soft-flow/overflow, winch beck) of knits: operator sews the fabric ends into a rope/loop, feeds the leading end through the loading port, over the reel or into the transport nozzle, and works in a confined, wet, hot machine opening.

Yarn/twine threading on yarn dyeing and yarn processing equipment (space-dyeing line, soft/package winding for package dyeing, yarn drying and take-up): threading single ends or sheets of yarn through eyelets, tensioners, guides, godets and take-up devices before processing.

Re-threading mid-run after a break, tear, wrap-up or jam: machine is hot and wet, the piece must be re-entered through the affected section quickly to limit off-quality and downtime, often with fabric or yarn ends in awkward, partly enclosed positions.

It is the same physical act as this task — threading yarn/twine ends through specified narrow sections of a machine before processing — with far tighter precision (heald eyes, reed dents) than dye-line guides and eyelets, but only with the warp fixtured in a purpose-built station.

tasks.label: Mount rolls of cloth on machines, using hoists, or place textile goods in machines or pieces of equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Continuous range / finishing machine feed: operator hooks a heavy batch roll of cloth (100-800 kg on an A-frame or shaft) with an overhead hoist, jib crane or lift truck, sets it into the let-off/unwind cradle of a bleach range, jig, padder, washer or tenter, secures the shaft and engages the leading end. Mill floor with aisles, forklifts and other workers; rolls arrive on carts or pallets.

Package (yarn) dyeing: operator slides yarn packages/bobbins onto the spindles of a dye carrier, caps and locks the columns, then lifts the loaded carrier with a hoist or bridge crane and lowers it into the vertical kier, closing the lid. Dyehouse bay with standard carriers, fixed machine positions, wet floors.

Rope dyeing machine loading: operator pulls the fabric rope from a truck/cart or roll through the loading port of a jet, overflow, soft-flow or beck machine, feeds the leading end onto the winch/lifter reel, runs the batch in, then sews the two ends together with a portable sewing machine to form an endless rope. Variable fabric weights and widths, cramped machine front.

Loose goods: operator places garments, hosiery, towels, hanks/skeins or loose stock fiber into rotary drum, paddle, or washer-extractor style machines by hand, by cart tipping, or in bags/slings, weighing out batch loads. Wet-processing floor of a dyehouse or commission finisher.

Beam work: operator mounts a warp or fabric beam (several hundred kg) with a hoist or beam trolley into a beam dyeing kier or onto a beam-loading carriage, aligns the shaft in the bearings and couples it to the flow connection. Dyehouse floor, standard beams and rails.

Laboratory/sample dyeing: operator places small swatches, mini-skeins or sample packages into holders, beakers or mini-autoclaves and sets them into a lab dyeing machine (IR beaker or high-temperature lab unit) for shade matching. Clean, air-conditioned dye lab bench.

tasks.label: Install, level, and align components such as gears, chains, dies, cutters, and needles.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: On the plant floor of a dye house or finishing mill, the operator locks out a jet dyer, washer, padder or continuous range and installs/replaces power-transmission parts on the drive train — gears, pinions, sprockets, pulleys, bushings, couplings on shafts — setting mesh/backlash, keying, and torquing set screws so the drive runs true.

Fitting or replacing chains in situ: a worn drive chain on a dye range or beam winder, or sections of pin/clip chain on a stenter (tenter) frame rail — threading the chain around sprockets and rails, joining links with connecting pins, setting tension and track, and checking run-out while jogging the machine.

Installing and aligning cutting elements on a finishing/inspection line: slitter or selvedge trim knives and counter-knives, rotary shear blades, doctor blades/scrapers on a coating or padding unit — setting blade positions across the width, gap/overlap and squareness to the web before a run.

Changing over applicator tooling: installing and aligning coating dies/knife-over-roll blades, pad-mangle nip inserts, spray-bar nozzle dies or rotary-screen squeegees for a new fabric width or finish, then setting the die to the roll/screen so the applied add-on is even across the width.

Replacing fine piercing elements: bent or broken pins/needles in stenter pin plates and pin bars, or needles in the tacking/sewing head that seams fabric batches together — seating each needle to depth and correct orientation so fabric is gripped or stitched without holes or misses.

Leveling and aligning larger assemblies after a component swap or machine move: guide rolls, expander/scroll bars, squeeze rolls and the machine frame itself — shimming feet, using a machinist level, straightedge and dial indicator (or laser) to bring rolls parallel and square to the fabric path in a hot, lint- and chemical-laden aisle.

tasks.label: Perform machine maintenance, such as cleaning and oiling equipment, and repair or replace worn or defective parts.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine wet cleaning/washdown of a jet, jig, beck or package dyeing machine and its surroundings at the end of a run or shift: hosing, foaming and wiping dye, chemical and lint residue off vessel exteriors, doors, dosing tanks, pipework and floors in the dye house.

Cleaning removable machine components: pulling lint filters, strainer baskets, screens, nozzles, spin packs/spinnerets or rotary print screens out of the machine, removing hardened dye, size, polymer or fiber deposits, and refitting them.

Scheduled lubrication round on dyeing/finishing equipment: greasing bearings and grease fittings on padders, winches and pumps, oiling tenter/stenter chains, rollers and drive chains, checking and topping up gearbox oil and lube reservoirs.

Replacing worn or defective parts with hand tools: pump seals and packing, gaskets, hoses, drive belts, spray nozzles, doctor blades, bearings, tenter clips/pins - diagnose, isolate the machine, disassemble, fit the new part, reassemble and test-run.

In-situ minor repair and troubleshooting during production: chasing a leaking fitting, clearing a fabric wrap or jam, freeing a stuck valve, swapping a failed sensor or solenoid, re-adjusting rollers and tension, then verifying the machine runs to standard.

tasks.label: Inspect products to ensure that the quality standards and specifications are met.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Apparel/home-furnishings cutting room: after a CNC cutter finishes a lay, the operator walks the table and checks the cut pieces against the marker — edge accuracy, notch placement, no fraying or melted edges, no ply shift — laying a hard pattern or template over a top piece, measuring with a tape, and flagging miscut pieces for recut.

Inspecting the material to be cut: incoming rolls and the spread on the table are checked for holes, slubs, stains, shade variation, width and ply alignment; defects are marked or spliced out, rolls are graded/accepted or rejected, and the decision is logged.

Technical-textile / converting operation (nonwovens, automotive fabric, airbag panels, medical textiles, filters): operator tends a slitting or die-cutting line, monitors continuously produced cut goods, pulls samples, checks dimensions and edge quality against spec, and culls defective pieces from the output stream.

First-piece and setup verification: after a setup, knife/blade change or parameter change, the operator cuts a sample, measures critical dimensions with rule or calipers against the spec sheet, checks edge seal/fray and cut-through of all plies, and records results on a QC log.

Audit of finished bundles/kits before they leave the cutting room: pulling bundles off carts, verifying piece counts and ply totals, size labels and bundle tickets, and spot-checking plies from the top, middle and bottom of each stack for shade and miscuts.

Small-shop / job-shop cutting (custom upholstery, sails, awnings, industrial fabric shops, sample rooms): short runs of many different items cut on hand-guided or small CNC cutters, each finished piece checked against a paper pattern or work order for dimensions, nap/grain direction and print or pattern matching.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume apparel / home-textile cutting room: a 20–100 ply spread of woven or knit goods is laid on the cutting table, the CAD marker (nested pattern layout) governs the cut, and a conveyorized CNC cutter with vacuum hold-down cuts the plies; the worker loads the spread onto the feed table, sets ply height/vacuum/blade parameters, watches for blade deflection or fusing, then pulls and bundles cut parts.

Small or mid-size plant / contract cut shop: a paper marker is laid over a spread on a static table, weighted or pinned, and the operator cuts around the printed pattern lines with a handheld electric straight knife or round knife, drilling notches and drill holes, working through heavy, bulky, or slippery material.

Sample room, made-to-measure, or on-demand work: hard oaktag/plastic templates or printed pieces are placed on one to a few plies (often digitally printed, striped, or plaid fabric requiring alignment), chalked around, and cut with shears, a small rotary cutter, or a low-ply cutter; short runs, frequent style changes.

Non-apparel industrial cutting: upholstered furniture, automotive interiors, and technical textiles — leather hides or foam-backed vinyl, carpet, canvas, or composite reinforcement fabric — where patterns must be placed to avoid hide defects and respect nap/grain, cut single or low ply on large tables.

Block and band-knife detail cutting: sub-blocks are separated from the lay, a hard pattern template is clamped to the block, and the operator guides the block by hand through a vertical band knife (or uses a die press) to cut small precise parts such as collars, cuffs, pockets, and welts.

instances.label: Apparel / home-textile cutting room: operator queues a marker on a CNC multi-ply cutter (Gerber Paragon, Lectra Vector, Bullmer, Tukatech), presses start, then watches the cutting head for blade deflection, fusing, ply shift and vacuum loss, pausing to change speed, vacuum, sharpening interval or notch settings before restarting.

Automotive-seating / furniture cutting line: conveyorized cutter handling leather hides or coated fabric. Operator starts the queued job, watches the scanning/nesting and cut, and adjusts buffers, blade parameters and feed when hides carry defects or material behaves differently lot to lot.

Textile / nonwoven mill slitter-rewinder or cut-to-length line: operator threads and starts the machine, then monitors web tension, edge alignment, slit quality, dust and roll build over a long run, adjusting knife positions, tension, speed and blade engagement, and handling splices and roll changes.

Smaller cut-and-sew or industrial-textile shop with semi-automatic equipment (band knife, straight knife, clicker/die press, hot-knife or ultrasonic slitter): operator starts the motor, listens and watches for bunching, scorching or dull blades, and adjusts guides, pressure, temperature or stroke by hand between and during cycles.

Difficult or variable multi-ply runs (plaids and stripes to be matched, high-pile, slippery knits, relaxed/stretchy goods): operator starts the cut but must repeatedly stop, reach into the spread to smooth or re-align shifted plies, re-tape or re-seat the plastic overlay film, and re-register the cut before continuing.

tasks.label: Adjust machine controls, such as heating mechanisms, tensions, or speeds, to produce specified products.

instances.label: Cutting room of an apparel, automotive-interior or furniture plant: operator sets up a job on a conveyorized multi-ply CNC cutter (Lectra Vector, Gerber Paragon, Bullmer, Zund), selecting/adjusting knife speed, cut speed, blade depth and angle, vacuum level and sharpening interval for the specified fabric, then verifying first parts and tweaking.

Spreading/feeding station in the same cutting room: operator adjusts spreader feed speed, unwind tension, overfeed and edge/selvage alignment so plies lay tension-free and square for the specified lay; re-adjusts at each roll change and when fabric weight or stretch changes.

Slitting/rewinding line in a textile mill or nonwovens converter: operator sets and trims unwind/rewind web tension, taper tension, line speed and blade/anvil pressure for the specified roll width and material, adjusting during the run to prevent telescoping, curl or web breaks.

Heat-based cutting/sealing (hot knife, ultrasonic slitter, laser) of synthetics and nonwovens: operator sets and adjusts heating element temperature or ultrasonic amplitude/power, dwell pressure and feed speed so edges seal without scorching or hardening, checking sealed edges during the run.

Troubleshooting or qualifying an unfamiliar material: parts come off fused, frayed, off-size or with poor notches, or a new fabric has no recipe; the operator inspects cut parts, diagnoses the cause and re-tunes several controls (speed, temperature, tension, vacuum, sharpening) through repeated test cuts until parts meet spec.

Legacy or light equipment in a small cut shop: band knife, straight knife, cloth-cutting/rolling machine or die press with mechanical knobs, hand-wheels, air regulators and rheostats; operator adjusts blade speed, feed tension, table height and press pressure/temperature by hand for the specified product.

tasks.label: Inspect machinery to determine whether repairs are needed.

instances.label: Pre-shift condition check of a computerized fabric cutter (e.g., Gerber/Lectra vector cutter) in an apparel cutting room: the operator walks the machine, checks the reciprocating knife edge for nicks and dullness, the sharpener stones, bristle-bed blocks, presser foot, vacuum hoses and seal, drive belts and lubrication, and notes anything needing repair before production starts.

Symptom-triggered inspection during a run: an unusual noise, vibration, burning smell, hot motor or drive fault appears; the operator stops the cutter, inspects belts, bearings, motors, drives and pneumatics at the machine to judge whether a repair is needed, and reports it to maintenance.

Inspection of a die-cutting/clicker press, band-knife or rotary-knife cutter: check blade tension and tracking, blade edge and guides, guards and safety interlocks, hydraulic/pneumatic hoses for leaks, and roller/table wear, deciding whether the machine can run or needs repair.

Scheduled periodic (weekly/monthly) checklist inspection of cutting machines and auxiliaries (vacuum blower, spreader, conveyor): lubrication points, worn parts, cords and hoses, gauge and sensor readings; findings logged on the PM checklist and turned into work orders.

Post-repair or post-blade-change verification: after a knife, belt or part replacement the operator inspects the reassembled machine, makes a test run, examines the cut and machine behavior, and confirms whether further repair is needed.

instances.label: Cut room of an apparel/upholstery/technical-textile plant: the CNC cutter (Gerber/Lectra/Zund) or straight-knife/rotary machine dulls or snaps a blade mid-job; operator powers down, removes the knife guard/clamp with hex keys and small wrenches, pulls the worn or broken blade, seats and aligns a new one, resets depth/offsets and makes a test cut.

Same plant, scheduled or as-needed swap of bolt-on wear consumables on the cutting machine: sharpening stones or abrasive belts, bristle blocks / cutting strips / cutting boards, presser foot, blade guides, drill and notcher bits, hold-down clamps - unbolt or unclip the worn item, fit the new one, tighten to feel, verify operation.

Deeper mechanical replacement on the machine in place: worn drive belt, chain, bearing, bushing, gear, sharpener motor, vacuum seal or conveyor lug - operator opens covers, disassembles with wrenches and screwdrivers (sometimes a puller), removes the worn part, installs the replacement, re-tensions/aligns, reassembles and runs the machine to check.

Unplanned troubleshooting fix during a job: after a jam, crash or fabric wind-up the operator finds a bent guide, cracked bracket, sheared fastener, damaged bristle bed area or loose hardware; must diagnose which part is at fault, decide repair versus replace, and correct it in place, often reaching into a confined area of the machine.

Pneumatic/electrical wear items on the cutter: split vacuum hose or fitting, failed proximity sensor or limit switch, chafed cable in the drag chain, blown lamp or worn connector - operator traces the fault, disconnects and replaces the component with hand tools, re-routes the line and verifies with a test cycle.

Wiping down with rags and cleaning solution: knife blades and guides, sharpening stones, table and bed surfaces, guards and covers, removing lint packed in oil, sizing/adhesive residue and old grease on a band knife, straight knife, rotary slitter or die-cutting press.

Oiling with an oilcan per the machine's lube chart: blade guides and knife bar, chains, guide rails, sharpener carriage and pivot points on band-knife, straight-knife, spreader or die press; applying a few drops at each point and wiping off the excess so oil does not mark fabric.

Weekly/monthly grease-gun PM: locating and wiping grease (zerk) fittings on bearings, drive shafts, cam followers and press rams — often behind guards, under the table or in confined spots — coupling the gun, pumping the specified number of strokes, and cleaning up purged grease.

Cleaning the waste and lint-extraction side of the machine: emptying scrap and dust bins, pulling and blowing out vacuum plenum screens/filter bags on the cutter, clearing choked ducts and hoses of packed fabric fluff.

tasks.label: Adjust cutting techniques to types of fabrics and styles of garments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Multi-ply apparel cutting room: changeover of a CNC multi-ply cutter (e.g., Lectra Vector / Gerber Paragon) between fabric types on the same shift — lightweight lining or slippery woven to heavy denim or fleece. Operator sets/verifies knife speed, blade sharpening frequency, cut depth and vacuum for the ply height, adjusts blade offset and notch/drill settings for the garment style, runs and checks the first cut for fusing, edge quality and part accuracy.

Small-batch, on-demand or sample-room single-/low-ply digital cutting: many short jobs across knits, mesh, fleece, coated and technical fabrics. Operator selects the cutting tool (rotary, oscillating, drag blade), sets oscillation/depth/speed and hold-down for each material, and tunes notch depth and seam-allowance handling to the style before running the marker.

Patterned goods: plaids, stripes, engineered prints and napped fabrics for suits, shirts or dresses. Cutting technique must be adjusted so parts land on the correct motif position, grids match across garment panels, and nap/one-way layout rules for the style are respected; often requires slower speeds and re-registration of the spread.

Specialty materials outside plain apparel goods: leather hides, foam-backed upholstery fabric, heavy canvas, coated or technical textiles for furniture, automotive interiors and industrial products. Technique is adapted to thickness, grain/stretch direction, hide shape and visible defects, with blade type, passes and hold-down changed accordingly.

Hand-guided cutting in a cut room or small shop: straight knife on a spread, band knife for small curved parts, or shears for samples. The worker changes blade type/grit, adjusts knife speed and stroke, uses paper overlay, clamps or weights for slippery chiffon or stretch knits, and varies hand technique for tight curves, corners and notches of a given garment style.

Problem fabrics and conditions: relaxed or distorted stretch knits, off-grain or bowed wovens, and rolls with flaws. The worker compensates on the fly — re-tensioning, shifting the marker, changing cut sequence or speed — and re-cuts rejected parts so the bundle meets the style's tolerances.

tasks.label: Operate machines for test runs to verify adjustments and to obtain product samples.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Cutting room of an apparel, furniture, or automotive-textile plant: after loading a new fabric and marker on a CNC flatbed cutter (Lectra Vector, Gerber Paragon, Bullmer, Zünd), the operator runs a short trial cut on a small spread, lifts the cut pieces off the table, checks them against the pattern for size, notch/drill placement, edge fray, ply fusing and undercut, then adjusts knife speed, sharpen interval, blade offset or vacuum and re-runs until the sample is accepted.

Die-cutting: clicker press, beam press, or rotary die cutter making textile/nonwoven parts (automotive interior trim, filters, gaskets, shoe uppers). Operator mounts the die, runs a test stroke on scrap material, pulls the sample, checks for complete cut-through on all plies and correct dimensions, shims or changes pressure/stroke depth, and repeats until a good first piece is produced.

Slitting/rewinding or cut-to-length line for rolled goods (webbing, elastic, narrow fabric, nonwoven, carpet, tape). Operator positions the knives, threads the web, runs a short test run, cuts a sample lane, measures widths and length with tape/caliper, checks edge quality and roll build, adjusts knife position/depth, overlap and tension, then releases the run.

Laser, ultrasonic, or hot-knife cutting machine on synthetic textiles. Operator runs a test cut on a piece of the production material, retrieves the sample, inspects the sealed edge for discoloration, melt bead, kerf width and complete separation, then adjusts power/speed/frequency or horn pressure and repeats before releasing the job.

Bench/hand-guided cutting: straight knife, band knife, or hand-held hot knife. Operator makes a trial cut on scrap or a single ply to verify blade sharpness, height, and guide setting, produces a sample piece for the supervisor's or customer's approval, and adjusts by feel before cutting the bundle.

tasks.label: Observe woven cloth to detect weaving defects.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Loom patrol in a broadwoven mill: the weaver walks an assigned set of shuttleless (air-jet/rapier/projectile) looms running plain, uniform grey goods (sheeting, denim, base cloth), glancing at the cloth at the fell and on the take-up roll under mill lighting to catch broken picks, mispicks, floats, warp streaks, oil stains and starting marks, and stopping the loom when a fault appears.

Technical / zero-defect woven fabrics (airbag cloth, coating base fabric, composite/carbon-glass fabric, automotive and industrial textiles): operator continuously watches the emerging cloth on the loom because a single missed fault scraps a high-value roll; defects are small and low-contrast, often on reflective or dark material.

Knitting-machine variant (circular knit and warp knit) in the same kind of mill: operator observes the fabric tube or open-width web coming off the machine for needle lines, dropped stitches, holes, oil marks and periodic faults, and stops the machine on detection.

Patterned/yarn-dyed styles on dobby or jacquard looms (upholstery, mattress ticking, plaids, terry, home textiles) with frequent style changeovers: the operator must separate the intended design from a genuine fault (broken pattern, missing repeat, wrong end, distortion) in the running cloth.

Doff / first-piece check: at roll change or after a style start-up the operator pulls out a length of cloth at the loom or runs the roll over a backlit perch table in the mill's inspection area, checks width, sett, selvedge, shade and accumulated defects, marks faults and assigns a grade before the roll moves on.

Narrow-fabric or specialty small-shop weaving (webbing, tapes, labels, sample looms) where many narrow tapes run side by side on one machine, styles change constantly and lot sizes are tiny; the operator eyeballs each tape for weaving faults.

tasks.label: Thread yarn, thread, and fabric through guides, needles, and rollers of machines for weaving, knitting, or other processing.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Weaving mill, warp preparation: for a style change or new beam, draw several thousand warp ends through drop wires, heddle (heald) eyes and reed dents in the correct repeat — or knot the new warp sheet to the old one so the ends pull through the existing harness. Yarn ranges from fine filament to fancy/slub cotton and wool.

Weaving mill, at the loom: thread weft/filling yarn from the supply package through the balloon breaker, pre-tensioner, weft accumulator/feeder drum and into the main nozzle or gripper at start-up, style change or after a break upstream of the feeder; also re-thread the occasional broken warp end through its drop wire, heddle eye and reed dent while the loom is stopped.

Circular knitting mill: at machine set-up, thread 30-100 yarn ends from the creel cones up through eyelets, disc/spring tensioners, stop-motion detectors, wrap them on positive storage feeders and lead them down through guides to the yarn carriers at the needle cylinder; re-thread individual ends after breaks during the run.

Flat-knitting (Stoll/Shima), hosiery and sock machines, narrow-fabric and sample machines: thread yarn through side tensioners, springs, guide tubes and the carriage yarn carriers/needles on small machines that are re-set frequently for short runs, with yarn type, carrier layout and machine differing job to job.

Threading fabric rather than yarn: lead the fabric web from the machine's take-down through spreaders, guide bars, rollers and nips and onto the batching/cloth roll at start-up on knitting and weaving take-ups and on downstream processing/inspection machines, keeping the web square and untwisted.

tasks.label: Remove defects in cloth by cutting and pulling out filling.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Weave room of a broadwoven mill: a shuttleless production loom (air-jet, water-jet or rapier) stops on a filling/weft-feeler fault with a single short, long or mis-inserted pick at the cloth fell. The weaver reverses the loom to pick-finding position, cuts the faulty filling at the selvage and pulls it out of the fabric, then restarts so no filling bar or stop mark remains.

Harder at-loom removals in the same weave room: the pick has broken into pieces inside the shed, repeated mispicks have been beaten up, or several picks must be unwoven after a smash, a warp-break repair, or to clear a start mark. The weaver backs the loom off and picks out multiple filling yarns by hand with a pick needle/tweezers, brushing the cloth fell clean before restart.

Defect found in cloth already taken up — at the loom's cloth roll or on a cloth inspection/mending frame in the cloth room. A coarse, doubled, wrong-colour or floating filling is located in beaten-up fabric under tension; the worker cuts that pick and pulls it out across the full width (often 1.5–3.4 m) with a pick needle without damaging the warp.

Knit fabric: on a circular or flat knitting machine (or at the knit inspection frame) a defective course caused by a broken needle, dropped stitch or bad yarn must be removed — the operator cuts the offending yarn course and pulls/unravels it out of the loop structure before re-knitting or re-running.

Specialty/technical weaving: terry towel, heavy denim, jacquard upholstery, or flat-yarn/tape technical fabric (e.g., airbag, tarpaulin, industrial cloth) where a single faulty pick at the cloth fell must be cut and drawn out of a stiff, wide or delicate fabric without disturbing the pile, selvedge or tape yarns.

instances.label: Modern shuttleless loom (air-jet or rapier) in a US weaving mill: the loom stops with the warp-stop indicator lit; the weaver walks the aisle to the machine, reads the display/indicator zone, opens the shed area, scans the warp sheet for the fallen drop wire and the broken or slack end, and determines the cause (broken end, weak place, entanglement, or a false stop from lint).

Same weave room, filling/weft stop: the loom stops on a weft-feeler signal; the weaver checks the shed, the weft detector, the insertion nozzle or rapier head, the prewinder and supply package, and determines whether the cause was a weft break, short pick, run-out, tangle or detector fault.

Mechanical or electrical fault: broken heddle or harness strap, bent reed dent, temple or take-up problem, dobby/jacquard or drive fault; the weaver/fixer inspects loom internals, hand-turns or inches the machine, removes guards, listens for abnormal noise, and identifies the defective part.

Chronic stopper: a loom stopping repeatedly on the same warp zone or pick; the weaver examines the beam, sizing condition, reed, drop wires and cloth at the fell, cross-references stop counts, and determines the underlying root cause rather than the immediate trip.

Knitting machine (circular, flat or hosiery) stoppage in a knit mill: machine stops on a yarn or fabric-fault detector; the operator examines needles, sinkers, feeders and the fabric tube to determine whether a needle is broken, yarn broke, or lint/oil caused the stop.

Older or specialty equipment: shuttle looms, narrow-fabric/webbing looms, sample and technical-textile looms in small shops with mixed-vintage machines and little instrumentation; the operator diagnoses the stoppage largely by eye, ear and touch.

Start-up / style change on patterned or specialty goods (jacquard, dobby, terry, technical or 3D warp knits, sample lots): first piece is compared against the customer sample or design file for pattern repeat, color placement, draw-in and hand feel before the run is released, with set-up corrections called out.

Shaped knit goods off the machine: socks/hosiery, seamless garments and sweater panels are picked up, turned, stretched over a form or held to the light to check size, toe closure, dropped stitches and holes, with the machine's needles or cams adjusted when a repeating fault appears.

instances.label: Weaving room of a fabric mill: operator is responsible for 20-40 modern shuttleless looms (air-jet/rapier) running apparel, home-furnishing or industrial cloth. Small shop, sample room or development lab: sample looms and older mechanical knitting/weaving machines with limited electronic control; operator starts the machine and continually nurses it by feel, sound and eye, adjusting cams, tensioners and take-up for novel yarns and one-off constructions.

instances.label: Weaving mill: operator running a bank of shuttleless (rapier/air-jet) looms must halt a loom when the woven piece reaches the specified cut length (yards/meters or pick count) for the order, so the piece can be cut off and doffed. Length is tracked by the loom's take-up/electronic length measurement.

Circular knitting mill: operator tending single-jersey/interlock/rib machines must stop the machine when the roll reaches the specified length or weight (revolution/meter counter target) so the roll can be cut and doffed and a new one started.

Flat-knitting, hosiery/sock or seamless knitting department: machine is to produce a specified number of pieces (panels, garments, socks) for an order; operator stops the machine when the set piece count has been knitted.

Warp preparation (direct/sectional warper, beamer, slasher, drawing-in machine): machine must be stopped when the specified warp length (meters/yards) or number of ends has been wound onto the beam for the order.

Small shop, sample room, or legacy equipment: older shuttle power looms, narrow-fabric or specialty machines without integrated order counters; operator watches an add-on counter or marks the fabric and stops the machine by hand at the specified quantity.

tasks.label: Inspect machinery to determine whether repairs are needed.

instances.label: A loom or knitting machine on the operator's assigned set stops or faults mid-run (stop light, weft/warp stop, needle stop, jam). The operator goes to the machine, opens or reaches into the affected mechanism (shed, gripper/rapier, take-up, cylinder, tension assembly), works out whether it is a simple yarn break they can piece up or a mechanical/electrical failure (worn cam, slipping belt, damaged shuttle, misadjusted let-off) that requires a fixer or mechanic, and calls it in. Mill floor: lint, noise, machines packed in rows.

Routine patrol of a set of running looms/knitting machines during the shift: walking the aisles watching, listening, and smelling for signs of trouble — unusual noise or vibration, smoking or hot bearings/motors, oil or air leaks, yarn wraps, misbehaving take-up — and flagging machines that need maintenance attention on the shift log or work-order system.

Scheduled preventive condition checks at the machine: oil/lubricant sight glasses and levels, air pressure gauges and indicator readouts, belt and drive condition, lint/filter buildup, guard and hose condition, panel indicator lamps; recording out-of-spec items for the maintenance department.

Close-up inspection of the knitting or weaving elements with the machine stopped or barred over by hand: examining needles, latches, sinkers and jacks on a knitting cylinder, or reed, heddles, drop wires and harnesses on a loom, for bends, breaks, burrs, or wear, and deciding which elements must be replaced or a mechanic called.

A fabric defect (needle line, streak, stitch drop, weft bar) is found in the cloth at the machine or reported back from inspection; the operator traces the defect to the responsible machine element, inspects that part, and determines whether a repair/replacement is needed before restarting.

instances.label: Knit fabric mill, circular knitting machine: after a pattern, yarn or needle change, the tender starts the machine at reduced speed, knits a short length, stops, inspects the tube on the machine or cuts a swatch, checks stitch length/weight/width and defects (holes, needle lines, elastane faults), tweaks stitch cams and take-down tension and re-runs.

Weaving mill, shuttleless loom (air-jet/rapier/projectile): after a style change, warp change or repair, the weaver inches then runs the loom, weaves a short length, checks pick density, selvedge, start marks and weft/warp faults, cuts a sample of greige cloth for QC or the customer, adjusts and restarts.

Warp knitting mill, tricot/raschel machine: after guide-bar/pattern setup or beam change, run in a few metres, check width, pattern repeat, courses per inch and fabric quality, take a sample to the lab, adjust let-off/take-up and re-run.

Hosiery/seamless mill, computerized circular sock or seamless-garment machine: run one or two trial articles off the machine, measure dimensions and tension, check pattern and toe closure, tweak the program or cam settings and re-run.

Sample/development room of a knitting or weaving plant: run an established sample program on a computerized flat-knit or sample machine to produce a swatch/garment for customer or QC approval, with familiar yarns and a proven construction.

Sample/development room: iterative development trial with novel yarn or a new construction — frequent yarn breaks and re-threading, repeated cam/tension retuning, and acceptance judged subjectively on hand, appearance and drape by a designer or technician.

tasks.label: Set up, or set up and operate textile machines that perform textile processing and manufacturing operations such as winding, twisting, knitting, weaving, bonding, or stretching.

instances.label: Weaving mill warp preparation: a new warp beam is brought to the drawing-in area and several thousand warp ends are drawn through drop wires, heddles and reed (or the new warp is tied/knotted end-for-end to the expiring warp), producing a harness and beam ready to be gaited into a loom.

Gaiting up and running looms: hoisting the prepared beam into the weaving machine, mounting harness frames, drop wires and reed, threading the weft insertion system, setting picks/tension/speed and starting the loom, then patrolling a set of running looms — piecing broken warp ends, clearing weft stops, doffing cloth rolls, cleaning lint.

Circular knitting machine (jersey, fleece, hosiery) setup and operation: loading dozens of yarn cones into the creel, threading each end through tensioners, stop motions and feeders to the needle cylinder or tying to running ends, setting stitch length, take-down and speed, knitting a trial, then tending — repairing yarn breaks, changing broken needles and sinkers, doffing fabric rolls, inspecting fabric.

Warp knitting (tricot/raschel) machine setup and operation: hoisting and mounting warp beams, threading yarn sheets through guide-bar eyelets, loading the pattern, setting runner lengths and take-up, starting the machine, watching for needle and guide damage, doffing batched cloth rolls.

Winding, twisting and beaming machine setup and operation in the yarn preparation room: loading bobbins/cops and creels, threading yarn paths through tensioners and clearers, setting package density and speeds, piecing breaks, doffing full packages, changing over between lots.

Bonding or stretching line setup and operation (nonwoven thermal/needle bonding, laminating, tenter or stretching frame): splicing in a new roll, threading the web through rollers, pins or needle boards, setting temperature, tension and line speed, running and monitoring, and doffing finished rolls.

Weaving mill: loom set-up for a new style — mounting and aligning the reed in the sley, hanging and levelling heald/harness frames, fitting drop-wire rails, temples and selvedge devices, and squaring them to the warp line before the warp is gaited in.

Either mill: changing drive-train components to change fabric specification or timing — fitting change gears, sprockets, pattern wheels and take-up gears, re-fitting and tensioning drive chains or timing belts, and checking mesh/backlash and machine timing.

Either mill: installing and aligning cutting elements — slitting knives on the take-up of a circular knitting machine, weft/selvedge cutters and trimmers on a loom, or dies/blades on trimming attachments — setting blade clearance and height so cut edges meet quality standards.

Either mill: installing/levelling a whole machine or a major assembly during machine installation or overhaul — shimming and adjusting levelling feet on the floor, plumbing the frame, and aligning shafts, take-up rolls or beams with levels and dial/laser alignment tools.

instances.label: Large-diameter circular knitting machine in a knit fabric mill: fabric shows a needle line or dropped stitches, so the operator stops the machine, locates the broken/bent latch needle among hundreds in the cylinder, removes a cam box or the needle-retaining band segment with hand tools, extracts the damaged needle and fragments, inserts a new needle, checks latch action, restarts. Work done in place on an oily, lint-laden machine while adjacent machines run.

Small-diameter hosiery/sock or seamless bodywear knitting machine: fine-gauge cylinder and dial needles, sinkers and jacks replaced with hook tools and tweezers after breakage detected by a needle detector or by a fault in the sock; very small parts, tight access, frequent occurrence, quick turnaround demanded.

Flat V-bed sweater/flat knitting machine: replace broken needles, needle jacks/selectors and sinkers in the needle bed — remove the retaining spring strip or comb with a screwdriver, slide the damaged needle out of its trick, fit the new part, refit the strip, run a test carriage pass.

Weaving loom in a broadwoven mill: replace broken heddles/healds on a harness frame, bent drop wires, damaged reed dents, worn gripper/rapier heads or shuttle parts, temple rings and springs; performed at the loom inside the warp sheet with pliers, screwdrivers and wrenches, followed by re-drawing the affected warp ends and restarting.

General worn/defective component repair on knitting or weaving machines: yarn feeders and guides, tensioners, belts, take-down rollers, cutters, bearings, warp-knitting needle-bar or guide-bar segments, sensors and switches — diagnose, unbolt, swap, re-align and adjust with hand tools in situ; diverse parts, fasteners and access conditions.

instances.label: Routine per-shift/per-doff lint blow-down: operator walks a set of weaving machines or circular knitting machines on the mill floor with a compressed-air hose, blowing fly, lint and dust off machine frames, guards, take-up areas, feeders and accessible working areas while machines run or are briefly stopped.

Wipe-down of machine surfaces with rags and cleaning solution: removing oil/grease/lint sludge from guides, tension devices, drip pans, guards, rails, control panels and cam boxes on a loom or knitting machine standing in its position on the mill floor.

Scheduled lubrication round: filling oil reservoirs, applying oil from an oil can to designated points (needles, sinkers, cams, gears, bearings) and shooting grease into fittings with a grease gun on looms/knitting machines, per the machine's lube chart.

Deep clean at scheduled maintenance or style change: removing guards/covers and some components, blowing and solvent-cleaning packed lint and oil residue from machine interiors, re-lubricating, and reassembling the machine before restart.

Fine cleaning of delicate working elements in place: clearing packed fiber and oil from needle slots and sinker rings, reeds, heddles, drop wires, air-jet relay nozzles and sensor faces, using picks, small brushes, rags and low-pressure air without damaging or misaligning parts.

instances.label: Weaving mill floor: weaver/loom technician sets warp tension, machine speed (rpm/picks per minute) and let-off/take-up parameters on a modern air-jet or rapier loom for a new fabric style, then fine-tunes after the first yards so pick density, cover and hand meet the style specification.

Circular knitting mill: knitter adjusts yarn feed tension at each feeder, stitch/quality cam setting, take-down tension and machine rpm on a large-diameter machine to hit specified fabric weight (GSM), course/wale count and stitch appearance, verifying against a weighed swatch.

Flat-bed or warp knitting: operator sets loop length/stitch density, yarn feed tension and carriage or main-drive speed through the machine controller and pattern program for a specified garment panel or tricot/raschel fabric.

Heat-related settings: operator sets and adjusts heater zone temperatures, dwell time/line speed and yarn or fabric tension on heat-setting, thermal fixation or draw-texturing equipment (stenter/fixation line, texturizing heaters, hosiery heat-set) to meet shrinkage, dimensional and hand specifications.

Older, mechanically adjusted equipment in small or specialty operations (narrow-fabric looms, sample looms, older knitting frames): hand-set spring tensioners, dead weights, change gears and manual heater dials, judged by feel and visual inspection of the cloth.

Running correction: operator sees a defect in fabric coming off a running machine (barre, tight/slack ends, weight drift, distortion), diagnoses the cause and tweaks tension, speed or heat on the fly to bring output back within specification.

Automatic cone winder (e.g., Autoconer/Muratec/Savio) in a spinning mill: at cop change, yarn break or clearer cut, the yarn end must be taken from the cop and from the package and re-threaded through balloon breaker, tension device, clearer head, splicer and guides so winding resumes with a correct thread path.

Two-for-one twister, cabler or thread-twisting frame: at lot start-up or after a break, thread yarn from the feed package down through the hollow spindle, out of the yarn storage disc, around the balloon guide and through delivery rollers and traverse guide to the take-up package; repeated across many spindles at start-up.

Draw frame, comber or slubber/roving frame in the spinning-preparation room: at can change, lap change or sliver break, thread the fragile sliver/lap from the can or lap roll through creel guide rollers, guide bars, trumpet/condenser and drafting rollers and piece it to the running end without disturbing draft.

Synthetic filament take-up winder or draw-texturing position in a man-made fiber plant: at start-up or after a break, string up the running filament bundle with a suction/aspirator gun through godets, guides and traverse into the winder chuck, at speed and with hot components nearby.

tasks.label: Inspect machinery to determine whether repairs are needed.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine in-shift condition round on a bank of running winders, twisters or drawing frames in a modern mill: walking the aisles listening for abnormal noise or vibration, watching for smoke, oil or compressed-air leaks, hot motors/gearboxes/bearings, loose guards; flagging findings to the fixer/maintenance.

Close-in check of yarn-path hardware at individual positions (tension discs, ceramic guides and eyelets, traverse cams, splicers, drafting cots and aprons) for grooving, glazing, nicks or lint-caused damage, deciding whether a part must be replaced or repaired.

Scheduled stopped-machine mechanical inspection with covers or guards off: drive belts and spindle tapes, gears, bearings checked for play and wear, lubrication levels and oilers, pneumatic hoses and fittings; deciding what needs a repair order.

Diagnostic inspection after a stop, alarm or repeated ends-down/defect at one unit: examining the unit to decide whether it is an operator-clearable condition (lint, tangled end, jam, mis-threaded yarn) or a mechanical/electrical fault requiring a fixer.

Routine condition round in an older or small mill: legacy machines of mixed vintage, heavy lint and dust, cramped aisles, dim lighting, non-standard guarding; checking running machines for signs of impending failure.

instances.label: Modern spinning mill, automatic cone/package winder (e.g. Autoconer, Murata, Savio) with 60-100+ winding units: each package must contain a specified yarn length or reach a specified size; the operator watches the unit displays, ensures units stop at the set length, and stops the machine at the end of ... run/lot. Lint, noise, continuous shift operation.

Drawing frame / breaker draw frame in a spinning mill: sliver is coiled into cans to a specified sliver length; delivery must be halted when the can is full and when the scheduled quantity of cans for the lot has been produced, then the frame is stopped for can removal or lot change.

Roving frame / slubber: bobbins are built to a preset roving length; the frame must be stopped at full-bobbin doff and again when the specified number of bobbin sets for the order has been made, before doffing and restart.

Twisting frames (two-for-one twisters, ring twisters, cabling machines) for carpet, industrial or sewing-thread yarn, often older equipment: run to a specified yardage per package or a specified number of packages, then stop the frame and doff. Machine-side counters, manual start/stop controls.

Small or specialty operation (technical yarn, cord, tape, sample or short-run winding) on machines without integrated automation: the operator monitors a yardage counter or weighs output and stops the machine when the specified amount is produced; frequent short runs and product changeovers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: BCF/carpet-yarn twisting and cabling department (e.g., Dalton-area carpet yarn plant): tender keeps a row of two-for-one twisting/cabling machines running — lifts 5-15 kg supply packages onto creel and pot positions, joins tails so feed is continuous, watches for stopped positions, removes finished twist packages from the machine conveyor onto carts, and feeds the heatset creel. Staple-yarn two-for-one twister bank in a spun-yarn or sewing-thread mill: tender patrols aisles of 200+ spindle TFOs plying cotton/poly yarn, spots frequently occurring ends down, re-threads the yarn through the hollow spindle and pieces up, swaps empty feed cheeses, doffs full cones onto trucks, blows lint off the frames and logs production.

Tire cord / industrial filament direct cabling machines: tender creels heavy supply packages, monitors cord regulator and quality readouts, performs block doffs of large twist packages using lifters/rail systems, moves packages to heatsetting, and pulls samples for length/twist checks. Institution-controlled plant floor, standard equipment.

Ring twisting / doubling frames (wool, specialty, cord, technical yarns): tender walks both sides of the frame, finds broken ends at ring-and-traveler positions, searches the end on the bobbin, threads the traveler and pieces up, doffs full bobbins at end of run, cleans lint and roller waste.

Small mill or job-shop twisting of specialty/technical product (glass fiber twisting, novelty yarns, cords/ropes) on older machines: frequent short lots, hand creeling of odd-sized packages, hand knotting/splicing of breaks, manual doffing into boxes, twist-per-inch sample checks between lots, machine set-up changes between products.

tasks.label: Observe operations to detect defects, malfunctions, or supply shortages.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Tending a bank of automatic package winders (cone winding) in a yarn mill: walking the aisle each hour watching for yarn breaks, slubs/foreign matter passing the clearer, spindles stopped or cycling repeatedly, bad splices, cobwebbed or soft packages, and cops running out in the feed - noisy, linty, fixed-layout production floor.

Monitoring two-for-one twisters, cabling machines or texturing/filament winders: watching for broken ends, wraps on rollers, spindles not turning, tension faults, and supply packages in the creel nearly exhausted, over a long multi-position machine.

Monitoring drawing frames and slubbers/roving frames: checking sliver quality and evenness, laps building on the drafting rollers, sliver breaks in the creel, choked trumpets, and can/roving-bobbin supply levels running low or cans full.

General shift rounds across the department: reading gauges, HMI screens and alarm lights, listening for abnormal noise or vibration, smelling hot bearings or burning, spotting oil leaks, lint build-up and safety issues, and confirming raw-material supply staged for the machines is adequate.

Close-in check of the output and material: pulling a cone or bobbin off the doffing area, eyeballing package build, ribbon, stitching, colour/lustre and stains, feeling the yarn, and comparing it against the standard while the machine keeps running.

Watching a machine closely during startup after a changeover or on an unfamiliar specialty lot (novel fiber, small run, new count/twist): judging whether the process is running correctly before it is released to run, with no established sensor thresholds or defect history.

tasks.label: Operate machines for test runs to verify adjustments and to obtain product samples.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Modern automatic package winder (Autoconer/Savio/Murata link system) in a yarn or thread mill: after a lot change or adjustment of winding tension, splicer, clearer limits or package format, the tender runs winding units as a test, watches splices and package build, and pulls a sample cone for count/tensile/density checks before releasing the lot.

Twisting frame (two-for-one twister, ring twister, cabler) making sewing thread, carpet or industrial yarn: after changing twist gears/spindle speed/feed ratio, the operator runs a group of spindles for a few minutes, doffs a sample bobbin from the aisle, and checks twist per inch and count on a bench tester, then re-adjusts.

Drawing frame / sliver line (breaker and finisher drawing, autoleveller frames) in a spinning mill: after changing draft, break draft or leveller settings, the operator runs the frame, watches the sliver at the coiler, takes a measured length of sliver, weighs it for hank/count and checks evenness before letting the frame run out cans.

Man-made filament winding/drawing position (POY/FDY winder, draw-twister or draw-texturing machine) in a synthetic fiber plant: after string-up and adjustment of draw ratio, heater or take-up settings, the operator runs the position, then takes a sample package for denier, tenacity and dye-uniformity testing in the plant lab.

Older or specialty operation (small industrial-yarn, carpet, glass or specialty coning plant) with legacy winders, twisters or drawing frames lacking integrated quality electronics: the operator threads up by hand, runs the machine briefly, feels package hardness and yarn hand, pulls off a sample skein or short length, weighs it on a shop scale, and adjusts tension weights, gears or guides.

tasks.label: Observe bobbins as they are winding and cut threads to remove loaded bobbins, using knives.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Staple-yarn spinning mill, winding department: operator patrols rows of automatic/semi-automatic cone winders, watches packages build, and when a package is full or faulty cuts the yarn with a hand knife, lifts the full cone off the cradle, sets an empty tube, and restarts the unit. Lint-heavy, noisy, fixed layout, work presented at fixed winding-head positions.

Older manual/semi-automatic winders, quillers and ring or two-for-one twisters in a staple, carpet-yarn or thread plant: operator walks the machine, judges package fullness by eye, severs the thread with a knife, doffs the loaded bobbin into a truck, and dons an empty tube by hand; frequent yarn breaks and stop-and-go tending.

Roving frame / slubber and similar bobbin-building machines: operator watches roving bobbins fill, breaks or cuts the strand at doff time, removes the full bobbins and places empty tubes, then restarts; heavy, standardized bobbins in a fixed rail arrangement inside the mill.

Filament / technical-yarn plant (nylon, polyester, industrial thread, glass or carbon fiber): operator monitors take-up winders, cuts the filament with a knife at package changeover, removes the loaded bobbin, sets an empty tube and moves packages to buffer or packing. Plant floor with people, carts and vehicles moving between winder rows.

Small specialty or sample operation (novelty yarn, elastic, narrow tape, custom lots): non-standard packages and tubes, frequent lot changes, mixed and sometimes aging equipment; operator watches each bobbin, cuts the thread with a knife, doffs, ties or tucks the end, and labels the package.

tasks.label: Unwind lengths of yarn, thread, or twine from spools and wind onto bobbins.

instances.label: Spinning mill winding department: tending an automatic cone/package winder that unwinds ring-spun cops or supply spools and rewinds the yarn onto cones/bobbins; the tender keeps the feed supplied, watches for blockages and yarn faults, and checks package build. Doffing and creeling: pulling full bobbins/cones off winding or twisting positions, placing empty tubes, and loading fresh supply spools into magazines/creels, moving them by truck between machines on the mill floor.

Piecing up: finding the broken yarn end on the supply spool and on the package, threading it through tension device, yarn clearer and guides, splicing or knotting, and restarting the winding position.

Lot/job change and setup: changing to a different yarn count or package format, fitting the right tubes, setting tension, traverse and package density, threading the first ends and running test packages until output meets the quality standard.

Specialty/finish winding in a thread or filament plant (sewing thread, dye packages, assembly winding, twine): smaller lots, precision packages and length measurement, machine tended in a fixed factory bay.

Small shop or sample room: winding thread/twine onto assorted sewing bobbins, quills or odd cores on a bench winder, spools hand-placed and thread hand-threaded, mixed job types with no standard package.

tasks.label: Adjust machine settings such as speed or tension to produce products that meet specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Yarn mill winding department, automatic cone winder (60-72 heads) running a lot: operator sees package density, yarn-tension readings or clearer-cut data drifting off spec and changes the yarn-tension setpoint and winding speed so packages meet density/quality specification. Machine running, lint and noise, fixed aisle layout.

Count/lot change on an automatic winder: for a new yarn count and customer spec the operator sets winding speed, yarn-tension setpoint and package build parameters at the machine's central control terminal, then checks the first packages and trims the values.

Spinning preparation: drawing frame or slubber/roving frame. After a sliver/roving count check or a raw-material change, the operator adjusts total and break draft, autoleveller/draft settings, delivery speed and tension draft so hank and evenness (CV%, A%) return to specification.

Twisting department (two-for-one twister, ring twister or cabler for carpet, thread and industrial yarn): operator sets spindle speed and twist level and adjusts take-up and yarn-brake tension, frequently by hand at individual spindles (ball brakes, tension weights, balloon controls), after twist and package checks.

Warp preparation / creel or multi-position winding: setting and correcting yarn tension across hundreds of creel positions together with machine speed, so the beam or package builds uniformly from first to last meter.

Older, mechanically adjusted winders, twisters or frames: operator changes gears/pinions, resets roller gauges with feeler gauges and spanners, repositions guides and adds/removes tension weights, choosing the change by feel and experience after finding off-spec product.

Twisting department (two-for-one twisters, ply twisters, cabling machines): removing full take-up packages from the cradle/take-up spindles and placing empty tubes on a running twisting frame, package by package as positions fill.

Specialty/older twisting and spooling plants: stripping spent supply bobbins, pot bobbins and residual yarn off spindles and reloading; mixed package shapes and sizes, short lots, machines of several vintages, no uniform presentation.

Maintenance/changeover work: pulling spindle assemblies (spindle, bolster, wharve, adaptor) out of the spindle rail with hand tools for cleaning, oiling, repair or replacement, or removing spindle inserts when changing tube size; machine stopped, awkward reach under the rail.

tasks.label: Install, level, and align machine components such as gears, chains, guides, dies, cutters, or needles to set up machinery for operation.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Winder/twister yarn-path hardware: on a winding, coning or two-for-one twisting frame standing on the mill floor, the tender removes worn ceramic yarn guides, eyelets, tensioner discs, balloon guides and traverse guides/cam followers, bolts or clips replacements into brackets, and aligns each to the spindle/package center by eye or gauge before running a test package. Lint-laden air, machine in a row of identical frames, cramped work between spindles.

Drawing frame / slubber drafting zone: press new rubber cots onto top-roller arbors, fit aprons and cradles, install trumpets/condensers and the coiler tube, then set and lock roller gauge spacings with gauge blocks/feeler gauges and check roller parallelism, before a test sliver run for evenness.

Drive train gearing: swap change gears/sprockets on shafts of a drawing frame, roving/slubber or twister to alter draft or twist ratio - remove retaining collar or circlip, slide the gear off, install the specified gear, check mesh/backlash and re-lock.

Drive train chains and belts: fit a replacement roller chain around sprockets (breaking/joining with a master link) or slip a new toothed/flat belt over pulleys, then set tension and tracking with a tensioner or by shifting a jackshaft.

Cutting and pinning elements: install and align cutter blades of yarn clearers/cutters, tow or staple cutter knives, or pins/needles in gill-box faller bars and needle boards - pressing many small pins into a board or bar to a set depth and pattern, or setting a knife to a fixed clearance.

Machine installation or major realignment: after moving or rebuilding a frame, level the multi-meter-long machine bed with a precision level using shims and jack screws, align head-end to tail-end and creel to machine over the full length, anchor to the floor, and align drive motor/coupling.

tasks.label: Place bobbins on spindles and insert spindles into bobbin-winding machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Staple-yarn spinning/winding mill: on the automatic package winder and the linked ring frames, the tender keeps empty tubes going onto spindles/cradles and keeps supply cops (bobbins) fed into the winding positions during a continuous run. Uniform plastic tubes and one yarn lot, standard machine rows, aisles kept clear by the mill.

Man-made filament plant (POY/FDY spinning take-up winders, DTY texturing machines): operator places empty paper/plastic tubes onto the winder chucks/spindles at each position and doffs the full packages in the winding aisle, on a fixed cycle, with one tube type per machine.

Twisting/cabling mill (industrial yarn, tire cord, sewing thread): operator brings supply packages from the yarn store on a trolley and loads them onto the creel pegs and pot/spindle positions of two-for-one twisters or cabling machines, several dozen positions per machine, packages of 2-8 kg.

Small or specialty operation (narrow fabric, technical/sample yarn, older rewinders): assorted tube and bobbin types of different lengths and materials are taken from bins, cartons or a scrap pile, inspected for damage and residual yarn, and pressed onto the spindles of hand-fed winders in tight, cluttered aisles, with several lot changes per shift.

Setup/changeover work: pulling removable spindles, skewers or mandrels out of the winding heads, slipping the correct bobbins/cores onto them, and reinserting and seating the loaded spindles into the machine's bearings or drive, checking alignment and free rotation before the run starts.
