tasks.label: Repair or replace worn or defective parts or components, using hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: On the mill floor, replacing small consumable wear parts at winder/twister positions during a shift: yarn guides and ceramic eyelets, tension discs and springs, splicer cutting blades and opening tubes, brushes, suction-nozzle tips. One or two fasteners or a clip; small parts; done at the stopped position with screwdriver, pliers, hex keys; part is standard stock.

Replacing worn rubber cots and aprons on drawing-frame / roving-frame top rollers: lifting the weighting arm, pulling the top rollers, pressing off the worn cots and pressing on new ones (often in the mill's roller shop with a mounting/demounting press and cot grinder), then refitting the rollers and re-setting the arm.

Replacing worn drive components: spindle tapes, timing and V-belts, idler pulleys, small bearings, gears and sprockets. Requires removing guards, routing a flexible belt or tape around pulleys/whorls, pulling and pressing bearings, re-tensioning and aligning, all with hand tools in confined, lint- and oil-covered machine interiors.

Troubleshooting an alarm or defect and replacing an electrical/pneumatic component: photocell or yarn-break sensor, solenoid valve, air line or fitting, limit switch, connector or damaged wiring. Involves locating the fault, isolating power/air, disconnecting and reconnecting leads, and verifying the machine runs correctly afterward.

Larger or structural repairs, often alongside a fixer under lockout/tagout: damaged creel rails and can guides, coiler tubes, traverse or doffer mechanisms, gearbox or drive-shaft components, guards and covers. Heavier parts, multiple fasteners, shimming and alignment before the machine is released to production.

Improvised or restorative fixes to keep the frame running: straightening a bent guide or wire, re-tapping a stripped thread, filing a burr off a worn surface, fabricating a shim or temporary bracket, refurbishing a part rather than replacing it because no spare is on hand.

tasks.label: Measure bobbins periodically, using gauges, and turn screws to adjust tension if bobbins are not of specified size.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Automatic/semi-automatic cone winding room in a spun-yarn mill: operator walks the machine, periodically checks wound packages with a diameter gauge/hardness tester against the lot spec, and turns the tension screw on the gate/disc tensioner at heads producing soft or oversized packages.

Twisting department (ring twister, two-for-one twister, cabler for carpet/industrial/sewing yarn): operator gauges take-up bobbin/package diameter and build periodically during a run and adjusts tension nuts/screws on the tension device or balloon setting when packages are off-size.

Roving frame (slubber)/drawing area: operator checks roving bobbin build and diameter with a gauge during the build cycle and adjusts roving tension/builder screws so bobbins doff at the specified size for the ring frame creel.

Older or specialty equipment in small plants and technical-textile operations (pirn/quill winders, sample winders, thread winders): many spindles with mechanical screw tensioners, mixed tube/bobbin types and frequent lot changes; operator uses calipers or go/no-go gauges across positions and turns individual tension screws.

Synthetic filament take-up winding or warping/beaming creel: operator gauges package diameter/traverse on precision winders or creel packages during a run and turns tension adjusting screws on the tension devices to bring packages back to specified size.

tasks.label: Clean, oil, and lubricate machines, using air hoses, cleaning solutions, rags, oilcans, and grease guns.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine shift blow-down: operator walks the line of winders, two-for-one twisters and drawing frames in the mill's production hall with a compressed-air hose, blowing lint and fly off machine exteriors, creels, headstocks, drives and guards while machines run or are briefly stopped; fly is swept/collected afterward.

Detail cleaning of the working zone: wiping winding drums, traverse guides, tension units, splicers, yarn clearers/sensors, drafting rollers, cots and aprons with rags and cleaning solution; picking off wound-on fiber laps and yarn wraps; opening covers and reaching into tight interiors between running positions.
Clearing fiber waste from the floor and aisles around the machine frames and hauling it to the waste bin, on a mill floor with pallets, cans, trucks and people moving through.
Emptying the machine's pneumafil/suction waste boxes and clearing clogged filter screens, hoods and suction ducts on the machine itself, then re-seating them.

Scheduled lubrication round: grease gun at bearing zerks on roller stands and drives, oil can on chains, guides and spindle bolsters, checking and topping up gearbox oil levels, wiping excess grease; machine stopped and guards opened for access.

Periodic deep clean at changeover or scheduled shutdown: removing guards and components, vacuuming and solvent-cleaning inside the frame, cleaning under and behind machines, washing removed parts, cleaning hoods and ducts.

roles.description: Set up, operate, or tend machines that extrude and form continuous filaments from synthetic materials, such as liquid polymer, rayon, and fiberglass.

tasks.label: Set up, operate, or tend machines that extrude and form filaments from synthetic materials such as rayon, fiberglass, or liquid polymers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Tending a running synthetic-filament melt-spinning line (polyester/nylon POY-FDY, PP BCF carpet yarn, spandex): patrolling the spinning and take-up levels, watching threadlines and gauges/HMI, adjusting temperatures, pump speeds, quench and finish-oil settings, responding to alarms, checking package build and yarn quality, pulling QC samples, clearing waste, logging data. Indoor plant floor, hot, standard machine layout controlled by the employer.

Doffing full yarn packages/bobbins from take-up winders on a filament spinning line and re-tubing: transferring the running yarn to empty tubes, removing full packages, loading them to carts/conveyors, labeling and moving them to interim storage or the next process. Repetitive, on a fixed doff cycle, at fixed positions along the machine.

String-up / re-threading after an end break, a doff failure, or a position start-up: aspirating the extruded filament bundle with a suction gun at the spin pack, drawing it down through quench and finish applicator, laying it over godets and through interlace jets, and transferring it onto the winder chuck at speed. Time-critical, done at the running machine.

Spinneret / spin-pack face care during production: wiping the spinneret face on a defined cleaning schedule, applying silicone release spray, removing drips and monomer build-up to prevent yarn breaks. Hot, overhead work along the spinning beam at each spinning position.

Set-up and product changeover: pulling and installing hot spin packs/spinnerets and metering pumps, changing extruder screens/dies, fitting new guides and tubes, entering the new product recipe, starting the extruder and line up to first good yarn. Heavy, hot, tool-intensive, non-routine work.

Tending a continuous glass-filament forming position: watching the bushing and filament cone, adjusting bushing temperature and sizing applicator, clearing flooded tips and gathering/restarting filaments with an air lance and water spray after a break-out, threading the strand through the gathering shoe to the winder, and doffing forming packages. Very hot radiant environment below a molten-glass bushing.

tasks.label: Press buttons to stop machines when processes are complete or when malfunctions are detected.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Synthetic-filament melt-spinning/extrusion line, planned stop: the batch, package set, or production run is complete (or a polymer/product changeover or scheduled maintenance shutdown is due). The tender brings extruder, metering pumps, godets, quench and take-up winders down in the correct sequence using stop buttons/HMI on the plant floor.

Running line, instrumented fault: a yarn/filament break, high head pressure, high melt or barrel temperature, drive fault, or level alarm annunciates on the panel or stack light. The tender presses stop on the affected winding position or the whole line quickly to limit waste, wraps, and equipment damage.

Safety-driven emergency stop in the production hall: a person enters the hazard zone of a running machine, material jams or wraps, or a hot-polymer/molten-glass hazard develops; the tender hits the E-stop button or pull-cord on the machine immediately.

Off-normal condition recognized by the operator's own senses and judgment rather than by an installed sensor - burning polymer smell, unusual bearing/drive noise, visible drips, laps or wraps on godets, off-colour or fluffing filament - the tender judges it a malfunction and presses stop.

Continuous-filament glass fiber forming room (hot, humid, glass shards): a break-out or glass flood occurs at the bushing, or a forming cake/package reaches full size; the tender stops the winder/forming position and initiates shutdown of that position.

instances.label: Startup/activation of a synthetic filament spinning line (polyester/nylon POY or FDY) in a fiber plant: at the line console/HMI the operator calls up the product recipe, energizes extruder barrel and spin-beam heats, waits for soak, starts the screw, metering pumps, quench air, godets and winders in sequence while watching melt pressure and temperatures, jogging drives as needed.

In-run adjustment to hold product to spec: operator moves controls (HMI setpoints, potentiometers, drive speed dials) to trim metering-pump/godet/winder speeds, quench air, barrel and spin-pack temperatures in response to denier/tension/break data and lab test results, on a spinning or extrusion line running continuously.

Fiberglass filament forming: at the forming-position control panel the operator activates and adjusts bushing power/temperature, winder speed, water spray and binder/sizing applicator flow to keep filament diameter and strand quality on target; hot, high-noise forming floor beneath the bushings.

Older or partly manual equipment (rayon/monofilament/small fiberglass or legacy melt lines): operator turns hand valves, rheostats, levers, and hardwired pushbutton stations mounted on the machine to start pumps, set flow and speed, and inch equipment, judging by eye and feel at the machine rather than from a central screen.

Abnormal-event response: on a filament break, wrap, plug, drip or spill, the operator hits local stop/E-stop or slows the line at the nearest control station, isolates the affected position, then re-activates and ramps the position back up after the problem is cleared.

Specialty, pilot or small-lot production (meltblown, monofilament, technical fibers, R&D pilot line): frequent product changeovers where the operator locally activates the machine and adjusts settings largely by observing the extrudate, with short runs and non-standard setups.

instances.label: Melt-spinning line (POY/FDY filament, staple, or spunbond): on a scheduled cycle the operator wipes/scrapes the hot spinneret (spin pack) faces at the spinning beam with a spatula/wipe stick and silicone spray to remove degraded polymer and oligomer, without stopping the position; done from a platform in a hot spinning floor.

Pack shop / cleaning station: spinnerets, spin packs, dies, filter screens, ceramic guides and interlace jets that have been taken off the machine are cleaned to spec (burn-off/pyrolysis, ultrasonic bath, scraping and brushing with hand tools), inspected for plugged holes, and set aside for reuse.

Between doffs or at a changeover: in-place clean-down of the yarn path and machine interior — wiping finish and oligomer off godets, separator and draw rolls with pads and solvent, picking wound fiber wraps off rolls and guides with a hook/knife, clearing fluff and waste polymer from the quench cabinet, aspirator and machine frames, blow-down with an air gun.

Routine preventive-maintenance round with hand tools: greasing bearings and chains, changing filters, seals and worn guides/belts/nozzles, checking and tightening fasteners, adjusting take-up and traverse components, reassembling and signing off a PM checklist on the production floor or at a maintenance bench.

Spin pack / extrusion die changeover: shut the position, break loose and unbolt the hot pack or die with wrenches and a pack cart or hoist, pull it, fit the cleaned replacement, torque to spec, check for leaks, restart and string up the position.

Glass fiber forming floor: clean the bushing face and tips of beads and flooded filaments with hand tools/torch, clean and swap sizing applicator rolls and pans, clear broken glass, fiber scrap and water from the forming hood, winder and surrounding area; radiant heat and glass shards throughout.

tasks.label: Observe flow of finish across finish rollers, and turn valves to adjust flow to specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Continuous-filament melt spinning line (polyester/nylon POY, FDY or BCF carpet yarn): operator walks the spinning deck during steady running, looks at the finish (spin-finish) applicators/kiss rolls at each of dozens of positions to see that finish is flowing evenly across the rolls, and turns supply/trim valves (or resets pump/flow setpoints) to bring finish flow back to the specified rate.

Staple-fiber or tow line: finish emulsion is applied to the running tow through a dip trough and finish rolls or spray bar; operator observes wet-out and film on the rolls, checks trough level, and turns valves on the finish supply header to adjust flow to the recipe specification.

Fiberglass forming room: sizing/binder is fed to a rotating applicator roll directly under the bushing; operator checks that sizing is flowing evenly across the applicator roll (no dry bands, no flooding) in a hot, humid, water-misted forming area and adjusts the sizing supply valve to specification.

Start-up, string-up or product changeover: finish flow is brought up from zero to a new specification; the operator watches roller wet-out and dripping while iteratively trimming valves, sometimes dealing with a dirty roll, air-locked or partially plugged supply line before the flow reads to spec.

Older or specialty line (rayon/solution-spun, aramid, small technical-yarn line) with gravity-fed finish troughs and manual needle/globe valves: operator judges flow by eye at the roll and level in the trough and hand-trims the valve to specification.

tasks.label: Remove polymer deposits from spinnerettes and equipment, using silicone spray, brass chisels, and bronze-wool pads.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Scheduled wiping of spinneret (spin pack) faces on a running POY/FDY filament spinning line: operator works along the spin beam, atomizes silicone oil, scrapes residual and degraded melt off the hot spinneret face with a brass tool, repeated across dozens of positions roughly every 48 hours, without stopping melt flow.

The same face-wiping duty on staple fiber, BCF/carpet yarn, industrial yarn or spunbond/meltblown spin beams: larger rectangular packs or wide dies, hot overhead work, silicone spray plus brass scraper, timed around can change/doffing so the line keeps running.

Off-line deposit removal in the pack/jet cleaning shop: spinnerets, filters, screens and pack components carrying baked-on polymer are de-polymerized (pyrolysis/vacuum calcining), ultrasonically and high-pressure-water cleaned, then hand-finished with brass chisels and bronze-wool pads until holes are clear.

Unplanned, event-driven wipe: after a yarn break, spin-in, or product/color changeover, the operator immediately re-wipes the affected position(s) with silicone and a brass wiper so filaments can be re-strung and the position brought back to quality.

Removing heavy, hardened polymer drips, lumps and 'candles' from the pack face, pack shroud and quench cabinet after a serious malfunction: chiseling and prying off irregular solidified masses with brass chisels, judging when the spinneret face is damaged and the pack must be pulled.

Cleaning polymer deposits and finish buildup off surrounding equipment in place: godets and rolls, yarn guides, quench screens and cabinet interiors, cutters, spin beam undersides and floor grating, using silicone spray, bronze-wool pads and hand scrapers in cramped, hot, cluttered spaces.

tasks.label: Press metering-pump buttons and turn valves to stop flow of polymers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Scheduled end-of-run or product-changeover shutdown at a synthetic filament spinning position: operator on the spin deck presses metering-pump stop buttons on the line's machine panel/HMI and closes the polymer feed valve to the spin beam. Hot melt lines (~280-300 C), catwalk access between positions, fixed equipment layout inside a producer's plant.

Upset/emergency response: spin-pack blowout, melt leak, or heavy filament wrap. Operator must within seconds hit the metering-pump stop/e-stop at the nearest station and close the manual shut-off or diverter valve, sometimes reaching into a cramped, hot, dripping-polymer area while other operators clear the position.

Isolation for spin-pack/spinneret change or maintenance: stop the metering pump, close the block valve on the polymer manifold to that position, crack a purge/drain valve, and confirm flow has stopped before the pack is broken loose. Torque on handwheels/valve stems, verification of no residual melt flow.

Glass-fiber forming line variant: shutting off flow at a forming position - stopping binder/sizing metering pumps at their control buttons and closing supply/recirculation valves, plus shutting the feed to the bushing/forehearth, in a hot, noisy forming room with standard fixed equipment.

Coordinated line shutdown run from a central control room/DCS console: operator stops the metering-pump drives and closes motor-operated polymer valves from the console in sequence, coordinating by radio with field operators who close local manual valves.

sources.claim: Commercial collaborative-robot machine-tending cells run unattended cycles in which the robot loads ... workpiece, closes the machine door and physically presses the machine's start button - i.e., a robot arm operating a machine's pushbutton control in a purpose-built cell.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: CNC machine tending. tasks.label: Record operational data on tags, and attach tags to machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine lot/production identification tag on the fiber line: after a doff or product changeover at a spinning position or winder, the operator writes lot/merge number, product code, date, shift and position number on a card or plastic tag and clips, hooks or ties it to the winder frame, creel or package tray so the running product can be traced. Done many times per shift on a fiber plant floor with standard equipment and controlled access.

Fault / out-of-service tag: the operator finds a position running off-spec or down (broken filaments, plugged spinneret, damaged winder chuck), writes the position number, problem description and time on a defect or 'do not run' tag, and hangs it on that specific machine position for the mechanic; the tag is removed and updated after repair. Location on the machine and wording depend on operator judgment.

Lockout/tagout or danger tag during spinneret change, pack change, cleaning or maintenance: operator writes name, date, machine and reason on a danger/hold tag and attaches it, together with a padlock, to the machine's energy-isolation point (breaker, valve, disconnect); later removes it after the work is complete.

Quality/test or hold tag: operator records test or process values (denier/tex, moisture, tension, break count, temperature) or sample identity on a tag and attaches it at the machine position or on the sample/package holder to identify material under test, on hold, or being trialed.

Digital/print hybrid: operator keys run data into the machine HMI or plant terminal, a station printer produces a barcoded tag or label, and the operator applies it to the machine's position card holder, tray or package at the machine.

tasks.label: Start metering pumps and observe operation of machines and equipment to ensure continuous flow of filaments extruded through spinnerettes and to detect processing defects.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Polyester/nylon melt-spinning line (POY/FDY) start-up after a spin-pack change or scheduled start: operator starts the metering (spin) pumps at the spin deck/panel, watches melt emerge from every spinneret, checks for drips, uneven or missing filaments and early breaks during ramp-up, and confirms all positions are running before the line goes to production. Hot, oily spinning hall built for operator access.

Steady-state tending of a running filament line: patrol rounds of spinning positions, quench cabinets, godets and winders; watch for broken filaments, fluff/wraps and oil-up; check spin-pump pressures, melt temperatures and drive readings on gauges/HMI; respond to break alarms and flag processing defects. Fixed-layout plant floor with other workers present.

Spunbond/meltblown nonwoven extrusion line: start polymer metering pumps at the spin beam, observe the filament curtain and web formation for drips, holes, streaks and shot, and watch pump/extruder pressures to keep continuous throughput through the spinnerette beam.

Fiberglass forming room: start sizing/binder metering pumps, observe filament formation at the bushings and the strand path to the winder, detect break-outs, flooding, fuzz and irregular filament flow in a very hot, high-glare setting.

Solution/wet spinning (viscose rayon, lyocell, aramid, carbon-fiber precursor): start metering pumps feeding spinnerettes in a coagulation bath, observe filament/tow flow through baths, godets and washing stages, detect broken filaments, gelling, spinnerette deposits and bath disturbances.

tasks.label: Remove excess, entangled, or completed filaments from machines, using hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Synthetic filament plant (POY/FDY/BCF/industrial or carbon fiber): operator removes completed filament packages from take-up winder positions when full — breaking/cutting the transfer tail, pulling full bobbins off the chuck or doffing shaft, and loading them onto a truck/peg rack while the line keeps running.

Fiberglass forming room: operator doffs completed cakes/forming packages from revolving two-spindle winders every 20-60 minutes — cuts the strand, removes wire rings/sleeves, pulls the cake off the collet and places it on a support frame/trolley for the drying oven.

Break recovery at a synthetic spinning position: after an end-down, filament laps/wraps build up on hot godets, separator rolls, guides, aspirator and winder chuck; operator stops or slows the position and uses a hook, knife or scissors to cut and pull the fused, entangled fiber mass off, clears the waste bundle, then re-strings.

Glass fiber bushing break-out: filaments break and tips bead/flood; operator works beneath the hot bushing with a hand lance/hook to clear beads and wads of broken glass filament from the tip plate and the fiber path, gathers the filaments and restarts attenuation.

Scheduled spinneret/spin-pack face cleaning in melt spinning: operator reaches into the hot spinning head and uses a brass wiping tool plus silicone oil to scrape residual melt and the excess extruded filaments off the spinneret face so filament formation stays clean.

Housekeeping between cycles: pulling accumulated waste filament, fly and stray strand out of machine guards, traverse zones, waste chutes and under-machine trays with hand tools, rakes or picks, and bagging or feeding it to the waste system.

tasks.label: Wipe finish rollers with cloths and wash finish trays with water when necessary.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Melt-spinning line, scheduled doff/string-up: operator stops or slows a spinning position, reaches into the deck/cabinet and wipes the ceramic finish applicator rollers and adjacent guides with a lint-free cloth to remove finish buildup, oligomer and fly, then restrings yarn. Hot, oily, cramped machine positions repeated down a line of many positions.

Finish tray/trough service: operator lifts the small stainless finish pan out from under the applicator roller, dumps residual finish emulsion, washes it with water (hose or wash sink) and scrubs gummy residue, dries and wipes it, refills with fresh finish and reinstalls it in the position.

Spot cleaning during running production: operator notices a gumming or dripping finish roller, or a wrap/lap, and quickly wipes the roller and immediate guides with a rag while the line runs at speed with yarn threadlines nearby, without breaking ends.

Fiberglass forming room: operator cleans the sizing/binder applicator roller and its pan beneath the bushing during a rebush or size change - wipes the roller with cloth, rinses/washes the pan with water to clear cured sizing, in a hot, humid, wet forming area.

Product/finish changeover or scheduled cleanout: multiple finish trays, applicator rollers and lines are removed from a line, carried to a wash station, washed with water and detergent, wiped, dried and reinstalled, with cleanliness documented to avoid cross-contamination between finish types.

sources.system: Flexo Wash parts washers / anilox cleaners
sources.title: Parts Washing - Label industry | Flexo Wash
sources.claim: Flexo Wash builds fully automatic washing units that clean removable press parts - ink trays, doctor blades and anilox rollers - in an enclosed machine with water-based cleaning liquid, on an unattended wash-and-rinse cycle.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: cleaning liquid-application trays and their applicator rollers. Ink trays and anilox rolls are the same class of object as a fiber finish tray and finish applicator roller - small metal/ceramic pans and fine-surfaced rollers coated in viscous liquid - washed with water-based liquid to a production-quality standard.

sources.claim: Baldwin automatic blanket-cleaning systems press a cleaning cloth and wash fluid against the press cylinder to remove ink and debris automatically, including while the press is running; they are long-established commercial products on offset presses.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated cloth wiping of a rotating roller in place. The machine holds a cloth against a fixed-position cylinder with wash fluid and cleans it during production - the same physical act as an operator wiping a finish roller with a cloth, at a quality accepted for print production.

sources.system: Kadant VeriLite roll cleaner assembly
sources.title: Synthetic Fibers - Kadant DCF
sources.claim: Kadant supplies VeriLite roll cleaner assemblies - blade, holder, beam and optional oscillation - installed on cantilevered draw-stand rolls in synthetic fiber production to keep rolls clean of fiber and residue and to remove operators from manual roll cleaning.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: continuous mechanized cleaning of production rolls inside a synthetic-fiber line, in the same plants and on the same class of rollers the operator otherwise wipes by hand; it shows roller-surface cleaning is achieved by machine when the roll is presented in a fixed, known position.

sources.system: Rosie
sources.title: Use Case: Hatcheries - Poultry Hatchery Sanitation Automation with Rosie | CleanBotix
sources.claim: Rosie is an autonomous mobile cleaning robot with a 6-DOF arm and precision spray that runs rinse-foam-rinse-sanitize routes in food and beverage plants and is in use in a poultry hatchery; sanitation crews still perform the scrubbing of machines after the robot foams.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: washing plant equipment with water in a structured facility. Cited to bound E2: the robot does hose/spray work while the crew 'focuses on scrubbing machines ...', so contact wiping of rollers and scrubbing of trays in situ is not covered.

sources.system: Dodman industrial tray washer
sources.title: Tray Washer Machine - Dodman Ltd
sources.claim: Dodman supplies continuous industrial tray-washing machines that wash and rinse crates, baskets, lids and metal or plastic trays with water as they are conveyed through the machine, at hundreds of trays per hour.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: washing trays with water. Food-plant trays and pans carrying greasy or baked-on residue are comparable to finish trays carrying finish emulsion; the machine delivers a hygiene-inspected clean when trays are conveyed to it.

tasks.label: Lower pans inside cabinets to catch molten filaments until flow of polymer through packs has stopped.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Polyester/nylon POY-FDY melt-spinning line: during a scheduled spin pack change at one spinning position, the operator lowers/slides the steel catch pan into the spinning cabinet beneath the spin pack so that ~290 C molten polymer and filaments drip into it while the pack bleeds down; work done from the spinning deck walkway, standard pans, fixed positions, radiant heat and fumes.

Line or block start-up/restart after pack changes or a melt interruption: pans lowered under several adjacent positions of a cabinet and kept in place until melt flow through the packs stops, then pans of congealed polymer pulled out and hauled to waste; time pressure, several operators working the same deck.

Unplanned event mid-run (blocked, leaking or flooding pack, spinneret bleed-through): operator works a pan into a cramped, partly obstructed cabinet around quench ducts, running filaments and polymer deposits, sometimes with non-standard or hand-held pans in an older plant.

Staple-fiber, BCF or industrial-yarn spinning position with large multi-pack beams: large/heavy trays lowered on rails or brackets under a row of packs at pack change or shutdown, held until flow stops; access from a platform, heavy handling.

Glass-fiber forming (bushing) position: catch/cullet pan placed and lowered under a bushing at start-up or when the bushing floods, catching ~1200 C molten glass and beads until flow is stabilized/stopped; forming room, extreme radiant heat.

sources.system: KUKA KR 1000 titan foundry robots (integrator ROBOTEC Engineering) at Georg Fischer
sources.title: KUKA case study: Casting at Georg Fischer AG
sources.claim: Two KUKA KR 1000 titan six-axis robots autonomously carry a casting ladle of 1400 C molten iron and pour into molds in a production foundry cell, protected by heat-resistant suits; shows deployed robotic handling of metal vessels amid molten material in a purpose-built cell.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic ladle handling/pouring in a foundry. Transfer: the pan task at E1 is positioning a metal vessel accurately beneath a molten-material outlet and holding it until flow stops; the cited system performs the same class of motion with a heavier vessel, at higher temperature, with tighter placement tolerance, in a fenced purpose-built cell.

sources.system: FANUC M-900iA/260L robotic heat-treat load/unload cell (MWES)
sources.title: Automated Heat Treatment Loading & Unloading | MWES Robotics
sources.claim: A FANUC M-900iA/260L cell with custom grippers, modular basket fixtures and vision autonomously loads and unloads metal parts into steel baskets in and out of a heat-treat furnace line at a metal-parts manufacturer.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: fixtured machine tending of a furnace with trays/baskets. Transfer: at E1 the catch pan is presented fixtured and the cabinet is a known machine geometry, so lowering the pan into its guides and later withdrawing it is the same presented-workpiece pick-and-place into hot equipment that this deployed cell performs.

sources.system: WIESHEU TrayMotion with FANUC robot cell (integrator ASA Automation)
sources.title: FANUC Relieves Heat Stress in Bakeries | Case Study
sources.claim: Robots that load and unload trays of goods into and out of hot ovens are commercially deployed in bakeries, with a FANUC robot cell extending the tray handling upstream and downstream of the oven.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated insertion/removal of flat metal trays into a hot enclosure. Transfer: the physical act rated here is inserting and later withdrawing a shallow metal pan in a heated cabinet on fixed guides, the same handling problem at comparable payload and placement tolerance.

sources.system: Oerlikon Barmag spin pack wiping robot
sources.date: 2018 launch; commercial deployments reported 2020-10; staple-fibre version reported 2025-08
sources.title: Wiping robots increase production efficiency in spinning
sources.claim: Oerlikon Barmag's wiping robot runs on a ceiling track along a filament spinning line and autonomously services up to 48 spinning positions, removing residual melt from the spinnerets inside the hot spinning heads; deployed at yarn plants in China and India and later extended to staple-fibre spinning packs.
sources.transferJustification: Closest in-environment system: it performs an operator melt-handling job at the very spinning positions and cabinets in question. It is cited to bound the judgment, not to support E2: it carries only a fixed wiping/spray tool on a rail and never grasps, transports, positions or removes a loose catch pan, so it does not substantiate completion of this task on the plant floor.

tasks.label: Open cabinet doors to cut multifilament threadlines away from guides, using scissors.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Start-up/string-up of a synthetic filament (POY/FDY/nylon/rayon) spinning position: after the threadlines are strung through godets and guides, the operator opens the spinning/take-up cabinet doors and cuts the waste multifilament threadlines away from the guides with scissors, directing the cut ends to the suction gun/waste aspirator. Hot enclosure, running machine, 6-12 ends per position.

Response to a threadline break or off-quality alarm at one position: operator opens the cabinet door, cuts the affected running multifilament threadlines free of the ceramic guides so the polymer flows to the waste aspirator, then prepares to re-string. Time-critical, machine running, other ends must not be disturbed.

Planned interruption — merge/lot changeover, spin-pack change, or shutting a position down: operator opens cabinet doors and cuts all threadlines away from the guides in the cabinet so the position can be taken off line cleanly, waste routed to the aspirator/waste bin.

Cleanup after a wrap/lap-up: filaments have wrapped around godets, rolls and guides inside the cabinet; operator opens the doors and cuts and pulls the tangled mass of multifilament away from guides and roll surfaces with scissors without scoring the rolls, then clears guide slots before re-string.

Glass-fiber forming variant: operator opens forming/winder enclosure doors at a bushing position and cuts continuous glass strands away from gathering shoes and guide eyes with shears, sending the strand to the waste chute; wet sizing spray, hot bushing, splashing water.

sources.system: Oerlikon Barmag wiping robot
sources.title: Wiping robots increase production efficiency in spinning
sources.claim: Oerlikon Barmag's wiping robot works autonomously at individual spinning positions of filament-yarn spinning plants, travelling on a ceiling track; deployed at plants in China and India.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated spin-pack wiping at the same spinning position the operator opens cabinets to reach. It shows machine-mounted robots servicing in-machine work at chemical-fibre spinning positions autonomously, i.e. the purpose-built (E1) form of position-side operator work; it does not itself cut threadlines.

sources.system: Yarn cutting-sucking device on spinning winders (TMT Machinery)
sources.title: EP2495203A2 - Yarn cutting-sucking device and spinning winder
sources.claim: Commercial spinning winders are fitted with a yarn cutting-sucking device ... severs the continuously supplied multifilament threadlines and sucks them to waste whenever the downstream process is interrupted — the machine-integrated equivalent of cutting threadlines free with scissors.
sources.transferJustification: Same operation, same objects: severing a sheet of running multifilament threadlines at the guide plane and diverting them to waste suction, performed by purpose-built machine hardware rather than an operator with scissors.

sources.system: Yarn cutting-sucking device / spinning winder (TMT Machinery)
sources.title: EP2567919B1 - Yarn cutting-sucking device and spinning winder
sources.claim: The yarn cutting-sucking device cuts ... holds them under suction automatically when an abnormality such as yarn severance ....
sources.transferJustification: Directly covers the break-response case: on a break the machine itself cuts the running threadlines free and takes them to waste, which is the accepted output of the operator's scissors cut.

sources.system: WINGS POY 2.0 winder with automatic string-up
sources.title: Barmag Presents The Next Generation Of POY Production – Energy-Efficient And Partial-Automated
sources.claim: Barmag's WINGS POY 2.0 take-up winder introduces an automatic string-up function, shortening string-up and reducing waste and take-up personnel; shown at ITMA Asia + CITME 2025 with pilot-plant interest.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated string-up of POY threadlines onto the winder, which includes taking threadlines from the waste aspirator and placing/releasing them at guides — the mechanised counterpart of the operator's cabinet-side cutting and rerouting of threadlines.

sources.system: ROBOspin piecing robot
sources.title: Automated Piecing Robot ROBOspin
sources.claim: Rieter's ROBOspin, on the market since 2019 and installed in the US, Turkey and India, is a machine-mounted, fully automated piecing robot that autonomously repairs yarn breaks — finding the end, handling the fine yarn and re-threading it — around the clock at ~95% success.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous handling, cutting and threading of fine yarn at guides on a spinning machine built to host the rail-mounted robot. Comparable objects (thin, flexible yarn), comparable precision at guide eyes, and the same class of in-machine intervention.

sources.system: Automatic yarn threading device (robot arm, suction device, cutter)
sources.title: TW201715104A - Automatic yarn threading device
sources.claim: An automatic yarn threading device uses a robot arm to lead multiple yarns onto the take-up guide with a suction device, positioning them so an integrated cutter severs the bundle.
sources.transferJustification: Same objects and precision: a robot arm plus cutter handling a sheet of multifilament yarns at guides inside a spinning take-up machine, i.e. the purpose-built machine form of cutting threadlines away from guides.

roles.title: Fabric and Apparel Patternmakers
roles.description: Draw and construct sets of precision master fabric patterns or layouts. May also mark and cut fabrics and apparel.

tasks.label: Create a master pattern for each size within a range of garment sizes, using charts, drafting instruments, computers, or grading devices.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Apparel brand or manufacturer tech-design/pattern studio: patternmaker takes the approved sample-size master pattern and grades it across the full size range (e.g., XS-3X) in CAD (Gerber AccuMark, Lectra Modaris, Optitex, TUKAcad) by entering grade rules from the size spec chart, checks the nested measurements against the chart, and releases a graded pattern set (DXF/AAMA) to the marker/cutting room and factory.

Digitizing/conversion workflow: an existing hardcopy master pattern is digitized on a digitizing table or pattern scanner, grade rules are applied in CAD to produce every size, and the nested set is plotted so hard patterns can be produced for the sample and cutting rooms.

Independent/freelance patternmaker or small brand working in a home or shared studio: grades the base pattern manually using charts and a grading ruler or the slash-and-spread method, tracing each size onto paper or oaktag and labeling the resulting set.

Costume, uniform, or custom/made-to-measure shop: creates a limited range of sizes from a block using grading charts, drafting instruments, or a grading device, producing per-size patterns for a specific order or production run.

tasks.label: Input specifications into computers to assist with pattern design and pattern cutting.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Draw details on outlined parts to indicate where parts are to be joined, as well as the positions of pleats, pockets, buttonholes, and other features, using computers or drafting instruments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production apparel CAD annotation: in Gerber AccuMark, Lectra Modaris, or Optitex, the patternmaker places notches/match points, drill holes for pocket and dart placement, buttonhole and button positions, pleat lines, and grainlines on the outlined pieces of a new bulk style, then releases the piece set for grading and marker making.

Marking a digitized or draped pattern: after a muslin drape or a hard pattern is digitized/scanned, the patternmaker cleans up and adds the internal detail lines and symbols (seam match notches, pocket placement, closure positions) in CAD before the first sample is plotted.

Hand drafting in a sample room or small studio: using rulers, curves, awl, and pencil, the patternmaker draws notches, pleat fold and roll lines, pocket boxes, and buttonhole placement onto paper or oaktag block pieces for a sample or made-to-measure garment.

Home-sewing/commercial tissue pattern publishing: adding the printed annotation layer -- notches, dots, 'place on fold' and grainline symbols, dart legs, pleat and buttonhole placement lines, piece labels -- to the pattern artwork for print or PDF release to consumers.

Non-apparel technical textiles (upholstery, automotive trim, sails, tents, industrial covers): indicating join/seam match points, welt and fastener positions, and other feature locations on nested layout patterns in CAD for automated cutting.

tasks.label: Make adjustments to patterns after fittings.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Apparel brand/manufacturer fit session: after a fit model try-on and recorded fit comments, the patternmaker revises the pattern in CAD (Gerber AccuMark, Optitex, Lectra Modaris, CLO) — moving points, reshaping armhole/neckline, adjusting dart intake, rise, sleeve pitch, walking seams, updating grade rules — and releases a revised pattern file for the next sample round.

Small design studio / sample room: corrections pinned, chalked or taped onto the fitted muslin or first sample are interpreted by the patternmaker, who marks new seam lines, unpicks/presses the muslin or measures the changes, and transfers the revisions into the pattern (often marking a paper printout, then editing the digital file).

Hand/hardcopy patternmaking in couture, bridal, or theatrical costume shops: the physical paper or oaktag pattern is altered after the fitting by slashing and spreading, taping in wedges or filler paper, redrawing seam lines with rulers and French curves, truing and re-notching, and cutting fresh pattern pieces.

Custom tailoring / made-to-measure: after a basted or try-on fitting on an individual client, the customer's block or personal pattern is adjusted for shoulder slope, balance, blade width, waist suppression and sleeve pitch, recorded either on the paper draft or in MTM/alteration software.

Non-apparel soft-goods patternmaking (upholstery covers, footwear uppers, bags, technical textiles, safety gear): after a prototype is fitted to the frame, last, or wearer, pattern pieces are revised in CAD or on hardcopy templates and re-issued for the next prototype.

tasks.label: Compute dimensions of patterns according to sizes, considering stretching of material.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Mark samples and finished patterns with information, such as garment size, section, style, identification, and sewing instructions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: CAD pattern room at an apparel brand/manufacturer: after drafting or digitizing a style, the patternmaker attaches piece information (style number, piece name/section, size, fabrication, grainline, notes) and plots full-size hardcopy pattern pieces on paper so the printed pieces carry the identifying text for the sample and cutting rooms.

Hard-pattern (oaktag/tagboard) production in a sample/pattern room: finished patterns are traced or cut onto card stock and marked by hand with style, size, piece name/section, grainline, drill/notch identification and short sewing instructions, then hung on the pattern rack.

Sample room: cut sample parts (muslin or self fabric) are marked with chalk, marker, or stick-on labels showing size, section, piece identification and sewing notes before being bundled for the sample sewer.
Production cutting room of a domestic apparel factory: cut plies/bundles coming off the spread are numbered and labeled with style, size, bundle number and piece ID for the sewing floor.

Freelance patternmaker, costume shop, or small custom/made-to-measure operation working in a home studio or client's improvised workspace: paper patterns are hand-marked at a table with size, style, piece identification and ad hoc sewing instructions, one or two styles at a time.

sources.system: Gerber AccuMark 2D / AccuMark plotting (Lectra)

tasks.label: Draw outlines of pattern parts by adapting or copying existing patterns, or by drafting new patterns.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Apparel manufacturer/brand product development room: patternmaker drafts a first pattern for a new style from a sketch, spec sheet and block, working in CAD (Gerber AccuMark, Lectra Modaris, Optitex, CLO) on a workstation; output is a digital pattern file of piece outlines sent to plotter or automated cutter.

Adapting/modifying an existing pattern: patternmaker pulls the stored block or prior season's pattern and alters outlines (new neckline, changed sweep, fit corrections from a sample fitting) to produce a revised set of piece outlines.

Copying/duplicating an existing physical pattern or garment: tracing a hard oaktag pattern or a rub-off of a sample garment onto paper (or digitizing it on a digitizing table/photo capture) to recreate the outlines of each piece.

Manual flat drafting in a small sample room, costume shop, or custom/bespoke workroom: patternmaker draws outlines on paper or oaktag with rulers, French curves and hip curves from body or block measurements.
Drafting pattern outlines for non-apparel sewn goods (upholstery, industrial textiles, footwear/technical soft goods) from engineering drawings or a drape/mock-up, in CAD or on paper.

tasks.label: Test patterns by making and fitting sample garments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Brand/manufacturer sample room: patternmaker cuts the newly drafted pattern in muslin, sews a first-pattern toile of a woven style (blouse, dress, skirt) with darts, facings and a temporary closure, puts it on a standard dress form, smooths and aligns grain/center-front, evaluates balance and drape, pins/slashes and chalks corrections, then trues the paper or CAD pattern.

Fit session on a live fit model in a design studio fit room: the sewn sample is put on the model, the patternmaker looks at fit across bust/waist/hip/armhole, has the model move and sit, pins excess, marks new seam and hem lines, records fit comments, and revises the pattern for the next proto.

Basics/knit and activewear proto: patternmaker or sample sewer makes a simple proto (tee, legging, hoodie, boxer) on production-type machines from the tested pattern, measures it against the spec point-of-measure sheet on the table and on a form, checks stretch fit, and adjusts the pattern.

Complex or structured sample: tailored jacket, coat, bra, or swimwear with linings, interfacings, boning, zippers and set-in sleeves; the patternmaker makes one or more successive samples in fashion fabric, fits on form and model, and works through several rounds of correction before the sample is approved.

Custom/bespoke or theatrical work: a patternmaker in a small dressmaking shop, bridal atelier, or costume shop makes a toile for an individual client or performer, fits it on that person (sometimes at the client's premises, rehearsal room, or a rented space), pins alterations to the individual body, and reworks the pattern.

sources.system: Siemens / Sewbo robotic sewing workcell (ARM Institute project)
sources.developer: Siemens Corporation with Sewbo, Levi's, Bluewater Defense
sources.title: Robotic Automation in Apparel Manufacturing: A Novel Approach to Fabric Handling and Sewing (arXiv 2503.00249)
sources.claim: Siemens/Sewbo/Levi's robotic sewing cell: a UR5 cobot with vacuum gripper, ultrasonic tacking, overhead pose-estimation camera and closed-loop visual servoing sews 2D seams on pre-cut, temporarily stiffened fabric panels inside a purpose-built workcell, producing items such as denim shorts; validated at a defense apparel production line and Levi's research facility.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic assembly-line sewing of garment panels. It covers only the 'making' half of this task — seaming pre-cut panels in a fixtured cell — and involves no dressing of a form, fit evaluation, or marking of pattern corrections.

sources.system: Robotic sewing workcell for denim manufacturing (digital-thread/digital-twin integration)
sources.developer: Siemens Corporation with Sewbo and Levi's
sources.title: A Deployment Case Study in Robotic Apparel Automation: Digital Twin Integration, Interoperability, and Workforce Enablement (arXiv 2606.16078)
sources.claim: Follow-on deployment study of the same robotic sewing workcell: two staged factory deployments on ..., with DXF pattern files parsed into robot trajectories, suction fixtures, and runtime seam monitoring.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: factory sewing operations on denim garments. Shows a robot can execute individual seam/pocket operations from a pattern file in a fixtured cell, but not build a novel one-off sample garment or perform any fitting step.

sources.system: SEWBOT workline
sources.title: The return of the Sewbot!
sources.claim: SoftWear Automation's Sewbot worklines use machine vision to steer fabric through the needle and sew T-shirts autonomously; the company continues to run a Sewbot machine-vision workline at its Atlanta plant, though commercialization has been limited by quality and recalibration challenges with fabric variation.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: high-volume automated sewing of simple knit garments. Demonstrates complete simple garments can be sewn in a purpose-built workline, but each workline is configured for a repeat style, and no fitting or pattern-correction step is performed.

sources.system: Aitu humanoid sewing robot with Ai10 AI sewing machine
sources.title: Taizhou enterprise showcases AI-powered humanoid sewing robot at 2026 WAIC
sources.claim: Aitu's purpose-built humanoid sewing robot moved between workstations and tables and performed material handling, positioning, template alignment ... of shirt/T-shirt components without manual intervention in a WAIC demonstration; the company's robotic sewing solution is reported deployed at garment factories in several countries.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: garment factory sewing-line operations (fabric loading, pocket placement). It works on repeat production styles on a factory floor and does no sample fitting, fit assessment, or pattern correction.

sources.system: Robot-assisted dressing system (Zhang & Demiris)
sources.title: A robot that can put a surgical gown on a supine mannequin
sources.claim: A bimanual robot learned garment manipulation policies to put a hospital gown on a supine mannequin, succeeding about 90% of the time over ... laboratory trials; this is the closest demonstrated capability to placing a garment on a form, and it involves a loose gown, a fixed supine mannequin, and no assessment of garment fit.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-assisted dressing of a mannequin. Transfer fails: dressing a supine mannequin with a loose gown in a lab does not establish smoothing a close-fitting toile on a dress form, judging drape and balance, or pinning corrections.

tasks.label: Position and cut out master or sample patterns, using scissors and knives, or print out copies of patterns, using computers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Apparel company CAD/pattern room: the patternmaker sends a finished or graded digital pattern set from CAD (AccuMark, Optitex, Lectra, Tukatech) to a wide-format plotter, prints full-size copies on roll plotter paper with all internal markings (grainlines, notches, drill points, piece labels), then collects, checks and labels the plot.

Sample/pattern room: the patternmaker positions the plotted or hand-drafted paper sheet on the pattern table and cuts each piece out with shears or a knife, cutting notches into the edges and punching drill holes, producing a working sample pattern for the sewing sample room.

Making a durable master pattern for repeated production use: pieces cut with a knife from heavy oaktag/manila tag board or plastic template stock, with punched hanging holes, notches and drill marks, on a pattern table in the pattern room.

Positioning master/sample pattern pieces on a single ply of sample fabric spread on the cutting table and cutting out the sample garment pieces with shears or a rotary knife — respecting grain, matching plaids/stripes, clipping notches and marking drill points — in an apparel sample room.

Small custom, made-to-measure, or costume/theatrical shop or home-based studio: patterns and sample pieces positioned and cut on a large table or on the floor in a space taken as found, with varied and unusual materials (canvas, leather, interlining, foam) and no standard layout.

sources.system: Zünd single-ply digital cutter (apparel configuration)
sources.title: Apparel | Zünd

sources.system: Zünd Notching Marking Module (NMM)

tasks.label: Create a paper pattern from which to mass-produce a design concept.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Pattern/sample room of an apparel brand or contract manufacturer: patternmaker receives a designer's sketch and tech pack, interprets it, drafts or modifies a company block in CAD (Gerber AccuMark, Lectra Modaris, Optitex), walks seams, adds seam allowances, notches, grainlines and piece labels, then plots the full-size pattern on pattern paper for the sample room.

Hand patternmaking in a design house or sample room: drafting the design concept onto pattern paper or oaktag from a sloper with rulers, French curves, tracing wheel and pencil; truing and walking seams; cutting the pieces out with shears; adding notches, drill holes and piece identification, then hanging the paper set.

Draping-derived pattern: patternmaker realizes an ambiguous design concept by pinning and marking muslin on a dress form, removes and presses the muslin, then transfers the marked shapes to paper, trues the curves and blends seams into a master paper pattern.

Pattern correction after a fit session: patternmaker interprets fit comments on a sewn first sample (on a live fit model or form), re-engineers the pattern (slash-and-spread, re-balance, ease changes), and issues the corrected paper pattern approved for production.

Production hard-copy output: after the digital master pattern is approved, the full-size paper/tag pattern set is generated for the cutting room — plotted on pattern paper with piece names, grainlines, drill marks and size, and the pieces cut out along the outline with notches.

Freelance or home-studio patternmaker working for a small brand: works on a home or shared studio table of whatever size is available, from a client's reference sample garment, photo or verbal concept, and delivers a cut paper pattern set by hand or via a small plotter.

instances.label: Apparel brand or design studio: patternmaker reviews a designer's sketch, tech pack, and reference measurements in a fit/design meeting, then drafts the first pattern in CAD (Gerber AccuMark, Lectra, Optitex, CLO), producing separate front, back, sleeve, collar, facing pieces with grainlines, notches and seam allowances, issued as a DXF/AAMA file for sample cutting.

Sample room or small design house working from a physical concept: designer presents a draped muslin or a garment prototype on a dress form; the patternmaker drapes/refines fabric on the form, marks style lines, removes and trues the pieces onto pattern paper or oaktag to form a master pattern set.

Reverse-engineering ('rub-off') of a designer's original model garment or a bought reference sample: the patternmaker measures and traces the existing garment's components and reconstructs each separate pattern piece to match, checking with the designer on intended fit and ease.

Revision cycle after a fit session: designer marks changes on the sample (raise armhole, reshape neckline, add ease), patternmaker discusses the intent and edits the existing pattern pieces, re-plotting or re-issuing the corrected piece set for the next sample.

Custom / costume / technical work (theatrical costume shop, bridal, uniform or performance apparel): patternmaker discusses a designer's rendering plus client or wearer measurements and drafts bespoke pattern pieces, often on paper, for one-off or short-run garments.

Sample/development room of a brand or small factory: single-size or short-run layout on a napped or one-way fabric for a sample or small batch; patternmaker positions hard pattern pieces on a table with grainlines and nap respected and chalks/traces the outlines, under a same-day deadline.

Layout on a plaid, stripe, engineered print or pile fabric where pieces must be matched to the fabric motif and repeat; marker must be laid with matching points aligned and marked on fabric that may be bowed or skewed.

Leather hides or flawed/variable material (furniture, automotive, footwear, outerwear): pieces must be nested around defects and quality zones on irregularly shaped hides or flagged fabric, then the placement marked on the material.

Custom/bespoke tailoring, costume or alterations workroom: one-off garment on customer-supplied or unique yardage, often folded double on a work table; layout decided by eye and marked with chalk/tracing wheel including allowances and notches.

Independent/freelance patternmaker in a home studio, or a small industrial-textile shop (marine canvas, awnings, drapery, upholstery) marking layouts on wide goods in a garage/loft workspace with no standardized layout or equipment.

Automotive/vehicle trim shop: installing new upholstery on a removed vehicle seat - stretching the sewn cover over foam and the seat frame, securing with hog rings, J-clips and listing wires - plus contact-cementing headliner cloth to a board and covering door panels; work partly at the bench, partly reaching inside the vehicle.

On-site / in-place installation: restaurant booth backs and church pew cushions recovered at the customer's premises, boat cockpit and RV/aircraft interior panels and cushions fitted inside the cabin - material cut to fit as found, glued with contact cement and stapled in awkward, confined positions.

tasks.label: Make, restore, or create custom upholstered furniture, using hand tools and knowledge of fabrics and upholstery methods.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Shop reupholstery of a residential sofa or armchair: strip old cover and tacks, inspect and re-glue/repair the frame, retie or replace coil springs and webbing, replace foam/batting, template and cut new fabric, sew panels with welt cord, then stretch, tack/staple and blind-stitch the cover to the frame and finish.

Shop build of a new custom piece from a bare frame to a designer's or customer's specification (custom sofa, wing chair, upholstered headboard, restaurant banquette): webbing/springs, foam build-up and shaping, pattern making, sewing 3D covers, fitting, stapling and trim.

Traditional restoration of an antique or heirloom piece in the shop: eight-way hand-tied springs, tack-and-twine edge rolls, horsehair/cotton stuffing, hand-sewn stitched edges, deep buttoning/tufting, matched to the original construction and finish.

Custom transportation upholstery in an auto/marine/aviation trim shop: strip seats to foam and frames, pattern from the worn cover, sew covers with piping, French seams or embroidery in vinyl/leather, then pull, hog-ring or staple covers onto seat frames and fit door panels and boat cushions.

Smaller, more repeatable shop jobs: drop-in dining chair seats, ottomans, bench pads, office-chair seat/back pads, replacement cushions — cut foam, cut and (sometimes) sew fabric, staple over a simple board or shell.

On-site custom work at the customer's location: re-covering a restaurant booth, a built-in window seat, an RV dinette or a boat cushion at the dock, or an immovable piece in a private home, working with portable hand tools in a space taken as found.

sources.system: Fanuc M-710iC automated upholstery cell (Dvolu integration)

sources.transferJustification: Closest existing system to this task: it handles upholstery fabric on furniture components. Transfer is limited — it performs a single stretching/stapling operation on standardized, palletized seat linings in a fenced production cell, with no frame repair, spring work, pattern making, sewing or fitting of a custom piece.

tasks.label: Examine furniture frames, upholstery, springs, and webbing to locate defects.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Reupholstery/repair shop: a customer's used sofa or armchair of unknown construction is on trestles; the upholsterer tips it over, pulls the dust cover and some cover fabric, presses and lifts the deck to find sagging or broken coil/sinuous springs and broken spring ties, tugs jute or elastic webbing for rot and slack, racks the frame by hand to find loose dowel/mortise joints, split rails and missing corner blocks, and lists every defect for the repair plan and quote.

On-site at a customer's home or office: the upholsterer inspects a piece in place (often against a wall, on carpet, with pets/clutter around), sits and presses cushions, tilts the piece to look underneath, checks springs, webbing and frame wobble by feel, and identifies defects to quote a reupholstery or repair job.

Automotive/marine/aircraft trim shop: a worn or damaged seat, bench or boat cushion is pulled into the bay or removed to the bench; the trimmer inspects seat covers for tears, seam blowouts and UV wear, checks foam collapse, listing/hog-ring failures, broken seat frame welds, rusted springs and torn diaphragm/webbing straps to determine what must be replaced.

Furniture plant, production upholsterer at a station: examines each incoming hardwood/plywood frame and its components for splits, knots, warp, misaligned or loose joints, protruding or missing staples, and rejects or tags defective frames before padding is applied.

Furniture or vehicle-seat plant: examines cut cover material (fabric/leather), foam and the just-covered unit for defects — fabric flaws, shade/pattern mismatch, wrinkles and puckers, crooked seams, show-through staples, poorly seated spring units and slack webbing — before the piece moves on.

Institutional/commercial setting (office suite, hospital, theater, transit terminal): upholsterer walks a floor of installed seating, inspecting fixed or stacked chairs and benches in place for torn upholstery, collapsed foam, broken springs/webbing decks and cracked or loose frames, logging which units need repair.

sources.system: Automated Defect Inspection cell for complex metallic parts (Univ. of Washington / GKN Aerospace, ARM Institute)
sources.developer: University of Washington, University of Connecticut, GKN Aerospace (ARM Institute project)
sources.title: Highlight: Automated Defect Inspection of Complex Metallic Parts — ARM Institute
sources.claim: An ARM Institute-funded robotic inspection cell autonomously positions non-contact imaging sensors around complex fixtured parts and localizes surface defects, with detection rates above 95% and roughly one minute per part; GKN Aerospace has built the cell in a factory.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic surface-defect inspection of fixtured manufactured parts. It transfers to examining fixtured furniture frames/components in a purpose-built cell because the robot itself plans and executes the sensor viewpoints and localizes defects on a part presented to it; the objects differ in material, so it is used only as general support for the E1 cell format alongside wood- and textile-specific systems.

sources.system: MiCROTEC Goldeneye 300/500/900 Multi-Sensor Quality Scanner

sources.title: MiCROTEC - Goldeneye 900
sources.claim: MiCROTEC Goldeneye multi-sensor quality scanners are installed in sawmill planer lines and glulam plants and automatically recognize wood defects (knots, cracks, splits, warp) on all four sides of boards, feeding automatic sorting and cross-cutting.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated detection of defects in wood stock on a production line. Furniture frames and rails are the same hardwood/softwood material and the defects sought (splits, knots, cracks, warp) are the same; the scanner is part of a purpose-built conveying line that then sorts or cross-cuts the piece, i.e. it acts on the workpiece.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated inspection of wood furniture components on a production line. sources.claim: EasyFlow's EasyODM AI vision system was deployed at a production facility of a global car seat manufacturer, inspecting finished seats in 2.2 seconds at 99% accuracy and identifying wrinkles, scratches, staining and creases by seat area, with defective seats routed for automated robotic or manual rework.

Car seats are upholstered assemblies of frame, foam and sewn cover, and the defects located (wrinkles, creases, staining, marks in a given seat area) are the same class an upholsterer looks for on a finished piece; inspection is on a purpose-built line station with parts presented to fixed cameras and defective units routed out.

sources.claim: USTER EVS Fabriq Vision performs automated intermediate and final fabric inspection on running fabric lines, detecting, recording and locating visible defects in every roll at line speed and supporting automated cutting, replacing manual inspection.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated defect location in rolled fabric. The upholsterer's inspection of cover goods and woven webbing is the same inspection of the same materials for the same flaws (holes, slubs, stains, weave faults); the machine transports the goods past its sensors and can trigger cutting.

sources.system: Dvolu / Fanuc M-710iC robotic upholstery work cell
sources.developer: Dvolu (Fanuc authorized system integrator) with Fanuc America
sources.title: Fanuc-powered robotic cell automates one of furniture manufacturing's toughest jobs
sources.claim: A Canadian furniture manufacturer runs a Fanuc M-710iC robotic upholstery cell that uses machine vision to locate seat cushions on pallets and then picks, stretches, staples, laser-trims and palletizes chair seat linings, adapting to part variation without manual adjustment.

It substantiates that in a purpose-built cell a robot can present and manipulate frames/cushions to a vision system with part-to-part variation, which is the handling half of an inspection station; it does not itself locate defects.

tasks.label: Adjust or replace webbing, padding, or springs, and secure them in place.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Custom reupholstery shop, one-off household piece (sofa, wing chair, antique): frame already stripped, worker removes old tacks/webbing, stretches and tacks new jute or elastic webbing, replaces or reties coil springs (eight-way hand tie) or clips in sinuous springs, then lays burlap, foam and batting and staples it down. Every frame differs in size, age and construction; tension and crown judged by feel.

Upholstered-furniture plant, serial production of a standardized seat/back deck: sinuous springs or webbing strips are attached to identical new wooden frames (clips, holders, staples) at a dedicated station, hundreds of identical units per shift.

Upholstered-furniture plant, serial 'padding up' of standardized frames and cushion units: foam blocks and polyester wrap are glued and stapled to arms, backs and seat decks of identical new frames, and seat pans have foam and lining stretched and stapled on.

Vehicle, marine or aircraft trim shop: a removed used seat is disassembled; collapsed foam padding is replaced or built up, broken sinuous springs, suspension wires or diaphragms are replaced, and the pad/cover is re-secured with hog rings, listing wires and staples on the model-specific frame.

Shop batch job on contract seating (restaurant chairs, office chairs, booth or theater seats): 20-60 identical used drop-in seat pans are stripped of old staples, fabric and crushed foam, re-webbed or re-padded and stapled back up, then reassembled.

On-site work at a customer's premises (home, office, restaurant, boat in a slip): sagging webbing on a built-in booth, church pew or boat cushion is re-tensioned or replaced and padding topped up in place, working around fixed structures with hand tools and no fixturing.

sources.system: Euroline robotized upholstery frame assembly line (spring insertion section)
sources.developer: Euroline sp. z o.o. / Poznan University of Life Sciences (study)
sources.title: Comparative analysis of the manual and robotic upholstery frame assembly processes. Study based on many years of research (MATEC Web of Conferences 338, 01028)
sources.claim: A deployed robotized production line at furniture-frame maker Euroline assembles upholstery frames including a dedicated spring insertion section in which a robot inserts all the corrugated (sinuous) springs into the frame's spring holders; over 30,000 frames were produced and robotic assembly showed under 2% defective frames versus ~25% for the manual line.
sources.transferJustification: Directly on task for the spring element: the robot attaches steel corrugated springs into holders on an upholstery frame and secures them, the same operation an upholsterer performs when installing sinuous springs on a standardized frame.

sources.system: Dvolu automated upholstery cell (Fanuc M-710iC + machine vision)
sources.developer: Dvolu (Fanuc Authorized System Integrator) / Fanuc America
sources.title: Fanuc-powered robotic cell automates one of furniture manufacturing's toughest jobs
sources.claim: A Canadian furniture manufacturer runs a vision-guided Fanuc M-710iC robotic upholstery cell built by integrator Dvolu that picks chair seat cushions off pallets, positions them, stretches the flexible lining, staples it, laser-trims it and palletizes the finished seats, adapting to part variation without manual adjustment.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (covering/lining a padded chair seat) transfers to securing padding in place in serial production: same objects (foam seat cushions and flexible sheet material), same fastening method (stretch-and-staple to a seat pan), same factory-cell environment and cycle-time requirement.

sources.system: Two UR10 collaborative robots at Fibreline (with OCTOPUZ programming)
sources.title: Removing Production Bottlenecks through Automation
sources.claim: Fibreline, a UK upholstery cushion fillings manufacturer, deployed two Universal Robots UR10 arms to process upholstery foam pieces (drilling tufting holes) in production.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (robotic processing of upholstery foam in a factory cell) shows only that foam padding can be handled and worked by robots on presented, fixtured parts; it does not show foam being fitted and secured to furniture, so it is supporting context for the serial-production padding instance.

tasks.label: Sew rips or tears in material, or create tufting, using needles and thread.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Reupholstery/furniture repair shop: worker hand-sews with a curved needle and waxed thread to close a rip or a burst seam in the cover of an assembled piece still on the workbench or upholstery horse — blind-stitching an arm panel, outside back, or cushion boxing so the stitches are invisible; each piece is a different frame, fabric and damage.

Auto, marine or RV trim shop: repairing a rip or tear in a vehicle seat cover, headliner, convertible top or boat cushion — hand-stitching a split seam on the seat in the vehicle or on a removed seat, matching original thread and stitch spacing on vinyl or leather.

On-site service call in a customer's home, office, restaurant or clinic: mobile upholsterer hand-sews a tear in a sofa cushion, booth seat or office chair in place, working around furniture, walls and occupants with a hand needle and thread.

Shop sewing bench: a torn or split cover panel is removed and re-stitched on an industrial walking-foot machine — restitching a failed seam, sewing in a patch or replacement section along the existing curved stitch line on used, stretched material.

Furniture/bedding plant production line: creating repeating tufting on flat production items — mattresses, futons, flat seat/back cushions and grid-tufted panels — driving twine or lace with a long needle through the padding and securing it with buttons or washers in a fixed pattern.

Shop or plant custom work: creating deep-button diamond or biscuit tufting on a chair back, headboard or booth back — laying out the pattern, hand-folding and dressing the pleats, driving twine through foam and frame with a long tufting needle and tying each button off at the back.

sources.system: MPT Group Autotufter
sources.title: MPT Group Meets Growing Demand — BedTimes Magazine
sources.claim: MPT Group's Autotufter is a fully automatic mattress/futon tufting machine that drives tuft lace through the product and secures it with washers/buttons, running in assembly lines without operator intervention; about a dozen units in operation in the US, tufting 200+ mattresses per shift.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is mattress tufting: the same operation as upholstery tufting — a long needle carries twine/lace through thick padding and is secured with a button/washer in a laid-out pattern — on comparable objects (thick foam/fibre cushions) at comparable precision, so it transfers to tufting flat cushions and panels in a production cell.

sources.system: GENMAX ACKJ automatic mattress/cushion tufting machine

sources.claim: GENMAX sells a fully automatic (ACKJ) button tufting machine with 4-axis button movement that the vendor states also handles sofa cushion and futon tufting, alongside a semi-automatic pneumatic model.
sources.transferJustification: Mattress button tufting equipment extended by the vendor to sofa cushion tufting: the workpiece (foam/spring cushion), the consumables (buttons, washers, tufting cord) and the required placement precision match the upholsterer's tufting operation on flat cushions.

sources.system: KMF RoQom 6000 robotic sewing system (Yaskawa Motoman GP7)
sources.title: The Future of Sewing in a Robot — IEN Europe
sources.claim: KMF's RoQom 6000, built on a Yaskawa Motoman GP7, is a fully automatic sewing cell that produces curved lockstitch decorative seams on leather automotive seat covers; parts are held in part-specific templates inside the cell.
