It shows automated seam sewing exists only for pre-programmed paths on new, template-fixtured cut parts; it does not substantiate locating and closing an arbitrary rip in a used, three-dimensional cover, so it supports no positive judgment on the repair instances.

sources.system: Lowry Sewbot
sources.title: Softwear launches new automated industrial sewing system with machine vision
sources.claim: SoftWear Automation's Lowry Sewbot performs fully automated loading, defect detection, sewing, seaming, cutting and stacking of sewn goods (towels, t-shirts, home textiles) inside a self-contained machine using machine vision; it makes new products rather than repairing damaged ones.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is automated sewing of new flat textile goods on a vacuum table. It handles limp fabric autonomously but only on cut panels fed into a purpose-built machine, giving no evidence of stitching a tear closed in an assembled, upholstered item.

sources.system: Dvolu automated upholstery cell (Fanuc M-710iC)
sources.title: Fanuc-powered robotic cell automates one of furniture manufacturing's toughest jobs
sources.claim: A Fanuc M-710iC cell integrated by Dvolu performs vision-guided upholstery of chair seat linings in a Canadian furniture plant — picking, stretching, stapling, laser trimming and palletizing — showing upholstery automation to date covers stapling/trimming, not needle-and-thread repair or tufting.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is robotic upholstering of new seat linings in a fenced production cell. It establishes the current frontier of furniture-upholstery robotics (fabric stretching and stapling of standardized parts) and shows no sewing, hand-stitching or tufting capability, so it cannot substantiate the repair instances.

tasks.label: Remove covering, webbing, padding, or defective springs from workpieces, using hand tools such as hammers and tack pullers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Custom upholstery shop: full strip-down of a residential sofa or armchair brought in for reupholstery. Worker flips the piece on trestles, pulls hundreds of staples/tacks with tack puller and ripping chisel, removes outside back/arm fabric, cambric, burlap, cotton and foam padding, cuts spring twine, tears out rotted jute webbing, and pulls broken coil springs — all without splitting the wood frame or losing the old pieces used as patterns.

Custom shop: simple small pieces — dining-chair slip seats, ottomans, bar stools, bench seats, loose cushion covers. Worker inverts the seat pad, pulls the staple line around a plywood/hardwood base with a staple lifter, lifts off fabric and foam, and checks the base. High volume, repetitive, but each seat's staple pattern, fabric, and base differ by piece.

Antique/heirloom restoration: hand-tacked Victorian or period frame with horsehair or moss stuffing, hand-tied coil springs on webbing, and delicate show wood. Worker must extract tacks from fragile rails without marring finished wood, salvage original stuffing or trim where required, and note the original construction for rebuild.

Auto/marine/RV trim shop: seat assembly removed from the vehicle and set on the bench. Worker cuts or unclips hog rings, releases listing wires and J-hooks, peels the cover off the foam bun, removes deteriorated foam and defective seat-frame springs/sinuous wires, working around heaters, airbag stitching, and wiring.

On-site or in-situ stripping: headliner and door panels stripped inside a customer's vehicle, boat cockpit cushions and built-in bench upholstery at a marina, or restaurant booths and church pews stripped in place at the customer's premises — cramped access, overhead work, varied fixings.

sources.system: Urban Machine 'The Machine'
sources.title: Nailed down — AI technology aids Urban Machine in reclaiming wood waste at Zanker facility
sources.claim: Urban Machine's robotic system autonomously locates and extracts nails, screws and staples from reclaimed construction lumber using AI vision and patented end effectors, in purpose-built machines run at C&D recycling facilities. It is the closest demonstrated analog to fastener removal from wood, but it handles straight dimensional lumber fed into the machine and does not remove fabric, padding, webbing or springs from a shaped furniture frame.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: extracting metal fasteners (nails, staples) from wood. It fails to transfer to upholstery stripping because the workpiece is a uniform board presented to a gantry, not a shaped frame; the system does not peel covering, cut spring twine, remove padding/webbing, or pull coil springs, and destroys nothing-but-metal rather than preserving a reusable frame with a recorded construction.

sources.system: Dvolu automated upholstery cell (Fanuc M-710iC)
sources.title: Fanuc-powered robotic cell automates one of furniture manufacturing’s toughest jobs
sources.claim: A vision-guided Fanuc M-710iC cell integrated by Dvolu performs upholstery attachment on chair seat linings — picking, stretching, stapling, laser trimming and palletizing — in a purpose-built industrial cell at a Canadian furniture manufacturer. It shows flexible-fabric handling is automatable in an E1 cell, but the demonstrated operations are assembly, not removal of existing covering, padding or springs.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic upholstering (attaching) of new seat linings on identical parts presented on pallets. It does not substantiate stripping: no fastener extraction, no removal of aged covering/padding/webbing/springs, and it relies on known, repeated part geometry rather than the one-off, unknown constructions an upholsterer strips.

sources.system: Kathedra upholstery robot
sources.title: Kathedra - Columbia Entrepreneurship
sources.claim: Kathedra is developing and piloting a robotic system aimed at upholstery manufacturing (attaching fabric), in partnership with Standard Bots; it is a pilot-stage manufacturing tool, with no demonstrated stripping/tear-down capability.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic upholstery in furniture manufacturing. Not transferable to this task: the stated target is producing new upholstered goods, autonomy is unestablished, and no source shows removal of existing covering, padding, webbing or springs.

tasks.label: Attach fasteners, grommets, buttons, buckles, ornamental trim, and other accessories to covers or frames, using hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Furniture plant, styled upholstered goods: at a trim station the upholsterer drives rows of decorative brass nailheads and tacks gimp/braid along arm fronts, outside backs and skirt edges of sofas and chairs with a pneumatic decorative nail gun and tack hammer; heads must be evenly spaced, head-to-head, following hand-shaped curved edges without marring the fabric or the nail heads.

Furniture plant production line, repeat models: fastening cover and deck material to the frame with staples and tack strip and installing accessory hardware on identical parts arriving in batches at a bench or line station - plastic clips and retainers, Velcro and zipper fittings, tufting buttons in flat padded panels, grommets in skirts and dust covers, glides, brackets and leg hardware.

Custom reupholstery / furniture repair shop: finishing a one-off residential or antique piece - decorative nailhead trim, hand-tied deep tufting buttons, gimp and welt tacking, skirt hooks, casters and customer-supplied hardware - each frame a different shape and size, worked on trestles with hand tools and judged on appearance.

Vehicle seating and interior-trim manufacturing line: attaching trim clips, retainers, listing rods, hog rings and fastener hardware to seat trim covers and interior panels on high-volume repeat parts at a fixed workstation.

Auto / marine / aircraft upholstery shop: setting snaps, grommets, buckles, webbing straps and hog rings on convertible tops, boat and tonneau covers and replacement seat covers, positioned to match the specific vehicle or hull, frequently test-fitted and finished on the vehicle itself.

On-site / field work: attaching accessories and fasteners to furnishings in place - restaurant booths, church pews, institutional seating, boat canvas at the dock, vehicle interiors - in the customer's space, working around fixed obstructions with hand tools.

tasks.label: Repair furniture frames and refinish exposed wood.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Shop reupholstery of a single used wooden-frame chair or rocker: worker strips the old cover, finds loose or racked joints, knocks the joint apart, scrapes old hide glue, re-glues and clamps, replaces broken corner blocks/dowels/springs rails, adds screws, then sands and refinishes the exposed show-wood arms, legs and back rail to match the customer's expectation. Every piece is unique and the damage is discovered as the work proceeds.

Sofa, settee or sectional brought into the shop with a cracked or broken hardwood rail, split frame member or failed corner blocks: worker cuts and fits a replacement rail or sister piece from stock lumber, glues/screws/staples it in place, re-squares the frame, and touches up or refinishes exposed wood trim and legs.

Antique or high-end restoration: repair of a period frame with missing or damaged carved members, custom-fabricating a matching replacement part by hand, repairing loose mortise-and-tenon joints, then chemically stripping, staining and hand-rubbing the exposed wood to match existing patina and adjacent surfaces.

Contract/commercial batch (restaurant, hotel, church, institution) of dozens of identical wood-frame chairs, in which many frames have structural damage: broken stretchers, split legs, elongated screw holes; worker repairs each frame individually and then refinishes the wood.

Contract/commercial batch of identical wood-frame chairs whose frames are structurally sound: worker re-tightens fasteners, then sands off scuffed/worn finish on the identical wood frames and re-sprays a uniform stain/clear lacquer, all in the shop with the pieces handled repeatedly in the same way.

On-site work at a customer's home or in a client facility: tighten a wobbly dining-chair or church-pew frame with glue/screws in place, fill and touch up scratches, gouges and worn spots on exposed wood with fillers, burn-in sticks and padding lacquer, working around furnishings and finished floors.

tasks.label: Interweave and fasten strips of webbing to the backs and undersides of furniture, using small hand tools and fasteners.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Custom/repair upholstery shop: a stripped antique or classic wood-frame chair or settee seat is re-webbed with jute webbing — strips cut from a roll, folded and tacked to one rail, tensioned with a webbing stretcher to high tension, tacked off, then cross strips threaded over-and-under the first layer and tacked at every rail. Each frame is a one-off with different rail spacing, wood condition, and tack-hold quality.

Custom/repair shop: a modern sofa or lounge chair with sagging support gets new elastic (rubber/Pirelli) webbing on the seat deck and back — parallel strips stapled or clipped to the frame under measured stretch, sometimes with a few crossing strips, plus new webbing under the frame's underside. Frames vary job to job; access is tight around arms and rails.

Furniture manufacturing plant: repetitive webbing of standardized seat and back frames during a production run — frames come from the frame shop on carts or a line, elastic webbing is pulled from a roll across the frame opening at a set tension, stapled at both rails, cut, and (for some models) crossed strips added; hundreds of units per shift to a fixed spec.

Vehicle, RV, marine or aircraft trim shop: webbing applied to the base and back of a custom bench, van, or boat seat frame — fewer, non-standard frames, sometimes metal or plywood, fastened with staples, hog rings, or clips inside a confined seat box.

On-site work at a customer's premises (home living room, office, restaurant booth, boat in a slip): the upholsterer flips the piece or works underneath it in place, removes failed webbing and re-webs the underside/back with hand tools, working around furnishings, flooring, and limited light.

sources.system: Fanuc M-710iC automated upholstery cell (integrator: Dvolu)
sources.title: Fanuc-powered robotic cell automates furniture upholstery process
sources.claim: A deployed robotic work cell at a Canadian furniture manufacturer uses a Fanuc M-710iC with machine vision to pick, position, stretch, staple, trim and palletize chair seat linings — i.e. vision-guided tensioning and stapling of flexible material onto chair seat components inside an industrial cell.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: stretching and stapling flexible seat covering material onto chair seat components. It transfers to fastening webbing strips on production frames because the objects (tensioned flexible textile stock), the fastening method (staples into the seat frame), the required precision, and the fixtured production-cell environment are the same; only the strip geometry differs.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic stapling of upholstered furniture frames held in molds. It transfers to the fastening half of this task because it is the same fastener (industrial staples), the same substrate (wooden upholstery frames), and the same fixtured-cell presentation of the work.

sources.transferJustification: Directly the same task (applying and fastening elastic webbing to furniture frames), but the machine is operator-loaded and machine-controlled only within each cycle, so it cannot by itself support a positive autonomous-completion judgment.

sources.system: Kathedra robotic upholstery cell (prototype/pilot)

tasks.label: Draw cutting lines on material following patterns, templates, sketches, or blueprints, using chalk, pencils, paint, or other methods.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Small custom reupholstery shop: worker spreads plain fabric on the shop cutting table, lays down hardboard/paper templates or the ripped-off old cover pieces, and chalks the cutting lines (with seam allowance) around each piece for one chair or sofa.

Patterned goods: stripes, plaids, or large printed motifs must be centered on inside backs/seats and matched across seams; the worker positions the pattern pieces on the fabric to align the repeat and nap direction before marking the cut lines in chalk or tailor's pencil.

Leather or vinyl hides for furniture or vehicle interiors: worker nests templates around brands, scars, holes and thin edges of an irregular hide and marks cut lines on the back or face with a silver pen/chalk.
Foam, batting and decking: worker marks cut lines on foam slabs, Dacron, burlap or deck material to templates or measured sketches using marker/pencil before cutting cushion cores and padding.

Production/contract upholstery shop: worker marks multiple identical sets of cover panels on a spread or roll of standard goods from production patterns, including notches and placement marks, working to a cut ticket.

Fit-and-mark on the piece itself: material is draped, pinned or stapled over a chair frame, boat cushion or vehicle seat and the trim/cutting lines are drawn directly on the material in place to capture the true 3D fit before removal and cutting.

sources.system: Zünd Marking Module (MAM) on G3/S3/D3/L3 cutters
sources.title: L3 leather cutter | Leather processing | Zünd
sources.claim: Zünd digital flatbed cutters (G3/S3/D3/L3) offer marking modules that hold pen and ink inserts and plot die-lines, seam lines, pattern outlines and guidelines directly onto the material, including silver-pen marking on leather.
sources.transferJustification: Directly the task: a CNC gantry draws cutting/seam lines with a pen on the same fabrics, vinyls and leathers an upholsterer chalks, but the material is presented on the machine's vacuum table.

sources.system: Zünd G3 L-2500 textile processing solution with MindCUT

sources.system: Mind / MindCUT Studio pattern matching

sources.transferJustification: Substantiates the pattern-matching judgment the upholsterer performs when positioning templates on striped/plaid fabric before marking cut lines.

tasks.label: Stretch webbing and fabric, using webbing stretchers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production furniture plant, upholstery line: worker stretches cut cover fabric taut over a standardized seat or back panel/deck (same model repeated through the run), pulls out wrinkles with stretching pliers, and staples it off before the part moves on.

Production furniture/frame plant: worker applies parallel strips of elastic (or polypropylene) webbing across standardized sofa/chair seat and back frames, tensioning each strip with a webbing stretcher or belt-tension tool and stapling/clipping both ends, dozens of frames per shift.

Custom reupholstery/repair shop: stripped one-off frame (antique armchair, dining chair, sofa deck) of unknown geometry is re-webbed with jute webbing — strips cut, tensioned by feel with a gooseneck webbing stretcher, folded and tacked, then interwoven basket-fashion across the opening.

Custom reupholstery shop: worker stretches and tacks cover fabric over a one-off frame with curved arms, backs and welted edges, pulling to even tension, aligning pattern/grain, easing fullness at corners before stapling.

Auto/marine/RV trim shop: worker stretches vinyl or cloth covers over varied vehicle or boat seat foam and frames (bucket seats, bench cushions, boat lounges), pulling with stretching pliers and securing with hog rings, listing wires or staples.

On-site at a customer's premises (home, office, restaurant booth, boat cabin, aircraft interior): worker re-stretches and secures webbing or fabric on furniture that cannot be moved, working in place with hand tools in cramped, as-found conditions.

sources.claim: A deployed robotic work cell built around a Fanuc M-710iC at a Canadian furniture manufacturer performs fabric stretching, stapling, trimming and ... of chair seat linings — tasks previously done by skilled upholsterers.

tasks.label: Operate sewing machines or sew upholstery by hand to seam cushions and join various sections of covering material.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Furniture/bedding plant sewing department: high-volume, repeat-SKU production sewing — seaming pre-cut standardized cushion cover panels, running boxing/border strips, closing filled cushions, sewing labels and zippers on a fixed pattern with folders and guides.

Custom/repair upholstery shop: one-off residential reupholstery job — sewing a new cover set from custom-cut goods, welt cord inserted into curved boxed-cushion seams, zipper boxing, pattern/stripe matching, seams trued to a frame that has been measured piece by piece.

Vehicle-seat, marine or RV trim manufacturing plant: repeat-production seat cover work — joining vinyl/leather/cloth panels to a fixed pattern, decorative topstitching, listing and hog-ring channels sewn in, on standardized parts running in volume.

Small auto/boat/aircraft trim shop: one-off custom seat cover or interior panel — 3D-shaped panels fitted to a specific seat, French seams around bolsters, tapered darts, sewn and re-fitted by eye against the foam bun.

Hand sewing on the assembled piece in the shop: blind/slip-stitching a cushion closure, closing an outside arm or back with a curved needle, hand-sewing welt to a finished edge, stitching through tufted areas — sewing done on the bulky, already-built furniture.

On-site sewing at a customer location (home, office lobby, boat cockpit, vehicle interior): hand-stitching a split seam or re-closing a cushion in place, working around fixed furniture and uncontrolled lighting/space.

tasks.label: Design upholstery cover patterns and cutting plans, based on sketches, customer descriptions, or blueprints.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Residential re-upholstery shop: customer describes desired changes to an existing sofa or armchair; upholsterer works out the cover panel shapes (from measurements, the old cover pieces, or a sketch), decides seam and welt placement, and lays out a cutting plan/yardage estimate for the chosen fabric, accounting for pattern repeat, nap and railroading.

Custom/one-off commission for an interior designer or client: upholsterer works from a sketch, photo, or shop drawing of a piece that does not yet exist, drafts each cover pattern piece (inside/outside back, arms, deck, skirt, boxing), adds seam and pull allowances, and produces a cut list and fabric requirement before any cutting.

Auto, marine, or aircraft trim shop: designs seat cover, door panel, headliner or boat cushion patterns from vehicle blueprints, factory templates, or a customer's description of a custom design (pleats, inserts, embroidery), and plans the cut layout on hides or vinyl rolls around hide defects and directional grain.

Furniture manufacturing plant: upholsterer/pattern maker digitizes or drafts master patterns for a new production model from engineering blueprints, grades them across size or SKU variants, and builds nested cutting plans (markers) for CNC cutters to minimize fabric or leather waste.

Small routine jobs: dining chair seats, box cushions, bolsters, simple slipcovers or a replacement panel; upholsterer measures, sketches a quick pattern, and calculates a simple straight-line cutting plan and yardage for the customer's quote.

tasks.label: Maintain records of time required to perform each job.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Discuss upholstery fabrics, colors, and styles with customers, and provide cost estimates.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Pick up and deliver furniture.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Residential pickup: upholsterer drives a van/box truck to a customer's house, walks the piece (sofa, sectional, recliner, wing chair) out through hallways, doorways, and often porch steps, wraps/blankets it, lifts it into the truck and straps it, then drives back and unloads at the shop. Access, floor surfaces, pets, parking and stairs differ at every address.

Residential delivery of the finished piece: load at shop, drive to the home, carry the reupholstered furniture in without marking walls or the new fabric, set it in the room the customer specifies, level/position it and get sign-off. Includes tight turns, elevators or narrow stairwells in apartments.

Commercial/institutional pickup or delivery: restaurant booths and chair seats, office or lobby seating, hotel or church furniture, medical waiting-room chairs. Often several pieces at once, through a service entrance or loading dock, scheduled around the client's operating hours, with public-street driving between stops.

Shop-side handling: unloading incoming pieces from the truck at the shop's door or small dock, carrying them into a crowded workshop, staging them on work stands or in a storage rack/loft, and moving pieces between stripping, frame, sewing and finishing areas.

Vehicle/marine upholstery collection: driving to a dealership, marina or storage lot, removing and carrying out car/boat/RV seats, cushions and panels, loading them into the truck, then returning and refitting them on site.

sources.system: KUKA AMRs (KMP fleet) + KUKA palletizing robot at Formetal
sources.title: How autonomous mobile robots optimize furniture manufacturing | KUKA Global
sources.claim: At furniture manufacturer Formetal, KUKA autonomous mobile robots pick up stacks of furniture product placed in loading bays and transport them to a palletizing robot, which builds shipment pallets that the AMRs return for pickup — i.e. autonomous internal pick-up-and-delivery of furniture goods in a purpose-built plant.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: intralogistics transport of furniture goods in a furniture plant. It substantiates the E1 counterfactual of 'pick up and deliver furniture' — work staged for the machine at a loading bay, moved autonomously to a designated destination and handed off — with comparable objects (furniture product stacks) in a machine-built setting.

tasks.label: Attach bindings or apply solutions to edges of cut material to prevent raveling.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Custom/repair upholstery shop: after cutting one-off panels (cushion boxings, skirts, decking, arm covers) from varied goods (velvet, chenille, linen, vinyl), the upholsterer runs a binder-folder or serger over the raw edges of curved and straight panels on an industrial machine, matching binding to the job and stopping/pivoting at corners.

Furniture manufacturing sewing room: production runs of identical cut panels; operator overlocks/serges or applies bias binding tape to edges of deck fabric, dust covers and cushion panels on dedicated machines before assembly, repeating the same operation hundreds of times per shift.

Auto/marine/RV trim shop: binding the edges of cut carpet pieces, canvas and vinyl panels (floor mats, cockpit carpet, kick panels) with binding tape or serging on a heavy-duty walking-foot/overlock machine; heavy stiff material, irregular outlines.

Shop bench work applying anti-ravel solutions rather than tape: brushing/dabbing liquid seam sealant, latex or Fray-Check along raw cut edges, notches and slit openings of synthetic and woven pieces, or melting/searing edges of synthetic goods with a hot knife/flame, on small pieces and partially assembled panels.

Mobile/on-site work at a customer location (boat, RV, van conversion, in-home repair): a piece of carpet or fabric is cut to fit on site and its edge must be bound or sealed, sometimes on or beside the installed item, with only portable tools.

instances.label: Auto trim shop: a used vehicle seat is unbolted and carried to the bench, the worn cover is stripped off, foam, springs and listing wires are repaired or replaced, a new pre-sewn cloth, vinyl or leather cover is stretched over the bun and secured with hog rings/clips, and the seat is refitted to the car. One or two model-specific seats per job.

Spot repair inside the vehicle in a shop bay (occasionally mobile at a customer site): cigarette burn, cracked bolster, pet-claw tear or split seam in a leather or vinyl seat, door panel or armrest, fixed by cleaning, sub-patching, layering filler, heat-cured grain matching and colour blending, or hand restitching in place.

Bench and sewing-room fabrication: taking a pattern off the old cover or a template, laying out and cutting cloth, vinyl or leather while working around hide defects, then sewing panels, welts, French seams, listing pockets and decorative stitching into finished covers, headliner panels or door-card wraps on industrial machines.

Convertible or vinyl top replacement on the vehicle in the shop: remove the old top, tacking strips, pads and rear window; align, glue, stretch and staple/bolt the new top to the bows and body; fit and seal the rear window; adjust tension so the top seals, folds and stows correctly.

Headliner, carpet and interior trim work: pull trim, visors and grab handles, remove the sagging headliner board through a door opening, scrape off deteriorated foam-backed cloth, spray adhesive and smooth new fabric over the compound-curved board, trim the openings and refit; also fitting molded carpet and re-wrapping door panels.

tasks.label: Verify dimensions or check the quality or fit of pieces to ensure adherence to specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Custom/small cabinet shop bench check: after ripping, crosscutting or CNC-machining parts, the worker measures stile, rail, panel and shelf lengths, widths and thicknesses with tape, rule, calipers and square against the cut list, checks squareness and flatness, and pulls out-of-tolerance parts for recut. Parts are stacked on carts and benches amid other work, dust and moving people.

Dry-fit / fit check of joinery and sub-assemblies in the shop: test-fitting dadoes, dowels, dominoes, mortise-and-tenon and drawer-box joints without glue, clamping up and measuring diagonals for square, checking that a drawer box or door fits its opening and reveals, and paring or re-machining where the fit is tight or loose.

Volume casework / millwork plant: in-process quality check of parts flowing off a beam saw, nested CNC or edgebander \- panviation panel size and squareness, edgeband adhesion and trim quality, surface tear-out, grain/color match, veneer defects \- with off-spec parts flagged, sorted out or re-run. Fixed line layout, standard machines, institution-controlled floor.

Final inspection of an assembled/finished unit before crating or delivery: overall cabinet dimensions to the shop drawing, door and drawer-front reveals and alignment, joint gaps, finish/surface quality under lights, and operating the hardware (drawers slide, doors close) in the shop's finishing or shipping area.

Field verification at the install/jobsite: measuring the as-built opening, wall plumb, floor level and obstructions and comparing them with the shop drawings and the parts already built, to confirm the casework will fit before it is delivered or during install. Site taken as found, other trades working, changing layout.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated dimensional inspection of manufactured parts. Transfers to checking cabinet parts because the geometric checks (length, width, squareness, flatness against a CAD/cut-list spec) are the same and the required precision is far tighter than cabinetwork tolerances; optical scanning works well on matte wood surfaces.

tasks.label: Produce or assemble components of articles, such as store fixtures, office equipment, cabinets, or high-grade furniture.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production cabinet/casework plant: machining carcase components from sheet goods for a job — panels cut to size on a beam saw or nested CNC router, edges banded, holes bored for shelf pins, hinge cups and dowels, parts labeled and stacked by cabinet. Repetitive sizes, engineered software output, indoor plant floor.

Assembling machined panel components into finished cabinet carcases: inserting dowels/glue or cam fittings, squaring the box in a case clamp, pressing, inserting and fastening the back panel. Shop or plant assembly area, standard boxes in varying widths.

Making and assembling secondary components in the shop: five-piece cope-and-stick doors, dovetailed or doweled drawer boxes, face frames — ripping and crosscutting solid hardwood, machining joints, gluing/clamping, and sanding the assembled component flat and clean.

Custom architectural millwork / store fixture components, batch of one: reception desk panels, display-case gables, laminated countertops and toe kicks machined to job-specific dimensions from shop drawings; mixed materials (melamine, veneer core ply, HPL, solid edging), each part a different size.

Bench assembly and fitting of a one-off high-grade piece (custom furniture case, store fixture, executive desk): dry-fitting joinery, adjusting fit with hand tools, glue-up with clamps and cauls, squaring, hanging and adjusting doors/drawers, installing hardware and trimming/scribing parts to fit the actual assembly.

tasks.label: Trim, sand, or scrape surfaces or joints to prepare articles for finishing.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production/custom cabinet shop: sanding flat components — slab doors, drawer fronts, veneered panels, shelves, table/counter tops — through a grit sequence to a finish-ready surface, removing mill marks and de-nibbing before stain or clear coat. Parts arrive in batches on carts.

Shop: sanding profiled and shaped parts — shaker and raised-panel door profiles, cope-and-stick joints, moldings, curved rails, turned or bandsawn legs — including easing/breaking edges and corners so the profile takes finish evenly.

Shop bench: after glue-up, sanding assembled articles — face frames, cabinet fronts, chair/table frames — flushing rail-to-stile joints and removing glue squeeze-out and clamp marks on exterior surfaces before finishing.

Shop: trimming operations — flush-trimming edgeband overhang and scraping the glue line, trimming protruding dowels, plugs, tenons and dovetail pins, and cleaning saw marks or tear-out at joints so the article is ready for finish.

Shop bench: detail work in confined geometry — hand-sanding and scraping inside corners of assembled cabinet boxes and drawer boxes, inside curves, rabbets and recesses, and joint lines that machines cannot reach.

Small custom shop: one-off or oversized pieces — live-edge tops, curved reception desks, restoration/repair work, figured hardwood — hand-scraping tear-out with a card scraper and progressive hand sanding to a fine-furniture standard, each piece unlike the last.

tasks.label: Measure and mark dimensions of parts on paper or lumber stock prior to cutting, following blueprints, to ensure a tight fit and quality product.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Custom cabinet shop: from shop drawings/cut list, worker measures 4x8 plywood/MDF sheets on a bench or saw table, squares off the factory edge and marks cut lines for case sides, backs, shelves and doors with pencil, tape and straightedge so parts fit the assembled box.

Shop or millwork plant: worker measures rough solid lumber boards, chalks/pencils crosscut and rip lines around knots, checks, wane and warp, and selects grain/color placement per the blueprint to yield clear parts of required finished dimensions.

Bench layout of joinery and hardware locations on cut parts or stock: dado/rabbet lines, mortise and tenon shoulders, dowel and shelf-pin centers, hinge and drawer-slide positions, marked with square, marking gauge, story stick or template per blueprint before machining.

Full-size pattern work: laying out the part on paper, hardboard or plywood (arched doors, curved rails, moldings, stair parts) from the blueprint, drawing the profile full scale, then transferring/tracing it onto the stock before bandsawing or routing.

Production millwork/component plant: repeat-batch layout of framing or cabinet components — measuring stock to length, marking part positions and identification per the approved shop drawing for a run of identical assemblies.

Field/installation work: measuring the actual opening at the customer's home or a renovated space (out-of-square walls, sloped floors, existing tile/stone), then marking a filler, scribe strip or countertop blank on site so the piece fits tight to as-built conditions.

tasks.label: Cut timber to the right size, and shape and trim parts of joints to ensure a snug fit, using hand tools, such as planes, chisels, or wood files.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Custom cabinet shop: cutting rough or S4S solid stock and sheet parts to final dimension (rip, crosscut, trim to a line), working off a cut list at the saw and bench, with a jointer/plane pass to clean edges to exact size. Boards vary in length, warp, and defect content.

Bench joinery on furniture/casework parts: laying out and cutting mortise-and-tenon, dovetail, dado, or lap joints, then paring cheeks and shoulders with chisel, block plane, and file through repeated test fits until the joint slips together snug with no gap.

Fitting components during assembly in the shop: planing/trimming cabinet doors, drawer fronts, face-frame stiles and rails so they sit in the opening with an even reveal, easing edges and shaving high spots where the assembled case is slightly out of square.

Production millwork/component plant bench work: repetitive cutting of stock to size and shaping joint members (tenons, dovetails, cope-and-stick, door blanks) in volume against a standard spec, using jigs, stops, and standard machines, with hand trimming of the occasional off-spec part.

On-site during installation: scribing and trimming filler strips, end panels, countertops, and trim to as-found walls and floors, planing and filing the scribe until the part fits tight against irregular surfaces in an occupied or under-construction building.

tasks.label: Match materials for color, grain, or texture, giving attention to knots or other features of the wood.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Custom/small cabinet shop: the cabinetmaker walks the shop's lumber rack and cart of S2S hardwood, sights down boards for color, grain figure and knots, culls and sets aside a matched set of stock for a specific job (door stiles/rails, face frames, drawer fronts), marking pieces for later machining. Mixed species and lots, variable shop lighting, boards stored on racks and carts.

Panel glue-up layup: planed narrow boards are laid edge-to-edge on a bench or clamp-carrier infeed for a wide panel (door, top, side); the worker flips, rotates and re-orders the boards so color and grain blend across the panel and knots/sapwood are hidden or balanced, then marks the sequence and feeds the glue applicator/clamps.

Veneer and sheet-goods matching in an architectural millwork/cabinet shop: selecting veneer leaves from a flitch and sequencing them for book- or slip-matched door and panel faces, or picking plywood sheets whose faces match each other and the solid stock, keeping the sequence and figure aligned across a run of doors.

Production cabinet/furniture component plant: at a grading and sorting station on a rough-mill or panel line, the bench worker takes ripped/defected parts off a conveyor, judges color, grain and knots, culls defects and routes parts into color/appearance bins so downstream panels and door parts are matched sets, at line rate.

Field/repair matching: at a customer's home or a jobsite, matching new stock or a replacement door/drawer front to existing installed, finished cabinetry (or a client-supplied finished sample), judging how raw wood will look after stain and aging, and selecting boards accordingly.

tasks.label: Set up or operate machines, including power saws, jointers, mortisers, tenoners, molders, or shapers, to cut, mold, or shape woodstock or wood substitutes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Cabinet shop: sizing sheet goods (plywood, melamine, MDF) on a panel/beam saw or nested-based CNC router for casework parts — loading sheets, running a cut list, labeling and stacking parts, checking dimensions.

Millwork/cabinet shop: ripping and crosscutting solid hardwood on a table saw, gang rip saw or chop saw for face frames, doors and drawer parts — reading grain, cutting around knots and defects, small batches and one-offs.
Shop: surfacing and dimensioning rough-sawn lumber on a jointer and thickness planer (or four-side planer) — flattening cupped/twisted boards, referencing an edge, bringing stock to final thickness.

Millwork shop: setting up and running a shaper or moulder to produce profiled parts (door sticking, mouldings, curved rails) — installing/aligning profile tooling, setting fences and power feeder, making test cuts and adjusting, then running the batch.
Shop: cutting joinery on a hollow-chisel mortiser, tenoner, dovetailer or CNC — mortises and tenons for doors/frames, dovetails for drawers, dados and grooves, fitted to mating parts.

tasks.label: Bore holes for insertion of screws or dowels, by hand or using boring machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production boring of flat cabinet parts in a shop: shelf-pin (32 mm system) lines, dowel/confirmat holes, and hinge-cup bores in melamine, MDF and plywood panels, run on a point-to-point CNC or multi-spindle/vertical boring machine from a cut list; batch-size-1 custom kitchens mixed with repeat parts.

Bench boring of individual parts with a hand drill, drill press, or jig in the shop: pilot and pocket holes, hinge cups on doors, hardware and drawer-slide holes on face frames, rails and stiles; parts held by hand, clamp or shop-made jig on a bench.

Boring into partly or fully assembled casework/furniture in the shop: reaching inside a glued-up box or drawer, boring for slide screws, pulls, locks, or repair/rework holes at awkward heights and orientations on a piece too large or odd to fixture on a boring machine.

On-site boring during cabinet installation where hole positions are pre-specified by shop drawings: pilot holes for hardware, joining screws between cabinet boxes, pulls and knobs, hinge-plate screws; done in a customer home, kitchen or office fit-out.

On-site boring where hole positions must be located from as-found conditions: pilot holes through cabinet rails into studs found with a scanner, screws through scribed fillers, out-of-square walls and uneven floors in an occupied home or renovation.

Boring shaped or solid-wood joinery components: dowel holes in chair/table legs and curved rails, angled and end-grain bores, boring on non-flat blanks that must be indexed or cradled rather than laid flat.

Cabinet shop: assemble solid-wood face frames from rails and stiles (glue plus pocket screws, dowels, or mortise-and-tenon), square and clamp them, then glue/nail the finished frame onto the completed box. Parts vary in species, size and straightness.

Production shop: assemble drawer boxes (dovetail, doweled, or tongue-and-dado sides with a bottom panel slid into grooves, glued and pressed) and five-piece cabinet doors (cope-and-stick rails/stiles with a floating panel, glued, squared and pinned).

Custom architectural millwork / small custom shop: assemble one-off units — a curved reception desk, an angled kitchen island, a large built-in wall unit or store fixture. Non-rectangular geometry, oversized subassemblies, benchwork with bar clamps, biscuits/dominoes, glue and screws, with hand fitting, shimming and scribing as the unit goes together.

Wood furniture / case goods factory bench assembly: join drawer-rail frames, dust panels, tops, ends and web frames of a dresser or nightstand with glue, dowels, staples and screws to form the finished carcass, working from a fixture or assembly bench on a moving line.

tasks.label: Perform final touch-ups with sandpaper or steel wool.

instances.label: Cabinet/millwork shop bench: final sanding of flat and shaker-style doors, drawer fronts and flat panels before finishing — knocking down mill marks and raised grain, easing edges, stepping 120/150/180-220 grit, checking by hand feel and raking light.

Shop finishing room: denibbing / scuff-sanding doors and panels between coats of sealer, stain or lacquer with fine paper (320-400) or steel wool — removing dust nibs and raised fibers without cutting through the coating.

Shop bench: touch-up sanding of profiled and contoured work — molding profiles, raised-panel and cope-and-stick edges, louvered shutter frames, turned or curved parts — abrasive must follow the contour without rounding crisp detail.

Shop bench: detail touch-ups on assembled casework — hand-sanding inside corners where face-frame stiles meet rails, cleaning dried glue squeeze-out at joints, blending a proud joint or scribe edge inside a cabinet box, judged largely by feel.
Shop finishing area: rubbing out the cured topcoat with 0000 steel wool, fine abrasive pads or polish on tabletops, high-gloss fronts and casework surfaces to a uniform sheen.

Job site or customer's home after installation: touch-up sanding of installed casework and trim — scuffs, filler at scribes and nail holes, blending a fitted piece — in a cluttered, uncontrolled space.

tasks.label: Repair or alter wooden furniture, cabinetry, fixtures, paneling, or other pieces.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Shop bench repair of an assembled, often finished wooden piece brought in damaged (chair with loose mortise-and-tenon joints, table with split apron, cabinet with a broken door rail): diagnose the failure, knock apart or clamp the joint, scrape old glue, re-glue and clamp or fabricate and fit a replacement member, then sand and blend the existing finish.

Shop alteration/re-machining of cabinet and millwork components that can be laid on a machine table: cutting a door or panel down to a new size, re-boring 35 mm hinge cups and shelf-pin lines in a new position, adding a dado or edge profile to a part before it goes back into the assembly.

Shop defect repair of unfinished panels and parts before finishing: filling knots, voids, chips and dents with putty or wood patches, routing out and plugging a bad spot, then sanding flush so the surface accepts stain or lacquer.

On-site punch-list repair and alteration in a customer's home or apartment: scribing and trimming an installed cabinet or filler to an out-of-square wall, re-hanging and adjusting sagging doors and drawers, replacing a scratched panel or damaged piece of paneling, filling nail holes and touching up the finish, working in a furnished occupied room.

On-site repair or alteration of fixtures and casework in a commercial/institutional building (store fixture, office reception casework, hotel casegoods, school wall paneling): cut out and replace a damaged section, re-machine and refit parts in place with a router and hand tools, then patch and touch up, working around the building's own layout and occupants.

tasks.label: Dip, brush, or spray assembled articles with protective or decorative finishes, such as stain, varnish, paint, or lacquer.

instances.label: Shop finishing room / spray booth of a production or semi-production cabinet shop: spraying stain, sealer and topcoat (lacquer or conversion varnish) onto batches of flat components — doors, drawer fronts, panels, face frames — laid on a spray table or hung on racks; multiple coats with scuff-sanding between; tens to hundreds of like parts per run.

Custom/architectural millwork shop booth: hand-spraying assembled three-dimensional articles — cabinet boxes, islands, built-in units, tables, chairs — of one-off geometry rolled in on carts; sprayer walks around the piece, sprays faces, interiors, undersides and edges, watching for runs and dry spots.

In-shop touch-up and spot repair: brushing lacquer or stain into scratches, nail holes and defects on assembled articles, spot-spraying a repaired area and blending sheen so the repair is invisible.

On-site finishing at installation: brushing or aerosol-spraying finish on installed built-ins, scribe pieces and trim in a customer's home or on a job site, masking surrounding surfaces and blending to the shop finish.

roles.description: Shape, finish, and refinish damaged, worn, or used furniture or new high-grade furniture to specified color or finish.

tasks.label: Brush, spray, or hand-rub finishing ingredients, such as paint, oil, stain, or wax, onto and into wood grain and apply lacquer or other sealers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Furniture/cabinet plant flat-line finishing department: finisher applies stain to panels, doors, drawer fronts and tops, wipes it back into the grain, then sprays sealer and topcoat as parts move on a conveyor through booths; repeated identical parts, standard colors, production-rate schedule.

Plant or large shop spray booth for assembled goods: spraying stain, sealer and lacquer/paint onto chairs, tables, bed frames and cased goods hung on a line or set on turntables; complex 3D shapes, backspraying legs, spindles and inside corners, models run in batches.

Custom / high-grade furniture shop: one-off or small-batch pieces sprayed with stain, sealer and lacquer in the shop's booth to a customer-approved sample color; each piece a different shape, finisher judges coverage, flash times and coat build.

Hand-rubbed oil or wax finish on high-grade flat surfaces (tabletops, panels, veneered case tops): flooding or wiping oil/hardwax onto the surface, letting it penetrate the grain, wiping and buffing off the excess, repeating for several coats and final waxing.

Antique / used-furniture restoration shop: a unique stripped or repaired piece is stained, padded with shellac or brushed with varnish, then toned, glazed and blended by hand-spray to match the surviving original finish and adjacent surfaces, and waxed into carvings and turnings.

On-site service call (customer home, office, hotel, showroom): hand-rubbing stain, oil or wax and brushing or aerosol-spraying lacquer onto scratched, worn or damaged areas of furniture in place, working around furnishings, carpet and occupants without a booth.

tasks.label: Fill and smooth cracks or depressions, remove marks and imperfections, and repair broken parts, using plastic or wood putty, glue, nails, or screws.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Furniture/cabinet plant, white-wood line: raw flat components (case panels, door fronts, table tops) come down the finishing line; finisher spots knots, checks, small splits and machine marks, presses in matching wood putty/filler, lets it set and sands the surface flush and smooth before stain/sealer. Standard-size flat parts, high volume, known defect types.

Furniture/cabinet plant repair-and-touch-up bench: assembled new case goods and chair frames arrive with nail/staple holes, glue squeeze-out dings, chipped edges and loose joints; finisher putties holes on the assembled 3D piece, re-glues and clamps a loose stretcher, sets a screw or brad, and sands/blends the repair before finishing.

Refinishing/repair shop, used furniture, flat surfaces: a stripped table top or dresser top with dents, gouges, small cracks and burn marks is on the bench; finisher fills depressions with wood putty/epoxy filler, levels and sands smooth ready for stain, matching surrounding surface flatness.

Refinishing/repair shop, structural repair of used furniture: wobbly chairs and drawers taken apart, old glue cleaned off, dowels/tenons replaced, joints re-glued and clamped, split rails screwed or nailed and pegged, broken carvings/mouldings pieced back; each piece is a different geometry and state of damage.

Antique/high-value restoration: chipped veneer patched with matched veneer, hide-glue re-adhesion of lifted banding, shellac burn-in of dents and worm holes, missing beading fabricated and glued, all with reversible materials and period-appropriate appearance on delicate, irregular pieces.

Off-shop repair at customer premises or in a warehouse/retail damage room: freight- or move-damaged furniture repaired in place in a home, office, hotel room or distribution-center back area — dents and scratches waxed/puttied and blended, loose legs re-glued and screwed, broken brackets refastened, working around finished surfaces and surrounding furnishings.

tasks.label: Smooth, shape, and touch up surfaces to prepare them for finishing, using sandpaper, pumice stones, steel wool, chisels, sanders, or grinders.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Furniture/cabinet plant, whitewood sanding station: finisher sands batches of flat components — cabinet doors, drawer fronts, case panels, table tops — with orbital sander and hand blocks through a grit sequence to remove machine and CNC marks before stain; parts arrive on carts, dust collection at the bench.

Same plant/custom shop: finisher hand-sands shaped and profiled new components — turned legs, curved chair rails and backs, moldings, raised-panel and profiled door edges — with sandpaper, profile blocks and small pneumatic sanders, following the grain and preserving crisp detail.

Finishing room: between-coat work — scuff-sanding sealer/primer coats and denibbing dust nibs with fine paper and steel wool, and rubbing out topcoats with pumice/steel wool to an even sheen on flat and paneled surfaces, without burning through the film.

Assembled new furniture (chair frames, case goods) at the whitewood bench: chisel or scrape off dried glue squeeze-out, level joints where rails meet legs, ease edges, sand into inside corners and around hardware pockets, spot-sand filler repairs before stain.

Refinishing shop: a used or antique piece (dresser, dining table, chair) brought in by a customer — after stripping, remove residual finish with scrapers, steel wool and pumice, sand flats, veneer, turnings and carvings without sanding through old veneer, feather repairs and burn-ins; every piece different.

On-site touch-up at customer premises — home, office, hotel or showroom — sanding out a scratch, dent or delivery scuff on installed or delivered furniture and blending the surrounding surface with fine abrasives and steel wool before touch-up finish.

tasks.label: Remove accessories prior to finishing, and mask areas that should not be exposed to finishing processes or substances.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Furniture/millwork plant finishing department, production run of identical or known-variant components (cabinet doors, chair frames, panels): per a fixed standard spec, tape off glue joints/tenons, pre-attached metal glides or hinge plates, and boundary lines for two-tone work, on parts moving through the finish room on carts or a conveyor.

Plant, custom/architectural millwork shop, or retail/warehouse touch-up bay: a low-volume or one-off assembled piece where the finisher must judge and then apply bespoke masking (tape plus paper or film) around glass, mirrors, upholstery, laminate, metal accents, or an already-finished area before spot or full spraying.

Plant or distribution-center finishing area: remove accessories already installed on new or returned production furniture (hinges, drawer glides, pulls, glass shelves, casters) before refinishing, then bag and label the hardware with the unit.

Refinishing/repair shop: a used or antique piece arrives for stripping and refinishing; remove old hardware — painted-over or corroded slotted screws, brass pulls with through-bolts, escutcheons, tacked felt, mirrors held by clips, casters — then mask upholstery, glass, and areas not to be stripped or finished.

Refinishing shop handling semi-repetitive modern casework (kitchen cabinet door/drawer-front programs, office furniture remanufacture): back out standard Phillips-screwed hinges and knobs from many similar doors, mask hinge cups and edges, and keep hardware sets matched to each unit.

On-site work at a customer's premises (home, office, hotel, restaurant): remove hardware from built-in cabinets, doors, banisters or fixed furniture, and mask the surroundings — adjacent walls, floors, countertops, glass and finished trim — with tape, paper and plastic sheeting before finishing in place.

sources.system: Astech X-Mask automated Turbine Blade Masking System

sources.claim: Astech Projects supplied a fully automated robotic masking cell to a UK aerospace manufacturer that masks defined areas of turbine blades before coating, handling fourteen blade variants with machine vision and 0.1 mm masking accuracy.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: masking areas of a manufactured part that must not receive coating. It transfers to production furniture masking because the objects are rigid known-geometry parts presented in fixtures, the required boundary precision (0.1 mm) far exceeds furniture tolerances, and the cell already switches automatically among fourteen part variants as a furniture line switches among models.

sources.system: Active Taping Kit (ATK) on a six-axis robot

sources.claim: Aerobotix and FerRobotics sell the Active Taping Kit, a robot end-effector with force-compliant control that automatically applies masking tape to aircraft parts of varying shape in straight, bubble-free lines.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic application of masking tape prior to painting on aerospace assemblies. Transfers to taping off boundaries on furniture components because the medium (masking tape), the contact-force control needed to avoid marring a high-value surface, and the straight-line boundary quality requirement are the same; furniture parts are smaller and simpler.

tasks.label: Remove old finishes and damaged or deteriorated parts, using hand tools, stripping tools, sandpaper, steel wool, abrasives, solvents, or dip baths.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Refinishing shop: an ornate solid-wood piece (Victorian dresser, carved chair, turned-leg table) is hand-stripped - brush on stripper, dwell, scrape flats, work steel wool, picks and brushes into carvings, turnings, moldings and crevices, neutralize/rinse, hand-sand to bare undamaged wood without cutting through veneer or losing detail.

Refinishing shop: essentially planar components - kitchen cabinet doors and drawer fronts, flush doors, shutters, table leaves, panels - with old lacquer/varnish/paint removed by random-orbit or belt sanding (often after chemical stripper) down to clean bare wood, edges and profiles included, without burn-through on veneer.

Commercial strip shop: chairs, frames, doors and shutters loaded on racks and dip-tank or flow-over stripped - immersion in caustic/solvent bath, soak, lift, rinse/wash off residue, dry - producing a stripped piece ready for sanding.

Refinishing/repair shop: removal of damaged or deteriorated parts - knocking apart failed glue joints, extracting broken spindles, dowels and split rails, peeling loose or blistered veneer, chiseling out old glue blocks, pulling hardware, nails and upholstery tacks with hand tools, saving reusable original material.

On-site work in a customer home, office or hotel: finish removed in place from installed millwork - built-in cabinetry, stair rails and balusters, doors, mantels, paneling - with surroundings masked, working around furnishings and occupants, no shop equipment available.

Furniture plant finishing department: rework and prep on new high-grade production parts - sanding off a blemished or defective cured finish coat, scuff/denib sanding cured sealer, cutting back runs and raised grain on chair parts, tops and case components before recoat.

tasks.label: Treat warped or stained surfaces to restore original contours and colors.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Repair/restoration shop bench: a finished antique or used piece arrives with a dark water ring, ink or heat mark, pet stain or sun-faded panel. The finisher tests the finish, locally strips or abrades, applies oxalic acid or two-part bleach, neutralizes, then re-dyes/tones and glazes the treated spot and blends topcoat so the repair disappears into the surrounding original color.

Warped component in a shop: cupped one-board tabletop, bowed door or drawer front, twisted table leaf. Worker reads grain and moisture, wets/steams and heats the concave face, weights or clamps between cauls for hours to days, sometimes kerfs the back or adds battens, then re-sands and re-colors the treated face to match.

Furniture plant finishing/rub-out room: a new high-grade piece comes off the line with a blotchy or off-shade stained area, blush, sink or run in the color coat. The finisher scuffs the area, sprays shading stain/toner by hand, blends into adjacent surfaces and re-coats to match the approved color standard.

Cabinet/furniture plant or millwork shop: unfinished panels, tops and solid boards carrying knots, checks, mineral streaks and discolored spots that must be milled or filled with color-matched putty, sanded flush and color-corrected so the surface takes an even stain.

On-site service call at a hotel room, office or private home: treat a water-stained or sun-bleached tabletop, burn mark, or a warped drawer front in place, working around occupants and furnishings, with a portable kit, masking, and no shop ventilation.

tasks.label: Select appropriate finishing ingredients such as paint, stain, lacquer, shellac, or varnish, depending on factors such as wood hardness and surface type.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Mix finish ingredients to obtain desired colors or shades.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production finishing department of a furniture plant: the finisher mixes a batch (gallons to a drum) of stain, glaze, toner or pigmented topcoat from a written/recorded formula — weighing or measuring bases, colorant concentrates, dye concentrates and reducers into a pail, agitating, straining, and checking the batch against a control panel or retained standard before it goes to the spray line.

Custom/contract finishing shop, repeat or catalog color: finisher pulls a filed formula or manufacturer color card, mixes a modest quantity (quart to 5 gallons) of stain or toner, reduces it to spraying strength, and sprays a test panel to confirm the shade before production.

Custom color development / match to a customer sample or an existing piece: the finisher blends dyes, pigments and stain concentrates in small increments by eye, wipes or sprays sample panels of the same wood species, evaluates them dry under shop light next to the target, and iterates until the shade, tone and clarity match.

Bench touch-up and repair blending in the shop: mixing very small quantities (a few ml) of pigmented lacquer, padding stain, glaze or graining colors, adjusting drop by drop while holding the cup against the repaired area of the specific piece, to blend a patch or spot repair invisibly.

On-site service technician (furniture medic / in-home or office repair): mixing touch-up colors and tinted finishes from a portable kit at the customer's home, office or showroom, with the piece in place, under whatever ambient light and surface are available.

tasks.label: Remove excess solvent, using cloths soaked in paint thinner.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production/semi-production wood finishing shop: flat components (cabinet doors, drawer fronts, panels, tabletops) that have just had stain, glaze or wiping-solvent applied; worker wipes off the excess with thinner-dampened cloths to leave an even, residue-free surface before topcoat. Pieces move on carts or a conveyor; pace is set by dry time.

Finishing room of a furniture plant or large shop: assembled case goods (dressers, cabinets, tables, desks) on a turntable or bench; worker wipes excess solvent/stain from broad faces, edges, corners and shallow profiles with thinner-soaked cloths, changing rags as they load up.

Custom or antique refinishing shop: one-off intricate pieces (turned spindles, chair backs, carved crests, ornate moldings, veneered antiques); worker works excess solvent out of crevices and around delicate or fragile old finishes by hand and eye, varying pressure and dwell so highlights and shadows in the carving are preserved.

Spot cleanup on an otherwise finished piece: a run, drip, sag, overspray, adhesive or filler smear, or a puddle of solvent left in one area; worker wets a cloth with thinner and wipes just that spot without disturbing the surrounding finish, then blends the area.

Small parts and profiled stock (mouldings, frames, turnings, small components) in a factory finishing line; excess stain/solvent removed to a uniform finish as parts are conveyed between coating and drying stations.

On-site refinishing at a customer's home or office: built-in cabinetry, a banister, or a piece too large to move; worker wipes excess solvent while working around the customer's furnishings, with drop cloths, variable lighting and no shop fixtures.

tasks.label: Examine furniture to determine the extent of damage or deterioration, and to decide on the best method for repair or restoration.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Intake at a small refinishing/restoration shop: a customer's used or antique piece (dresser, dining chair, table) is set on a bench; the finisher turns it over, rocks joints to find loose glue blocks and mortises, checks veneer for lifting/blisters, looks for water rings, sun fade, cigarette burns, insect damage and prior repairs, tests the existing coating with solvent to identify shellac/lacquer/varnish, then decides strip-and-refinish vs. clean-and-touch-up vs. re-glue/part replacement and quotes it.

Finishing department of a furniture plant: newly finished high-grade case goods, chairs and components arriving off the sanding/spray/rub line are examined under inspection lighting for dents, sand-throughs, raised grain, runs, sags, blush, dirt nibs and color mismatch; the finisher judges severity and decides rub-out, spot touch-up/blending, re-sand and re-spray, or reject.

On-site field service in a customer's home, hotel room or office: technician examines a piece damaged in delivery or in use (scratched top, chipped corner, dented edge, loose leg, torn finish) in whatever light and space is available, decides whether it can be repaired in place with burn-in/touch-up, must go back to the shop, or should be replaced.

Retail warehouse or distribution-center back room: freight-damaged, returned or floor-model pieces are uncartoned on the floor; the finisher inspects each for structural vs. cosmetic damage, grades repairability, and decides the repair method or write-off/markdown disposition.

High-value antique or conservation assessment: probing for rot, worm channels and hidden cracks, checking structural integrity of joints and seat frames, distinguishing original surface and prior restorations, weighing historical accuracy, then planning a conservation-grade approach (consolidation, reversible repair, preserving original finish).

tasks.label: Distress surfaces with woodworking tools or abrasives before staining to create an antique appearance, or rub surfaces to bring out highlights and shadings.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Furniture plant finishing department: batches of flat components for an 'antique-look' line (table tops, cabinet doors, drawer fronts, flat panels) are mechanically distressed before stain — wire-brushed to raise grain, edge-worn, dented, saw-marked — to a repeated house standard, then passed to staining.

Furniture plant: assembled or three-dimensional parts of a repeated production style (dining chair back and front subassemblies, turned legs, shaped rails) are distressed with punches, files, hatchet marks and 'rocks' to simulate worm holes, dents and wear before stain; parts are clamped in forms and run in volume.

Furniture plant finishing line: wiping stain or glaze is applied to flat panel components, then wiped/rubbed back so color stays in the grain and low spots and the field lightens — producing even shading and highlight across the panel before topcoat.

Finishing room or custom shop: glaze/antiquing color is brushed or sprayed onto a profiled, carved, turned or fully assembled piece (raised-panel door, carved crest rail, molding, chair) and then rubbed through by hand with cloth or abrasive pads so highlights appear on crowns and edges and shadow stays in recesses.

Shop bench: rubbing out the cured finish on a piece with abrasive pads, steel wool, pumice/rottenstone or compounds and a buffer to level the film and bring the surface to an even satin sheen on the large flat show surfaces (top, sides, doors) at the end of finishing.

Small custom/refinishing shop: a one-off piece (a customer's reproduction chest, a repaired antique, a bespoke table) is distressed by hand to a look agreed with the customer or matched to an existing antique — the finisher decides where wear, dents, worm holes and rub-through belong on that particular shape, occasionally doing the same blending work at the customer's home.

tasks.label: Stencil, gild, emboss, mark, or paint designs or borders to reproduce the original appearance of restored pieces, or to decorate new pieces.

Restoration/period shop: reproducing painted decoration on a restored piece — hand-painted floral or classical motifs, stenciled patterns on a Hitchcock-style chair back, pinstriping on turned legs, replacement transfer decals — matched in color, sheen and wear to the aged original surface around it, on curved and turned 3D surfaces.

Custom/small-batch shop: applying a specified decorative design to new or reproduction pieces — stenciled borders, painted banding or striping on a painted chest, a stenciled motif on a flat door or drawer front. Design given by pattern or spec; no matching to a worn original required.

Plant finishing line: antiquing/distressing new production furniture and cabinet parts — physical distress marks (worn edges, dents, wormholes, wire-brushed grain) plus glaze, spatter/fly-speck and rub-through effects applied to panels, doors and components moving through the finishing room in batches.

Factory/production shop: embossing, branding or marking decorative elements on new pieces — embossed or foil-stamped borders and medallions, branded maker's marks, laser-engraved patterns on wood or leather inserts, applied in repeatable runs on components.

On-site work at a client's home, office or historic interior: touching in gilded striping, painted borders or stenciled decoration on installed furniture, built-ins or paneling, working around the room's furnishings and lighting as found.

tasks.label: Disassemble items to prepare them for finishing, using hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Furniture plant finishing department, production run of new high-grade case goods: identical assembled units arrive on carts; the finisher backs out temporarily fitted knobs, pulls, hinges and catches with screwdriver and nut driver, pulls the drawers, lifts off doors and glass/mirror panels, and bags hardware by unit so components can be sprayed separately. Fasteners are new, of one or two known types, at the same positions on every unit.

Plant, warehouse or showroom rework/touch-up: a one-off damaged or defective piece (varied model, varied damage) must be partly taken apart before refinishing - pop off a split drawer front, unscrew a glass door or seat frame, remove trim, drive out a dowel - with the finisher deciding on the spot how far to go, which fasteners are hidden, and what is glued rather than screwed.

Restoration/refinishing shop, antique or heavily used case piece: remove drawers (some with stops requiring a lift-and-tilt), unscrew painted-over, rusted, slotted or stripped screws holding pulls, hinges and escutcheons, pry small brads and nails with pliers and nail set, take off mirrors, glass, marble tops and felt, keeping original hardware intact and not chipping veneer or scratching surrounding surfaces.

Chairs, stools and small upholstered pieces: knock loose glued joints apart with a rubber mallet and wedges without splitting the tenons, unscrew slip seats from corner blocks, pull staples and tacks from webbing and seat covers with tack puller and pliers, remove glides and casters.

On-site work at customer premises (kitchens, offices, hotels, restaurants): remove doors and drawer fronts from installed built-in cabinetry and fixed furniture, back out hinge screws overhead and under counters, take off pulls and knobs, and label/organize the parts before they are refinished in place or carted back to the shop.

instances.label: Furniture/cabinet plant finishing line: flat components (doors, panels, table tops, drawer fronts) arrive on a conveyor after sanding; worker blows off, brushes and wipes sanding dust and residue from each face and edge so the sealer/stain lays down clean. Repetitive, high volume, known part sizes.

Production shop / spray-booth staging area: assembled or shaped goods (cabinet boxes, case goods, chair frames, shaped fronts) on carts or turntables; worker blows off dust and tack-rag/solvent-wipes all show surfaces immediately before spraying. Large smooth-to-moderately-contoured surfaces, pieces staged by humans.

Custom refinishing/repair shop: a stripped or freshly sanded table top, dresser case, door or cabinet on a bench or sawhorses; worker wipes the whole piece with mineral spirits or denatured alcohol and a tack cloth to lift sanding dust and stripper residue before stain. Mostly flat and simple curved surfaces.

Custom shop, intricate piece: spindle-back chair, turned legs, carved moldings, fretwork or grooved veneered panels; worker must work solvent-dampened rag, brush and air into every crevice and around joints without soaking joints or raising grain, then check by eye and feel that no residue remains.

Antique/high-value restoration bench: washing decades of old wax, grime, polish and silicone contamination off a fragile original finish or veneer, deciding piece by piece how aggressive to be (mild soap, naphtha, solvent) to avoid cutting patina, lifting veneer or damaging gilding, before recoating or touch-up.

On-site work in a customer's home or office: kitchen cabinets, built-ins, handrails or doors cleaned in place with degreaser/TSP and rinsed, working around counters, appliances, plumbing and occupants, before on-site refinishing.

tasks.label: Follow blueprints to produce specific designs.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Furniture/cabinet plant: the finisher works from the job's blueprint/finish schedule (specified stain, sealer, topcoat, sheen, film build) and produces the specified finish on a run of parts or assembled pieces — spraying coats, sanding between coats, checking against the spec panel. Indoor plant with spray booths, conveyors, drying ovens.

Custom cabinet/furniture shop: reads shop drawings/blueprints for a piece, lays out and machines the components to the dimensions, profiles and joinery shown (panels, rails, curved parts), and verifies parts against the print before assembly and finishing.

High-grade furniture or architectural millwork: produces the decorative elements shown on the drawing — carved panels or brackets, turned/shaped legs and posts, profiled moldings, routed patterns — to the drawn profile and dimensions.

Custom color/finish development in a shop finishing room: from the blueprint's finish schedule or an approved sample, mixes stains/dyes/toners, sprays step panels on the actual species, judges and adjusts the match, then applies glaze, distressing or padding by hand until the specified appearance is approved.

Restoration/reproduction shop: from a measured drawing or sketch of a damaged or missing element on an existing piece, fabricates the replacement part, fits it to the piece by hand, and finishes it so it blends with the surrounding aged finish.

tasks.label: Paint metal surfaces electrostatically, or by using a spray gun or other painting equipment.

instances.label: Production finishing line in a metal/mixed furniture plant: batches of identical metal chair frames, table bases or cabinet shells hung on an overhead conveyor or cart line and sprayed (liquid or electrostatic/powder) inside a ventilated booth, then cured; finisher checks film build, coverage of undercuts and gloss.

Custom/job-shop refinishing of one-off metal pieces (a vintage steel tanker desk, wrought-iron patio set, metal bed frame) in a small shop's spray booth: piece hung or set on stands by hand, masked, primed and top-coated with a hand-held spray gun to a customer-specified color and sheen; every job a different geometry.

On-site electrostatic refinishing in a customer's occupied building: metal desks, file cabinets, lockers, shelving, partitions and door frames are cleaned, masked and recoated in place with a portable electrostatic gun, working around carpet, walls and other furnishings, often overnight.

Spot repair / touch-up of a damaged or mismatched painted metal component: locating the scratch or run, feathering, matching color, spraying only the affected area and blending it into the surrounding finish so the repair is invisible.

Decorative or antique metal finishing: ornate wrought iron, brass-toned or multi-color effects, shading, rub-through and antiquing applied by spray gun over a base coat on irregular scrollwork, judged by eye against an approved sample.
